docs.text: Welcome to BMac's Nonsense Hey there. I'm Brian MacDonald, and this is the place where I keep stuff that I want to be on the web, but is too big for including on socials. It's a blog site, in other words. If you came here looking for professional or serious stuff, you're in the wrong place. These links lead to more official resources about me. MacDonald Editorial , my professional website with my portfolio and services. My Mastodon , pretty much the only social media I bother with anymore. My LinkedIn , for all the usual LinkedIn stuff. What's going on here? I'm verbose. This is a known flaw, known to myself and anyone who's talked to me for more than a few minutes. I often record my thoughts and memories in written form. I'm also fond of "projects," meaning that if I become interested in woozles, I probably won't be happy until I collect all the woozles and write down some thoughts about each. ADHD symptom? Seems likely. At some point, I look at my woozles document and think, "Oh, gosh, that's 100 pages long now." And once I noticed that I had lengthy writing on multiple different topics, I thought I'd put them on a web site, where at least they might persist in some form or be useful to others. Doctor Who Tabletop RPG Adventures I like Doctor Who . Like, a lot. A lot a lot. I also like tabletop role-playing games (TTRPGs). There have been attempts at a Doctor Who RPG in the past, but they've faded out over time. The latest attempt is Doctor Who the Roleplaying Game from Cubicle 7 . I stumbled upon it in the fall of 2023, just as the second edition was coming out. I have a weekly RPG group who is often open to trying new things, and which includes some fans of the show, and everybody else is polite and humors me. After running an initial adventure from the rulebook, I started coming up with my own, and I really enjoyed the writing. I'm putting them here in case anybody else wants to run some adventures. Big Finish Pocket Reviews As I mentioned, I'm a huge Doctor Who fan, and have been since the 1980s. But Doctor Who isn't always around, and these days, you get ten episodes and then a two-year pause. Fortunately, Big Finish is there to fill the gaps with audio dramas. They've got full-length, full-cast audio dramas created by amazing writers and directors, some of whom have worked on the TV show, and as many former actors from the show as they can convince to sit in front of a microphone. They're audio stories, sure, but they've got the feel of real Doctor Who , both the classic and the modern series. When I say Big Finish is there to "fill the gaps," I really mean "stuff as many stories as possible into every possible crack, no matter how small." They've been doing their thing since 1999, which has resulted in a massive library of stories. Although Big Finish doesn't restrict themselves to one era or a specific release order, a few years back I decided to listen to as much of the library as I could, in the order the stories take place in the Doctor's personal timeline, or as close as I could determine. Things...got a little out of hand. And of course I had to write down my thoughts, briefly (for me), and that's what you'll find here. Roller Coaster Journal One of my other unusual hobbies is riding roller coasters. There's a whole community of "coaster enthusiasts" (what we call ourselves) who love to compare and contrast, collect experiences, and rank things. Oh, do we love to rank things. Rankings are always in flux, so I won't subject you to mine. However, I do like to keep a journal of coasters I've ridden and parks I've visited, because it helps with my later recall. Built with mkdocs.org , because if you're a tech writer and spend all day in Markdown, there's no more natural-feeling static site generator.

docs.text: Big Finish Pocket Reviews I’m writing this at the end of 2019, and I’ve been a fan of Big Finish Doctor Who for a while now. As a long-time fan of the show, I learned about Big Finish at some point during the “wilderness era,” but they weren’t commonly available in America at the time, so much like the novels, I ignored them. Sometime in 2012, I realized that downloads were available, and I made a few purchases...which I failed to listen to, because I fell asleep while listening. In late 2013, I tried again with the 50th anniversary special, " The Light at the End ." Because I was recovering from an injury, the only exercise available to me was walking, so I listened while I walked. That gave me the revelation that the stories are better listened to while doing something that occupies my hands or feet, but not my mind. From that point, I was off to the races. Big Finish has sales quite frequently, and by the time I’m writing this, I’ve acquired all of the Main Range, the Short Trips series, and a good chunk of the Companion Chronicles, as well as the box set specials for a number of the other Doctors. I generally stick to stories in which the Doctor appears, because I have to draw the line somewhere, but I’ve also purchased all the UNIT and River Song sets. I find that I need to have a “project,” some order in which I’m listening to the stories. I usually listen to new ones right as they come out, but that’s not enough for the amount of listening I do. I can’t just pick stories at random to listen to, unfortunately; maybe it’s a lack of creativity. So a few years back, I listened to everything I own in release order, and that took me about three years to finish. In the first part of 2019, I decided to start over, but listening to the stories in chronological order, according to the Doctor’s timeline, as laid out by Craig Brawley in the Big Finish Listeners Facebook group. However, Mr. Brawley doesn’t include a lot of the Short Trips from before 2018 or so. I had to make my best guesses about where those go. At the end of November 2019, I decided to take a few minutes after each story and write down what I thought. I started with the Fifth Doctor, because he’s my favorite, and because my collection has only a few gaps in his era. After I finished with that, I planned to loop back around to the First Doctor, then jump back to the Sixth, then the Second, and so on. I hope that by the time I get to the eras with more gaps, I’ll have filled them in. I’ll present these reviews in chronological order for the Doctor, but I’ll tag each with the real-world date I wrote the review. That means that for most stories, I’ll write the review shortly after listening to the story, but for the Fifth Doctor, I had to backfill some earlier stories I listened to. I don’t know how long I’ll continue this project; it depends on whether I get bored. Update, November 2025: Clearly, I didn't get bored. Equally clearly, this project accelerated my acquisition of Big Finish stories. I now have almost no gaps anywhere in the Doctor's timeline, and I have complete collections of a number of the spin-off series as well. And because Big Finish never stops, my collection of stories from the modern era has grown to a size I never could have imagined when I started this project.

docs.text: UNIT UNIT was a pretty steady presence in televised Doctor Who through most of the classic series, especially during the Third Doctor ’s tenure. It then reappeared from time to time in the modern series, usually on the same basis: UNIT is who you go to when you need an organization that knows about aliens, and has some resources the Doctor can use: a base, equipment, transportation, connections to world governments, or even some guns and bombs, as much as the Doctor claims not to like those. Which means having a handful of recurring characters whom the Doctor knows and trusts, or at least can get along with. When you consider that these established characters presumably fight aliens when the Doctor isn’t around, that’s the perfect basis for a Big Finish spin-off. They’ve actually done this more than once, resulting in three separate eras of UNIT stories.

docs.text: 2000s UNIT This particular series was released in 2004, meaning it predates the new series, and was produced well before the “ Brave New World ” series, although it takes place later. It takes place in the year it was released, but mostly seeks to update the Classic-series version of UNIT into the 21st century. As such, it features Nicholas Courtney as Brigadier Alistair Gordon Lethbridge-Stewart, but only in some of the stories, sadly. Although it’s not stated, I imagine this series got curtailed when the new series premiered, with a new version of UNIT appearing almost immediately on TV.

docs.text: Snake Head UNIT #2 Released: January 2005 Listened: 3/25/23 This one actually seems a bit like filler, in as much a short series can have filler. Colonels Chaudhry and Dalton head to Southend to investigate some mysterious murders. They’re in civilian clothes, and refer to each other by name without rank for most of the story, making this seem much more “private detective” than UNIT. In fact, it doesn’t make a lot of sense that the two highest-ranking UNIT officers would go out on a mission alone, but Dalton is still being a skeptic, and Chaudhry wants to convince him…or else she just wants to get out of London. There’s an archaeological dig run by a lecherous professor who won’t stop hitting on Chaudhry; his primary purpose seems to be explaining Albanian legends, specifically the Vârkolak, a kind of invisible Balkan vampire, which of course nobody but Chaudhry believes in. Issues of race and immigration get a lot of airing here, from the illegal Chinese and Kosovan refugees smuggled in by the “snake head” (what Americans would call a “coyote”), to the Kosovan vampire hunter (who doesn’t have a valid visa), to Kevin Lee and Chaudhry herself, both British citizens back several generations, but with foreign names that can result in racism. Actually finding and killing the monster isn’t that big of a deal, but it definitely makes a believer out of Dalton, after quite some time looking like it wouldn’t. The story’s fine, for what it is.

docs.text: The Coup UNIT #0 Released: 9 December 2004 Listened: 3/20/23 This story was released through Doctor Who Magazine, and was intended as a teaser to the UNIT series proper. In that, it succeeds quite well, for a 20-minute story. UNIT is in the process of standing down, to be replaced by ICIS, an organization with the same remit, but answerable to the British government, not the UN. We get plenty of chances to see that ICIS isn’t very nice, as they “put down” a group of Silurians , and then torture a journalist who was covering the event. We’re introduced to Colonel Emily Chaudhry, apparently UNIT’s liaison officer with the government and the press, and someone who trusts Sir Alistair implicitly. Colonel Brimmicombe-Wood (a version of whom had appeared in “Sympathy for the Devil”) is mentioned, but doesn’t appear. Sir Alistair is officially retired, and he’s supposed to give a bland speech handing over responsibility from UNIT to ICIS, but without saying what either group does, because Secrets Act. Instead, he introduces a Silurian who’s been trying to broker peace, which presumably ICIS had been trying to stop. We’ve got the basic conflict, we’ve got tagonists both pro- and an-, and we’ve got a link into the classic series. Not bad for 20 minutes.

docs.text: The Longest Night UNIT #3 Released: March 2005 Listened: 3/25/23 Now things really ramp up between UNIT and ICIS, with the whole of England caught in the crossfire. The PM is about to sign a treaty creating greater integration between the UK and Europe, which is met with mixed reactions (and this story was a good decade before Brexit). A group of extremists carry out terrorist bombings throughout London and the rest of England, done in such a way that immigrants appear to be responsible, although in fact they aren’t. Chaudhry and Dalton are out for the evening after their adventure in Southend, and Hoffman is at a club that gets bombed. Since that uses up all the UNIT characters with speaking roles, UNIT is remarkably ineffective in mounting a response, and it’s not even their jurisdiction anyway. But it’s Chaudhry and a reporter friend who figure out that the terrorists are using the media to stir up racial unrest, which works like a charm. Of course ICIS is in the middle of it, although it’s not clear whether it’s the organization itself or a few individuals who’ve gone rogue and tried to seize power. The adult content in this one is more violence and language than anything else. While justified by events, there are some words used that you won’t hear elsewhere in Doctor Who . And the body count is ridiculous, not just random Londoners, but also named characters and members of government. The racism behind the story is brutal, and I wish I could say unrealistic, but it really isn’t. The three stories so far have seemed kind of disconnected, without a thematic or plot thread. We’ll see if that continues.

docs.text: The Wasting UNIT #4 Released: June 2005 Listened: 3/25/23 Why, look – it’s that David Tennant bloke! He’s playing Colonel Brimmicombe-Wood, and while I’d like to call this his only recurring role in pre-2005 Big Finish, in fact the only other appearance of this character is in an Unbound story, so it’s technically not the same character. If you only knew him from his various Big Finish appearances (and Harry Potter , really), you’d probably think of him as the guy who yells a lot, because he certainly does that here. In fact, it’s not really clear why the rest of UNIT think so highly of him, even though we’re told that they do, repeatedly. Plot-wise, there’s a pandemic, which has spread rather quickly around the world, with nations all pointing fingers at each other. (Which, in 2023, gives a chill.) Of course, it’s actually alien, spread by ICIS, so UNIT need to fix the problem and track down the baddies, which means finding Brimmicombe-Wood. Fortunately, Sir Alistair has resurfaced to help out. He keeps insisting that he’s retired, and Chaudhry is in charge, but then he turns around and gives orders, keeps everybody calm, and provides moral support. In fact, he’s wearing some pretty hefty plot armor, because he succeeds in just about everything he does. Which takes some of the suspense out of the plot. The only big twist is that (Spoiler: Brimmicombe-Wood turns out to be the bad guy. Which might be a shock if we’d ever heard him before, or had any reason to be sympathetic towards him.) Once again we have a huge body count, and characters who can’t seem to stop being offensive toward Chaudhry. Less swearing, though, which is odd. On the whole, the boxed set is a bit of an odd artifact, being made in a distinctly “wilderness years” style, but terminated before it got any further. Still, it’s great to hear Nicholas Courtney in the role.

docs.text: Time Heals UNIT #1 Released: December 2004 Listened: 3/21/23 Now we’re into the series proper, and it’s clear it was planned as four parts, because this is basically all setup. We’ve got several plot threads that don’t intersect until the very end, and even then, there’s more going on than anyone knows. In plot 1, UNIT is moving an alien spacecraft to storage under secrecy, but it gets stolen, and Colonel Brimmicombe-Wood is taken as well. Although he doesn’t appear in the story, we hear repeatedly how devoted the troops are to him. That leaves Colonel Chaudhry in charge, until she’s told to call off the search for Brimmicombe-Wood, and Colonel Dalton is assigned as a temporary replacement. Dalton knows squat about UNIT, and of course doesn’t accept any sci-fi explanations, because he’s doomed to be that kind of character, and that puts him in conflict with Chaudhry. Plot 2 involves some scientists working on a matter transporter. It’s all very shady, and they never say directly who they’re working for, only that they’ve crossed ethical lines by working with a military group. Except they think their tech will end world hunger, so it’s worth it. Unless it isn’t. Both scientists flip-flop continuously on whether they’re being noble or criminal, whether their project will be helpful or harmful, and whether they’re justified or not. The project itself seems to have time-related side-effects, like causing a train to jump forward 30 minutes, so it collides with another train that occupies the same spot, or causing a plane to crash (into Windsor Castle!), or causing a nuclear submarine to go into meltdown. And like all good scientists, once they learn the project is killing people, they go right on with it. Plot 3 involves the Brigadier, back to being retired, noticing the time-blips, although he’s somehow the only one who does, investigating on his own, and passing the info to Chaudhry, enabling her to track down the scientists. This is a pre-new-series story, so it tries a little too hard to be “adult.” The body count is extraordinary, including at least one member of the royal family. There are also several references to a UNIT lieutenant's romantic conquests, and the scientists banter about how famous scientists still don’t get the girls. The dialog is amazingly strained, and would have been awkward in the 1970s, much less 2004. I also have to make special note of the soundtrack, or lack thereof. Big Finish was likely operating on a smaller budget back then, but the only music is a repetitive bass line that seems to have been lifted from Excellis, and some occasional drums, neither of which seem appropriate to the story. It’s nice to see UNIT operating on their own, and competently, but as a story, this has an awful lot of rough edges.

docs.text: Brave New World UNIT This 90s version of UNIT started on TV in “ Battlefield ,” with Angela Bruce playing Brigadier Bambera. Never one to let a gap in the chronology go unexplored, and with Angela Bruce more than willing to return to the role, Big Finish took advantage of the opportunity to create a new series. This probably helped to bridge the period when Big Finish had to put its primary UNIT series on pause, for reasons not yet explored.

docs.text: Dark Side of the Moon UNIT: Brave New World #1.3 Released: 13 July 2022 Listened: 3/27/23 Now that we’ve got things established, we can start them rolling. As often happens in Doctor Who , the state of UK space exploration is variable; sometimes matching real-world history, and sometimes more advanced. In this case, Britain is sending space shuttles to orbit the moon in the 90s, which is a neat trick. Except the last shuttle to go didn’t make it back, and it’s possible the accident was a cover-up. At least, astronaut Helena McNamara thinks that, because she died on that mission, and now she’s possessing people on Earth to try to stop the next one. In addition, Helena was a friend of Dr. Rix from when they were in university. Which means Rix isn’t exactly thinking straight on this one. Which would be an interesting character development if we’d already established Rix as level-headed and confident, but she’s been established as a bit of a loose canon. Bambera is growing increasingly frustrated that despite all UNIT’s experience, they always seem to be starting from behind when one of these events happens. No telling where that’s going to go.
docs.title: Dark Side of the Moon

docs.text: Haunt UNIT: Brave New World #2.2 Released: 8 December 2022 Listened: 3/28/23 Lizzie Hopley writes the second story, and if that makes you suspect it’ll be a spooky one, you’d be right! Rix has gotten wind of a haunted hotel at a northern seaside town, and dragged Bambera out to investigate. Why exactly Bambera agreed, I don’t know. Savarin doesn’t accompany them, getting a small over-the-phone cameo, probably because his normal role would be keeping peace between Rix and Bambera, and we don’t want that here. Rix thinks that something paranormal is going on. Bambera, despite being head of UNIT, is certain it’s a hoax. Herein lies the conflict. In fact, it’s slightly absurd how much Bambera argues, given that she could leave any time, or even order Rix to leave. Of course, because this is a Doctor Who story, it’s not a hoax, but nor is it clear exactly what it is. The Doctor would build a doohickey to figure it out, but this UNIT is stuck with 1990s technology – Rix needs an Internet cafe to do online research, which is a nice touch. The other thing that makes it different is that we really don’t care about the how or the why; we’re just gonna make things spooky. I’m sure there are some small details from Rix’s or Bambera’s lives that you can glean from their fears, but I’m not that meticulous about it.
docs.title: Haunt

docs.text: Rogue State UNIT: Brave New World #1.1 Released: 13 July 2022 Listened: 3/26/23 This story sets up the premise for the entire series, and opens the box entitled “Seabird One,” which is Bambera’s call sign. Getting some background details out of the way: At the time of “ Battlefield ” (1997), Bambera was one of several officers in UNIT, assigned all over the world. As a result of her performance in that story, she’s now offered the leadership of UNIT’s UK division. She apparently got together with Ancelyn, but that ended because they couldn’t reconcile their respective duties. Also, UNIT seems to be used as a generic global peacekeeping force (again, in accord with “Battlefield”), but also with a specialization in what Bambera calls “the woo-woo stuff,” which she doesn’t care for. As the story opens, Bambera has just narrowly missed capturing an arms dealer she’s been tracking, and is considering resigning. Dame Lydia Kingsley is introduced as Bambera’s boss at UNIT, and assigns her a new second, Sgt. Jean-Paul Savarin, a French soldier. He’s played by Alex Jordan, but his French sounds quite good to me. According to Rob Valentine and Emily Cook, the aim of the story is to create “a 2020s version of what the 1980s thought the 1990s would be like.” The technology level seems historically accurate, but the primary concerns seem to be global terrorism and rogue states getting their hands on former Soviet weapons (see also: 90s James Bond). The story moves at a rapid pace, which can make it hard to discern exactly what’s going on. Bambera does an awful lot of shouting, which Angela Bruce is admittedly very good at. She’s not as directly insulting as Brimmicombe-Wood, but it does sound like she’s unhappy all the time. Savarin is her foil, generally keeping a cool head and pointing out when she’s wrong. The soundtrack is extremely energetic, with a lot of electric guitars, and seems kind of over the top. That extends to the new theme as well. It’s a decent start, but I don’t think they can maintain this pace.

docs.text: The Frequency UNIT: Brave New World #2.1 Released: 8 December 2022 Listened: 3/27/23 The second boxed set is called “Visitants,” although it’s not clear from the first story why that is. It’s by new writer Tajinder Singh Hayer, and it’s a slower-paced story with a smaller focus. The US military has some new tech that they’d like UNIT to evaluate, so Bambera, Savarin, and Rix (with nobody else, apparently) are on a US Air Force base to investigate. Ostensibly, they’re evaluating some new robots, which aren’t really combat-ready yet. However, Colonel Hagen, the head of the project, has something else in mind, a method of forcing unit cohesion. Hagen is played by American David Menkin, and he sounds much more like a techbro sales guy than an Air Force Colonel. If anything, the story’s a bit basic; it’s pretty obvious what the big revelations are going to be, to the point where I was waiting for them to get on with it. I didn’t expect the focus to stay small; I kept assuming the scene would broaden out, but it never happened. Still, there’s some good character work done between our three leads.

docs.text: The Last Line of Defence UNIT: Brave New World #2.3 Released: 8 December 2022 Listened: 3/28/23 I wasn’t really expecting a big slam-bang ending in this story, but I got one. Lots of the plot threads that were seeded in the previous stories come together here, along with several reveals: the mysterious aliens from earlier, the mysterious phone calls Bambera was getting, and a mole on the good guys’ team. And there’s a world conference that UNIT has to provide security for, because that’s something UNIT is always doing, whether it’s in their remit or not. Unfortunately, I found the aliens kind of absurd and non-threatening, both in their audio presentation, and in their plot choices. It made it hard to take them seriously as a threat, which also made it hard to believe that people would betray their own side out of fear. Angela Bruce gets to show off her shouty side again, but also has scenes of quieter exposition. I wish there’d been a bit more emotion when she discovered the betrayal, but apparently when Bambera’s betrayed, she gets angry. Which is what Bambera does in response to anything else, so I wish that had gone differently. The story takes place on December 31, 1999, and includes UNIT’s move to the Tower, so with the big ending, this feels like the end of an era. There’s certainly room for more stories with this team, but I get the feeling there may not be. Either way, it’s a decent addition to the canon, maybe not the best, but certainly not bad. The theme song is really a banger, though; it kind of grew on me.
docs.title: The Last Line of Defence

docs.text: UNIT: Brave New World #2.3 Released: 8 December 2022 Listened: 3/28/23 I wasn’t really expecting a big slam-bang ending in this story, but I got one. Lots of the plot threads that were seeded in the previous stories come together here, along with several reveals: the mysterious aliens from earlier, the mysterious phone calls Bambera was getting, and a mole on the good guys’ team. And there’s a world conference that UNIT has to provide security for, because that’s something UNIT is always doing, whether it’s in their remit or not. Unfortunately, I found the aliens kind of absurd and non-threatening, both in their audio presentation, and in their plot choices. It made it hard to take them seriously as a threat, which also made it hard to believe that people would betray their own side out of fear. Angela Bruce gets to show off her shouty side again, but also has scenes of quieter exposition. I wish there’d been a bit more emotion when she discovered the betrayal, but apparently when Bambera’s betrayed, she gets angry. Which is what Bambera does in response to anything else, so I wish that had gone differently. The story takes place on December 31, 1999, and includes UNIT’s move to the Tower, so with the big ending, this feels like the end of an era. There’s certainly room for more stories with this team, but I get the feeling there may not be. Either way, it’s a decent addition to the canon, maybe not the best, but certainly not bad. The theme song is really a banger, though; it kind of grew on me.
docs.title: The Last Line of Defence

docs.text: Time Flies UNIT: Brave New World #1.2 Released: 13 July 2022 Listened: 3/26/23 One of my favorite word-play jokes: “Time flies like an arrow. Fruit flies like a banana.” In this story, you get much more literal time flies, or butterflies, or caterpillars; there’s a lot of bugginess going on. This one’s got a straight mad science plot, with a scientist genetically engineering butterflies to age backwards, a trait they can pass along by biting. Which makes this the right story to introduce UNIT’s latest scientific advisor, Dr. Louise Rix. Presumably Rix looks like her actor Yemisi Oyinloye, and dresses neither like a soldier nor like a scientist, because she finds it hard to get people to take her seriously. In the finest UNIT tradition, she pretty much does what she wants, investigates what she wants, and steamrolls anybody who gets in the way. Which would be fine if she were the Doctor (or knew as much as he does), but she hasn’t proved herself yet, and Bambera clashes with her almost immediately. She disappoints Bambera by not being able to magic up a solution to rewrite genetic code on the fly, which is completely preposterous, unless you’re used to working with the Doctor. She does get the job done, though. It’s also a bit rich of Bambera to be annoyed at Rix’s disrespect for the chain of command, when she herself is pretty insubordinate, but that’s the way it usually goes. The science in the story seems a bit dodgy, but nothing entirely out of the ordinary for Doctor Who . The resolution, in fact, is a bit of a letdown.

docs.text: Modern-Era UNIT UNIT appeared almost immediately in the new series, but they were a sporadic presence, appearing most prominently in “ The Sontaran Stratagem ,” “ Journey’s End ,” and “ Planet of the Dead ,” as well as various links to Torchwood (TV and audio) and The Sarah Jane Adventures . However, “ The Power of Three ” in the Eleventh Doctor’s era introduced the new-and-improved UNIT, led by Kate Stewart, with science taking the lead over military functions. In 2013, Big Finish acquired the rights to all new-series concepts up to and including the 50th anniversary special, which for UNIT mostly meant the characters of Kate and Osgood. So in their burst of new content that didn’t include the new-series Doctors, they kicked off a new UNIT series, filling in the gaps when the Doctor wasn’t around. Which lasted until 2019 or so, until “ Spyfall ” revealed that UNIT was defunct, and Big Finish put the series on hold. It returned in 2021, and was shown to be active on TV again in “ The Power of the Doctor .” The gap has not yet been fully explained.

docs.text: Agents of the Vulpreen UNIT Nemesis #2 Released: 3 March 2022 Listened: 4/25/23 - 4/27/23 The Man from Gallifrey The last story left us with the cliffhanger of Jacqui McGee being lost through the arch. This box is called “Agents of the Vulpreen,” because that’s who lives on that other world. It starts off with a nice cold open that explains just about everything we wanted to know in the last box: What’s the arch, where did it come from, and what was the Eleven doing on the other side? Turns out it was another Time Lord who put him there, a CIA agent named Hasper, and he’s popped up on Earth now to find out who the heck is poking at the arch that was never supposed to be found. Hasper's got piles of the typical Time Lord condescension, but he’s really mostly helpful to the UNIT squad…mostly. The other big development in this story is the introduction of Jimmy Tan, played by Chris Lew Kum Hoi. I guess Warren Brown and Ramon Tikaram are unavailable now, because we haven’t seen Sam or Shindi in quite some time. Jimmy’s the skeptic who’s nevertheless hyper-competent, and Kate pretty much recruits him on the spot, which seems like a bit of a stretch, but maybe she’s aware that she’s short on main characters. Not a ton really happens here, except introducing new characters. In fact, the net result is to reverse the end of the previous story, which is sort of a step backwards. Power of the Dominators Just like the second story of the last box, this one is a distraction from the story of Eleven and the arch. Unlike last time, though, this is a straight comedy. Because apparently you can’t bring back the Dominators and the Quarks and be serious. The Dominators are pretending to be developers building an enclosed planned community, except that nobody’s been able to see the inside of it, and of course there are disappearances. The comedy comes from the fact that the Dominators are absolutely terrible at pretending not to be aliens, with the same stilted speech and apparently the same absurd outfits. They’re also still terribly concerned about conserving energy in their bizarre late-60s way. And of course Osgood thinks the Quarks are adorable…because they are. Beth Chalmers provides the Quark voices, but I never would’ve guessed that. Naomi and Harry feature in this one, because they recognize the Dominators, having faced them in a not-yet-unreleased Fourth Doctor adventure . Which means we get Harry’s charming 70s-ness on top of the Dominators’ silly 60s-ness. And basically, it’s all a laugh. In the background, Josh is training Jimmy, so he can be an officer next story, and Jacqui has discharged herself from the hospital. Osgood thinks that’s unwise, and she’s right, because Jacqui’s a Vulpreen sleeper agent. This one is funny enough to be the standout from this box. The War Factory We’re back to the main plot again, this time with a Lizzy Hopley story, and I’m sorry to say that I found it tough to follow. There’s an awful lot of timey-wimey going on here, and I’m probably hampered by the fact that I’m unfamiliar with the Royal Arsenal at Woolwich , which has a central role in the story. For whatever reason, Eleven is messing around with the arch in such a way that time fissures are opening all over the place, and since he’s doing it at the Arsenal, that means soldiers from various eras are shooting kinda randomly at things they see through the gaps, which is bad news, especially as the site was home to Britain’s post-WWII nuclear weapons program. The rifts allow Osgood and Jacqui to accidentally bounce into the future, where there’s a Vulpreen war going on, and Jacqui reveals her brainwashing by helping the Vulpreen out. But more important, Kate and Josh get bounced to the late 90s, where Brigadier Bambera is in charge. (Sir Alistair is still active, but not present. One wonders if he’s getting tired of receiving reports about incursions from Future UNIT and specifically his daughter .) Bambera and Kate get along like a house on fire, which is nice, because the building soon is. Angela Bruce, as always, plays Bambera as larger-than-life. This time, she’s acting protective toward a young private who’s facing trouble with the military’s glass ceiling. We also get one passionate “Oh, shame ,” which is something I missed in the “Brave New World” sets. But really, it’s more runaround, and I wonder if anything was actually accomplished. Ten Minutes in Hell A rather ominously titled story by John Dorney finishes off this box. We’ve really spent quite a while back-and-forth-ing with the gate, and as of this point we’ve ended up with the Eleven free on Earth, and Kate a prisoner of the Vulpreen on their prison world. With the time differential, Kate could be on this world for hours while minutes pass on Earth, and there’s another gate that makes the situation even worse. This is an acting spotlight for Jemma Redgrave, as she gets to resist torture and then try to start an uprising among the prisoners. Josh and Osgood mount a rescue, which seems a bit absurd for just the two of them in unfamiliar territory, but hey, they’re really capable, so it’ll be all right. Osgood is a bit more flippant in the face of danger than previously, but by this point, she’d have to be. There’s no sign of flirting between them; that seems to have stopped after the parallel Earth incident a few boxes back. While it’s a pretty gripping episode, and Kate gets to do a lot of emoting, not that much really happens. This whole box, while mostly fine, has the feel of a middle episode. We can’t eliminate the threat altogether, but we have to have some kind of a win, so it ends up as a net zero.
docs.title: Agents of the Vulpreen

docs.text: Armageddon UNIT #1.4 Released: 9 November 2015 Listened: 4/3/23 Lots of shooting and explosions in this ending. It’s perhaps inevitable that you’d want your first boxed set to end with a pitched battle, but since UNIT is fixed in time and place, they can’t keep threatening the planet in every set. Still, you can get away with it the first time. So we’ve got UNIT troops fighting Autons in London, and all over the world. Of course, the key to the whole thing is at Devlin’s headquarters, where Kate, Josh, and Jacqui are all stuck from last episode. Devlin uses a rather nasty process to line Josh’s skeleton with plastic, and threatens to do so to Kate. This is quite painful, but also has the effect of letting the Nestenes control your mind. Of course, you’d only need to coat the skull if your goal is mind-control, but this way we get a super-strong UNIT operative for use in future stories. Jacqui really doesn’t handle all this well. Like, at all. Admittedly, UNIT plans to stage a global cover-up and Jacqui’s a journalist, so who’s to say she’s wrong? It’s big, it’s loud, but it doesn’t really hinge on anybody being particularly clever, just folks doing their jobs. On the whole, it makes for a competent first boxed set, and establishes some characters you’d like to see more of.

docs.text: Between Two Worlds UNIT Nemesis #1 Released: 16 November 2021 Listened: 4/22/23 - 4/24/23 After boxed set 8, Big Finish paused UNIT for a couple of years. At the time, they said it was because they were doing a number of different series on a twice-yearly basis, and needed to get on top of them all. It also coincided with a period when the TV show declared UNIT to be defunct, although that didn’t last too long. Coincidence? Hard to say. Anyway, the series came back in 2021 with a new umbrella story called “UNIT: Nemesis,” which consists of four boxed sets. They no longer have individual covers, and each box is pretty self-contained, so I'm going to review the whole set on a single page. The Enemy Beyond The primary baddie here is The Eleven, one of Big Finish’s periodic villains that they invent , see it become popular , and then over-use (see also: the Eminence ). In this case, though, it’s been a while since we’ve seen the Eleven. Thanks to a tip from Jacqui, UNIT discovered a stone arch that’s been buried since prehistoric times. The arch turns out to be a portal, because of course it does. There’s a planet on the other side, and the Eleven has been there for an undetermined period of time. (I don’t know where this fits in the Eleven’s personal history, unfortunately.) UNIT doesn’t have any records on the Eleven, but they know enough about Time Lords to understand his regenerative dissonance pretty quickly. Eleven makes his escape by distracting everybody with a toxin that makes a sticky, almost indestructible, web substance? That seems pretty odd, and very indirect for the Eleven. Looks like this arch is going to be a thing for a while, but this story is mostly setup. It’s fine for what it is, and Mark Bonnar always impresses as the Eleven, so there’s nothing to object to. Fire and Ice Although this boxed set, in fact, this entire run, seems to be one long story, this particular episode takes a hard left turn to accomplish some other things. Specifically, it’s got Ice Warriors in the Australian outback, which is a really bad place for Ice Warriors to be. It’s also got Harry Sullivan and Naomi Cross , the out-of-time UNIT agents. Thing is, this was Harry and Naomi’s first appearance in release order, and as of the time of this writing, the Fourth Doctor story that explains it all still hasn’t come out, so we just have to take them at face value. We also have to accept the coincidence that Harry and Naomi happened to be in Australia at a medical conference, and thus available to help. When Ice Warriors are around, you always have to ask whether they’re friendly or hostile, and this time, it’s a bit of both. There’s one warrior who’s gone rogue, and another bunch who want him back, preferably with no witnesses. Which makes it a generally terrible idea for a social media influencer to butt in and try to figure out what’s going on, although pairing her with Harry for a while provides plenty of humor. Unfortunately, Ice Warriors speak slowly, and that always slows down the pace of the story, especially if negotiations are involved. The toxin from the previous story makes a surprise appearance…or rather, an appearance that makes it clear why it was introduced in the previous story. Which feels a little bit clunky, but sometimes that’s what you get. Eleven’s Eleven It feels like this is one of those stories where the title came first, and the plot came second. The Eleven is still trying to get back to that arch, but UNIT has moved it, so he needs to build an arch-detector. Which means he needs some alien tech. Fortunately, alien tech is scattered rather liberally around the planet. Some of it is disguised as, or mistaken for, jewelry. So the Eleven takes over a gang of jewel thieves to get what he wants. It’s not nearly as clever as the movie, though. We’re not really saddled with ten new characters; it’s mostly the ringleader Ava and a bunch of mostly-silent bystanders. This story seems like it wants to be a heist movie, but it’s a bit more procedural, with Josh and Kate trying to outsmart the Eleven and figure out where he’ll be next, while the Eleven tries to fake out UNIT while still getting the goods. Jacqui McGee makes another appearance, because a series of major jewel thefts is big news. Oddly, Kate and Josh treat her as an adversary, even though she just helped them out in the first story. It’s like she’s an informant of occasional value, but not trusted. That certainly annoys Jacqui, who takes it upon herself to find out where Osgood is researching the arch. This story feels fairly middle-ish, and I’m afraid it’s not one that will stick in the mind. The Curator’s Gambit This boxed set marks a shift in Big Finish’s licensing game, which affects UNIT possibly more than any other series. The events of “ The Day of the Doctor ” (and presumably later) are now free game, which means that the Undergallery and the Curator can be used. (It presumably also means that there are two Osgoods, but that never comes up in the story.) More significantly, it means there’s a lot of Tom Baker in this story, and he can use his natural voice, which is a bit slower and deeper than his Doctor voice. The Curator isn’t my favorite character, but if he exists, he should be enigmatic and used sparingly, which is what Big Finish does. And this story is seriously high-concept. The Curator has been asked to hide the arch, and does so inside the Undergallery, at a place that isn’t really intuitive. And the use Andrew Smith makes of that space, and the possibilities it contains, are surprising and creative. And would only make sense from a character like the Curator, as it’s outside of UNIT’s capabilities. So points for that, as well as clever use of the history of British art. However, the Eleven isn’t really a planner; he mostly just reacts to things, so while he starts with the upper hand in the story, it’s a lot of running and shouting by the end. And because this is the first boxed set of several, while the story and the box both wrap up nicely, it’s not a clean win. It’s a decent opening chapter of the larger story, and while it’s a little draggy in the middle, it’s got enough action and pacing on the ends.

docs.text: This boxed set marks a shift in Big Finish’s licensing game, which affects UNIT possibly more than any other series. The events of “ The Day of the Doctor ” (and presumably later) are now free game, which means that the Undergallery and the Curator can be used. (It presumably also means that there are two Osgoods, but that never comes up in the story.) More significantly, it means there’s a lot of Tom Baker in this story, and he can use his natural voice, which is a bit slower and deeper than his Doctor voice. The Curator isn’t my favorite character, but if he exists, he should be enigmatic and used sparingly, which is what Big Finish does. And this story is seriously high-concept. The Curator has been asked to hide the arch, and does so inside the Undergallery, at a place that isn’t really intuitive. And the use Andrew Smith makes of that space, and the possibilities it contains, are surprising and creative. And would only make sense from a character like the Curator, as it’s outside of UNIT’s capabilities. So points for that, as well as clever use of the history of British art. However, the Eleven isn’t really a planner; he mostly just reacts to things, so while he starts with the upper hand in the story, it’s a lot of running and shouting by the end. And because this is the first boxed set of several, while the story and the box both wrap up nicely, it’s not a clean win. It’s a decent opening chapter of the larger story, and while it’s a little draggy in the middle, it’s got enough action and pacing on the ends.
docs.title: The Curator’s Gambit

docs.text: Breach of Trust UNIT #7.3 Released: 21 November 2018 Listened: 4/20/23 This boxed set is called “Revisitations,” and for the Wirrn story, that was pretty obvious, but this one is more complicated. In fact, this story is more complicated in a number of ways. An alien woman with a powerful voice comes to Earth with her child, claiming asylum. She’s being pursued by her people, who have turned war-like under the influence of their current leader, and she claims they’ll destroy the Earth to get her back. David K Barnes is setting this up as a variation on a “believe women” story, with complications. It even opens with Kate having a business dinner with a misogynistic general accused of harassing a soldier under his command. Why exactly Kate would discuss that over dinner, I have no idea, and the general would be a complete caricature if he weren’t also accurate. Where it gets complicated is that the woman insists on using a bit of tech from her race that UNIT recovered back in the 70s to destroy the fleet she says is coming for her, and she isn’t willing to give much explanation. Osgood, of course, is all-in on the woman’s side, especially with a small child involved. Kate, however, is torn between sympathy and her duty to protect the planet. She’s not about to start an interstellar war on the word of one person. The “revisitation” part comes because this alien tech was recovered in an earlier encounter, handled by Mike Yates, and the Doctor had it sealed away because humans “weren’t ready,” the way he often does. Notes from that encounter are scarce, but indicate that the aliens aren’t trustworthy, which just makes Kate’s dilemma worse. It seems like that older story might be “ The Rings of Ikiria ” or “ The Other Woman ,” both stories in which Mike and UNIT encountered alien women who couldn’t be trusted, but it’s neither of those. Where the story becomes dark, and even hard to listen to, is that Kate believes she’s in a no-win situation, and is trying for minimal damage, whereas Osgood believes she’s in a Doctor Who story, in which there’s always another way out. And while it’s fun to deconstruct your show’s premise, especially after 50-plus years, I don’t like nihilism in my Doctor Who . It’s the same problem I had with “Torchwood: Children of Earth,” which makes it more of a me problem than the story’s problem, but there it is. In the interest of fairness, I’ll mention that this story does not feature a mass slaughter of UNIT troops, which is a nice change. As an ethical drama, it’s effective, but as a one-part story with no connection to anything on either side, it suffers a bit.

docs.text: Bridgehead UNIT #1.3 Released: 9 November 2015 Listened: 4/2/23 This is pretty much the proper Act 2, in which our folks figure out what’s going on. (Without Sam, because conservation of characters.) The good guys are pretty sure that Devlin’s company is the problem, but they need hard evidence. So Josh goes undercover at Devlin. Meanwhile, Jacqui is becoming steadily more irritated by the bits she’s been able to work out, but without evidence, her producers won’t let her on the air, so she infiltrates Devlin too. Josh breaks cover to rescue her, to no avail, as Jacqui and Kate are both captured. Jacqui does a lot of screaming in this episode. Admittedly, she’s not trained for any of this, but her reactions go beyond panic toward hysteria. Kate, on the other hand, is cool and collected at all times. And Josh isn’t much of an undercover agent, unfortunately. Nick Briggs plays a put-upon TV news presenter, and while it’s clearly Nick, he does a good job. The 3-D printers finally print some Autons, which is the image we’ve been waiting for this whole box, but it does seem a bit slow as invasions go. There’s a pretty good cliffhanger that will have ramifications for quite a while.

docs.text: Call to Arms UNIT #4.1 Released: 23 May 2017 Listened: 4/10/23 Since the new UNIT series started, a team-up between modern UNIT and 1970s UNIT was pretty much inevitable, and well done to Big Finish for holding off as long as they did. Of course, that means even more characters, so the carousel of who’s sitting out this story is rather pronounced this time around. Shindi doesn’t appear at all, and Sam and Josh have reduced roles. Naturally, if you’re going to bring in old UNIT heroes to help, the threat has to be the Silurians , because who else? In fact, because of the levels of nostalgia going on here, the plot kind of takes a back seat, in contrast to the previous boxed set. Osgood and Kate, along with a squad, were doing a routine checkup on some sleeping Silurians when, oops, turns out they’re not sleepy anymore. In past Silurian stories, we got a mix of peaceful and aggressive leaders, but this particular colony just has one military leader, Jastrok, who’s very clear on a “wipe out the apes” strategy. Things go very badly for UNIT, and Kate and Osgood end up fleeing to a local country pub, which happens to be owned by one John Benton, who’s having a retirement party, which luckily means there’s several old UNIT folks there, including Mike Yates. Benton spent a few years selling cars, but eventually bought this pub and married Margery Phipps, who he met in “ Council of War .” Yates has been reinstated to UNIT (somehow), but seems to be mostly administrative. Unfortunately, the other UNIT alumni don’t make out very well in this story, which seems like poor treatment, even though they were made up just for this story. The story is primarily occupied with having the main characters get away alive, although they do tend to stop to reminisce a bit more than you’d expect for a life-threatening situation. Richard Franklin does a good job as an older, professional UNIT officer. John Levene seems thrilled to have been invited, and that comes through in his acting. He seems far too upbeat for the situation, and continually fanboys all over Osgood (who is fairly impressive, but still). Jastrok is played by Richard Hope, who played the scientist Malokeh in “ The Hungry Earth ,” but this character is nothing like that one. Unfortunate body count aside, this one gets the job done.
docs.title: Call to Arms

docs.text: Code Silver UNIT #6.3 Released: 10 May 2018 Listened: 4/16/23 OK, we all knew that the Cybermen would be turning up in this story, and yes, that’s who created the VR helmets. They’re other-dimensional Cybermen, who can send the helmets through to a new dimension, then establish a link to the local sentients, partially convert them, and use that to create a tunnel to bring through Cybermen properly. We’re told that these Cybermen probably aren’t any ones UNIT has met before, since there are so many different origins for them, and of course these are from another dimension entirely. Key differences in this bunch is that they have the sing-song voices of Mondasian Cybermen (probably because Nick Briggs loves those voices), and they convert folks really, really quickly. Which makes them even more Borg-like than Cybermen usually are. Shindi, Sam, and Osgood are all “partially converted,” which means that Shindi and Sam do nothing at all, but Cyber-Osgood wants to help the invasion effort, which means retaining her individual personality because that’s the key to her creative thinking. And apparently, Cyber-Osgood is really snotty. She’s completely unimpressed by the Cybermen and their invasion plans, and thinks she can do a lot better. That leaves Josh and Kate dealing with the base-under-seige, running around, hiding, and trying to find effective weapons. But what Kate and Osgood are both doing is dropping exposition. Oh, so much exposition. Kate covers Cybermen 101, their origins, motivations, variations, and potential weaknesses. Osgood has to spell out their game plan, because it’s admittedly complicated. And every other UNIT staffer on the base is busy getting slaughtered or converted. I know I keep complaining about this, but having a 100% death rate for anybody not in the credits is starting to get annoying. Of course, Cybermen are tough, and sometimes you have to have a story where UNIT just can’t win on their own, don’t you?

docs.text: Death in Geneva UNIT #2.2 Released: 30 June 2016 Listened: 4/4/23 Based on the events of the previous story, Kate fears an information leak in the UK government, and tries going over their heads by going physically to Geneva. After Osgood’s experience in the last story, Kate takes her along for safety. Which turns out to be a terrible idea. The bad guys are in Geneva too, and we learn that they’re the Kamishi, and specifically that the things that sound like space-ninjas are in fact space-ninjas called Tengobushi. Their leader, Dokan, is played by Dan Li, with a Japanese accent that’s not quite as stereotypical as I remember from my first listen, but the whole thing combined makes the Kamishi seem borderline inappropriate. Speaking of accents, we meet the head of UNIT, General Grant Avery, played with a decent American accent by Harry Ditson. Credit where it’s due: I thought there was something fishy with Avery as soon as he was introduced, but there’s a swerve there that makes it non-obvious. Osgood gets nearly murdered a couple of times (again), to the point where she’s only surviving because her name is in the credits. Josh gets to do some decent soldiering, commanding actual troops instead of just rushing in to do things himself, so that’s good. The change of pace and setting is pretty nice, and I can see the attempt at some political intrigue, but it’s let down by the bad guys being inscrutable.

docs.text: Earthfall UNIT #1.2 Released: 9 November 2015 Listened: 3/30/23 This story has the shortest running time of the set, less than 40 minutes. So not a lot gets done, but that’s not terrible. It seems Big Finish has a limit on the number of main characters per story, so Shindi is sent off to Geneva so that we can introduce Lieutenant Sam Bishop (Warren Brown). Sam is established as ultra-competent action hero dude, which you’d think would make Josh jealous, but Sam seems to always be in the field, so they don’t interact much. In this case, Sam and Osgood are in the Gobi desert, tracking down a Nestene energy unit that fell to Earth a bit early (as they do). This gives Osgood a lot of opportunity to complain about how she’s not cut out for field work, and for Sam to demonstrate his competence. Meanwhile, Kate confronts Simon Devlin, having put together the 3D printer connection. Turns out Simon had a congenital condition in his skull, so he had it replaced with a plastic one, which is the sort of thing you can do if you’re ultra-rich. Except oops, that gave the Nestenes a direct line to his brain. It’s a little hard to fault the guy; I doubt he anticipated that. Andrew Smith writes this one, and he’s always pretty good at making the bad guys at least partially sympathetic, but so far it’s by-the-numbers storytelling.
docs.title: Earthfall

docs.text: False Negative UNIT #5.4 Released: 29 November 2017 Listened: 4/14/23 Looks like it’s time for a parallel-universe story, and it’s amazing that we haven’t had one before. While following up a lead on the Auctioneers, Osgood and Josh get popped over to a parallel universe. Unfortunately, it’s just about the most cliched type of parallel universe imaginable, where everybody’s the same, just evil. Much like the Star Trek version, it’s hard to imagine how this civilization could have produced the exact same people in the exact same positions, when they’re constantly backstabbing each other (sometimes literally). And of course Sam gets killed in the first few minutes, because apparently Warren Brown just wasn’t available for this set. Despite the “everybody’s evil” trope, the story doesn’t take itself very seriously. Josh and Osgood are a couple in this universe, because that causes maximum embarrassment for “our” Josh and Osgood as they try to impersonate their counterparts. Shindi, oddly, is mostly the same, just crankier. And Kate, for no reason I can tell, is not so much evil as lazy. She spends most of the story trying to check her emails. Our Osgood once again does a pretty decent job operating in the field, despite some initial confusion. She figures out what’s going on very quickly and adapts better than Josh. And the characters left in “our” universe figure things out awfully quickly as well, because Kate’s pretty smart. (And she’s heard of this before – she specifically asks whether her alt-self wears an eye-patch, a reference to “ Inferno ,” but she treats it as an inside joke.) And that pretty much wraps up the boxed set. It’s a mixed bag, because that was the intention. I think my favorite is probably the Sontaran story, but that could vary depending on the day.

docs.text: Game Theory UNIT #6.1 Released: 10 May 2018 Listened: 4/14/23 Sam’s back! This is the beginning of the boxed set entitled “Cyber-reality,” which evokes some obvious associations for long-time fans. However, this time we’re starting with the VR flavor of Cyber-reality. Sam wakes up as a prisoner on a ship, along with fellow prisoner Julia. Seems like a pretty basic hostage-escape scenario, tailor made for Lieutenant Sam Bishop of UNIT…or is that what’s going on here? Meanwhile, Kate and Osgood track down a lead on the Auctioneers that leads them to an abandoned warehouse containing a VR headset and a message. That kicks off the Overseer of the Auctioneers leading Kate and Osgood around on one of those Batman-style “bad guy has planted deadly devices all around and gives the heroes clues they have to solve.” Which they can, because they’re Kate and Osgood, but admittedly the puzzles aren’t particularly complex, and Kate is very unwilling to play along. She’d rather cut to the chase than follow the instructions, which makes sense. Osgood’s level of amazement at the VR headset, and need to exposition about it for the audience, probably was a lot more necessary in 2018 than in 2023, but that’s the dangers of sci-fi. Although this story has a definite conclusion, it’s not as self-contained as the previous box. And we’re getting payoff for the Auctioneers plotline. Plus more Sam, and who doesn’t want more Sam?
docs.title: Game Theory

docs.text: Hosts of the Wirrn UNIT #7.1 & 7.2 Released: 21 November 2018 Listened: 4/19/23 In which we learn that Osgood makes a terrible people manager. This boxed set features a whole raft of new writers, and a new format, with the first two discs being a single story, this one by Chris Chapman. When the Master cleared out in the last story , he left a note for UNIT indicating that the Auctioneers had a Wirrn egg, which UNIT now needs to dispose of safely. Of course that doesn’t work, and a soldier gets infected before we even get going. UNIT is trying to take the egg to a secure biohazard facility hidden under Lake Windermere, never mind that there’s a town nearby. We get a ton of description of how secure the facility is, with decontamination chambers between each of its seven levels, each of which can independently self-destruct. We also get Shana Siddiqui, entomologist and science geek, who gets recruited by Osgood after the world’s most awkward interview. Because even in a UNIT where “science leads,” Osgood is apparently the only scientist who can be trusted with anything, unless she decides to recruit somebody else. (And Malcolm , who’s eternally off-screen.) Although Shana seems like she’s being set up as a new recurring character, things go badly almost immediately, and of course the super-secure facility isn’t secure enough to cage a Wirrn. Osgood is portrayed as more flippant than usual, even careless, which really isn’t like her. I’d think she’d be especially careful after her recent cyber-conversion, but apparently we’re glossing over that. Once again, UNIT troops are shown to be disposable unless they’re main characters. Clearly Chapman wanted to show that the Wirrn are a threat, because the body count includes not just numbers of troops, but also people from the nearby town, which seems a bit egregious. It also represents a big failure on Kate’s part, who has the chance to stop things sooner, but doesn’t, because it would mean losing characters whose names are in the credits. She gets some dialog where she beats herself up about that (apparently at Jemma Redgrave’s insistence), but it doesn’t lead to any growth on her part. Osgood doesn’t even get that much. She talks a good game about wanting to give all life a chance, but she should have some feelings about the collateral damage she caused because she didn’t supervise the new recruit. There’s some snappy dialog, but I’m kind of disappointed in this one. Maybe it would be different if I liked the Wirrn better, but I’m kind of indifferent to them.

docs.text: UNIT #7.1 & 7.2 Released: 21 November 2018 Listened: 4/19/23 In which we learn that Osgood makes a terrible people manager. This boxed set features a whole raft of new writers, and a new format, with the first two discs being a single story, this one by Chris Chapman. When the Master cleared out in the last story , he left a note for UNIT indicating that the Auctioneers had a Wirrn egg, which UNIT now needs to dispose of safely. Of course that doesn’t work, and a soldier gets infected before we even get going. UNIT is trying to take the egg to a secure biohazard facility hidden under Lake Windermere, never mind that there’s a town nearby. We get a ton of description of how secure the facility is, with decontamination chambers between each of its seven levels, each of which can independently self-destruct. We also get Shana Siddiqui, entomologist and science geek, who gets recruited by Osgood after the world’s most awkward interview. Because even in a UNIT where “science leads,” Osgood is apparently the only scientist who can be trusted with anything, unless she decides to recruit somebody else. docs.text: House of Silents UNIT #3.1 Released: 23 November 2016 Listened: 4/7/23 Another new boxed set, this one called “Silenced,” because, well, it features the Silence , an Eleventh Doctor monster from series 8. The Silence’s big thing is that you forget them as soon as you’re not looking at them, an effect that persists even through recordings. Which is tricky to do on audio, but fortunately the TV show provided a nice sound effect for “I’ve just forgotten about the monster,” and it gets used here. The other big issue is that UNIT doesn’t have any records of them, because the Doctor, River, Amy and Rory dealt with them in 1969 by implanting a subliminal “kill on sight” order within humanity, and called it a day. That’s fairly sloppy, even by the Doctor’s standards, and it means UNIT has to figure out a lot of stuff that listeners already know. In other news, remember Colonel Shindi? I do, and I liked him. Unfortunately, Ramon Tikram was unavailable for the last boxed set, but he’s back this time. He’s still recovering from the events of “Extinction,” and using a wheelchair, but he’s getting fidgety, so Kate assigns him to surveil the house of one Mrs. Faversham, noted wealthy recluse and philanthropist (and possibly crazy cat lady, judging from the sound effects). Osgood spotted a strange energy discharge there, but nobody else can find anything wrong…or at least, nobody can remember seeing anything wrong. Fortunately, we don’t do a “everybody thinks Shindi’s crazy” plot; he’s too good an operative for that, and everybody else is too smart. 2016 UNIT also has better resources than making marks on your arm with a sharpie when you see a Silent. But there’s still a lot of mystery to figure out, and they’re just getting into it. Also, remember Jacqui McGee? She’s gone from investigative journalist to free-speech vigilante during the time she’s been away. She keeps trying to expose UNIT secrets under a pseudonym, and Osgood keeps taking them down. But Jacqui’s onto the Silence and knows that UNIT is a step behind, so she breaks cover to tell Kate what she knows, which admittedly isn’t much. Jacqui is still fundamentally right that UNIT keeps more secrets than they ought to, but she’s still addressing the problem with blunt force, and it’s not getting her anywhere. It’s kind of cool that UNIT has to approach this as a mystery to solve, rather than an invasion to fight. And the fact that both sides are concerned with secrecy means there won’t be any attention-grabbing street battles. It’s a decent start.

docs.text: Ice Station Alpha UNIT #2.4 Released: 30 June 2016 Listened: 4/7/23 We had a slam-bang episode in the last story, so now it’s time for one that’s almost equally violent, but with UNIT in a different role. You’d think that after the Kamishi got their power cell back in the last story, they could just take it and go home. Problem is, Felicity Lyme still has the tech, and is building an even bigger power generator in Antarctica. Which really should be a good thing, solving the world’s energy problems, but Kate’s against it, on the rationale of a) Lyme will use it to corner the energy market for herself (that’s probably true), and b) we’re not ready yet as a species, and need to get there by ourselves. Says the woman who runs the government agency that uses bunches of alien tech. Kate gets away with it because Lyme is Evil, but there’s some hypocrisy there. This sets up a conflict between Lyme’s Cerberus mercenaries and the Tengobushi, with UNIT trying to stop both sides. Which, again, is kinda hypocritical because UNIT just kicked Tengobushi butt at the Tower, but talking is always better in Doctor Who . I’m not 100% sure that Kate’s argument would have swayed the Kamishi, but they do seem to like self-sacrifice, and both Josh and Osgood are up for that. (Which leads to a tender moment between them that totally isn’t followed up on.) On the whole, I salute what Matt Fitton and Andrew Smith were trying to do, but the Kamishi just aren’t much more than “space ninjas,” and can’t help feeling just a touch racist. It’s probably fine that they faded away quickly.

docs.text: In Memory Alone UNIT #3.4 Released: 23 November 2016 Listened: 4/10/23 Throughout this whole story, it’s never been clear (to UNIT, anyway) exactly what the Silence want, mostly because the Doctor never told them. Which means that we haven’t been invited to think about what it’s been like for them, stuck on Earth for over 50 years with every single human programmed to kill them on sight. Basically, they’d really like to leave. Unfortunately, they also want revenge on humanity, which, again, is understandable, but it’s the Doctor who did this; humanity was just a tool. After the last story, everybody’s forgotten the Silence again , and even the UNIT staff who know about them were subliminally conditioned to think the threat was dealt with. Osgood and Sam have gone up to the UNIT space platform…because of course UNIT has a space platform. However, it’s not much more advanced than the ISS, so that keeps it within the realm of plausibility. Unfortunately, there’s a Silent on the station with them, who reprograms Sam and Osgood to its own ends. Jacqui McGee is back, and once again frustrated that UNIT is apparently ignoring her info about the Silence. Fortunately, she and UNIT don’t stay confused for too long, and Jacqui is able to contribute much more positively than she did back in “Extinction.” Josh has only a minor role this time, but he makes clear the confusion and frustration experienced by those who’ve been exposed to the Silence for a long period of time. On the whole, this boxed set is more about the plotting than anything else, which I think plays more to Dorney’s strengths than Fitton’s, but only by a little bit. The Silence on the whole are one of Moffat’s one-trick-pony monsters, who work really well for the story they’re in, but you can’t think about them as a society, or even as individuals, or they stop making sense. This set nicely walked the line of considering the aftermath of “ Day of the Moon ” without having to humanize the Silence all that much. Aside from some unintentional comedy, it works quite well.

docs.text: Invocation UNIT #5.2 Released: 29 November 2017 Listened: 4/13/23 This story, from Roy Gill, takes advantage of the anthology format to go for the straight-up scary. The story is told in several parts, but definitely centers around a haunted house. Specifically, an old manor that UNIT owns but isn’t using, so Kate decides to go have a look, and remembers having been there as a child. Josh attends a Halloween party that’s crashed by some actual ghosts (or what appear to be actual ghosts to everyone except Josh), and Osgood picks up a signal from a 1960s-era satellite that really shouldn’t be broadcasting, especially not in Latin. It’s a bit of narrative convenience that all of our main characters happen to be in the right places to each get a piece of the puzzle and then put them all together. (Osgood does a lot of odd things, but listening to a dead satellite?) There is a human element to the whole story, with a scientist who was funded by UNIT years ago, but now resents having her project terminated. But the main thrust is to create a spooky feeling that can’t entirely be explained away by the science. No mention of the Auctioneers here, but Sam is mentioned as still being missing.

docs.text: Master of Worlds UNIT #6.4 Released: 10 May 2018 Listened: 4/16/23 So the wheezing, groaning noise at the end of the last story wasn’t the TARDIS, or at least, not the Doctor’s TARDIS. It’s the Master, specifically the War Master. Which is kind of awkward, because from UNIT’s point of view, they’re well past him, but that particular continuity point doesn’t come up. The Master, of course, can thwart Cybermen pretty easily, but he does need to have the right gear. Plus, Osgood is still Cyber-ized, and doing everything she can to help the Cybermen with their conquest plan. Apparently that involves sending an app to the phone of everyone on Earth, which is supposed to get everybody, but would really be more like 80% of everybody. Sir Derek Jacobi is delightfully snarky throughout, because all of this is a bit beneath him, really. If you’re going to have to cooperate with the Master, it’s certainly lucky for UNIT that they got this version, as opposed to the Simm, Missy, or Dhawan versions, who are all considerably more impulsive and mad. You can usually trust the War Master to have a decent plan. That doesn’t stop him from playing all kinds of mind-games, mostly with Kate, but really with anybody he comes across. Kate and Sam especially are determined not to be swayed, and Sam seems almost furious that the Master would even try. Kate treats him like the scorpion he is, which is about as good as it gets with him. Caught between two formidable enemies, the death toll is once again high, but Kate is primarily concerned with getting Osgood back safely, because she’s in the credits. The Auctioneers pop up briefly, but are quickly dealt with. It’s almost a disappointment, given they’ve been in the background for two boxed sets, and much of this is their fault. I also would have expected some additional reaction from Osgood, having been mind-controlled for so long and having done some fairly awful things, but that’s not here. This story isn’t too heavy on the plot, mostly to give Sir Derek time to be awesome, which he certainly does. On the whole, the boxed set is kind of a mixed bag. It makes sense that UNIT would eventually face something they couldn’t defeat alone, but having the Cybermen and the Master in it together makes the back half seem rushed, and the first half needlessly drawn-out.

docs.text: Masters of Time UNIT Nemesis #4 Released: 12 July 2023 Listened: 4/28/23 - 5/1/23 One Way or Another We’re into the fourth and final boxed set for this story, which is called “UNIT: Nemesis: Masters of Time.” Which is awfully generic, and could mean just about anything. It’s been a few months in story-time since the last box, so this story needs to recap where we are and set up the new status quo. Which it does mostly by info-dumping, unfortunately. The Vulpreen have taken over the Earth, but they’ve time-locked most of the population centers, except for some out-of-the-way places where they’re manufacturing arches and unimaginatively named “super arches.” And Missy is working with them now, but she doesn’t appear in this story, which is annoying. It’s written by John Dorney, who’s one of my favorite writers, but this one is just disappointing. Dorney says he was going for a “single take” kind of story that focuses on one character’s perspective. Unfortunately, the story requires parallel perspectives from Kate (breaking into a Vulpreen base with Harry and Naomi) and Osgood (imprisoned in said base with Jimmy and Josh). So the story ends up being Kate’s perspective for 20 minutes, then rewinding and starting over from Osgood’s perspective. Which I really think was a mistake; some tight cross-cutting would have ramped the tension better. We also run up against the limitations of audio, in which Kate’s team conducts the chattiest stealth infiltration ever, as well as explaining the plan as she goes, instead of, say, working out the plan in advance and briefing people. The only thing worse than that is Osgood talking to herself in her section, while she’s trying to be stealthy. And the Vulpreen don’t seem to be very clever either, even though they’ve got UNIT outgunned, outnumbered, and have the ability to freeze time. Overall, it’s a pretty disappointing start that isn’t giving me a lot of hope for this box. Traitor’s Gate This story has a reasonably tight focus, with most of it being on Osgood. She’s a prisoner, being held in the Tower, because the Vulpreen want access to the Black Archive. Osgood uses the memory-wipe feature to stall for quite some time, which you think the Vulpreen would notice sooner than they do. In fact, the Vulpreen just aren’t very bright in this story, or any of the stories, really. This time, we’ve got the trope of the villain who can’t trust his underlings, so he has them executed whenever they fail him, which means the underlings don’t trust him and want to take him down, and around and around. We get the introduction of the “time knife” in this story, which is basically a knife that can cut through Vulpreen time-stops, among other things. Either the Vulpreen are bad at naming things, or maybe Andrew Smith is. While all this is going on, Kate and Josh sneak into the Tower through the submarine dock. It’s supposed to be a reverse parallel to Andrew Smith’s “ The Battle of the Tower ” from Series 2, but the parallels really aren’t that strong. We get two new minor characters: Ashley the Ravenmaster of the Tower, who has somehow stayed hidden all this time, and Lorraine, a schoolteacher who’s joined the resistance. Both seem prone to heroic self-sacrifice, because that’s what minor characters do around here, evidently. There’s a twist around Lorraine that’s sadly obvious, and once again Missy is mentioned frequently, but doesn’t appear. Sarah Grochala is one of Big Finish’s newer writers, and I understand she’s skilled at mysteries, but I think she was tasked with moving some pieces around, and simply did the best she could. The Destiny Labyrinth The last three boxes have featured one episode that seems to be a distraction from the main plot. This box doesn’t have that, but it does have this runaround instead. Kate, Osgood, Josh, and Jimmy are chasing through various arches after Lorraine, hoping to find Missy. Missy has changed the rules on the arches: several are now one-way, and they move through time as well as space. They waste some time determining that they’re at prehistoric Niagara Falls. It’s a stretch that Osgood can figure this out just by looking, and then they don’t actually do anything with the setting. They hop over to 1530s France, where Josh needs some medical attention, so they enlist an apothecary named Michel, who turns out to be Nostradamus. Alison Winter seems to have done her homework on Nostradamus, and uses him as a macguffin to guide Team UNIT through the proper arches. Oscar Batterham does a good job portraying him as kind, intelligent, and capable, but it’s still odd that he’s in the story at all. They all spend a while on a Pacific Island during WWII that just serves to split the party. The story makes a lot of use of Missy’s hypnotic powers, which never really came up on TV, and seem to be a lot stronger than the Master’s ever were. He was able to plant the idea that people in power should trust him, but he usually wasn’t able to hypnotize people into being double-agents of their own accord. Missy’s thralls are able to run long cons on our main characters and make independent choices, which seems a bit much. And they’re all dead by the end of this story anyway. Some good elements in this story, but I’m not excited about where the whole arc is going. True Nemesis It’s time for an ending, and there’s a lot still to do. For one thing, Michelle Gomez actually has to turn up this time. It seems that Big Finish was only able to get her for one story, which makes it seem like they swapped the Eleven out for Missy because of actor availability, although Andrew Smith says that was always the plan. Missy realizes, which the Eleven didn’t, that the Vulpreen are refugees from an aborted timeline, and shouldn’t be around at all. That’s the cause of all the time-glitches going back to the beginning of this arc. She can use them to conquer the universe, then get rid of them and take over. Probably. Kate spends a while trying to tell Lord Varliss what happens to every group who’s ever teamed up with Missy, and of course he doesn’t believe her. I can see where Andrew Smith is going, trying to have Kate and Varliss talk it out rather than shoot it out; Andrew Smith is always one for humanizing the bad guys. But Varliss has been one-dimensionally evil up until now, so it’s odd that he becomes reasonable once he loses most of his resources. I don’t really buy the scene where Missy gets taken off the board; she’s smarter than that. Maybe they’re just following the new-series pattern of her improbable deaths and unexplained returns. Harry and Naomi return in this one, to do basically nothing, and get shunted off to the Seventh Doctor stories offscreen. And because most of the world was time-locked while this was happening, the general public neither knows nor cares. This boxed set, and the entire arc, was disappointing to me. Sam and Shindi are apparently gone and never mentioned. Jimmy looks to be a Sam replacement, but he doesn’t have much to do. Josh’s special abilities are never mentioned or used. The Time Lords involved don’t seem as clever as they should be, and the Vulpreen are basically cartoon villains. I understand that Big Finish are trying to do things differently, switch up some writers, bring in new ideas. That’s important, to keep things fresh. But this arc didn’t do it for me, and that’s a shame to say about a 16-story arc. (9/1/23)
