The only thing worse than that is Osgood talking to herself in her section, while she’s trying to be stealthy. And the Vulpreen don’t seem to be very clever either, even though they’ve got UNIT outgunned, outnumbered, and have the ability to freeze time. Overall, it’s a pretty disappointing start that isn’t giving me a lot of hope for this box.
docs.title: One Way or Another

docs.text: This story has a reasonably tight focus, with most of it being on Osgood. She’s a prisoner, being held in the Tower, because the Vulpreen want access to the Black Archive. Osgood uses the memory-wipe feature to stall for quite some time, which you think the Vulpreen would notice sooner than they do. In fact, the Vulpreen just aren’t very bright in this story, or any of the stories, really. This time, we’ve got the trope of the villain who can’t trust his underlings, so he has them executed whenever they fail him, which means the underlings don’t trust him and want to take him down, and around and around. We get the introduction of the “time knife” in this story, which is basically a knife that can cut through Vulpreen time-stops, among other things. Either the Vulpreen are bad at naming things, or maybe Andrew Smith is. While all this is going on, Kate and Josh sneak into the Tower through the submarine dock. It’s supposed to be a reverse parallel to Andrew Smith’s “ The Battle of the Tower ” from Series 2, but the parallels really aren’t that strong. We get two new minor characters: Ashley the Ravenmaster of the Tower, who has somehow stayed hidden all this time, and Lorraine, a schoolteacher who’s joined the resistance. Both seem prone to heroic self-sacrifice, because that’s what minor characters do around here, evidently. There’s a twist around Lorraine that’s sadly obvious, and once again Missy is mentioned frequently, but doesn’t appear. Sarah Grochala is one of Big Finish’s newer writers, and I understand she’s skilled at mysteries, but I think she was tasked with moving some pieces around, and simply did the best she could.
docs.title: Traitor’s Gate

docs.text: The last three boxes have featured one episode that seems to be a distraction from the main plot. This box doesn’t have that, but it does have this runaround instead. Kate, Osgood, Josh, and Jimmy are chasing through various arches after Lorraine, hoping to find Missy. Missy has changed the rules on the arches: several are now one-way, and they move through time as well as space. They waste some time determining that they’re at prehistoric Niagara Falls. It’s a stretch that Osgood can figure this out just by looking, and then they don’t actually do anything with the setting. They hop over to 1530s France, where Josh needs some medical attention, so they enlist an apothecary named Michel, who turns out to be Nostradamus. Alison Winter seems to have done her homework on Nostradamus, and uses him as a macguffin to guide Team UNIT through the proper arches. Oscar Batterham does a good job portraying him as kind, intelligent, and capable, but it’s still odd that he’s in the story at all. They all spend a while on a Pacific Island during WWII that just serves to split the party. The story makes a lot of use of Missy’s hypnotic powers, which never really came up on TV, and seem to be a lot stronger than the Master’s ever were. He was able to plant the idea that people in power should trust him, but he usually wasn’t able to hypnotize people into being double-agents of their own accord. Missy’s thralls are able to run long cons on our main characters and make independent choices, which seems a bit much. And they’re all dead by the end of this story anyway. Some good elements in this story, but I’m not excited about where the whole arc is going.
docs.title: The Destiny Labyrinth

docs.text: It’s time for an ending, and there’s a lot still to do. For one thing, Michelle Gomez actually has to turn up this time. It seems that Big Finish was only able to get her for one story, which makes it seem like they swapped the Eleven out for Missy because of actor availability, although Andrew Smith says that was always the plan. Missy realizes, which the Eleven didn’t, that the Vulpreen are refugees from an aborted timeline, and shouldn’t be around at all. That’s the cause of all the time-glitches going back to the beginning of this arc. She can use them to conquer the universe, then get rid of them and take over. Probably. Kate spends a while trying to tell Lord Varliss what happens to every group who’s ever teamed up with Missy, and of course he doesn’t believe her. I can see where Andrew Smith is going, trying to have Kate and Varliss talk it out rather than shoot it out; Andrew Smith is always one for humanizing the bad guys. But Varliss has been one-dimensionally evil up until now, so it’s odd that he becomes reasonable once he loses most of his resources. I don’t really buy the scene where Missy gets taken off the board; she’s smarter than that. Maybe they’re just following the new-series pattern of her improbable deaths and unexplained returns. Harry and Naomi return in this one, to do basically nothing, and get shunted off to the Seventh Doctor stories offscreen. And because most of the world was time-locked while this was happening, the general public neither knows nor cares. This boxed set, and the entire arc, was disappointing to me. Sam and Shindi are apparently gone and never mentioned. Jimmy looks to be a Sam replacement, but he doesn’t have much to do. Josh’s special abilities are never mentioned or used. The Time Lords involved don’t seem as clever as they should be, and the Vulpreen are basically cartoon villains. I understand that Big Finish are trying to do things differently, switch up some writers, bring in new ideas. That’s important, to keep things fresh. But this arc didn’t do it for me, and that’s a shame to say about a 16-story arc. (9/1/23)
docs.title: True Nemesis

docs.text: Narcissus The Eighth of March #1.4 Released: 8 March 2019 Listened: 4/22/23 In 2019, Big Finish decided to celebrate International Women’s Day on the Eighth of March with an eponymous boxed set. Although they didn't have access to the Thirteenth Doctor yet, they have plenty of spin-offs led by women, and they just barely have enough women writers and directors to pull it off. This story was part of the first set, by Sarah Grochala and directed by Helen Goldwyn, and focuses a lot on Osgood. In fact, it’s got twice the Osgood, because for the first time, the Zygon Osgood is acknowledged. And unlike what we saw on TV, they’re quite clear on which of them is human and which is Zygon (which means the one Missy killed was definitively a Zygon, a fact they acknowledge). The story involves an alien who feeds on beauty (apparently), and uses a dating site to find its victims, meaning Josh ends up a distressed dude very early on. Jacqui also has a key role, making some points about identity theft that Zygons just don’t understand. It’s a fairly short story, so the climax isn’t particularly elaborate, but does demonstrate that there’s more than one kind of beauty. This story may also close the door on any Josh/Osgood relationship. The flirting has dropped dramatically over the last few sets, and Osgood makes it pretty clear here that she doesn't see Josh that way. Not so sure what Josh thinks, though. It does push the empowerment thing a bit hard, in my opinion, but I’m not the target audience, so maybe someone else would think differently.

docs.text: Objective: Earth UNIT Nemesis #3 Released: 15 November 2022 Listened: 4/28/23 - 5/1/23 The Vulpreen Encounter We’re on another new boxed set, this one called “Objective: Earth,” basically indicating that the Vulpreen are ready to show up in force, instead of being all mysterious with gates. Which doesn’t mean we’re done screwing around with the gates, not by a long shot. This one is a pair of two-handers: Osgood and Jimmy in space, and Kate and Jacqui at a UNIT safe-house. Osgood and Jimmy are investigating a big asteroid spotted near Jupiter, and yeah, of course it’s Vulpreen. Unfortunately, a whole pile of UNIT troops get slaughtered in the process; we’d had a pretty good streak of low fatalities for a while there. They’re mostly running around gathering intel and trying to figure out how to get home. Jacqui has been in self-imposed isolation at a safe-house in Norway, trying to recover from her Vulpreen brainwashing. Kate goes to visit because there’s been no word from her in a while. Jacqui is being even more spikey than usual, and doesn’t seem terribly recovered. In fact, it’s a pretty clear setup to make you think that she’s still working for the Vulpreen…or is she? The acting between Tracy Wiles and Jemma Redgrave is pretty top-notch, but not a lot is going on from a plot perspective. By Jacqui McGee As the title indicates, this is a Jacqui spotlight episode. Jacqui is captured by the Vulpreen early on, and while we learned last time that she’s not working for them, sometimes she doesn’t have a choice in the matter. However, while imprisoned, she’s able to file verbal reports to the UNIT cloud, always giving herself a byline. The Vulpreen have taken to lobbing rocks at the Earth, which are dismissed as meteorites, but each contains an arch. Specifically, one of the first arches ends up in Beijing, where we meet Yang Li, tour guide at the Forbidden City, who’s apparently far too curious for her own good, and ends up prisoner as well. We also get Naomi in this story, orchestrating an aerial rescue. Unfortunately, dramatic chase scenes are a little difficult to do on audio, because people have to describe the action, which keeps slowing things down. In fact, writer Lisa McMullin includes a lot more “describing what’s in front of them” lines than I normally expect from Big Finish, enough to draw me out of the story, so that’s rather disappointing. Big Finish has done a spotty job of making UNIT seem like a large organization, rather than just the people in the credits. They’d been improving over time, but the stories in this box really narrow the scope again, which is unfortunate, as there’s a big invasion going on. Axos Unleashed In the previous two boxes, episode 2 was a distraction with a classic monster ( Ice Warriors and Dominators ). This time, it’s episode 3, but it’s still a distraction. It turns out that the invasion force that comes out of the arches isn’t Vulpreen, but Axos . It’s not clear how Axos escaped its time loop, because it deliberately avoids explaining. It’s also not at all clear why the Vulpreen would team up with Axos, but the intent seems to be to further obscure the Vulpreen’s motives. We’re 75% of the way through the story, and it’s still not completely clear what they want. It seems like they want to take over, but maybe not? Just about everyone in UNIT knows what Axos is and what happened last time, but that doesn’t give a ton of solutions. Naomi figures they need a Time Lord to pop Axos back in its time loop, and then only one available is the Eleven, so she fetches him, but surprise, he’s not particularly helpful. At least, not voluntarily. Li is still hanging around from last story, despite everybody saying she should go home and they can’t endanger a civilian. She turns out to be a mini-companion for Osgood, saying just the right thing at the right time to give her an idea to solve the problem. Although Katharine Armitage said she did a lot of science research for this story, I have to say I find the science a bit dodgy. It also feels more like a distraction than the Ice Warriors or Dominators did. The story should be picking up pace at this point, but it isn’t. Time of the Vulpreen Now that we’re done with Axos, we let the Vulpreen back in the room. And really, they’re pretty much just invading. Or dropping arches all over the world, anyway. Including one on the Isle of Wight, of all places; big strategic advantage there. But that’s the one where Varliss happens to turn up in order to taunt Kate, because he’s really annoyed by her at this point. Osgood press-gangs the Eleven into helping do a sciency thing to disable the arches, which gives Ingrid Oliver the chance to be snarky, and it goes quite well. She’s grown some since she started at UNIT, and it shows. There’s a noble sacrifice with a fake-out, and although writer Roland Moore says he really likes those, I found this one transparent enough to be annoying. Admittedly, Jacqui’s death a couple of stories ago gives it a tiny bit of weight, but not really. So we end with UNIT on the back foot, which they had to be, because it’s box three of four. There’s a good cliffhanger, although it’s overplayed just a little. Ultimately, this whole box feels like it has middle-episode syndrome, which is unfortunate.
docs.title: Objective: Earth

docs.text: Open the Box UNIT #7.4 Released: 21 November 2018 Listened: 4/20/23 It appears that despite Osgood’s and Josh’s insubordination last story, they faced no consequences, because Kate has them with her pseudo-undercover investigating a training organization called Pandora. It seems the government wants UNIT to take “mental resilience training,” but Kate wanted to check it out first, and uncovered a series of mysterious deaths, so now she’s investigating personally. The callback in this story is to “ The Mind of Evil ,” which seems like an unexpected reference. However, “Mind of Evil” was unusual for its time in casting Pik-Sen Lim as a Captain in the Chinese army, and a somewhat sympathetic character. Ms. Lim has been acting steadily for decades, and was available for this story, so we get to find out what happened to Captain Lee after her encounter with the Master and the Keller Machine. We also learn that Osgood is extremely cranky and sarcastic before she’s had her coffee. We also discover the biggest fears of each of our three main characters, none of which is actually surprising. It’s a fine story, with references I didn’t expect, but nothing too revolutionary. On the whole, this boxed set shakes up the format, which is good, but the characterizations seem a bit off.

docs.text: Power Cell UNIT #2.1 Released: 30 June 2016 Listened: 4/4/23 The second boxed set is called “Shutdown,” but not for any good reason, as far as I can tell. Big Finish wanted to establish the series with new, original bad guys, and…that didn’t really come off, in my opinion. However, this set goes a lot more slowly than the last, and the story takes a while to unfold. A scientist working on alien tech for UNIT has been killed, and another evil corporate type, Felicity Lyme, has taken an interest and used her government connections to seize UNIT’s other doodads. Generally speaking, I wouldn’t want another evil corporate type after the last series, but Lyme is played by Alice Krige, so that’s a point in her favor. The character development this time around is focused on Osgood, who goes out with old friends from college, and potentially even starts the beginning of a relationship…which is promptly ruined. It’s not quite a fridging, but it does inform Osgood’s actions in the rest of the story. The bad guys don’t have much of a presence yet; they’re just whispering and whooshing noises, mostly. As an aside, we’re told that Colonel Shindi is recuperating from events of the previous box, and likely Ramon Tikram was unavailable for this recording, so he’s out for now.
docs.title: Power Cell

docs.text: Retrieval UNIT #4.3 Released: 23 May 2017 Listened: 4/11/23 No classic characters this time around. The hybrid creatures from last story are heading toward London (this is apparently just a UK problem, not a global one), and Kate and Osgood are hoping to find a solution from the Silurians’ own technology. So they visit a Silurian R&D facility to look for one, which they both admit is a long shot, but they’re out of options. By sheer bad luck, a Silurian named Tryska is also visiting the base, in order to find a weapon that stimulates primate fear-centers. She’s played by Neve McIntosh, which doesn’t cause any continuity problems because it’s already been established that many Silurian warriors look and sound like Neve McIntosh. And Tryska is very, very angry and bloodthirsty, so she’s an awful lot like Restac from “ Cold Blood .” Except I’m so used to hearing her as Vastra that it’s rather jarring. It feels like Vastra is having an incredibly bad day. Osgood and Kate are a good pairing, and Kate gets a chance to show off her science chops, although she’s a bit snotty about it. Both women end up debilitated, Kate by venom, and Osgood by the fear weapon, which means it’s Sam to the rescue. Which isn’t a great look, but Kate gets to do a lot of teeth-gritted determined-while-poisoned acting. Osgood gets to panic a lot. And considering that Osgood is nervous at the best of times, she has to reach pretty high to get to panic. And once again, anybody whose name isn’t in the main credits isn’t making it out. Which is a small thing, but it’s starting to become irritating. We’ve now had three standalones in a row, and this is probably the weakest of them.

docs.text: Silent Majority UNIT #3.3 Released: 23 November 2016 Listened: 4/9/23 This one opens with another time-jump, to just before the election that was called in the previous story . Osgood (and John Dorney) have come up with a tech-y solution to the Silence: goggles that let the wearer see 360 degrees, so a Silent can’t evade your view, and also with a small image of a Silent so you won’t forget them when they aren’t around. Josh is working for the LeBlanc campaign full-time, running security, although neither LeBlanc nor his aide can recall just where Josh came from. Unfortunately, the Trumpian parallels continue, as LeBlanc makes it clear he doesn’t actually have any policies, and didn’t particularly want to be Prime Minister, but he’s about to have no choice. Once Osgood figures out the subliminal messaging trick, she can use a portable hologram of a Silent to get anyone to do anything she wants, which is really rather scary, but she uses it sparingly. Hearing Josh spout right-wing bile at Osgood is disquieting, and underlines the point that there’s no flirting in this boxed set. Kate’s the one who realizes what the Silence are really up to, because why would they need to have a hand-picked Prime Minister in office, when they could just mind-control the one who’s already there? And yet, “seize power” is such a standard play for alien baddies that you don’t realize it until Kate says it, so good on John Dorney for playing that well. Also well-plotted for giving UNIT a win and a loss simultaneously.
docs.title: Silent Majority

And yet, “seize power” is such a standard play for alien baddies that you don’t realize it until Kate says it, so good on John Dorney for playing that well. Also well-plotted for giving UNIT a win and a loss simultaneously.
docs.title: Silent Majority

docs.text: Square One UNIT #3.2 Released: 23 November 2016 Listened: 4/8/23 John Dorney takes over the writing duties for parts 2 and 3 this time, instead of Andrew Smith. Although you might expect a twisty story from Dorney, the Silence are twisty enough on their own. The title is an accurate one, because UNIT has clean forgotten what they discovered in part 1 . Fortunately, Sam Bishop is in town while on leave, and he’s worried that folks are acting funny. Specifically, Osgood and Kate are both very dismissive of the raid on Mrs. Faversham’s house, although they remember it differently. Fortunately, Sam is persistent, and technology has advanced since 1969, because UNIT can review CCTV footage and see a Silent. This leads to an honestly comedic scene in which Kate, Sam, and Osgood all learn the hard way that looking away from the image causes you to forget about it. Sam and Osgood follow up a lead in a scene that has an abrupt jump cut indicating a Silent encounter, just like the TV show did. And then there’s the part that hurts: There’s a politician, Kenneth LeBlanc, who’s making a name for himself being loud and criticizing the Prime Minister, but offering nothing constructive, just empty slogans. He’s portrayed as a complete moron, and he’s only getting attention because the Silence are using their subliminal abilities to influence the public to trust him. This was recorded in early 2016 and released just after the US election, and it’s a sharp reminder that nobody thought Trump was going to win in 2016, and most of the world thought him a moron. Portraying a candidate who was so clearly idiotic that he’d need alien intervention to get support was probably a lot more amusing before the real-world idiot actually won. And oh yeah, the Silence have brainwashed Josh into helping them, and specifically supporting LeBlanc. While his friends have noticed his abrupt change in politics, they aren’t connecting it with the Silence yet.
docs.title: Square One

docs.text: Telepresence UNIT #6.2 Released: 10 May 2018 Listened: 4/15/23 We’ve got Sam back now, but even he can’t bounce back immediately, so both he and the VR headsets are taken to a secure, offshore location for analysis. Osgood figures out that these are some seriously advanced VR, that in fact transport the wearer’s consciousness to another dimension. But it should be safe, because VR, right? So Shindi, Josh, and Osgood go to reconnoiter, And they find a blasted, burnt-out Earth, that doesn’t seem to have the same level of tech as whoever made the headsets. There are also dangers in the form of local wildlife, but also cybernetic monsters, and it seems that the danger they pose is quite real. Josh and Shindi get to do their military thing, except of course they have no gear or weapons, but they still have their tactical minds. Naturally, getting them out isn’t nearly as easy as they thought it was going to be, because something has been waiting for people to use the headsets. While all this is going on, Sam is supposed to be recovering in sickbay, except he’s not doing as well as he should be. That’s because he’s not as disconnected from the VR network as he should be either. Something’s still got a grip on him, and it’s trying to establish a bridgehead in our dimension. Basically, this is a “middle story,” where our heroes think they’re figuring things out, only to discover that oops, things are more complicated than they thought. It’s fine, but it’s treading water.
docs.title: Telepresence

docs.text: Tempest UNIT #8.2 Released: 30 April 2019 Listened: 4/22/23 Another one-parter, this time by Lisa McMullin. We’re swapping Josh out for Sam in this story as the soldier who goes with Osgood. UNIT is investigating freak atmospheric disturbances in the northern hemisphere. Specifically, Kate goes to visit an oil rig where workers are hearing voices, and Osgood and Sam investigate an old woman in an isolated shack who’s hearing voices down her chimney. This one is definitely set up as a mystery; it takes a fair chunk of the one-part story before we have any idea what’s going on. McMullin’s creation of Mother McCracken is inspired, as it provides an information source without actually providing too much information. Plus she’s got some excellent lines. Kate, unfortunately, gets the oil rig supervisor who only cares about the company’s profits, which is straight out of 70s UNIT, no matter how justified it actually is. It’s a pretty normal story, with UNIT doing what they’re supposed to and sciencing up the mystery. This one is also very light on the bloodshed, which is a nice sign.
docs.title: Tempest

docs.text: The Battle of the Tower UNIT #2.3 Released: 30 June 2016 Listened: 4/5/23 This one does what it says on the tin: it’s a battle, at UNIT’s Tower of London HQ. In fact, there’s so much detail provided about the Tower that I almost expected the story to be sponsored by the London Tourism Bureau. Still, if you’ve been to the Tower – which I have, and which Andrew Smith admits he hadn’t until he was writing this story – it’s remarkably easy to visualize the action. The plot has become clear now: The Kamishi lost an energy cell, UNIT has it, UNIT now know what it is, and the Kamishi are going to raid the tower to get it back. The irony is, by the end of the story, UNIT agrees with the Kamishi that this tech is too dangerous for humans at their current level of development, but they don’t have a chance to peacefully hand it over. You might expect, as I did, that because the Tower is a real-world building and a major historical site in the middle of London, it would have the equivalent of plot armor. But we’d be wrong. Pretty much every bit of the Tower comes in for a major bashing, which somehow heightens the tension, even though that’s not logical. Not a lot of time for character development this time around, but Josh does some more commanding, and he’s pretty good at it.
docs.title: The Battle of the Tower

docs.text: The Dalek Transaction UNIT #5.1 Released: 29 November 2017 Listened: 4/12/23 Big Finish originally planned for just four UNIT boxed sets, because that’s the number they arbitrarily chose for most of their series at the beginning of the boxed set era. However, the popularity of the series was such that they kept right on going, at the rate of two boxes a year. However, they did decide to change things up a little bit with #5, entitled “Encounters.” The original idea was that they’d do four stand-alone stories, and they mostly still are, but as the set developed, the thread of “the Auctioneers” wove itself into the background of each story. For this one, the big deal is that there’s a Dalek (it’s right there in the title). It crashed somewhere in the South Atlantic, and some generic Central American revolutionaries have salvaged it, removed its eye, arm, and gunstick, and are selling off the rest. UNIT isn’t sure what the alien is, so they go undercover as shady alien-buyers to find out. Colonel Shindi is back for this one, although he’s not great at playing a mercenary. Kate, Osgood, and Josh are the rest of the squad, because of course they are. Everybody involved knows what a Dalek is, Shindi from personal experience, the others by reputation. But they all know enough to be properly terrified, as they should be, with the Daleks having gotten their new-series upgrade. And this Dalek is proper scary, even without its casing. It’s a trained scout, and it knows what it’s doing. Matt Fitton has done a great job of making this truly frightening. My only complaint is the body count. Yes, a Dalek can kill a lot of people; but having it kill everybody except the people with their names on the cover is a bit much. Still, UNIT had to face a Dalek eventually, and this is a good example of how to do it right.
docs.title: The Dalek Transaction

docs.text: The Power of River Song UNIT #8.3 & 8.4 Released: 30 April 2019 Listened: 4/22/23 This was pretty much inevitable. River has worked with 1970s UNIT , so why not modern UNIT? Except in River fashion, she’s trying to keep her identity hidden, especially because Kate probably has records of who she is. Also in River fashion, she enjoys being enigmatic and irritating at the same time. Kate’s snark level is turned all the way up, which seems a bit unusual, although it’s mentioned several times that she hasn’t slept in days. Plus, early events of the story put her even more on edge. Somehow, River seems to have gotten herself put in charge of a microwave solar power transmission project, which is exactly the thing that would solve the UK’s power problems, if it actually works. But does it? By part 2, we’re deep into temporal shenanigans. Jacqui and Sam are running around in the marshland avoiding dinosaurs and Vikings; Osgood and River are off in the future dodging robots; and Josh is dealing with overlapping quantum-possibility Kates. It’s actually kind of difficult to follow, but I’m not sure that’s really important. We do get to see Kate doing a lot of sciencing, which is nice, but unusual for her. It’s even more unusual for her to keep reminding herself that she’s a genius; that’s more of a Doctor thing, really. Osgood, unfortunately, is out of her element, and lacks sciency things to do, which is annoying to her. And River’s being especially River, which isn’t the best thing for Osgood’s nerves. She ends up liking River anyway, though, because everybody does. I’m not really sure why we had Jacqui back for this set, she doesn’t seem particularly necessary, although it’s nice to see her again. Colonel Shindi is nowhere to be found; I guess Ramon Tikaram was busy. On the whole, this one is a romp, I think it’s safe to say. It just runs along at such a pace that you have to go with it rather than stop to think. Which makes the boxed set kind of uneven in tone, but that’s not a terrible thing.
docs.title: The Power of River Song

docs.text: The Sacrifice of Jo Grant The Legacy of Time #3 Released: 17 July 2019 Listened: 4/12/23 I covered this story in the Third Doctor section , where I mostly focused on the 1970s aspects. For Jo, Osgood, and Kate, it takes place here. The characterizations are ever so slightly off, but not so much that it would cause distress. Jo and Osgood are now close friends, and Jo’s trying to draw Osgood out of her shell, taking her to a water park, and planning on paintball later. But of course this is UNIT, so they have to go deal with a time distortion that results in Jo and Kate getting shunted back to the 1970s, where the Doctor is also dealing with the same distortion. Osgood stays in the present, dealing with all kinds of side effects, and she seems more panicky than usual while also seeming rather a bit smarter, able to understand temporal physics on the Doctor’s level. (Jo doesn’t show the talent she had in the last story.) For her part, Kate seems to be beating herself up a bit more than she usually would, and gets rather wound up by the idea of talking to her Dad. Jo has a chance to spend more time with “her” Doctor, and grabs it with both hands, probably bending the rules of causality a bit, but the Doctor is good at keeping secrets. The focus isn’t on the science, of course, but rather on the interactions between the characters, and that works just fine.
docs.title: The Sacrifice of Jo Grant

docs.text: The Sontaran Project UNIT #5.3 Released: 29 November 2017 Listened: 4/13/23 Continuing with the anthology, this is an Andrew Smith story about Sontarans. One thing about Andrew Smith: he likes to make the monsters misunderstood rather than just baddies. In this case, there’s a Sontaran missing on Earth, and his fellows have come to rescue him, but they have to find him first. Sam is still missing, so Shindi is the first to encounter them, and after some initial distrust (and light torture), they actually work alongside UNIT, if somewhat uneasily. Meanwhile, Osgood meets an old Defense Department colleague who’s working on cloning therapies…and in this case, yes, mad scientist cloners leads directly to Sontarans. Osgood is operating on her own for most of the story, and although she’s initially too trusting of her old friend, she handles herself quite well, better than in previous boxes, certainly. However, much like the Dalek in the first story, she’s sympathetic to an alien being held prisoner and experimented on. Fortunately, this Sontaran is more Strax-like, and willing to meet her halfway. Dan Starkey plays all the Sontarans, investing each of them with a different persona. None of them are deliberately comedic, but there are some pretty good one-liners with Starkey’s patented dry delivery. We’re getting closer to the Auctioneers as well, actually capturing one of their agents, but we’re told that’ll just make the rest vanish and cover their tracks. I really can’t turn down a Sontaran story with Dan Starkey, especially ones in which the Sontarans are more honorable than aggressive.
docs.title: The Sontaran Project

docs.text: The Turn of the Tides The Eighth of March #2.3 Released: 8 March 2022 Listened: 5/2/23 This special story is a bit of a mash-up, kind of hard to categorize, so it’s going here. It doesn’t feature any of the regular UNIT cast, but it does feature Jo Jones and her assistant Rio; Jac, the poor UNIT scientist who never got a last name on TV; and Rani Chandra, presumably before her own series begins. Whew, that’s a thing. There’s a group of aliens who are messing about with the moon, with the effect of disrupting the tides, causing earthquakes, and generally damaging the ecosystem. That’s enough to draw Rani’s attention in the UK, but it’s a bit beyond her skills, so she gets in touch with Jo. Jo is in the Amazon with Rio, so of course they notice the disruption. Jac is stationed at Gibraltar, where they gather data on it as well, but without more info, she can’t get the funding to launch an operation. All of them meet up in the Amazon and eventually head to the moon. As with many Eighth of March stories, the plot is less important than the interactions between the characters. This one does a very good job of making the story not about women’s empowerment specifically; it’s a group of women who each have different agendas. Jo is concerned about ecology, but cares about a lot of people, and wants to follow the Doctor’s example. Rani is following in Sarah Jane’s footsteps, with similar goals to Jo, but more focused on freedom of information. Jac seems more concerned with her authority and UNIT status than anything; she’s not afraid to use violence to achieve her goals. And Rio thinks that Jo and others like her are thinking too small, that the world has problems that can’t be solved by individuals. I note that Rani has Sarah Jane’s sonic lipstick, and Jo has psychic paper, although I have no clue where she got it. This is writer Nina Millns’ only contribution to Big Finish so far, but she does a pretty good job capturing the voices of the disparate characters, and throws in a couple of nice twists I didn’t see coming.
docs.title: The Turn of the Tides

docs.text: This Sleep of Death UNIT #8.1 Released: 30 April 2019 Listened: 4/21/23 This boxed set is called “Incursions,” which could mean anything at all, really. This one is written by Jonathan Morris, and calls back to his Main Range story “ Static ,” which is one of the creepier Big Finish stories I’ve ever heard. Bottom line: UNIT has jurisdiction over Abbey Marston, which has been proven to be a place where you can bring back the dead, so long as you put them back when you’re done. This is the sort of thing that UNIT should probably destroy, but a power like that is just too useful to ignore entirely. So what could drive Kate to use it? When there’s a hidden threat to the whole human race, and only a deceased UNIT soldier knows where it is. Except that very little is what it seems in this story. After the last boxed set, Osgood seems a little more tentative this story, not necessarily because she’s learned, but because she’s being written by someone else. Both she and Josh are remarkably skeptical of the whole back-from-the-dead thing, and you’d think that two seasoned UNIT operatives would be a little more open-minded. The previous story also involved a fair bit of body-swapping, which comes up again here, but it’s kept to a minimum because it’s only a one-parter, and frankly, the rules around that are complicated. But it means that Ingrid Oliver has to play yet another Osgood-but-not-Osgood, which is getting a bit overdone (even though the Zygon complication hasn't appeared in this series yet). Once again, there’s no mass slaughter, unless you count an awful lot of people who were already dead to start with. It’s not as creepy as the original, but I didn’t expect it to be.

docs.text: UNIT #8.1 Released: 30 April 2019 Listened: 4/21/23 This boxed set is called “Incursions,” which could mean anything at all, really. This one is written by Jonathan Morris, and calls back to his Main Range story “ Static ,” which is one of the creepier Big Finish stories I’ve ever heard. Bottom line: UNIT has jurisdiction over Abbey Marston, which has been proven to be a place where you can bring back the dead, so long as you put them back when you’re done. This is the sort of thing that UNIT should probably destroy, but a power like that is just too useful to ignore entirely. So what could drive Kate to use it? When there’s a hidden threat to the whole human race, and only a deceased UNIT soldier knows where it is. Except that very little is what it seems in this story. After the last boxed set, Osgood seems a little more tentative this story, not necessarily because she’s learned, but because she’s being written by someone else. Both she and Josh are remarkably skeptical of the whole back-from-the-dead thing, and you’d think that two seasoned UNIT operatives would be a little more open-minded. The previous story also involved a fair bit of body-swapping, which comes up again here, but it’s kept to a minimum because it’s only a one-parter, and frankly, the rules around that are complicated. But it means that Ingrid Oliver has to play yet another Osgood-but-not-Osgood, which is getting a bit overdone (even though the Zygon complication hasn't appeared in this series yet). Once again, there’s no mass slaughter, unless you count an awful lot of people who were already dead to start with. It’s not as creepy as the original, but I didn’t expect it to be.

docs.text: Tidal Wave UNIT #4.2 Released: 23 May 2017 Listened: 4/10/23 Following the law of conservation of characters, this story is mostly Osgood and Jo Grant-Jones, with a side of Kate. Katy Manning is a familiar voice around Big Finish, playing both a younger Jo and Iris Wildthyme, and even an older Jo on occasion, but this is really the first time she’s played the older Jo, post “Death of the Doctor,” and the story really leans into her eco-warrior status. Which is why she’s called in as an expert to help test an eco-friendly submarine, which is a terribly flimsy excuse, but it gets her there. Osgood, of course, fangoobers all over Jo, to the point where Kate has to rein her in. We know Osgood’s a fan, but it’s fairly unprofessional. Of course, the whole submarine plotline is an excuse to bring in the Sea Devils . Captain Burmeister was brainwashed by the Silurians in the last story and is now using the sub to awaken a Sea Devil base, specifically one where some monster dinosaur hybrids are stored, and pin the blame on the humans. (An opportunity to mention the events of “ Bloodtide ,” but that doesn’t happen.) Which works pretty well, so that Kate and UNIT are forced to defend themselves. Of course, Jo wants to see if she can negotiate, to honor the Doctor, if nothing else, and naturally Osgood is going to help, even if that means going behind Kate’s back. Despite the contrived setup, what follows is exactly what Jo, Kate, and Osgood would do, so credit to Guy Adams for that. And the Jo / Osgood combo just sparkles every time they’re in a scene together. You can see why they were willing to go back to that later . So far, we’ve had two entirely self-contained stories, but it’s clear this is building to something.

docs.text: United UNIT #4.4 Released: 23 May 2017 Listened: 4/11/23 We’ve reached the end, and it’s time to get the band back together, or most of it, anyway. The Silurians are using modified dinosaurs to control the sea and airspace around Britain, and everybody Colonel-level and above is out of the country and can’t get back. It’s pretty contrived, but that gives Kate the excuse to delegate to Mike Yates, with Jo and Benton as his advisors, as they’ve fought Silurians before. Josh and Osgood manage to teleport back in to help. Kate is mostly left giving orders from outside. Yates and Benton get to work prepping a military response, because that’s their job. Jo, though, objects strenuously. She still wants to pursue diplomacy, because it’s what the Doctor would have done. So she goes along to help Osgood, displaying a much greater technical knowledge than she ever has before. I know she learned from the Doctor and Cliff, but this seems a bit of a stretch. And, of course, being Jo, she goes off to try to negotiate without telling anybody else. At this point, I think Mr. Fitton was in trouble: we’ve established that just killing all the Silurians isn’t the right thing to do, but also that Jastrok is a fanatic and unwilling to negotiate. So that seems to leave our heroes with no options, but this is Doctor Who , so we can always come up with a deus ex scientia to save the day. And it does feel a bit like a deus ex, but you really can’t write a Silurian story that doesn’t end with “and then they all went back to sleep,” because that’s the rules that we’re stuck with now. So: the story is fine, and all the stories in the box are fine. What we paid our admission for is to see UNIT team up with 70s UNIT, and we certainly got that. In fact, as we’ll see, establishing Jo as an occasionally recurring character and friend of Osgood will pay off down the road.

docs.text: Vanguard UNIT #1.1 Released: 9 November 2015 Listened: 3/29/23 Welcome to the most recent, and most successful era of UNIT. This series premiered in 2015 with the burst of new-series spin-offs, and started with this boxed set called “Extinction.” Kate and Osgood appeared from TV, and new characters Colonel Vikram Shindi (Ramon Tikaram) and Captain Josh Carter (James Joyce) were introduced. Although the speaking cast isn’t much bigger than previous iterations, the writing and sound design manage to give an impression of a much larger, better-funded, and better-equipped UNIT than ever before. And yet, somehow still a secret, despite the multiple public alien encounters over the past couple of decades. Which means we need a nosy journalist character, Jacqui McGee (Tracy Wiles). The stories in this set are fairly short, under 45 minutes each, and form basically one long story. And if you’re going to start a new era of UNIT, why not start with Autons ? I’m not sure who came up with this idea, but Autons plus 3D printers is a fairly clever concept. So we have Simon Devlin, a super-rich business type who’s selling the printers cheap, and is extremely shady. UNIT, to their credit, don’t stay in the dark for long, recognizing a Nestene signal almost immediately. It’s just going to take a while to put the pieces together. Because this is a Matt Fitton story, we get a lot of focus on characters: Kate is cool, calm, and efficient, and wants to change the “shoot first” policy UNIT seems to have had in the early 21st Century. Osgood is twitchy and nerdy, and no good in the field. Shindi is by-the-book, and not entirely comfortable with the “science leads” policy, but fiercely loyal to Kate. And Josh Carter is a maverick, overly convinced of his own invincibility and way too headstrong. He also flirts with Osgood a lot; at this point, I’m not sure if he’s sincere (which might be odd) or teasing (which would be cruel). This one is all setup, but it’s good setup.

docs.text: The Eighth Doctor The Eighth Doctor, more than any of the others, is largely (but not entirely) an invention of Big Finish. Although the Eighth Doctor has a long run in both novels and comics, lasting from his inception in 1996 to the return of the new series in 2005, the bulk of the stories featuring Paul McGann during that period were found on Big Finish, which gives them a bit of extra weight. Unlike the Seventh Doctor stories, Big Finish didn’t try to keep their timeline consistent with the other media (mostly) which allowed them to keep the Doctor’s timeline mostly straight, and avoid the temporal complexities that were going on in the novels. Big Finish also kept going long after the novels and comics had finished, and the Eighth eventually became the first Doctor to see a new TV story (sort of) while his Big Finish adventures were still ongoing, tying this Doctor directly to events created for the new series, specifically the Time War. That gives the Doctor a destination and an arc to his life that had previously been open-ended. As a result of the way Big Finish executed the Eighth Doctor stories, release order runs closer to chronological order than for any other Doctor, although there are exceptions of course. His tenure can also be divided into three large chunks: the early period with Charley, when he was one of several Main Range Doctors, and also considered the “current” Doctor; the middle period with Lucie, in which he became the first Big Finish Doctor to have his own specialized series, influenced by the style and pace of the new series; and the “boxed set” era, in which his adventures tended to be part of large sweeping arc of four boxed sets, each containing four stories. This last era tends to be more tied to new-series concepts and characters, and is still ongoing as I write this.

docs.text: The Eighth Doctor and Bliss We had to end up here eventually. Thanks to the 50th Anniversary special , we know how the Eighth Doctor’s tenure ends, and we know it happens in the middle of the Time War. After several years of saying they’d stay away from the Time War period, Big Finish kept edging closer and closer, until eventually they did the War Doctor series , and then it was Time War for everybody! Well, mostly everybody. The Eighth Doctor is the only other one we know who had direct contact with the war, so we’ve got several boxed sets dedicated to that. Fortunately, Bliss is his companion through much of that time, so I can name this section after her rather than having to call it “The Time War.” Curiously, for a section about the Time War, these stories take place almost exclusively in release order, right up until the end.

docs.text: Dreadshade The Time War #4.3 Released: 16 September 2020 Listened: 2/2/22 The Doctor and Bliss bounce back to the “prime” timeline, where the Time War is still over, but now nobody can remember that the Daleks existed, which is awkward, given that the Time Lords are trying to wind down a war against an enemy they can’t remember. Worse, the Doctor and Bliss also seem to have lost part of their memories, and can’t remember each other. And worse still, the Twelve is awake and about, with her memories intact, and she’s got control of a Dreadshade, a rather strange sentient weapon. It’s terrified of just about everything, but the more afraid it gets, the more dangerous it is. But it’s not mythical or anything; it just starts throwing out energy bolts once it gets to a certain level of terror. It was trained to fear Daleks most of all, but since it can’t remember the Daleks now, the Twelve gets it to lash out at the Time Lords. Unfortunately, the Twelve isn’t as cleverly written as in her last appearance. Most of the time, her other personas are suppressed, and she’s mostly vicious and scheming, instead of the nice little old lady act she did before. It’s still funny to hear Julia McKenzie doing evil, but it’s kind of one-note. Bliss spends most of the story being confused, but steadily becoming more dismayed by the Time Lords’ conduct during the war, the more she learns. The Doctor’s moral high-handedness seems a bit overdone here, since the war is over, and nobody can recall the enemy, but he’s still leaning into it. Casting-wise, Ken Bones appears as the General, although he doesn’t do anything specific that couldn’t be done by another Time Lord character, unfortunately. Rasmus is here too, having regenerated from Damian Lynch into Chris Jarman. He’s not much different, though; he just sounds older. While it’s interesting to see how the Time Lords would have acted in the aftermath of a Time War that they won, this story doesn’t really do a whole lot.
docs.title: Dreadshade

docs.text: Echoes of War The Time War #1.2 Released: 26 October 2017 Listened: 1/17/22 This story follows directly from the previous , as all of the stories in this box are pretty tightly connected. Having just escaped the Theseus in a Dalek time ship, the Doctor, Bliss, and a pile of refugees are now stranded on a planet undergoing terrible pockets of temporal instability. Their only hope is to find their way to the wreck of the Theseus and hope they find the TARDIS there. As it happens, there’s a Dalek standing in their way…an amnesiac Dalek, who doesn’t know what he’s doing here or what his purpose is. It’s kind of fun to have the Dalek be amnesiac for a change, although we’ve seen plenty of “is this Dalek actually good?” stories many times before. And oddly enough, we’ve seen “The Doctor refuses to admit that a Dalek could ever be good” stories before, at least two of them with this Doctor, so it doesn’t ring entirely right that he’d see something in this one. Bliss gets a turn in the spotlight as the Doctor vanishes partway through the story. She proves herself to be the kind of companion who probably would have done fine on her own, even if she’d never met the Doctor (see also: Martha Jones, Sarah Jane Smith). She’s uncomfortable with being in charge, but rises to it. As with the last story, it doesn’t feel entirely complete, and the ending is kind of sudden, but taken together, it’s pretty good?
docs.title: Echoes of War

docs.text: Fugitive in Time The Time War #3.3 Released: 13 August 2019 Listened: 1/27/22 The third story shifts gears again, with a small link to the previous story. The Doctor wants Tamasan to agree to protect the planet from the last story , so Tamasan demands he do her a favor in return, by coming with her on a mission. There’s a medieval-ish planet where spaceships tend to crash, and the people there scavenge the tech. They’re harboring the last member of a race called the Helixara, whom the Time Lords deleted from history long ago. If they can find out how this one person managed to escape deletion, they could use that as a defense against further time-meddling. Of course, there’s probably a Dalek agent around trying to find out the same thing. Naturally, the Doctor disapproves of the whole “deletion from time” thing, and thinks it must be absolutely horrible to be the last survivor of one’s race. (Foreshadowing!) Tamasan doesn’t really care, so long as she gets the data. We see a lot more of Tamasan in this story; she makes a nice contrast to Veklin, because she’s not going to “come around” and start to admire the Doctor. She doesn’t dislike him personally; she just disagrees with his point of view, and won’t be changed. But in holding to her own viewpoint, she justifies actions that the Doctor can’t condone. We don’t really get to see a lot of the society, just the poor Helixara, played by Wendy Craig in a way that makes you feel her intense pain in every line. It’s fairly dark, but still rather Doctorish.

docs.text: In the Garden of Death The Time War #2.3 Released: 10 July 2018 Listened: 1/24/22 After the events of the last story , the Doctor, Bliss, and the Twelve have been captured by Daleks and are trapped in a prison camp, with their memories erased. They’ve got their skills and personalities, but any personally identifying information is gone. Although the Doctor still merits special treatment; while the others have the run of the camp, he’s in a separate bunker behind a force-field. Bliss gets to bring him food twice a day, but she can’t stay long. People periodically get transmatted away for interrogation, and returned with their memories of it wiped. The Doctor has a bit of a crisis of faith. Without knowing who he was fighting against, or what he was fighting for, and with the available evidence indicating he’s a very dangerous prisoner, it’s possible that he’s some kind of monster. It’s an interesting line of thought, but very little is made of it, because there is a monster present, several in fact, hiding in the Twelve’s head. Unfortunately, she doesn’t know why she’s hearing voices, or why they’re so ruthless, but she does fairly quickly realize that following them gets results. Unfortunately, this story really feels like killing time until the next one. Maybe it’s the amnesia combined with the prison plot, but it really leaves the impression that the characters are just sitting around waiting for something to do.
docs.title: In the Garden of Death

docs.title: In the Garden of Death

docs.text: Jonah The Time War #2.4 Released: 10 July 2018 Listened: 1/25/22 Here we’ve got another narrative jump from the previous story , although it seems to take place not long after. After being rescued from the Daleks, the Doctor, Bliss, and the Twelve are taken to the ocean planet of Uzmal, where the Daleks are looking for something. The Doctor is put in charge of a submarine with Bliss and the Twelve aboard, while Tamasan has charge of another. Putting the Doctor in charge of a group, especially a military group, is a terrible idea, which quickly shows, but he does manage to win over the crew with some unorthodox thinking. Mostly, though, it’s a submarine thriller, with depth charges and silent running and hull pressure and all that stuff. Timothy X Atack creates some impressive secondary characters, especially Tania Rodrigues as Chief Panath, having to put up with being the Doctor’s second. All of the native Uzmali have Indian accents, which sound very lovely, but there’s no reason given for it. And the Twelve more or less loses her mind, which gives Julia McKenzie a lot of acting to do, managing to be convincingly scary. Once the Daleks actually reach their goal, it’s a bit anticlimactic, because they don’t seem to have much of a plan for what to do next. Good worldbuilding, great character work, but the plot is just kind of fine. As a boxed set, it’s clear that they want the Time War as a setting, but this one isn’t nearly as desperate as the first, nor is the Doctor pushed as far.

docs.text: Lies in Ruins The Legacy of Time #1 Released: 17 July 2019 Listened: 2/4/22 “Legacy of Time” was the special release for the 20th anniversary of Big Finish, which meant a big multi-Doctor story. As with the other Doctors, each story is pretty much standalone, but features elements specific to Big Finish. This one kicks off the box in a big way, with a meeting fans have long awaited: Professor Bernice Summerfield and Professor River Song. It turns out that River was Benny’s student at Luna University, which was intentional on River’s part, as she knew of Benny’s history with the Doctor. Benny, however, didn’t know who River was – until right now – and considered her a poor student. There’s some sniping, because really, it would be disappointing if there weren’t, but actually not a ton, especially once the Doctor shows up. He seems kind of subdued, especially for the Eighth Doctor, and has a new companion, Ria, who’s bouncy and cheerful and thinks the Doctor is fabulous, and that’s the first clue that something isn’t right there. And once the plot really starts rolling, we see just how damaged this Doctor is, how close to the edge the Time War has pushed him, and how far he’s willing to go without someone to stop him. Fortunately, Benny’s pretty good at stopping him, and River’s even better. If the “ Time War ” series has been strange because the Doctor isn’t as dark as you’d expect, this story goes all the way into the darkness. This Doctor is broken, and has no idea how to fight against a war without fighting in the war. If there’s any complaint about this story, it’s that there’s no parity between Benny and River. Benny may be a better archeologist, but River has knowledge that Benny just doesn’t, about the Time War, about Gallifrey, about the Doctor’s future. So she’s better positioned to see what’s going on than Benny is, which means there can’t really be parity. I have no idea if we’ll ever see them together again, but they do seem to be on good terms, which is nice to see.
docs.title: Lies in Ruins

docs.text: Meanwhile, Elsewhere The Time War #5.1 Released: 18 January 2023 Listened: 2/2/23 In Production time, there was a sense that the Time War series might have run its course. The pandemic threw all the schedules off, and then it was a couple of years real time between sets. In that time, Rakhee Thakrar got more famous, and became unavailable to play Bliss, so the series had to pivot, which apparently they’d been thinking about doing anyway. Which leads to this boxed set, entitled “Cass.” Yes, that Cass, from “ The Night of the Doctor ,” played by Emma Campbell-Jones. Except she and the Doctor had never met before that final episode, which is the mystery that runs behind the whole set. If that weren’t enough, Alex Campbell is back, played by Sonny McGann (who no longer goes by Jake). He was mentioned at the end of the previous story, but in this one, he’s clearly been traveling with the Doctor for a while, long enough to be very comfortable, even cocky. He doesn’t seem to be the same character as the one who died fighting the Daleks , or at least, he’s had a lot more fun in his life. Susan and Lucie aren’t mentioned, and there’s probably a reason. There’s also a story here, from Tim Foley. Cass is an engineer on an “errand-class” ship, not terribly exciting, but she still wants to explore. Problem is, the ship is manifesting gateways to other times and places. And other people on the ship start dying. The Doctor and Alex turn up, being particularly enigmatic, especially Alex, in part because of some timey-wimey on their end, so they have a much better idea of what’s going on. Also aboard is the wonderfully named Hieronyma Friend, who’s a “temporal diplomat” who knows an awful lot about the Doctor and the Time War that he’s avoiding. It’s all twisty enough that it needs a big exposition-dump at the end to straighten it all out, but that’s not too awkward. The main point of the story is reintroducing Alex and Cass, and setting up the bigger story arc.
docs.title: Meanwhile, Elsewhere

docs.text: One Life The Time War #1.4 Released: 26 October 2017 Listened: 1/18/22 It’s time to wind up this boxed set, and yet, this story is in many ways small and personal. Plot-wise, it’s just the Doctor, Bliss, Ollistra, and the refugees trying to run from a Dalek fleet, first in the TARDIS and then on a planet. But the deeper part is that it’s about an amazingly powerful Time Lord weapon, where it’s been hidden, and what using it will mean for everyone involved. In between, we get glimpses of Quarren and Rupa’s life together, with both happy and tragic moments, because they’re the ones who’ll be paying the price. John Dorney pulls another one of his tear-jerker stories, and even if this one isn’t on the level of “ Absent Friends ,” it’s still affecting because David Ganly and Nimmy March sell the relationship well. It’s possible that this story justifies the attitude the Doctor displayed in the last one , but in fact it’s more complicated than that. It’s a good story, but one that suffers a bit from other stories going to the same well afterwards.
docs.title: One Life

docs.text: Palindrome The Time War #4.1 and 4.2 Released: 16 September 2020 Listened: 1/31/22 This boxed set starts with a two-parter from John Dorney that’s really one long story. As you’d probably expect from him, there’s some timey-wimey going on, but also some universe-hopping. One thing that got glossed over quickly in the last story is that the Valeyard’s actions apparently ended the Time War, with the Time Lords winning. In fact, they’ve enjoyed peace for quite a while. But the Dalek Time Strategist managed to escape through a portal to another universe, with the Doctor and Bliss following, but the timing has gotten screwed up. In this other universe, the Daleks never existed, and Davros is a genial scientist married to a Thal named Charn, and together they’re building a dimensional portal. However, because of the timey-wimey, this Davros is living the five days since the Doctor’s arrival in reverse order, complicating his relationship with the Doctor and Bliss, and requiring a lot of info-dumping. It’s somewhat fun to see a “good” Davros, and it’s nice to hear Terry Malloy play a kind character, without the screechy modified voice. In fact, it’s almost hard to tell it’s the same actor. The first part is fairly tight, with everyone trying to figure out what’s going on, and in fact, all three characters get killed multiple times, so even knowing that it doesn’t stick, it’s still alarming. As you can imagine, part one ends when Davros reaches the end of “day one,” and then part two goes forward from there. Sadly, that part isn’t as interesting as the setup. The Time Strategist tries to win Davros over, and honestly, if you’re counting on a Dalek’s charm and charisma over the Doctor’s, that’s a slim hope. Eventually we start to get multiple parallel universes converging into one, which gets us more Daleks, and the kind Davros slowly metamorphosing into the one we know. Malloy does an awfully good job portraying the sudden personality shifts, and it would be fairly tragic, except that we already know Davros’ destiny and just how evil he actually is. Good setup; not too sure about the payoff.
docs.title: Palindrome

docs.text: Planet of the Ogrons The Time War #2.2 Released: 10 July 2018 Listened: 1/23/22 After this level of darkness, we’re due for a lighter story, and this Guy Adams story is definitely that. For starters, we get the Eleven’s successor in the Twelve, played by Julia McKenzie, who is apparently helping the Time Lords during the war, and has her other personas under control thanks to a neural inhibitor chip. She can let them out at will, and hearing McKenzie do Mark Bonnar’s multi-voice trick is really quite disturbing. She’s quite capable of verbally sparring with the Doctor, and can be quite ruthless when she needs to be, while sounding like a little old lady the whole time. If that wasn’t strange enough, she’s accompanied by a “Doctor Ogron,” that is, an Ogron who claims to be a future regeneration of the Doctor, or at least an Ogron who has the Doctor’s memories and skills. And dress sense, as he wears a cravat and a tail-coat, much like the Eighth Doctor’s original costume. As voiced by John Culshaw, he gives off a strong Third Doctor vibe, with an imposing physical presence and a lot of self-confidence. This provides an opportunity for lots of continuity references, as the Doctor Ogron keeps spouting old memories. Beyond that, we learn that the Daleks are using the Time War to insert Ogrons into past events, specifically “ Day of the Daleks ” and “ Frontier in Space ,” which kind of spins one’s brain. That doesn’t leave a ton of room for plot, so it’s basically just a quick rescue mission to the Ogron homeworld, where a twisted scientist Dalek is conducting genetic experiments that creep out even other Daleks. Which is fine, because the main point of this one is the usual shenanigans that a multi-Doctor story brings…when one Doctor is an Ogron. It’s a lot more fun than you’d expect from the Time War.
docs.title: Planet of the Ogrons

docs.text: Previously, Next Time The Time War #5.3 Released: 18 January 2023 Listened: 2/4/23 It’s a Time War boxed set, so we have to have Daleks in it at some point, and to deliver that, they got writer James Moran, writer of “The Fires of Pompeii” and various Torchwood episodes. This two-part story is a puzzle box of continuity, as the Doctor, Alex, and Cass try to destroy a Dalek temporal weapon, and find themselves tossed backward a year in the middle of a civilization that didn’t exist before they interfered. It’s not quite as twisty as a Moffat or a John Dorney story, but it does have plenty of temporal confusion going on. The story is mostly told as an “interrogation turned flashback device,” and the interrogators are from a pre-spaceflight civilization, so that provides lots of opportunities for exposition. And snark. Oh, so much snark. Cass was already pretty good at it, but in this story, everybody’s on another level. The Doctor’s initial conversation with the interrogator is a masterpiece by itself. Even the natives have a good grounding in sarcasm, for reasons that are actually part of the plot later on. And the mystery of what happened to Bliss is still running, but barely mentioned here. As a Dalek runaround story, it’s pretty good, but the dialog is the real star in this one.
docs.title: Previously, Next Time

docs.text: Restoration of the Daleks The Time War #4.4 Released: 16 September 2020 Listened: 2/3/22 Having reached the end of the boxed set, it falls to Matt Fitton to provide the slam-bang ending. That’s been hit-and-miss in the past, but this time, it is fairly big while still keeping the personal interaction that Fitton’s known for. It also ties together quite a lot of story, going back to the previous boxed set. The Daleks are back now, and the war is back on, but the Strategist is the one pulling the strings, and Davros is mostly forgotten…except he isn’t, really. Because he’s Davros – a combination of many possible Davroses from across the multiverse – he’s taking advantage of that status to create something that’s even worse than Daleks. And that threatens every living thing in the universe, because Davros never thinks small. However, by bringing back every possible Dalek, the Strategist has also resurrected the Emperor, particularly the delusions-of-godhood one from “The Parting of the Ways.” Of course, Davros has no patience for that, or for being usurped, and you know where this is going. The only real weak point is the worse-than-Dalek warriors, who we never really get a description of, except that they’re really bad. So that’s kind of a shame. The Doctor is still in the mode of “I won’t fight, I just want to help people,” which gets him in trouble as usual. Bliss is rather a bit more pragmatic, but she’s also seen her people destroyed by the Daleks. She’s quite willing to pull a gun on Davros, and to go behind the Doctor’s back to contact Rasmus for help. Even though the Doctor has been depressed and darkened by events going back to his series with Lucie , that’s all pointing him toward “ The Night of the Doctor ,” whereas these Time War boxes seem to be taking a line of “but he’s not there yet,” meaning he’s actually more up-beat here, toward the end of his tenure. But you could think of it as a reprieve, something Bliss inspires in him that will come crashing down eventually. Right now, we don’t know, but this story has a fairly big surprise at the end, so it’s clear Big Finish want to continue.
docs.title: Restoration of the Daleks

docs.text: Salvage Short Trips #12.1 Released: 2 February 2023 Listened: 3/7/23 This short trip is set sometime during Bliss’s tenure with the Eighth Doctor, so it might as well be here. It’s written by new writer Max Curtis, and narrated by Adele Anderson, who does a decent job of capturing Bliss’s voice, but not so much the Eighth Doctor’s delivery. It’s also one of the more fairy-tale sounding stories. The TARDIS lands on a very long train streaming through the vortex, with passengers frozen in time. The train is supposedly heading for Salvage, the planet where lost things go, from socks and pens to people and planets. Maybe; if such a thing actually exists. Although the Doctor provides the exposition, Bliss definitely drives the plot for this one, as it’s her story in large part. In a way, it’s nicer to have a story that isn’t overcome with terror at the war, but rather a kind of melancholy.
docs.title: Salvage

docs.text: Short Trips #12.1 Released: 2 February 2023 Listened: 3/7/23 This short trip is set sometime during Bliss’s tenure with the Eighth Doctor, so it might as well be here. It’s written by new writer Max Curtis, and narrated by Adele Anderson, who does a decent job of capturing Bliss’s voice, but not so much the Eighth Doctor’s delivery. It’s also one of the more fairy-tale sounding stories. The TARDIS lands on a very long train streaming through the vortex, with passengers frozen in time. The train is supposedly heading for Salvage, the planet where lost things go, from socks and pens to people and planets. Maybe; if such a thing actually exists. Although the Doctor provides the exposition, Bliss definitely drives the plot for this one, as it’s her story in large part. In a way, it’s nicer to have a story that isn’t overcome with terror at the war, but rather a kind of melancholy.
docs.title: Salvage

docs.text: State of Bliss The Time War #3.1 Released: 13 August 2019 Listened: 1/25/22 The third set, like the second, kicks off with a story that’s unconnected to the rest of the set, and focused on Bliss. Specifically, the Doctor wants to try to fix her “orphan of the Time War” status, which means using the psychic circuits to try to get a grip on her past, which is variable at the moment. So we get several different versions of Bliss’s history, some in which she studies robotics, sometimes quantum mechanics, sometimes from a war-torn world, other times from a peaceful one. And stranger, there’s a number of realities in which she meets a Professor Deepa, who has a “visualizer” that shows Bliss other versions of her own life in different realities. Which admittedly gets confusing, even for Bliss. Rakhee Thakrar seems to excel at the “sputtering, confused” state, but balances it out with genius at other times, so it’s OK. The climax gets a bit twisty, but the focus stays on Bliss almost the entire time, with the Doctor just advising. I think we did need a story that established where Bliss came from, and made her OK with traveling and helping out during the war, as opposed to being despondent about her temporal status. She hasn’t had a lot of stories, but she’s proving herself to be a quite capable companion.
docs.title: State of Bliss

docs.text: The Conscript The Time War #1.3 Released: 26 October 2017 Listened: 1/18/22 This story is probably the toughest listen of this boxed set, possibly of the entire range. Basically, the Doctor gets drafted and sent to basic training, which goes about as well as you’d think. Cardinal Ollistra knows that the best way to control the Doctor is to threaten his friends, so the refugees from the last story are held in “protective custody” for a while. That keeps the Doctor around, but can’t make him follow orders. The camp commandant has a “tough but fair” reputation, and seems to be quite skilled at the “break them down to build them up as a unit” technique. Objectively, he appears to be reasonable, and good at his job. However, the Doctor questions the premise of the entire war, and is determined to undermine discipline at every opportunity. It doesn’t really start to bite until the Doctor is sent to solitary, and we see what happens to the recruits who’ve decided to follow the Doctor’s example. Basically, the Doctor’s normal tactics have no place in a war, and yet he’s opposed to the very idea of fighting in a war on the Time Lords’ terms, which leaves him stuck. The last conversation between the Doctor and the Commandant is very revealing, with each side trying to do what they believe to be right, but having no middle ground. Knowing what happens to the Doctor not very long from now puts a sad cast over the whole thing. Fortunately, we can be pretty sure Ollistra is in the wrong, and the story isn’t that long, so there’s not as much time for examination as might be warranted. Still, this is the story that sticks with me from this set.
docs.title: The Conscript

docs.text: The Famished Lands The Time War #3.2 Released: 13 August 2019 Listened: 1/26/22 Having decided that they want to help people affected by the war, the Doctor and Bliss end up on a planet suffering a global famine, because they’re dependent on trade for food, and the war has disrupted their trade routes. Unfortunately, there’s rather more going on here, as the artificial food substitute they’ve created…isn’t food, and is rather more sinister. Bliss and the Doctor get separated, so Bliss gets to do her confused stammering thing, followed by her technical brilliance thing. The Doctor gets an inadvertent dose of hallucinogens, which honestly proves pretty darned funny. The rest of the story, though, is rather grim, and illustrates what people will do in the desperation of the war, even those who are only tangentially affected by it, and don’t really know what’s going on. A new Tamasan appears, played by Adele Anderson. Unfortunately, Jacqueline Pearce had passed away by the time this was recorded, so Ollistra no longer appears. This is a decent enough war story, although not a standout.
docs.title: The Famished Lands

docs.text: The Lords of Terror The Time War #2.1 Released: 10 July 2018 Listened: 1/19/22 This boxed set starts off with much the same tone as the previous, essentially, dark and horrible. Jonathan Morris is the author this time, rather than Dorney or Fitton, but the tone stays the same. The Doctor has taken Bliss back to her home, although whether for a visit or to stay is unknown. Unfortunately, the Time War has changed the planet’s history, and it’s now the victim of a Dalek attack 20 years ago, after which the Time Lords converted it to a missile factory. If Bliss’s family still exists in this timeline, there’s no sign of them. The main thrust of this one is not just Bliss’s personal anguish at the destruction of her planet, but also the Doctor confronting just how far his people will go to win the war. There’s no Ollistra this time, just a new incarnation of Tamasan, but she’s definitely incorporated the “ends justify the means” attitude. Unlike in the previous box, though, the Doctor gets to keep the moral high ground and be as righteous as he likes. There’s a handful of good twists here, and that mixes nicely with the moral issues.
docs.title: The Lords of Terror

docs.text: The Night of the Doctor Webcast Special Aired: 14 November 2013 This very short webcast was released as part of the 50th Anniversary, written by Stephen Moffat, to give viewers the chance to see the Eighth Doctor regenerate into the War Doctor. For those of us who got to see it unspoiled (and I did), the appearance of Paul McGann was so unexpected as to be jaw-dropping. Even more significantly to this project, just before regenerating, the Doctor specifically mentions his Big Finish companions: Charley , C’rizz , Lucie , Tamsin , and Molly . He left out Liv , Helen , and Bliss simply because they hadn’t been written yet, but if you want, you can imagine he was in a rush before regenerating. For many fans, this is as close to an “official” acknowledgment of Big Finish’s canon status as we’re ever likely to get, and it adds a nice coda to an unbelievable little story. Which brings an end to the "Classic" portion of the Doctor's life, but modern Big Finish isn't stopping there, not by a long shot.
docs.title: The Night of the Doctor

docs.text: The Silent Priest Classic Doctors, New Monsters #4.3 Released: 14 March 2024 Listened: 4/8/26 Another Classic Doctors, New Monsters story, this time with the Silence. Normally in these CDNM sets, the Doctors involved appear in chronological order, and the stories usually aren't connected. This time, though, the Eighth Doctor's story comes first, and is a prequel to the Seventh Doctor story " The Silent City ." Which means, for the purposes of this project, I've listened to the stories backwards. But ultimately, it doesn't matter much. The Eighth Doctor turns up two years before the events of "The Silent City," when the city is still ruled by crime lords of two main factions, and the police can't do anything about it. However, there's a church, and everybody who visits it leaves feeling better, although they don't know why. The Doctor specifically visits to unburden himself of things he's done related to the Time War. I think it's a bit of a stretch that the crime lords want to control something that makes people feel better about themselves. Maybe if they thought it was a drug they could package and sell, I suppose, but mostly it seems that they don't like the idea of a secret existing on their turf. And the Silent, well, he's awfully independent for one of his kind, but at the same time has a rather limited imagination. There's an interesting difference in that the Seventh Doctor doesn't trust the hypnotic suggestions he's received, whereas the Eighth is more likely to trust his gut (or what he thinks is coming from his gut). Because of the nature of the story, it can't end well for the Doctor, but he also can't know that, which leaves the whole thing feeling a bit insubstantial.
docs.title: The Silent Priest

docs.text: The Starship of Theseus The Time War #1.1 Released: 26 October 2017 Listened: 1/17/22 This story is unique in that you can see the effects of the Time War actually occur from the outside. Naturally, John Dorney was tapped for this one. In a presumably Pre-Time War timeline, the Doctor lands on a luxury spaceliner with his companion Sheena. Something shady is going on, and they start on a fairly typical story, except that Sheena’s name changes to Emma mid-story, and nobody notices. It’s so smooth even the listener might not catch it the first time through. Just when you’ve forgotten why that’s odd, it happens again, and Emma becomes Louise. They’re all played by Olivia Vinal, so presumably they’re intended to be the same person, but you could be forgiven for thinking they’re not. They all sound like perfectly normal companions: young women who are curious, brave, and clever, and willing to snark at the Doctor, which is what makes the trick work. Unfortunately, there’s another shift where the Doctor has no companion at all, and the starliner has become a refugee ship. There’s still one couple who seem not to have changed much, Quarren and Rupa Maguire. This may be Important Later. Of course, Daleks invade, looking for “the Renegade Time Lord,” which sets the Doctor off on his usual thing, and also introduces Bliss, another refugee who’s smart and capable and not afraid to blast a Dalek if necessary. She’s got “companion” written all over her. The point of the story is the timey-wimey, and it takes the time and space to set that up properly. However, that doesn’t leave much room for the rest of the story, so it doesn’t really have a proper ending.
docs.title: The Starship of Theseus
