docs.text: The Eighth Doctor and Lucie Lucie Miller’s era was pretty much the direct result of the revived TV series. As the show grew in popularity, there was pressure on Big Finish to provide content from the classic series, but in a format more comfortable for fans of the new series. Hence “The New Eighth Doctor Adventures,” which first aired on BBC Radio 7, and were then released on CD by Big Finish. Much like the new series, the stories are roughly an hour, with occasional two-parters, there are ongoing story arcs, and the Doctor has a bit more of an edge to his personality. Most significantly, the companion is a street-smart young woman with an attitude from contemporary times (that is, just like Rose Tyler). Lucie Bleedin’ Miller certainly fulfills the role, being distinctly different from Charley, yet hitting all the companion boxes, and importantly, not in love with the Doctor...at least at first. Because of the season structure, most of these stories go in production order. However, there have been some later inserts, many of which are stuck between Series 1 and 2, because that’s the only spot where they wouldn’t interfere with a cliffhanger.
docs.title: Eighth Doctor and Lucie

docs.text: All The Fun of the Fair Short Trips #3.8 Released: 11 May 2011 Listened: 9/21/21 Oddly, I think of these first Short Trips as being too early to include a story with Lucie, but in fact this came out in 2011. It’s narrated by India Fisher, paradoxically, but since the Doctor and Lucie don’t appear for most of it, that doesn’t really matter. It’s told from the point of view of a carnival con-man, who has somehow gotten hold of the TARDIS and is busy sending fairgoers into the future with it, from which they don’t return. Which is something of a problem, but this is a Short Trip, so it gets sorted fairly quickly. India Fisher does a remarkably good job of imitating Lucie, very nearly a direct impression. Her Doctor, as always, sounds a bit off, but that’s expected. It’s a fine little story, neither here nor there.

docs.text: An Earthly Child Special Released: 8 December 2009 Listened: 10/26/21 After the events of the last story, the Doctor is alone, which provides another convenient place to stick some Eighth Doctor solo stories. This story is specifically placed at this spot, and released at the same time as “ Death in Blackpool ,” and you could certainly infer that the Doctor goes to find Susan because he’s upset after losing Lucie, but that’s not stated. It’s now 20 years after “ The Dalek Invasion of Earth ,” and things have changed for Susan. She has a son, Alex, for one thing (played by Paul McGann's son Jake), and David Campbell is dead. Susan has decided to dedicate herself to helping the Earth, a process that started in “ After the Daleks ” (written and recorded much later). In this case, that means calling for help to rebuild, even though Earth is turning increasingly xenophobic. And she ends up calling the wrong race, needing her grandfather to bail her out. The real core of this story, though, is the Doctor reuniting with Susan and meeting Alex for the first time. The Eighth Doctor is perfect with Susan, being more demonstrative and empathetic than his previous incarnations. Unfortunately, he’s also rather more idealistic, and has some unrealistic expectations for Alex. That won’t resolve until later , though. This is really just an introduction to these characters, setting up a plotline for Season 4. Susan doesn’t really come out looking best in this story, but it is good to see her again.
docs.title: An Earthly Child

docs.text: An Ocean of Sawdust Subscriber Short Trips #2019-3 Released: 3 October 2019 Listened: 10/28/21 This is one of those short stories with a dream-like quality, which makes it appropriate that Stephen Critchlow is doing the narration, because his calm delivery is excellent for a dream. It’s also one of those stories in which the Doctor comes across a small child in need of rescue, not unlike “Night Terrors,” and once again, the situation isn’t what it looks like. In fact, after the Doctor pulls out one of his patented scientific explanations, it’s still not what it looks like. There’s a bit of melancholy to this story, especially at the end, but that’s intentional, as writer Paul Starkey drops several foreshadowing hints of the Time War. It’s a nice change of pace in between these seasons.
docs.title: An Ocean of Sawdust

docs.text: Blood of the Daleks, Part 1 Eighth Doctor Adventures #1.1 Released: 23 December 2006 Listened: 9/7/21 The new era starts off with a bang: Lucie suddenly appears in the TARDIS without explanation -- it’s very similar to how Donna appears, in an episode that came out at the same time. Also much like Donna, Lucie initially doesn’t explain how she got there or why, and doesn’t get along with the Doctor at all. It eventually comes out that she’s been placed with the Doctor by the Time Lords as a form of witness protection because of something she saw, but Lucie doesn’t know what that was. The Doctor isn’t very sympathetic; we don’t know how long it’s been since Charley and C’rizz, but he doesn’t seem very welcoming to the idea of a new companion. However, because this is a new-series style story, they don’t get much time to discuss this before ending up on planet Red Rocket Rising (a Russell T Davies name if ever I heard one), and immediately bump into a bunch of important characters. Red Rocket Rising suffered an asteroid strike (that wasn’t supposed to happen), so most of the population fled, leaving some behind. The leader of the remainers is a low-ranking government official who promptly fails the Laura Roslyn test by accepting an offer of help from the Daleks. The Daleks’ reputation has gotten a new-series boost; the Doctor considers them a universal threat, and expects that a colony of humans would remember them from history (they do, but it was a long time ago). For their part, the Daleks immediately react to the Doctor’s name. Hayley Atwell (pre-Peggy Carter) plays a scientist whose boss was arrested for immoral experiments, who carries a secret of her own, and she’s wonderful as always. There’s also a conspiracy theorist who remembers the Daleks, and in new-series style, is completely right about everything, but no one will listen. It’s a lot of plot and running around packed into an hour, even as the first part of a two-parter. Lucie is an absolute breath of fresh air with her accent and language choices. It’s a promising start.
docs.title: Blood of the Daleks 1

docs.text: Blood of the Daleks, Part 2 Eighth Doctor Adventures #1.2 Released: 7 January 2007 Listened: 9/8/21 Lucie Miller’s debut continues, with suitably high drama. Lucie still doesn’t trust the Doctor much, but it’s clear to her early on that the Daleks are seriously bad news. In fairness, the Doctor’s plans are fairly desperate, as there’s not a lot he can do against the Daleks at this point. The scientist from last story is revealed to be transferred to Haley Atwell’s body, and he’s been busy creating a new race of Daleks out of humans, adding a new dimension to the conflict. Haley Atwell is excellent as this proto-Davros, who has just a touch more morality than the original. The Daleks, of course, react the way they always do to “impure” Daleks, but the lengths they’ll go to are pretty horrible this time. The Doctor, for his part, treats the Daleks as a very serious threat, more than he has in the past. He’s not quite up to the Ninth Doctor’s reaction, but he currently believes that his decision in “ Genesis of the Daleks ” was wrong, and that genocide is justified when the target is the Daleks. Lucie is a bit afraid of the Doctor, and not really impressed, but does decide that he’s a good person. She still wants to stay behind when he leaves, but the Time Lords don’t really offer them that choice, for reasons yet to be determined. This premiere definitely achieves the goal of having new-series pacing and scale, with the Daleks as a major threat. Still a bit too much friction between Doctor and companion, but that’ll change.
docs.title: Blood of the Daleks 2

docs.text: Brave New Town Eighth Doctor Adventures #2.3 Released: March 2008 Listened: 9/24/21 The TARDIS lands in a quaint English seaside village...except there’s no sea. According to the inhabitants, it’s September 1, 1991...every day. And the TARDIS says it’s 2008. This is one of those new-series style stories where the Doctor and companion are trying to figure out what’s going on for more than half of the story. This time, though, the pacing is about right for a 48-minute story, and the reveal is gradual and satisfying, with a classic-series tie-in. Once again, though, the Doctor and Lucie leave after solving most of the problem, but not all of it. Lucie doesn’t seem to like this particular story, and some of the friction from Series 1 is present, but only a little bit. On the whole, the mystery makes this one a pretty good entry.
docs.title: Brave New Town

docs.text: Dead London Eighth Doctor Adventures #2.1 Released: January 2008 Listened: 9/22/21 This is the beginning of the second series of Lucie Miller stories, although no longer transmitted on BBC radio 7. Lucie seems to have had her hair done in between seasons, as she’s portrayed as blonde on the covers. This story is a bit on the lightweight side, but still with that new-series feel of dropping the characters into the middle of the action, where they spend half the story trying to figure out what’s going on. In this case, really in the middle, as Lucie and the Doctor start out already separated, and already in trouble. Lucie had wanted to go shopping in London, 2008, but both she and the Doctor quickly discover that London is shifting time zones with its geography, except for the rivers. This allows for lots of accents and archaic language from the guest cast, with the Doctor frequently needing to translate for the audience. Claire Buckfield returns, having last appeared in “ Horror of Glam Rock ,” but this time she’s playing a circus performer who moonlights as a thief. She makes a decent substitute companion while Lucie is missing, and there’s a bit of friction once she returns, but the story is too short to make much out of that. In fact, the plot doesn’t so much resolve as stop, with the Doctor and Lucie leaving without really setting everything to rights. It’s an OK episode, not a slam-bang opener like last season had .
docs.title: Dead London

docs.text: Death in Blackpool Eighth Doctor Adventures #4.1 Released: 9 December 2009 Listened: 10/25/21 The last story was released in June of 2009, and this one was released just six months later. However, the rest of Season 4 wasn’t released until July 2010, making this something of a Christmas special. A really depressing Christmas special, for which Alan Barnes apologizes in the extras. The purpose of this story is to resolve the dangling plot thread of Auntie Pat, revealed in “ The Zygon Who Fell to Earth ” to have been replaced by a Zygon in 1985, so Lucie never knew her “real” aunt. The Doctor tries to get Lucie to Christmas in Blackpool, 2009, but “Pat” uses a device that pulls them off-course, to 2008, because she wants to see them again. That means Lucie can’t go to her parents’ home, because she’s already there. Worse, she gets hit by a car and ends up comatose in the hospital. She has an out-of-body experience in which a different Zygon tries to take over her body. Fortunately, she’s too strong-willed for that, but she does learn Pat’s secret by accident, which shatters her faith in both Pat and the Doctor. Pat’s storyline ends here, but so, apparently, does Lucie’s. The Doctor’s anguish is pretty real in this story, as he’s been stuck in an untenable situation, and as he points out, he’s not perfect. It’s short, it’s small-cast, and it’s not really very Christmassy, but it is powerful, and it sets up the idea that this last season is going to be different than what’s gone before. Small notes: The theme music is the same from Season 3, but the cool intro to the extras is gone, which is a shame, because I liked it. They’ve also abandoned the mid-story break, which isn’t really needed in an hour-long story.
docs.title: Death in Blackpool

It’s short, it’s small-cast, and it’s not really very Christmassy, but it is powerful, and it sets up the idea that this last season is going to be different than what’s gone before. Small notes: The theme music is the same from Season 3, but the cool intro to the extras is gone, which is a shame, because I liked it. They’ve also abandoned the mid-story break, which isn’t really needed in an hour-long story.
docs.title: Death in Blackpool

docs.text: Deimos Eighth Doctor Adventures #4.5 Released: 8 October 2010 Listened: 11/3/21 This story has links all over the place. As a title and a concept, it’s a reference to “ Phobos ,” the story from Season 1 named after the other moon of Mars. As an Ice Warrior story, it references several other such stories, as the Doctor relies on his familiarity with the Ice Warriors to try to negotiate with them. And it’s got David Warner starring in an Ice Warrior story, three years before “Cold War” on TV. As for the story, this is a sneaky two-parter, so not a lot actually goes on in this one. There’s Ice Warriors threatening a bunch of tourists on Deimos, and the Doctor is trying to get them out of it. For Tamsin, this is the first time she’s encountering the Doctor’s unique approach to morality, where it’s worth risking the lives of hundreds of people he can’t see in order to save the one person in front of him. Her point of view doesn’t quite match up, and it gives her something to think about. There’s another twist at the very end, much like the previous story , that will catapult you right into the next part.
docs.title: Deimos

docs.text: Flashpoint Short Trips #7.7 Released: 13 July 2017 Listened: 9/22/21 The last of these interlude stories is almost all Lucie. The Doctor takes her to a viewing platform above a storm-wracked planet, but of course they’re attacked by raiders, and Lucie ends up stuck down on the planet, without the Doctor, protecting a child. This Lucie is a little more contemplative, as the narration sticks tightly with her, instead of having a ton of secondary characters. Despite her apparent recklessness, she seems to be aware that there’s just as much danger in her life as there is excitement, and sometimes there’s a cost for that. Sheridan Smith’s narration fits the tone perfectly, and the whole thing feels very Lucie. Her impression of the Doctor isn’t all that great, and makes him sound somewhat dismissive and arrogant. The story is relatively brief, but that’s expected. It’s a nice short story, if a bit dark.
docs.title: Flashpoint

docs.text: Grand Theft Cosmos Eighth Doctor Adventures #2.5 Released: May 2008 Listened: 9/30/21 After a bunch of standalone adventures, we now step lightly into some continuity, with the return of Karen and the Headhunter from “ Human Resources .” Karen is working for the Headhunter now, and although they claim to be acting for the greater good, their plans seem somewhat profit-oriented. Karen’s also miffed at Lucie for leaving her for dead in “Human Resources,” and at loose ends in general because she believes her life to this point was a lie. It’s a heist story, revolving around stealing some artwork in 1905 in Stockholm. In this case, though, the Doctor knows that the art was created by an alien, and therefore dangerous, so he wants it destroyed, which means he’ll have to steal it first. Lucie gets a big kick out of the idea that the Doctor will knowingly commit a crime, and also leans into the heist-movie tropes. It would be a bit ridiculous except that Karen is doing the same thing. You’ll also find Christopher Benjamin in this one, playing his only non-Jago role for Big Finish, but you’ll be hard-pressed to spot him with his accent. Ultimately, Karen and the Headhunter get away to appear again later, so the story is sort of unresolved, again.
docs.title: Grand Theft Cosmos

docs.text: Horror of Glam Rock Eighth Doctor Adventures #1.3 Released: 14 January 2007 Listened: 9/10/21 Paul Magrs provides what may be the greatest Big Finish title of all time here. Even better, it stars Bernard Cribbins shortly before he appeared as Wilfred Mott on TV (the extras are impressive for his interview alone). The TARDIS lands in 1974 at a highway services station frequented by touring glam rockers. There’s an alien menace taking advantage of one of the acts, but the menace part is kind of perfunctory, even the resolution. The focus is more on the characters and how they react to being trapped in a dangerous situation, much like “Midnight” would do later. Cribbins and Una Stubbs are both fantastic characters with very different attitudes that add flavor to the story. In addition, Lucie meets her Auntie Pat and inadvertently reveals that she’s from the future, giving Pat some info she shouldn’t have, and setting up other stories down the line . Lucie’s relationship to the Doctor seems far more trusting and cordial than it did in the previous story , or the following one , which reflects the order in which they were recorded, but it’s a bit of a snag in the development of their relationship. Be sure to stick around for the glam-rock version of the theme tune; it’s worth it. This one’s a favorite from this season, not to be missed.
docs.title: Horror of Glam Rock

docs.text: Hothouse Eighth Doctor Adventures #3.2 Released: 21 March 2009 Listened: 10/9/21 If the title makes you think of Krynoids and “ The Seeds of Doom ,” well, you’d be right. It’s a fairly small cast for what seems like a fairly small story, although it has global implications. In the near future, the Earth’s ecology is getting worse, and there’s a wealthy activist who thinks that Krynoids will solve the problem, for some reason. The activist is played by Nigel Planer, who’s pretty well known, so that’s cool casting. Even in this slightly longer format, the story still seems a bit truncated, with a rather swift resolution. The Doctor is still having trouble adjusting after his long stay on Orbis , having forgotten a lot of things about humanity, and not completely sure about Lucie. But she pulls out all the stops to prove herself worthy of his trust, and mostly pulls it off.
docs.title: Hothouse

docs.text: Human Resources, Part 1 Eighth Doctor Adventures #1.7 Released: 11 February 2007 Listened: 9/13/21 We’ve reached another tradition adopted from the new series: the two-part blockbuster season finale with one of the Doctor’s old enemies. In addition, this one also adopts the new-series trope of something that seems like ordinary modern life actually being sinister. In this case, it’s an ordinary office job, specifically the one that Lucie had been hired for just before meeting the Doctor. It seems like ordinary, bland data-entry, but the inconsistencies start to add up: nobody ever takes breaks, the windows don’t open, and no one can go outside. The Doctor, meanwhile, is sent after Lucie by the Time Lords, specifically Straxus, making his introductory appearance (although we saw him in “ The Light at the End ”). Both the Doctor and Lucie play along with the charade in order to figure out what’s going on, which allows writer Eddie Robson to get in plenty of corporate satire and jargon, most of which is pretty funny. Lucie eventually gets herself fired, which leads to discovering that the world outside the office is rather grim and war-torn. The Doctor tries to get to the bottom of the mystery, and discovers that he may have been helping the wrong side. As a two-parter, the plot has more room to breathe, and allows for the main characters to be kept in the dark for quite a while. This may not be the strongest of this season’s stories, but it definitely accomplishes the remit.
docs.title: Human Resources 1

docs.text: Human Resources, Part 2 Eighth Doctor Adventures #1.8 Released: 18 February 2007 Listened: 9/13/21 Much like the second part of the new series finales, this one is somewhat loud and dramatic, but not as high-concept as the first part. It’s revealed in the cliffhanger that the “innocent victims” whose planet was getting invaded were the Cybermen, licking their wounds after the last war. And although the Doctor inadvertently helped them out, they’re still getting their butts kicked all over the place, against probability. Which is because of the Time Lords, specifically the CIA, who believe that Lucie has a rather specific destiny...unless they’re wrong and she doesn’t. It’s hard to tell. In the end, though, the win comes because the humans work together for the common good, and more specifically because Lucie decides to trust the Doctor, bringing the whole emotional arc of this season to its endgame. Once again, the Doctor is pretty hard on the Cybermen, as well as the Time Lords (although he’s usually angry with them), and Lucie doesn’t mind all that much. When she decides to stay with him at the end, it’s a bit of a surprise to him, but the viewers are very happy. This final episode isn’t the strongest of the bunch, but it’s been a really strong season, with all of the stories at least good, and some excellent.
docs.title: Human Resources 2

docs.text: Immortal Beloved Eighth Doctor Adventures #1.4 Released: 21 January 2007 Listened: 9/11/21 This one is fairly high concept, but doesn’t really have the room to breathe at this length. The Doctor and Lucie land in the middle of what appears to be a Romeo & Juliet scenario, but turns out to be much more complicated, with cloning, mind-swapping, and individual rights all involved. It takes half the story for the Doctor and Lucie to figure out what’s going on, so the resolution seemed rather rushed. The “high tech but devolving” society doesn’t really get much attention, and the characters we should sympathize with don’t have time to establish themselves. Watch out for a pre-Churchill Ian MacNeice playing Zeus, though. The distrust between the Doctor and Lucie that was missing in “ Glam Rock ” is back here, as a major development hinges on Lucie’s inability to tell when the Doctor is running a bluff and automatically assuming the worst. However, it seems like the Doctor isn’t really trying to get Lucie home anymore, but is just having the usual sort of adventures.
docs.title: Immortal Beloved

docs.text: Island of the Fendahl The Further Adventures of Lucie Miller #1.4 Released: 10 July 2019 Listened: 9/21/21 The monster is spoiled right in the title, which is a bit of a shame: It’s the Fendahl, who hasn’t appeared since the Tom Baker era, because the Doctor destroyed it. Or did he? Turns out that’s the answer to the plot thread left over from the first story in this set . It helps if you remember “ Image of the Fendahl ,” because this story has a lot of references to it, which unravel rather slowly. There’s a spooky island, cut off from the mainland, with a few villagers and their strange customs. There’s an abandoned monastery, currently occupied by a cult. There’s a missing girl, and the police detective sent to look for her. And the scientist who seems to just be here to study caterpillars. Almost none of these elements are what they seem on the surface, and finding out where they all fit is most of the fun. The actual resolution, again, is mostly just OK. The Doctor seems a little harsher in this particular story, but he does spend a bunch of it under the influence of evil, so there’s that. Because this is an Alan Barnes story, Lucie gets all the best lines; clearly all the writers in this set really enjoy writing her dialog. Heard in release order, this is a really nice nostalgia trip. In the order of this project, it’s just a nice interlude between seasons.
docs.title: Island of the Fendahl

docs.text: Lucie Miller Eighth Doctor Adventures #4.9 Released: February 2011 Listened: 11/9/21 This is where it gets dark. This is also the point where all the plot threads of this season come together, although not entirely together; that’s for next time. Lucie and Alex have been touring the world, as promised, but they get stuck when a plague sweeps the planet. Possibly because this story was written in 2010, after seeing Rose, Martha, and Donna all put through the wringer on TV, Lucie comes out much the worse for wear. Of course this is the Daleks, re-invading Earth using almost the exact same plan from “ The Dalek Invasion of Earth ,” which Susan comments on. But originality was never their strong suit. The Monk is here as well, because he’s allied with the Daleks before , and doesn’t seem to have learned that you can’t trust the Daleks as your allies. The first part of the story is told partially narrated from Lucie’s point of view, as the world falls apart and things get progressively worse for her, Alex, and Susan, eventually taking Lucie past the point of having any faith in the Doctor. He does show up eventually, of course, but far too late to prevent slaughter. Tamsin is around too, but still operating under the impression that the Monk is benevolent, because she has no clue how Daleks operate. And it ends with a pretty strong cliffhanger, not that anybody would believe it. Far from a fun story, but powerful.
docs.title: Lucie Miller

docs.text: Max Warp Eighth Doctor Adventures #2.2 Released: February 2008 Listened: 9/23/21 This is one of those stories that’s a direct parody of some other part of pop culture, in this case Top Gear , but with spaceships. I wasn’t familiar with Top Gear the first time I listened to this, and I’m only a little familiar with it now, but the parody part is incredibly obvious, with the characters being paper-thin parodies of the usual presenters and style. Which is mostly OK, because this episode is intended to be humorous. It takes place in one of those new-series style future cultures, where everyone behaves somewhat stupidly, in this case, politicians obsessed with their approval ratings. There’s a murder mystery to provide a plot, but the Doctor seems to be having fun with it, while Lucie can barely take it seriously, suspecting everyone who happens to be nearby. She also has some good lines at the expense of the spaceship fans and the TARDIS in particular. Graeme Garden plays the Jeremy Clarkson character with perfect smarminess, and he’ll be back as a different character in a couple of seasons . Don’t look for depth in this one; it’s just fun.
docs.title: Max Warp

docs.text: Museum Peace Short Trips Rarities #1.2 Released: 30 September 2016 Listened: 10/27/21 This is one of the longer Short Trips, one that started as a prose story. It features Kalendorf, and ties to the Dalek Empire storyline, which the Doctor mostly didn’t appear in. There’s not a ton of action, just a very vivid description of a museum commemorating the Dalek War. Specifically, the room where Dalek equipment is stored scares away most citizens, which is why Kalendorf likes to go there, alone with the hatred he still harbors. The Eighth Doctor turns up, with a need to make a decision (probably about the Time War , except he’s described as wearing his original outfit, likely because this was written before we knew about his change, or the War Doctor , or any of it). Kalendorf thinks like a soldier, and would like to use the TARDIS to wipe out the Daleks before they existed. The Doctor, of course, has been there , and is now second-guessing the decision he made then. There’s a plot twist that’s wholly unexpected, and makes up the Doctor’s mind for him, perhaps. It’s a strong story, if you can remember the Dalek Empire stories, and if you can put aside later revelations about the Time War.
docs.title: Museum Peace

docs.text: Nevermore Eighth Doctor Adventures #4.3 Released: 12 August 2010 Listened: 11/2/21 Now that Tamsin has been established as the official companion, she needs a proper adventure to start her off. In this case, it takes place on a planet that’s one of those single-inhabitant prisons, and very heavily influenced by the writings of Edgar Allen Poe . We’ve got robotic raven guards, a pit and a pendulum, and a giant black cat. Tamsin does a decent job her first time out: her snark is pretty good, although it’s hard to beat Lucie in that department. In exchange, she gets the Poe references that Lucie probably wouldn’t. The secondary characters all have American accents for some reason, and are mostly played by Americans, except for Fenella Woolgar playing the villain with a rather heightened American accent, but it still sounds good. The story itself isn’t the strongest, plot-wise, but it’s mostly about seeing how many Poe references can be shoved into a one-hour story (answer: quite a few). We also learn that Tamsin is partial to cats, although Time Lord-agent cats are a new one on her. It’s a good first step.

docs.text: No More Lies Eighth Doctor Adventures #1.6 Released: 4 February 2007 Listened: 9/12/21 This one also has quite a new-series influence, in that it starts in the middle of an adventure (or possibly at the end of one), and tells you how you got there through flashbacks. It also contrasts a genteel English garden party with temporal shenanigans on a spaceship. In fact, we never really learn what the baddie did to start all the trouble in the first place, or what his plan was, because it’s a very human story at the core. There’s an extremely small cast, including English acting luminaries Nigel Havers and Julia McKenzie, but also Tom Chadbon, who wonderfully played Duggan in “ City of Death .” The sci-fi trappings are there, but very much in the background. The Doctor isn’t as harsh as he has been in the last few stories, but Lucie is very active and take-charge, almost reckless. She also seems to have a strong trust in the Doctor at this point. So it’s a bit of a bummer when her “Bad Wolf” plotline pops up at the end and kidnaps her into the next story. Although this story isn’t loud and dramatic, it’s one of the few this series that gets the pacing exactly right, by keeping a lot of the plot outside the story. The quality has stayed high all throughout.

docs.text: Orbis Eighth Doctor Adventures #3.1 Released: 7 March 2009 Listened: 10/8/21 A new season begins, and it’s probably a good idea to take a little break between the last episode and this one (I did). There’s some format changes that go with this season: Episodes are longer than 48 minutes now, which means they’re all divided in two parts with cliffhangers and theme music, which is also a slightly different arrangement (I think). There’s also substantially cooler music introducing the extras. It’s been months since the events of “ Vengeance of Morbius ” for Lucie, and...considerably longer...for the Doctor. Personally, I’ve never liked stories where the Doctor stays in one place for years for plot purposes before jumping back into the action. The classic series never did that, but the new series has done it with the Eleventh and Thirteenth Doctors, so I guess I shouldn’t complain. The Headhunter brings Lucie to find the Doctor (no sign of Karen, though), but the Doctor can’t remember her because it’s been so long, a frankly heartbreaking sequence. In fact, the Doctor is pretty damaged throughout this story, and things don’t go so well for him as a result. It remains to be seen how long this new status quo will affect the stories, but it does shake up the relationship between Lucie and the Doctor that became awfully friendly last season.
docs.title: Orbis

docs.text: Phobos Eighth Doctor Adventures #1.5 Released: 28 January 2007 Listened: 9/12/21 The new-series vibe continues in this one, when the Doctor and Lucie land on Phobos, the moon of Mars, part of which has become an extreme-sports mecca, attracting thrill-seekers from Earth and beyond. But there’s something else on this moon, and it’s killing the thrill-seekers, so of course the Doctor needs to investigate. The Doctor is once again more harsh than he was with Charley; he responds badly to threats, and is willing to take down monsters instead of learning more about them. Lucie isn’t too sure about that side of his attitude, but she seems to trust him a bit more than last story . The resolution is a little bit too easy, one that the new series goes to a bit too often, and once again the Doctor leaves before making sure of the clean-up. The extras mention that because of BBC 7, there’s a hard limit of 50 minutes on these stories, but this one still feels a little rushed. The secondary characters are well-drawn, and have their own personal issues that are also very much new-series, and that makes the story. This is another good one.
docs.title: Phobos

docs.text: Prisoner of the Sun Eighth Doctor Adventures #4.8 Released: January 2011 Listened: 11/8/21 Since Lucie has gone off with Alex , the Doctor is alone again. However, this doesn’t seem to have led to a long period of solo adventures. Instead, we come in close to the end of a story, after the Doctor tried to help a rebellion and then spent six years trying to keep a sun stable so that it doesn’t fry a couple of inhabited planets. I normally have a negative opinion of stories that have the Doctor sit in one place for a long time, but this one isn’t all that long, and we’re seeing the end of it. Eddie Robson shows good insight in determining that the only prison that can hold the Doctor is one made of his own responsibility. There’s multiple layers of misdirection throughout, because the Doctor is isolated, with limited information from outside, so when a rescue squad shows up, he (and the listener) isn’t sure what to believe. When the Rebels turn out to have conflicting hidden agendas, you could be forgiven for getting lost, but it keeps the tension pretty high. Although Lucie doesn’t appear in the story, Sheridan Smith is quite present, because she plays the Doctor’s android assistants, who he programmed with Lucie’s voice and persona. Beth Chalmers also has a tiny role, but you won’t know it’s her until the extras. You could imagine this story is just killing time, because it isn’t connected to the larger series arc, but a breather is necessary for pacing, and a story that keeps you guessing is engaging as a breather.
docs.title: Prisoner of the Sun

docs.text: Relative Dimensions Eighth Doctor Adventures #4.7 Released: December 2010 Listened: 11/7/21 After the last story , a bit of a breather is necessary. Tamsin has gone off with the Monk, and Lucie is back with the Doctor, but not to stay. By way of apology, he offers her Christmas in the TARDIS, and also invites Susan and Alex. “ An Earthly Child ,” released a year prior, is pretty much required listening before this one, as there’s a direct connection. It also connects to “ Quinnis ,” but that’s far from required. The Doctor has ulterior motives with almost everything he does in this story, consciously or not. He doesn’t tell Lucie who Susan and Alex actually are until they turn up; he never told Susan about Lucie at all. And he’s testing Alex the whole time to see if he’ll make a suitable companion and heir. That infuriates Susan, who’s convinced that her Grandfather is just as short-sighted and irresponsible as he’s ever been. Her ability to treat the Eighth Doctor as exactly the same person as the First, while also acknowledging her own maturity, is one of the highlights of the story, and Carole Ann Ford pulls it off perfectly. There is, of course, a threat to the TARDIS, because we can’t just have a Christmas dinner story. Marc Platt does a decent job of making it seem dangerous, but in fact it’s mostly just an interruption and a conversation starter. In the end, the Doctor doesn’t really get what he wants, although he may have gained some understanding of the other people in his life, specifically that they have lives of their own to live without him.
docs.title: Relative Dimensions

docs.text: Running Out of Time Short Trips #1.8 Released: 5 November 2010 Listened: 10/27/21 This very short Short Trip is one of the first, read by India Fisher, although Charley isn’t in this one. There’s also nothing to indicate it should take place at this point, but also nothing to say it doesn't. This is one of those where the point-of-view character doesn’t know the Doctor, and so we see him from the outside. docs.text: Sisters of the Flame Eighth Doctor Adventures #2.7 Released: July 2008 Listened: 10/2/21 We’re now at the end of the season, so that means a two-parter with an old enemy, in this case, Morbius. This episode is mostly setup, but it allows time for the plot to build, and to flesh out the secondary characters so we’ll care about them, aspects the previous stories have lacked. In this case, the character that benefits most is Rosto, space cop, all-around good guy, and who just happens to be a 10-foot tall centipede. He’s played by Alexander Siddig of Deep Space Nine fame, and his voice is remarkably calm and soothing. The Doctor is mostly absent in this one, which means that Lucie gets the starring role, overcoming her initial reaction to Rosto and helping him figure out what’s going on. Specifically, there’s a zillionaire named Zardonix buying up planets, including ones belonging to Rosto’s people, and also Karn, the setting of “ The Brain of Morbius .” The Sisterhood have abandoned Karn, but they’ve got a plot to get it back, because they believe Zardonix is obsessed with Morbius. It’s a Nick Briggs story, so it’s not particularly twisty, but the listener has an advantage over Lucie, who presumably never saw “Brain of Morbius.” And of course it ends on a nice cliffhanger with imminent death, because of course it does.
docs.title: Sisters of the Flame

docs.text: Situation Vacant Eighth Doctor Adventures #4.2 Released: 15 July 2010 Listened: 11/1/21 With the interlude over, we can get back to Series 4, or more accurately, start Series 4, because “ Death in Blackpool ” seems more like a holiday special. The Doctor is alone, and has been for a bit, so he’s auditioning for a new companion, Apprentice -style. That leads to four candidates with really distinct personalities, which is a good start. Then the sci-fi things start happening, and it’s not clear to anyone whether these are tests the Doctor set up, or real threats. It’s never entirely clear where the threats came from or how they were resolved; that’s secondary to how the characters react. And pretty much nothing here is what it appears to be, from the contestants to the secondary characters to the contest itself. From here in 2021 America, a reference to The Apprentice leaves a bad taste in the mouth, but Big Finish seemed to be thinking of the UK version, and in 2010, who would have known? It’s a funny premise, especially since none of it goes down as planned, and it does make you wonder who planned it and why. In other notes, the mid-story break is back, with attendant cliffhanger. Also, in this story, there are a number of references to the names of previous companions or actors. I don’t think they mean anything; they’re just fun to spot. This story definitely sends the signal that this series will be different.
docs.title: Situation Vacant

docs.text: The Beast of Orlok Eighth Doctor Adventures #3.3 Released: 4 April 2009 Listened: 10/10/21 The TARDIS lands in the Black Forest in Germany, 1827. There’s a legend of a beast in the woods, and an evil baron who used to torture people, but disappeared 20 years ago. Not to mention the twins found as babies in the woods, Hans and Greta. However, this is not at all a historical, and pretty much nothing is what it seems. The guest stars are really impressive in this one, with Miriam Margolyes playing Frau Tod, who is a remarkably impressive character, very level-headed and smart, given the time period and her social station. Sam Barnett plays Hans, the first of many Big Finish roles for him. The relationship between the Doctor and Lucie is pretty much back to normal, with Orbis entirely forgotten. In fact, the Doctor gives his age as 900, which sort of rules out Orbis at all. Barnaby Edwards plays fast and loose with all kinds of fairy-tale references in this story, and it works well. He also gives Lucie some of the best lines, which Sheridan Smith uses to the fullest.
docs.title: The Beast of Orlok

docs.text: The Book of Kells Eighth Doctor Adventures #4.4 Released: 13 September 2010 Listened: 11/2/21 Now that the dynamic between Tamsin and the Doctor is established, it gets shaken up a bit in this story. The TARDIS is pulled off-course, to Ireland, 1006, near Kells Abbey. Tamsin has a fairly bad time of it, getting soaked, covered in chalk, and then falling down a midden, all in the first few minutes. She also proves to be terrible at improvising a cover story, despite having attended drama school. She and the Doctor aren’t quite in sync yet, and she makes some new-traveler mistakes. In fairness, the Doctor isn’t really helping her much, and is willing to leave her on her own for long periods. But this isn’t a true historical, because the Meddling Monk is at Kells, and has designs on the Book of Kells . In production time, this is the first time the Monk has been seen since 1966, and the Doctor certainly acts as though he hasn’t seen the Monk since “ The Daleks' Master Plan .” Of course, since then Big Finish has used the Rufus Hound version of the Monk in quite a few stories, and he’s had multiple encounters with the Doctor. Here, though, he’s played by Graeme Garden, which seems like a good choice for comedy, except this Monk is more calculating and less blustering than either of his other two incarnations. (However, his choice of “ Thelonius ” as an alias is such a bad pun, even the Doctor calls him on it.) The Monk is also working with an associate, Lucianus, who isn’t what he appears to be. You’ll have to stick around after the credits for that reveal, but it’s effectively shocking on first listen, and adds a vein of humor to re-listens. I kind of wish Tamsin had gotten more of a fair shake before the series arc took over, but this story stands reasonably well on its own.
docs.title: The Book of Kells

docs.text: The Cannibalists Eighth Doctor Adventures #3.6 Released: 16 May 2009 Listened: 10/19/21 Another fairly high concept, as the Doctor and Lucie run across an abandoned space station, full of robots that have become self-aware and turned to cannibalizing each other for parts. Which is kinda creepy, and provides lots of opportunities for running away, but the scary mood is undercut by most of the actors doing goofy caricatured voices for the robots. And the rather doofy cover. The vocal effect on the robots is somewhat annoying to listen to for long periods, and unfortunately there’s a bunch of exposition. This is another story where the pacing feels a bit off, because as soon as they figure out what’s going on, it ends. There’s a happy-ending coda, though, so clearly this adventure is meant to be on the light side.

docs.text: The Caves of Erith Short Trips Rarities #4.2 Released: 30 January 2026 Listened: 4/28/26 After years of thinking I was never going to get my hands on this one, it came out in 2026 as part of the "Short Trips Rarities: The Eighth Doctor Collection." This one is a Christmas story, and a bit on the longer side for a short trip, although the time is mostly spent building atmosphere rather than a complex plot. The Doctor wants to attend a lecture by a scientist friend; Lucie wants to check into a B&B to watch The Sound of Music on Christmas. The B&B owner has a teenage son who's obsessed with the local bat population. When he goes missing, the Doctor and Lucie search for the inevitable evolved bat-creatures the boy has been working with. The Doctor knows how this story goes , but manages to solve the problem with diplomacy this time. It's a nice Christmas story, but a little longer than it needs to be.

docs.text: The Curse of the Fugue Short Trips #6.4 Released: 21 April 2016 Listened: 9/22/21 This Short Trip is read by Sheridan Smith, so Lucie gets a somewhat larger role. In particular, she’s in the 1970s, during the time of labor strikes and power cuts, undercover at a nursing home, many of whose residents lived through World War II. In particular, one of them has a secret from the war, both in how she served her country, and something that she found at the time. Perhaps because Alice Cavender specializes in creating vivid characters with unusual quirks, this one seems to be entirely an invention, not drawn from any historical figure. Because it’s a Short Trip, there isn’t a lot of chasing around or action, but that’s to the good, because the dialog sparkles in this story. Having Lucie’s lines read by Sheridan Smith enhances the whole thing.

docs.text: The Dalek Trap The Further Adventures of Lucie Miller #1.1 Released: 10 July 2019 Listened: 9/19/21 In 2019, Big Finish brought back Lucie Miller, eight years after her last appearance. For reasons that will become clear later, this boxed set of four stories is specifically set between series 1 and 2 of the Eighth Doctor Adventures. This story specifically establishes that the Doctor and Lucie have been traveling around since “ Human Resources ,” having generally fun adventures, with any tension between them now diffused, so that’s nice. This particular story has the TARDIS falling into the event horizon of a black hole, in response to a distress call. They end up in a strange place that erodes your memories the longer you stay, and the Doctor is acting mind-controlled...by the Daleks. Which would be unfortunate, except the Daleks mostly seem to want to get out of there, which involves the Doctor doing...a thing, which doesn’t get resolved in this story. Since the Doctor spends a large chunk of the story out of it, Lucie carries most of the dialog, interacting with a couple of other memory-damaged characters. It shows her using her initiative, and although she’s not as clever as the Doctor, she’s been doing this long enough to know the standard strategies, which is good. Giving her the spotlight in this first story was definitely intentional. There’s a little bit of foreshadowing of future events, but not so much that it hits you over the head.
docs.title: The Dalek Trap

docs.text: The Eight Truths Eighth Doctor Adventures #3.7 Released: 30 May 2009 Listened: 10/20/21 The end of the season means another big two-part adventure, and also the return of the Headhunter and Karen . As often happens with these two-parters, the first part is almost entirely setup, but it’s pretty good setup. The Doctor and Lucie have landed on Earth in the near future, and the Doctor immediately pops off to help with a lost space probe, waving his UNIT credentials about. Lucie doesn’t tag along, because the plot calls for them to be separated early. Instead, she meets up with Karen, gets introduced to Karen’s life-coaching service, which turns out to be a cult, and promptly gets brainwashed. That means Sheridan Smith gets to play Evil Lucie, or at least Mind-Controlled Lucie, which is pretty fun, because Lucie can be quite forceful when she wants to be. The Doctor gets a temporary companion in Kelly Westwood, a journalist who’s trying to expose the cult. Unfortunately, the cult’s prophecies start coming true, which leads to a reappearance of the stellar manipulator from “ Orbis ,” and a callback to a classic series villain. Knowing that it’s all setup lets you appreciate the minor characters more, and the cliffhanger is pretty good on the first listen.
docs.title: The Eight Truths

docs.text: The Four Doctors Special Released: 15 December 2010 Listened: 10/27/21 This is another subscriber special, released in 2010, but in a period that requires the Doctor to be alone (all the Doctors, really), and that fits best here. The underlying plot device is seriously timey-wimey, but the story itself isn’t as much as you’d expect. The Eighth Doctor arrives at a space station conducting time experiments, but the Fifth Doctor is already there. Fortunately, they don’t meet, but the Daleks arrive and invade, because a colonel from the cybernetic race that controls the station has betrayed his people. The Fifth Doctor does a clever thing, and a couple of the Daleks and the colonel get sucked away down the vortex. That results in them bouncing into other points in the Doctor’s timeline, which affect the development of the race itself. Each segment is separate, and only involves one Doctor, so it’s more anthology than multi-Doctor. The individual pieces are pretty good, except for the Seventh Doctor’s, which takes place on Earth and involves Michael Faraday , for no good reason at all. The various Doctors only meet up at the very end, after the story has ended, because it would be a cheat if they never met up at all. On the whole, it’s a fine “bonus” story, in that it’s a bit of fan-service that doesn’t really affect anything much.
docs.title: The Four Doctors

docs.text: The House on the Edge of Chaos The Further Adventures of Lucie Miller #1.3 Released: 10 July 2019 Listened: 9/21/21 The TARDIS lands on another random planet, hazardous to life, but full of robots building a massive house occupied by humans, Winchester Mystery House style. For the inhabitants, it’s more “ Upstairs, Downstairs ,” as a strict class system is maintained, despite the fact that they’re all working for survival on an alien planet. That order seems to keep everything in line, and is the key to preventing the terrors outside from getting in, or so we’re led to believe. Lucie almost immediately gets carted off as a potential mate to the scion of the house, although the daughter brings a hint of lesbian subtext. The big secret is what the lord of the manor is up to in his private study, which leads to a lot of inevitable running down hallways and sciency things. The twist isn’t bad, and the setting is very evocative, but the larger plot is kind of standard. It’s also on the short side, for this set.
docs.title: The House on the Edge of Chaos

docs.text: The Resurrection of Mars Eighth Doctor Adventures #4.6 Released: 15 November 2010 Listened: 11/6/21 This story follows on immediately from the last one , but the Ice Warrior threat takes kind of a back seat. To be accurate, the threat is still there, but its primary purpose is to provide the Doctor with an ethical dilemma. Lucie Miller returns, having been dropped on Deimos by the Monk, and the Monk is revealed to have been the driving force behind almost everything since “ Situation Vacant .” Which is a lot more planning than other incarnations of the Monk usually do, but he’s still got it all wrong. The Doctor explains that his current morality is a reaction to his previous “ chessmaster ” incarnation, so he won’t countenance the death of even one innocent, if he can prevent it. However, he’ll also tolerate the death of whole planets if needed to keep the Web of Time intact. The Monk doesn’t seem to care about the Web of Time, and he uses that difference to subvert Tamsin, making her think the Doctor is a hypocrite. The story runs the risk of being just a discourse on moral philosophy, but Paul McGann sells it pretty well, and you can tell the Doctor’s experiences brought him to this point. There are some brief scenes where Lucie and Tamsin get together, but given that they’re coming from opposite perspectives, they don’t really get along. Resolving the main conflict is almost pro-forma, and the ending is mostly about how these characters feel about each other. In that sense, it’s pretty enjoyable.
docs.title: The Resurrection of Mars

docs.text: The Revolution Game The Further Adventures of Lucie Miller #1.2 Released: 10 July 2019 Listened: 9/20/21 It’s Lucie’s birthday! Or a day she’s chosen to call her birthday anyway. So she wants to do something special, and ends up with...space roller-derby. For a short episode, there’s a lot of content here and several high concepts. There’s the horribly corrupt company keeping the populace under its thumb, which is standard, as are the low-level employees looking to rebel. The roller derby is a bit of a twist, though. The oppressed natives are also pretty standard, but having them be fans of old Earth movies is different, and generational differences on how to fight back is pretty unusual. There’s plenty of action, with scenes that would make excellent visuals if this were a TV episode. The unique aspects of the writing by Alice Cavender make this the story from this boxed set that stands out most to me.
docs.title: The Revolution Game

docs.text: The Scapegoat Eighth Doctor Adventures #3.5 Released: 2 May 2009 Listened: 10/16/21 You could be forgiven for thinking the title of this one is metaphorical, and it kind of is, but there are also actual goats. Lucie wants to visit the Moulin Rouge in the late 1800s, hoping to meet Ewan McGregor (somehow), but they land in Nazi-occupied Paris instead, which is something of a disappointment. They still get to go to the theater, but a horrible Grand-Guignol style of show where a man is executed live on stage. Which is where the alien goats come into it, but that’s better experienced by listening. Author Pat Mills is most famous for writing some of the best Fourth Doctor comic strips back in the day, and here he’s produced another very visual story, which mostly succeeds. Like the others this season, though, it’s a bit on the compact side, with a plot that sort of fizzles out rather than a climax. Look out for Samantha Bond as the leader of the goats. In addition to playing Moneypenny in several James Bond films, she was also Mrs. Wormwood in The Sarah Jane Adventures . Amusing if only for Lucie enthusiastically slaughtering the French language.
docs.title: The Scapegoat

docs.text: The Skull of Sobek Eighth Doctor Adventures #2.4 Released: 16 April 2008 Listened: 9/25/21 In which we learn that Lucie doesn’t like crocodiles. It’s a somewhat high concept story, centered around a monastery that’s supposed to provide solace and sanctuary, but is currently hiding an ancient secret. That brings in an ancient race of crocodilians, who’ve been fighting a war for thousands of years. Writer Marc Platt jams together a bunch of interesting ideas, as he often does, but the story itself feels somewhat slight. A lot of it hinges on a physical combat between a mind-controlled Lucie and the Doctor, which is hard to pull off properly on audio, and it doesn’t really come across. Again, the Doctor seems to leave with the problem not quite resolved. This is one of the more forgettable stories from this season.
docs.title: The Skull of Sobek

docs.text: The Vengeance of Morbius Eighth Doctor Adventures #2.8 Released: August 2008 Listened: 10/2/21 This is the second half of the two-parter, and where most of the action is...kind of. The Doctor and Lucie are reunited, but still spend a lot of time wandering around trying to figure out what to do, first with the Sisterhood, then on Gallifrey. Unfortunately, the Doctor isn’t very effective this time out, being mostly out of clever ideas, which I think we have to blame on the writer. We don’t really get an idea of what the Gallifreyans we know are up to, which is fine, as the Gallifrey series was on hiatus at this point. So we’ve just got Straxus, who’s pretty much the typical CIA agent. We get almost none of Alexander Siddig this time around, as his character is mostly forgotten, which is a shame. Samuel West has a good presence as Morbius, but he doesn’t have a ton to do except for megalomaniac rants. Lucie, however, demonstrates how far she’s come in the past year. She’s pretty capable, and completely devoted to the Doctor, in contrast to her first season. For his part, the Doctor seems to really appreciate and admire her. All of which comes to a head at the ending, in which (spoiler) the Doctor and Morbius fall off a balcony into a really deep ravine, and are both presumed dead. As cliffhangers go, it’s not bad, and although the extras try gamely to be mysterious, it’s pretty clear there will be another series very soon.
docs.title: The Vengeance of Morbius

docs.text: The Young Lions Short Trips Rarities #2.5 Released: 29 December 2017 Listened: 9/21/21 This Subscriber Short Trip from 2015 was re-released in 2017 as a Rarity. It’s set in an English village in 2005, where the local military barracks is about to be decommissioned, to the dismay of both the soldiers and the town, for political reasons this American doesn’t quite follow. The military post has a secret, though, an alien secret that an alien is willing to go to great lengths to protect. Alice Cavender only has a few Big Finish credits, but one of her hallmarks seems to be slightly odd juxtapositions, like the local group of Buddhists who are involved in local activism, and prove very handy in preventing psychic attacks. Lucie doesn’t have as much to do in this story, which is fine, because Stephen Critchlow, while an excellent narrator, doesn’t attempt Lucie’s northern accent. Although the story is long, it doesn’t really feel like all that much happens.
docs.title: The Young Lions

docs.text: The Zygon Who Fell to Earth Eighth Doctor Adventures #2.6 Released: June 2008 Listened: 9/30/21 This is another story with connections in both the past and the future. Auntie Pat from “ Horror of Glam Rock ” (both by Paul Magrs) appears again, rather later in her life, when she’s taken up running a B&B in the Lake Country, married to a former folk singer. Which is fine until the Zygons turn up. This is the first time that Big Finish used the Zygons, since shapeshifting doesn’t lend itself well to audio, but also the Zygons just aren’t used as often as people think, “Day of the Doctor” notwithstanding. Here, they’re played somewhat for comic relief, as you might expect from Paul Magrs, somewhat like the Sontarans have become on TV. There’s a twist that I never saw coming, and it ends with the Doctor having to lie to Lucie, which will come back to haunt him much later . This is a memorable story, but probably more for what it leads to later.
docs.title: The Zygon Who Fell to Earth

docs.text: To the Death Eighth Doctor Adventures #4.10 Released: 31 March 2011 Listened: 11/10/21 Now we’re at the end. The Doctor isn’t dead from the cliffhanger , of course, but he’s not doing well, and he’s too late to stop most of the catastrophe. Still, Lucie and Susan still believe in him; Alex isn’t as sure. Tamsin finally realizes that the Monk has been feeding her lies for months, and her loyalties start to shift, but again, it’s mostly too late. Although the Daleks are carrying out the same plan as before, the presence of the Dalek Time Controller makes them more dangerous this time around. Because writer Nick Briggs needs to prove they’re deadly, and because this phase of the Doctor’s life is ending, they get to kill off some people we actually care about. Also because this is Briggs, the story connects to “ Patient Zero ” and the Amethyst viruses, although fortunately no Virans turn up. The Monk seems to spend most of his time spluttering about how things are “complicated” and not really his fault, which kind of undercuts this whole season building him up as a major threat, and not a joke. Big Finish will totally abandon that characterization once they replace Graeme Garden with Rufus Hound, but if you want to see what the Monk did next, that’s in “ The Secret History .” The ending is sad, with the Doctor failing to save the day, leading you to wonder why he couldn’t pull off a miracle this time. Nick Briggs is good, but it doesn’t have the same level of emotion that Russell T Davies would bring to a similar story. It leaves the Doctor in an extremely dark place, so much so that he can’t even comfort the survivors, which will lead him into the next phase of his journey . That’s a wrap for Sheridan Smith and Lucie Miller in this project, who was loud, brash, and cared a lot. It was good to know her.
docs.title: To the Death

Also because this is Briggs, the story connects to “ Patient Zero ” and the Amethyst viruses, although fortunately no Virans turn up. The Monk seems to spend most of his time spluttering about how things are “complicated” and not really his fault, which kind of undercuts this whole season building him up as a major threat, and not a joke. Big Finish will totally abandon that characterization once they replace Graeme Garden with Rufus Hound, but if you want to see what the Monk did next, that’s in “ The Secret History .” The ending is sad, with the Doctor failing to save the day, leading you to wonder why he couldn’t pull off a miracle this time. Nick Briggs is good, but it doesn’t have the same level of emotion that Russell T Davies would bring to a similar story. It leaves the Doctor in an extremely dark place, so much so that he can’t even comfort the survivors, which will lead him into the next phase of his journey . That’s a wrap for Sheridan Smith and Lucie Miller in this project, who was loud, brash, and cared a lot. It was good to know her.
docs.title: To the Death

docs.text: Wirrn Dawn Eighth Doctor Adventures #3.4 Released: 18 April 2009 Listened: 10/15/21 Big tones of Starship Troopers in this one, which frankly is a pretty obvious way to go with the Wirrn, but Big Finish had never used them before this. The Doctor and Lucie stumble into the middle of an all-out war between Wirrn and humans, during the post-abandoning-Earth era . For once, they both realize just how dangerous the situation is and plan to leave, so of course they’re promptly separated from the TARDIS. For all that it’s got a big war going on, the story seems very compact, with only a few other characters. And the Doctor doesn’t really do very much. Nick Briggs puts an interesting spin on how to handle the Wirrn if you can’t fight them, but also has the Doctor basically shrugging and going “In nature, creatures do what they need to survive” instead of sticking up for humanity as he usually does. The Extras indicate that’s an effect leftover from his time on Orbis, but he was pretty normal in the previous story. Keep an ear out for Daniel Anthony (Clyde Langer in The Sarah Jane Adventures ) playing a young soldier, and doing a nice job of it. Overall, though, I don’t think one lands quite the way it was intended to.

docs.text: Worldwide Web Eighth Doctor Adventures #3.8 Released: 13 June 2009 Listened: 10/21/21 The cliffhanger of the previous story revealed that the baddies here are the Eight-Legs from “ Planet of the Spiders ,” but they really hate being called spiders. However, there’s dissension within the ranks, much worse than last time, and that eventually leads to their downfall. Sheridan Smith gets to spend about half the episode being evil, and another chunk engaging in mental combat, which reveals that she’s actually fairly tough. Her bond with the Doctor is still fairly strong, even though they spend much of the story apart. It’s also the end of the Headhunter’s and Karen’s arcs, perhaps ending a bit more flat than one might have expected, without any big revelations. On the whole, it’s good-not-great. The plot isn’t all that memorable, but the secondary characters are well drawn.

docs.text: The Eighth Doctor and Mary Shelley This is a somewhat vague period of stories inserted at the beginning of the Eighth Doctor’s life. Several feature Mary Shelley as a companion, produced later in real time, but returning the Eighth Doctor to the Monthly Range after he’d moved out. Some other stories with a younger, solo Eighth Doctor are wedged in here as well. The novels and comics could take place during this time period, or could be ignored altogether, depending on your tastes.

docs.text: Army of Death Main Range #155 Released: 12 December 2011 Listened: 7/17/21 The horror tropes keep on coming, as this time we have the walking dead. Mary doesn’t sympathize with the monster this time, though, as it’s just an animated skeletal army from the get-go. Oddly, the army pretty much becomes a background event, as there’s a bunch of politics between two competing cities on this planet. It comes across as rather strange, as both cities’ leaders are dead, except maybe not, and who killed whom at whose instigation becomes thoroughly muddled. David Harewood plays the leader of one city, and although he’s a good actor, his character comes off as out of his depth and desperate, wanting the Doctor’s help, but never quite able to ask for it. The monster is played by Mitch Benn, and that’s completely over-the-top to the point of absurdity. And I know we’re not supposed to worry much about the science in Doctor Who , but “bone control” is one of the sillier bits of pseudo-science, without much attempt at all to explain it. Mary spends most of the story away from the Doctor, but unlike last time, not doing anything important. She finally calls the Doctor out on enjoying the threat-of-death stuff just a little too much, and asks to go home. Whether she actually gets there right away or not is uncertain. It’s a poor last episode for her, compared to the other two .
docs.title: Army of Death

docs.text: Benny's Story Main Range #123 Released: 28 July 2009 Listened: 7/10/21 We’re starting in a weird place: This is an anthology release with four short stories, featuring characters who mostly associated with the Eighth Doctor in print: Bernice Summerfield, Fitz Kreiner, Izzy...and then Mary Shelley, who’d become a companion later on. These adventures would have been separated by a fairly long period of time, but since we’re assuming all the comics and novels happen in this phase, it’s pretty much chronological, I guess? In “Benny’s Story,” it’s pretty clear that this is the first time she’s seen him since “ The Dying Days ,” and a lot has happened for her since then. As for what she’s up to, it’s a standard (for Benny) dodgy archaeological dig, where she’s not sure who’s signing the checks or what they’re up to. The Doctor turns up, there’s a time bubble and a bit of a paradox, but it’s all pretty standard really. Benny, as always, lays on the snark pretty thickly, and Lisa Bowerman sounds great doing it.
docs.title: Benny's Story

docs.text: Fitz's Story Main Range #123 Released: 28 July 2009 Listened: 7/11/21 This story features Fitz Kreiner , a character from the novels. It has Fitz pretending to be the brains behind the Doctor’s exploits, but it doesn’t go nearly as poorly as any other time a companion has pretended to be the Doctor. That’s because the Doctor is behind the deception, although Fitz is more than happy to play along. Fitz is clearly portrayed as a character who doesn’t mind personal benefit (in the form of female attention), but is also fiercely loyal to the Doctor. Matt di Angelo plays Fitz as hammy and over the top, but that’s somewhat appropriate. Anji is conveniently asleep in the TARDIS for the whole story; Sam is mentioned, but only briefly. Fenella Woolgar has a small role, which is pretty cool. Even though there’s an alien invasion going on, the Doctor doesn’t take it terribly seriously, and seems to be having fun.

docs.text: Five Hundred Ways to Leave Your Lover Classic Doctors, New Monsters #5.4 Released: 21 January 2025 Listened: 4/15/26 This story pits the Eighth Doctor against the Monks from "The Pyramid at the End of the World." If you've forgotten their deal (and I had), they like to use virtual environments, and can only invade planets with the consent of specific individuals. But none of that is clear at first, because we're dropped in on the Doctor visiting various tourist spots with some guy named Chris, who believes he's romantically involved with the Doctor. Except that Chris wants to break up with the Doctor; possibly because their lives seem to be in danger wherever they go. And since they never stop long enough to breathe, Chris never actually manages to get the words out. It's more or less a romantic comedy, or the Doctor Who version of one. The Doctor seems to be trying his absolute best to keep Chris both calm and distracted, and it's really kind of sweet. But Chris can tell something is wrong and gets steadily more upset as the story goes. In worldbuilding terms, this may be an early part of the Monks' story, showing how they got their modus operandi. Lord knows the TV episodes didn't give us any motivation for them. And there's a decent reason why the Doctor won't remember them in a few regenerations; one you can see coming, but is fairly well handled nonetheless.
docs.title: Five Hundred Ways to Leave Your Lover

docs.text: Izzy's Story Main Range #123 Released: 28 July 2009 Listened: 7/11/21 This one is even more over cartoonish than the last, but that’s fitting for a character from the comics. Even more fittingly, the plot revolves around Izzy trying to use time travel to get a copy of a rare comic, because she’d never seen the end of a story. When the aliens and other time travelers turn up, things get really strange. The story is written by Alan Barnes, who created Izzy in the comics, so she’s written accurately (as far as I can tell). Jemima Rooper is fantastic as Izzy, with breathless enthusiasm and total sincerity about nerdy stuff; it’s a shame this is her only appearance. The comic itself is a thinly veiled parody of Judge Dredd , so that’s nice for folks who get the reference. There’s also a swipe at gender issues in comics and fandom in general, which is even sharper now given some fans’ objection to Jodie Whitaker. Again, the Doctor mostly seems to be enjoying himself, and certainly enjoys Izzy’s company, deadly danger or not. It’s good to see him having fun, given the amount of pain waiting for him later in life.
docs.title: Izzy's Story

docs.text: Mary's Story Main Range #123 Released: 28 July 2009 Listened: 7/11/21 Although the last couple of stories were fun and games, this one isn’t so much, except for the paradoxes. It’s the infamous trip to Villa Diodati with Percy and Mary Shelley , Lord Byron , Claire Clairmont and John Polidori . A horribly burned and scarred Eighth Doctor drops into their laps, mentioning companions that clue us in that he’s late in this incarnation’s life (Charlie and Lucie, but also the unknown Todd and Rita, but not Liv or Helen, because they hadn’t been introduced yet). Shelley and Byron really take it on the chin here, as neither of them are particularly nice people (although the Doctor admires Byron’s outfit, in an inside joke), but Shelley is particularly mad, wanting to conduct medical experiments that will inspire Frankenstein . Another, much younger Eighth Doctor turns up to set everything to rights, more or less. The older Doctor is rude and ungrateful, but he’s probably envious of his younger self’s carefree existence. All of which leads to Mary going off with the Doctor for a while, which leads into the next set of stories. That would all make perfect sense if it didn’t conflict with the Thirteenth Doctor’s “ The Haunting of Villa Diodati ,” and I really can’t see any way of reconciling the two stories, which is a shame, so the only valid response is to just ignore the conflict. It’s a decent story, but it’s really just an intro. On the whole, the four stories in this set don’t really hang together, as their styles are quite different, and it’s probably best to consider them that way.
docs.title: Mary's Story

docs.text: Shada Bonus Release #2 Released: 21 November 2003 Hang on, kids; this is where it gets complicated. “ Shada ” was a Fourth Doctor story from 1979 that was started but never completed as a result of one of the BBC’s infamous strikes. However, because it was partially complete, and written by Douglas Adams, there’s always been a great deal of interest in it. Short clips from the partial episode formed the Fourth Doctor and Romana’s appearance in “ The Five Doctors ” in 1983. In this case, though, for the 40th anniversary in 2003, the BBC and Big Finish created a webcast version featuring the Eighth Doctor, along with Romana and K-9. The conceit was that the Fourth Doctor’s version of the story had been aborted because of the meddling from “The Five Doctors,” and now the Eighth has sought out Romana and K-9 later in his life to finish it. However, in 2017, the Fourth Doctor version of “Shada” was restored and released, with the unfinished bits filled by animation, possibly returning it to the canon timeline. That leaves the 2003 version in limbo. Big Finish released an extended version on audio, but it’s only available on CD, so I don’t have it. The webcast version still exists, but ironically it’s only available as a Flash animation, and in 2021, Flash no longer exists, possibly rendering this a lost story. Bottom line: I don’t have it.
docs.title: Shada

docs.text: The Silver Turk Main Range #153 Released: 15 October 2011 Listened: 7/13/21 The Doctor thinks he’ll take Mary for an easy first trip, and hops over to Vienna without changing the time coordinates, ostensibly to pick up Samson and Gemma . However, that doesn’t go to plan, and they end up in the 1870s, where the local fair has another “ mechanical Turk ” exhibit going. Except of course this Turk is actually a badly damaged Cyberman, which you can see coming. What you can probably also see coming is that a damaged, suffering mechanical man is going to elicit the sympathies of the author of Frankenstein . The Doctor really doesn’t see that coming, because he has a really bad reaction to the presence of Cybermen; maybe not quite as bad as his Dalek reaction, but he’s clearly upset. There are, of course, a variety of humans looking to use the Cybermen for their own ends, and you know how that’s going to go. These particular Cybermen seem a bit different than usual: they’ve got personal names, and apparently the power to hypnotize, which I didn’t remember as being part of their abilities. Things get a little murky around who, exactly, the main antagonist is, but that’s necessary if you’re going to make the Cybermen sympathetic. Although the difference of opinion on the Cybermen could strain the relationship between Mary and the Doctor, they seem to get over it fairly quickly. A Cybermen story is pretty much a requirement if you’re going to have Mary Shelly as a protagonist, and they pull it off well.
docs.title: The Silver Turk

docs.text: Doctor Who: The Movie TV Special Released: 14 May 1996 This is the Eighth Doctor’s only TV adventure, from 1996. It has his regeneration early in the story, so he spends a lot of it amnesiac or acting confused. It also features the Master adopting his Eric Roberts body, which Big Finish has made some use of. Daphne Ashbrook appears as Dr. Grace Holloway, and Yee Jee Tso as Chang Lee, who take the temporary companion roles, but neither leave with the Doctor. Although both actors have appeared in Big Finish, they play other characters, as Grace and Chang are off limits.

docs.text: The Witch from the Well Main Range #154 Released: 8 November 2011 Listened: 7/15/21 From one classic horror trope to another, this one has the titular witch wreaking havoc in the 21st century, causing the Doctor and Mary to jump back to the 17th to see how it all got started. They’re accompanied by two oddly-named teenage twins, Finicia and Lucern, who are related to the nobility in the area. Much like in “The Witchfinders,” the Doctor really doesn’t get along with people who want to hunt and persecute witches. However, in this case there’s a bunch of backstory around a race of aliens who use energies that would be considered paranormal, and generally inaccessible to the rest of the universe. That provides a metaphor for persecution on a couple of levels, as well as what it does to the psychology of the persecuted, which is interesting, but not fully explored. As often happens in Doctor Who stories, who the monster is, and who the villains are, is confused and muddled and swaps around during the story, all of which is complicated by the fact that the story jumps between the 1650s and the present. Mary spends much of the story separated from the Doctor, but having to take charge of the two teens puts her in the driver’s seat for her part of the plot, and then she has to motivate the current lord of the manor, who’s not exactly decisive. She has the usual issues companions from the past face with present-day technology, but her sci-fi writer’s mind grasps the concepts well enough, and she’s even used to the TARDIS capabilities in quite a short time. The story seems to have a tragic ending, but there’s a cop-out after the fact that cheapens the drama, in my opinion. Overall, it’s a good showcase for Mary, adjusting on her own, and a story with more timey-wimey than usual, so the twist works fairly well.
docs.title: The Witch from the Well

Mary spends much of the story separated from the Doctor, but having to take charge of the two teens puts her in the driver’s seat for her part of the plot, and then she has to motivate the current lord of the manor, who’s not exactly decisive. She has the usual issues companions from the past face with present-day technology, but her sci-fi writer’s mind grasps the concepts well enough, and she’s even used to the TARDIS capabilities in quite a short time. The story seems to have a tragic ending, but there’s a cop-out after the fact that cheapens the drama, in my opinion. Overall, it’s a good showcase for Mary, adjusting on her own, and a story with more timey-wimey than usual, so the twist works fairly well.

docs.text: Tuesday Subscriber Short Trips #2018-4 Released: 1 December 2018 Listened: 7/18/21 This is one of the Christmas-themed Subscriber Short Trips, or rather lack-of-Christmas, because the Doctor comes to London to discover that December 25 is just a regular day. Fortunately, he bumps into his old friend Harry Sullivan...who doesn’t remember him. Which is a good start for what could be a longer story, but this is just a short trip, so it resolves fairly quickly, and with very little harm done. We do find out that Harry has some concern about how his medical research is being used, which we’ve seen in other stories, but the Doctor tells him it’ll be OK. Stephen Critchlow reads this one, and as usual doesn’t attempt to mimic any voices, although he does have the Eighth Doctor’s cadence pretty well down. It’s a nice addition to the collection of Christmas stories, although not a standout.

docs.text: The Eighth Doctor and Molly (and Liv) With this phase, the Era of the Boxed Sets began. The Eighth Doctor Adventures had ended in early 2011, followed by the Mary Shelley stories from the beginning of this Doctor’s tenure in late 2011, and then this blockbuster set not until late 2012, making a break in the publishing schedule, and a good jumping on point for new listeners (including myself). The experiment worked so well that Big Finish published all the subsequent Eighth Doctor stories in boxed sets, and then expanded the format to other Doctors and series as well, to the point where the Main Range ended in 2021 , replaced by boxed sets. The new companion is Molly O’Sullivan, played by Ruth Bradley, except that Big Finish didn’t really plan Molly’s arc, or Bradley’s involvement, beyond the first box, which...complicates things.
