docs.text: A Life in the Day Dark Eyes #4.1 Released: 2 March 2015 Listened: 11/23/21 With this fourth box, a new pattern emerged in the writing, which becomes the standard going forward for Eighth Doctor Adventures: Matt Fitton and John Dorney splitting the episodes two-and-two. As they’re two of my favorite Big Finish writers, I’m very happy about this. Dorney has the first episode of this set, and it’s as timey-wimey as we’d expect from him. As of now, Liv is the official sole companion, but I’m not about to change my organizational structure for this project because of that. The Doctor is still concerned about Molly, so he goes to London in 1920, where he hopes to find her in this new timeline. Unfortunately, she’s not there, although Kitty Donaldson (still played by Beth Chalmers) and her brother Martin are. As is a temporal anomaly, which of course requires investigating. The Doctor wants Liv to relax, and tries to get her to take some time off, eventually pairing her up with Martin for a day out. What happens then is too good to spoil, but it evolves gradually, giving just enough hints that the listener might figure it out before the Doctor does. There’s also real emotion attached to it, not just clever plotting, which is what makes it beautiful. The dialog in this one is sharp, with just about everybody getting some clever lines. The boxed set formula is coming together here, with this story being complete, and yet still with a link that drives the action to the next part. The only complaint I have about this story is that it’s on the short side, as are all the stories in this box.
docs.title: A Life in the Day

docs.text: Eye of Darkness Dark Eyes #4.4 Released: 2 March 2015 Listened: 11/26/21 This one had to end with a bang, as it was the conclusion of the whole Dark Eyes series, as well as this boxed set. Which meant bringing back Molly O’Sullivan in the previous story , but not played by Ruth Bradley. Having gotten rid of most of the other players, this one is just the Doctor and friends versus the Daleks, with the prototype Eminence as the prize, all fought on the Eye of Orion, for no real good reason. There’s a lot of stuff blowing up, Dalek blasting, betrayals, and a Dalek rebellion for good measure. However, it does suffer from trying to make the last episode big and meaningful, which often gets confused with “noisy.” And trying to tie the origin of the Eminence into the whole thing stretches credibility just a bit. And of course there’s a noble sacrifice, because there has to be. There’s a bit of philosophy going on that asks the question of how many lives can be sacrificed to save billions more. We know where the Doctor stands on that, especially this Doctor, but not everybody agrees. Which would be interesting to explore, but there’s too much stuff blowing up. At least the Doctor isn’t left in such a dark place this time around, and he has a friend for company. So that’s it for Molly O’Sullivan, who really wasn’t around all that long, and hasn’t appeared again since. She had presence, for sure, but was too often played as a plot device. The Dark Eyes epic as a whole wasn’t bad, but suffered a bit from shifting focus and writers.
docs.title: Eye of Darkness

docs.text: Eyes of the Master Dark Eyes #2.4 Released: 12 February 2014 Listened: 11/18/21 We’ve got a villain gambit pileup in this story, or at least the beginnings of one. The Time Lords think it would be a good idea to use the Daleks against the Eminence, and have tasked the Master with making that happen. What could possibly go wrong? This, incidentally, seems to be where the Master got his new regeneration cycle, and was being prepped for a role in the Time War. Of course the Master is betraying the Time Lords, and wants to control the Eminence for his own purposes, which means getting hold of Molly and her dark eyes. So naturally he’s set himself up as an optician in 1970s London, and is removing people’s eyes and replacing them with artificial substitutes. Because that’s what constitutes a “normal plan” to the Master, or at least this one. Alex MacQueen is a fantastic Master for audio, with an amazing range to his voice, flipping easily from jovial to sinister. He’s also closer to the crazier end of the Master’s spectrum than the suave Delgado end. He seems genuinely pleased to see the Eighth Doctor, at least at first. The interactions between almost all the characters in this story are excellent; this is an area where Matt Fitton shines. Whether it’s the banter between the Doctor and the Master, Molly and Liv trying to navigate 1970s London, or Molly with her elderly friend David Walker, it’s all believable and natural. Molly plays the experienced time traveler here with Liv as the novice, and it’s fun to see Liv be uncertain, as she so rarely is. Her interactions with David demonstrate her kindness, which is often hard to see in life-or-death situations. We’re left with an ending that wraps around to the beginning of the boxed set , with the Doctor helping the Daleks on Nixyce, but we’re left with a cliffhanger as to the outcome. The individual stories with a single plot thread is a better format than the first box, and the writing is stronger on the whole, but they also threw the kitchen sink into this one and didn’t really resolve it.
docs.title: Eyes of the Master

docs.text: Fugitives Dark Eyes #1.2 Released: 10 November 2012 Listened: 11/14/21 If the first episode was setup, this episode is “runaround.” Although Nick Briggs wants this to be a big epic, he’s structuring it like one long story. The Doctor and Molly spend the whole episode running from the Daleks, who always seem to turn up wherever they go. They bounce to 1940 Dunkirk, 1972 London, and the planet Halalka, which has nice tourist beaches, all of which gives Molly a good opportunity for culture shock, but she seems to adapt rather quickly. More oddly, she claims to recognize this TARDIS interior, and can’t seem to keep her hands off the controls, although she can’t remember just why they’re familiar. The Doctor tries to warm to this new companion, but he’s still carrying around a lot of grief, and he hates mysteries where the Time Lords know more than he does. As a result, he sometimes speaks quite harshly to Molly, but she gives as good as she gets. In subplot land, Straxus turns up on a mountain range and tries to kill himself, but fails repeatedly. Toby Jones gets a name (Kotris) and is revealed to be working with the Daleks. Final note: Although supposedly this episode is where the Doctor gets a haircut and his new costume, I’ll be darned if I can find where it happens, no matter how many times I listen to it.
docs.title: Fugitives

docs.text: Master of the Daleks Dark Eyes #4.3 Released: 2 March 2015 Listened: 11/25/21 And we’re back to John Dorney, as the action and chaos heat up. The Doctor spends most of this one dazed and confused from the explosions at the end of the previous story , so Liv carries much of the plot. Which works out fine, because she’s quite willing to snark at both the Master and the Daleks. The Master and the Dalek Time Controller have worked together to create a divergent timeline where the Daleks conquered Earth in the mid-20th Century, then used it as a base to take over the rest of the universe. Which is fine as far as it goes, but this is the Master and the Daleks, so of course neither one trusts the other, with good reason. And there’s Sontarans in the mix too, because why not? Actually, they don’t really do a whole lot, but they’re all played by Dan Starkey, which is always a pleasure. And Molly O’Sullivan returns as well, a much older version, played by Sorcha Cusack because Ruth Bradley was unavailable. She does a decent job of imitating Molly’s accent, and she hasn’t lost any of her sass in the intervening decades, so she and Liv together are quite a team, although they spend most of their time captured. This is the last we’re going to see of the Alex MacQueen Master for quite some time, and this is his chronologically latest appearance (which is a shame, because I like him a lot). So it’s a good thing that he gets to ham it up completely in this one, with some of his dialog veering pretty close to Missy’s style (who had been created by the time this was recorded). This makes a nice part 3 to head into the finale.
docs.title: Master of the Daleks

docs.text: Masterplan Dark Eyes #3.3 Released: 17 November 2014 Listened: 11/21/21 Having hit his breaking point in the last story , the Doctor decides he’s OK with breaking the Laws of Time and preventing the Eminence from being created, so he heads back to its origins. However, the Master has done his homework this time, and although his plan is absurdly complicated, he does seem to have thought it all through. If he can influence the creation of the Eminence, he can take control of the Infinite Warriors later on, after they’ve converted most of humanity. Except the Doctor, playing it by ear as usual, has screwed things up enough that he and the Master are forced to work together. And neither of them banked on the scientist who created the Eminence being totally binky-bonkers. This episode is mostly about putting pairs of characters in one room and seeing what happens, both the Doctor and the Master, and Liv and Sally Armstrong, which doesn’t go well at all for Sally. Molly isn’t in this story either, at least, not as a speaking part, but her presence is felt. It’s a good quiet episode before the big explosions.
docs.title: Masterplan

docs.text: Rule of the Eminence Dark Eyes #3.4 Released: 17 November 2014 Listened: 11/21/21 And this is where things go bang, at least as far as this boxed set is concerned, and the Eminence. The Doctor’s meddling in the last story doesn’t seem to have changed much, and now both Molly and Liv are in the hands of the Master. The action comes back to Earth, where the Master is going to orchestrate the Eminence’s takeover of humanity, so he can subvert it later. In the end, though, the Eminence realizes that it’s been a somewhat gullible ball of gas, and doesn’t really know who to believe anymore. The actual solution has a bit of deus ex machina to it, as the Doctor doesn’t really do much clever, aside from putting himself at the center of things and talking a lot. There’s also a bit of clunky descriptive dialog, but it’s hard to properly convey the actions of an evil gas on audio. But there’s a good pace, appropriate levels of action, and a heartfelt conclusion, which Matt Fitton is quite good at. Also check out Beth Chalmers, doing a convincing American accent and reprising her role from “ The Seeds of War ,” and Georgia Moffett in a small role. And this is a wrap for Ruth Bradley in this series, although not for Molly herself. It’s a bittersweet exit, and too short a time as a companion, but she made an impression.
docs.title: Rule of the Eminence

docs.text: Tangled Web Dark Eyes #1.3 Released: 10 November 2012 Listened: 11/14/21 Things start to come together a bit more here, as you’d expect from the title. But if we’ve had the setup and the runaround, this episode is the misdirection, a plot thread that distracts the heroes and the audience while the bad guys get on with their plot. It’s the typical problem with converting a three-act arc into a four-part Doctor Who story, and it’s a bit ironic that Big Finish changed the format, but still wound up with the same problem. The misdirect in this case is a timeline where the Daleks reformed, and became a force for good in the universe. While it’s amusing to hear the Daleks playing with children, the thematic purpose is to explore the psychological damage that the Doctor’s long-running war with the Daleks has done to him. Molly is uniquely qualified to help with this, as she’s seen war weariness, and she’s also a brand-new companion, so hasn’t yet internalized the idea that the Daleks are pure evil. There’s some Time War foreshadowing here, but at this point Big Finish was still being coy with new-series references, as they didn’t have the license yet. We also find out that Molly got lost as a child, and was found by Kotris, which started her on her special destiny. Kotris and the Daleks have a “relativity map,” which is a rather benign name for a device that allows them to see all of time and apparently avoid paradox somehow. The image of the peaceful Daleks is one of the strongest from this set, but that doesn’t change the fact that this story is mostly filler.
docs.title: Tangled Web

docs.text: The Death of Hope Dark Eyes #3.1 Released: 17 November 2014 Listened: 11/20/21 In the previous set, we had reduced Nick Briggs, and now we have none at all, as this set is entirely the Matt Fitton (writing) / Ken Bentley (directing) show. They also deliberately slow the action down and simplify a bit, so as to appeal to new listeners, something I don’t think they’ll do with the later boxes. This set is primarily the Doctor vs the Master, which is quite fine by me. This story provides the setup, which means it’s kind of perfunctory, and the Doctor does very little. Having kidnapped and brainwashed Molly , the Master and Sally Armstrong take her to a planet that’s been pretty much destroyed by the Eminence, to test out how exposure to the retrogenitor particles affects the population. However, the Master is incapable of doing anything covertly, so he has to show up like a hero who’s going to liberate the town from the Eminence. He even has a cowboy hat. The Master is usually fabulous when he’s pretending to help people, and this Master is no exception. It’s sad hearing Molly be dazed and confused throughout this story, thinking she’s doing the right thing. Meanwhile, the Doctor has been hijacked by Narvin, who wants him to intervene directly to stop the Master. Whether it was really necessary to show him this much backstory is debatable. This is the first time that Sean Carlson has appeared in a story with the Doctor, but he’ll be retconned into earlier meetings with the Doctor in other stories, establishing him as a chief CIA honcho. As a result, the acting and characterization in this story is excellent, but the plot is a little bit thin.
docs.title: The Death of Hope

This set is primarily the Doctor vs the Master, which is quite fine by me. This story provides the setup, which means it’s kind of perfunctory, and the Doctor does very little. Having kidnapped and brainwashed Molly , the Master and Sally Armstrong take her to a planet that’s been pretty much destroyed by the Eminence, to test out how exposure to the retrogenitor particles affects the population. However, the Master is incapable of doing anything covertly, so he has to show up like a hero who’s going to liberate the town from the Eminence. He even has a cowboy hat. The Master is usually fabulous when he’s pretending to help people, and this Master is no exception. It’s sad hearing Molly be dazed and confused throughout this story, thinking she’s doing the right thing. Meanwhile, the Doctor has been hijacked by Narvin, who wants him to intervene directly to stop the Master. Whether it was really necessary to show him this much backstory is debatable. This is the first time that Sean Carlson has appeared in a story with the Doctor, but he’ll be retconned into earlier meetings with the Doctor in other stories, establishing him as a chief CIA honcho. As a result, the acting and characterization in this story is excellent, but the plot is a little bit thin.
docs.title: The Death of Hope

docs.text: The Great War Dark Eyes #1.1 Released: 10 November 2012 Listened: 11/13/21 Welcome aboard, Molly O’Sullivan -- except not quite yet. The first story in this box is very much setup, without much of a story of its own, something that future boxed sets try to avoid. But this box is the Nick Briggs show, both writing and directing, and feels more of a single piece. We have the Doctor, despondent and a bit unhinged from Lucie’s death , heading to the end of the universe in search of hope, only to be intercepted by the Time Lords and sent to find...well, we don’t know what yet. We have Straxus the CIA agent, sent by somebody to do something. And Toby Jones, whose character doesn’t even have a name yet, monitoring something for somebody. Lots of setup. The Doctor ends up in World War I, which is where Molly comes in, a Voluntary Aid Detachment worker -- kind of like a nurse. Historically, these were noblewomen volunteering to “do their part,” but they sometimes brought their servants. Molly came along with Kitty Donaldson, to whom she was extremely dedicated (and hints of something more, but of course not confirmed), but has found herself on her own. Ruth Bradley plays Molly with a thick Irish accent, sounding borderline cliche with her wording and strong attitude, but that may have been appropriate for a lower-class woman in 1915. Molly is pretty determined not to like the Doctor, and certainly looks sideways at any of his explanations. She addresses him as “the Doctor,” including the article every time, and you can hear the sarcasm slathered on it. But she’s definitely tough and capable, and she’s going to have to be. Because this is a Nick Briggs story, and it’s a big epic, so you know who’ll be turning up as the bad guys. It’s hard to evaluate this story on its own, when it’s a large pile of loose ends.
docs.title: The Great War

docs.text: The Monster of Montmartre Dark Eyes #4.2 Released: 2 March 2015 Listened: 11/24/21 We flip over to Matt Fitton for this story, in which the TARDIS has been stolen, but politely stayed on the same planet in the same time period, so the Doctor and Liv are able to track it to Paris. Which means we get to have fun with eccentric artists, criminals, and dancers against a decadent Parisian background. Except the Moulin Rouge has become a Red Pagoda for some reason. It’s tricky to see where this one is going, as the Doctor and Liv each pursue their own clues. Liv holds up her end quite well, seeming more confident in her past than she has before. The Doctor, in contrast, seems rather judgmental of the ethically shady characters he encounters, but then, someone has stolen his TARDIS. How it unravels is a good surprise that I won’t spoil. Although several necessary plot elements come together here, there’s a slight sense of killing time in this one. The climax is approaching, but this story lacks the urgency you’d expect, until the very end.
docs.title: The Monster of Montmartre

docs.text: The Reviled Dark Eyes #3.2 Released: 17 November 2014 Listened: 11/21/21 Because of Ruth Bradley’s limited availability, Molly is less of a presence in this box, and she’s not in this episode at all. This is one of the weaknesses of the boxed set format: with a story this long, sometimes there are episodes that feel tangential or unrelated. Which should be no problem, because the Doctor does tangential stuff all the time, but when the larger arc is a universe-ending threat, side tracks can feel like filler. In this case, the Time Lords drop the Doctor off on Ramossa, where a human colony is having trouble with the natives, a race of sentient scorpions, and they’ve dropped Liv there too, to make sure he stays. The idea is that the Ramossans have rounded up the humans in camps, because the presence of humans makes them a target for the Eminence. Sally Armstrong is there to scoop up the humans for the Master, and the Doctor wants to hide them instead. Problem is, the Ramossans want the humans either gone or dead, and they’re not picky about which, resulting in the sort of moral dilemma the Doctor specializes in. Which should be fine, but he’s fighting against three separate agendas with the Master, the Eminence, and possibly the Time Lords all wanting different things. When things start to go sideways, the Doctor is driven a bit over the edge. Some good guest stars in this one: Sarah Mowat, who starred as Susan Mendez in the Dalek Empire series, plays one of the Ramossans, and future Master Sacha Dhawan plays another. This is the first set of Eighth Doctor stories recorded after the 50th anniversary redefined the Time War and the Eighth Doctor’s role in it, which gives a destination for the character’s arc, which Big Finish can now move towards. However, there’s a long way from here to “ Night of the Doctor ,” and they don’t want to go back to “despairing and desperate” too often. As a hint here and there, it works.
docs.title: The Reviled

docs.text: The Traitor Dark Eyes #2.1 Released: 12 February 2014 Listened: 11/16/21 Dark Eyes 2 is a whole different animal than its predecessor. It was released a year and a half later, and in the interim, the 50th anniversary happened, Big Finish started gaining the rights to new-series characters, and we finally saw the Time War . This expanded the canvas that Big Finish could work on, both in terms of re-using old characters and telling new stories. In addition, Nick Briggs isn’t the sole writer on this one, adding Alan Barnes and relative newcomer Matt Fitton, who would go on to write a ton of Eighth Doctor and new-series stories. This boxed set was intended to be part of a group of four, and each story is self-contained, unlike Dark Eyes 1. The situation was complicated by Ruth Bradley’s shrinking availability, requiring a reduced role. However, Nicola Walker was able to step in and reprise her role of Liv Chenka from “ Robophobia .” In addition, the stories are told out of order, depending on whose viewpoint you’re following. So this story reintroduces Liv, working as a medic on the Dalek-occupied planet of Nixyce VII. The Daleks are following the playbook from Dalek Empire (likely suggested by the Dalek Time Controller) and allowing Liv to carry out her work as a way of creating hope in the populace, thus making them easier to control. When the Doctor turns up, he’s alone, and although he recognizes Liv right away, she hasn’t seen him since “Robophobia,” and doesn’t recognize the Eighth Doctor. Although the Doctor goes about his usual business of defeating Daleks, he seems kind of cavalier about it, almost casual. At least until the big plan is revealed, at which point he becomes extremely cagey about what’s going on. Liv is a much more forceful character here than she was in “Robophobia,” giving orders, talking back to Daleks; she’s definitely seen some stuff. And it all leads up to a massive cliffhanger.
docs.title: The Traitor

docs.text: The White Room Dark Eyes #2.2 Released: 12 February 2014 Listened: 11/16/21 You could be forgiven for thinking of Cream’s song “ White Room ” (which also mentions “dark eyes” in the lyrics), but it seems to be a coincidence. This story doesn’t continue directly from the last , and might be in a different time period altogether. It begins nicely in media res , with the Doctor showing up at his house in Baker Street just before Armistice Day, 1918, to find Molly O’Sullivan living there (she saw it in the 1970s as the Ides Institute , but that was erased), harboring Irish deserters from the war. Of course, things start going sideways as soon as the Doctor turns up, and Molly’s retrogenitor particles get reactivated (a cheap retcon, but the series is called Dark Eyes after all). And then the Viyrans turn up, and not just any Viyrans, but temporally insane Viyrans. A bit odd, since they’re usually one of Nick Briggs’ favorite toys. Molly has always been commanding, but now she’s much more so, without the stress of being on a battlefront, as well as being more in her element. The conflict itself resolves somewhat quickly, but puts Molly back on the board, which is good.
docs.title: The White Room

docs.text: The World Beyond the Trees Short Trips #7.1 Released: 31 January 2017 Listened: 11/19/21 This isolated Short Trip takes place concurrently with “ Damascus ,” also by Jonathan Barnes. That’s possible because Liv is currently in 1972, living in Baker Street with Molly . Liv receives a strange message from the Doctor in a dream, and wakes the next morning to find all the humans asleep, or at least dazed and inattentive. Of course an alien did this, for pretty good reasons, and Liv helps her get to Project Damascus. The whole story has a strange, dream-like quality to it, which even Liv remarks on, but it leaves a lot of plot elements unexplained. If you listen to both this and “Damascus,” you’ll supposedly get the whole story, except it doesn’t really feel that way. The story is told in first-person by Liv, in the form of a letter to her father, so it’s fitting that Nicola Walker narrates. It fits nicely as a connection to “ Absent Friends ,” but that’s still a ways off yet.
docs.title: The World Beyond the Trees

docs.text: Time's Horizon Dark Eyes #2.3 Released: 12 February 2014 Listened: 11/17/21 Pieces start coming together in this story. There’s a gap between this story and the last for Molly and the Doctor, but not a big gap, and she’s starting to think it’s time to go home. There’s also a much longer gap for Liv, as they all meet up on a spaceship at the edge of the universe, although that’s a fuzzy definition. Unfortunately, the Eminence is also hanging out here as a big orange cloud. The Eminence is one of those Big Finish baddies they come up with once, and then re-use in multiple stories in unrelated ranges released around the same time. There’s quite a bit of jumbled timelines going on here. For the Eminence, this is apparently the first time it meets the Doctor, although it’s come back from the end of time, so who knows what’s going on there. For Liv, this is after “The Traitor,” and as a result, she has a very poor opinion of the Doctor. And herself, because she joined an exploratory sleeper ship with three other people to get as far away as possible from anyone who knows what she did on Nixyce. But for the Doctor, that hasn’t happened yet. And there’s a time traveler who popped back a few hundred years to set all this up, but it went terribly wrong for him. The other three crew members are well-drawn secondary characters, as Matt Fitton often writes, each quite driven toward their own goals. Molly shows signs of being a seasoned companion, which she hasn’t done before. She’s clearly of her own time, but has enough experience to handle the strangeness of being in a sci-fi environment. She and Liv bond over their medical training, and Molly displays the empathy that makes her a good nurse. She gains Liv’s trust almost immediately, which is no easy trick. The plot, again, resolves quite quickly, especially defeating something as powerful as the Eminence, but that thread isn’t completely over. The interaction with Molly and Liv makes this a good one.
docs.title: Time's Horizon

docs.text: X and the Daleks Dark Eyes #1.4 Released: 10 November 2012 Listened: 11/15/21 This story is the explosive conclusion to the Dark Eyes story, with lots of timey-wimey, twists revealed, and exposition. So, so much exposition. It looks like Nick Briggs wanted to create a Moffat-style puzzle box, and it certainly is puzzling, but the explanation isn’t simple, and requires a lot of spelling out. Unfortunately, a lot of the explicating is left to Straxus, explaining to Nadeyan (played by Ian Cullen from “ The Aztecs ”), as the latter splutters and exclaims that he doesn’t understand. That’s OK, Nadeyan, we don’t really understand either. As best I can tell, it looks like the Doctor didn’t really do anything to defeat the Daleks’ big plan; that was somebody else. All the Doctor did was be in the right place at the right time (inadvertently). And it’s never really made clear why Molly, specifically. Most of the Daleks don’t seem to know what’s going on either. The Dalek Time Controller does, but he’s turning into a favorite character of Nick’s, popping up all over the place. As a climax, it’s big and loud, but it’s not a particularly good story. The boxed set as a whole, taken as a single story, isn’t bad, and Molly is definitely a contrast to Lucie and Charley, but it doesn’t have either the clever storytelling or the emotional heft of later Eighth Doctor stories.
docs.title: X and the Daleks

docs.text: The Eighth Doctor Solo As with all Big Finish Doctors, there needs to be a part of their tenure where the writers can stick stories that feature the Doctor alone, without companions. The real-world reason is usually budgetary, or actor availability, or a general feeling that having an additional character around would complicate the story. In this case, we can assume a gap after the Liv & Helen era, the only such gap currently in the Eighth Doctor’s era. Fitting into that spot are two main plotlines: The “Time Lord Victorious” multimedia story from James Goss, which covered the Eighth, Ninth, and Tenth Doctors; and the “Pre-Time War” stories, which cover the period when the Doctor was actively trying to stay out of the war, but before he was dragged in, during the next section. That means he’s mostly appearing in stories as a supporting character, rather than as the protagonist. Plus a couple of other bits and bobs that require the Doctor to be solo.
docs.title: Eighth Doctor Solo

docs.text: A Heart on Both Sides Short Trips #7.9 Released: 27 September 2017 Listened: 1/13/22 The Time War seems to be in full swing now, with various other races getting involved. Former companion Nyssa is running a hospital ship, providing aid to victims of the war, no matter who they may be. It’s not clear where in Nyssa’s timeline this is, whether before her time with her family or after, or maybe the war messed everything up. The story is narrated by Sarah Sutton, and carries the Fifth Doctor’s theme music. In fact, it’s not clear to Nyssa whether the Doctor was ever there at all. Writer Rob Nisbet tosses in an awful lot of continuity references here, especially about the Fifth Doctor’s celery, but also various other new-series nods, to the point where I think it was overdone. The Time Lords here are shown in their vicious, “win at all costs” mode that the Doctor particularly objects to. It seems a bit early in the war for that kind of behavior, but it’s hard to tell just when this is.
docs.title: A Heart on Both Sides

docs.text: All Flesh Is Grass Time Lord Victorious Novel #2 Released: 10 December 2020 This part of the crossover rightly belongs to the Tenth Doctor , so I’ll leave details for later. Short version: The Eighth and Ninth Doctors confront the Tenth, who has gone all “I am the master of time!” again, believing himself to have defeated death for all time. Eventually, they convince him he’s wrong, and the Eighth Doctor bops off with the Daleks again, in a badly damaged time-ship.

docs.text: All Hands on Deck Short Trips #7.10 Released: 3 October 2017 Listened: 1/15/22 This 2017 Short Trip serves as a prequel to the "Susan's War" boxed set, although Eddie Robson didn’t intend it that way. It’s narrated in the style of a Companion Chronicle, read by Carole Ann Ford, which feels very natural. Susan is still living on Earth, after the events of the Eighth Doctor Adventures , so she’s on her own, without David or Alex, and feeling somewhat melancholy. She lives in a flat built from the remains of Coal Hill School, with a tree dedicated to Ian and Barbara growing in the quad. She’s still serving as a scientific advisor to the world government, so she’s called in when strange, alien-ish stuff happens, which suddenly occurs quite frequently…because the Doctor is trying to distract Susan and keep Gallifrey from contacting her to drag her into the war. I’m not sure what I think of Susan’s choice, really, but I do agree with her reasoning that there’s nothing left for her on Earth.

docs.text: Short Trips #7.10 Released: 3 October 2017 Listened: 1/15/22 This 2017 Short Trip serves as a prequel to the "Susan's War" boxed set, although Eddie Robson didn’t intend it that way. It’s narrated in the style of a Companion Chronicle, read by Carole Ann Ford, which feels very natural. Susan is still living on Earth, after the events of the Eighth Doctor Adventures , so she’s on her own, without David or Alex, and feeling somewhat melancholy. She lives in a flat built from the remains of Coal Hill School, with a tree dedicated to Ian and Barbara growing in the quad. She’s still serving as a scientific advisor to the world government, so she’s called in when strange, alien-ish stuff happens, which suddenly occurs quite frequently…because the Doctor is trying to distract Susan and keep Gallifrey from contacting her to drag her into the war. I’m not sure what I think of Susan’s choice, really, but I do agree with her reasoning that there’s nothing left for her on Earth.
docs.title: All Hands on Deck

docs.text: Darkness and Light War Master #3.4 Released: 3 July 2019 Listened: 1/14/22 This boxed set comes to a close with this story, where it’s become clear that the Master is hiding back in the mists of time building a weapon for the Time Lords, one of those nasty sentient, humanoid weapons that has all kinds of power and can wipe out whole planets. Naturally, the Master intends to install a back door so that he can control it himself. Also naturally, it’s gotten out of control and is rampaging around the facility. The Doctor and the Master are forced to combine their abilities to shut the thing down, or at least limit its power. Derek Jacobi does just enough to make the Doctor think he’s panicking and actually needs help, while letting the listener know who’s really in charge. There’s some wistfulness here on the Doctor’s part, as he misses his old friend. It must have been a while since they last met, because he never acted that way toward the Alex MacQueen Master. But then, the Doctor is searching for hope in the midst of the war, so he’s likely to clutch at straws. It’s highly likely the Doctor would be quite angry at being used the way he was, but fortunately he won’t remember any of it.
docs.title: Darkness and Light

docs.text: Day of the Vashta Nerada Classic Doctors, New Monsters #2.4 Released: 27 July 2017 Listened: 1/12/22 This time around, the “new monsters” are the Vashta Narada, which does qualify nicely as “new series.” However, they’re invisible, hide in shadows, and don’t talk (the ones from “Silence in the Library” were an exception), all of which makes them tricky to capture on audio. Even more astoundingly, they’re in two stories in this box: the Fourth Doctor story that started the box had them on Funworld, and this story transplants the same colony to a research station. It’s not really a direct sequel, just a link, and nothing really comes of that. The Vashta Narada are being engineered for a variety of benevolent purposes, but of course they could also be a weapon, and surprise, the Time Lords are subsidizing that for the war. Specifically, Cardinal Olistra is overseeing the program, which means the wonderful Jacqueline Pearce is in this story, and she’s amazingly snotty and dismissive throughout, even when her life is in danger. Because naturally one of the human scientists decides to pull a Jurassic Park , and then all hell breaks loose. There really isn’t a lot more to the plot than a standard run, hide, run some more story, but the tension is kept up pretty well, given that the antagonist can’t verbally menace anybody. The Doctor’s attitude toward the war hasn’t changed any, but Olistra is already getting sick of his dodging. At the moment, she just wants him out of her way, but that will change. It’s a decent story, but that’s about all.
docs.title: Day of the Vashta Nerada

docs.text: Death Will Not Part Us Short Trips #11.4 Released: 15 February 2022 Listened: 2/17/22 This story is a bit tricky to place in the Doctor’s timeline, because it’s not really about the Doctor. But it takes place during the Time War, and the Doctor is most definitely trying to control the damage. It’s about a woman whose planet was destroyed in the Time War, and now she’s out for revenge against the Time Lords. Specifically, she’s got her hands on a gun that uses time as bullets; she has to “feed” it pieces of her own history, which then affects her timeline. However, by ripping out parts of her own timeline, she affects the lives of her loved ones as well. It’s very tragic, and makes for an appropriate Time War story.

docs.text: Echoes of Extinction Time Lord Victorious Special Released: 14 October 2020 Listened: 1/09/22 The Time Lord Victorious storyline was a bit hard to follow. It was a multimedia project including audios, novels, YouTube videos, comics, and I think there was an escape room in there too? The idea was that you were supposed to be able to follow it by just reading the bits you wanted to, which may have been true, but in practice that meant that the individual threads were kind of disjointed, and it wasn’t clear how they connected up. This story is a pretty key example. The gimmick is that it was released on LP (with a limited download availability); one side had an Eighth Doctor story, the other a Tenth Doctor story, and they connected up, such that you could listen to either side first. Except the Eighth Doctor story is pretty much standalone, and because it’s only 30 minutes, to fit on the LP, it’s pretty short. Basically, there’s a space station with a genocidal monster, a hostage woman, and a robot butler. The Doctor turns up, does his thing, leaves. I guess the Tenth Doctor section has the connection points, because there’s no sign of another Doctor here. Minor note: The theme music has switched to the “War Doctor” theme, and I believe will remain that way for the rest of the Eighth Doctor’s tenure.
docs.title: Echoes of Extinction

docs.text: He Kills Me, He Kills Me Not Time Lord Victorious #1 Released: 16 April 2021 Listened: 1/10/22 The primary purpose of this TLV story is to introduce Brian, the Ood Assassin. (That is, he’s an Ood, not that he assassinates Ood.) Brian’s origin isn’t explained here; he’s just on a contract to retrieve a princess and kill the commoner she’s married and run off with. Silas Carson plays Brian, as he’s voiced all the Ood on the TV series and Big Finish up to this point, so Brian sounds as authentic as you can get, even though his dialog is rather un-Ood-like. The Doctor stumbles across all three of them while trying to visit a beautiful oceanic planet that’s now inexplicably a desert wasteland. Equally inexplicable is what appears to be an Old Western town apparently occupied only by a barkeep, a sheriff, and a doctor. Writer Carrie Thompson hasn’t done much Doctor Who writing yet, but she has a distinctive voice for making absurdities sound plausible, and for creating secondary characters who have interesting backstories and motivations that go beyond just the story they’re in. The western characters all sound authentically American, although slightly stereotyped with Old West twang. The only weak part is the ending, where the story doesn’t really resolve or even “just end.” Instead, the Doctor and Brian are just taken out of the story, to get on with their next respective parts.
docs.title: He Kills Me, He Kills Me Not

docs.text: Mutually Assured Destruction Time Lord Victorious #3 Released: 9 December 2020 Listened: 1/11/22 The big battle of Time Lord Victorious is over, the Daleks are fleeing in their wrecked ship, containing the TARDIS. The Doctor is hiding out on board, believed to be dead, so yeah, it’s Die Hard on a Dalek Time-Ship . The Doctor continues with his lighter attitude from the previous story, mocking the Daleks’ ineptitude, and even waltzing with one in zero-G, admittedly to stay out of the way of its gun, but still. The Daleks with separate personas are all still around, and the Executioner in particular really gets to shine here. He’s a psychotic who just wants to kill everything, but he’s finally had enough and not listening to orders anymore, which is cool. The Commander and the Strategist are no longer operating from the same playbook, which means we have the unusual sight of Daleks undercutting each other, but that also makes things easier for the Doctor, since he can play them off each other. There are a couple of last-of-their-race beings being held in cryo-sleep on board, but they don’t really have a connection to the larger plot; they just seem to be there to give the Doctor someone to talk to. Which is a shame, because this event has been so full of small links otherwise, like the heat shield the Doctor picked up in “ He Kills Me, He Kills Me Not .” The three stories are pretty successful as standalones, which is good, but if you didn’t know about the event, you’d have a distinct sense of missing something between the second and third stories.
docs.title: Mutually Assured Destruction

docs.text: The Castle of Kurnos 5 War Master #5.3 Released: 28 October 2020 Listened: 1/14/22 If the last couple of stories were odd, this is downright silly. The Doctor is present for all four stories in this War Master set, but out of order. Which ruins the surprise of the first two episodes, but that’s the price we pay for strictly following the Doctor's timeline. Anyway, the Master has stolen the corpse of some ancient Gallifreyan scientist, and come to this planet, where the old guy once kept a castle and a lab, to find one of his genetic descendants so he can contact the dead guy through time, and find out where he kept his greatest weapon. Or as the Master would call it, Thursday. The Doctor shows up to stop him, and happens to arrive just as the Master has found the genetic match he’s looking for. Because this is the Master’s story, the Doctor basically charges straight in with little subtlety or plan, and it goes about as well as you’d expect. The Master gets to be suitably evil, sacrificing a few lives for his own ends, but really, nothing too dastardly. Told in the proper order, this would be a nice break, and a flashback. Looked at this way, it’s kind of a slow and unimpressive start.
docs.title: The Castle of Kurnos 5

docs.text: The Cognition Shift War Master #5.4 Released: 28 October 2020 Listened: 1/15/22 After quite a bit of time getting to the where the plot is happening, we’ve got the climax here. The Master (played by Paul McGann) is building a “Cognition Shift,” which will do something horrible, universal, and mind-swappy, giving the Master control of the universe, as usual. The Doctor (still played by Sir Derek Jacobi) is trying to get there with his motley companions to stop it. McGann is using the same tactics as Jacobi: They’re not trying to mimic the other’s inflections or line readings; they’re just doing the dialog as they would in their normal voices. Which really makes everything kinda spookier, because Paul McGann playing the Master impersonating the Doctor sounds like the Doctor we know, but with just a little bit of an edge to him to throw everything off. But that doesn’t really leave a lot of time for plot twistiness, nor for getting the story on this planet and its inhabitants. It’s just rush to the conflict, then resolve it. There is, as you might expect, a “that’s not me; I’m me!” scene, but it’s not belabored, which is good. A lot of the other stories in this set have been equally fun on a re-listen, but I’m not so sure about this one.
docs.title: The Cognition Shift

docs.text: Edge of Redemption War Master #5.1 Released: 28 October 2020 Listened: 1/15/22 If you haven’t heard this boxed set before, you’re really better off listening to it in the proper order, or else you’ll ruin the surprise. Big spoiler coming, so turn away now. As we saw in the last story , the Master swapped bodies with the Doctor, which means the Doctor is played by Derek Jacobi in this story, and the Master doesn’t appear at all. But the listeners aren’t supposed to know that, so we think this is about the CIA ordering the Master to track down and stop the Doctor. Why exactly Narvin would be the one giving that assignment at this point in Galifrey’s timeline, I can’t say, but here we are. So how well does it hold up on a re-listen? The opening conversation with Narvin is awfully stilted, for a start. Sir Derek doesn’t seem to be trying to “play” Paul McGann’s Doctor at all; he’s giving line deliveries in the same way he normally would. There’s a little more anxiety and less suave surety, but that’s all. Which leaves the plot to do a lot of the work, and it’s kinda mixed. This episode is basically a heist movie – the Doctor needs to get to the planet where the Master is, without a TARDIS. So he’s on a nearby planet, but only smugglers will fly where he needs to go. He gets a Local Knowledge guy, who gets him a pilot, but the pilot’s ship is impounded, so they need to break in, and for that they need a contortionist, and before you can say “Ocean’s 11,” they’ve got a team. The biggest plot-based clue that something is wrong with the Master is that he declines to carry a gun, although he threatens Kriket with a weapon after the latter picks his pocket. The second-biggest clue is that the heist plan goes wrong in a variety of little ways, and the “Master” has to improvise, which he does well, and succeeds anyway. There are, however, a couple of deaths, due entirely to the fact that one of his new allies recognizes the “Master,” and carries a grudge. The first time through, you’re trying to figure out what’s going on, and you may twig that something’s not right with this story. The second time through, it’s almost as fun when you already know the secret, so that works out.
docs.title: The Edge of Redemption

docs.text: The Enemy of My Enemy Time Lord Victorious #2 Released: 11 November 2020 Listened: 1/11/22 The Eighth Doctor continues through this crossover without actually knowing he’s in it. He’s pitched up (without Brian ) on a Dalek ship holding a Dalek time squad with an unusual collection of Daleks with distinct personalities: the Commander, the Scientist, the Executioner, and the very curious Strategist, who has an old, beat-up casing, and an agenda of his own. The Daleks are very interested in whatever’s been causing temporal distortions lately, and they want the Doctor’s help. We seem to be pre-Time War at this point, for the Daleks to consider recruiting the Doctor at all. For his part, the Doctor seems distinctly flippant with the Daleks, teasing them and playing them off one another without any fear of extermination, as though they don’t impress him at all. The Daleks are headed for the planet Wrax, where the natives have a device that can devolve an entire species, anywhere in the universe, if they have a DNA sample. Which is kind of bonkers, but that’s because it comes from the Kotturuh, a race that the Doctor believes is extinct…but also alive, which means they’ve got something to do with the time anomalies. This Doctor seems incongruously optimistic – although he’s getting close to the Time War, he’s still not willing to contemplate genocide of the Daleks, even though he felt differently after Lucie’s death , and when he was with Molly . He’s still able to make speeches about the sanctity of life and such. Maybe his time with Liv and Helen restored his optimism; I don’t know. The story ends with the Doctor and the Daleks heading off into the Dark Times, which is where the rest of the crossover takes place.
docs.title: The Enemy of My Enemy

docs.text: The Missing Link War Master #3.3 Released: 3 July 2019 Listened: 1/14/22 Once the War Master stories became an ongoing series, one of the obvious things fans wanted was an appearance from the Doctor, which would have been the Eighth Doctor, following continuity. (Although having Sirs John Hurt and Derek Jacobi together in a story would have been beyond awesome, it was established that the War Master was gone before the War Doctor came on the scene.) So we get stories like this, where the Doctor essentially drops in as a secondary character to the Master’s story, and is doomed not to remember it, because otherwise the Tenth Doctor might have recognized Professor Yana in “Utopia.” Which makes these stories a little silly, from the perspective of this project, because the listener knows about as much as the Doctor does. In this case, the Master has built a giant medical facility on some planet, and he’s got a number of scientists researching…something. Something to do with lycanthropes, or psychic abilities, or both. The Doctor pops up rather randomly and rescues one of the subjects, a psychic woman named Alice (who was introduced in the earlier stories I’m not covering). The Doctor is unusually fuzzy-headed because of her powers, and keeps forgetting what he’s doing as he and Alice run around the spacious ventilation system. He’s being even more flippant than usual, which is a bad sign, but Alice doesn’t know him well enough to know that. The Doctor fulfills his role as semi-antagonist fairly well, although the Master is continually one step ahead, because it’s his story.
docs.title: The Missing Link

docs.text: The Rulers of the Universe The Diary of River Song #1.4 Released: 25 December 2014 Listened: 1/12/22 This one is from the first River Song boxed set, and that early in her tenure, Big Finish was trying to be careful with how River interacted with older Doctors who shouldn’t know her. This caution didn’t last very long , it should be noted. River’s boxed sets often have a single plot thread running through them, so for River, this is the climax of a longer story, whereas for the Doctor, it’s just some crisis he stumbled into. Listening to it in isolation, there are references to a huge party, and a group called the Rulers of the Universe, which don’t make a lot of sense, but for this project, that’s kind of appropriate. The Time War is definitely happening by now, but the Doctor is busy avoiding it, as he did in the beginning. He’s entirely aware of the horrors of the war, though, and actively tries to dissuade a race that wants to join in. He’s still pretty cavalier about his personal safety, though, and remains somewhat light-hearted. He and River don’t actually meet; they just talk over a radio link, and River never gives her real name. The Doctor seems interested, and grateful for her help, whereas River seems pained by the idea that she can’t help him directly. That emotion is less prevalent later in River’s series, where she seems to enjoy dancing around the prior Doctors. As a story for the Doctor, this one isn’t easy to follow, so it’s best enjoyed by not worrying about the things he doesn’t know about, because River’s got it covered.
docs.title: The Rulers of the Universe

docs.text: The Scaramancer War Master #5.2 Released: 28 October 2020 Listened: 1/15/22 If you were listening to this boxed set for the first time, you could be forgiven for thinking that the plot is taking a long time to get going (I certainly did). The previous story was all about getting a ship. This story is about flying the ship to the planet. The third (in order) story is a flashback. Having killed off a couple of interesting characters in the last story, we immediately replace them with more interesting characters, Dorada the mercenary, and the Scaramancer, a pirate. Again, Sir Derek is mostly playing the Doctor, although the Master does appear in a short flashback, perhaps for the purpose of reminding us what the Master really sounds like, to make a contrast. Because while the Doctor isn’t acting typically Doctor-ish here – he seems somewhat hardened, and more angry than usual – he’s not really acting like the Master either. The purpose of this story seems to be lining up some more characters who are really unhappy with the Master, and then drop the big reveal at the end. Honestly, I wonder if that couldn’t have been done in the first story.
docs.title: The Scaramancer

docs.text: The Shoreditch Intervention Susan's War #1.4 Released: 16 April 2020 Listened: 1/16/22 The Short Trip " All Hands on Deck " inspired Big Finish to create a sequel series starting in 2020, explaining exactly what Susan was up to during the war. Which I'm not sure was a crucial question to answer, but Carole Ann Ford was available and willing, and remains an excellent voice actress, so I think it was justified. But this project follow's the Doctor's timeline, and for him, he skips over most of the first boxed set to appear in the last story. It's presumably been a while for him since "All Hands on Deck," but maybe not so long for Susan. She's sent back to Shoreditch, 1963, and we know what that means. Alan Barnes fills this story with continuity, both Susan’s personal history with the Daleks, and remembering Alex, as well as broader references to “ Unearthly Child ” and also “ Remembrance of the Daleks .” There’s even a tiny cameo from David Bradley as the First Doctor. Everybody is clearly after the Hand of Omega, so it’s a bit odd that it never gets mentioned by name, but whatever. There’s a fair bit of timey-wimey going on, as you might expect, although we do finally learn that Earth was time-locked during the war, presumably for its own protection. It’s fun to see Susan getting nostalgic for 1963, but also seeing the teenagers through adult eyes. The references continue even up to the end, in which we learn where this series falls in relation to Gallifrey: Time War . I’m not sure all of these machinations were strictly necessary, but sometimes it’s fun to have a good continuity wallow, so long as it’s entertaining, which this one is.
docs.title: The Shoreditch Intervention

docs.text: The Sontaran Ordeal Classic Doctors, New Monsters #1.4 Released: 28 July 2016 Listened: 1/12/22 The CDNM series is supposed to pair old Doctors up with new-series monsters, and they really fudged the definition by putting the Eighth Doctor with the Sontarans. The argument is that new-series Sontarans look and act differently than “classic” ones, but c’mon. Admittedly, these Sontarans are looking to get into the Time War, and they’re played by Dan Starkey and Christopher Ryan, and that’s about as new-series Sontaran as you can get. And Andrew Smith gets everything just about right, too. The Doctor is still trying to “clean up” around the Time War without getting involved, and he’s pretty torn up about the fact that he’s not making a difference. We get to actually see a planet have its entire history altered in a few seconds by the war, and it’s clear why the Doctor is horrified. Dan Starkey plays the honorable Sontaran, who wants to defeat his enemies, but wants to do it the right way, and is willing to ally with the Doctor if that’s what it takes to satisfy honor. He’s not humorous like a lot of Dan Starkey Sontarans are, and Starkey sells him quite well. Aside from the tenuous link to the boxed set’s theme, it’s really quite good.
docs.title: The Sontaran Ordeal

docs.text: The Truth of Peladon Peladon #4 Released: 28 January 2022 Listened: 2/6/22 I’m placing this story here, because the Doctor is solo, and seems rather stern, but he’s not yet fallen into despair. He also seems to spend quite a bit of time in this story. From a storytelling perspective, this Tim Foley story is drastically different from the others. It’s very small and tight, with the Doctor trying to win over Arla Decanto, a seamstress, and slightly influential figure in Peladon’s trade class. She’s played by Meera Syal, who played Nasreen Chaudry in “The Hungry Earth” and “Cold Blood,” but this is her first Big Finish appearance, and she’s magnificent. The Doctor is really playing a long game here, setting things up slowly to change the mind of one person; it’s more Seventh Doctor than Eighth, really. Except that early in the story, he displays the bubbly side of his personality, and proves remarkably good at being an apprentice tailor. We’ve heard of the Doctor doing things like that off-screen before, but normally when we actually see him trying to blend in, he’s a colossal failure. It’s nice to know that he really can pull it off if he wants. The politics are kind of off-beat in this one, as the Doctor is working very much from the outside, rather than having the monarch’s ear as he normally does. As a result, he seems very short with Arla, sometimes downright angry, which is unusual for him. It’s tough to figure what Big Finish meant here, because Peladon is often used as a stand-in for Earth’s political problems, but things don’t seem to get any better after the Doctor leaves. Maybe they will this time? As an individual story, it’s quite strong. As the closing story of the boxed set, it just offers more questions.
docs.title: The Truth of Peladon

docs.text: The Turn of the Screw Short Trips #8.3 Released: 27 March 2018 Listened: 1/09/22 This short trip is narrated by Yee Jee Tso, in character as Charlie Sato from the handful of UNIT stories where he’s appeared. There’s also a tiny cameo from Daphne Askbrook as Ruth Matheson. Charlie is in San Juan, trying to track down some alien tech, which turns out to be the broken sonic screwdriver that the Eleventh Doctor lost in “The Eleventh Hour.” Paradoxically, the Eighth Doctor comes to retrieve it, saving Charlie’s life from the various aliens who are also after it. Because the story takes place in North America, Yee Jee Tso’s American accent is very appropriate, especially in-character. He’s never suffered from the over-enunciation that Americans in Big Finish often have, even when they’re played by actual Americans, so it sounds very authentic. Unlike most narrators, he doesn’t attempt to mimic the Doctor’s voice or cadence, which makes the story a bit flat, but it’s probably best he didn’t try. It’s a nice little story with good continuity references.
docs.title: The Turn of the Screw

docs.text: The Eleventh Doctor The Eleventh Doctor: The old man in a young man’s body. The one who likes fish fingers and custard. The one who thinks bow ties are cool (also fezzes). The one you never put in a trap. The one who likes big, loud speeches. The one who Matt Smith hasn’t yet portrayed for Big Finish. The one who, fortunately, sounds a lot like Jacob Dudman, who will appear in Big Finish, so that’s all right then. It’s hard to fault Matt Smith for not having time to give to Big Finish just yet. He’s been busy playing Prince Philip in The Crown and Daemon Targaryen in House of the Dragon and appearing in some truly regrettable sci-fi films. He’s a busy guy. In fact, the only one more busy is Karen Gillen, who appears in the MCU under a ton of blue makeup, and has also done a bunch of TV shows. Jenna Coleman is equally busy, playing Queen Victoria, starring in The Sandman , and appearing in a bunch of stuff in between. Arthur Darville is plenty busy too, particularly appearing on Legends of Tomorrow , but he’s made the time for some Big Finish. In short, it’s a scheduling nightmare to get the original cast together, so the Eleventh Doctor’s audio appearances are mostly chronicles and short trips. But there’s always hope.
docs.title: Eleventh Doctor

docs.text: The Eleventh Doctor, Amy, and Rory Amelia Pond, the Girl Who Waited, and Rory Williams, the Last Centurion. Moffat clearly wanted Amy to be different from the companions who’d come before, and she’s loud, assertive, and probably overconfident. Rory, meanwhile, is patience and devotion incarnate. Except when he’s dead. It’s a different team dynamic for a new Doctor, one who seems to be more open and vulnerable, but who’s concealing an awful lot of what he feels.

docs.text: A Tragical History The Eleventh Doctor Chronicles #2.4 Released: 16 September 2021 Listened: 12/27/22 This one takes place in London, 1770, which is a bit unusual, as the Eleventh Doctor didn’t do many quasi-historicals. It also mostly takes place in a debtor’s prison, where something or someone is making some pretty grandiose promises to inmates. In continuing with the theme of this set, the “baddie” isn’t exactly a baddie, but misunderstood. And yes, humanity, specifically humans’ inhumanity to each other, is once again the bad guy, which is kind of much when several stories in a row end up that way, but it was a pretty common theme of this era. This is writer Tessa North’s only contribution to Doctor Who thus far, but she does a good job of capturing the feel and the vocabulary. She’s also created some very strong secondary characters in Sarah Ellison, the companion-substitute and pickpocket, and Lady Dora Smith, noblewoman and prison reform crusader. The characters are memorable, even if the story isn’t so much.
docs.title: A Tragical History

docs.text: Living History The Churchill Years #1.3 Released: 14 January 2016 Listened: 12/18/22 We’re back to the Churchill stories, but this one is distinctly odd. It takes place in the middle of “ A Christmas Carol ,” in which the Doctor takes teenage Kazran to meet Churchill in his post-war era. On top of that, he takes them both to an era Churchill would like to investigate, Roman Britain, circa 55 BC. On landing, though, the TARDIS slips out of phase, stranding Kazran and Churchill on their own, and relieving anybody of having to do an Eleventh Doctor impression. Churchill gets to meet Caesar and even help direct a battle; Kazran meets a British queen; and everybody meets (spoiler, although it’s on the cover) a Dalek. In this case, Churchill knows what Daleks are, and even Kazran has heard of them, so there’s no time spent in subterfuge. Justin Richards really took the brief in both hands and ran with it – having Churchill actually travel in time is a first for this series (and for him), and combining it with Kazran gives another perspective on events, as well as providing an action-type to do all the running. Danny Horn returns as Kazran, and apparently loves every minute of it. There’s nothing at all Christmassy about this story, nor is there any advancing of Kazran’s development, but that’s about the only thing that’s missing.
docs.title: Living History

docs.text: The Calendar Man The Eleventh Doctor Chronicles #1.1 Released: 15 August 2018 Listened: 12/17/22 In this first Eleventh Doctor audio story, AK Benedict isolates the major themes of Series 5 and leans in. Leans way, way in. We’ve got fairy tales, both thematic and literal. We’ve got the one person who no one believes, except for the Doctor. We’ve got a bad guy that erases things from history. And we’ve got a fairly unnecessary connection to the Time Lords that makes the Doctor actually the center of the story. There’s references to the Doctor’s guilt, he gets to make a sacrifice play in a battle of wills, AND he gets a big speech. Ticks all the boxes. And unfortunately leaves one with that vaguely dissatisfied feeling that Series 5 stories often had, that some bits went unsaid or were unexplained. There’s also a mention of the Doctor being in his last incarnation, which didn’t feel necessary to the story, and is mostly there to show that people paid attention to “ The Time of the Doctor .” Amy’s pretty accustomed to being with the Doctor at this point, knowing when to listen to him and when to ignore him, and pretty capable of acting on her own. However, there’s nothing that refers to her having forgotten Rory, despite the fact that the forgotten settlers would give the writer a perfect excuse. Jacob Dudman does a fantastic job playing the Eleventh Doctor, as that’s his speciality. He also does quite a good job with the various secondary characters. His impersonation of Amy isn’t as good, but that’s an awfully big ask. It’s a very representative start, if not a standout.
docs.title: The Calendar Man

docs.text: The Chartwell Metamorphosis The Churchill Years #1.4 Released: 14 January 2016 Listened: 12/28/22 The stories in the first Churchill Years boxed set went in chronological order for both Churchill and the Doctor, so this one finds him close to the end of his life, when he was retired and residing at Chartwell House. And boy, is he cranky about that. Not the house specifically, but his physical deterioration, which requires him to rely on his staff. Said staff specifically including Lily Arwell, last seen as a girl in “ The Doctor, the Widow, and the Wardrobe ,” and played again by Holly Earl, although that’s not obvious when the story starts. This time around, there actually is a baddie, being bad, and unfortunately, taking advantage of Churchill’s vanity and desire for youth. The Doctor actually isn’t in this one all that much, which gives Earl a chance to shine. She’s got some excellent lines, demonstrating the quickness of mind and ready sarcasm she had as a kid. Once the Doctor shows up, things tend to devolve into a runaround rather quickly. Ian McNeice doesn’t do the best Eleventh Doctor, and it’s hard to fault him for that, but there it is. Points to Ken Bentley for pulling off an energetic story with an elderly Churchill.
docs.title: The Chartwell Metamorphosis

docs.text: The Day Before They Came The Eleventh Doctor Chronicles #2.2 Released: 16 September 2021 Listened: 12/23/22 Another small-scale story, fitting for this period where the Doctor has deleted himself from the historical record, and is trying to keep a low profile. It takes place entirely within a boring seaside town where an alien scout has accidentally invaded, and someone else is watching out for alien activity. It’s set in 1986, and is very of its time, with a video arcade featuring appropriate sound effects. The Doctor sounds extremely Doctor-y in this one, with his random asides all over the place, and Jake Dudman handles that perfectly. Daniel Blythe has written prose Doctor Who before, but this is his first time in audio, and he seems to have adjusted quite well. There’s a twist, but not an overly elaborate one. The overall impression of the story is that it’s “nice.”
docs.title: The Day Before They Came

docs.text: The Evolving Dead The Eleventh Doctor Chronicles #2.1 Released: 16 September 2021 Listened: 12/20/22 Unlike previous Chronicles sets, which jump all over the Doctor’s timeline, this second set of Eleventh Doctor Chronicles takes place all in a row, in the gap between Series 6 and Series 7. They’re also closer to full-cast than previous Chronicles, which only had two actors. In this case, the Doctor is traveling sans companion, which means he has to talk to himself more often than usual, except for the Eleventh Doctor, it doesn’t really seem out of character. He lands on a space station where the whole crew is dead, and has become nanobot-infested zombies. Including a couple who are unusually talkative and clever, for zombies. Writer Doris V Sutherland is relatively new to Big Finish, and she crafts a sort of small-scale story here, definitely base-under-seige. It’s a little unclear why the zombies are hungry for human flesh here, or exactly how their biology works, but that doesn’t matter, so long as there are groaning shamblers about. I think the Doctor is a bit more ruthless in dealing with a sentient AI than he would be in other stories, but he does go back and forth on those.
docs.title: The Evolving Dead

docs.text: The Infinite Today Short Trips #10.1 Released: 30 January 2020 Listened: 12/29/22 This is an absurdly long Short Trip at 46 minutes, but it’s a pretty special one, because it puts Jo back with the Eleventh Doctor again. It’s read by Katy Manning, which is kind of a shock after all the Jacob Dudman. Although Katy is a gifted impressionist, I don’t expect her to get the voice, but unfortunately she doesn’t quite get the rhythm either. Matt Smith can be a motormouth like David Tennant, and he’s exceptionally fond of nonsensical asides, but it’s when he slows down unexpectedly that you really have to pay attention, and Katy doesn’t capture that. Her version of Jo, of course, is spot-on. This is after “ Death of the Doctor ,” so Jo recognizes the Eleventh Doctor. She’s also quite busy doing her activist thing, but gets stuck in a time loop. When the Doctor turns up, he’s even more cryptic than usual about what’s causing the loop, and for what reason. Jo puts a great deal of effort into liking this Doctor, but it’s pretty clear she’s looking for the protective, avuncular version to make everything OK, and that’s not Eleven’s style. She also demonstrates her fiery, assertive side, especially when she thinks he might be downplaying her activist mission. It’s also terribly hard to write an ending for these “old companion visits” stories, so this one just kind of stops. It’s a lovely effort, but falls a bit short as a story.
docs.title: The Infinite Today

docs.text: The Jago and Litefoot Revival Short Trips #7.4 Released: 4 April 2017 Listened: 12/17/22 This is the second half of the Short Trip from the very end of the Tenth Doctor’s tenure , and features both the Tenth and Eleventh Doctors, but this half is definitely more Eleven. Which means more Henry Gordon Jago and his florid narrative style, which may not be to your taste. In fact, this second half doesn’t really live up to the setup. There’s a bit of a runaround, the Doctor does a clever thing, resolution. The Tenth Doctor bows out early, and he admits that he’s on his farewell tour, but there isn’t much more to it than that. You could consider it a love letter to Jago and Litefoot, if you like, and it works perfectly well on that level.

docs.text: The Light Keepers The Eleventh Doctor Chronicles #1.3 Released: 15 August 2018 Listened: 12/18/22 The Doctor is alone at this point, presumably leaving Amy and Rory alone for a bit. He does, however, crash at the Maldovarium, because Simon Fisher-Becker ( Dorium Maldovar ) is the guest star for this story. This isn’t the first time he’s met Dorium, but it may be the second, because the Doctor has a bar tab, plus damages from the crash. Dorium convinces him to pay off the debt by ridding him of the “Beacon People,” natives who inhabit the planetoid the Maldovarium sits on, and who are digging it up piece by piece. Oddly, this all forms a big callback to “ Tales of New Earth ,” with the Lux involved. Probably. Or maybe not. The Doctor is written as extremely Eleventh Doctory in this one, full of non sequiturs and random observations, most of which seem to be designed to irritate Dorium. It’s a little hard to see how this ends up with Dorium owing the Doctor a big favor, but maybe that’s not this time.
docs.title: The Light Keepers

docs.text: The Melting Pot The Eleventh Doctor Chronicles #2.3 Released: 16 September 2021 Listened: 12/24/22 I hope you like trilling, because you’re going to hear a lot of it in this story. The Doctor lands on the planet of the Piir, adorable-sounding mouse-like aliens who trill a lot when they talk. They apparently had a lovely world, existing in balance with nature, until the nasty human colonizers showed up and exploited everything, then left. There’s a human named Preacher Stem, apparently a philanthropist, but actually stirring up class warfare among the Piir. Given his name, he should be another of the Master’s aliases, but he’s not, and that’s never explained. Writer Christopher Cooper gives Jacob Dudman some choice lines in this one, as well as a big old speech about religion or the lack thereof. It really gives Jacob a chance to show off his Eleventh Doctor, and a fine job he does of it too. Except the only thing you’ll remember about this story is the adorably trilling mouse-creatures.
docs.title: The Melting Pot

docs.text: The Top of the Tree The Eleventh Doctor Chronicles #1.2 Released: 15 August 2018 Listened: 12/19/22 You might think, given the title, that this could be a Christmas story, but it isn’t. It’s another of Kazran’s Christmas outings with the Eleventh Doctor, but there’s nothing Christmassy about it, except for the fact that it takes place in a tree. A really, really big tree. With odd gravity, acidic sap, a huge insectoid ecosystem, and devolved proto-humans who crashed there a long time ago. As high concepts go, this one is awfully high. There’s also an absurd amount of climbing up and down the branches, which can get tiring just to listen to. In fact, as stories go, this is one of the most punishing I’ve seen or heard for both the Doctor and the companion. And given that Kazran is a once-a-year companion, you could probably forgive him for wanting to check out of the whole story, which he does want to, at times. But this is a young adult Kazran, and he’s developing a sense of altruism, which is the whole point of the Doctor’s larger plan, after all. The physics and ecology of this story is nearly enough to break disbelief, but manages to just hang on to the right side of it, and for that, it’s memorable. But that’s all for Kazran, of any age, in this project.
docs.title: The Top of the Tree

docs.text: The World Tree Short Trips #12.X Released: 29 December 2022 Listened: 12/29/22 This is the Paul Spragg Memorial Short Trip for 2022, coming out at the last week of the year, which means it’s by a brand-new writer, Nick Slawicz. Like many of them, this story is less about what actually happens, and more about the feelings it evokes. In this case, the Doctor visits an elderly woman, living alone in the 1980s, whose memory is starting to fade, so that some days are better than others. And that’s pretty much it, except that she acts very human, and the Doctor appreciates that. There is, however, just a hint at an unspecified future Doctor. Lisa Bowerman is the narrator, and she does a better job of capturing the rhythms of the Eleventh Doctor’s speech than a lot of other narrators do.
docs.title: The World Tree

docs.text: False Coronets Eleventh Doctor Chronicles #1.4 Released: 15 August 2018 Listened: 1/4/23 This is pretty much the only audio story so far in this project where Clara figures as a character. We also know from later stories that Clara admires Jane Austen quite a bit, so it’s nice that they get to meet in person. You can’t say they get along immediately; they seem to like one another, but Clara’s arrogance and stubbornness is on full display here, acting on her own, getting into trouble, and eventually getting in over her head. The plot involves an alternate timeline where history has gone off the rails and the monarchy was overthrown in the 19th century. As an American, it’s a little hard to sympathize with the idea that a republic would be an obviously bad thing, but there it is.The baddie in this story isn’t so much evil as simply amoral, not caring about humanity or what happens to history; they just want to get off the planet and go home. Which isn’t that different from others the Doctor has helped, but this time around he’s furious. I guess this story would go down better if I were more interested in this period of English history – or in Jane Austen – but this one didn’t click for me. Which is a bummer, because it’s the end of the Eleventh Doctor’s tenure in this project.
docs.title: False Coronets

docs.text: Rearguard Short Trips #11.1 Released: 15 February 2018 Listened: 1/2/23 This Short Trip isn’t really short, nor does it follow the usual formula. There’s no narration, and two actors: Jacob Dudman playing the Doctor, and Dan Starkey playing a Sontaran trooper, because nobody does it better. Trooper Stron has been left behind on an abandoned planet as a “rearguard” for the Empire…unless they just forgot about him. Like any good Sontaran, he goes about his business until the Doctor turns up and offers to rescue him. Make no mistake, Stron is a good soldier by Sontaran standards, even excellent. The Doctor hopes he can get another Sontaran to make the same choice Strax has, but it’s looking like Strax was a one-off . The whole story is kind of sad, and if you didn’t think that a Sontaran could make you feel sympathetic, you have Alfie Shaw to thank.
docs.title: Rearguard

docs.text: Young Winston The Churchill Years #2.1 Released: 15 February 2022 Listened: 1/2/23 This rather unusual story relies on the coincidence that Churchill was a young man in the late Victorian Era, meaning that he was alive while the Paternoster Gang were active. Stranger yet, the story takes place in 1899, with flashbacks to Churchill’s time in Cuba in 1895, when he was an “observer” of the war going on at the time. This means that Ian McNeice does the narration, but Iain Batchelor plays Churchill as a young man. Neve McIntosh also has a share of the narration, for the parts of the story from Vastra’s point of view.The Doctor is in his post-” Snowmen ” period, in both costume and demeanor, but Clara is nowhere to be seen. Which is kind of a shame, as I think she’d like Winston. As for Winston himself, his verbosity and arrogance are both evident even at this younger age, but at least the older narrator admits when he’s making mistakes. He’s also met the Doctor several times before this point, presumably a reference to the various meetings in prose stories. Writer Paul Morris has definitely done his homework on the Cuban portions of the story, as the events and people depicted, and the La Huerfana pearl, are all historically factual, although there was no alien influence in actual history. The split narrative, and the inclusion of other actors, make this different from most of the Churchill stories, and probably the most memorable of them. However, that’s the last of them for this project.
docs.title: Young Winston

docs.text: All of Time and Space The Eleventh Doctor Chronicles #4.1 Released: 21 February 2023 Listened: 3/18/23 This is the start of a new box, with both the set and this story called “All of Time and Space,” which is an Eleventh Doctor catchphrase, but I think there could’ve been better titles for this one. The last story ended with the TARDIS exploding, and this one picks up there, except it doesn’t, because this story is all about meta. It’s so meta, in fact, that one of the characters provides the theme music. Tim Foley is turning it up to 11 for this one. The main character, more or less, is one Ellery Quest (any resemblance to Ellery Queen completely intentional), a writer from London, 1956, who’s trying to sell his idea for a story called Doctor Who . He knows all about the Doctor and Valerie, who eventually start talking to him from…a variety of places, really. Which makes the story rather tricky to follow, even for Ellery. Fortunately, Valerie seems to be establishing herself as the empathy conduit. She’s willing to talk to the bystanders, and willing to call the Doctor out on his crap. In a lot of ways, she’s the companion that Clara should have been, before Clara started trying to take control. All of this culminates in a discussion about the Web of Time, and how some points are fixed and others aren’t. Valerie really isn’t happy with the amount of “because the Doctor says so” involved here, but claims that she understands.
docs.title: All of Time and Space
