docs.text: Curiosity Shop The Eleventh Doctor Chronicles #4.3 Released: 21 February 2023 Listened: 3/20/23 Let’s get the easy part out of the way: Jacob Dudman blows this one out of the water. The Doctor has suffered some mental damage and forgotten who he is, so he cycles through the personas of several regenerations in the story. Which means that Jacob Dudman plays the Eleventh Doctor playing the First, Third, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, Ninth, and Tenth Doctors, and it’s amazing. His Hartnell and Pertwee are frankly astonishing, and we’ve seen elsewhere that he can do a great Eccleston and Tennant. His two Bakers are not quite so polished, but you can see what he was going for. The little breaks where the Matt Smith accent comes through are so natural, I can’t imagine how he pulled that off. I’m amazed that James Goss felt able to write it, with the guilt that must surely follow. With that bit aside, Valerie gets put through the wringer in this one. With the Doctor not himself, she’s put in a “ Human Nature ” situation of taking care of him, even though he doesn’t know it. Mostly, she tells him stories about adventures they’ve had (so there have been quite a few by this point that we haven’t seen). More than that, though, this not-Doctor keeps paying her for bits of her cybernetic components. Valerie keeps providing them because she needs to keep him on the hook, but her abilities decline throughout the story as she gives up progressively more vital components. They’re not taking the easy way out here – it’s clear that Valerie considers this a violation of her person, but she does it anyway. And like many other companions before her, she discovers that sometimes the Doctor does ask too much. Saffiya Ingar totally sells it, the hope and the grief of believing the Doctor may be lost, all the way down into despair. It’s honestly heart-rending, and I hope it’ll have an impact on her character development in the future. As a set, it’s a little hard to know what to think. It’s got two episodes that underscore how the Doctor’s life is essentially made out of stories, which is appropriate for the Eleventh Doctor, but maybe would have done better split apart? I’m not sure.

docs.text: Regeneration Impossible Short Trips #10.5 Released: 23 May 2020 Listened: 12/29/22 While the Doctor is moping around in Victorian London, he meets the king of grumpy, the Twelfth Doctor, who’s also the king of showing up too early. The Eleventh is more than a little puzzled by this, because he believes himself to be his final regeneration. He’s also especially puzzled by the fact that the Twelfth keeps regenerating without changing, having the energy siphoned away. Of course, neither of them know about the Timeless Child yet, so they assume there’s a limit to how often he can do this. Of course, the plot is less important than putting two Doctors in a room and letting them snark at each other, a task for which the Twelfth Doctor is overqualified. He hasn’t mellowed from his time at St. Luke’s yet, and he’s quite dismissive of the Eleventh’s “retirement,” even though he knows how that’ll end. What’s really amazing is that Jacob Dudman plays both Doctors, even through all the snark, and the bad guy as well. It’s not narrated like a short trip at all; it feels like a full-cast story, even though there’s only one actor. For that reason alone, it’s worth a listen.
docs.title: Regeneration Impossible

docs.text: The End The Eleventh Doctor Chronicles #3.3 Released: 6 October 2022 Listened: 12/31/22 This story, with its fairly deceptive title, is written by relative newcomer Rochana Patel, although you could be forgiven for thinking it’s John Dorney, given the amount of timey-wimey involved. It’s got time spiders, which are pretty much what they sound like, and incredibly dangerous. Which means repeating time loops happen in this story, starting at the very beginning. Nobody takes it entirely seriously when the Doctor dies before the opening credits, but Safiyya Ingar really sells it. In fact, her whole distress situation throughout the story is really well sold. A companion with no TV history is always at greater risk of jeopardy, since we don’t know how their story ends, but that’s only part of the formula. Of course, this isn’t the end, but just the beginning. We know there will be more stories in this block, and the episode ends on a cliffhanger. Valerie is a promising new companion, although the stories haven’t quite lived up to her potential yet.

docs.text: The Galois Group Short Trips #12.6 Released: 2 February 2023 Listened: 3/19/23 And here we have a Short Trip that just drops right into the middle of this set, fitting in perfectly. It’s by Felicia Barker, a relatively new writer at this point, having mostly contributed Short Trips, and narrated in first-person by Safiyya Ingar, providing smooth continuity. The story plays off the discussion that Valerie and the Doctor just had regarding fixed points , but this pushes it to the extreme. The TARDIS lands in Paris, 1832, in the attic of mathematician and revolutionary Évariste Galois , shortly before his death. Galois is a real historical figure, an amazing mathematician, and if you haven’t heard of him, the reason is probably because his accomplishments are hard for most people to understand. Speaking of hard to understand, Valerie wants to try to prevent his death, and ends up causing a paradox. She even runs afoul of the Blinovitch Limitation Effect, and the way that Felicia Barker describes it is about as well as anybody else ever has, which makes for a fascinating visual as well as a strong feeling of melancholy. Most of the story is standing around talking and doing math, so it’s clear why it’s a short trip and not part of the boxed set, but that gives Safiyya Ingar a chance to do the Eleventh Doctor’s rapid-fire dialog, which she does quite well. It’s a very nice addition to the ongoing set.
docs.title: The Galois Group

docs.text: The House of Masks The Eleventh Doctor Chronicles #3.2 Released: 6 October 2022 Listened: 12/31/22 In the manner of boxed sets, we need a historical setting now, so the TARDIS gets yanked off-course and lands in Venice at Carnival, late 1700s. They gate-crash a masquerade in a palazzo, and quickly discover that not everything is what it seems, because of course it isn’t. There are a few references to Valerie’s cyborg extras: enhanced strength, on-board scanners, and a universal translator, but they’re not key plot points. Her general tech-savviness and future-person status make her a little more capable of operating solo than Amy was. Fortunately, even though they’re in Venice, the Doctor doesn’t spend much time mourning Amy and Rory, which is probably good, because Valerie is still in mourning herself. Writer Georgia Cook seems to be trying to set up a moral dilemma, but it hinges on the difference between primitive robots (which are OK to deactivate) and sentient AI (which is murder). And maybe there’s an interesting point to be made there, but it’s not really relatable to most listeners, and Doctor Who has tromped all over that line from both directions in its history. Which is to be expected for a show that’s 60 years old, but does undercut this story a bit. However, it does provide an opening for the Doctor to explain the Time War, and his own actions in ending it, in plain language, which he almost never did on TV. Which itself is undercut by the knowledge that he didn’t do what he thinks he did, but he doesn’t know that yet. It’s a good try, but it’s full of contradictions.
docs.title: The House of Masks

docs.text: The Inheritance The Eleventh Doctor Chronicles #3.1 Released: 6 October 2022 Listened: 12/30/22 This third boxed set with Jacob Dudman takes the conceit a little further. The first set was just a bunch of separate stories. The second were full-cast stories that all took place around the same time, but were unconnected. This time out, they’ve added a new companion, Valerie, and it looks like she’ll be sticking around for a while. She’s from the future, and a cybernetics expert (but nothing to do with Cybermen; she says humanity has outgrown that). She’s extremely sharp, strongly emotional, and seems to know what she wants. Alfie Shaw channels the new-series vibe in this one, with the story mostly from Valerie’s point of view when the Doctor blows into her life like a tornado. Everything moves along at a rapid clip from there, including minor characters dying somewhat abruptly, but the new series is like that sometimes. The big nod to continuity is that the Doctor is still looking for Clara, and willing to bend his altruism a bit to find her…but exactly how far is the question. Arabella Hendricks also makes a very clever baddie, one who’s always calm and calculating, and knows how to push the Doctor’s buttons to get what she wants, which is kind of rare. It’s a promising start.
docs.title: The Inheritance

docs.text: The Time Machine Destiny of the Doctor #11 Listened: 12/29/22 This one is unusual for a number of reasons. It’s the final part of the “Destiny of the Doctor” series, released in 2013, so it’s also an anniversary special. It’s read by Jenna Coleman, even though Clara doesn’t appear in the story. That makes this Coleman’s only appearance in this project. The intent was to wrap up all the threads from the previous 10 stories, a tall order for anybody. Although Matt Fitton is fantastic at writing character relationships, tricky plots have never been his specialty. He gives this one a game try, introducing a timey-wimey threat great enough to require all 11 Doctors to do their bit. However, when it all comes together, it seems like an overly convoluted plot, even for the Eleventh Doctor. Much like Katy Manning before her, Coleman doesn’t quite get the Doctor’s intonation right. The rapid-fire part she can do just fine, but the changes in pacing just aren’t there, which makes the Doctor sound somewhat unhinged (more than usual). It’s a reasonable story, and credit for all the logistics involved in pulling it off, but I’m glad we had other anniversary stories as well.
docs.title: The Time Machine

docs.text: The Yearn The Eleventh Doctor Chronicles #4.2 Released: 21 February 2023 Listened: 3/19/23 This second story is unrelated to the first , pretty-much a stand-alone adventure. In fact, it had been scheduled for spots in other boxed sets before ending up here. There’s a base under siege, something is going on that nobody understands, and the Doctor has to do a clever extra-dimensional thing to save everyone. That much is fairly standard. However, there’s evidence that the Doctor and Valerie are beginning to work together as a team. The banter is thick and fast, so credit to Angus Dunican for that, and Jacob Dudman and Safiyya Ingar sell it quite nicely. The fact that Valerie is from the future and has her own level of tech-tinkering skills helps, as she can contribute to the solution in a more direct way. Valerie also gets her own love interest, or at least the beginnings of one. But she’s still figuring out what she wants from her new travel experience, so that’s complicating.

docs.text: Thin Time Main Range #267 Listened: 12/29/22 This one is properly a Fifth Doctor story , but for the Eleventh, it takes place here. The Eleventh Doctor turns up at the end of the story, because the Fifth’s shenanigans happened to take place in Victorian London, so the Eleventh noticed. The Fifth Doctor is in a bit of a sulk, having left Nyssa, Tegan, and Marc behind for their own safety, and the Eleventh is in a monumental sulk after losing Amy and Rory, so there’s a parallel here. However, it’s the Fifth Doctor who gets inspired, not the Eleventh. He’s played by Jacob Dudman here, thus making him the only modern Doctor to appear in a Main Range story, and the only one to be recast.

docs.text: The Fifteenth Doctor Ncuti Gatwa’s Fifteenth Doctor sprang to life through “bi-generation,” which makes very little sense, but hey, Russell T Davies is back in charge, so it’s best not to lean too hard on the logic. The intent here seems to be a Doctor who’s less burdened by his past and all the trauma he’s absorbed, and one who’s refocused on exploring and helping people, like he was in the beginning. As of this writing, this era has just recently ended, so it’s too early for Big Finish speculation. In fact, at this moment, we don't know anything about the Sixteenth Doctor either.

docs.text: The Reality War TV Series 15, episode 8 Aired: 24 May 2025 In which just about everything that was built up this season is wasted. Omega is a giant skeletal beast, for no reason. The newer Rani gets eaten alive, but Mrs. Flood escapes. The alternate reality resets itself, which means Poppy ceases to exist, but only Ruby remembers, for some reason. The Doctor sacrifices himself to bring Poppy back into existence, forcing Belinda into single-motherdom without actually getting her consent. This story was supposed to carry into another season, but Disney didn't approve one, so the revelation that Poppy is Susan's mother got jettisoned at the last moment. The Thirteenth Doctor shows up for a quick cameo chat at the end, and then the Fifteenth Doctor regenerates into...Billie Piper? As of this writing, that hasn't been explained yet.

The Thirteenth Doctor shows up for a quick cameo chat at the end, and then the Fifteenth Doctor regenerates into...Billie Piper? As of this writing, that hasn't been explained yet.

docs.text: The Fifth Doctor The Fifth Doctor’s era stands out in the TV series as having a lot of companions. That made for some logistical difficulties on Big Finish’s part, both in getting the actors to return (Janet Fielding and Matthew Waterhouse were unwilling for several years), but also finding spots where the stories could fit between the TV episodes. The solution was to add a lengthy period of the Doctor traveling with just Nyssa, and then a period at the end of his tenure when he traveled with Peri for much, much longer than the TV series ever indicated, even adding an original companion into the mix with Erimem. As of 2019, all the actors have returned to their roles, leading to a wide variety of stories scattered throughout the Fifth Doctor’s tenure. This is also the portion of the project where the "Main Range" or "Monthly Range" stories start to appear. Original Big Finish, back in 1999, had one range of stories that alternated between the Fifth, Sixth, and Seventh Doctors, adding the Eighth after a short period of time. That lasted until 2021, when they had so many other Doctors with their own dedicated series, it made little sense to continue with the monthly releases. As a result, some of the oldest Big Finish stories are found in this section. This is also the place where I started my project, as the Fifth is my favorite of the classic Doctors. I wasn't taking careful notes in the first stage, so many of the "listened" dates are approximations. Also, some of these reviews are very short; I may revisit them someday.
docs.title: Fifth Doctor

docs.text: The Fifth Doctor, Adric, Nyssa, and Tegan It took a very long time, but Matthew Waterhouse eventually became one of the last actors to reprise his role for Big Finish, starting with a box set, and then a series of Main Range stories. The writers were then presented with the challenge of making Adric somehow not annoying, while still keeping him recognizable, and for the most part, they succeeded. Most of the Big Finish insertions come later in the season, when the characters have gotten to know one another a bit better, but also because the early stories in this season are linked pretty tightly together. There’s no indication yet of whether this team will do more together, but I’d welcome it.

docs.text: Cold Fusion Novel Adaptations #11 Released: 15 December 2016 Listened: 1/8/22 This is one of the novel adaptations, and I normally don’t care for those all that much, but it was on sale, so. It’s also a fairly impressive story, featuring both the Fifth and Seventh Doctors, as well as the mysterious Time Lady called Patience. Normally I place multi-Doctor stories with the “latest” Doctor involved, but this is really a Fifth Doctor story that intersects with the Seventh. For Adric, Nyssa, and Tegan, it’s still early days, but fortunately all of them have seen a regeneration quite recently, so they’re clued in to that aspect. The Seventh Doctor is with Roz Forrester and Chris Cwej , so after Ace and Benny, and well into his “chessmaster” phase. It’s also quite long, being a novel adaptation. However, it has several aspects common to the novel series, where things are slightly more adult: Tegan wants a beer, both Nyssa and Tegan are on the receiving end of flirting from Chris, but Nyssa completely misses it and makes some inadvertent innuendo of her own. There’s danger to the entire multiverse, there’s Time Lord history involved, and of course the Seventh Doctor is acting the mastermind while appearing to be somewhat silly. The interactions between the Fifth Doctor and Patience are full of references and vague hints of events in other novels, and none of it is explained properly, which was rather a feature of the novels. The Seventh Doctor is pretty mournful about Adric, but keeps it carefully hidden. However, this adaptation has a few unique features, particularly references to the events of “The Day of the Doctor” and “ Time Crash .” Like most of the novel adaptations, I find the plot to be not very memorable, but the character interactions are worth it. And because it’s a Fifth Doctor story, we don’t get a ton of the Seventh Doctor being super-manipulative, which can get old fast.
docs.title: Cold Fusion

docs.text: Ghost Walk Main Range #235 Released: 13 February 2018 Listened: 12/26/19 As Big Finish often does in these trilogies, when one story is silly, the next is dark and scary. The TARDIS crew is split up in this one, which allows them each some solo spotlight time interacting with the minor characters. Specifically, Nyssa gets a romance with Sacha Dhawan (who hadn’t been cast as the Master yet, so this is retroactively creepy), and Adric nearly gets himself hanged. Tegan spends a fair amount of time with the Doctor, which goes about as you’d expect, but you also get to see that the Doctor appreciates Tegan’s determination and perseverance, even while finding her annoying at times. The Fifth Doctor also spends a lot of time with Leanne, played by Fenella Woolgar, who played Agatha Christie in “The Unicorn and the Wasp” on TV, and several other Big Finish roles. It’s not the most memorable spooky Big Finish story, but it’s pretty good.
docs.title: Ghost Walk

docs.text: God of War Forty #1.2 Released: 4 January 2022 Listened: 1/7/22 This is a shorter two-part story by playwright Sarah Grochala, who’s only recently started working with Big Finish. This is still the younger Doctor, having bounced here from “ Secrets of Telos ,” but for Tegan, Nyssa, and Adric, it’s shortly after “ Kinda ,” possibly after “ The Visitation ,” because the sonic screwdriver is mentioned, but not used. The story takes place in ninth-century Iceland, and deals with a group of outcast Vikings, all women, who’ve gone off to make their own settlement. Unfortunately, they come across some Ice Warriors and mistake them for gods, which goes poorly. The Ice Warriors have a tendency to be written as misunderstood, or at least partly sympathetic, but there’s very little of that here. The Doctor seems to be trying to juggle his relationships with his companions based on what he learned in the last story, giving Adric more leeway, being more patient with Tegan, and taking advantage of Nyssa’s scientific expertise. However, the overall effect is to make the characters seem a bit out of sync with how they should be at this point. The resolution is also a bit farfetched. I’d like to hear more from this author, but this story doesn’t quite seem to click.
docs.title: God of War

docs.text: Iterations of I Fifth Doctor Boxed Set #1.2 Released: 12 August 2014 Listened: 12/26/19 This is the second half of the inaugural Fifth Doctor boxed set. The first story was set as early in this crew’s tenure as possible, and this one is deliberately set as late as possible, shortly before Adric’s departure. It’s also a John Dorney story, so you can expect some mental exercises, and he doesn’t disappoint. There’s a locked-room mystery, a creepy cult, lots of early-80s tech, and plenty of math, including a sentient imaginary number. As you can imagine, that gives a lot for Adric to do, but Nyssa and Tegan also get their turns to be helpful. The actors do an impressive job of conjuring the versions of their characters from late in season 19, especially since they recorded this shortly after doing the early versions. I’m glad the boxed set went over well, enough to get us more stories with Adric.
docs.title: Iterations of I

docs.text: Kingdom of Lies Main Range #234 Released: 17 January 2018 Listened: 12/26/19 Although I listened to this story near the beginning of this project, these Adric stories were among the more recent that Big Finish had released at the time of writing, with this second trilogy in 2018. This first entry is silly to the point of being a farce, with a Duke and Duchess vying for control of their shared kingdom, splitting everything down the middle. The Fifth Doctor and Nyssa end up on one side, Adric and Tegan on the other, which allows for some novel character interaction (although the Doctor and Nyssa will get plenty of that shortly in this chronology). The resolution is clever, but manages to be almost equally silly. How much you like this one depends on your tolerance for the silliness, but I enjoyed it. Random note: This is the first release to feature two covers, one with the traditional Big Finish logo (the silver version of the one from the TV movie), and the other with an “era appropriate” logo, in this case the early 80s “neon” logo. This sets the stage for later in 2018, when all releases would have the Jodie Whitaker logo, with an alternate cover with the “era appropriate” logo.
docs.title: Kingdom of Lies

docs.text: Prisoners of London Prisoners of London #5 Released: 5 July 2023 Listened: 8/20/23 Placing this here because they’ve just come from London, and they mention the loss of the sonic screwdriver. This is one of the line of audio novels, although as the fifth, maybe I should stop thinking of them as “new.” It’s written and narrated by Matthew Waterhouse, who presumably knows these characters pretty well. It’s also the second entry by him, so I guess Big Finish is happy with his work. Personally, I find his ideas to be somewhat surreal, and a bit over-descriptive. On audio, some things just have to be described visually, I get that, but Waterhouse seems to delight in bizarre landscapes that can only exist in novel/audiobook form. In this case, the image of a giant theme-park London, with four Tower Bridges and oversized monuments, patrolled by police boxes that continually appear and disappear. It’s a novel, so it’s longer than the usual Big Finish story, but once you’re finished with it, not all that much seems to have happened. The team is split up very early, which almost always happens, but Tegan specifically gets packed off to a prison on the moon, for the crime of being rude to an officer of the law. Although we check in on her periodically, she doesn’t really have any agency in the story. Adric and Nyssa don’t fare a whole lot better, being kidnapped by rebels who want to make changes to the government of the planet. They’re together, so we’re treated to Adric’s inner thoughts much more than Nyssa’s. Which makes sense, given the author, but is kind of a lost opportunity. What’s unusual is that the Doctor intervenes in the assassination of the Emperor, gets arrested, and is almost immediately believed, freed, and trusted (by the Emperor, anyway). In fact, the Emperor remains honest, trustworthy, and responsible throughout the story, which is really rare. Waterhouse does a decent job imitating the Doctor’s breathless delivery, but he’s got a few too many “posh” characters who aren’t easily distinguishable. I’ve enjoyed some of the audio novels, but this one was a slog for me.
docs.title: Prisoners of London

Waterhouse does a decent job imitating the Doctor’s breathless delivery, but he’s got a few too many “posh” characters who aren’t easily distinguishable. I’ve enjoyed some of the audio novels, but this one was a slog for me.
docs.title: Prisoners of London

docs.text: Psychodrome Fifth Doctor Boxed Set #1.1 Released: 12 August 2014 Listened: 12/26/19 In 2014, Matthew Waterhouse had been working with Big Finish on Dark Shadows, but hadn’t reprised his role as Adric yet, but was open to it. Before bringing Adric into the Main Range, they tested the waters with a boxed set. This story is appropriately set right after “ Castrovalva ,” and they make that obvious -- Adric talks about the Fourth Doctor, all the characters reference recent adventures, and really the whole theme of the story is about how these four people see each other, and how they feel about this new status quo. The characters get split up in pairs and then recombined, so that all of them have a chance to interact. Each character also encounters parody versions of how they see the other three, although that’s not obvious at first. The actual plot isn’t hugely important, as this story is distinctly about the character interactions, and it does the job well. The Fifth Doctor gets to use the sonic screwdriver in this story, one of the only times the Fifth Doctor can use it in Big Finish before it’s destroyed in “ The Visitation .”
docs.title: Psychodrome

docs.text: Secrets of Telos Forty #1.1 Released: 4 January 2022 Listened: 1/6/22 This story, from the boxed set celebrating the Fifth Doctor’s 40th anniversary, is a little hard to place. For the Doctor, it takes place right after “ Four to Doomsday ,” but the Doctor is immediately bounced through his own timeline, taking the place of the Doctor right after “ Arc of Infinity .” Which means he doesn’t know Tegan had left and come back, or that he’d spent a long time with just Nyssa…or what happened to Adric. If that wasn’t timey-wimey enough, the TARDIS lands on a ship containing the surviving characters from “ Tomb of the Cybermen ,” who’ve just left Telos following that story. The Doctor does a rather poor job of convincing them of who he is, worse than usual, but he’s a bit time-lagged himself. Tegan and Nyssa, on their part, do OK with keeping quiet about the Doctor’s personal history. It would be interesting if the Doctor behaved a bit differently here, acting more tentative because he’s younger, or wondering why he doesn’t have his sonic screwdriver, but none of that happens. The only change is on the part of Nyssa and Tegan, who are both more experienced travelers than they were when this Doctor met them. The plot itself is mostly just fine, very much fitting with “Tomb of the Cybermen,” as most of the humans have ulterior motives for getting involved with the Cybermen, and that goes as well as you might expect. The Doctor spends a lot of time trying to figure out how the Cybermen relate to his time-hopping, but it doesn’t come together, so that feels like a dangling plot thread.
docs.title: Secrets of Telos

docs.text: Serpent in the Silver Mask Main Range #236 Released: 20 March 2018 Listened: 12/26/19 This one is deliberately a high-concept murder mystery, referencing Kind Hearts and Coronets , with Samuel West playing seven different characters, all from the same family. This story is also fairly silly, giving a whiplash effect to the trilogy, but it’s less farcical and more clever, with a legitimate murder mystery with a timey-wimey solution, which only works on Doctor Who . All of the characters get to use their personal skills to good effect, Tegan gets a love interest (she hadn’t had one yet in the chronology), and Samuel West shows off his range well.

docs.text: Smoke and Mirrors Destiny of the Doctor #5 Released: 1 May 2013 Listened: 12/26/19 This story is part of the 50th Anniversary “Destiny of the Doctor” series, which means it’s a narrated story, in this case by Janet Fielding, who does her best at mimicking the other characters’ speech patterns while still using her Australian accent. This is one of the various times the Doctor has met Houdini, although one of the few where he actually appears as a character, instead of being name-dropped. This is one of my favorites of the “Destiny” stories, not necessarily because of the plot, which goes kind of how you’d expect for a Fifth Doctor story, but for how well it captures the companions’ personalities and reactions to a 1920s fun-fair. The “Destiny” stories also all feature an appearance by the Eleventh Doctor, which is inevitably amusing, and is so again here.
docs.title: Smoke and Mirrors

docs.text: The Auton Infinity Forty #2 Released: 7 September 2022 Listened: 1/7/22 This story, which makes up the whole of the second “Forty” boxed set, is one bumper-sized six-parter. Except this time-lost version of the Doctor isn’t really the focus this time, and in fact doesn’t appear until part 3. Which makes this story a bit tricky to describe for this project. This Doctor is still bouncing through time, and ends up much, much later in his tenure, shortly after “ Frontios .” He drops in on an adventure on Earth in the 80s, when he, Tegan, and Turlough accidentally crash a UNIT training exercise with the Brigadier as an observer. An awful lot goes on that’s fairly spoilery, but we get the origin of the Autons (maybe), two different Doctors, and the Master trying to interfere as always. John Culshaw stars as…lots of folks: the Brigadier, the Master, and Kameleon. As an anniversary story, the whole sequence is a bit confused, as it can’t really change anything we know about the Doctor’s history, nor can it be a fun reunion-type story, because of Adric. I’ll have to call it a good try, and leave it at that.
docs.title: The Auton Infinity

docs.text: The Contingency Club Main Range #222 Released: 14 February 2017 Listened: 12/26/19 The second part of this trilogy takes place among the Gentlemen’s clubs of Pall Mall in the 19th Century, a setting that the Fifth Doctor takes to with obvious relish. His companions, not so much, particularly Tegan, as you’d expect. Nyssa gets to be the clever one here, spending a lot of time with Adric and Marjorie. That leaves Tegan and the Doctor together, which works out rather better than you might anticipate. Particularly noteworthy is Lorelei King, an American using her own accent, although she’s playing an alien. Oddly, it still comes out sounding over-enunciated, as Americans often do in Big Finish. I think this one works better for the setting than the story.
docs.title: The Contingency Club

docs.text: The Darkening Eye Companion Chronicles #3.6 Released: 3 December 2008 Listened: 2/1/20 This is an early Companion Chronicle, the first one Sarah Sutton had done, so it follows the pattern of a later-in-life Nyssa telling someone else a story of something that happened when she was with the Doctor. The frame story makes some odd changes to “ Terminus ” and what Nyssa did after. The flashback story features the Dar Traders, who’ve appeared in one Main Range story , and are interesting enough that I’m surprised they haven’t appeared more. The Doctor spends most of the story off-camera, which relieves Sarah of having to portray him, but she does a pretty good job of capturing the tone of both the Doctor and Adric, and especially Tegan, where she incorporates just a hint of Australian accent. The story itself is a bit hard to follow, and gives a sense that there’s a lot more going on outside the story, but we don’t get to see that.
docs.title: The Darkening Eye

docs.text: The Ingenious Gentleman Adric of Alzarius Short Trips #7.11 Released: 7 November 2017 Listened: 4/19/20 Placed here because the sonic screwdriver features. This is Adric’s story, in which he gets separated from the rest of the crew and ends up in a Don Quixote reference (as you can tell from the title). Unfortunately, Adric isn’t human, and so doesn’t get the reference. Quixote’s role is played by a doppelganger of the Fourth Doctor, conjured from Adric’s subconscious desires. This lets Matthew Waterhouse do a Tom Baker impression, which isn’t half bad, and a Peter Davison impression that’s just OK, and a frankly terrible Janet Fielding impression, but that feels somehow appropriate. There’s not a lot of drama in this story, just some character development for Adric, but it’s mostly about the references.
docs.title: The Ingenious Gentleman Adric of Alzarius

docs.text: The Star Men Main Range #221 Released: 10 January 2017 Listened: 12/26/19 After the Fifth Doctor box set proved popular, Adric appeared in a couple of Main Range trilogies, starting with this one in 2017. Andrew Smith often writes these Adric stories, as he created the character. This one is clearly intended to be a showcase for Adric, as he gets to be clever, heroic, and even has a love interest. As with many Andrew Smith stories, it’s pretty high-concept, with sentient pan-dimensional beings and humanity’s first trip to the Andromeda galaxy. As a showcase for Adric, it works fairly well.

docs.text: The Toy Short Trips Rarities #1.1 Released: 28 September 2018 Listened: 2/1/20 This Short Trip focuses almost entirely on Nyssa, and takes place within the TARDIS, but it’s also full of continuity references. Nyssa’s been having bad dreams about her father, and stumbles onto a device of Susan’s that allows communication with a much earlier Gallifrey, specifically with a memory of the First Doctor, who believes Nyssa to be Susan, but also with the original Master, who tries to corrupt her. All the imagery on Gallifrey reflects the depictions in the modern series, and there are also descriptions of the first eight Doctors, many of whom Nyssa doesn’t know. Sarah Sutton does a very credible job of imitating Tegan, Adric, and the Fifth Doctor for their parts. It’s got atmosphere, if not a lot of plot, but the atmosphere it conveys is quite satisfying.
docs.title: The Toy

docs.text: The Fifth Doctor and Nyssa These stories made up a large chunk of the early Big Finish output. Sarah Sutton was one of the only companion actors available at the time, and since there was only a short period between stories (and seasons) where the Doctor and Nyssa traveled by themselves, they all have to go here. As with the Big Finish stories with original companions, release order and chronological order seem to match up during this time, with only a couple of exceptions. It certainly gives Nyssa a chance to grow as a character, but she ultimately can’t change all that much, because she needs to get back to the same person she was in “ Arc of Infinity .” Still, Big Finish keep returning to this period from time to time, based on actor availability.
docs.title: Fifth Doctor and Nyssa

docs.text: Circular Time, Autumn Main Range #91 Released: 20 January 2007 Listened: 12/8/19 I’m a fan of Paul Cornell, and I like stories that tie the Big Finish timeline to Stockbridge, the small town from the comics where the Doctor likes to show up to rest. Mostly because the Doctor often gets to relax and play cricket while he’s there, and so much of his timeline is about loss, that I like to see him get a break. This story, though, is more about Nyssa’s character than anything else, where she makes some choices that perhaps set her up for her departure in the future.
docs.title: Circular Time, Autumn

docs.text: Creatures of Beauty Main Range #44 Released: 24 May 2003 Listened: 12/21/19 In this story, writer Nick Briggs gets clever with narrative structure, as well as an examination of the connection between morality and physical beauty. The games with flashbacks and recordings make it easier to come up with cliffhangers, but you have to pay attention while listening, and there’s a faint sense that it’s showing off cleverness, rather than serving the story. I’m also not very fond of the “twist” at the end; that’s not the sort of thing that Doctor Who often does.

docs.text: Downward Spiral Short Trips #10.7 Released: 28 July 2020 Listened: 7/31/20 I’m setting this one here because the Doctor and Nyssa have been together long enough to start arguing with raised voices. This story is remarkable because it’s told by Nyssa in the second person, to an astronaut named Siobhan, who’s on one of the first trips from Earth to Venus (why an expedition would have only one astronaut, I can’t say). She’s got an AI for company, but runs into...something...that affects both her AI and her ship. Fortunately, the Doctor and Nyssa are there to help. It’s a fairly standard story from their end, although the Doctor seems a little less empathetic than usual, a little more like the Sixth than the Fifth. The writer also uses the word “roared” quite a bit to indicate shouting, and neither the Fifth Doctor nor Nyssa strike me as the roaring type. Still, it’s a nice emotional short trip for Nyssa, and Sarah Sutton reads these very well.
docs.title: Downward Spiral

docs.text: 1963: Fanfare for the Common Men Main Range #178 Released: 11 September 2013 Listened: 12/21/19 I absolutely love this one, and it’s my favorite of the “1963” trilogy. I’m a sucker for alternate histories around the Beatles, and this definitely delivers. There’s a lot of well-plotted timey-wimey in this one, and that keeps you guessing. The fact that Big Finish provided the Common Men with their own Beatle-esque songs is the perfect touch that takes it over the top. The thick Liverpudlian accents might be a little hard to process on first listen, but that’s part of the price you pay.
docs.title: 1963: Fanfare for the Common Men

docs.text: Masquerade Main Range #187 Released: 18 June 2014 Listened: 12/21/19 This is one of those trippy alternate realities where everybody has amnesia at first and has to slowly figure out what’s going on. However, there’s also rather a lot of proper upper-class behavior, which I can really take or leave, so this story doesn’t do a lot for me until the sci-fi part actually gets going. Hannah departs in this one, and I’m not overly upset about that. She seemed to grow as a person in her travels, but ultimately stuck to the same worldview she started out with, which isn’t great for a companion.

docs.text: Spare Parts Main Range #34 Released: 31 July 2002 Listened: 12/13/19 This is one of the legendary Big Finish stories, often referred to as “Genesis of the Cybermen.” I think it’s pretty good, with some interesting minor characters, and Nyssa gets put through the emotional wringer. I have to say, though, that I’m not quite sure it lives up to its billing. The idea that Mondas isn’t just Earth’s twin, but an exact copy of Earth, down to the streets and the holidays, has never rung quite true for me. As an origin story for the Cybermen, it’s strong, and Davison does a great job depicting the Doctor’s anguish here. I’m just not sure if it’s as strong as “The Doctor Falls” from the end of the Twelfth Doctor’s tenure.
docs.title: Spare Parts

docs.text: The Boy That Time Forgot Main Range #110 Released: 30 July 2008 Listened: 12/21/19 Given its position in the sequence, the boy of the title seems like it could refer to Brewster, but (spoiler) it’s actually Adric. Or an alternate version, anyway. Like many Paul Magrs stories, it’s somewhat off-kilter and complicated, with plenty of timey-wimey as well. At the time this was recorded, Adric hadn’t appeared in Big Finish, and seemed unlikely to, so this must have been something of a pleasant surprise to listeners. Of course, old Adric isn’t a particularly nice person, so he comes off the worse in the story. The two Victorian adventurers, Beatrice and Rupert, are remarkably well-drawn and quirky for secondary characters, and make a good impression.
docs.title: The Boy That Time Forgot

The Doctor is alarmed at first, but then decides to test it by taking them to the bottom of the ocean, where the TARDIS improbably becomes a whale and spits them out. Fortunately, it’s a short story, so the Doctor’s idea to get it back works the first time. It’s a nice contrast between Nyssa asserting herself and the Doctor’s recklessness.

docs.text: The Game Main Range #66 Released: February 2005 Listened: 12/21/19 This one, I flat-out dislike, although it does have some positives. William Russell appears as a famous diplomat, one who’s an old friend of the Doctor’s, but who the Doctor keeps meeting out of order -- that’s more of a new-series trick, even though the new series hadn’t started when this was recorded. On the other hand, the idea of a sanctioned “sport” in which hundreds of people die in every match is just silly, and worse that the Doctor ends up participating without knowing what’s going on. I also found the athlete characters with their shifting loyalties hard to keep track of, as their accents are all similar.
docs.title: The Game

docs.text: The Haunting of Thomas Brewster Main Range #107 Released: 30 April 2008 Listened: 12/21/19 This story introduces semi-companion Thomas Brewster. As with many stories in Victorian London, it’s fairly dark, and the haunting use of “ Oranges and Lemons ” will make it more of an earworm than it already is. It’s also got a lot of time travel and paradoxes in it, showing a fairly clear influence of the new TV series. Brewster himself is both sympathetic and entirely untrustworthy, an interesting combination for a companion, and perfectly suited to take advantage of the Fifth Doctor and Nyssa, who are both fairly trusting, especially without Tegan or Turlough nearby to be more skeptical. At the end, Brewster steals the TARDIS and leaves, creating a rare cross-story cliffhanger, or at least rare for this era of Big Finish.
docs.title: The Haunting of Thomas Brewster

docs.text: The Land of the Dead Main Range #4 Released: January 2000 Listened: 12/8/19 Going by release order, this is the first Nyssa story from Big Finish. Unfortunately, like a lot of the very early stories, it’s not very good at all. It’s set in Alaska, which means characters with dodgy “American” accents, and Native mysticism handled rather poorly. Doctor Who doesn’t usually do well when they try to bring in mysticism respectfully, and the psuedo-science story behind it this time doesn’t hold up particularly well.

docs.text: The Fifth Doctor, Nyssa, and Tegan Once Janet Fielding agreed to return for more Big Finish audios, but Matthew Waterhouse hadn’t yet, this section became the obvious choice to insert the stories. Tegan is more relaxed than in her earlier stint, with the pressure to get to Heathrow removed. There is some awkwardness in that they really don’t address the fact that it’s been much longer for the Doctor and Nyssa than it was for Tegan, but there was no evidence of that on TV, so it’s best to keep that pretense up. There’s also a large section of this period where the Doctor is traveling alone. That doesn’t correspond to anything from TV, but the idea that he left them in Amsterdam for a bit, which turned out to be much longer than “a bit,” works reasonably well. So any “Fifth Doctor alone” story tends to get shoved into this part of the timeline.
docs.title: Fifth Doctor, Nyssa, and Tegan

docs.text: A Requiem for the Doctor The Diary of River Song #3.2 Released: 23 January 2018 Listened: 12/7/19 The next three stories come from the third Diary of River Song box set. At this point, Big Finish had given up on having River try to tiptoe around the Doctor’s older incarnations, and she just interacts with him directly, for an extended period. It’s implied that the Doctor travels with first Brooke, then River, for quite some time, which stretches credulity on the “trying to get back to Amsterdam” story, but it’s what we’ve got. This is more River’s story than the Doctor’s, but he does get to be fairly sharp and action-oriented. River relates a little differently to each Doctor, but she seems to have basic affection for the Fifth, probably because of his similarity to the Tenth. The ending is perhaps a bit contrived, but Jac Rayner and Alex Kingston really sell it.
docs.title: A Requiem for the Doctor

docs.text: Aimed at the Body Main Range #269 Released: 1 October 2020 Listened: 10/16/20 I’m not 100% sure where these go yet, so I’ll slot them in this “Fifth Doctor solo” period until I learn otherwise. This is another quartet of short stories, under the heading “Shadow of the Daleks 1,” which is odd coming so soon after " Time Apart ," with the same format. However, this form was a necessity because of the 2020 Covid lockdown, which rendered some actors unavailable. In this one, the Doctor ends up in Australia in 1933, where he immediately runs into cricketer Douglas Jardine , his girlfriend Flora, and her mother, who are on a trek in the mountains, but have lost their guide. Douglas is a famous, and somewhat controversial cricketer, known for an aggressive style of play, and of course the Fifth Doctor has opinions about this. As an American, it went almost completely over my head, but writer James Kettle does put in enough Cliff’s notes that I wasn’t entirely lost. I don’t know how an actual cricket fan would feel about it. There are Daleks lurking about -- and the one the Doctor sees looks like a new-series Dalek, a fact that he comments on -- but they don’t seem to be doing much of anything, except causing a temporal problem. As a one-part story, it’s nearly meaningless, but as part 1 of an eight-part story, it sets the scene and starts the mystery off nicely.

docs.text: Main Range #269 Released: 1 October 2020 Listened: 10/16/20 I’m not 100% sure where these go yet, so I’ll slot them in this “Fifth Doctor solo” period until I learn otherwise. This is another quartet of short stories, under the heading “Shadow of the Daleks 1,” which is odd coming so soon after " Time Apart ," with the same format. However, this form was a necessity because of the 2020 Covid lockdown, which rendered some actors unavailable. In this one, the Doctor ends up in Australia in 1933, where he immediately runs into cricketer Douglas Jardine , his girlfriend Flora, and her mother, who are on a trek in the mountains, but have lost their guide. Douglas is a famous, and somewhat controversial cricketer, known for an aggressive style of play, and of course the Fifth Doctor has opinions about this. As an American, it went almost completely over my head, but writer James Kettle does put in enough Cliff’s notes that I wasn’t entirely lost. I don’t know how an actual cricket fan would feel about it. There are Daleks lurking about -- and the one the Doctor sees looks like a new-series Dalek, a fact that he comments on -- but they don’t seem to be doing much of anything, except causing a temporal problem. As a one-part story, it’s nearly meaningless, but as part 1 of an eight-part story, it sets the scene and starts the mystery off nicely.

docs.text: Echo Chamber Main Range #270 Released: 10 November 2020 Listened: 11/10/20 For the second month running, the covid lockdown necessitated a release made of short stories with a very limited cast, continuing directly from last month , which means this is “Shadow of the Daleks 2.” The opener finds the Doctor involuntarily hosting a radio call-in show, but he has no idea why. Someone seems to want very angry callers, but the callers don’t seem to know why either. It results in a lot of talking and filler. I can understand why “radio call-in show” would seem an appealing device for an audio story, especially under lockdown conditions, but this one doesn’t seem to advance the story any. The Daleks only appear after the Doctor has already gone.

docs.text: Effect and Cause Main Range #270 Released: 10 November 2020 Listened: 11/10/20 The final part of this eight-part story is by John Dorney, but even by his own admission, it’s less twisty than one of his stories normally is, because the other writers have done most of the high concepts. The Doctor figures out what’s going on, and there are finally Daleks doing something other than intoning ominously in the background. Precisely what that is, I can’t say, and the explanation for the repeated characters is something of a surprise, but not really a big shock. If you’re looking for a major tie-in to the Time War, I’m afraid you won’t find it. On the whole, it’s a bit of a let-down. Maybe listening to it at another time, it won’t be so obvious, but this story really shows that it was made in lockdown with limited resources, and while I salute Big Finish for not interrupting their monthly schedule, it didn’t result in brilliance.
docs.title: Effect and Cause

docs.text: Empire of the Racnoss Classic Doctors, New Monsters #2.2 Released: 27 July 2017 Listened: 12/7/19 After the success of the first CDNM box set, Big Finish immediately did another, and because the Doctor is alone, the story is placed here, chronologically. This time the Fifth Doctor meets the Racnoss, but the Racnoss’ long history with the Time Lords allows him to go pretty far back in Time Lord history as well. The Fifth Doctor seems desperate to give the Racnoss the benefit of the doubt, which is fitting for this incarnation, and a contrast with how the Tenth Doctor treated them. The events of this story justify the Tenth Doctor’s attitude, though. Unfortunately, I find the Racnoss voices grating, and a little ridiculous, and boy are there a lot of them in this story. Adjoa Andoh plays the queen, having played a variety of roles in the TV series, but not a Racnoss. So that’s something, but it’s really not enough.
docs.title: Empire of the Racnoss

docs.text: Fallen Angels Classic Doctors, New Monsters #1.1 Released: 28 July 2016 Listened: 12/7/19 When Big Finish got the rights to use elements from the modern series, one of the first things they did was create some stories with the Big Finish Doctors encountering monsters introduced in the new series, being careful to use only ones the modern Doctors had indicated they’d met before. Obviously, the Weeping Angels topped the list of monsters to use, and yet presented a serious challenge because they’re very visual monsters who don’t speak. This does lead to characters overtly describing what the angels are doing, and announcing when it’s light or dark, rather unlike the Angels’ TV appearances, but it’s not too intrusive. Joel and Gabby make good temporary companions (and it’s always great to hear Sacha Dhawan), in the tradition of Sally Sparrow, and there’s a bonus appearance of Michelangelo, acting grumpy and pompous, rather like Rembrandt from a few stories ago . There’s a fair bit of timey-wimey, which you’d expect in a story with the Angels, even though the Doctor doesn’t actually say the phrase. So far, Big Finish has only used the Angels sparingly, but this is a decent start.
docs.title: Fallen Angels

docs.text: Friendly Fire Conflicts of Interest #1 Released: 5 April 2023 Listened: 5/13/23 This is a John Dorney story, but not the kind you were expecting. Sometimes he goes nuts with twisty stories, and sometimes he just demonstrates how rubbish humans can be. Something goes awry with the TARDIS, forcing the Doctor, Tegan, and Nyssa to evacuate onto a space station. Fortunately, there’s a planet nearby where the Doctor’s old friend Velar (from “ Gobbledygook ”) lives. Velar has apparently taken up mining in his retirement, which is a bit odd, but maybe not so much if you’re an armadillo-person. The miners that the team encounter are evasive, paranoid, and borderline hostile. It’s clear they’re covering something up, and it’s just as bad as you might think it is. And once they’re in over their heads, they have to go to even greater lengths to continue covering it up. The Fifth Doctor gets to have a moment or two of real anger, which is kind of unusual for him. But mostly he sounds disgusted, which is something Peter Davison didn’t do so easily when he was younger, but he can pull it off now. Even Tegan modulates somewhat, especially once she realizes that “her people” (or some of them) are the bad ones. It’s somewhat dark and sad, but not overly so, as it’s only a three-parter.
docs.title: Friendly Fire

docs.text: Ghost Station Main Range #266 Released: 1 July 2020 Listened: 8/1/20 This story, the first part of a collection called “Time Apart,” follows on immediately from “ Conversion ,” with the Fifth Doctor alone, recovering from the trauma of that story. Although these are unrelated short stories, they have related themes of forgiveness, and the Doctor not needing to be responsible for other people’s actions. It has a small cast, and was released during the COVID-19 lockdown, but it was recorded much earlier, so the events are unrelated. This first story is a two-hander, set in an abandoned train station in East Germany, where a guard has an experience he wasn’t meant to have, and could potentially change his life. This one is very dark and atmospheric, a good ghost story, best listened to at night with the lights down.
docs.title: Ghost Station

docs.text: Gobbledegook Interludes #4 Released: 5 April 2023 Listened: 5/14/23 The Doctor is solo and says he’s heading for Earth, so I’ll assume this takes place hereabouts. It’s an interlude, so it’s told in a narrated style, but it’s read by Dan Starkey, who can do lots of different voices, so it feels rather full-cast. The Doctor visits Velar, an old friend of his, a member of a race of evolved armadillos called the Batearian. He comes up again in “ Friendly Fire ” a bit further down the line. At this point, he’s retired from being an ambassador, and is chief librarian at a university on his homeworld. If you’re familiar with university libraries, this immediately creates a visual image…with a giant armadillo. Unfortunately, there’s something wrong with the books; they’re being rendered unreadable, somehow. Lucky for Velar, the Doctor is here to help. It’s not too often that we get to see the Fifth Doctor take over and steamroll people into helping by force of personality, and I wish we did, because he’s terribly nice about it, unlike most of his other incarnations. Maybe he can get away with it when Tegan isn’t undercutting him every second. Because of the narrated format, the story is slow, almost textual, which gives Velar the opportunity to think about the previous times he met the Doctor (an earlier version, apparently), and about his place in his current society. Which is nice character work, if we’re ever going to see Velar again outside of “Friendly Fire,” and I kind of doubt that.
docs.title: Gobbledegook

docs.text: Interlude Main Range #269 Released: 1 October 2020 Listened: 10/16/20 The final of the four stories is even more surreal than what’s come before. The Doctor lands in Renaissance Florence, where he’s roped into performing a play based on Dido and Aeneas for a hostile Duke. But something is wrong, and the world seems to keep getting smaller around him. Dan Starkey wrote this one, and like many things he writes, there’s a lot of fancy language, which can be somewhat distracting. Unfortunately, none of it reveals any more about what the Daleks are doing. I understand this was written and recorded under very trying conditions, and the lockdown messed up the Monthly Range schedule just as the line was coming to an end, but this whole release really feels like filler.

docs.text: Madquake Main Range #267 Released: 12 August 2020 Listened: 8/16/20 This is a primarily Doctor-less story, with Nyssa, Tegan, and Marc dealing with the aftermath of “ Conversion ,” on the unnamed planet where the Doctor left them. The planet seems to have some pacifying properties, which Tegan objects to, but in fairness, that’s because the memory of the Mara is still fresh for her, not just Tegan being irritable. Marc, of course, has it worst of all, as his cyber-conversion has left him feeling disconnected, and his physical strength makes him a danger to the others. Because the Doctor isn’t in the story, that means they can use the Slitheen without causing any continuity errors. And it’s kinda fun to see the Slitheen again, but they’re not my favorite new-series villain, and they aren’t used very creatively here. They’re just implacable hunters, a role that could have been filled by a variety of monsters (the unnecessary fart joke is all Slitheen, though). But the Slitheen aren’t really the important part; the internal conflict is. And that isn’t really resolved, so the story is a bit dissatisfying on the whole.
docs.title: Madquake

docs.text: My Dinner with Andrew The Diary of River Song #3.3 Released: 23 January 2018 Listened: 12/7/19 This is a John Dorney story with an artificial structure, and the timey-wimey turned up to the point where even River gets confused, and I love every second of it. This is the sort of time-hopping that’s only really been common in Moffatt-written stories, but that’s fine because River is a Moffatt creation, and Dorney handles it expertly. The Fifth Doctor is basically just a prop in this one, but Davison gets to put on a fake accent and ham it up a bit, which I’m sure he enjoyed.

docs.text: Nightmare of the Daleks The Lost Resort #3 Released: 8 September 2021 Listened: 9/15/21 We close out the boxed set with a Dalek story, which happens to be Tegan’s first encounter with Daleks. (I guess “ Resurrection ” is vague enough on whether she knows what they are.) Marc collapses in the TARDIS, as a result of some signal he’s received with his cyber-parts, and he steers them to a drilling platform on a water world. The Doctor thinks that the sleep pods on the rig should help Marc stabilize, but there’s a problem: The crew of the rig have been having nightmares, and sometimes they don’t wake up. It’s Daleks invading the dreams, which is a trick they haven’t used before, and makes for a heck of a title. But things get a little confusing as there’s a lot of hopping in and out of the dreamscape, and once again the short length of the story means we don’t get to know much about secondary characters who we should care about. Mark departs the crew in this story, which unfortunately was fairly well telegraphed throughout this boxed set; it seems they’d run out of things to do with him. It’s a better departure than Adric’s, but in a story this short, it doesn’t feel entirely justified. I know part of it was due to the pandemic shaking up the schedule, but Marc doesn’t feel like he got a fair chance. So this one ends up somewhat flat.
docs.title: Nightmare of the Daleks

docs.text: The Lost Resort #3 Released: 8 September 2021 Listened: 9/15/21 We close out the boxed set with a Dalek story, which happens to be Tegan’s first encounter with Daleks. (I guess “ Resurrection ” is vague enough on whether she knows what they are.) Marc collapses in the TARDIS, as a result of some signal he’s received with his cyber-parts, and he steers them to a drilling platform on a water world. The Doctor thinks that the sleep pods on the rig should help Marc stabilize, but there’s a problem: The crew of the rig have been having nightmares, and sometimes they don’t wake up. It’s Daleks invading the dreams, which is a trick they haven’t used before, and makes for a heck of a title. But things get a little confusing as there’s a lot of hopping in and out of the dreamscape, and once again the short length of the story means we don’t get to know much about secondary characters who we should care about. Mark departs the crew in this story, which unfortunately was fairly well telegraphed throughout this boxed set; it seems they’d run out of things to do with him. It’s a better departure than Adric’s, but in a story this short, it doesn’t feel entirely justified. I know part of it was due to the pandemic shaking up the schedule, but Marc doesn’t feel like he got a fair chance. So this one ends up somewhat flat.

docs.text: Relative Time The Legacy of Time #4 Released: 17 July 2019 Listened: 12/7/19 This story is a chunk of the Big Finish anniversary box set "The Legacy of Time," and probably best listened to as part of that set. The stunt for this story is reuniting the Doctor with Jenny, the first time she’s encountered him since “The Doctor’s Daughter,” so there’s lots of explaining to do. And of course there’s a meta-stunt because Georgia Tennant is Peter Davison’s daughter. It goes more or less as you’d expect, with the Doctor trying to distance himself from Jenny at first, and later coming to like and appreciate her. The “father-daughter driving lesson” is probably the most obvious aspect, and yet they pull it off. Of course, it can’t last, and the Doctor can’t remember it, but you know that going in. The gimmick works, and that’s all you can ask for.
docs.title: Relative Time

docs.text: Sock Pig Short Trips #2.5 Released: 28 February 2011 Listened: 4/11/20 The wiki says this story comes between “ Kinda ” and “ The Visitation ,” but there’s no gap there, and the Doctor is alone, so I’m placing it here. This is one of those stories like “ Cuddlesome ,” where something odd is happening to a perfectly ordinary English household, the Doctor bursts in and takes charge through a combination of charm, bluster, and not listening to anyone who objects, solves the problem, and goes. In this case, there’s a force animating objects in the house of an unnamed woman who lost her infant son recently, including a stuffed pig she knitted for him. The Doctor banishes the invading force, but leaves the pig animated, at least for a while, so the woman can heal. The bluster feels rather new-series, but the kindness is appropriate from the Fifth Doctor. This is one of the more memorable short trips.
docs.title: Sock Pig

docs.text: The Burning Prince Main Range #165 Released: 19 September 2012 Listened: 2/1/20 This is one of Big Finish’s “multi-Doctor trilogy” entries, in which a single story crosses between the Fifth, Sixth, and Seventh Doctors, who all operate without companions. Which means for the Fifth Doctor, it takes place as he’s trying to get back to Amsterdam, but he ponders taking a more scenic route until he can come to terms with having Tegan back on board. The story is by John Dorney, but it’s one of his earlier stories, so perhaps not quite as twisty as you’d expect. It’s a story of politics, war, and a royal wedding that’s supposed to solve everything, but in typical Fifth Doctor fashion, it doesn’t, there are betrayals galore, and everybody ends up dead. Oddly, the legitimate monsters, the Igriss, don’t seem to figure all that much, except being a generalized threat for much of the story, and the “burning” aspect of the burning prince doesn’t seem particularly relevant, although there’s hints that it could become important in the next story. The Doctor is written as particularly snarky in this one; perhaps he gets that way when Tegan’s not around. It’s a decent enough solo story, but as always with these trilogies, probably best listened to together, which I’m not doing in this project.
docs.title: The Burning Prince

docs.text: The Edge of the War Conflicts of Interest #2 Released: 5 April 2023 Listened: 5/14/23 This story, by Jonathan Barnes, has a different pace to the previous one; it’s nearly dream-like, or fairy-tale-ish. It starts out with one of those “I don’t remember how I got here, and I’ve been shunted into an identity that makes sense for the context” plots, but it doesn’t really stay there very long at all. The setting is a small town in France, near the Maginot Line, not long before the war. That seems like it should be tense, but instead everything is peaceful, languid even. Except nobody will tell team TARDIS what’s going on, for much longer than usual in these sorts of stories. The Doctor and Nyssa get on with working it out, while Tegan spends time with a local soldier. In fact, she gets pretty close to him, despite knowing what’s going to happen to France shortly. It’s nice to see Tegan doing something other than complaining, but she’s still Tegan, and pretty much shouts at people until they listen to her. The villain isn’t quite what you’d expect, or what the Doctor expects. In fact, it’s not really clear what’s going on there. On the whole, it’s more atmosphere than story, but the atmosphere is memorable.
docs.title: The Edge of the War

docs.text: The Lions of Trafalgar Short Trips #4.5 Released: 10 August 2011 Listened: 4/11/20 Placing this story here because Tegan says they’ve come from 1982, so she’s presumably not trying to get back to Heathrow. The Doctor and company have arrived in Trafalgar shortly before Nelson’s Column was completed, when the architects hosted a large dinner atop the column. Except they’ve been taken over by aliens, who animate the lions (which aren’t supposed to exist yet) to attack the people in the square. There’s an unusual amount of action and bystander deaths for a Short Trip, and the Doctor solves the problem with an “I know you’re in there somewhere” solution, which isn’t terribly satisfying. They also leave behind an unusual number of anachronisms. I usually enjoy stories that take place around familiar landmarks, but this one kind of falls flat.
docs.title: The Lions of Trafalgar

docs.text: The Lost Resort The Lost Resort #1 Released: 8 September 2021 Listened: 9/14/21 This 2021 release is a boxed set continuing the story that was in progress after the end of the Main Range. In this four-parter, after picking up Nyssa, Tegan, and Marc, all of them still on edge, the Doctor promises that they’ll talk, and tries to head for Gallifrey to do so. They end up instead on a planet with a crumbly, spooky sanatorium. Marc hopes he can get treated for his cyber-conversion, but the robot who runs the place seems most interested in the Doctor’s mental fatigue. As the Doctor tries to induce a trance state, he’s confronted with a vision of Adric (played by Matthew Waterhouse). This is one of those stories with an isolated location and a very eccentric guest cast, with almost too many quirks to keep track of. Tegan is annoyed, surprising no one, but even she is careful around the idea that Adric is alive in some way. Marc maybe comes to some acceptance of his condition. And Nyssa proves that she’s capable of acting independently (which should have been obvious from the long stretch she was alone with the Doctor, but never mind). Although there’s a certain amount of deception, and some peril, there isn’t really a bad guy or an evil scheme, just a series of sad circumstances. Because the point of the story is the Doctor coming to terms with Adric’s death, and being able to finally say some last words and let go. Matthew Waterhouse certainly does his level best with the dialog, and I’m glad he was able to show up for this story, but it does give Adric a level of gravitas that he never really had on TV. I’m not sure it accomplishes all it set out to do, but it does hopefully bring to a close the friction that started back in “ Warzone/Conversion ,” and allows this group to go on to further stories.
docs.title: The Lost Resort

docs.text: The Mistpuddle Murders Short Trips #8.11 Released: 29 November 2018 Listened: 4/21/20 I’m placing this here to give Tegan and Nyssa a little break after “ Peterloo ,” in the absence of other clues. It’s an Agatha Christie style drawing-room mystery, or at least the end of one. The twists are that the Doctor isn’t around for most of it, and the villagers are anthropomorphic animals created by a children’s book author. Simon Forward does a great job of capturing Nyssa’s and Tegan’s personalities, and Sarah Sutton does an amazing job playing Tegan, narrating a chunk of the story and interrupting Nyssa at times. The Doctor shows up at the end, rather ex machina , but the bulk of the story lets the two women take the spotlight, to good effect. This story is my Exhibit A in why the next spin-off (TV or Big Finish) should be "The Tegan and Nyssa Mysteries."
docs.title: The Mistpuddle Murders

docs.text: The Perils of Nelly Bly The Lost Resort #2 Released: 8 September 2021 Listened: 9/15/21 Why not follow up a grim, emotional story with a two-part true historical? The TARDIS team lands on the ship carrying Nellie Bly on the last phase of her round-the-world trip, just before it reaches San Francisco. Historical figures in Doctor Who tend to be overwhelmingly awesome, or else rather arrogant and full of their own reputations. Nellie here is the latter, but everyone seems to like her anyway. None of the team have any idea who she is (not that Nyssa or Marc would), which is somewhat amusing. I'd heard her story before, but I know most people haven’t. Tegan is at first concerned about messing with history, but Nellie has such a force of personality that they’re quickly swapping outfits so Nellie can go incognito and find out what people are saying about her. This one is written by mystery novelist Sarah Ward, and as such, it has a lot of plot happenings, but not really much drama, as all the perilous situations get resolved pretty easily. It’s apparently fairly historically accurate, except that Nellie Bly probably didn’t have someone dogging her steps, actively trying to sabotage her. The story feels very slight, almost cartoonish, and the characters all seem somewhat shallow. It’s OK as a two-parter, but I wonder if it could have been better if it had more room to breathe.

docs.text: The Lost Resort #2 Released: 8 September 2021 Listened: 9/15/21 Why not follow up a grim, emotional story with a two-part true historical? The TARDIS team lands on the ship carrying Nellie Bly on the last phase of her round-the-world trip, just before it reaches San Francisco. Historical figures in Doctor Who tend to be overwhelmingly awesome, or else rather arrogant and full of their own reputations. Nellie here is the latter, but everyone seems to like her anyway. None of the team have any idea who she is (not that Nyssa or Marc would), which is somewhat amusing. I'd heard her story before, but I know most people haven’t. Tegan is at first concerned about messing with history, but Nellie has such a force of personality that they’re quickly swapping outfits so Nellie can go incognito and find out what people are saying about her. This one is written by mystery novelist Sarah Ward, and as such, it has a lot of plot happenings, but not really much drama, as all the perilous situations get resolved pretty easily. Unfortunately, like many pure historicals, it’s bleak, and this one is even darker than usual, with rather a lot of death and pretty much nobody coming off well, even the reporter sent to cover the events. It’s one of the ones dark enough to make you wonder why Nyssa and Tegan would want to continue traveling.

docs.text: The Waters of Amsterdam Main Range #208 Released: 11 January 2016 Listened: 12/7/19 A later story, in Main Range numbering, but an early one chronologically. I think that’s a good thing, as it allowed Janet Fielding to get comfortable playing Tegan again before recording her “rejoining” story. As far as the plot goes, it’s more about Tegan and her personal life than the villains as such. Tegan’s ex Kyle makes for an interesting character with a slow unwinding of his backstory. Rembrandt features, with the Big Finish trick of “famous historical figure is actually cranky, put-upon, and rather egotistical.” At the end of the story, the Doctor leaves Nyssa and Tegan in Amsterdam for a bit, which allows him to have a handful of solo adventures...a period which seems to keep growing.

docs.text: Thin Time Main Range #267 Released: 12 August 2020 Listened: 8/16/20 The Main Range entry for this month is divided into a pair of two-parters. It’s a bit odd that a significant story would be told this way, but that’s how it is. At first, this story seems to be a continuation of the short stories from “ Time Apart .” The Doctor ends up at an English manor house on Halloween 1890. The house is occupied by a writer, his visiting friend, a butler, and a cook, but something is quite wrong. There’s a bit of Lovecraft feel as Things from Outside are trying to get into our dimension where time is thin. The mystery involves the Doctor figuring out who started it, why, and where they currently are, which plays out to a satisfactory conclusion. What happens after that is a major spoiler, so I won’t go into it. However, the Doctor has a good think about the price paid by his companions, and whether he’s responsible for them, or if they choose to associate with him despite the risks. His conclusion leads to the end of the second story .
docs.title: Thin Time

docs.text: Towards Zero Main Range #270 Released: 10 November 2020 Listened: 11/10/20 Once again, we’ve got the same bunch of characters, and this time in a time loop built around an Agatha Christie-style manor-house murder mystery, where the Doctor is both the detective and the victim. At least now he’s starting to get an inkling of what’s going on in the larger story, recognizing what the time loop is built from, and that the other four characters are unreal fragments, but this seems like another exercise in letting the guest actors stretch out again. The Daleks are back to being shadowy voices in this one, and barely figure. There are some amusing clues that point to the Master’s involvement, but they don’t come to anything. Seems like more filler.
docs.title: Towards Zero

docs.text: Warzone Main Range #258 Released: 12 November 2019 Listened: 12/7/19 The two stories in this release are directly linked, but their tone is sharply divergent. The first part has Team TARDIS dropping involuntarily into the middle of an amped-up “Tough Mudder” race, with a certain amount of silliness, at least in the first part. Because I often listen to Big Finish while running, including the first time I heard this story, I was particularly amused. Tegan admits that her normal shoes aren’t appropriate for running, and Nyssa seems to want nothing to do with physical exercise, which seems odd, given that she’s in good shape, but maybe Trakenites maintain their figures in other ways. Marc comes off best, as he’s physically suited for the task and enjoys it...until he gets hurt, after which things get very dark, very quickly.
docs.title: Warzone

docs.text: What Lurks Down Under Main Range #266 Released: 1 July 2020 Listened: 8/1/20 The TARDIS lands on a ship of women prisoners being transported to Australia. (Amazingly, he only mentions Tegan once, and doesn’t go for the cheap shot.) It’s one of those “something’s gone wrong, there’s aliens involved, and it’s nobody’s fault” sort of stories that’s more common in the new series. The historical character Mary Ward is the companion substitute for this story, and much like Astrid Peth or Lady Christina, she makes an amazing companion, because she can’t come along. This was the last work by Tommy Donbavand before he passed away, fulfilling his desire to write a Big Finish audio.

docs.text: The Fifth Doctor, Nyssa, Tegan, and Turlough This is an interesting section designed to make use of a TARDIS team that didn’t really get much time together on TV. There seems to be a general agreement not to set stories in the period where Turlough is controlled by the Black Guardian (except for one Short Trip), so in order to get Nyssa back on the team, she needs to return after her departure. It feels a little awkward, but Tegan already did it, and they handle it as best they can. This is another long stretch of stories where the release order mostly matches up with chronological order for the characters.

docs.text: Cobwebs Main Range #136 Released: 15 July 2010 Listened: 12/6/19 This story is one of the more interesting long-term twists Big Finish pulled. In order to get Nyssa, Tegan, and Turlough all together without Turlough being evil, the story has to be set after “ Enlightenment ,” which means they need to bring Nyssa back at a point in her life after she left, 50 years in this case. At least they deal with it up front, and give Nyssa other concerns in her life, although she keeps some of them secret for now. The rest of the story is serviceable, with some confusing timey-wimey that’s worthy of the TV series. The trick to get out of the big cliffhanger seems contrived. Ironically, behind the scenes this is the first story that Janet Fielding did in her return to playing Tegan on a regular basis, so the extras are more about that than Nyssa, who has been appearing in Big Finish pretty much since the beginning.
docs.title: Cobwebs

Main Range #172 Released: 10 April 2013 Listened: 12/6/19 Interestingly, while the last Main Range story with this crew was a prequel to “ Talons ,” this one is a sequel to “ The Hand of Fear ,” and also written by Marc Platt. You don’t need to know as much about the earlier story this time, though. Turlough gets most of the spotlight this time, once again having difficulty with mind control and crystals, but as the Doctor points out, all of them have been susceptible to mind control at one time or another. I hope you don’t mind hearing the title, because the characters say it rather a lot.

docs.text: Freakshow Companion Chronicles Special Released: 4 March 2010 Listened: 5/17/20 I’m not sure exactly why this story was released as a special, instead of a regular Companion Chronicle, but there it is. Mark Strickson narrates, and it’s a Turlough-focused story in the American Old West, but it’s sci-fi, rather than a true historical. The first half has Turlough alone for much of it, and we get a lot of insight into how he feels right after having left the Black Guardian. The second half is more straight-up action story, with the Doctor taking a bigger role, and frankly a deus ex machina resolution. Strickson does a good job of playing both the Doctor and Tegan, just enough of an impression without being a parody. It’s a decent story for the peek inside Turlough’s head, if not for the plot.
docs.title: Freakshow

docs.text: Heroes of Sontar Main Range #146 Released: 14 April 2011 Listened: 12/6/19 This one is probably my favorite of this trilogy, because it doesn’t take itself too seriously. Even as an American with only slight familiarity with Dad’s Army , I immediately recognized it for the parody that it is. The story holds up reasonably well outside of the parody though, with an interesting plot that takes a while to unravel. Turlough’s character is used effectively here, both his survival instincts and his military background. The Sontarans are all distinct characters with their own motivations, a good trick with clones. And surprisingly for a Sontaran story, Dan Starkey is nowhere to be found.
