docs.text: The Doctor's Tale Early Adventures #1.2 Released: 17 October 2014 Listened: 1/31/20 This is another longer story, from the first set of Early Adventures. The formula hadn’t quite gelled yet, so the story mostly focuses on Ian and Vicki, with Barbara off-stage for almost the entire story. I imagine the story is more effective if you know more about the death of Richard II and the rise of Henry IV , but I don’t, really. One of the main historical characters is Richard’s queen Isabella, who is portrayed as being around Vicki’s age, and a firebrand, although historically, she would have been rather younger. The other figure is Geoffrey Chaucer, who seems like he should play an important role, but mostly just seems to tag along with the others. The plot itself is typical for a second-season historical, with the characters stumbling into trouble, getting separated, and spending the rest of the story trying to find one another again and get back to the TARDIS. It’s not a particularly strong story, which makes it a shame that it leads directly into “ The Chase ,” which means this is the last appearance of Ian and Barbara in this project.
docs.title: The Doctor's Tale

docs.text: The Fifth Traveller Early Adventures #3.2 Released: 13 October 2016 Listened: 1/30/20 Early Adventures are four-parters, so we’re back to a longer story. Which is good, because the Doctor, Ian, Barbara, Vicki, and Jospa -- what’s that? You don’t remember Jospa? There’s a reason for that. The writer doesn’t really try to trick you for too long about that, but with the longer running time, the mystery can simmer in the background just long enough for you to accept Jospa. The only real flaw is that James Joyce, who plays Captain Carter in the UNIT series, doesn’t really sound like he’s Vicki’s age, which is what we’re supposed to believe. Speaking of voices, though, Jemma Powell plays Barbara again, William Russell plays both Ian and the Doctor, and Maureen O’Brien plays a much younger Vicki. It shouldn’t work with that many different actors, but for the most part, it comes off fine. Russell isn’t the best Hartnell impersonator, but he captures the essence. His Ian mostly sounds the right age, except for a few moments. Maureen O’Brien somehow makes you think she’s a girl without fail, and Powell’s accent, which sounded a bit out of place in the other Early Adventure she’s in, doesn’t really jar here. As for the rest of the plot, it’s serviceable, but a story about psychic orangutans is a little hard to get your head around.
docs.title: The Fifth Traveler

docs.text: The Revenants Companion Chronicles Special Released: 31 May 2012 Listened: 1/17/23 There’s only one story in this gap between Susan leaving and Vicki joining, this Companion Chronicle special. It’s on the long side for a Companion Chronicle, clocking in at a bit over an hour. I have no clue what makes this story warrant a special, but here it is. As often happens, Ian and Barbara get separated from the Doctor early on, but in this case, it’s the TARDIS that leaves, which in this era, means they’ll likely never see him again. So they’re stuck on Orkney, but fortunately, quite close to their own time. And, of course, there’s something weird going on, connected to the ancient legends of Orkney, because of course it is. William Russell continues to sound good as both Ian and the Doctor, but like many Chronicles, this one uses the conceit of Ian telling the story much later in life. The story itself is actually fairly small-scale, without a whole lot of actual peril, but the cliffhanger at the end of Part 1 and the twist at the end of Part 2 are quite well executed.
docs.title: The Revenants

docs.text: The Rocket Men Companion Chronicles #6.2 Released: 10 August 2011 Listened: 1/31/20 I’ve been looking forward to this story for a while, because I’ve heard other Rocket Men stories, but I hadn’t heard the original. Plus, I love a John Dorney story. This is one of his earlier ones, so it’s relatively straightforward, and not as twisty as his later stories. The storyline is split in two, though, alternating between different time periods within the story, before catching up at the end. That serves to preserve the suspense of the cliffhanger before it happens, but there’s no narrative reason for the story to be split like that. Unlike the older Companion Chronicles, this is just a straight story, without a frame of an older Ian telling a story. While the cliffhanger is very dramatic, and probably would have looked amazing on TV, I was able to figure out the resolution, which takes a little bit away from it. The focus of the story is mostly on Ian, with Vicki in a minor role, and the Doctor mostly off-screen. Specifically, it’s about Ian and Barbara’s relationship finally moving forward, something that the extras imply they felt confident doing because The Sarah Jane Adventures had stated that they end up together. It’s emotionally satisfying, and appropriate that this story takes place late in their tenure. The Rocket Men may not be to everyone’s taste, since they’re modeled on 50s movie-serial villains, but I like them. They’re a legitimate recurring threat, and because their goals are relatively simple, they just have to be stopped when they appear, not completely crushed.
docs.title: The Rocket Men

docs.text: The Sleeping City Companion Chronicles #8.8 Released: 13 February 2014 Listened: 1/28/20 A bit further down the chronology now, this Companion Chronicle’s frame story takes place after Ian and Barbara have returned home, and seem to be in a lot of trouble with spy agencies because of their disappearance, which is realistic, but more of a new-series idea. So Ian decides to tell a story of some random visit to a planet where the citizens all engage in shared dreaming. Except not everything is what it seems, and it wraps up rather nicely. docs.text: The First Doctor, Steven, and Dodo Jackie Lane was the only living companion actor from the classic series who refused the invitation to be part of Big Finish. She quit acting and became a voice-over agent, representing Tom Baker, Nicholas Courtney, and Janet Fielding, among others. However, she retired in 2000, before Big Finish really got started. Although Big Finish could get around her unavailability with Companion Chronicles, they mostly just avoided Dodo for a long time. There were a handful of Companion Chronicles and Short Trips until 2021, when they recast Lauren Cornelius as Dodo. Sadly, Jackie passed away in June 2021, a few months before the first story with Cornelius was released. Since then, Big Finish have released a number of stories with Steven Noonan as the First Doctor and Cornelius as Dodo, filling out what was really a brief period on TV.
docs.title: First Doctor, Steven, & Dodo

docs.text: Mother Russia Companion Chronicles #2.1 Released: October 2007 Listened: 2/27/20 This is one of the very earliest Companion Chronicles recorded, so it’s a bit more narrated than usual, and Peter Purves’ First Doctor impersonation isn’t quite as polished. It’s an early appearance for Dodo, but it’s definitely set after they’ve been to Tombstone, so she’s more confident as part of the crew. She doesn’t have a ton to do, staying mostly “off-camera,” but the writer has pegged her rebellious streak, and given her some 1960s slang to differentiate her from Susan and Vicki. The story itself features the “companion telling a story to a hostile interrogator” trope that the Companion Chronicles used to use a lot. This time, it’s set in 1812, in Russia, so while it’s not a true historical, there’s still plenty of grimness as they get caught up in Napoleon’s march on Moscow. The baddie is a shapeshifter, who takes several different forms throughout the story, and Steven is really slow to pick up on it. Even accounting for the fact that he’s never met one before, several events hinge on his gullibility. On the whole, it’s a good enough entry for a first appearance.
docs.title: Mother Russia

docs.text: Return of the Rocket Men Companion Chronicles #7.5 Released: 10 November 2012 Listened: 3/2/20 This is a sequel to “ The Rocket Men ” from earlier in this chronology, and where that one was definitely an Ian story, this one is decidedly a Steven story. It’s written by Matt Fitton instead of John Dorney, and although Fitton tries to mimic some of the structure of Dorney’s story, it doesn’t quite come off. What does come off well is making the Rocket Men seem like a serious and credible threat, which works well with the 60s atmosphere. I don’t think they’re as dangerous in their subsequent appearances. It’s also a good showcase for Steven, operating within his own native era, so he’s the most knowledgeable character for once, and he gets to use his piloting skills, something that never happened on TV. It’s not quite as good as the original, but it’s a strong sequel.
docs.title: Return of the Rocket Men

docs.text: The Demon Song First Doctor Adventures #2.1 Released: 16 February 2023 Listened: 2/26/23 The first boxed set with Stephen Noonan and Lauren Cornelius was a success, so here’s another. This time around, the two-parter comes first. It’s set in Camden in the 2020s, post-pandemic anyway, which is a heck of a thing for Dodo, but she seems to take it all pretty much in stride, once she gets over everybody’s phones. The First Doctor is written brilliantly here, as he clearly knows about the history and technology of this period, but doesn’t seem to have experienced it himself, so he’s both familiar and unfamiliar. The story involves an alien (considered a demon by many) who’s spreading a song that hypnotizes people, and then kidnaps them. Of course, that turns out to be pretty standard stuff. A lot of the scenes with the Doctor are played for humor, as he’s either confused or confusing people. Once again, I feel like Stephen Noonan is playing him too high-pitched, and they’ve still got the tic of Hartnell blowing his lines, which I don’t like. And yet the scenes with Dodo are often serious and very grim, although the wild tracks of screaming and moaning in the background seem rather overdone. On the whole, it’s OK, but the tonal clash hurts it.
docs.title: The Demon Song

A lot of the scenes with the Doctor are played for humor, as he’s either confused or confusing people. Once again, I feel like Stephen Noonan is playing him too high-pitched, and they’ve still got the tic of Hartnell blowing his lines, which I don’t like. And yet the scenes with Dodo are often serious and very grim, although the wild tracks of screaming and moaning in the background seem rather overdone. On the whole, it’s OK, but the tonal clash hurts it.
docs.title: The Demon Song

docs.text: The Doctor's Gambit Short Trips Special Released: 21 June 2025 Listened: 3/17/26 This is a Short Trip from a special collection of two stories, called "A Feast of Steven," along with " A Forest of All Seasons " much earlier in the chronology. It's another story where Steven is playing hero, but also supporting his friends in having agency of their own. The plot involves the TARDIS team getting forcibly recruited for a deadly game of human chess, which even Jacqueline Rayner admits isn't the most original trope. But what makes this story different from "Forest" is that we spend a good chunk of time in Dodo's head, which we didn't in Vicki's. The selection process gives Dodo flashbacks to school, where she was an outsider because of her accent, as well as feeling unwanted in her family after the death of her parents, which had only been alluded to briefly on TV. This story also has more explicit continuity references, as Dodo worries that the chess game might be the work of the Celestial Toymaker . On his part, Steven reflects on the number of friends he's seen die in his time with the Doctor, specifically mentioning Bret, Katarina, and Sara , as well as Oliver , which is the first reference to Oliver I've heard outside the stories where he appears, so that made me smile. The Doctor is largely absent for this one, but Peter Purves continues to do a good job invoking William Hartnell without imitating him. In the extras, he admits that he no longer hears Hartnell in his head as he did when he first started with Big Finish, which is a reminder that we're lucky that he's still both willing and able to participate.
docs.title: The Doctor's Gambit

docs.text: The Horror at Bletchington Station Short Trips Rarities #3.1 Released: 15 March 2016 Listened: 3/4/20 When this was released, it was a very rare story, with just the Doctor and Dodo. As a result, it’s the first Big Finish story that deals with Dodo’s internal thoughts. That’s an interesting perspective, because we don’t really have enough Dodo around to get a sense of what she’s like. This story also features some introspection on the Doctor’s part, as he seems to realize that he’s reaching the end of his life and reflects on how he’s changed since he started hanging out with humans. The story itself is a bit spooky, but mostly standard, with a Time Lord twist at the end that doesn’t really change much, but lets you feel a bit clever for understanding the reference.

docs.text: The Incherton Incident First Doctor Adventures #2.2 Released: 16 February 2023 Listened: 3/3/23 This four-parter, by Nick Briggs, is set in 1947, in an isolated seacoast town, because Nick Briggs likes both those things. Unfortunately, as a result of a collision in the Vortex, a spaceship has crashed into Incherton and killed a lot of people. In First-Doctor style, it takes quite a while for the Doctor and listeners to figure out what the heck is going on, during which time the Doctor and Dodo are separated, and both of them end up getting shot, although they aren’t badly hurt. Much of the story involves early Cold War politics, with the British army trying to claim alien tech for their own, an American spy claiming that allies should share technology, and a Soviet spy that everybody assumes must be somewhere (see if you can spot them; it’s not actually very hard). There’s something deeper going on here, though, as the aliens are time-travelers looking to arrest the Doctor for things he hasn’t done yet. There are hints that his crime relates to enabling humanity throughout their history, allowing them to become a major power in the universe eventually. We’re not really sure, though, because the First Doctor just assumes it’s all a misunderstanding. There are some pretty heavy-handed parallels about the line between fanaticism and patriotism, but it’s hard not to default to assuming the post-WWII English are the “good guys.” The Doctor has a lengthy speech at the end of the story laying out his purpose in traveling, which seems a bit odd to just drop in at the end here, but it leads to a cliffhanger.
docs.title: The Incherton Incident

docs.text: The Miniaturist First Doctor Adventures #1.2 Released: 12 April 2022 Listened: 4/20/22 The second story of this boxed set is only a two-parter, but it’s lengthy for a two-parter. Still, it feels like it has just the right pacing, keeping things moving while preserving the mystery. It’s a very mysterious, almost dreamlike story, one that wouldn’t be out of place in the modern series, something like “ Midnight ” or “ Amy’s Choice .” Writer Lizzie Hopley drops in some scientific facts, like the Zechstein seabed , and geological quiet points. The mystery, though, revolves around a psychic entity that seems to pull images from people’s minds, and also plays with dimensions, leading to some very surreal experiences. Dodo is on her own for a while, and there’s some vague hinting here about traumatic events in her childhood, which weren’t revealed on TV. I liked Stephen Noonan’s performance better in this story; he spends more time pitching the Doctor at a threatening growl than the high-pitched giggle. While both stories are decent, I much prefer this one.
docs.title: The Miniaturist

docs.text: The Outlaws First Doctor Adventures #1.1 Released: 12 April 2022 Listened: 4/19/22 This is the first of a new era of First Doctor Adventures, featuring Stephen Noonan as the Doctor, with Lauren Cornelius continuing as Dodo. It allows an opportunity to flesh out this part of the First Doctor era, and give Dodo a consistent character, which she never really had on TV. Cornelius has really mastered her choices as Dodo, sounding a lot like a modern companion with her accent, word choice, and shaky grasp of history. Stephen Noonan isn’t doing an impersonation, but he’s certainly closer to Hartnell’s performance than David Bradley is. However, he plays the Doctor as frequently high-pitched and silly-sounding, so that when he drops into his gruff, outraged tone, it’s an odd transition. Worse, they’ve kept Hartnell’s tic of stumbling over words. I wish they hadn’t done that, as it seems like a Hartnell thing, rather than a Doctor thing, and as such, it’s rather disrespectful. As for the story itself, it’s almost a pure historical, taking place in Lincoln in 1216. King John is on the throne, the French are about to invade, and Nicholaa de la Haye is Sheriff of Lincoln. Which would be fine, except that Dodo has a 1960s interpretation of John’s reign, and gets herself in trouble. There’s also a band of thieves who appear to be doing the Robin Hood thing, but without the “give to the poor” part. The thing that makes it not a pure historical is that the Monk is here, the Rufus Hound version, helping the outlaws. Although this is much later in the Monk’s personal timeline, he was expecting the First Doctor, and seems to hold a grudge against him specifically for the events of “ The Time Meddler .” However, he’s still the Rufus Hound Monk, so it’s always fun to hear him become apoplectic, even if it seems like it would fit better in a more modern story. There are minor historical characters scattered about: the sheriff’s granddaughter, the head of her guards, and the bandit leader, but to be honest, their plot threads don’t really go anywhere, or at least, they aren’t much influenced by the Doctor and Dodo. Their part seems to be mostly “get back to the TARDIS” with a side of “stop the Monk.” On the whole, it feels like the story isn’t all that important, and we’re just listening to the actors do their thing.
docs.title: The Outlaws

docs.text: The Secrets of Det-Sen Early Adventures #7.2 Released: 17 August 2021 Listened: 8/19/21 This is the first story featuring Lauren Cornelius as Dodo. It’s also a trip to Tibet, forming a direct prequel to “ The Abominable Snowmen .” If you know that story well, you can probably guess at some of the plot twists here, but most people don’t know it, as it’s currently a lost story. But all the same trappings are in place, including the monks, the monastery, and even yeti, although in this case natural creatures rather than robots. Cornelius plays Dodo with a distinct accent, which doesn’t seem quite what Jackie Lane did on TV, but is closer to the accent that Dodo would’ve had. Dodo herself seems to be doing well in this story, getting along with the pilgrims and the monks, and even the yeti. Fortunately, they all seem to find her irreverence amusing. Steven is having a much harder time of it, starting with altitude sickness that makes him cranky for the whole story. Worse, he’s distrustful of several of the other characters, and flatly dismissive of the monks’ pacifist beliefs. That’s probably not out of line for the 1960s, but I’d expect a character from the future to be less parochial. Peter Purves does his usual fine job voicing the Doctor, who mostly seems respectful towards the monks, but also barges around the monastery like he has the right to go wherever he wants, and considers his own philosophy to be superior. As a true historical and a 1960s story, it’s a little on the slow side compared to modern stories, but probably better paced than other stories from the period. It’s a nice start for full-cast stories featuring Dodo.
docs.title: The Secrets of Det-Sen

docs.text: The War to End All Wars Companion Chronicles #8.10 Released: 9 April 2014 Listened: 3/3/20 This story is the first part of a trilogy, at least as far as the frame stories are concerned, but told out of order for this chronology. The story continues from here to “ The Founding Fathers ,” which appeared earlier, and then to “ The Locked Room ,” which comes at the end. But the frame story itself follows Steven’s life from the events of “ The Savages ,” although much later. We sort of find out what he’s been doing since then, but much of it is kept a mystery. As for the flashback, it’s a pretty heavy allegory, with Steven and Dodo getting caught up in an endless war, and brainwashed into fighting. Although they give it their best shot, it’s an off-screen Doctor who solves everything, which is kind of an odd resolution. The frame story is really the meat of the action here, with Steven interacting with his granddaughter and explaining why he’d done the things he’d done since assuming control of this society in “The Savages,” which plays into the follow-up stories. This was the last Companion Chronicle recorded in the main series, but clearly the plan to continue as boxed sets was already in place, because this story sets up a sequel. It seems reasonable this would be the last appearance of Peter Purves in this chronology, but it isn’t, quite.
docs.title: The War to End All Wars

docs.text: This Sporting Life Short Trips #6.5 Released: 31 May 2016 Listened: 3/4/20 This one is lightweight, and mostly a joke on the title, which refers to a film Hartnell was in , in 1963. The story itself revolves around the theft of the World Cup in 1966 , which is a strange story that's worth reading about if you're not familiar. Much of the humor derives from the fact that it’s set in Dodo’s native time, so she understands what’s going on, and Steven is totally at sea. The rest of the story is serviceable, with a small amount of misdirection that’s not too hard to see coming.

docs.text: The First Doctor, Steven, and Oliver Oliver is a real rarity in Big Finish: a brand-new companion inserted into the earliest stories. Original companions are unusual, but not unheard of, but this is the only one who was created in the Companion Chronicles, instead of in the Main Range. The stories after that are the Doctor traveling with just Steven, which is technically what they’re doing in “ The Massacre ,” but that period tends to be overlooked, since it didn’t last very long.

docs.text: Helmstone Subscriber Short Trips #2017.3 Released: 12 September 2017 Listened: 2/25/20 This is one of the bonus Short Trips for subscribers, which means very little music, minimal sound effects, and in this case, the narration is by Stephen Critchlow, which is something of a surprise after hearing Peter Purves for so long. Some time has probably passed since the last story, as Steven isn’t overcome by grief. It’s one of those stories where the TARDIS crew seems to be welcomed by a group of people, and they have some odd customs the crew doesn’t really understand, which turn out to be masking something horribly wrong. Except in this case, even the natives themselves don’t know what’s wrong, so we’re spared the usual tying up the outsiders and sentencing them to death. The Doctor seems to be unusually tight-lipped for this period, leaving Steven to stumble around by himself, trying to solve what he believes to be the problem. Being a short and rather spare story, it doesn’t exactly stick in the mind, but it’s a nice brief diversion.
docs.title: Helmstone

docs.text: Peace in Our Time Short Trips #9.12 Released: 23 December 2019 Listened: 4/30/20 Setting this one here because it fits in the short gap where Steven is alone with the Doctor. They end up in 1906, tracking some folks who are trying to steal the plans for the HMS Dreadnaught , for mysterious reasons. But most of the story is told from the point of view of Ruby, a servant who gets mixed up in all of this, and has to continually remind people (including Steven) that she’s neither deaf nor stupid, and rather refuses to be put off. This all occurs against the backdrop of the Suffragette movement, but Steven doesn’t mention having encountered that before .

docs.text: Short Trips #9.12 Released: 23 December 2019 Listened: 4/30/20 Setting this one here because it fits in the short gap where Steven is alone with the Doctor. They end up in 1906, tracking some folks who are trying to steal the plans for the HMS Dreadnaught , for mysterious reasons. But most of the story is told from the point of view of Ruby, a servant who gets mixed up in all of this, and has to continually remind people (including Steven) that she’s neither deaf nor stupid, and rather refuses to be put off. This all occurs against the backdrop of the Suffragette movement, but Steven doesn’t mention having encountered that before .
docs.title: Peace in Our Time

docs.text: The Cold Equations Companion Chronicles #5.12 Released: 2 June 2011 Listened: 2/23/20 The second part of Oliver’s trilogy again dials down the sci-fi elements, in favor of the human element, and in this case, actual science. When Steven and Oliver end up trapped on a bit of space junk that’s losing air rapidly, Steven gets to show off his pilot’s training, in the form of orbital equations, to help get them out of it. And he narrates every bit of it while he does it, which certainly demonstrates that writer Simon Guerrier did his homework, but also smacks of the writer showing you his homework, which can break the suspension of disbelief. Of course, since they’re going to die, Oliver confesses his “crime” to Steven: he’s gay. In fairness, Steven had been concerned about having a companion who was hiding something, possibly something serious. Once he knows, Steven naturally laughs it off, which isn’t the best reaction, but to be fair, the story doesn’t immediately turn to “well, it’s the future, so you’re fine now.” Oliver’s still left behind everything he knows, and can’t go back, so everything isn’t really OK just because he’s in the future. It’s a strong story, maybe a bit slight given the running time, but a good listen.
docs.title: The Cold Equations

docs.text: The First Wave Companion Chronicles #6.5 Released: 8 November 2011 Listened: 2/24/20 Poor Oliver. Only three stories, and he never left the solar system. Once again, there’s a lot of hard science in this story, perhaps a touch too much. The Vardans are the bad guys, which is somewhat unexpected. The Doctor is aware of them before this story, but it seems to be the first time the Vardans meet him, and they find out about Gallifrey, which will play a role in the future . The Doctor gets rather arrogant again about his responsibility to the Laws of Time, and Oliver calls him out on it in a big way. I won’t spoil Oliver’s final fate, but I find myself wishing he’d stayed around longer. The Doctor and Steven don’t really need more sad departures at this point, and Oliver deserved to be able to see more, I think. I liked him as a companion, and it’s a good trilogy on the whole.
docs.title: The First Wave

docs.text: The Perpetual Bond Companion Chronicles #5.8 Released: February 2011 Listened: 2/23/20 The setup here is strong, with Oliver getting a cold open, and then Steven clearly grieving from the events of “ The Daleks' Master Plan ,” and then the TARDIS landing in Totter’s Lane, perhaps as a kindness. Oliver has a serious problem, which isn’t revealed in this story, but it’s ruining his life enough that he wants to leave and never come back. He’s capable and quick-witted, which is always key in a potential companion, a bit confused by what’s going on, but he adapts quickly. His voice is engaging, and sounds a little bit like James Joyce from the UNIT series. The Doctor is clearly suffering some shock from having lost two companions recently, and he comes off as rather cold, much like he sometimes gets in the new series when he’s pushed far enough. He’s quite willing to let unscrupulous characters suffer the punishment they’ve unknowingly set up for themselves, which is more of a new-series thing. On top of that, it’s got great 1960s flavor. On the whole, it’s a good episode.
docs.title: The Perpetual Bond

docs.text: The Vardan Invasion of Mirth Companion Chronicles #13.3 Released: 18 September 2019 Listened: 2/26/20 This one is somewhat unusual, as it’s not a very serious story, but rather focuses on the state of British comedy in the 1950s, which Steven unwittingly gets involved in. The bad guys are the Vardans, which seems odd in this chronology, because they appeared not long ago , but Steven doesn’t reference Oliver at all. A lot of the humor stems from Steven being bewildered by 1950s British culture, although I wonder how many in the target audience can remember it.

docs.text: The First Doctor, Steven, and Sara Speaking of characters who didn’t have any room for their own story, Jean Marsh as Sara Kingdom shouldn’t have any space for added narrative, but “ The Daleks’ Master Plan ” specifically has a gap in the middle of it, and Jean Marsh seemed to enjoy doing Big Finish, so there’s more stories packed in there than you’d expect, some of which are quite good. Jean Marsh herself appears in most of them, which is only slightly unexpected, but pleasant. There’s a trilogy of Companion Chronicles in here that are all part of a connected story, but it’s the frame stories that follow release order, and the flashbacks take place in reverse order. If you’re doing this project yourself, I’ll strongly recommend that you break from the chronological order and listen in release order, just this once.
docs.title: First Doctor, Steven, & Sara

docs.text: An Ordinary Life Early Adventures #1.4 Released: 16 December 2014 Listened: 2/22/20 These last two stories are from the Early Adventures series, which means they’re longer, full-cast stories, which is nice, because Peter Purves and Jean Marsh play off each other quite well. This story is one of my favorites from this era, not because of the high concept, but because of the character focus. The TARDIS lands in London in the 1950s, and it appears the Doctor has left Sara and Steven behind. Because they’re both from the future, they have some trouble adapting, and end up living in a boarding house upstairs from a Jamaican family, newly arrived in London. With their limited knowledge of history, Steven and Sara just don’t comprehend the racism the family faces; they just can’t get it through their heads at all. Which is a nice thought from the writer, but Purves and Marsh have to sell it, and they succeed. The sci-fi plot doesn’t actually start until halfway through, and I don’t mind. It’s a pretty normal body-snatchers subplot, but that’s not really the important bit. I have to salute the guest actors, whose Jamaican accents make a nice change from the voices normally found in these stories.
docs.title: An Ordinary Life

docs.text: Home Truths Companion Chronicles #3.5 Released: November 2008 Listened: 2/22/20 This story is the first part of the trilogy, and therefore the first appearance of Jean Marsh as Sara since 1967, so it’s worth listening to the interviews. This time, the frame story and the flashback are both part of the same story, so listening to this one first sets up the other two properly. It’s creepy and atmospheric, and like a lot of such stories, especially early Companion Chronicles, which are narrated, there’s more telling than showing. In this case, that works to the story’s advantage, as it puts the focus on Sara and what she’s thinking about her situation, both in this story and with the Doctor in general. Also, the ending is ambiguous, which works better if you haven’t heard the subsequent stories. Because the frame story and the flashback mesh so well, this story is more coherent than the other two, and makes this the best of the three, in my opinion.
docs.title: Home Truths

docs.text: The Anachronauts Companion Chronicles #6.7 Released: January 2012 Listened: 2/19/20 The next batch of Companion Chronicles take place in reverse order to their release order. This one is a bumper release with both Jean Marsh and Peter Purves, who once again plays both Steven and the Doctor. Half of it is set on a strange planet, and the other half in 1966 Germany, but there’s head games all around, so you need to be careful about what you’re hearing. Jean Marsh sounds distinctly older than Sara did originally, but she has the advantage that she didn’t have many episodes back then, so most listeners don’t remember what she sounded like. She plays Sara as tough and capable, with a military mind, which makes a distinct contrast to pretty much all the companions so far, women or men. Because it’s a longer story, there’s some time spent on her relationship with Steven, with the Doctor out of the picture, but that relationship is one of strong friendship and loyalty, even though they haven’t known each other very long. There are a number of minor characters who aren’t voiced, because it’s a Companion Chronicle, which detracts from the impact of the story -- a failing that this line doesn’t normally fall victim to. The overall plot may not be the strongest, but it’s a decent story.
docs.title: The Anachronauts

docs.text: The Drowned World Companion Chronicles #4.1 Released: 28 July 2009 Listened: 2/21/20 This is the middle story of the trilogy, both in the frame story and in the flashback. Which you’d think would make things easier, but the frame story seems to be the real story the author is trying to tell. The flashback, regarding some miners trapped by semi-sentient water, is dramatic, but brief, almost inconsequential. It’s the frame story with Sara and the visitor Robert that seems to be important, and in this case, it’s slightly let down by there being only two actors, and in this case, by my knowing already how that part of the story ends. It’s not as surreal as the previous story, but doesn’t carry a lot more impact.

docs.text: The Guardian of the Solar System Companion Chronicles #5.1 Released: 15 July 2010 Listened: 2/20/20 For the first time in this project, I’m disadvantaged by trying to go in chronological order and conflicting with the Companion Chronicles format. These three stories form a trilogy with Sara, where the frame stories go in release order, but the flashbacks go in reverse order. So listening to this story first gives me spoilers for “ Home Truths .” Alas. But turning to the flashback, it relies a lot on the listener’s knowledge of “ The Daleks Master Plan ,” or at least Sara’s role in it. The story about Mavic Chen using a giant mystical clock to keep the Earth Empire running is...kind of surreal, which doesn’t really match my limited knowledge of the “Master Plan,” so that kind of jars, but the frame story is also a bit surreal, so that fits. Even though this is the final part of the frame story, it doesn’t really resolve, just suggests, and maybe that’s appropriate.
docs.title: The Guardian of the Solar System

docs.text: The Little Drummer Boy Short Trips Rarities #1.4 Released: 30 September 2016 Listened: 2/18/20 This is a short trip, set explicitly after the Christmas special “The Feast of Steven” from the middle of “ The Daleks’ Master Plan ,” and read by Beth Chalmers, veteran of a number of Big Finish roles, but most known for Raine Creevy. Her style doesn’t really match any of the characters in this story, Steven least of all, but that’s all right, because it’s a narrated story. As a Christmas short trip, it’s more whimsical than anything else, and it’s definitely Christmas-related, featuring a boy reliving various Christmases throughout time. The Doctor’s solution to the dilemma may seem a little heartless, and certainly violates the rules of paradox as we’ve been led to understand them, but hey, it’s Christmas, so why not?
docs.title: The Little Drummer Boy

docs.text: The Sontarans Early Adventures #3.4 Released: 14 December 2016 Listened: 2/23/20 This is the most recent release featuring Sara, and with Jean Marsh's passing in 2025, there won't be more. It’s a shame that she doesn’t have more to do in this story, as Peter Purves does all the narration, and the story clearly leads into the second part of “ The Daleks’ Master Plan .” It features the Doctor’s first encounter with Sontarans, and I’m a bit surprised the BBC let Big Finish do something definitive like that, but maybe they don’t care. In a twist, both Steven and Sara know about Sontarans, but haven’t encountered them. New-series Sontarans have been treated as lightweight, often comic relief, thanks to Strax , so making them a credible threat in an early story like this is tricky, especially when you’ve got Dan Starkey playing most of them. These Sontarans seem to be scary and military, but they’ve also got an overdeveloped sense of honor and fair play, to the point of foolishness, which the Doctor uses against them. The Doctor seems a little out of character too, letting people take terrible risks, even fatal ones, to his benefit. Add in some very dodgy geophysics and mountaineering, and I can’t rate this one very highly. It’s a nice expansion into a full-cast story, but not as strong as its predecessor.
docs.title: The Sontarans

docs.text: The First Doctor, Vicki, and Steven With both Peter Purves and Maureen O’Brien actively participating in Big Finish, there’s plenty of room for stories with the two of them, even though they didn’t have much TV time together. The end of this section gets a little strange. “ The Destroyers ” features none of the regular characters, and is a lead-in to “ Mission to the Unknown ,” which does the same. Then Vicki leaves and Katarina arrives in “ The Myth Makers .” Adrienne Hill passed away in 1997, so she’s unavailable, which hadn’t really mattered as Katarina doesn’t really have a place to fit a story...except this is Big Finish, so they added one in 2019, except it’s also a Second Doctor crossover, so I’ll deal with it then .

docs.text: A Forest of All Seasons Short Trips Special Released: 21 June 2025 Listened: 3/17/26 This Short Trip is from a special collection of two stories, called "A Feast of Steven." Apparently this came about shortly after the recording of " The Living Darkness ," when Jacqueline Rayner wanted to write some more stories with Steven, and Peter Purves wanted some more time playing the First Doctor. The emphasis in both stories is Steven trying to take care of his younger companion, but also getting glimpses into his own potential future. In this story, they're on a planet where the same people and places seem to exist in different time zones simultaneously. This gives Steven the opportunity to meet an attractive woman of his own age, and see them as a young married couple, and again as an older man after her death. The actual sci-fi explanation of how that happens is somewhat weak, in my opinion, but the point of the story is presenting a "life in a day" kind of future that gives Steven something to chew on.
docs.title: A Forest of All Seasons

docs.text: Across the Darkened City Companion Chronicles 11.2 Released: 15 June 2017 Listened: 2/10/20 This next two stories are slightly odd, because normally the boxed-set Companion Chronicles go in chronological order within a set, but Craig Brawley figures in this case, the second story happens first, because of one aside from Steven in the first story . This box set starts with two Steven & Vicki stories, unlike the previous set (probably because of the unavailability of William Russell again). This is a fairly tight story, with mostly only Peter Purves as Steven, and Nick Briggs as a lone Dalek. It starts in media res , with an awful lot of Daleks killing people, but quickly ends up with just two characters. From there it becomes an “Enemy Mine” story (Nick Brigs even says so in the extras) with Steven and the Dalek being forced to cooperate. But this is a Dalek, so the whole “sympathetic enemy” trick is an open question. I’d say it resolves fairly satisfactorily. The narration works pretty well for this story, because it lets us inside Steven’s head when he’s got nobody else to talk to.
docs.title: Across the Darkened City

docs.text: An Ideal World Early Adventures #5.2 Released: 17 October 2018 Listened: 7/24/22 We head straight into another story with an ethical dilemma, but unfortunately this one is even more heavy-handed. The TARDIS lands on a planet that’s being surveyed for terraforming. The surveyors are making every effort not to disturb the planet’s natural ecosystem until they’re sure there’s no intelligent life. They even have an ethicist in a senior position, which is apparently standard procedure. Unfortunately, the planet doesn’t really have a breathable atmosphere; the surveyors just created a small, temporary one, which tricks the TARDIS crew into going outside without survival gear, with unfortunate consequences. And which splits up the party, because that always has to happen. We learn that both Vicki and Stephen have nanotech in their blood that protects them from alien diseases, although the Doctor does not…which seems very odd, as the Doctor is normally more resilient than his companions when it comes to disease. Much like the last story , there’s a political power play going on here between the Captain and the Ethicist, and it doesn’t play out well. The Doctor insists on standing on his principles no matter what the cost, which brings strong reactions from Vicki and Stephen, and seems somewhat inconsistent with his later behavior. I think author Ian Potter was trying to set up a “both sides are right” argument, but it really doesn’t look that way to me. It’s unsettling, but not in a good, thoughtful way.
docs.title: An Ideal World

docs.text: Entanglement Early Adventures #5.3 Released: 14 November 2018 Listened: 7/25/22 It’s pretty rare, but every once in a while Big Finish comes up with a story that only really makes sense if you’re English. In this case, it also helps to have a knowledge of the English university system, particularly Cambridge, the works of Lewis Caroll, who Kim Philby and Guy Burgess were, and a smattering of quantum theory as well. As I only have some of that background knowledge, the story didn’t work for me as well as it could have. I’m also not sure why writers Robert Khan and Tom Salinsky chose to fictionalize Trinity College into Sedgwick College, but leave virtually all the other historical names intact. Maybe it’s tradition? Anyway, the TARDIS lands in Cambridge in the 1930s, and it eventually becomes clear that Something Is Off. But it takes a while to get to that point, because it’s a university, so how can you really tell if a student or professor is acting strangely? And Stephen and Vicki really lack the context for this particular situation. These writers have a tendency to show off their cleverness in stories that don’t take themselves entirely seriously. It’s an acquired taste, and not always successful.
docs.title: Entanglement

docs.text: Fields of Terror Companion Chronicles 11.1 Released: 15 June 2017 Listened: 2/11/20 This episode is a true historical, set during the tail end of the French Revolution, which means it’s unrelentingly grim and dark. At least the Doctor knows this, because he’s been there before, and for a change, even he wants to just leave, but events prevent them. Out in the French countryside, Republic armies are ravaging the landscape and killing indiscriminately, which the TARDIS crew blunders into. It’s one of those stories where all they’re trying to do is stay alive long enough to leave again, which makes for a bleak story, but fortunately this one is short. One notable aspect is that the Doctor is correct in all of his observations and assumptions, which is pretty rare for the First Doctor. Maureen O’Brien narrates and plays most of the parts. Unlike the previous story, the Doctor is a main character, so O’Brien has to do her Hartnell impersonation, which honestly isn’t the best, but she does have his mannerisms down. It’s a dark downer of a story for Vicki’s last appearance in this project, but there it is.
docs.title: Fields of Terror

docs.text: Frostfire Companion Chronicles #1.1 Released: 19 February 2007 Listened: 2/7/20 The very first Companion Chronicle, but there’s no evidence that the formula hadn’t come together. In fact, this story has a distinct “new series” feel, although it came out in early 2007. The TARDIS lands in London, at the last Frost Fair (good thing they didn’t bump into Eleven and River , or Twelve and Bill (and Pete!)). They quickly get caught up with an alien killing swathes of people in Regency London, and meet up with Jane Austen late in her life, who acts unexpectedly heroic (although Clara isn’t there either ). Even the frame story references the new-series concept that a companion’s life after they leave the Doctor may not be all happily-ever-after, which one would really expect for Vicki, living in ancient Carthage. As often happens in these early Companion Chronicles, the frame story and the flashback seem to be entirely separate, but end up being related, in this case by some time-travel trickery. The second actor doesn’t do much, really, leaving Maureen O’Brien to handle all the parts in the flashback, which she does admirably. It’s a good start to the series.
docs.title: Frostfire

docs.text: The Bounty of Ceres Early Adventures #1.3 Released: 14 November 2014 Listened: 2/5/20 Another full-length, full-cast (ish) story, this one from the first box of Early Adventures. As the title implies, this story takes place on Ceres, which lends itself to a “base under siege” scenario, where some of the characters grow increasingly paranoid, except not everything is what it seems. The story proceeds a bit slowly, which is appropriate for the era, but I think it probably could have been compressed without too much difficulty. Peter Purves gets to give his First Doctor impersonation a workout, and does a pretty good job of it. There’s also a good bit of the Vicki/Steven sibling relationship, with a lot of the trope of “Steven is from the future, but Vicki is from further in the future, so she teases him.” On the whole, the story is middling, and not all that memorable.

docs.text: The Crash of the UK-201 Early Adventures #5.4 Released: 11 December 2018 Listened: 7/25/22 This one is deeply timey-wimey, and in fact has a very modern-series feel, as it’s more or less “Turn Left,” but for Vicki. Something unexplained happens within the TARDIS that sends Vicki back down her personal timeline. It turns out the UK-201 is the spaceship that crashed on Dido, putting this right before the events of “ The Rescue .” Given an opportunity like that, of course Vicki tries to set things right, particularly saving her father. Of course, that means she never meets the Doctor, which creates a great whopping paradox, but first we get to see Vicki’s alternate life play out. This gives Maureen O’Brien a chance to really stretch, as she has to play Vicki at various ages from 15 to 170. Peter Purves gets a break as well, as the Doctor is barely present, and Steven seems to randomly bounce around Vicki’s timeline, as he’s also caught in the paradox (without Vicki, the TARDIS may have never gone to Mechanus, so Steven never gets rescued). It’s hard to describe much more without spoiling, but Vicki goes through the same sorts of decisions and anguish that Donna does, and learns that even when you have foreknowledge, “fixing” things doesn’t always get you what you want, and even trying to put things back may not have the same results. It’s a pretty effective tearjerker, even though we know how it has to end up. On the whole, this boxed set brought a lot of newer concepts to an old team, and mostly executed on them successfully. With the Early Adventures winding up, this may be the last story in recording order for this particular team, in which case it’s a good ending.
docs.title: The Crash of the UK-201

docs.text: The Dalek Occupation of Winter Early Adventures #5.1 Released: 12 September 2018 Listened: 1/5/22 These next four Early Adventures break with the previous formula, featuring the same characters, and occurring all in a row. I imagine that had to do with the unavailability of William Russell, or possibly with the “Adventure in Space and Time” team taking over most of the stories featuring the original team. This story, by David K Barnes, takes a look at a different kind of Dalek invasion, and different ways that people might react to it. The TARDIS lands in the city of Winter on an unnamed planet, where winter lasts 500 years. It was colonized by speculators hoping to mine rare ores, but that didn’t pan out, and when they called for help, the only response came from Daleks, who were talked into varying from their standard procedures. In exchange for food, the population builds Dalek casings, not as slaves, but as paid workers with decent conditions. They have no idea what the Daleks are actually used for, thinking them exploration and aid robots. Naturally, the Doctor, Vicki, and Steven react with shock and horror, and immediately try to get a rebellion going. The chief administrator isn’t a fan of the Daleks, but will do whatever’s necessary to keep his people safe and himself in power, not necessarily in that order. The security chief simply wants to be on the winning side, and thinks she can manipulate the situation to her own ends. Even the factory worker who befriends Steven is worried; she can be convinced that the Daleks are evil, but kicking them off the planet would cut off their food supply, and the people would starve. For Vicki and Steven, at least, this is a genuine moral dilemma, and their arguments with the natives are interesting. Barnes is usually a comedy writer, but there’s very little of that here. In fact, the ending is grim even by the standards of Dalek stories. But it’s fitting to have a First Doctor story where they can take time to consider the implications of fighting the Daleks.
docs.title: The Dalek Occupation of Winter

docs.text: The Destroyers Lost Stories #2.2 Released: December 2010 Listened: 2/12/20 This is a prequel of sorts to “ Mission to the Unknown ” (itself a prequel) which doesn’t feature the Doctor, any companions, or the TARDIS. It does, however, feature Sara Kingdom, and was intended as a pilot for Terry Nation’s proposed Dalek spin-off series, which never happened. It even has its own 60s-style theme music, which wouldn’t be out of place as an unused track from The Incredibles . Sara seems decidedly younger and less tough than in her later appearances, but she spends much of the story worried about her brother David, who never appears again, so we don’t know what happened to him. It also introduces android Mark Seven, who was intended to be a major character if the series took off, and turns up again much later in the Tenth Doctor “ Dalek Universe ” stories. Like many Dalek-focused stories, the Daleks are an implacable force, and everybody else is just trying to survive. From that perspective, it has a fairly unsatisfying ending, but given that it’s a pilot to a series that never happened, that’s probably expected.
docs.title: The Destroyers

docs.text: The Founding Fathers Companion Chronicles #9.3 Released: 3 June 2015 Listened: 2/6/20 This story is a shorter-form Companion Chronicle, but unlike many of the others, the frame story is almost as important as the flashback, and the frame story forms a sequel to the frame story of “ The War to End All Wars ,” which comes much later in this project, and unusually, that later frame story really is required listening for this one. The story continues into “ The Locked Room ,” which takes place at the end of this era. Turning to the flashback story itself, well, I’m a Philadelphian, so any story involving Benjamin Franklin and the Penn family will have some personal appeal for me. Knowing what I know about Franklin’s history, I think the story treats him fairly. It also has a trick for forcing the travelers to stick around that I haven’t seen anywhere else -- the Doctor locks himself out of the TARDIS accidentally. How you get from that to Franklin is kind of a stretch, but there’s a strong implication that the Doctor is manipulating events so that he can meet Franklin. Because this is a Companion Chronicle, Peter Purves plays Steven, the Doctor (fairly well), and Franklin...somewhat less well. He’s clearly aiming for a generic American accent, which probably isn’t accurate, but it’s reasonable for Steven telling a story. Alice Haig does a decent job playing Vicki, but she doesn't have a lot of lines. The story itself has some decent misdirection, but it’s a bit slight.
docs.title: The Founding Fathers

docs.text: The Ravelli Conspiracy Early Adventures #3.3 Released: 10 November 2016 Listened: 2/8/20 Another Early Adventure, which means full cast and a longer running time, with Peter Purves playing the Doctor. It’s also a pure historical, but instead of massacre and plague, we’ve got 16th Century Italian politics, which means the Medicis and Machiavelli, because why not go all the way? It’s not nearly as grim as one might expect from that setup; in fact, nobody dies at all, not even minor characters. Aside from all the machinations, the plot could almost be described as silly, with guards regularly giving up on understanding what’s going on and just doing whatever the nearest character tells them. As far as the TARDIS team is concerned, it’s one of those “get back to the TARDIS and leave without upsetting history” stories, where they just happen to fall into the middle of things. And the plots are very complicated, as you’d expect, given the historical characters. Giovanni de’Medici (Pope Leo X) seems to be portrayed accurately, as a great lover of the arts and interested in keeping the peace at all costs, whereas his brother Giuliano is painted as a bloodthirsty villain. It’s not the most memorable of stories, mostly because the TARDIS crew spend much of it reacting to events.
docs.title: The Ravelli Conspiracy

docs.text: The Suffering Companion Chronicles #4.7 Released: 20 February 2010 Listened: 2/4/20 This is a slightly unusual release, a double-length story (so the same as a Main Range), with both Peter Purves and Maureen O’Brien voicing Steven and Vicki, with no guest actors. It’s a semi-historical, taking place in 1912 not far from London, and is largely concerned with the Women’s Suffrage movement. I didn’t realize that the movement was more violent, on both sides, than it was in America (or at least more than I’ve heard in American history), so there are some pretty brutal descriptions in this story. It’s also a little more heavy-handed than usual on the gender conflict, although it’s subtly tied to the origin of the Drahvins of “ Galaxy 4 ,” so maybe it’s par for the course for this era. The narrative plays a little with the traditional Companion Chronicles format, with Vicki and Steven collaborating to make an intentional recording of these events (Steven somewhat reluctantly), so there’s a little bit of mocking and false starts as they get the story going. It’s a pretty good showcase for their sibling-like relationship, and for Steven’s “action hero” status, replacing Ian. The historical details make it an uneasy listen, though.
docs.title: The Suffering

docs.text: Companion Chronicles #4.7 Released: 20 February 2010 Listened: 2/4/20 This is a slightly unusual release, a double-length story (so the same as a Main Range), with both Peter Purves and Maureen O’Brien voicing Steven and Vicki, with no guest actors. It’s a semi-historical, taking place in 1912 not far from London, and is largely concerned with the Women’s Suffrage movement. I didn’t realize that the movement was more violent, on both sides, than it was in America (or at least more than I’ve heard in American history), so there are some pretty brutal descriptions in this story. It’s also a little more heavy-handed than usual on the gender conflict, although it’s subtly tied to the origin of the Drahvins of “ Galaxy 4 ,” so maybe it’s par for the course for this era. The narrative plays a little with the traditional Companion Chronicles format, with Vicki and Steven collaborating to make an intentional recording of these events (Steven somewhat reluctantly), so there’s a little bit of mocking and false starts as they get the story going. It’s a pretty good showcase for their sibling-like relationship, and for Steven’s “action hero” status, replacing Ian. The historical details make it an uneasy listen, though.
docs.title: The Suffering

docs.text: Upstairs Companion Chronicles #8.3 Released: 12 September 2013 Listened: 2/8/20 This is another Companion Chronicle where both Peter Purves and Maureen O’Brien work together, without any other actors, but this time O’Brien plays the Doctor, and it has to be said, not as well as Purves’ version, but that’s not overly surprising. It’s also a very twisty, brain-hurting story that almost seems to take place in an alternate reality. This one probably would have worked quite well on television, with limited sets and cast, but the story is so bizarre that I wonder if they would have dared such a thing in the 1960s. I hesitate to say more about it for fear of spoilers, but the characterizations of the TARDIS team are quite well-written, especially the First Doctor.

docs.text: The First Doctor, Susan, Ian, and Barbara As the original TARDIS team, Ian, Barbara, and Susan have a fair number of stories. Full-cast stories have been hampered by the unavailability of Jacquiline Hill, who died in 1993, but William Russell and Carole Ann Ford have been willing to work with Big Finish almost since the beginning. Carole Ann has the advantage of having been quite young when she was on the show, so was still in prime working age when Big Finish came calling. William Russell was also game at first, but as Big Finish has gone on for quite some time, he eventually retired from active participation. As a result, the stories in this set are a mix of Companion Chronicles, Short Trips, and Lost Stories told in a narrated style.
docs.title: First Doctor, Susan, Ian, & Barbara

docs.text: A Star Is Born Short Trips #4.1 Released: 10 August 2011 Listened: 4/26/20 Placed here pretty arbitrarily. The TARDIS lands on a failing generation ship inhabited by sea-lion-like aliens, who are also dying of radiation poisoning. It takes the Doctor some time to determine that the problem is sabotage, not a mechanical fault. There’s some dodgy science here, of both radiation and genetics, and the TARDIS saves everybody by making a controlled short hop, which wasn’t really possible in this era. On the whole, I’m not impressed with this story.

docs.text: After the Daleks Early Adventures 7.1 Released: 17 August 2021 Listened: 8/18/21 This Early Adventure is a departure for the series, as it focuses entirely on Susan, and the Doctor doesn’t appear. It starts immediately after “ The Dalek Invasion of Earth ,” and addresses the fact that maybe leaving Susan on a war-torn planet with a guy she just met wasn’t exactly the best recipe for happily-ever-after. Because humans are humans, and as we’ve learned in the real world, when people are frightened and desperate, they’ll turn to an autocratic strong-man for leadership. It might have been better if the former governor had genuine reasons for believing himself the best leader, but the story was deliberately written in a 1960s style, so he’s basically just a selfish collaborator. The plot also has some 60s-style contrivances, like a creature whose origin is never explained, but who happens to secrete a substance that reverses the Roboman conversion process. But it’s Susan’s arc that’s done properly here, as she goes from feeling somewhat helpless, to trying to channel what her grandfather would do, to trying to stick to her people’s non-intervention policy, to finally taking brave action and making an active choice to stay on Earth with David, instead of having it made for her. David and Jenny from the original story are recast, with David played by Sean Biggerstaff, who’s turning into a Big Finish stalwart. His accent is pretty distinctive, but it’s also fantastic, so I don’t mind at all. Jenny is played by Lucy Briers, taking the role originated by her mother in the original story. All new stories from this early period have to choose between trying to imitate a 1960s style, or going for more modern pacing and storytelling. This time, Big Finish chose the former, and while it gets the job done, I think it might have been a bit more enjoyable if it had gone the other way.
docs.title: After the Daleks

docs.text: Domain of the Voord Early Adventures 1.1 Released: 4 September 2014 Listened: 1/3/20 The Early Adventures are like the Companion Chronicles on steroids. They’re full-cast stories, although because of the lack of William Hartnell and companion actors, they’re still partially narrated. They also tend to be longer, a traditional four-part story, which enables the story to expand in a way that feels more true to the original stories. This story feels like it could have fit nicely into the first season. It features the return of the Voord, but like many Andrew Smith stories, we discover a lot more about the villains and their society. There are a number of First Doctor tropes: The Doctor puts Susan’s safety, and the TARDIS, over that of the other people they meet. Ian is strangely competent at a number of skills (SCUBA diving, commando raids). The only real difference is that Barbara doesn’t get as much to do. She and the Doctor get sidelined and are missing for most of episodes 2 and 3, which lets the story concentrate on Ian and Susan, who have actual actors. As often happens, the Doctor wins in the end by doing something clever and sciency that’s never entirely explained. Russell and Ford sound closer to their actual ages, and Russell has William Hartnell’s mannerisms down, but doesn’t quite match the voice. Still, there’s enough of the feel of an early story here that it’s a success.
docs.title: Domain of the Voord

docs.text: E Is for... Early Adventures 13.1 Released: 18 September 2019 Listened: 1/6/20 This story is from much later in Big Finish’s recording history, and it shows. Susan spends almost the entire story separated from the others, and Carole Ann Ford is starting to sound more like Old Susan than Young Susan. But the key point of this story is that it’s a superhero pastiche, specifically the X-Men. Doctor Who has always stayed away from superheroes in the past, but after “ The Return of Doctor Mysterio ,” it seems they’ve become fair game. From the extras, it seems like most of the creators (except the writer, of course) don’t realize just how much of an X-Men reference this story is, but if you’re at all familiar with Marvel history, the references stick out a mile. I think you could have gotten away with this story with different characters, possibly one of the modern series Doctors, but it just seems strange and out of place in the First Doctor era.
docs.title: E Is for...

docs.text: Farewell, Great Macedon Lost Stories #2.1a Released: 10 November 2010 Listened: 1/1/20 All of the stories in this part of the project so far have been on the shorter side. Companion Chronicles and other such formats run about an hour. Which is unusual, because this early era had some lengthy stories, and this is one of them. Also written by Moris Farhi, this is a true historical in the way that they really only did them in the First Doctor’s era, hanging out with historical figures, getting tangled in historical events, and yet not changing the overall course of history. The chronology establishes this as the first true historical, before “ Marco Polo ” or “ The Aztecs ,” but it does rely on the listener having some knowledge of those stories, and how this team behaves when they’re in Earth history. Alexander is presented as nuanced, mostly being a good man with strong ideals and some rather progressive ideas about race relations, but also prone to flying into rages and jumping to conclusions, which can make him look quite stupid at times. The villains, on the other hand, are straight-up baddies; if they had mustaches, they’d twirl them. But the villains’ plot isn’t really the important part of the story, because the course of history is set, and there’s nothing the travelers can do about it, except get caught up and falsely accused. This leads to the Doctor using his scientific knowledge to do something unexpected, and Ian being unexpectedly proficient at hand-to-hand fighting, both of which are pretty standard for this sort of story. The only divergence is that Barbara hides her historical knowledge of what’s going to happen from her companions, who have no idea until nearly the end of the story. As a production, Big Finish did this in a narrated style, with William Russell and Carole Ann Ford playing all the parts except for Alexander, who’s played by John Dorney (usually a writer, but he’s an experienced actor too). The music and sound effects are minimal, in a nod to how stories from this era were made. As with many historicals, how much you like it depends on how much you like that era, but I think it’s a fantastic example of both a First Doctor story, and a historical, one that Big Finish has only rarely matched.
docs.title: Farewell, Great Macedon

docs.text: Flywheel Revolution Short Trips #5.1 Released: 5 January 2015 Listened: 4/29/20 The first of the monthly Short Trips range isn’t a complete story by itself, but an interlude set in the part of some other story when the Doctor has been imprisoned and is separated from his companions for a while. It’s read by Peter Purves, but Steven isn’t in it; the Doctor specifically wants to get back to Susan, Ian, and Barbara. A lot of this story depends on the unique point of view of its narrator, so I’m reluctant to spoil it, but it’s fun for a listener, seeing the events of a normal Doctor Who story from an outside perspective. It’s a strong start for the series.
docs.title: Flywheel Revolution

docs.text: Here There Be Monsters Companion Chronicles #3.1 Released: July 2008 Listened: 1/6/20 After several stories in a row featuring Ian, now we get two focusing on Susan. This is the earliest Big Finish story focusing on Susan (she appeared in a couple of Unbound stories before this), and Carole Ann Ford sounds distinctly younger here than she does in other stories. However, it’s an early Companion Chronicle, which means it’s rather talky, with very little in the way of music or sound effects, which is appropriate for this era, but it makes the story tricky to get into. It’s a nice spotlight for Susan, but not a great story.

docs.text: Home Again, Home Again Subscriber Short Trips #2020.2 Released: 10 November 2010 Listened: 7/4/20 Placed here, later in Ian and Barbara’s timeline, because they’ve lost track of how long they’ve been traveling. The TARDIS comes back to Coal Hill School , and Ian and Barbara think they’re home, but unfortunately it’s June, several months before they left. They try to stay anyway, which results in some comedy as they try to avoid their earlier selves. The Doctor has a very early-seasons understanding of the laws of time, and won’t explain just why it’s so bad to cross one’s own timeline. Of course we know Ian and Barbara can’t stay, because of the larger narrative, but you’d think they could do a bit better job of hiding than they do. Stephen Critchlow’s First Doctor is getting to be quite good. I get a little tired of the “they’re home, but something’s wrong” stories with Ian and Barbara, but there aren’t quite as many of them as I thought.
docs.title: Home Again, Home Again

docs.text: Rise and Fall Short Trips #1.1 Released: 5 November 2010 Listened: 4/23/20 Placed here because Ian says they’ve just come from France . As the very first Short Trip, this one goes high-concept. The Doctor and Ian step out of the TARDIS, leaving the women behind momentarily. The natives of this world are primitive, but occupy a separate time stream, so they evolve, form a civilization, and then destroy themselves in the span of a few moments for the travelers. There’s barely a plot, more of an impression, but it’s a strong impression, and a story that sticks with me.
docs.title: Rise and Fall

docs.text: The Age of Endurance Early Adventures #3.1 Released: 14 September 2016 Listened: 1/3/20 This Early Adventure was recorded a few years after the previous one , and there are some differences. Jemma Powell steps in to play Barbara, but she’s still sidelined for most of the story, which seems an odd choice. Then again, Carole Ann Ford and especially William Russell sound quite a bit older than even the last story, and might make a poor contrast to Powell. Russell even plays the Doctor sounding rather older than previously, although he does spend most of the story injured and fatigued. As for the story itself, it seems like it should be part submarine thriller, and part morality tale regarding the dangers of genetic engineering, but the baddies don’t really stick in the memory, and the sacrifice play at the end is fairly obvious. The nebula the story takes place in probably would have looked great on TV if this story were made with modern-series special effects, but likely not in 1964 black-and-white.
docs.title: The Age of Endurance

docs.text: The Flames of Cadiz Companion Chronicles #7.7 Released: 9 January 2013 Listened: 1/5/20 This is a departure from the Companion Chronicles formula, being four parts (the length of a Main Range story), and featuring both William Russell and Carole Ann Ford, in addition to a supporting actor. It’s another historical, set in Spain in the 1580s, which means the Inquisition and the Armada, so it’s pretty grim, as historicals often are. The spotlight is definitely on Ian, but he’s unusually reckless in this one, beyond his normal levels. Getting arrested by the Inquisition because he doesn’t want to see injustice done is typical Ian, but running off to meet Francis Drake just for fun, while he’s still wanted by the Inquisition, is over the edge. The Doctor also mis-steps badly, in a way that’s unexpected for him. And there’s a definite push in developing a relationship between Ian and Barbara, although it can’t go too far while there’s still TV episodes left to cover.
docs.title: The Flames of Cadiz

docs.text: The Fragile Yellow Arc of Fragrance Lost Stories #2.1a Released: 10 November 2010 Listened: 12/31/19 These next two stories come from the “Lost Stories” First Doctor box set. There’s no telling whether these two were originally intended to appear at this spot in the chronology, but this is where the timeline cues place them, and oddly, the second story in the boxed set happens first. This is a one-part story, written as a “proof of concept” by Moris Farhi, never really intended for production. And you can see why, because it’s a very high concept, too far out there for the classic series, and maybe even the modern one, but it’s good as a short audio story. The early placement means that Ian and Barbara are just friends at this point, and the Doctor is still making arbitrary decisions for the whole group, which is required for the plot to work.
docs.title: The Fragile Yellow Arc of Fragrance

docs.text: The Library of Alexandria Companion Chronicles #7.10 Released: 10 April 2013 Listened: 1/6/20 This story was released just a few months after the previous one , and there’s definite connections. It starts out seeming like yet another historical, and it acknowledges several stories that have come before, specifically the fact that the travelers met Alexander the Great and Ptolemy . However, that all quickly gets turned on its head with an alien invasion, giving this story a much more modern-series feel. The Ian/Barbara relationship that was gently hinted at in the previous story is much more obvious here, which seems a bit out of place with the TV stories, but a reasonable development within the audio timeline. The Doctor also has a more modern-series attitude as well, striding up to the alien monsters and demanding that they listen to him. It’s probably not a particularly accurate early-era story, but within this project, it makes a nice palette-cleanser.
docs.title: The Library of Alexandria

docs.text: The Masters of Luxor Lost Stories #3.7 Released: 16 August 2012 Listened: 7/23/22 This Lost Story was originally intended to be the second serial of the series, but fortunately, we got “ The Daleks ” instead. In its current form, though, it’s established as taking place immediately after “ Farewell Great Macedon .” The characters are still a bit uneasy with each other, and Susan addresses Ian and Barbara by their titles. It’s a six-parter, and those often feel stretched out. Plus, it’s of its time, meaning the story is kind of pokey. As an example, it gets most of the way through Part 2 before the travelers even begin to figure out what’s going on. Even “The Daleks” wasn’t that slow. “Luxor” implies Egyptian, but there isn’t anything like that here, except that the huge building where the story takes place is pyramid-shaped. The TARDIS lands, and is drained of power, so they have to go exploring to figure out what’s wrong so they can leave. This leads to lots of wandering around, exploration, and speculation before they eventually discover the building is pretty much a way-station for Luxorites, staffed by robots, and currently empty. (So the story isn’t even set on Luxor, and only one of the “Masters” ever makes an appearance.) What follows should be rumination on the nature of artificial life and robot rights, except it’s held back by a rather basic understanding of what robots are capable of, for which you can blame 1963. Even the Doctor states several times that one action or another is “impossible” for robots, when moderately advanced AI could probably handle it. It eventually turns into one of those “mad computer thinks it’s god” stories, and while those are somewhat tiresome, this would have been the first time the show had told such a story, had it been televised. Much like “Macedon,” the story is partially narrated, with William Russell playing both Ian and the Doctor, Carole Ann Ford playing Susan and Barbara, and Joseph Kloska playing everybody else…which is to say, mostly robots. Unfortunately, William Russell’s age is showing, and it’s sometimes difficult to tell if a line was meant to be spoken by the Doctor or Ian. Sadly, it’s not the best Lost Story, especially compared to “Macedon.”
docs.title: The Masters of Luxor

docs.text: The Time Museum Companion Chronicles #7.1 Released: 23 July 2012 Listened: 1/1/20 For the first time, I’m not certain why Craig Brawley placed this story at this point. It’s a Companion Chronicle told by a much older Ian, or maybe an alternate Ian, from near the end of his life. Normally Companion Chronicles flash back to a single story that can be placed, but this story features bits and pieces from throughout Ian’s time as a traveler, brought up in random order. The plot isn’t too involved, as most of the enjoyment of the story comes from Ian’s memories, and you’ll probably see the twist coming. But if you’re looking for an explanation, you’ll find part of one after the closing credits.
docs.title: The Time Museum

docs.text: The Transit of Venus Companion Chronicles #3.7 Released: 22 January 2009 Listened: 1/4/20 This was the first Companion Chronicle to feature Ian, and therefore the first to be read by William Russell, in 2009, although the series had been going for a little while at that point. It very much follows the “classic” Companion Chronicle formula, with Ian relating the story to an “off screen” listener, later in his life, which relieves Russell of having to make himself sound younger, but he does do a good job playing the Doctor as well. As for the story, Susan and Barbara spend most of it off-screen, even though Barbara is on the cover. It’s a historical, in the sense that there aren’t any aliens or monsters, just the Doctor and Ian on Captain Cook’s voyage to Australia, but the time travelers accidentally present themselves as aliens from Venus, and Susan’s telepathy plays a role, so it’s not quite a “pure” historical. Unlike a lot of historicals, it’s not unrelentingly grim, with most of the danger coming from Ian himself, entirely by accident. In that respect, it’s lightweight, but it’s valuable because it gives a lot of insight into Ian’s frame of mind, how his attitude toward the Doctor is softening, and his feelings toward Barbara.
docs.title: The Transit of Venus

docs.text: Sidestep In 2013, as part of the 50th Anniversary celebrations, the BBC produced the docudrama An Adventure in Space and Time by Mark Gatiss, a semi-fictionalized account of the creation of Doctor Who. It starred David Bradley as William Hartnell / The Doctor, Claudia Grant as Carole Ann Ford / Susan, Jamie Glover as William Russell / Ian, and Jemma Powell as Jacqueline Hill / Barbara. Jemma Powell was recruited by Big Finish to play Barabara in the third series of Early Adventures in 2016, and in 2018, Big Finish decided to go whole-hog and cast all the actors to recreate the roles of the first TARDIS team. This would be the second time that Big Finish specifically recast a Doctor, and the first time they recast parts whose original actors are still alive -- although in fairness, William Russell was over 90 at the time, and had retired from Big Finish. What nobody knew at the time was that the BBC was about to cast Bradley to play the First Doctor in “Twice Upon a Time,” which came out around the same time as the first box set here. Craig Brawley, whose timeline I’m following for this project, doesn’t consider these stories to be canon, as they feature none of the original actors, so he isn’t placing them in the timeline. The Big Finish covers feature the likenesses of the new actors, not the originals, and they haven’t made any reference to these stories from others, thus “canonizing” them, although James Dreyfuss has appeared as the First Master in other Big Finish stories . I’m not including any other “unbound” stories in this project just yet, but I think these are pretty good stories, so I may as well include them at this point, just after Susan’s departure.
docs.title: Sidestep

docs.text: For the Glory of Urth First Doctor Adventures #5.1 Released: 27 April 2021 Listened: 5/1/21 In release order, it’s been a while since there was a release in this series, so hearing these actors again is welcome. As usual, there’s one sci-fi story and one historical, but the sci-fi is a bit off the usual path. The TARDIS crew have landed on a planet called Urth, which claims to have the last descendants of humanity living in a squalid city. However, it’s a dystopia of the fairly silly variety, not unlike “ The Happiness Patrol ” or possibly “ Vengeance on Varos ,” where the people in charge are so terrible that you wonder how they could have gotten there at all. Ian and Barbara don’t really have a lot to do in this story (aside from being generally appalled), and Ian’s “hero moment” goes decidedly poorly this time around. Susan has a lot of the action, as does Phyllida Nash as a blobby gestalt alien. The various revelations are interesting the first time through, but the ruling-class characters are annoying enough to discourage a re-listen.
docs.title: For the Glory of Urth
