docs.text: Last of the Romanovs First Doctor Adventures #4.2 Released: 18 March 2020 Listened: 3/24/20 This is the true historical for this boxed set, and as you might expect from the title, it’s a grim one. The TARDIS lands in Russia in 1918, right outside the palace where the Romanovs are being held, because of course it does. To their credit, as soon as the Doctor and company realize where they are, they immediately want to leave, but of course it’s too late. In a twist, Ian and the Doctor are merely sent to hard labor, but the women end up caught in a British plot to smuggle the Romanovs out of Russia. Interestingly, Susan is displaying a much broader independent streak, which fits with “ Tick-Tock World ,” but wasn’t much in evidence in “ Return to Skaro .” The plot itself has the characters wandering around, trying not to get killed, and bumping into the Romanovs, but a number of the secondary characters are not what they seem. In the background, though, there’s some “ Aztecs ”-like discussion of what can and can’t be changed, with the Doctor invoking “fixed points” quite deliberately. In the end, though, he seems to be questioning just how fixed they actually are, putting a new-series tinge on everything.
docs.title: Last of the Romanovs

docs.text: Return to Skaro First Doctor Adventures #4.1 Released: 18 March 2020 Listened: 3/21/20 These stories were released a couple of months after I was at this point in the chronology, and it’s a welcome return. Either the actors are relaxing into their roles and toning down the RP a bit, or I’ve just gotten used to it. This story is an interesting one to place in the chronology, because it’s made clear that the crew haven’t encountered Daleks since the first time, and think they were all destroyed at the end of that adventure. It’s also the first time they’ve explicitly returned to a place they’ve been before (courtesy of the Fast Return Switch) although many years later. The Thals have apparently taken over and all the Daleks are gone...except ha-ha, of course they’re not. Susan gets bullied into going to the Dalek city...except she’s the one who wants to explore once they get there, so that’s a nice twist. There’s also the scientist who’s gulled into believing that the Daleks want to be nice this time, except none of the listeners are going to buy that, so the plot dispenses with it early. The TARDIS crew split up and recombine often, allowing everybody to get a chance to play the hero. The Daleks, for their part, get the idea to investigate time travel, and the Black Dalek is introduced. However, the crew leaves things pretty much as they found them, believing that the Daleks are gone for good. On the whole, it’s not as exciting of a story as I would have hoped.
docs.title: Return to Skaro

docs.text: The Barbarians and the Samurai First Doctor Adventures #2.2 Released: 25 July 2018 Listened: 1/13/20 Keeping with the pattern of these box sets, we’ve had a sci-fi story first, then a pure historical. The TARDIS crew arrives in 19th Century Japan, during the isolation, and for once realize that they need to just get back in the ship and leave. But of course that doesn’t work out. The crew ends up separated, the Doctor blusters a lot at the local lord, who wants Barbara as a concubine (of course), while Ian and Susan meet a local ronin who has not only extraordinary fighting skills, but also knowledge of the lord’s castle, and is in love with the lord’s daughter. It follows pretty much the path of a typical 1964 historical, with escapes, recaptures, more escapes, and noble sacrifices. According to the extras, they cast Japanese actors to play the appropriate roles, but they still sound rather badly stereotypical. I have this feeling, probably unjustified, that American stories handle Japanese culture better than British ones. It’s a perfectly acceptable story, but not a stand-out.
docs.title: The Barbarians and the Samurai

docs.text: The Destination Wars First Doctor Adventures #1.1 Released: 25 December 2017 Listened: 1/10/20 The first thing I notice with this series is the voices. None of the actors are attempting to imitate their predecessors, but to capture the spirit of the characters. Jamie Glover does that reasonably well, I think, but Jemma Powell and Claudia Grant especially are emphasizing their RP accents, which makes Susan sound like a parody of herself, sometimes. David Bradley is definitely playing his own version of the First Doctor, which is a reasonable substitute, but it’s noticeably different. The writing also changes the characters somewhat, emphasizing some of their characteristics at the expense of others. The Doctor in particular is supercilious to the humans, and quicker to argue than William Hartnell’s was. Ian seems to have been toned down a bit, in order to give the others more “hero time,” which is probably to the good. This story features James Dreyfuss as the Master, presumably the “first” version of the Master. He’s more of a “suave” Master than the later “insane” Masters of TV, somewhat like Delgado, with some clever phrasings. There’s rather more use of time travel, and of the Fast Return Switch, than normally would have happened in the First Doctor era, but this story seems to be straddling the line between a traditional story and the style of the new series.
docs.title: The Destination Wars

docs.text: First Doctor Adventures #1.1 Released: 25 December 2017 Listened: 1/10/20 The first thing I notice with this series is the voices. None of the actors are attempting to imitate their predecessors, but to capture the spirit of the characters. Jamie Glover does that reasonably well, I think, but Jemma Powell and Claudia Grant especially are emphasizing their RP accents, which makes Susan sound like a parody of herself, sometimes. David Bradley is definitely playing his own version of the First Doctor, which is a reasonable substitute, but it’s noticeably different. The writing also changes the characters somewhat, emphasizing some of their characteristics at the expense of others. The Doctor in particular is supercilious to the humans, and quicker to argue than William Hartnell’s was. Ian seems to have been toned down a bit, in order to give the others more “hero time,” which is probably to the good. This story features James Dreyfuss as the Master, presumably the “first” version of the Master. He’s more of a “suave” Master than the later “insane” Masters of TV, somewhat like Delgado, with some clever phrasings. There’s rather more use of time travel, and of the Fast Return Switch, than normally would have happened in the First Doctor era, but this story seems to be straddling the line between a traditional story and the style of the new series.
docs.title: The Destination Wars

docs.text: The Great White Hurricane First Doctor Adventures #1.2 Released: 25 December 2017 Listened: 1/11/20 The second story of this set is a pure historical, set in New York during the Great Blizzard of 1888 , which I had never heard of before this story, much to my embarrassment. As with most historicals, it’s a little on the slow side, and a bit grim, but not bleak as they often are. The pace is sustained by separating Ian and Barbara from the Doctor, and all of them from Susan. Ian and Barbara get involved in a domestic dispute, and then a rescue of some folks from a train, while the Doctor and Susan get caught up in some gang warfare. Ian gets sidelined early, so he can’t go into full Hero Mode until later. The Doctor is particularly cantankerous, but he’s worried about Susan and stuck with a bunch of violent Americans. The American accents are rather good, better than usual for Big Finish, although they tend toward stereotypical “Noo Yawk” accents, and there are still some English phrasings. I’m rather fond of this story; although historicals usually aren’t my favorites, I gravitate toward stories that take place in locations I’m familiar with.

docs.text: The Hollow Crown First Doctor Adventures #5.2 Released: 27 April 2021 Listened: 5/1/21 The second story means it’s time for a historical, and unusually for this particular series, they don’t land someplace entirely horrible and immediately want to leave again. It’s time to meet Shakespeare! Again! This story takes place later in Shakespeare’s life than “ The Shakespeare Code ,” so he remembers meeting someone called “The Doctor,” but the First Doctor doesn’t react to that. Shakespeare is not played by Dean Lennox Kelly, as he was on TV, but rather by Nicholas Asbury, who’s had a tiny role on TV and several Big Finish parts. Writer Sarah Grochala (an award-winning playwright, but with only a few Big Finish credits yet) tells a tight story, leaning in on the Shakespearean tropes of noble rebellion, main characters in disguise, and gender-swapping, as well as slipping in rhyming couplets here and there. The TARDIS crew can’t seem to help quoting the plays at every opportunity, but it’s not like the Tenth Doctor resisted either. There’s also a nice subplot where Ian and Barbara once again test the limits of how much one can go against recorded history, which sometimes records incorrectly. In the end, though, this is the Essex Rebellion (which I knew very little about), and it has to go more or less to form, but with a nice romantic twist that’s very appropriate to the tone. And it ends on a sudden cliffhanger, a nice 1964-ish twist, so I hope it won’t be long before that’s resolved. I enjoyed this story much more than I expected to, and I hope to hear more from this writer in the future.
docs.title: The Hollow Crown

docs.text: The Invention of Death First Doctor Adventures #2.1 Released: 25 July 2018 Listened: 1/12/20 This is the first John Dorney story in this series, and as might be expected, it’s high-concept. The TARDIS crew happens upon a species of aliens who appear to be immortal, and therefore have no fear of death, no concept of pain or discomfort, no means of reproduction, and no spur toward scientific progress. That last concept seems to be most important in this story, as far as it provides some motivation for some very alien characters. Otherwise, there isn’t really a “bad guy” or any sort of threat, which makes the story drag a little bit. There’s also an odd interlude in which the cast sings “ London’s Burning ” as a round, for no real reason. This is another one of those stories that I don’t think could have been done on TV, not just because of the special effects, but because the concept is too far out there for the TV audience.

docs.text: The Phoenicians First Doctor Adventures #3.1 Released: 29 January 2019 Listened: 1/16/20 This third box set switches up the order a bit and puts the historical first, for reasons that will become apparent. This time they’re in Tyre, participating in the events that led to the founding of Carthage -- and I do mean participating, as they’re interfering more than they would have in 1964. Unusually for historicals from this era, there’s no real “good guy.” Princess Elissa is sympathetic, but also acts in her own self-interest most of the time, which doesn’t always coincide with our heroes’. King Pygmalion is almost a caricature, with no redeeming qualities at all; he’s possibly mad, which is apparently appropriate to the story. The Phoenecians are all played by actors of appropriate backgrounds, which wouldn’t have happened in 1964, but they still sometimes sound stereotypical, as did the actors in “ Samurai .” Ian still jumps into hero mode at the drop of a hat, but it goes badly for him much of the time, which leads to a pretty good first-episode cliffhanger. Susan gets some character growth too, and seems to be seeking some independence from her grandfather. Not the most memorable of the historicals, but not bad either.

docs.text: Tick-Tock World First Doctor Adventures #3.2 Released: 29 January 2019 Listened: 1/16/20 The gimmick in this story is that Carole Ann Ford appears, credited as “Woman,” but it becomes clear quickly that she’s an older version of Susan. Not the Susan from Earth, but an alternate future Susan. Claudia Grant still sounds quite different than Carole Ann, but either she’s toned down her RP accent some since starting, or I’m just getting more used to it now. The oddest vocal clashing is that the guest characters all use their own regional accents, which makes the four leads stand out more than usual. This is another high-concept time-traveley story, from Guy Adams, and another that probably wouldn’t have worked on TV in 1964. Susan, as you can imagine, is the focus, with a lot of attention being paid to her growing up and becoming more of her own person. If they were in the regular timeline, it would make a great lead-in to “ The Dalek Invasion of Earth .” There are also much stronger hints at a deepening relationship between Ian and Barbara, which kind of fits in the timeline as well. Carole Ann Ford does well in the role, despite being mostly a phantom with not much to do. She bounces off Bradley in just the same way she would Hartnell, which works nicely.
docs.title: Tick-Tock World

docs.text: The Fourth Doctor The Fourth Doctor: the scarf, all teeth-and-curls, that mellifluous voice. This is the Doctor who everyone thought of first, at least until that Tenant chap came along. Unfortunately, Tom Baker had a bit of a troubled relationship with the character, and often declined to reprise the role. For quite some time, Baker declined to work with Big Finish, for a variety of reasons. However, from 2009 to 2011, he participated in the “ Hornets Nest ” series for BBC Audio, and after that joined Big Finish for some Lost Stories in 2011, and his own series starting in 2012. I suspect that long-time Big Finish participant Louise Jameson may have had a part in his return to the role. Now, he’s extremely enthusiastic about the audios, having recorded several series years in advance, and popping up in specials and guest roles. Although he doesn’t sound precisely like his younger self anymore, his voice is unmistakable, and a great fit for audio.

docs.text: The Fourth Doctor and Ann You say you don’t remember a companion named Ann in 1978? That’s because she only exists in Big Finish. There’s a gap of undetermined length between “ The Invasion of Time ” and “ The Ribos Operation ,” but rather than sneaking in another solo period, or having the Fourth Doctor with just K-9, the folks in charge created a new companion, and a new adventure running through eight stories. Unlike other stories that feature TV companions, listeners don’t come in already knowing how Ann’s story ends. Even better, this is a complete story arc for Ann, making this boxed set self-contained…except it’s more complicated than that, because it always is.

docs.text: Fever Island Fourth Doctor Adventures #8.6 Released: 13 February 2019 Listened: 5/2/22 This story appears to be a standalone, the only one in this boxed set. And boy, is it trippy. The Doctor and Ann investigate a temporal anomaly taking place on an isolated Scottish island in 1978. There’s also a secret agent there, by the name of Jason Vane, who’s basically a parody of every spy novel ever. He even does narration in deeply purple prose, until Ann reveals that she can hear him doing it. Turns out there’s something here that’s changing the nature of people and things, and for a while, the Doctor behaves like a cliche spy villain. Which is silly on the face of it, but Tom Baker leans in to the sinister element of the role, and his lines drip with menace. The actual plot isn’t really any great shakes; it’s mostly an excuse to let people run around and play secret agent. But at that goal, it succeeds handily.
docs.title: Fever Island

docs.text: Planet of the Drashigs Fourth Doctor Adventures #8.2 Released: 16 January 2019 Listened: 4/26/22 This story is technically the first chronological appearance of K-9 Mark II, as the Doctor has just finished building him as the story opens. It’s also Ann’s first TARDIS trip, and unfortunately for her, she’s got a full-blown Jurassic Park reference, complete with electric fences, a mad billionaire owner, a laconic gamekeeper, and a panicky safety inspector. (Sadly, no Wayne Knight or Sam Jackson, but the story is only an hour.) And instead of foolishly messing with dinosaur DNA, the scientist is foolishly messing with mind-controlling Drashigs. Even though they only appeared in “ Carnival of Monsters ,” Drashigs have become kind of synonymous in the fandom with “unstoppable beasts.” (Although their name is an anagram of “dishrag.”) Introducing smaller, smarter variants creates even more parallels to Jurassic Park , but it does allow the baddies some agency, instead of just being a force of nature. As for Ann, although she drew an unusually dangerous first adventure, the Doctor does try to keep her out of mortal peril. She’s asking a lot of questions and making inferences here, which makes her a nice step between Leela and Romana.
docs.title: Planet of the Drashigs

docs.text: The Enchantress of Numbers Fourth Doctor Adventures #8.3 Released: 16 January 2019 Listened: 4/27/22 Doctor Who is rather fond of Ada, Countess of Lovelace, and honestly, why not? As a result, Ada’s timeline is getting as crowded as her father’s and Mary Shelley’s with visits from various Doctors. This visit takes place toward the end of Ada’s life, after she’s retired to the countryside and given up working on mathematics. Ada is played well as a woman hovering on the edge of madness, afraid of what she’s inherited from her father along with his genius. Of course, it doesn’t help that there are actual apparitions and sinister plague doctors popping up around her. Ann gets to do some more investigating in this story, and she’s pretty happy to violate cultural norms about her “place” in order to get her job done. K-9 is noticeably absent from this one, probably because a mobile, talking computer would change the story dramatically. The monsters are a little anticlimactic, but they’re not given a lot of space in the story. Good characterization, so-so plot.
docs.title: The Enchantress of Numbers

docs.text: The False Guardian Fourth Doctor Adventures #8.4 Released: 16 January 2019 Listened: 4/30/22 This is where things start to get a bit strange. Because it turns out that to follow this storyline, you’re going to have to remember things from “ The Daleks’ Master Plan ,” which is a lost episode, so you’ll have to know the plot somehow. You’ve got the planet Kembel, somehow still around, complete with Varga plants, you’ve got Mavic Chen (or someone who thinks he’s Mavic Chen), and you’ve even got Zephon, son of Zephon, from the planet Zephon (not very imaginative). Ann, K-9, and the Doctor spend the first half of the story in mortal peril from the elements, and the second half split up, trying to figure out what’s going on in this institution that calls itself a retreat, but is very probably an asylum. And that’s pretty much it. Ann gets to use her skills, but then the story ends on a cliffhanger, which in this case, was also the end of the first boxed set of Season 8.
docs.title: The False Guardian

Ann, K-9, and the Doctor spend the first half of the story in mortal peril from the elements, and the second half split up, trying to figure out what’s going on in this institution that calls itself a retreat, but is very probably an asylum. And that’s pretty much it. Ann gets to use her skills, but then the story ends on a cliffhanger, which in this case, was also the end of the first boxed set of Season 8.
docs.title: The False Guardian

docs.text: The Perfect Prisoners, part 1 Fourth Doctor Adventures #8.7 Released: 13 February 2019 Listened: 5/15/22 This two-part finale is what the whole boxed set has been building to. It’s a John Dorney story, so that means it’s twisty. The Doctor and Ann continue their investigations, finally involving the Space Security Service. The Syndicate turn out to be the members of the Galactic Council from “ The Daleks’ Master Plan ,” or their descendants, and they all have an issue with the Doctor. Their big plot involves controlling the minds of everyone in the galaxy, or rather, controlling their perceptions, which amounts to the same thing. However, most of the Syndicate members end up getting killed while in close proximity to Ann, which finally becomes suspicious.
docs.title: The Perfect Prisoners, part 1

docs.text: The Perfect Prisoners, part 2 Fourth Doctor Adventures #8.8 Released: 13 February 2019 Listened: 5/15/22 The big secret is finally revealed: Ann Kelso is revealed to be Anya Kingdom of the Space Security Service, operating as a sleeper agent on Earth in the 1970s. In fact, Ann Kelso never existed at all. Beyond that cover, Anya is a brainwashed agent of Zaal of the Syndicate, using her to wipe out the other members. That explains, among other things, Ann’s ability to fly the TARDIS accurately. Which makes for a great reveal the first time around, but knowing that doesn’t really add much to a relisten. However, Jane Slavin’s portrayal makes Ann/Anya vicious and cunning at many points, but ultimately sympathetic when it becomes clear she wasn’t responsible for her actions. If Anya never appeared again, it would seem odd that nothing was ever made of her family connections. However, she’ll be back again in the Dalek Universe stories, when considerably more time has passed for the Doctor, and he’s got a better perspective on the matter. On the whole, this season represented a strong attempt to do something different, give the Fourth Doctor a new companion, and give that story a strong twist, all of which succeeded. Having the story tied so tightly to “ The Daleks’ Master Plan ” seems like a less-good idea, partially because it’s a lost story, but also because the villains didn’t do much in that story, so they don’t seem very effective or threatening here.
docs.title: The Perfect Prisoners, part 2

docs.text: The Sinestran Kill Fourth Doctor Adventures #8.1 Released: 16 January 2019 Listened: 4/25/22 With the Doctor at loose ends, he answers a signal indicating unusual technology being used on Earth in 1978 (when the story would have aired, if this had been a TV season). Investigating, he discovers an area of London that’s having some trouble with organized crime. WPC Ann Kelso patrols the area, but doesn’t normally deal with the gang unit. Except the Doctor knows there’s more going on here, and it turns out that both the gangsters and their targets are aliens, or being controlled by aliens. All we know about this group right now is that they’re called the Syndicate, and that’s what this boxed set is all about. Ann has all the hallmarks of a good companion right from the start, being logical, open-minded, cool under fire, and yet empathetic. She even comments that she would expect to freak out after seeing a giant insectoid alien, but she didn’t. Equally unflappable is DCI Neilson, played by Frank Skinner, comedian and super-fan. Fortunately, Neilson was in Special Branch for several years, so he’s conversant with UNIT in general and the Doctor specifically, which really saves a lot of time in this story. Writer Andrew Smith was in an anti-terrorism squad himself during his time in the police, so his knowledge of procedure adds a little bit of realism to the story. It’s a pretty good kickoff, and the gangsters give it some 70s flavor.
docs.title: The Sinestran Kill

docs.text: Time's Assassin Fourth Doctor Adventures #8.5 Released: 13 February 2019 Listened: 5/1/22 The second boxed set of Season 8 opens right after the cliffhanger of the last one. A few things become slightly clearer…but not really. Most intriguingly, Ann reveals one layer of her deception, but only to the listener, not the Doctor. As for the rest, it’s a Guy Adams story, so there’s plenty of absurdity. In fact, just about every character in this story who’s not part of Team TARDIS is mad in one way or another. Special credit goes to Blake Ritson as Dr. Elmore, the maddest mad scientist I’ve seen in a while, and Jon Culshaw as Zephon, son of Zephon, who takes pettiness, paranoia, cruelty, and vengeance to the next level, while still remaining pathetic at the core. The only real downfall to the story is that the Doctor doesn’t seem to solve any problems. Bad guys lose, but not as a result of the Doctor’s actions, and the Doctor himself only survives through a deus ex machina. (Well, machina ex machina, or something.) What’s clear, though, is that the first half of this season appeared to be just a bunch of disconnected stories, and now we’re finding out that it definitely isn’t.
docs.title: Time's Assassin

docs.text: The Fourth Doctor and Leela (and K-9) Louise Jameson has been one of the biggest supporters of Big Finish almost since the beginning. She’s now written and directed for them, as well as playing Leela, which she does with astonishing skill. Even though Leela is a very physical character, Jameson manages to perfectly recreate her on audio. Unfortunately, without Tom Baker, she could only participate in some Companion Chronicles and Short Trips. This has never been confirmed, but I imagine she’s played a large part in getting Tom Baker to return on audio. That makes this section unusually long, given her somewhat short tenure on TV, but that’s fine, because Big Finish is able to flesh out the “education” subplot that didn’t see much action on TV.
docs.title: Fourth Doctor and Leela

docs.text: A Ghost of Alchemy The Eighth of March #3.1 Released: 8 March 2023 Listened: 5/6/23 This story is from the third "Eighth of March" collection, and it plays a little bit with the formula. It’s a full-length story, which is unusual for these sets. It’s also written by Louise Jameson, who is multi-dimensional in the Big Finish realm. It has Leela, but also the Fourth Doctor. The Eighth of March stories tend to minimize the Doctor to accentuate the women in the story, but this one doesn’t. Maybe Louise didn’t think it was necessary, because the big historical guest of this story is one Madame Curie, pioneer of radioactivity research. Of course, that same research also killed her, and the story never lets you forget it, with Marie’s continual cough, exhausted manner, and terrible stage-fright. The story takes place in America in 1920, when Marie had a national tour. Unfortunately, a scientist named Browman believes that Curie is a fraud riding on her husband’s success, and is determined to discredit her. He also believes that he should have access to the radium that Curie is being gifted with. He’s sexist, which makes sense in an Eighth of March story, but he’s so remarkably foolish and evil that he might as well be twirling his mustache. His henchman in Curie’s party is also pathetic and weak-willed. On top of which, President Harding is presented as rather foolish as well, delegating most responsibility to his wife Florence. This isn’t out of line with Doctor Who ’s treatment of American presidents, or even with historians’ assessment of Harding, although I don’t recall hearing that he was dominated by his wife. Leela, as you might expect, does reasonably well for herself, and the Doctor expresses quite a lot of confidence in her. However, she does end up captured and drugged at one point, which is fairly unusual for her. On the whole, it’s kind of a runaround, not too different from most stories, except for the fairly low stakes and caricatured presentation of the men.
docs.title: A Ghost of Alchemy

docs.text: Antillia the Lost Fourth Doctor Adventures #12.2 Released: 2 March 2023 Listened: 5/6/23 For her second trip, Margaret again gets a sci-fi setting. The TARDIS ends up unexpectedly on Antillia, a huge space station with its own environment that was host to a lot of scientific research, then disappeared, leaving a legend. They’re here because a ship with an experimental drive has located the station, and drawn the TARDIS off-course. Author Phil Mulryne has a lot of high concepts here, from the mystery of the disappearance to what happened to the inhabitants, to what the explorers are really up to. The secondary characters are very well-drawn, including a journalist played by Anjli Mohindra (Rani Chandra), who is always awesome, and a bodyguard who Leela forms an unusual respect for. And speaking of respect, she’s getting closer with Margaret, although they do spend a chunk of the story apart. Younger Leela might not see this so readily, but she recognizes Margaret’s innate bravery and sense of adventure, even if she hasn’t lived a life that brought that out of her before. Admittedly, there’s a lot of plot in this one, and not so much time for personal relationships. It zips along readily, with perhaps a touch too much capture and deathtraps and escapes and running, but that’s fairly common for the period. It’s good, but not a particular standout.
docs.title: Antillia the Lost

docs.text: Black Dog Short Trips #5.4 Released: 6 April 2015 Listened: 2/20/22 This story doesn’t have to do with depression, at least, not directly. The TARDIS lands on an Earth mining colony that’s now been mined out, so the few remaining humans are about to leave. There are natives on the planet, but for once, they’re not in conflict with the humans; in fact, they don’t seem to care whether the humans stay or go. Both groups are troubled by a black dog that appears in dreams, and marks the dreamer for death. The natives believe it’s a god, who has supplanted their other gods, and honestly the humans pretty much believe that too. When Leela has the dream, and has her energy sapped, the Doctor goes into full atheist mode to get to the bottom of the problem. In fairness, the Doctor has been vanquishing gods quite a bit lately ( Sutekh , Xoanon ), so he’s got form. He ends up praising Leela’s skills rather a lot, to inspire her, which gives Leela a glimpse into how he sees her.
docs.title: Black Dog

docs.text: Death Match Fourth Doctor Adventures #4.4 Released: 16 April 2015 Listened: 4/5/22 After a rather impressive cliffhanger, in which Leela left the Doctor and then found herself kidnapped by the Master, we find out what’s going on. The Master has used Leela to take over a multi-system deathmatch competition. With her as his champion, he’s amassing plenty of resources and attracting the attention of the rich and powerful of this corner of space. It’s a little small-fry for him, but he seems to be enjoying himself. Marshall, the reformed Rocket Man with an attachment to Leela, calls in the Doctor to help, and amazingly, he shows up in time. This story is much more straightforward than the previous, with the Doctor and the Master in their accustomed roles, because this is a Matt Fitton story, not a John Dorney one. Which means that there are layers of emotional content, Marshall’s for Leela, Leela’s more complex ones for Marshall, the Doctor’s for Leela, and even K-9’s, although he claims not to have any. Of course we know what the outcome has to be, but that doesn’t make it any less heartbreaking, mostly because Louise Jameson is awesome.
docs.title: Death Match

docs.text: Destination: Nerva Fourth Doctor Adventures #1.1 Released: 9 January 2012 Listened: 2/23/22 Now we’re getting into it! In 2012, Big Finish began releasing a dedicated series of Fourth Doctor Adventures. These were similar to the Eighth Doctor Adventures in format, being shorter stories of two parts, each 25-30 minutes. That results in a somewhat zippier pace, intended to appeal to new-series fans. Unfortunately, this story isn’t the strongest premiere. It starts immediately after “ Talons ,” and goes only a few years into the future, where some English military-types manage to get their hands on a crashed alien spaceship and somehow use it to get into space, despite the technological difficulties, where they proceed to colonize “for Queen and Country.” This could be an interesting investigation of British history and colonialism, but instead it just jumps forward a thousand years, where the Victorians are now just a generic “ooze monster” threat to the brand-new Station Nerva. There’s no good reason for it to be Nerva; aside from a couple of references only the Doctor could get, its history doesn’t figure in. Baker and Jameson both sound in good form; I could believe this is from Season 14. Also, a pre-Third-Doctor Tim Treloar plays Lord Jack, the chief baddie, but he doesn't really have a lot of lines.
docs.title: Destination: Nerva

docs.text: Destroy the Infinite Fourth Doctor Adventures #3.6 Released: 18 June 2014 Listened: 3/7/22 In 2013/2014, Nick Briggs created the Eminence and the Infinite Warriors as a “big bad” exclusive to Big Finish. As such, it pops up in a variety of stories, with its timeline out of order relative to the Doctor’s. This story, however, is their first meeting from the Doctor’s point of view. Beyond that, though, it’s a fairly standard story. The Eminence is busy waging war on humanity, the Doctor turns up and tries to stop it. Leela gets a lot of agency in this one because she’s separated from the Doctor and has to fight her way back on her own. There could probably be some interesting questions of identity in this story, or perhaps some timey-wimey nonsense given the out-of-sync timelines, but there isn’t. It’s mostly military action and explosions, which is fine for what it is. The Doctor can’t get a clean win, however, because the Eminence is needed further down the timeline. Although he finds that disturbing, he doesn’t really seem to do anything about it right now.
docs.title: Destroy the Infinite

docs.text: Empathy Games Companion Chronicles #3.4 Released: October 2008 Listened: 4/2/22 The frame story picks up directly from the previous one : Leela is still a prisoner, but the Z’nai have all been wiped out. Oddly, the torture machines are now keeping her alive. She hears a child crying nearby, and tries to tell it a story, leading to the flashback. Which is, honestly, very strange. The Doctor spends a large chunk of it in a coma, so Leela is left to function on her own, which means things are going to get a bit violent. The planet they’re on is very high-concept, supposedly totally peaceful, with an astonishing water sculpture that would look amazing with modern SFX, and some rather odd hunting “games” that Leela takes to right away, although they’re not what they seem. David Warner is the backup actor in this one, and although his character doesn’t actually do a whole lot, I’ll take David Warner in anything, thanks very much. Unexpectedly, we get an explanation for what happened to the wooden console room, and why it hasn’t been seen since. Even with the strangeness, there’s a strong visual quality to the story that makes it stand out. The frame story, however, is quite weak this time out, and doesn’t resolve, so we’ll have to wait for that.
docs.title: Empathy Games

docs.text: Companion Chronicles #3.4 Released: October 2008 Listened: 4/2/22 The frame story picks up directly from the previous one : Leela is still a prisoner, but the Z’nai have all been wiped out. Oddly, the torture machines are now keeping her alive. She hears a child crying nearby, and tries to tell it a story, leading to the flashback. Which is, honestly, very strange. The Doctor spends a large chunk of it in a coma, so Leela is left to function on her own, which means things are going to get a bit violent. The planet they’re on is very high-concept, supposedly totally peaceful, with an astonishing water sculpture that would look amazing with modern SFX, and some rather odd hunting “games” that Leela takes to right away, although they’re not what they seem. David Warner is the backup actor in this one, and although his character doesn’t actually do a whole lot, I’ll take David Warner in anything, thanks very much. Unexpectedly, we get an explanation for what happened to the wooden console room, and why it hasn’t been seen since. Even with the strangeness, there’s a strong visual quality to the story that makes it stand out. The frame story, however, is quite weak this time out, and doesn’t resolve, so we’ll have to wait for that.
docs.title: Empathy Games

docs.text: Energy of the Daleks Fourth Doctor Adventures #1.4 Released: April 2012 Listened: 2/27/22 Of course, if you’re launching a new Big Finish series, you need to have Daleks in there somewhere, especially since Leela has never encountered Daleks on TV. So they land in 2025 London, when apparently holograms are common, and the National Gallery has been turned into the HQ of an energy company, but nobody has smartphones, they have “tiny TVs” instead. Leela gets to wear contemporary clothing, including trainers, which she likes quite a lot. These Daleks are a fairly classic bunch; they’re trying to wipe out humanity in 2025 to alter the timeline. Which is a nice reversal of “ Genesis of the Daleks ,” although 2025 seems a bit early to try it. It’s a fairly straightforward story, as Nick Briggs stories often are, with not much in the way of surprises, but that’s OK. It’s mainly about a standard Dalek conflict, and it works well for that.
docs.title: Energy of the Daleks

docs.text: Ice Heist Fourth Doctor Adventures #12.1 Released: 2 March 2023 Listened: 5/5/23 This particular series brings in Nerys Hughes as Margaret Hopwood, introduced a while back in “ The Ravencliff Witch ,” but not invited as a companion. Back then, the Doctor was alone, but this time Leela is also present. She’s pretty experienced by this point, and almost immediately takes Margaret under her wing. A bit unusual, as Leela doesn’t really care for people who flap around and panic, but she knows Margaret helped the Doctor before. He’s picked her up to bring her to an art auction a few hundred years in the future, where one of her sculptures is going for an absurd amount of money. He thinks of it as a treat, but Margaret sees it as a sign of her own mortality and blows a fuse, which sets off Leela’s protective instincts. The Doctor spends an unusual amount of time being wrong in this story, and also spouting nonsense as he does when he wants to impress a new friend, which Leela isn’t willing to let him get away with. There’s some actual story going on as well, with Ice Warriors who are also present at the auction for nefarious reasons. Writer Guy Adams deliberately wanted to subvert the idea of Ice Warriors as honorable Klingon-types, and he succeeds here. The only flaw is that results in a lot of Martian bickering, which means lots of hissing Ice Warrior dialog. Nick Briggs normally does monster voices extremely well, but when he’s got a lot of exposition to fire off, you can tell it’s him. Adele Lynch, who played the Ice Warrior empress on TV, returns here as a different Ice Warrior, and she’s clearly enjoying herself. There are also quite a few memorable secondary characters, including a curator who’s completely determined to ignore anything that might be going wrong, her laconic head of security, a pompous artist who holds the buyers in contempt, and even a guard with a remarkably upbeat outlook on life. The story gets a little hard to follow at times, especially when so many characters are around, but ultimately it's worth it.
docs.title: Ice Heist

docs.text: Kill the Doctor! Fourth Doctor Adventures #7.7 Released: 16 May 2018 Listened: 4/15/22 This is the first half of a two-part story by Guy Adams, which brings back Sutekh , but in a futuristic setting, which hasn’t been done before. Fortunately, Gabriel Woolf is still around to voice Sutekh, but I’m not sure anyone else could, and he sounds just as quietly menacing as ever. However, he’s not really the main driver of this first half. The Doctor and Leela arrive on a planet not unlike present-day earth. People are obsessed with their smartphones, in a not-veiled-at-all reference. But more important, Leela runs headfirst into late-stage capitalism, and is appalled by the treatment of the underclass. She assumes the Doctor will help overturn the government, a reasonable guess on her part, but he’s not willing to go stomping on inequality wherever it exists. Leela ends up angrier than she’s been yet with the Doctor, and decides to go fight the power on her own. The Doctor, meanwhile, gets chased by zombified mobs everywhere he goes, which he has to admit is a bit extreme even for his lifestyle. As far as the dialog goes, it’s an open secret that Tom Baker likes to punch up his lines, and he might be taking it a bit too far this time around. The Doctor seems positively flippant, even goofy at times, which isn’t really what he was like back in this season. Still, it’s a well-paced setup for a longer story.
docs.title: Kill the Doctor!

docs.text: Last of the Colophon Fourth Doctor Adventures #3.5 Released: 14 May 2014 Listened: 3/6/22 This Johnny Morris story is also a bit slight, or at least the threat doesn’t get to be quite as big as it should. The planet Colophos is a dead world, destroyed by a virus centuries ago and lost to history. However, an Earth Empire survey ship turns up to assess the planet at exactly the same time the Doctor and Leela show up for a (questionable) holiday. That leads to their uncovering Morax, the titular last of the Colophon, who’s been imprisoned all this time. The first half of the story has a kind of Indiana Jones feel, with the trap-laden tomb and such. The second half is The Invisible Man , by the writer’s own admission. Doctor Who is famous for using invisible monsters as a budget-saving tool, but they rarely have a sentient invisible psychopath, which works reasonably well on audio. Gareth Thomas (Blake of Blake’s Seven ) plays Morax with lots of gravely menace, which is good. However, the short length makes it feel like either half of the story could have been longer.
docs.title: Last of the Colophon

docs.text: Night of the Stormcrow Fourth Doctor Adventures Special Released: 12 December 2012 Listened: 3/1/22 This bonus release is a bit odd because it feels like it should be part of Series 1 of the Fourth Doctor Adventures, and it was released between Series 1 and Series 2, yet it’s labeled as a special. Anyway, it’s a spooky, atmospheric, “ Fang Rock ” kind of story. The Doctor and Leela land near an observatory on a small Pacific island, where the lead astronomer has found something unusual orbiting the Earth, something she’s chosen to call “Stormcrow.” It’s never entirely clear what the Stormcrow is, just a kind of sentient blackness, as are the scavengers that follow it, which the Doctor calls “no-things.” Apparently they eat time, and cause despair and jealousy in people. It’s a Mark Platt story, so the whole thing has a semi-mystical feel, and most of it you have to take on faith. In the absence of a hard plot, you’re left with the performances, which are quite good all around. Ann Bell does a great job as the astronomer, seeming like the “older eccentric scientist” character common in this era, but there’s a lot more going on there. American Chase Masterson (of Deep Space Nine ) plays the authority figure with bad intentions, for the Doctor to bounce off of. Tom Baker gets an interesting turn when the Doctor is affected by the scavengers, giving Louise Jameson the chance to air Leela’s feelings of homelessness. She hasn’t really expressed how she feels about traveling before, so this makes for an interesting twist. Mark Platt stories, while interesting, usually leave me feeling like I’ve missed something, and this one is no different. It’s a fine addition to the first series, but not particularly memorable.
docs.title: Night of the Stormcrow

docs.text: Requiem for the Rocket Men Fourth Doctor Adventures #4.3 Released: 13 March 2015 Listened: 4/4/22 The Rocket Men have appeared in a few stories , and usually end up losing badly to the Doctor, which is starting to hurt their reputations. However, the Doctor still treats them as a serious threat. This story is by John Dorney, creator of the Rocket Men, and it has some nods toward his original story, like an extended bluff in Part 1 that’s explained by a flashback in Part 2. Unfortunately the misdirect isn’t as strong as in the original, but I don’t think it was trying to be. The misdirects lie in other places: any time you use the Master as a secondary character, something fishy is going on. The only real hitch is that it requires substantial planning on the Doctor’s part, which isn’t something the Fourth Doctor normally goes in for. That’s more of a Seventh Doctor thing, but maybe he felt that the Rocket Men merited that level of attention. The last couple of scenes, though, are entirely unexpected, and create a strong desire to listen to the next story .
docs.title: Requiem for the Rocket Men

docs.text: Return to Telos Fourth Doctor Adventures #4.8 Released: 11 August 2015 Listened: 4/10/22 This story follows on directly from the previous , but it’s a little more traditional. A little, anyway. K-9 has been suborned by the Cybermen, unfortunately in one of their Borg-like phases where a single touch can cause complete conversion. But the Doctor does a clever thing that accidentally drops them into “ The Tomb of the Cybermen ,” except in a way where the Doctors never meet, and the original story is undisturbed. So it’s not really a multi-Doctor crossover. In fact, there’s a lot of time spent on the timey-wimeyness of it all, with the Doctor’s moral dilemma from the last story brushed aside because the Cybermen cheated first. Unfortunately, a 60s-era Cyberplanner and Cybercontroller talking to one another, while probably fun for Nick Briggs, is a ring-modulated slow-speed assault on the ears, and tough to enjoy. I get what Briggs was going for here, but I don’t think that either story really succeeds fully.
docs.title: Return to Telos

docs.text: Shadow of the Sun Fourth Doctor Adventures special Released: 12 May 2020 Listened: 4/16/22 This one is slightly unusual. It was recorded in March 2020, the first remote recording Big Finish did because of the pandemic. The intent was to shelve it and release it with series 13. (The Fourth Doctor Adventures are recorded years in advance, at Tom Baker’s request.) However, Big Finish thought it would be a nice gesture to release it early, to help fans cope with lockdown. Unfortunately, they had no way of knowing just how long Covid would last, and that remote recording would become standard procedure. Listening to the extras is almost surreal. Anyway, the story involves a cruise liner rented by a society of spiritualists, on which the TARDIS lands for emergency repairs. Which would be fine, except this particular cult believes there’s a habitable area inside the sun, and intend to prove it by going there. Their leader is a charismatic, but disgraced, scientist, who’s basically dragging everyone else along by force of will. The Doctor has about as much luck as ever talking down insane tyrants. However, he does seem a bit more desperate than usual, and confused by the cult’s behavior. The theme of people ignoring science in favor of their own personal beliefs is pretty clear here, probably hammered a bit too hard, really. Tom Baker and Louise Jameson both sound a bit closer to their actual ages in this story; I don’t know if that’s a result of when it was recorded, or the new recording process, or just my imagination. It was a nice gesture as an early release, but ultimately it’s just OK.
docs.title: Shadow of the Sun

docs.text: Sound the Siren and I'll Come to You Comrade Short Trips Rarities #1.5 Released: 22 December 2014 Listened: 3/15/22 Short story, long title. It seems like the title should be a reference, but I can’t find out to what. The Doctor wants to take Leela to the court of Peter the Great, but they miss and land in a Soviet H-bomb testing site in the 1950s, most likely this test . There’s a monster around, a beast that thrives on radiation, but the Doctor is more concerned about the fact that they’re testing an H-bomb. In the end, history is history, and the Doctor really does nothing, and solves nothing. However, it’s a look into the Soviet mindset of the time, and a really close look at what the first milliseconds of a nuclear explosion actually look like, so writer John Pritchard has done his homework here. Stephen Critchlow narrates, and does an excellent Fourth Doctor. He also gives the Russian characters distinct accents, so it feels like a full-cast play.
docs.title: Sound the Siren and I'll Come to You Comrade

docs.text: Stone Cold Fourth Doctor Adventures #12.5 Released: 21 June 2023 Listened: 7/22/23 This is one where if you can manage to avoid the spoilers right on the cover (and the hint in the title), you’ll be much better off. The Doctor is trying to take Margaret somewhere pleasant, but the nice forest planet he’s aiming for turns out to be a barren rock with some active volcanism. It’s just rocks and more rocks…until they find the grave. And then the crashed spaceship. Which is bad, because there weren’t supposed to be any people here, ever. We do the usual runaround with the travelers being accused of murder before the crew start trusting them. The tension builds all throughout the first half of the story, before the monster is revealed. And as I said, if you don’t know, it’s a fairly effective reveal as the hints pile up. At least, it worked that way for me. The rest of the story is tight and claustrophobic, which is appropriate for these particular monsters, and writer Roland Moore uses what we know about them to great effect. There’s also a Bob Holmesian double-act in the form of a couple of tourists from the ship, who bicker and snipe most of the time. It might be a shade long, but I think it’s well-executed.
docs.title: Stone Cold

docs.text: Suburban Hell Fourth Doctor Adventures #4.5 Released: 21 May 2015 Listened: 4/8/22 At the halfway point of the season, this is a much lighter story, despite the title. The Doctor and Leela land in a suburban English town, and the TARDIS immediately leaves with K-9 aboard, writing him out of this story. They crash a dinner party, and assume they’re in 1977 again, but it turns out to be a 70s-themed party, and they’re actually in the 2010s. That doesn’t mean there’s no temporal shenanigans going on, though, as events in the present are linked to those in 1977, causing paradoxes, slippages, “long way rounds,” and the whole timey-wimey ball. It’s a well-paced story, with the first half entirely occupied with figuring out what’s going on, and the second taking a distinctly sci-fi turn as they try to use the temporal shenanigans to fix the problem at the root. Annette Badland makes yet another guest appearance, as Thelma-from-over-the-road. Alan Barnes gets special credit for creating a couple of characters in Belinda and Pete who are thoroughly unpleasant from the get-go, and stay that way even through mortal peril, which is a neat trick. It’s a small story, but it’s memorable.
docs.title: Suburban Hell

docs.text: The Abandoned Fourth Doctor Adventures #3.7 Released: 11 July 2014 Listened: 3/8/22 This story is remarkable for a number of reasons: It’s written by Nigel Fairs and Louise Jameson, in her writing debut. It also takes place entirely within the TARDIS, although there are more than two characters present. The gist of this one is that there’s a malevolent entity trapped in the TARDIS, which has been there since before the Doctor “borrowed” it. And now it’s doing something that involves other people’s imaginary friends? You’d best be in the mood for giggling and cackling, wailing and shrieking, because there’s a lot of all of those in this story. And painting. Lots of painting, which doesn’t really translate on audio. Louise Jameson seems to like the stories that have a more dreamlike quality, but I prefer them to have a bit of internal logic, and I wasn’t finding that here. I remember liking this one on my first listen, but it didn’t work for me this time around.

docs.text: The Age of Sutekh Fourth Doctor Adventures #7.8 Released: 16 May 2018 Listened: 4/15/22 The concluding part of the story isn’t quite as good as the setup , but it does come close. The issue is that Sutekh has a very primal objective: He wants to wipe out everything, full stop. That’s a little tricky to work with, so Guy Adams has him in a situation where his power is limited, and he needs to conserve it. Which leads to the best sequence, Leela out-maneuvering him in a jungle while calling him “horse-face” all the while. Leela versus a god is a match I wouldn’t really like to bet on, but don’t tell Leela that. She’s very nearly at the peak of her capability in this story, able to read and pretty good at understanding technology, while still retaining her fighting and tracking skills. The guest cast in these stories, beyond Gabriel Woolf, is worthy of note: Sophie Myles (Reinette from “The Girl in the Fireplace”), Eleanor Crooks (Naomi Cross in various UNIT stories), John Dorney as Carlton Joyce, and Barnaby Edwards as the entire rest of the population of the planet. That’s some quality Big Finish casting there. Oddly, K-9 is left out again, meaning he’s barely appeared at all in this season.

docs.text: The Bad Penny Fourth Doctor Adventures #7.6 Released: 16 May 2018 Listened: 4/14/22 This one is written by Dan Starkey, and although it doesn’t have the excessive verbiage that his stories sometimes do, it’s stuffed full of ideas, perhaps more than are needed. It’s a “mysterious hotel” story, of which Doctor Who has had plenty, and a big old time paradox as well. It’s also got a “self-made man” taking advantage of the paradox, various characters out of their time, and also a monster. I’m not sure the monster was strictly necessary, but someone decided that Doctor Who stories should have a monster in them. Leela does fairly well, for a story that takes place entirely inside a hotel, using her skills to read people. The Doctor seems a bit more banter-y than usual, but that’s probably the writing. (K-9 is absent once again.) One element to note is that there are more characters than usual in a Big Finish story, because Dan Starkey is able to voice them all himself, which gives him a bit of leverage in the scope, which is ironic considering the claustrophobic nature of the story.
docs.title: The Bad Penny

docs.text: The Beast of Muir Subscriber Short Trips #2020-3 Released: 9 September 2020 Listened: 4/28/26 This Short Trip puts the emphasis squarely on Leela, and provides a look into her mindset. She's feeling frustrated that most of her adventures with the Doctor take place on spaceships or in urban environments (and going by the TV stories, she's right). She wants to see some wilderness, so the Doctor offers to take her to Muir, named after conservationist John Muir . Of course, a pleasant walk in the woods isn't what they end up with. They're stuck in a research facility, with a rather dangerous creature on the loose. Leela spends most of the story tracking it down, and thinking about how her habits and even her thought patterns have changed since she met the Doctor. She reflects that she couldn't go home again, even if she wanted to, which she doesn't. For his part, the Doctor is balanced between the protectiveness he shows all his companions, and his absolute trust in Leela's skills. It's an interesting little story.
docs.title: The Beast of Muir

docs.text: The Catalyst Companion Chronicles #2.4 Released: January 2008 Listened: 4/2/22 A couple of Companion Chronicles slip in before we jump back to the full-cast stories, which gives Louise Jameson a chance to stretch by playing several characters, including the Doctor. She says it’s difficult to do a Tom Baker impersonation, but hers is one of the better ones I’ve heard. Like most early Companion Chronicles, the frame story takes place later in Leela’s life, but for her, that’s complicated, because this was recorded in 2007, when not a lot of detail was known about the Time War. So she survived, Gallifrey didn’t, and now she’s prisoner of a race called the Z’nai. The flashback relates her first encounter with the Z’nai, which involves visiting a Victorian-era mansion (again). The owner, Joshua Douglas, was apparently a previously unknown companion of the Third Doctor, never mentioned in any other story, who parted ways with the Doctor after a disagreement about how to stop the warlike Z’nai. Leela seems pretty inexperienced herself; her reading is rudimentary, she doesn’t know table manners, and she’s very quick to violence, but the story has to be placed here for Reasons. The story itself is quite dark. The body count is absurdly high, but also the Doctor has to try to convince several people that genocide is bad, even in self-defence. And he fails. It’s really kind of a grim moment in Leela’s relationship with the Doctor, and if we didn’t have a whole bunch of Fourth Doctor Adventures to offset it, it might be quite depressing. But Louise Jameson’s fantastic acting makes up for a lot.
docs.title: The Catalyst

docs.text: The Cloisters of Terror Fourth Doctor Adventures #4.6 Released: 4 June 2015 Listened: 4/8/22 Unlike the last story , this time they really do land in 1977, at a women’s college that’s part of Oxford. Like the last story, K-9 doesn’t feature at all. The Dean of the college is Dame Emily Shaw, mother of Liz, and still the most well-connected and influential woman in England , aside from the Queen. I can’t see any reason for her to return, aside from the fact that she’s awesome, and Rowena Cooper is awesome, so that’s enough. It does save time to have an authority figure who trusts the Doctor completely, once he establishes his credentials. Because the college is haunted by three nuns, girls are disappearing, and all the living nuns seem to be determined to hinder the investigation. Naturally, the explanation turns out to be less supernatural than it appears, as it almost always does, but it takes a good while to unravel. Leela gets to engage in a good bit of action, and has a solid respect for Dame Emily, who admittedly earns it. I think this one would have done quite nicely on television.
docs.title: The Cloisters of Terror

docs.text: The Crooked Man Fourth Doctor Adventures #3.3 Released: 14 March 2014 Listened: 3/6/22 This is a bit of a surreal one, but then, it involves the Land of Fiction . But not in the way you’d expect – there’s no famous characters here, just characters from unpublished novels, TV spin-offs, and tabloid representations of actual people. It’s unusual, but not twisty in the way that John Dorney stories normally are. There is, however, room for some really cracking dialog. The Crooked Man himself, the monster of the piece, is a pretty amazing visual (good thing the cover helps with that), and definitely scary. There’s a certain amount of parenting horror in this one as well, so be warned. And yet a lot of the dialog is quite funny, with a few very gentle jabs at the idea that Doctor Who is of course fictional as well.
docs.title: The Crooked Man

docs.text: The Crowmarsh Experiment Fourth Doctor Adventures #7.2 Released: 18 January 2018 Listened: 4/10/22 This story, though, is all about Leela. It’s one of those where a main character wakes up in a different life, and everyone keeps telling them the old life is a dream. Which is pretty standard stuff, but Louise Jameson plays it brilliantly as always, to the point where you can hear her starting to unravel and doubt herself. A big part of that is because Damian Lynch is back as Marshall, but a human version, not a Rocket Man this time. This is much more effective listening to those stories close together, rather than years apart as I originally heard them, having totally forgotten who Marshall was. Dan Starkey also has a small role as Linus Strang, a milder human version of his Sontaran Strang from “ The King of Sontar ,” and he’s subtle enough that I missed it completely. I was expecting a slightly ambiguous ending or a twist or double-bluff, none of which happen, but the emotional impact is probably stronger because of it.
docs.title: The Crowmarsh Experiment

docs.text: The Dalek Protocol Fourth Doctor Adventures special Released: 13 April 2021 Listened: 4/17/22 This one, unfortunately, is one of those times when the timeline of this project doesn’t serve well. If you listen to this before the next era’s boxed set, you’ll run into a major spoiler. It also connects to the Dalek Universe stories in the Tenth Doctor era, but it can be safely viewed as a prequel to those. You can tell it’s a Nick Briggs story, because it starts out on Exxilon, and Briggs loves “ Death to the Daleks ” to pieces. You can also tell because Briggs is playing Captain Bernard with his “northern” accent, which could double for “congested” if need be. This story is the first meeting of Space Security Service agents Mark Seven and Anya Kingdom, who will make up a lot of Dalek Universe, so they get plenty of screen time here. However, Mark spends a lot of time “not himself,” and Anya spends a lot of time trying to avoid the Doctor, for…reasons. She’s not entirely successful, but that seems to be OK. Leela doesn’t have the biggest role here, but she’s clearly come a long way. She remembers Exxilons , Daleks don’t phase her, her reading skills are improved, and she’s starting to learn when the Doctor is blowing smoke. The Doctor himself seems a little too flippant again, especially when Daleks are involved, but I think that’s the influence of Tom Baker on the scripts. Bottom line: If you like the Dalek Universe characters, you’ll like this.
docs.title: The Dalek Protocol

docs.text: The Darkness of Glass Fourth Doctor Adventures #4.2 Released: 12 February 2015 Listened: 4/3/22 This is one of those stories that grabs onto a particular historical phenomenon and explores it from multiple angles. In this case, that’s the “magic lantern” practice of slide projection from the 16th to the 19th centuries, when it fell into disuse after movies became popular. In this case, a bunch of enthusiasts are gathered in a spooky castle to remember the work of a (fictional) famous lanternist, who was said to be so skilled that he captured a demon in his images. Which means, of course, the Doctor and Leela will have to deal with that demon. K-9 stays behind, which happened from time to time on TV, but it does seem a bit odd here, given that K-9 has recently joined the crew. That gives Leela more space to shine, and although stone castles aren’t her forte, shadowy creatures that need hunting is right up her street. There are a number of secondary characters, well-drawn, if briefly, which makes it hard to determine the villain. The monster itself doesn’t get a lot of explanation. It’s mostly a macguffin while everybody else figures out the mystery. Not the strongest story from this set, but it’s a quality outing.
docs.title: The Darkness of Glass

docs.text: The Day of the Comet Fourth Doctor Adventures #10.2 Released: 20 January 2021 Listened: 3/19/22 This one moves out into space, to a doomed planet that’s about to get smacked by a comet. Most of the population left months ago, and the remainder…well, it isn’t going well. Unfortunately, the Web of Time has spoken on what happens to these people, because the consequences would be terrible otherwise. Writer Jonny Morris wanted to trap the Doctor in a no-win situation, and it shows. The story has a lot of room to breathe, enough that it’s essentially got a separate plot for each half: one in which they figure out the problem and struggle to help the survivors, and one where some other folks come along to try to exploit the planet. The first part has the moral dilemma, and the second has all the running around in corridors. There are some plot twists that allow for some convenient deaths, relieving the Doctor of that particular dilemma, and sometimes the seams show. Special mention must be made of Janet Henfrey, an actress who’s appeared in both the classic and new TV series, and has had several Big Finish roles , as an astronomer who gets increasingly fed up that everyone calls her “old woman” instead of using her name. In the end, though, it might last just a bit too long.
docs.title: The Day of the Comet

docs.text: The Demon Rises Fourth Doctor Adventures #7.4 Released: 18 January 2018 Listened: 4/12/22 The tone of this story is about the same as the last one , but the focus becomes different. The Doctor is still trying to figure out what’s going on and who’s hunting the Mind Runners, but the emphasis shifts to locating the Nightmind and what’s going on with the evacuation rocket. If you guessed “something sketchy,” you’d be right. I’ve seen the “sneak on board the mysterious evacuation rocket” more than a few times in Doctor Who , but this particular variant is probably the most unusual, and comes with the most body horror as well. Dorney’s reach may have exceeded his grasp a little bit here. He tries for an even higher concept than the ones he created in the last story, and in my opinion pushes the boundaries of plausibility a bit. The well-drawn characters are still around, but they’re less individualized this time, and more playing their expected roles in a Doctor Who story. There’s lots of running around, the Doctor talking the bad guy into a corner, and K-9 blasting things. The build-up is a little more dramatic than the actual climax. I’ll remember this one more for all the wild ideas zipping around than for the actual plot.
docs.title: The Demon Rises

docs.text: The Devil's Armada Philip Hinchcliffe Presents #1.2 Released: 5 September 2014 Listened: 4/1/22 This one is a four-parter, but it still feels nicely paced, like the previous story . It’s almost a historical, taking place in 1588, at the time of the failed Spanish Armada . There’s also plenty of witch-hunting and Catholic-hunting going on in the countryside. Against that historical backdrop, there’s an alien invasion to deal with, of demonic-looking creatures who are crossing a dimensional barrier, which plays right into the witch-hunters’ hands. All the Catholics who appear are quite sympathetic characters on the wrong end of unfair persecution. The action bounces from a village to a castle to London and then to the English fleet and back, so this story likely would have been unfilmable as a TV episode. The monsters are fairly stock, and not particularly clever, which leaves room for the humans to be the real monsters. Watch out for Beth Chalmers as one of Queen Elizabeth’s handmaidens, but the Queen herself doesn’t appear, nor do Raleigh, Drake, or Walsingham, which is probably good, given the number of versions of the Doctor running around in this time period. Although there are some tonal similarities between this story and the last, the historical elements make for a nice differentiator.
docs.title: The Devil's Armada

docs.text: The Dying Breed Classic Doctors New Monsters #5.2 Released: 21 January 2025 Listened: 3/30/26 This is one of the "Classic Doctors, New Monsters" sets where the "new" element isn't so much a monster as a species, in this case the Lupari, who appeared in "Flux," mostly in the person of the cranky-but-huggable Karvanista. That makes this the most recent "new monster" in the series to date. The Doctor and Leela arrive on the Lupari homeworld, the Loop (or possibly "Loupe"?), which turns out to be a ringworld rather than a planet. They're fairly early in Lupari history, before contact with humans, when the Lupari seem to be in a medieval phase, except they have energy weapons. They ingratiate themselves quickly with the local lord by pretending to be servants of K-9, who is accorded all the rights of a Lupari citizen. Personally, I find it hard to imagine that any bipedal canid species would recognize K-9 as one of them, or anything other than a box on wheels, but maybe I have less imagination than the Lupari. There's a standard-issue succession crisis going on, but also earthquakes, mysterious trees, unusual weather, and a temporal anomaly, all of which takes the Doctor a while to untangle. We learn an awful lot more about the Lupari than we did from "Flux," and writer Tim Foley puts a lot of effort into making the nonsensical parts at least somewhat plausible. As you might imagine, Leela is pretty comfortable in a warrior society, but she also uses her wits effectively when she judges that strength alone won't cut it. Bottom line: I love Karvanista, as many fans do, but I think the Lupari as a whole were rather half-baked in "Flux." I found myself liking this story more than I expected to.

docs.text: Classic Doctors New Monsters #5.2 Released: 21 January 2025 Listened: 3/30/26 This is one of the "Classic Doctors, New Monsters" sets where the "new" element isn't so much a monster as a species, in this case the Lupari, who appeared in "Flux," mostly in the person of the cranky-but-huggable Karvanista. That makes this the most recent "new monster" in the series to date. The Doctor and Leela arrive on the Lupari homeworld, the Loop (or possibly "Loupe"?), which turns out to be a ringworld rather than a planet. They're fairly early in Lupari history, before contact with humans, when the Lupari seem to be in a medieval phase, except they have energy weapons. They ingratiate themselves quickly with the local lord by pretending to be servants of K-9, who is accorded all the rights of a Lupari citizen. Personally, I find it hard to imagine that any bipedal canid species would recognize K-9 as one of them, or anything other than a box on wheels, but maybe I have less imagination than the Lupari. docs.text: The Evil One Fourth Doctor Adventures #3.4 Released: 11 April 2014 Listened: 3/6/22 It’s time for another story with the Master, because he’s going to be recurring for the Fourth Doctor, especially since Geoffrey Beevers is willing and available. However, this Nick Briggs story is kind of slight. It starts well, as an investigation into the murder of the passengers and crew of a luxury star-liner, but that part fizzles out fairly quickly, as the focus is on the Master brainwashing Leela into becoming an assassin tasked with killing the Doctor. Michael Keating (Vila from Blake’s Seven ) has a nice role as an investigator, but he’s written out rather abruptly. The coda with Leela reflecting on what her father meant to her is great, but the whole story is unfortunately less than the sum of its parts.

docs.text: The Exxilons Fourth Doctor Adventures #4.1 Released: 15 January 2015 Listened: 4/3/22 Now we’re back to the Fourth Doctor Adventures, but with added John Leeson! K-9’s presence does make a distinct change to the dynamic. Specifically, they’re toting around a third party with a ranged weapon, and a distinct willingness to use it. Even though he only shoots sentient beings with a stun ray in this story, he quite frequently threatens with it, and does quite a bit of plot-relevant property damage. I can’t help thinking that the Doctor couldn’t have solved problems this way just a couple of stories ago. It’s also to Leela’s detriment, as she doesn’t get to show off her growing knowledge when there’s a talking computer with all the answers hanging around. As for this story, it’s related to “ Death to the Daleks ,” as you might be able to tell from the title, but it’s not a sequel. In fact, it takes place long before that story, and gives some insight into just what the Exxilons were doing when they were a functioning civilization (hint: it wasn’t great). Of particular note is Jacqueline King (Sylvia Noble in the modern series) playing another role where you’d never recognize her, particularly this time, because she’s using an American accent just for fun. Tim Treloar also features, doing a rather guttural native. The pacing is a bit better than previous one-hour stories, although the ending is a little abrupt.
docs.title: The Exxilons

docs.text: The Fate of Krelos Fourth Doctor Adventures #4.7 Released: 8 July 2015 Listened: 4/8/22 This story and the next are connected, but not so tightly that they can be considered one story. In fact, in this first part, not a lot seems to be happening at first. Basically, the Doctor wants to go fishing, and convinces Leela to come along. The planet where he chooses to go, Krelos, is at a point in its development where most of society’s tasks are automated, although there are still some citizens who object to that. It’s a very small plot, with the Doctor and Leela basically trying to rescue one person. There’s also an extended sequence where K-9 reactivates an older control room, in which a piece of Jamie’s kilt is snagged on the console, leading to the Doctor telling Leela about Jamie. (I’m guessing neither of them remember the events of “ Dumb Waiter .”) After a timeslip, Leela and the Doctor have an argument about interference. It’s one of those in which the Doctor pulls out the “I can’t interfere” card for reasons known only to Time Lords, and the companion simply doesn’t buy it, except even more so, because it’s Leela. Parts of it are interesting, and parts seem kind of drawn out and repetitive (the number of times they climb up or down the mountain). Kudos to Nick Briggs for wanting to do a story without mortal peril (to the TARDIS team, anyway), but I’m not sure it really works, except as an extended lead-in.
docs.title: The Fate of Krelos

docs.text: The Foe from the Future Lost Stories Special Released: 9 January 2012 Listened: 2/21/22 This story comes from a boxed set of Lost Stories released during Series 3, but not officially part of that series. Why, I have no idea. This story was originally intended as the finale to Season 14, but writer Robert Banks Stewart was unable to finish it, so Robert Holmes wrote “ The Talons of Weng-Chiang ” instead, and it’s hard to argue that wasn’t the better choice. Anyway, that means this is a six-parter, making a sharp contrast to the Short Trips we’ve been doing for the last little while. There are a number of elements that are present in “Talons,” such as a man from the future coming back to the present and being badly damaged in the process, an interesting and sadistic henchman, and the involvement of the police. However, unlike “Talons,” this story jumps to the future, where we see exactly what the people of that time are afraid of, and spend a lot of time running around there. It’s still early days for Leela, but she’s starting to get the hang of things, and is generally pretty fearless in the face of danger. She’s still fairly vicious, though, threatening the villains when the Doctor isn’t around, and wanting to hunt down giant insects for fun. The villain, Lord Jalnik, is quite memorable, especially because he doesn’t have despotic ambitions for a change. Special mention should go to Charlotte-from-the-village (as she’s often called), who was apparently invented by John Dorney for the adaptation, but it’s hard to imagine the story without her. I’d never want to replace “Talons,” especially not Jago & Litefoot, but this probably wouldn’t have been a bad story either.
docs.title: The Foe From the Future

docs.text: The Friendly Invasion Fourth Doctor Adventures #12.4 Released: 21 June 2023 Listened: 7/21/23 This one is a reasonably nice historical. It’s Westbourne, England, 1943, the middle of WWII. There are a bunch of American troops stationed in the town: Dainty company, who will soon leave for deployment and play a critical role in the invasion of Normandy. Their presence is causing some friction with the locals, but that’s not really the problem. There’s another temporal anomaly here, and it’s pulled the TARDIS off-course. Turns out there’s some time-tourists here from the 51st century, inhabiting other people’s bodies. And since 51st-century time travel tech is rubbish (ask Magnus Greel ), things are going sideways. It ends up with a big scene of zombie villagers with flaming hands attacking an old pub defended by Leela and a bunch of Americans. It’s certainly fun to watch her order around the “Dainty men,” as she calls them. Margaret, meanwhile, faces the fact that she’s alive in this time, if a teenage girl. She’s not very good at keeping her future knowledge hidden, but it mostly turns out all right. So it’s a nice mix of adventure, character-building, and drama, along with some rather decent American accents for a change.
docs.title: The Friendly Invasion

docs.text: The Genesis Chamber Philip Hinchcliffe Presents #2 Released: 6 September 2016 Listened: 3/26/22 This next run of stories is from the “Philip Hinchcliffe Presents” range. We’re lucky enough that Hinchcliffe is still with us, and for this range, he came up with the story concepts and provides feedback on the scripts. So they’ve got that thread of darkness to them, with some Bob Holmes dark humor, and they’re long, a mix of four- and six-parters. This one has some interesting concepts, but I’m not sure it really gels properly. There’s a colony planet with a bunch of pampered city dwellers beholden to a central computer, and an outside group of back-to-the-land luddites. Which is a decent start, but it gets interesting when you throw in some invaders, and an alien “helper” who’s a bit too good to be true. There’s a Romeo & Juliet story, which works reasonably enough because the actors sell it well. Unfortunately, the Doctor and Leela aren’t really controlling events all that much, and mostly just seem to be along for the ride. The bad guys are done in by infighting and a deus ex machina, which is kind of unsatisfying.
docs.title: The Genesis Chamber

docs.text: The Ghost of Margaret Fourth Doctor Adventures #12.6 Released: 21 June 2023 Listened: 7/23/23 Margaret has had enough. After the last story, where she came pretty close to doom, she wants to get off the ride, although she’s sad and her life is still empty. Unfortunately, in putting her back, the TARDIS jumped a time track, which isn’t clear until after they’ve already left (the Doctor not being one for goodbyes), leaving Margaret stranded in a “nowhere place,” with manifestations of her depression out to get her. Oddly, Captain Ray Hunter turns up, one of the soldiers from “ The Friendly Invasion .” He’s 30 years older, as we’re in Margaret’s present. Apparently Margaret sent for him, but she doesn’t remember doing that. So we’ve got timey-wimey, and spooky dreamscapes, and time slippage. It’s a fairly tight story, as it’s mostly concerned with Margaret’s personal anxieties. In the end, she manages to decide what she wants, which is a nice closing to her story. There are enough stories here that it doesn’t feel like Margaret outstayed her welcome, but few enough to justify her not coming up again later.
docs.title: The Ghost of Margaret

docs.text: The Ghost Trap Short Trips #5.4 Released: 6 April 2015 Listened: 2/20/22 This Short Trip is probably longer than it actually needs to be, but it lets us spend time in Leela’s head while she’s still relatively new. They land on an entirely organic spaceship, but unfortunately the crew is dead, as are a bunch of humans who don’t belong there. While trying to figure out what’s going on, they encounter some ghosts, which gives Leela some more mental trouble trying to figure out exactly what’s going on. Like a lot of short trips, there’s not so much an enemy to fight as a problem to resolve. Louise Jameson puts a lot of effort into this one, ramping up the tension.
