docs.text: The Ghosts of Gralstead Philip Hinchcliffe Presents #1.1 Released: 5 September 2014 Listened: 3/31/22 This story, the first of the Phillip Hinchcliffe collection, leans in hard on the tropes that era is famous for. It’s a ghost story with a scientific explanation, set in Victorian England, with strong secondary characters. Leela even mentions wanting to see Jago and Litefoot again, but they’re 40 years too early. Plot-wise, it bounces around somewhat, from ghost story to Africa to gods in epic combat, and yet it’s paced quite well, so it doesn’t feel over-long. The origin of the bad guys is never fully explained, nor their motivations, but that’s also appropriate to the era. Leela does pretty well in Africa, better than she did in the Amazon in the last story . She also gets to do a more-than-usual amount of fighting, and isn’t at all hesitant to kill if she thinks it’s warranted. A large component of the story is a macguffin that can heal or even resurrect the dead, which allows for more dramatic cliffhangers in which our main characters actually do die, but cheapens it by making resurrection easy. You’d think there’d be some psychological repercussions to that, but apparently not. Also of note are the bit characters: an unscrupulous poor-house matron, and a pair of body-snatchers that fit the Robert Holmes mode quite nicely. A decent story, especially for a six-parter.
docs.title: The Ghosts of Gralstead

docs.text: The God of Phantoms Philip Hinchcliffe Presents #4 Released: 19 August 2021 Listened: 3/28/22 This one is huge, long even for a six-parter, and there’s a lot going on. There’s a planet with a bunch of Earth colonists, but instead of living as one civilization, there are multiple factions, some back-to-nature types, some more traditional, and some aggressive. One thing they all have in common is that they’ve regressed technologically, and while they’re aware of their ancestors’ tools, they can’t use them. So the battles are nasty, but not horrific. There’s also some rudiments of religion, with the villagers seeming to hold to a mild form of Christianity, and the commune-dwellers worshiping forest spirits and ghosts. And there’s a bunch of ghosts in this story, which are mostly treated as rather matter-of-fact. The Doctor is dismissive of ghosts as always, but he seems more on edge than usual in this story, and there’s a reason for that. Leela fits into the society better than she has in quite a few stories, although formal dancing eludes her. You’d think that would be enough to go on with, but as the story goes on, it gets more and more complex, getting involved in the Doctor’s personal history, and extending all the way to a war of the gods. Even though the story is quite long, seeming to have several different climaxes along with a lengthy coda, some parts of the backstory are still fuzzy, but Philip Hinchcliffe seems to like it that way. The secondary characters here are well-drawn, with differing agendas and motivations. Many of them have nuanced relationships to the Doctor and Leela, instead of the stubborn caricatures you often find in these stories. It’s a quality entry, although boy is it long.
docs.title: The God of Phantoms

docs.text: The Helm of Awe Philip Hinchcliffe Presents #3 Released: 11 April 2017 Listened: 3/26/22 This story is a four-parter, and yet it packs a lot of ideas into its running time. It’s set way up north in the Shetland Islands, on an island so small and insular that official records say that it’s uninhabited, and the locals like it that way. It has an unusually warm climate for its latitude, and rather spectacular aurora (the titular “Helm of Awe,” which really doesn’t play into the plot at all). In addition to the people’s distrust of strangers, there’s the local laird, who’s heavily into archaeology, his daughter, who’s caught between the urge to see the world and her deep roots on the island, and a family curse that’s more than it seems. Because this is a Philip Hinchcliffe story, we need a local ancient ritual, this one an annual Viking celebration of the turning of the year. Which heightens the emotions nicely, but also gives Leela a chance to participate in a longboat race, which she likes very much. There’s a timey-wimey jaunt back to WWII, to determine the roots of the mystery. As before, the actual sci-fi element is a bit of a disappointment, and the story just sort of ends instead of wrapping up, but that seems to be par for these stories.
docs.title: The Helm of Awe

docs.text: The King of Sontar Fourth Doctor Adventures #3.1 Released: 15 January 2014 Listened: 3/4/22 This next season with Leela looks like it’s trying to take some more chances with the Doctor and Leela’s relationship, as their philosophies on the necessity of killing come into conflict. They’re dropped into a conflict between a rogue Sontaran superman and, well, every other Sontaran. Super-Sontaran was a genetic anomaly, and in the way of such entities, he’s judged himself superior to the rest of his race, and therefore needs to wipe them out and take over. Rather than just getting some popcorn, the Doctor thinks that would be bad for the timelines, and sets about stopping him. Leela gets separated early on, and ends up leading a slave rebellion, because that’s what happens when you leave a Companion alone with some slaves for more than 10 minutes. Leela does quite well on her own, because battle is something she knows, possibly even more so than on TV. Unfortunately, she’s also becoming quite skilled with a variety of weapons that were far outside her experience before, and that’s what’s got the Doctor worried. John Banks and Dan Starkey provide the Sontaran voices, because of course they do. Starkey is still recognizable, but he puts enough of a spin on Strang that there’s no danger of mistaking him for Strax. And John Dorney accomplishes the goal of making the Sontarans believable and scary, which isn’t always easy in the modern era.
docs.title: The King of Sontar

docs.text: The Mind Runners Fourth Doctor Adventures #7.3 Released: 18 January 2018 Listened: 4/11/22 The next two stories are really a single four-parter, no matter how they’re numbered, although the tone of each is different. This is a John Dorney story, and it’s stuffed with high concepts. There’s the Mind Runners, who use headsets to tap into the consciousness of strangers and look out through their eyes. All they do is watch, though, so it’s less intrusive than other such tropes. There’s the “Digitals,” people who’ve uploaded their consciousness into robots, and would like everybody else to do the same. There’s a mysterious assassin of unusual abilities. There’s a malevolent force that’s apparently killing mind runners. There’s a rocket that’s supposed to evacuate the population of the planet, but oddly this is only a minor point in the first story, barely mentioned. All of it against a Blade Runner style sci-fi-noir backdrop. K-9 is present in this one, which is good, because he’s quite useful. Leela also transfers her hunting skills quite easily to the urban jungle, in ways that are surprising, but explained plausibly, because Dorney is just that good. The secondary characters are well drawn and sympathetic. The longer format really benefits the story here, because we still have very little clue what’s happening at the end of the first part, even though rather a lot has happened.
docs.title: The Mind Runners

docs.text: The Oseidon Adventure Fourth Doctor Adventures #1.6 Released: June 2012 Listened: 2/28/22 This is the second part of the finale of the first season of Fourth Doctor Adventures, and honestly, it’s a bit odd. It continues from the previous story, but it’s almost completely different. The previous story seemed rather of its time period (the classic series) with the small-town mystery. This one is full-blown alien invasion, and much of it is borderline farcical. All the nonsense from the last episode was so that the Master could bring the Kraals to Earth. Having failed in “ The Android Invasion ,” they want another go. Which forced the Doctor to call in UNIT, just not any characters we actually recognize, but rather the second string. And Kraals mean androids, specifically android duplicates who are so convincing that they can fool almost anyone, including themselves. Alan Barnes plays this for laughs, as he so often does, but it does become a little silly with duplicates on top of duplicates, most of them created almost instantly. Nobody seems to take the Kraals particularly seriously, so they end up more or less stand-ins for the Sontarans, and it’s not helped that they’re clearly voiced by veteran Sontaran actors Dan Starkey and John Banks. Add in some absurd dialog about Z-radiation, and O-radiation, and Z-O-radiation, and it’s hard to take any of it seriously. The entire cast seems to be having a ball, but it’s kind of a weak finish for a new series. Fortunately, there was never any doubt whether Big Finish would continue it.
docs.title: The Oseidon Adventure

docs.text: The Primeval Design Fourth Doctor Adventures #10.4 Released: 10 February 2021 Listened: 3/21/22 Leela and the Doctor have seen a handful of dinosaurs recently, so the Doctor takes her to meet Mary Anning , an English pioneer in the field of paleontology. Unfortunately, as a woman in the early 19th century, her work has gone unrecognized for over 100 years after her death. The Doctor is in full bluster mode, plowing into Mary’s life and getting himself involved in an investigation into an unusual death. Leela, of course, is a source of inspiration to Mary, as she fails to abide by any suggestions that she should “know her place.” Unfortunately, the story has an absurd amount of shouting and shrieking, which is kind of tough to listen to. I have to ascribe that to director Nick Briggs, rather than writer Helen Goldwyn or any of the actors. Still, these are the loudest exhausted, drowning people I’ve ever heard, especially since one of them has literally just given birth. Obviously, in this kind of a story, you can expect dinosaurs for monsters, but the theory posited is that the alien creatures designed to be the “ultimate killing machines” are not dinosaurs, but dinosaur skeletons . Which is kinda strange no matter how you slice it. But the Mary Anning parts are pretty cool.
docs.title: The Primeval Design

docs.text: The Renaissance Man Fourth Doctor Adventures #1.2 Released: February 2012 Listened: 2/24/22 One of the themes of the Fourth Doctor Adventures was that the Doctor was attempting to educate Leela about her heritage, so in this story, they visit a museum covering anything and everything related to Earth. However, somewhere along the line, the museum got the idea to drain specialists of their knowledge, leaving them empty shells. The casting is very referential: the baddie and his henchman are played by Ian McNeice, not playing Churchill for once, but still unmistakeable, and Gareth Armstrong, who starred in “ The Masque of Mandragora ” a very long time ago. Also of note is Daisy Ashford, daughter of Caroline John and Geoffrey Beevers, in a minor role. Leela is certainly exposed to many different aspects of Earth history, but it’s all somewhat random, and leads to her pronouncing “Renaissance” as “runny-science,” which will never not be funny. But it’s clear that she’s starting to get the hang of the Doctor, particularly determining when he’s trying to snow her with technobabble. The acting and dialog make this one more memorable than the plot.
docs.title: The Renaissance Man

docs.text: The Revisionists Short Trips #9.1 Released: 31 January 2019 Listened: 2/20/22 The first part of this subsection is mostly a lot of short trips, but that’s OK, because Louise Jameson often reads them. Her Tom Baker voice isn’t an impersonation, but usually gets the effect right. In this story, Leela is clearly very new in her travels, still getting used to a lot of things. The Doctor takes her to Geneva, where they meet the Brigadier, who’s in the process of retiring from UNIT. Of course, something weird is going on, in this case, people encountering the ghosts of their ancestors, after which they forget ever having known them. Solving the problem isn’t particularly dramatic, but that’s not the point. The idea is to get Leela and the Brig talking, and each coming to terms with the heritage that caused them to become warriors. The Brig and Leela are definitely kindred spirits here, and it’s great to have a story that puts them together.
docs.title: The Revisionists

docs.text: The Shadow of London Fourth Doctor Adventures #7.5 Released: 16 May 2018 Listened: 4/14/22 This one is OK, pretty much. It’s another one of those stories in which the TARDIS lands in what seems to be London, in this case in 1940, but something is off. There aren’t enough people, it’s unusually quiet and cold, and the few people they meet are acting oddly. Experienced listeners might suspect Kraals, which isn’t the case, but that just points up how often the show does this plot. K-9 isn’t in this one either, probably because his scanners would reveal what’s up far too early. This story continues the pattern from this set of spending all of Part 1 trying to figure out what’s going on, rather than resolve it. Of course, there’s a monster, because there has to be, but it doesn’t leave much of an impression. Leela is getting a little better at operating in urban areas, but the Doctor seems oddly annoying this time. He often doesn’t explain his odd phrases to Leela, but this time he seems on the verge of mocking her with them. And he’s much less concerned about people getting killed than he has been in other stories. It’s a fine story, but no more than that.
docs.title: The Shadow of London

It’s not a terribly involved story: The Doctor and Leela land on a war-torn planet, help a young person, and maybe inspire the people to think differently about their enemy. The Doctor is pretty good at that sort of thing. It’s read by Stephen Critchlow, which is the first narration other than Louise Jameson we’ve had in a while. As usual, he does an excellent job, but his Fourth Doctor is the closest to Tom Baker of any of the various narrators.

docs.text: The Sons of Kaldor Fourth Doctor Adventures #7.1 Released: 18 January 2018 Listened: 4/10/22 A new season starts here, with some twists on the formula. This story is a reference to “ Robots of Death ” without being a direct sequel, because it takes place a considerable time later, when the political situation has changed and robots are no longer trusted. K-9 doesn’t appear, perhaps because he could have shortcut parts of the story. The Doctor has always been particularly sympathetic toward Kaldor robots, and that’s still true here. Andrew Smith is pretty good at stories where the antagonist isn’t what you think they are, and that’s in here too. Leela doesn’t get quite as much to do, but it’s clear that she’s growing in experience, handling robots and spaceships with ease.

docs.text: The Talents of Greel The Diary of River Song #6.4 Released: 27 August 2019 Listened: 2/22/22 This is another one from the River Song set where she jumped in right before, or during, some classic stories, in this case, the imminent “ Talons of Weng-Chiang .” In this case, she pops up beforehand, and the Doctor doesn’t even figure, which is fine, because the Doctor has Jago and Litefoot to help in “Talons,” and River would just get in the way. That doesn’t mean she can’t tweak some things before the story starts, though. Specifically, she gets to meet up with Jago and perform at the Palace Theater, which allows her to push Greel’s plans back a bit. And along the way, explain some things about “Talons” that hadn’t been before, such as: Why is Greel’s lab beneath a theater? How did Greel get so messed up in the first place? What were Greel and Chang doing before coming to London? What happened to Chang’s monkey? Oh, did you not know that Chang had a monkey, who was more popular than Mr. Sin? That’s because he was invented for this story. Angus Wright does an awfully good job capturing the voice of Greel, returning to the role from “ The Butcher of Brisbane ,” and Nicholas Goh helps fix the racist casting from “Talons,” so that’s a good thing. Come for the references, but stick around for the River/Jago banter.
docs.title: The Talents of Greel

docs.text: The Time Vampire Fourth Doctor Adventures special Released: 31 May 2010 Listened: 4/17/22 This story continues the trilogy from “ The Catalyst ” and “ Empathy Games ,” supposedly putting a final end to Leela’s story…which is now completely unnecessary, because of all the other appearances she’s made. Frankly, this is a very strange one, full of time loops and paradoxes and reincarnation and other strangeness. The secondary actor in this is John Leeson, playing K-9 as well as other characters. It covers Leela’s rescue from the Z’nai torture machine where she’s been for…a long time? However, that kicks off a loop of paradox that’s…well, it’s really hard to follow, especially with just one listen. Honestly, I found it hard to focus on. I can see what Nigel Fairs is going for, as he’s done similar work on other Companion Chronicles, but this one just didn’t work for me. And unfortunately, that’s the end of Leela’s part of this project. However, both she and Louise Jameson will be back, in plenty of other stories.
docs.title: The Time Vampire

docs.text: The Tivolian Who Knew Too Much Classic Doctors New Monsters #3.2 Released: 28 July 2022 Listened: 8/4/22 Like the previous CDNM3 story , the “monster” in this one is more of a friendly alien we’ve seen before, in this case the Tivolians from “The God Complex” and “Before the Flood.” They’re the folks who like to be conquered, to a degree that’s nearly disturbing. The title is a reference to The Man Who Knew Too Much , but it doesn’t have much in common with the Jimmy Stewart film except for a tourist who becomes unwittingly involved in a greater plot. Our poor Tivolian protagonist is trying to have a restful holiday in Rome, 1977 (Tivolians apparently look human enough to pass, in Rome), when he gets caught up in a web of organized crime and blackmail where almost nobody is what they say they are. Writer Rob Valentine apparently couldn’t resist the idea of Tivolians in actual Tivoli, hence the Italian setting. The translation circuits also get a workout, with lots of Italian phrases dropped in, as well as every figure of speech involving “Rome” that you can imagine. Unfortunately, Big Finish was unlikely to get David Walliams or Paul Kaye to reprise their Tivolian roles, but the ones we got work just fine. There are a few moments in this where Tom Baker and Louise Jameson sound closer than usual to their actual ages, but it isn’t too much of a distraction. On the whole, it’s a lighter story, and everyone involved seems to be having a good time.
docs.title: The Tivolian Who Knew Too Much

docs.text: Classic Doctors New Monsters #3.2 Released: 28 July 2022 Listened: 8/4/22 Like the previous CDNM3 story , the “monster” in this one is more of a friendly alien we’ve seen before, in this case the Tivolians from “The God Complex” and “Before the Flood.” They’re the folks who like to be conquered, to a degree that’s nearly disturbing. The title is a reference to The Man Who Knew Too Much , but it doesn’t have much in common with the Jimmy Stewart film except for a tourist who becomes unwittingly involved in a greater plot. Our poor Tivolian protagonist is trying to have a restful holiday in Rome, 1977 (Tivolians apparently look human enough to pass, in Rome), when he gets caught up in a web of organized crime and blackmail where almost nobody is what they say they are. Writer Rob Valentine apparently couldn’t resist the idea of Tivolians in actual Tivoli, hence the Italian setting. The translation circuits also get a workout, with lots of Italian phrases dropped in, as well as every figure of speech involving “Rome” that you can imagine. Unfortunately, Big Finish was unlikely to get David Walliams or Paul Kaye to reprise their Tivolian roles, but the ones we got work just fine. There are a few moments in this where Tom Baker and Louise Jameson sound closer than usual to their actual ages, but it isn’t too much of a distraction. On the whole, it’s a lighter story, and everyone involved seems to be having a good time.
docs.title: The Tivolian Who Knew Too Much

docs.text: The Tribulations of Thadeus Nook Fourth Doctor Adventures #10.3 Released: 10 February 2021 Listened: 3/2/22 We’re jumping a ways ahead from a production standpoint, but it’s made clear in this story that Leela is still learning to read, so it belongs here. In later seasons, the Fourth Doctor Adventures converted back to full-length stories, so this one stands out at two hours. The Doctor and Leela run across the titular Thadeus and his girlfriend, who have stumbled into possession of a rather sketchy time machine, one that causes temporal damage when used. Thadeus doesn’t know that, though, and he’s running tours to critical flashpoints in history, like D-Day and the Kennedy assassination. Leela ends up with him, with the Doctor trying to catch up. Leela expresses a lot of confidence in the Doctor’s abilities, which is partially unwarranted. There’s something bigger going on, though, involving acolytes of a dead warlord who want to change history. It’s a very mobile story, with scenes in lots of different places and times, which wouldn’t really work on TV, so Andrew Smith is really taking advantage of the medium here. The secondary characters are well developed, with Brendan Murphy playing the con man with a good heart, and Laura Riseborough as his long-suffering girlfriend who sees him as more than what he is. The baddies don’t make as much of an impression, but that’s OK, because it’s the character growth that’s important. Running across other time travelers is always good fun, and this story plays with the conventions nicely.
docs.title: The Tribulations of Thadeus Nook

docs.text: The Valley of Death Lost Stories Special Released: 9 January 2012 Listened: 3/29/22 This particular entry is a Lost Story, rather than a Philip Hinchcliffe Presents, so it lacks the same sense of gothic horror, but it’s still a four-parter. It involves an explorer who went missing in the Amazon in 1873, and a follow-up expedition in 1977 that the Doctor and Leela join under UNIT credentials. Leela should be in her element here, and she certainly thinks she is, but she fails to track one tribe, and then fails to notice another before they capture her. She’s clearly having an off day. In fact, the whole story is slightly off, just a bit too whimsical and humorous. Even though it came from an idea from Philip Hinchcliffe, it’s a Jonathan Morris story, with the attendant off-kilter tone. In that sense, it feels like it belongs in the Graham Williams era of the show. Halfway through, the setting abruptly changes to London, and UNIT gets involved, but only ineffectually without the Brigadier. It does have slightly higher stakes and a more dramatic ending than the previous few stories, but mostly it feels a bit strange. Of particular note is Jane Slavin, playing an American journalist with a pretty decent New York accent. We’ll see more from her in a little while .
docs.title: The Valley of Death

docs.text: The Wizard of Time Fourth Doctor Adventures #12.3 Released: 21 June 2023 Listened: 7/20/23 The second half of series 12 goes by the name “Angels and Demons,” which is kind of unfortunate, because it’s awfully close to a spoiler. This half has three two-part stories and one four-parter, which gives a feeling of a lot of content, so that’s nice. This story is by Roy Gill, and has a distinct fairy-tale feeling to it. In fact, it’s one of those where the TARDIS crew don’t really feature that much, as the emphasis is on the narrator, Jacob Harmer. The story starts with an older Jacob at the end of his life, telling a caretaker stories in flashback of when he’d met the Doctor, Leela, and Margaret. Jacob eventually went on to become a famous writer, using the TARDIS crew as inspiration for his “Dirk Forever” stories. Jacob stumbles into a pesky temporal anomaly behind his house, and eventually stumbles back out of it again. As a result, he meets the Doctor and friends at several different points along his lifespan, but doesn’t stay with them long. One of the latest meetings features a distinctly older Doctor, and I don’t really like it when the Doctor solves a problem by simply waiting around for decades, but there’s enough timey-wimey going on in this story that maybe that’s not really what happened. It’s definitely a departure in storytelling terms, which may be enough for variety.
docs.title: The Wizard of Time

docs.text: The World Traders Fourth Doctor Adventures #10.1 Released: 20 January 2021 Listened: 3/17/22 The next block is a bunch of full-length stories, making a contrast to the previous series. This one takes place in London, in the early 21st century, probably around 2021, given the release date. There’s a corporation that's acquired an extraordinary amount of wealth in a short time, which is slightly suspicious, but they’re also very secretive and have tech that’s too advanced for the time. That results in a bunch of interesting alien races, some time travel, and some very creative real estate investment strategies, some of which border on the silly. There’s a bonus companion in journalist Emma Fremantle, mostly so that the Doctor has someone to bounce off of while separated from Leela. Unfortunately, she’s not a patch on Sarah Jane, but she also spends a good chunk of the story brainwashed. Leela gets to be in her element, hunting an alien in the late Cretaceous. She’s also quite a bit more primal, even violent, in this story. She’s not even attempting to adapt to the culture she’s in; instead, she’s using her skills to take advantage of people who don’t have them, and being frankly disdainful of the trappings of a high-tech society. It’s a bit of a change for her, and I don’t know if it’ll serve her well long-term, but she’s definitely more confident.
docs.title: The World Traders

docs.text: The Wrath of the Iceni Fourth Doctor Adventures #1.3 Released: March 2012 Listened: 2/26/22 This story is the stand-out of this first series, for me. Of course, it’s a John Dorney story, but there’s no twist, no timey-wimey. It’s a straight historical, initially pitched as “Leela meets Boudica ,” which is an amazing idea, and executed even better. Because of the speedy nature of this story, the Doctor and Leela run into Boudica almost immediately, Leela immediately recognizes her as a kindred spirit, and pledges herself to Boudica’s cause. The Doctor doesn’t like that at all, mostly because of the Web of Time, but he has no real way of explaining that to Leela that she’ll understand. It goes far enough that Leela is forced to choose between them, and although we know how the story will end up, the anguish in the Doctor’s voice is unmistakable. It’s a powerful story, with both characters doing what they believe is right, based on the values of their own cultures; it gives Leela more agency than just doing whatever the Doctor says all the time. Boudica, as played by Ella Kenion, is also impressive; she has a bold, commanding presentation that radiates self-confidence. It’s easy to see why Leela would be attracted to her. Even better, Leela makes her own decision about who’s right in the end, and adds some nuance to what she considers an “honorable warrior” to be. As a result, this is one of my favorite historicals, period.
docs.title: The Wrath of the Iceni

docs.text: Trail of the White Worm Fourth Doctor Adventures #1.5 Released: May 2012 Listened: 2/28/22 Since the only Master who Big Finish had access to in 2012 was Geoffrey Beevers, they mostly didn’t use him, but if they’re going to do a Fourth Doctor series, he’s fair game. He seems to have recovered a bit from the events of “ The Deadly Assassin ,” so he’s a little more physically capable, but this version of the Master is more cruel and less suave than the Delgado or Ainley versions. This story is set in a contemporary time to where it would have fallen in the classic series, although it’s set in Derbyshire, so the values are a little old-fashioned. And that’s what it appears to be at first: a murder mystery in the country, with legends of a monster, and a couple of eccentric figures for the Doctor and Leela to bounce off of. Except it’s not that at all. There is a monster, the titular White Worm, but it’s not monstrous. The Lord of the Manor isn’t just eccentric; he chases Leela around with a tank. And on top of all that, the Master is here, with a typically convoluted plan. Because this is the first half of a two-part story, it gets more time to breathe, which really just means the Doctor and Leela are separated, and spend a fair amount of time running around on their own. The oddly named Demesne Furze is played by Rachael Stirling, known as the daughter of Dame Diana Rigg, both of whom appeared in “The Crimson Horror” in the new series not long after this. However, I wouldn’t get used to any of the characters from this story, as they won’t stick around.
docs.title: Trail of the White Worm

docs.text: White Ghosts Fourth Doctor Adventures #3.2 Released: 14 February 2014 Listened: 3/5/22 The second story is intriguingly linked to the first , as the Doctor forgives Leela, she takes a stronger hand in her own education, and we see what can push the Doctor close to the ultimate sanction. They land on one of those permanently dark planets, which Big Finish is fond of because they wouldn’t work on TV, but are great on audio. The danger starts almost immediately, as violent, speedy plants grow with any tiny bit of light, and there’s a missile headed for the planet as well. Writer Alan Barnes has a brilliant insert where we hear a battle from Leela’s internal point of view, with her instincts doing the narrating, more or less. But it’s vampires, and the Time Lords’ instinctive hatred of them, that dominates the closing part of this story, and provides a contrast to Leela’s treatment of the Sontaran clones from the previous story. No breakthroughs yet, but I wonder if there will be. On the side, Leela’s reading skills are improving rapidly, and she’s learning the difference between reality and fairy tales.
docs.title: White Ghosts

docs.text: Zygon Hunt Fourth Doctor Adventures #3.8 Released: 15 August 2014 Listened: 3/7/22 We don’t get Zygon stories very often, and it’s nice to see one with the Fourth Doctor. Even more unusually, these Zygons aren’t on Earth, although they’d still like to invade it. A jungle planet gives Leela a good opportunity to practice her skills, and the Zygons are also doing a better job of infiltration than they normally do. There’s a bit of moral dilemma, as the defenders of Earth are shown to be thoroughly reprehensible people, but that doesn’t mean the Doctor can just abandon them. Although it has some good flashes, the story just isn’t all that memorable in the end. That seems to be true of most of the stories from this season; they simply don’t have as much time to develop as I’d hoped. I don’t know if that’s because of the shorter format, or some other reason.

docs.text: The Fourth Doctor and Romana I This era of the TV show was something of an experiment. It was the first full season to have a single story arc, the search for the Key to Time. It also introduced Romana, played by Mary Tamm, intended as an extreme contrast to Leela. Since the Key to Time stories are all pretty much connected, it wouldn’t initially appear that there’s much space to fit in more. However, nobody had yet accounted for the space after the Key to Time story finished, which could have gone on for a while before “ Destiny of the Daleks .” Although Mary Tamm appeared as Romana in small parts in Gallifrey stories, and in a few Companion Chronicles, once Tom Baker returned to the role, she was able to star in one season of full-cast dramas before her death in 2012. Although she died too young, it’s remarkable that there’s one season of stories to better flesh out her character.
docs.title: Fourth Doctor and Romana I

docs.text: Ferril's Folly Companion Chronicles #5.11 Released: 12 May 2011 Listened: 6/4/22 The first appearance of Romana in this project is a Companion Chronicle, which means lots of Mary Tamm. It doesn’t have the usual form of a companion telling a story later in their life, because that’s not possible for Romana I. Instead, it takes place in “real time” as it were, which means in the middle of the hunt for the Key to Time, which is a little odd, but doesn’t take too much handwaving to fix. The action takes place in Norfolk in 2011, which is a bit odd right after “ The Stones of Blood ,” but oh well. The baddy is played by Madeleine Potter, with a fairly strong American accent. She also does half the narration, which means sometimes Lady Ferril’s point of view conflicts with Romana’s, which is kind of amusing. Her impersonation of Tom Baker is fairly dire, but she doesn’t get to do it that often. Mary Tamm’s, while not really an impression, has a nice cadence to it that’s very effective in evoking the Doctor. The story itself, about a former NASA astronaut badly injured on a mission, and now possessed of numerous prosthetic parts, and the ability to control metal, is a bit far-fetched, even by Doctor Who standards. There’s rather a lot of sciency bafflegab, mostly to prove how clever Romana is, but it does threaten to overwhelm the story at times. Still, it’s a nice start to this section.
docs.title: Ferril's Folly

docs.text: Luna Romana Companion Chronicles #8.7 Released: 17 January 2014 Listened: 6/5/22 This story is also a Companion Chronicle, but it’s a bit more complicated. It’s part of the 50th Anniversary celebration, so it continues from “ The Beginning ” and “ The Dying Light ” in continuing the story of Quadrigger Stoyn. The story is constructed in four parts, featuring both Romana I and II. Unfortunately, Mary Tamm had passed away by this point, so the first Romana’s story is told in flashback by Romana III, played by Juliet Landau. Her voice is a bit of an acquired taste, and doesn’t really mesh that well with Romana I’s imperious personality, but at least she’s written properly. The Doctor and Romana stop off in ancient Rome, where they believe the last segment of the Key To Time will be found. Except the Doctor would rather see the latest comedy by Plautus instead, a play called Luna Romana . Romana eventually gets fed up with the Doctor (as she often did), and goes to finish the job on her own, except she ends up in peril at the cliffhanger. That cliffhanger waits until part 3, because of timey-wimey shenanigans, because part 3 continues from part 2, even though part 2 takes place later. Yeah. It’s a little odd that we get another insert with a segment of the Key to Time that’s not what it appears to be, but there’s an interesting bit implying that the Doctor is stalling on finding the last segment because he’s not sure what the outcome will be. The coda with Romana III is a bit elegiac of Romana I, which is appropriate after Mary Tamm’s passing, but most Time Lords aren’t often nostalgic about their earlier personas (“Time Crash” notwithstanding). Then again, Romana was always pretty well in touch with herself.
docs.title: Luna Romana

docs.text: Phantoms of the Deep Fourth Doctor Adventures #2.5 Released: 8 May 2013 Listened: 6/10/22 It’s Doctor Who meets The Abyss . The Doctor parks the TARDIS at the bottom of the Mariana Trench so they’ll be undisturbed while he repairs K-9. So of course a handful of explorers happen upon them almost immediately, and there’s something alien going on nearby. Something alien that uses a force field so that the local pressure is just 3 atmospheres instead of over 1,000, because otherwise the story wouldn’t work. Because there’s swimming, an awful lot of swimming. K-9 sat out the last story, and in this one, he ends up getting mind-controlled on multiple occasions. He’s just not having a good series. There’s nothing particularly special about this one, although Alice Krige is in it, best known as Star Trek ’s Borg Queen.

docs.text: The Auntie Matter Fourth Doctor Adventures #2.1 Released: 14 January 2013 Listened: 5/30/22 The official full-cast stories start out, rather oddly, with a farce, a P.G. Wodehouse parody, with all that entails. The Doctor decides to hang out in 1920s London for a while, annoying Romana, who goes in search of intellectual stimulation. Enter stereotypical upper-class twit Reginald "Reggie" Comely-Bassett, along with his stereotypical dry valet Grenville. Reggie’s searching for a bride at the insistence of his maiden aunt, and being not terribly bright, he latches onto Romana as the first person he sees, and brings her home to meet Auntie. It seems that something odd is going on at Bassett Hall, which independently attracts the Doctor’s attention. The cast is top-notch, with Robert Portal putting on an outrageous speech impediment as Reggie, Alan Cox doing his best Stephen Fry as Grenville, and national treasure Julia McKenzie as the evil Auntie, well before she played The Twelve . Most of the plot is dedicated to keeping the Doctor and Romana apart as they work at the same problem from opposite ends, and giving Reggie as many absurd lines as possible. It’s a strange choice to start this run with a comedy, but it’s definitely a memorable story.
docs.title: The Auntie Matter

docs.text: The Dalek Contract Fourth Doctor Adventures #2.6 Released: 11 June 2013 Listened: 6/10/22 Big Finish, and Nick Briggs especially, like to make sure that every companion gets a turn with the Daleks, especially those who didn’t have a crack on TV, so that’s where this story comes in. And if you’ve got David Warner signed on to your series, you’ll want to use him as much as possible, so he’s back as Cuthbert, along with Toby Hadoke as Dorrick. It’s rather later in Cuthbert’s life at this point, but he’s still conducting whatever transdimensional experiment he was up to in “ The Sands of Life .” Unfortunately, that means damaging some unsuspecting planet and ticking off the populace, so he’s actually hired the Daleks to be his muscle. Or at least, he thinks that’s what he’s done, because anybody who’s seen a Dalek story knows better than that. Because this is the first half of a two-parter, not much really gets done in this story. There’s a lot of running around with the rebels on the planet, Romana and K-9 get separated from the Doctor, and the usual threats and surrenders take place. It’s always fun to have Nick Briggs as the Daleks, but the story itself is a bit ordinary.
docs.title: The Dalek Contract

docs.text: The Final Phase Fourth Doctor Adventures #2.7 Released: 15 July 2013 Listened: 6/11/22 Cuthbert may very well be the single most stubborn opponent the Doctor has ever dealt with. Although he’s smart enough to realize that the Daleks have screwed him over…when the evidence slaps him in the face repeatedly…he’s determined not to reveal why he wants to build a dimensional gateway. The Daleks are very nearly equally stubborn in trying to get it away from him. K-9 gets to be clever in helping the rebels fight the Daleks. Romana gets to be clever in figuring out much of what Cuthbert is doing, but not all of it. And the Doctor gets to have a go at making the Daleks see sense for once in their lives, but you can imagine how well that goes. The nice bit of character development is Romana coming to realize that she does like the Doctor somewhat, laying the seeds for her regeneration. There’s plenty of sound and fury here, but on the whole, the story feels a bit unfinished. And it’s kind of a shame to have four out of seven stories this season taken up with Cuthbert, when “ The Auntie Matter ” and “ The Justice of Jalxar ” are pretty clear stand-outs. One wonders if more could have been done, but without Mary Tamm, that’s unlikely to happen.
docs.title: The Final Phase

docs.text: The Iron Legion Comic Strip Adapatations #1.1 Released: 13 March 2019 Listened: 6/5/22 This little interlude is a bit unusual, because it’s an adaptation for which I’ve read the source material. It’s an adaptation of a couple of the most popular stories from Doctor Who Magazine from that era. Oddly, neither Romana nor K-9 is with the Doctor at this point, and no explanation is offered. The action starts in the village of Stockbridge, its first appearance in the Doctor’s timeline. They’re invaded by the Iron Legion, a robot army from a parallel dimension where Rome never fell. The Doctor pursues them back home to rescue everybody. Although the original comics were short, the audio story follows the plot quite closely (deviating a bit at the end), adding dialog and embellishments to make it a full-length story. There’s more action than in a usual story, and it’s noticeably more fanciful and wider-screen. Also, the Doctor behaves a bit more broadly, with heightened dialog, and more action, which you’d expect from a comic strip. If you like your Doctor Who with some farce, this one is for you.
docs.title: The Iron Legion

docs.text: The Justice of Jalxar Fourth Doctor Adventures #2.4 Released: 11 March 2013 Listened: 6/9/22 This story is a bit more actiony than the last one , at least on the part of our heroes. The Doctor and Romana detect alien tech where it shouldn’t be, and go to investigate, ending up in Victorian London. It’s just about 10 years after “ Talons of Weng-Chiang ,” so they go looking for Jago and Litefoot to help. They’re unaware that J&L have probably met his later incarnations at this point, and have their own series by now. For their part, George and Henry are pleasantly surprised to see the Fourth Doctor again, and are very surprised by Romana, since they were expecting Leela. In fact, Romana gets a lot of agency in this story, running around solving mysteries on her own, with Jago in tow, who has developed a crush on her. This is a John Dorney story, and although the plot isn’t as twisty as he normally writes, it is interesting. There’s a vigilante running around London punishing wrongdoers, but neither Jago or Litefoot, nor the Doctor or Romana, have the cultural context for a “super hero,” so it just never gets mentioned. The ending is a bit darker than anticipated, but not in a bad way. It’s another strong story in this set.
docs.title: The Justice of Jalxar

docs.text: The Sands of Life Fourth Doctor Adventures #2.2 Released: 11 February 2013 Listened: 5/31/22 This story is the first half of a two-parter, and oddly, it’s an extended story, told in three parts. The big draw here is David Warner as Cuthbert, wealthiest and most famous man on Earth, and head of the Conglomerate, which is conducting some dodgy time experiments. It seems to take place in the future, although not too far, as capitalism is still running strong, and the military still seems to use conventional weapons. However, the story is a bit drawn-out to fit. A species of time-sensitive space whales are headed for Earth, disrupting both the TARDIS and Cuthbert’s experiment. Naturally, the powers-that-be react badly to a few billion creatures dropping in on the Sahara. And they have a point, because their spawning process will be destructive to the planet. They’re willing to psychically talk to Romana because she’s a female, but we don’t really know yet how far the connection goes. It’s a decent enough opener, but it’s just an opener.
docs.title: The Sands of Life

docs.text: The Star Beast Comic Strip Adapatations #1.2 Released: 13 March 2019 Listened: 6/8/22 Although I don’t have nostalgic memories of “ The Iron Legion ,” like many nerdy Whovians, I’ve heard of Beep the Meep , so this story holds more interest for me. Unlike the comic story, K-9 doesn’t feature, but the well-drawn secondary characters of Sharon and Fudge, teenagers who find Beep after he crashes on Earth, make up for it. Fudge has more of a role this time, although he’s still slightly pathetic. Of course, if you already know that (spoiler) Beep is the baddie of the piece, that takes quite a bit of the suspense out of the story. Sharon, Fudge, and Fudge’s mother all have rather thick Sheffield accents, and speech patterns that I assume are normal for the era. I can deal with most accents in Big Finish, but the characters’ tendency to drop articles from their sentences was remarkably distracting, more than I’ve encountered before. As in the comic, Sharon ends up as a companion, which was perhaps intended as an ongoing role for Rhianne Starbuck, but to date, there haven’t been any more comic adaptations. I think that’s probably fine by me, as some of the later stories get rather surreal, which is perfect for comics, but not so good for audio. (Addendum: This review was written before the Fourteenth Doctor's version of "The Star Beast," which likely blows continuity to smithereens, but why not enjoy as much Beep the Meep as possible?)
docs.title: The Star Beast

docs.text: The Stealers from Saiph Companion Chronicles #3.12 Released: June 2009 Listened: 6/12/22 This was the first Companion Chronicle (in release order) to feature Mary Tamm as Romana I, and they absolutely gave her a workout in this story. There’s no second actor, so Mary plays everyone, from the Doctor and Romana to upper-class twit Tommy to a German professor to an American millionaire to alien sludge. The storyline is a little bit convoluted, with body-snatching and some “whodunnit” qualities that take the Doctor and Romana time to unravel. Romana is mostly treated like an equal partner in this one, except in a few spots where the Doctor has greater experience. The story as a whole is serviceable rather than excellent, but the acting is really amazing, so that’s a good one on which to bid farewell to Mary Tamm for this project (mostly).
docs.title: The Stealers from Saiph

docs.text: The Warren Legacy Short Trips Rarities #3.4 Released: 28 September 2018 Listened: 6/12/22 This short trip is read by Stephen Critchlow, who does an excellent Fourth Doctor, so that makes this one special. It’s also on the long side for a Short Trip at 35 minutes. That gives enough room to tell a full story, one full of timey-wimey and paradoxes, where the Doctor and Romana come in on the end and have to work their way backwards. The baddies don’t leave much of an impression, and you wonder if maybe this would have been better if expanded somewhat. There’s no particular reason that Romana I is in this story; it really could have been any companion.

docs.text: War Against the Laan Fourth Doctor Adventures #2.3 Released: 11 March 2013 Listened: 6/1/22 If you thought the guest stars in part 1 were fun, I didn’t mention Toby Hadoke as Cuthbert’s right-hand-man, Jane Slavin in her first-ever Big Finish role, and Haley Atwell as the President of Earth (not a bad promotion, Agent Carter!). Unfortunately, as far as the plot goes, I’m a bit unimpressed. Although Haley Atwell is always awesome, her “unexpected presidential candidate” is just a little too naive and trusting to be believable as the president of a planet, new to the job or not. And no matter what the Doctor says, if you’ve got a species that’s about to wipe out all life on Earth because they made a mistake and got lost, well, there’s a point where you stop talking and take the tough action to save all your constituents. But this is a Nick Briggs story, so it all comes out well in the end. I wish Romana had a more active part, although she has some moments of brilliance. And Cuthbert is interesting enough that he’ll be back again later .
docs.title: War Against the Laan

docs.text: The Fourth Doctor and Romana II Although Mary Tamm is awesome, Lalla Ward made a strong impression as Romana II. She was smart enough to equal the Doctor, and in her new form, a little more whimsical and flexible, deliberately chosen to match the Doctor’s lifestyle better. There was certainly plenty of chemistry between this Doctor and Romana, as the actors married, but only briefly. Lalla Ward has also been a strong supporter of Big Finish, appearing in a number of Companion Chronicles and also headlining the Gallifrey series. It seemed somewhat inevitable that she’d participate in the Fourth Doctor Adventures series. Although Big Finish goes to great lengths to hide it, it seems that she never actually records with Tom Baker, but always does so remotely. Unfortunately, it seems like some of that bleeds into her performance, as she quite often seems exasperated, with little of the joy from her first few TV stories.
docs.title: Fourth Doctor and Romana II

docs.text: Babblesphere Destiny of the Doctor #4 Released: 1 April 2013 Listened: 7/6/22 This one is from the “Destiny of the Doctor” series, which means it’s a narrated story, in this case by Lalla Ward. She’s got Roger Parrott to play the various male roles, but Lalla narrates the Doctor, and doesn’t attempt Tom Baker’s voice at all. Unfortunately, a lot of the banter doesn’t come across as well with the constant “he said,” “she replied,” and so on. As for the story itself, it’s a critique of social media and the inanity it entails. That was probably more insightful in 2013, but in 2022, it’s not very impressive. Johnny Morris can do better. It also has another over-used trope, the “mind-sucking monster is feeding on human brains, so we’ll give it a Time Lord brain and it won’t be able to handle the volume.” Which is fine if done properly, but there isn’t any interesting twist on this one, really. As always in these Destiny stories, there’s an insert from the Eleventh Doctor, but it doesn't add a whole lot, except giving the Fourth Doctor the opportunity to comment on the Eleventh’s youthful looks.
docs.title: Babblesphere

As for the story itself, it’s a critique of social media and the inanity it entails. That was probably more insightful in 2013, but in 2022, it’s not very impressive. Johnny Morris can do better. It also has another over-used trope, the “mind-sucking monster is feeding on human brains, so we’ll give it a Time Lord brain and it won’t be able to handle the volume.” Which is fine if done properly, but there isn’t any interesting twist on this one, really. As always in these Destiny stories, there’s an insert from the Eleventh Doctor, but it doesn't add a whole lot, except giving the Fourth Doctor the opportunity to comment on the Eleventh’s youthful looks.
docs.title: Babblesphere

docs.text: Casualties of Time Fourth Doctor Adventures #5.8 Released: 10 August 2016 Listened: 7/1/22 The closing half of this story brings us answers to a bunch of questions: Who exactly is Cuthbert, and where did he come from? What is his actual goal? Why does he only have one name? What’s up with that parrot in the TARDIS? What does the Black Guardian have to do with all of this anyway? As to whether those answers are particularly satisfying…well, maybe not so much. Some things still seem arbitrary, and the science is kind of wonky, even by Doctor Who standards. It seems to be one of those stories that aims for “charmingly ambiguous,” but lands on “confusing” instead. Romana continues to sound irritated with everyone and everything. Toby Hadoke’s Mr. Dorrick gets to be properly menacing this time around, even if it’s ineffective.

docs.text: Dethras Fourth Doctor Adventures #6.4 Released: 20 April 2017 Listened: 7/6/22 This story has a fairly high concept: creatures that can hyper-evolve to withstand any environment, and the people who want to weaponize them. So of course it starts on a WWII-era submarine. In space. And there’s also a monkey. All of which seems kind of wacky for a story, and in fact, there doesn’t seem to be as much story here as one would think. The hitch is that the villain is fairly irrational and gives up way too easily, but this is only a one-hour story. The Doctor also seems rather angrier than usual, and even says so outright. It’s also somewhat odd in that it leaves a potentially dangerous resource around for anyone to find, and the Doctor is OK with that. Writer Adrian Poynton has only done a few stories for Big Finish; this and a couple of “Jenny” stories, which is probably why it seems kind of different. Not necessarily good different or bad different, just different. And it leads directly into “ The Leisure Hive ,” which is the first instance we’ve seen of one of these series taking a break in the middle.
docs.title: Dethras

docs.text: Gallery of Ghouls Fourth Doctor Adventures #5.5 Released: 10 May 2016 Listened: 6/28/22 This one is set in Brighton, 1833, where two competing exhibitions of waxworks are competing rather aggressively for customers. One of them is a thinly-veiled copy of Mme. Tussaud’s (although they also reference her by name), and the other is slightly more gruesome, but neither is entirely what they appear to be. Apparently the public was fascinated by the French Revolution at the time, particularly beheadings, so there are a lot of figures of Frenchmen hanging around. The guest cast is an impressive list of Big Finish talent: Celia Imrie, Nikolas Grace, Stephen Critchlow, and Helen Goldwyn…not that you can tell, because most of them are doing accents of one sort or another. The Doctor continues being somewhat antic, and Romana, unfortunately, keeps being irritated, although usually at people other than the Doctor, at least this time. I’m sure the actors all had a lovely time, but the story doesn’t really stand out.

docs.text: Legacy of Death Fourth Doctor Adventures #5.4 Released: 13 April 2016 Listened: 6/27/22 This story continues on from the previous , with 100% more timey-wimey. In particular, the flavor of timey-wimey in which people in the past can leave messages for people 1,000 years in the future, and people in the future can leave messages that later travel to the past to affect earlier events. Even Doctor Who doesn’t go to this well all that often (Steven Moffat notwithstanding), but Douglas Adams wasn’t afraid of it, and Johnny Morris is channeling that here. There’s also an unusually high body count, given that in the first half, the two sides tried to avoid killing each other. There’s also a religious cult and double agents confusing things, and I think only K-9 knows the whole story. I’ve said before I’m not really a fan of “wait here for 1,000 years and then do a Thing” plans, and this one isn’t giving me reason to make an exception. Still, if you’re going to do a time-twisty plot, doing it when the companion is also a Time Lord, and therefore doesn’t need to ask for exposition, isn’t a bad idea. So far, this story is the most notable of the season.
docs.title: Legacy of Death

docs.text: Luna Romana Companion Chronicles #8.7 Released: 17 January 2014 Listened: 6/16/22 This is where the rest of the story from the last segment comes in, and as Romana herself says “where it gets complicated.” The TARDIS lands on the moon, which in the future was host to a Westworld -style theme park of historical recreations, including a Roman section (hence “Luna Romana”), all abandoned now. Except Stoyn is here again, an even more bonkers, raving version of Stoyn, which Terry Malloy excels at. Stoyn is trying to approximate Gallifreyan technology with only several thousand years of Earth tech as a starting point. So things get timey-wimey in short order, which allows part 2 of the story to come between parts 1 and 3, even though it seems to take place later. Romana is rather better at crossing her own timeline than the Doctor is, in that she manages to avoid meeting herself or planting any memories that shouldn’t be there. In fact, the Doctor is portrayed at his most annoying and supercilious in this story, and Romana is a willing accomplice. Admittedly, it’s the easiest way to get Stoyn riled so he’ll make a mistake, but it also has the effect of making Stoyn’s hatred of the Doctor almost sympathetic. In the end, that’s the problem I have with this whole trilogy: Although Stoyn does some terrible things in his madness, he should never have been there in the first place, and that’s the Doctor’s fault. Stoyn doesn’t handle his situation well, but he was never temperamentally suited to leaving Gallifrey, so it’s kind of hard to blame him for anything. I don’t know if that was the goal, but the Doctor doesn’t seem very self-reflective here.
docs.title: Luna Romana

docs.text: Subterranea Fourth Doctor Adventures #6.6 Released: 14 June 2017 Listened: 7/8/22 This story isn’t an unfortunate sequel to “ Underworld ,” thank heavens. Instead, it takes place on a planet covered in porous rock, easily burrowed through. The inhabitants are evolved mole-people, dressed for some reason in 19th-century outfits. (Good thing they weren’t trying this on TV.) They live on large steampunk vessels that burrow continuously through the ground, because the surface is no longer habitable, after a war long ago. Unfortunately, they’re being stalked by a mysterious force of cyborgs…which aren’t terribly original, as they go in for capture and conversion, like some other famous cyborgs we know. However, they’re also not terribly bright, so resolving the story doesn’t seem like much of a challenge. Jane Slavin makes an appearance as a plucky young rebel, and seems to be having a ton of fun with it. There’s one plot twist that may catch you off guard, but other than that, the setting is more original than the plot.
docs.title: Subterranea

docs.text: The Beast of Kravenos Fourth Doctor Adventures #6.1 Released: 11 January 2017 Listened: 7/3/22 This new series of Fourth Doctor Adventures is meant to take place during Season 18 of the show (or a bit before), and carries the new theme music that John Nathan-Turner requested. However, the story itself is a return to Gothic horror, as it features Jago & Litefoot. It’s clearly later in J&L’s personal timeline, because they remember meeting Romana I (although they believe Romana II is a different person with the same name). Also, Inspector Quick is here, played by Conrad Asquith, who originated the role in “ Talons .” And it’s written by Justin Richards, who created the Jago & Litefoot series. Outside of all that, though, the story is a bit low-key. Jago and Litefoot are now pretty experienced with otherworldly stuff, so they’re not as credulous or cowardly as they may have been earlier. The Doctor and Romana aren’t concerned about blending in this time either, so they openly bring K-9 around with them. And with K-9’s abilities of computation, scanning, and defense, they don’t actually need long to deal with a J&L-style mystery. Which is more or less fine, as it’s a one-hour story, but it does seem to be a bit of a wasted opportunity. Romana seems a bit more cheerful and less exasperated than usual, but who could be exasperated with Professor Litefoot?
docs.title: The Beast of Kravenos

docs.text: The Beautiful People Companion Chronicles #1.4 Released: 19 February 2007 Listened: 6/13/22 Welcome Lalla Ward to the project! This is a very early Companion Chronicle, and that shows in some peculiarities. The story is four parts, with (increasingly punny) episode titles, even though the full thing is only a little over an hour. The Doctor gets sidelined early on, which gives plenty of focus to Romana, but the actual explanation for his sidelining is laughable. Writer Jonathan Morris is definitely trying to channel some of the Douglas Adams era here, with some overt references, as well as a general sly humor to the dialog. Unfortunately, the “exasperated Romana” persona is in full effect here. Although Romana supposedly regenerated to be more in sync with the Doctor, she sounds annoyed with him most of the time, as though she’s outgrown him. The story takes place at a health spa, where the super-wealthy go to get miraculously thin, but of course there’s something sinister going on with the process. This results in rather a lot of cheap shots about fat people. Although both Romana and the Doctor profess that it doesn’t matter what someone looks like on the outside, it’s clear from Romana’s inner thoughts that she does harbor some prejudice and refuses to acknowledge it. It’s also fairly hypocritical coming from a character who looks like Romana, and especially from someone who can change their physical appearance. On the whole, the story seems rather badly dated, even though it’s only 15 years old, and it caused some cognitive dissonance to listen to it while working out.
docs.title: The Beautiful People

docs.text: The Doomsday Contract Lost Stories #6.2 Released: 17 March 2021 Listened: 6/18/22 This is one of the more recent Lost Stories, a “B-Side,” if you will, to go with “Return of the Cybermen,” which I didn't cover because it's an Unbound version of " Revenge of the Cybermen ." As such, this story didn’t really get a ton of attention. It was originally commissioned by Douglas Adams and written by John Lloyd. Here, it’s adapted by Nev Fountain, and they lean into the Douglas Adams schtick so hard, they’re nearly horizontal. All the minor characters and the planets have absurd Adams-type names, bureaucracy has run amok to the level of absurdity, and the Earth is an insignificant planet in danger of being bulldozed in the name of development, unless the Doctor can prove it has sentient life on it…without revealing that he’s ever been there, as that would be a violation of the law. There’s not a lot of plot to be had, as the emphasis is on the style, and Douglas Adams stories have never been huge on plot. Still, the resolution stretches the timey-wimey well past the breaking point. If you’re not looking for seriousness, this is good, Adams-y fun.
docs.title: The Doomsday Contract

docs.text: The Eternal Battle Fourth Doctor Adventures #6.2 Released: 15 February 2017 Listened: 7/4/22 Who’s up for some Sontarans? We haven’t seen them in a while , and Romana never has, so that’s a good start. There’s an attempt here to do something both different and traditional with Sontarans, as we see a whole bunch of them engaged in a huge campaign, which we haven’t really seen them do on TV. In fact, this campaign has gone on for so long that even the Sontarans are getting tired of it, which is something that really doesn’t happen. Plus, the dead keep coming back as zombies, which is a bit tough on the usual “honorable death” trope. Clearly, something fishy is going on here, and it’s up to the Doctor to find out what. As usual, Dan Starkey plays a whole bunch of Sontarans, and as usual, he’s excellent. I’m a particular fan of Sergeant Major Stom, a Sontaran with an unfortunate habit of thinking, and a wonderful habit of snarking at the Doctor under his breath. Even the Doctor starts to like him. Romana is back to being fully exasperated again, although to be fair she has plenty of good reason. I just thought she’d be a bit more collected by now.
docs.title: The Eternal Battle

docs.text: The Haunting of Malkin Place Fourth Doctor Adventures #6.5 Released: 17 May 2017 Listened: 7/8/22 We’re back into the Adventures season proper, this time with a good old-fashioned ghost story. It’s slightly past the end of World War I, and Malkin Place is inhabited by a pair of twins, Maurice and Beatrice, who lost their father not long ago. Maurice is haunted by events that happened to him during the war, and the house seems to be just plain haunted on top of that. So they invite in a spiritualist to help, who bumps into the Doctor and Romana on the train. The Doctor is once again rather angry with the spiritualist, and dismissive of his “arts.” Romana just flatly disbelieves and doesn’t bother getting upset. Of course, ghosts in Doctor Who always have another explanation, but the story takes its time getting there, leaving the listener plenty of time to guess about it. It holds together rather nicely as a story, mixing the period and time travel together.
docs.title: The Haunting of Malkin Place

docs.text: The Labyrinth of Buda Castle Fourth Doctor Adventures #5.2 Released: 18 February 2016 Listened: 6/22/22 We’re dumping any silliness with this story, which seems to be aiming for Hinchcliffe-style horror. Buda Castle and its labyrinth are in Budapest, where Vlad the Impaler was once imprisoned, which in 1980 makes it popular with vampire hunters. Except that what’s here isn’t exactly a vampire, just an alien using blood as a gestalt organism, and taking people over. Romana is a lot more clinical about the possibility of vampires than the Doctor normally is, but she hasn’t met one yet , so probably regards them as myths. The Doctor is rather unusually shouty and righteous in this one, perhaps more appropriate to season 18 than 17. Mark Bonnar is unrecognizable as the baddie, but has a laconic tone that’s fitting for an immortal, and manages to be all the more sinister for it. Not too scary, but effective.
docs.title: The Labyrinth of Buda Castle

docs.text: The Movellan Grave Fourth Doctor Adventures #6.7 Released: 12 July 2017 Listened: 7/9/22 With this TARDIS crew, it makes sense to include some Movellans eventually. Although I think the best thing about Movellans is their striking visual, the characters do a pretty good job of describing them on audio, so it works out. And this time around, it’s just Movellans, with no Daleks around, although creating a weapon to win the Dalek war is part of the Movellans’ motivation. Unfortunately, they crash-landed just south of London around 1 AD, and weren’t uncovered for 2,000 years. These Movellans no longer have the weakness of deactivating when somebody pulls their power pack off their belt, which was a silly flaw to start with, and means we don’t have to endure any slow-motion deactivations on audio. In fact, this story gets a lot of mileage out of the fact that Movellans generally, and one in particular, are much stronger than humans. There’s still not a ton of peril going on, but it’s a decent enough story.
docs.title: The Movellan Grave

docs.text: The Old Rogue Short Trips #4.4 Released: 10 August 2011 Listened: 6/15/22 This is one of those early, short Short Trips where not much happens. It’s told from the point of view of the villain, an alien conqueror stuck in the body of a London cafe owner, for reasons that become apparent later in the story. The Doctor drops in to check on him once a decade, and this time it’s the Fourth Doctor’s turn, along with Romana. It’s kind of fun to see the alien’s impressions of the various Doctors; he calls this one “the lunatic,” which seems on-the-nose. He’s also very dismissive of Romana, but Romana is being unusually snotty on this story. Which is pretty much all there is to it, but the ancillary action is fun: K-9 is forced to wait outside, and gets up to various antics with the passersby (that would be fun to see on TV, action going on through the windows while the main characters chat in the cafe). There’s also a tiny twist at the end, more of a mint than a real plot development. The story is read by Louise Jameson, although Leela doesn’t appear in the story. Her acting gift comes through clearly, as she captures the tone of the various characters quite well.
docs.title: The Old Rogue

docs.text: The Paradox Planet Fourth Doctor Adventures #5.3 Released: 16 March 2016 Listened: 6/27/22 This story attempts to channel another part of the Douglas Adams era: not the silliness, but the high-concept sci-fi of ideas. In this case, it’s a planet at war with its own past. The people of the past era used up their fossil fuels and let many species of animal go extinct, despite having access to high-energy zenox crystals. So their descendents from the future travel back in time to snatch up both the animals and the crystals. You can probably see where this is going. Romana gets separated from the Doctor almost immediately, and they each spend a good portion of the story trying to puzzle out what’s going on, a process that takes some time, because this is the first half of a two-part story. Romana II seems to work better when she’s not just parroting things back at the Doctor, but instead she finds entirely new people to be exasperated with. Admittedly, the people of both time periods are fairly exasperating.
docs.title: The Paradox Planet

docs.text: The Pursuit of History Fourth Doctor Adventures #5.7 Released: 13 July 2016 Listened: 6/30/22 It’s the end of the season, which means it’s time for a dramatic two-parter, and in this case, the return of Cuthbert , his quantum gateway , and his time-sensitive space manatees . Who once again kidnap Romana to save them, so she and the Doctor are separated early on. She’s ever-so-slightly less exasperated than usual as she figures out the technological end of what’s killing the Laan, and is mostly in control of her situation. The Doctor is much less in control, as he ends up following Cuthbert up and down the timeline, discovering that he’s gone as far back as 1853 to plant the seeds of his business empire. Unfortunately, following a quantum tunnel is tough on the TARDIS, so there’s a lot of crashing sound effects. Because this is a two-part story, not a lot more happens in the first half.
docs.title: The Pursuit of History

docs.text: The Pyralis Effect Companion Chronicles #4.4 Released: October 2009 Listened: 6/15/22 Another early Companion Chronicle, this one has the potential to be something special, but unfortunately falls short. The action takes place in Kasterborous, not far from Gallifrey, where a colony ship carrying a gene bank is looking for the Doctor, as he helped their planet in the past. Unfortunately, they only remember the First Doctor, so they don’t believe the Fourth is the same person. Worse, they accidentally open a prison that the Time Lords sealed 1,000 years ago. (The Time Lords are really bad at cleaning up their trash.) You’d think this would have some interesting implications for the Doctor and the Time Lords, but it just turns into a standard-issue “strange invader” story mixed with a murder mystery. The story is told in present tense from Romana’s perspective. Fortunately, there’s much less “exasperated Romana,” but unfortunately, there’s quite a lot of “terrified Romana” instead. Lalla Ward oversells the cliffhangers, putting too much emotion into the narration. She also seems to have less agency in this story, making for a dissatisfying story overall.
docs.title: The Pyralis Effect

docs.text: The Silent Scream Fourth Doctor Adventures #6.3 Released: 22 March 2017 Listened: 7/5/22 The Doctor and Romana visit 1930s Hollywood, which at the time is full of silent movie stars suddenly unemployed because they’re not suited for talkies. And there’s something out there made of celluloid and stealing actresses’ voices. James Goss is the writer, and as you might expect, it’s a love letter to the silent film era, with lots of sympathy for silent film actors trying to stay relevant. And of course it’s a little bit meta as there’s talk of lost film reels hidden in back rooms, but also whether the Doctor and Romana’s regular lives are actually “adventure stories.” K-9 becomes a GPS about 60 years early. Of course, there are lots of actors trying out American accents, and on the whole, it comes off better than usual for Big Finish, so well done them. The ending is a little more deus ex sonic than I’d like, but there is at least an effort made at handwaving it. A decent story.
docs.title: The Silent Scream

docs.text: The Skin of the Sleek Fourth Doctor Adventures #6.8 Released: 16 August 2017 Listened: 7/9/22 We’ve reached the end of the season, so it must be time for a two-parter. The stakes don’t initially seem very high, as the TARDIS lands on a fairly primitive planet. There’s a nature-documentarian here, along with his assistant and pilot, but they’ve crashed and need help. Mark Platt throws in a twist, though: the planet’s surface is one big, sluggish ocean. You can walk on it, but if you stop, you’ll sink. And that’s just the start of things. Romana’s old friend from the Academy is here as well, but strangely reluctant to say what’s going on. And there’s more going on with the natives than meets the eye too, but we get only the vaguest of clues. It seems like one kind of story, yet the fact that it doesn’t end after two parts indicates it’s an entirely different kind.
docs.title: The Skin of the Sleek

docs.text: The Thief Who Stole Time Fourth Doctor Adventures #6.9 Released: 13 September 2017 Listened: 7/9/22 The second part of this story provides an awful lot of sturm und drang, with people chasing about on the dangerous surface, giant electric eels threatening everybody, and oh yeah, it turns out the planet is a gigantic gelatinous mass engineered by the Time Lords eons ago to plug up a space-time rift, as one does, and then forgotten about. Romana’s old friend Sartia, it turns out, has always hated her, and in addition she’s got a plan to take over all of space and time, as renegade Time Lords often do. When it comes to evil villain ranting, Joannah Tincey has it down. In the extras, several people think she might make a good recurring villain, but that hasn’t happened yet. Jane Slavin and Kieran Hodgson put on their best Cornish accents as natives, and yet still somehow managed to sound like themselves. It’s a big, blowout season finale, but having Mark Platt do it instead of Nick Briggs gives a different quality to the whole thing.
docs.title: The Thief Who Stole Time

docs.text: The Trouble with Drax Fourth Doctor Adventures #5.6 Released: 14 June 2016 Listened: 6/29/22 This one is a John Dorney story, so you can expect twists…and more twists…and some more on top of those. The story brings back Drax, Time Lord, friend of the Doctor’s, and general reprobate, last seen in “ The Armageddon Factor .” He was played there by Barry Jackson, who had agreed to reprise the role, but sadly passed away shortly before recording. He was replaced by Ray Brooks, also with a thick Cockney accent. While the previous version of Drax was a troublemaker, this one is a bit more nefarious. He needs something stolen, and has no problem forcing the Doctor to do it. He also carries a “Blinovitch Limitation Effect Limiter,” which is the sort of nonsense Douglas Adams would make up. Other cast members are particularly notable, including John Challis, Hugh Fraser, and Miranda Raison, all of whom have some history with the show. Eventually, the plot becomes so convoluted that it passes the point of absurdity, but by that time, you probably won’t care anymore. It has just the right lightness of touch that you can’t really blame anybody.
docs.title: The Trouble with Drax

docs.text: Wave of Destruction Fourth Doctor Adventures #5.1 Released: 12 January 2016 Listened: 6/20/22 As we move into the full season of Fourth Doctor Adventures, it looks like the Adams-style sensibility is continuing, if not quite as overtly. The story is set in the 1960s, with the Vardans trying to invade a planet that’s currently swimming in radio waves. Which gives the characters the opportunity to say things like “modulated frequency wave cancellation signal generator,” which they do, in full, many times. I’m not sure that the science actually works the way it’s described, but that doesn’t matter too much, as it’s all technobabble. More fun is the pirate radio station “Radio Frantic,” which is described as having remarkably catchy jingles, and darned if they’re not right. Some of these may be stuck in your head for days. “Exasperated Romana” is back here, even though she does get some plot to do on her own. She’s particularly dismissive of shopping for shoes and 60’s plastic handbags. I can see why that style may not be to her taste, and she probably doesn’t want to shop simply as a distraction for a young woman who’s witnessed traumatic events. But still, someone who wears outfits as fabulous as hers must spend some time shopping and accessorizing. Kind of a forgettable kick-off to the season.
docs.title: Wave of Destruction

docs.text: The Fourth Doctor, Romana, and Adric For many years, Matthew Waterhouse didn’t want to work with Big Finish, mostly because he didn’t think he could reproduce the voice of his younger self. However, after doing some Dark Shadows stories for them, he came around. At first, he did exclusively stories with the Fifth Doctor’s TARDIS crew , but eventually he did a handful of Fourth Doctor stories as well. This period on TV was kind of tumultuous, and took its toll on Tom Baker. As a result, his Doctor appears a bit darker and more reserved in this era.
docs.title: Fourth Doctor, Romana, and Adric

docs.text: A Full Life Short Trips #6.9 Released: 29 September 2016 Listened: 7/16/22 This is an awfully long short trip, a full story and then some. In fact, it’s an alternate timeline in which the Doctor and Romana sacrifice themselves, and Adric ends up living a whole life, which he doesn’t get to do in the main timeline. It takes a while for the horror to dawn that Adric really is stranded alone forever, and there’s a gut-punch at the end with “I’ll never know if I was right.” Matthew Waterhouse narrates in-character as a much older Adric, and it really works. He doesn’t pull any punches about what he was like as a kid. This is one time when the extended short trip is justified.

docs.text: Chase the Night Fourth Doctor Adventures #9.2 Released: 22 January 2020 Listened: 7/11/22 The TARDIS answers a distress call from a pretty high-concept planet: it’s too close to its star, but the night side is habitable. However, it’s not tidally locked, so the only way for anyone to survive is to keep moving, at about 10 mph. Which this particular ship did by constructing a railway track all the way around the planet. Unfortunately, if anything goes wrong, they’re all dead…and things are going wrong. The Doctor and Romana cause some of the problems themselves by lying when first asked who they are and where they’re from. Still, the colony has been engaged in some pretty brutal social Darwinism for a while now, and that’s impairing their ability to trust anybody. The image of being stuck while the terminator creeps closer is pretty tense, although the story goes to that well a few too many times, resulting in a few false climaxes. Where the story gets weird is in the resolution, and the revelation of how life on this planet actually works. There’s an interesting coda in which Romana ponders what she wants to do with her life, and wonders if it’s compatible with the Doctor’s lifestyle. Credit for a good concept, and some strong tension, although it maybe goes on a bit too long.
docs.title: Chase the Night
