docs.text: Erasure Short Trips #8.4 Released: 30 April 2018 Listened: 7/20/22 Story time with Narvin! This is an unusual Short Trip, told in the style of a Companion Chronicle, with a narrator relating a flashback. In this case, though, it’s Narvin talking to Leela. The frame story takes place after Gallifrey: Enemy Lines and before the Time War series. They’ve been in a battle, Leela is injured, and Narvin tells her a story so she’ll stay awake. Except it really is more of a “young Narvin” story than a story about the Doctor. As a young CIA agent, Narvin gets sent to stop some other species from mucking around with time, except he finds the Doctor and Adric already there. The aliens try to strong-arm the Doctor by popping back in history and blowing up the star-liner carrying Adric’s ancestors, erasing him from history. In response, the Doctor sends Narvin to fix it. Sean Carlson narrates quite well, telling the whole thing from Narvin’s biased point of view. He’s never seen the Doctor before, and is well-positioned to relate how intimidating the Fourth Doctor can be, especially when he’s angry. docs.text: Short Trips #8.4 Released: 30 April 2018 Listened: 7/20/22 Story time with Narvin! This is an unusual Short Trip, told in the style of a Companion Chronicle, with a narrator relating a flashback. In this case, though, it’s Narvin talking to Leela. The frame story takes place after Gallifrey: Enemy Lines and before the Time War series. They’ve been in a battle, Leela is injured, and Narvin tells her a story so she’ll stay awake. Except it really is more of a “young Narvin” story than a story about the Doctor. As a young CIA agent, Narvin gets sent to stop some other species from mucking around with time, except he finds the Doctor and Adric already there. The aliens try to strong-arm the Doctor by popping back in history and blowing up the star-liner carrying Adric’s ancestors, erasing him from history. In response, the Doctor sends Narvin to fix it. Sean Carlson narrates quite well, telling the whole thing from Narvin’s biased point of view. He’s never seen the Doctor before, and is well-positioned to relate how intimidating the Fourth Doctor can be, especially when he’s angry. docs.text: Purgatory 12 Fourth Doctor Adventures #9.1 Released: 22 January 2020 Listened: 7/10/22 This series of Fourth Doctor Adventures promises to focus on the interpersonal relationships between the Doctor, Romana, and Adric, and boy, this one dives right in. Adric is already feeling ignored and out of place when the story starts, and almost immediately decides to leave the ship. The Doctor thinks he’s being clever by dropping him off and jumping 15 minutes ahead in time, but this is Doctor Who , where a whole lot can happen in 15 minutes. In this case, getting kidnapped by an entire prison asteroid full of convicts and very strange rust storms. Gotta give Adric credit for committing to the bit; for a while, he even insists he wants to stay at the prison rather than going with the Doctor and Romana. He’s really at his most petulant here, but the story makes the point that he’s never processed his grief for his brother Vash, and both the Doctor and Romana pretty much ignored that. He does get a bit of the “Artful Dodger” act that was supposed to be part of his persona, but rarely showed up. Unfortunately, that can undermine the reader’s trust in him. Romana does a decent job of sticking up for him, but she’s really not experienced at being the big sister, and I’m not sure she’s sorted out her own feelings about Adric. There’s some sci-fi in this story too, with a bodiless entity who feeds on brains, but honestly the resolution to that drags out a bit longer than it should have. Writer Mark Platt knows how to create interesting secondary characters, and there are a bunch of them here, all with their own agendas. It doesn’t leave a ton of room for the plot, though.
docs.title: Purgatory 12

docs.text: The Invasion of E-Space Companion Chronicles #5.4 Released: 13 October 2010 Listened: 7/16/22 This Companion Chronicle takes place rather late in Romana’s tenure in the TARDIS, when Adric is present, but K-9 isn’t. In good Companion Chronicle style, the Doctor gets sidelined early and stays that way for at least half the story. That allows Romana to take the lead, but also allows her to spend a little time with Adric, whom Romana admits she hasn’t given much of a chance. It’s kind of her to realize that Adric really didn’t fit in with his home society, and doesn’t have many alternatives. Of course, the story is written by Andrew Smith, Adric’s creator, who always puts him in a good light. The other speaking role goes to Suanne Braun, a well-known actress who’s also appeared in Stargate and Red Dwarf , so she gets a bigger role than usual as a police inspector investigating a series of murders. Oddly, though, she doesn’t interact with Romana all that much, but carries the narration for parts of the story where Romana’s not around. She also sounds enough like Lalla Ward that it can cause confusion. It’s no fault of this story, but the whole “search for the CVE” thing is starting to get a little tired. This is also the final appearance of Lalla Ward in this part of the project, although she’ll be back later in various Main Range stories, and in Gallifrey .
docs.title: The Invasion of E-Space

docs.text: The Planet of Witches Fourth Doctor Adventures #9.3 Released: 12 February 2020 Listened: 7/13/22 The third story in the set finds the Doctor and Romana taking a methodical approach to finding a CVE and getting out of E-space, which bores Adric to death. Although Romana was defending him not too long ago, she seems frustrated by him now, even though he’s being less peevish and more typical teenager. This story emphasizes the fact that the entire TARDIS crew is extremely intelligent and rational-minded, because although everybody else is concerned with witchcraft and magic, none of the four of them believe it for even a second. This is one of those stories that seems to change dramatically which each part, starting out with prisoners on a ship, then wandering a mysterious planet with an enigmatic godlike being lurking nearby, to trying to stop religious fanatics. All that contrast makes the story more engaging, but it does seem like the characterizations jump around a bit, even if there is an in-story explanation for all of it. There’s an awful lot of bluffing and concealed identities in this story, to the point where it can be tricky to figure out what’s going on. Romana always seems exasperated these days, but in this story it’s worse than usual. Some of Lalla Ward’s line readings seem quite off, as if she can’t find an emotion other than “really annoyed.” There’s some interesting stuff going on here, but I don’t know if it adds up to much.
docs.title: The Planet of Witches

docs.text: The Quest of the Engineer Fourth Doctor Adventures #9.4 Released: 12 February 2020 Listened: 7/16/22 Andrew Smith, writer of “ Full Circle ,” where Adric and E-space were introduced, writes this one. He’s known for writing stories with monsters who turn out not to be so monstrous, or at least are only following their natures. This time, though, while the villain does have an understandable motivation beyond conquest, it’s still an amoral one. The action mostly takes place on an artificial planet that the Engineer has constructed, and can move portions of its crust around seemingly at will. It’s a fascinating image that probably wouldn’t have worked on TV, and unfortunately is hard to capture on audio. No sound effect can convey “a huge chunk of rock has ripped itself out of the surface and is carrying three people away at speed.” So the characters are forced to verbally describe things that are right in front of them, an audio trap Big Finish usually avoids. The various minor characters are well drawn and acted, although the main plotline itself doesn’t seem like enough for a four-parter. Oddly, although there are several stories left to go in this section, this is the last full-cast one, so that’s the last of Tom Baker in this part of the project, except for the inevitable multi-Doctor appearances later on.
docs.title: The Quest of the Engineer

docs.text: Watchers Audio Novels #2 Released: 12 January 2022 Listened: 7/19/22 This is the second of the original audio novels, written and narrated by Matthew Waterhouse, which is an interesting twist. Unfortunately, he’s not as adept a mimic as John Culshaw (who is?), so we’ve got his David-Warner-sounding Fourth Doctor. Because it’s an audio novel, it’s also quite long, which allows for lots of additional detail, but also affects the structure of the story. The Time Lord “Milady” and her companion Marcel are introduced early in the story, but don’t join the main plot until much later. This mostly gives Waterhouse the opportunity to describe the features of an advanced TARDIS in detail, followed later by tons of other TARDISes of various times and purposes, even a child’s “play” TARDIS with a cardboard console and painted controls. The majority of the story takes place in a timeless spot in the Vortex, where something is pulling other time ships together and fusing them into a single mass. (TARDISes are more advanced, so they just land inside, but can’t get away.) Of course there are Daleks here, because who can resist telling a story with Daleks? Plus it allows Nick Briggs to be a second voice actor, relieving the monotony. The Daleks act like Daleks always do, but at least it gives Adric the opportunity to encounter them, which he never did on TV. Much of the story revolves around a couple of other groups of aliens, one a race of cyborgs with a superiority complex, and one a race of lizard-types with a penchant for slavery. There’s not much here that affects the larger story of the Fourth Doctor, except that he becomes exhausted by the end of the story, perhaps contributing to his tiredness in “ Logopolis .” The pace seems unnecessarily languid to me, but maybe that’s because I’ve been listening to radio plays, not audio books. Maybe if this were in print, it wouldn’t bother me so much. But as it is, there’s too much description, too much musing, and way too much denouement.
docs.title: Watchers

docs.text: The Fourth Doctor and Sarah Jane (and Harry) In a tragedy of bad timing, Tom Baker’s joining Big Finish happened right around the same time as Elisabeth Sladen’s death. According to Baker’s website, he had just agreed with Big Finish to do a series of stories with Sladen as Sarah when she died. She did record two series of solo adventures with Big Finish in 2002 and 2006, which are covered elsewhere, and while she was making The Sarah Jane Adventures on TV, she was unavailable to Big Finish. As of 2022, They’ve very tentatively started using Sadie Miller (Sladen’s daughter) as Sarah Jane, but mostly in Third Doctor adventures for now. UNIT Doctor Harry Sullivan is around for the first half of this era, but Ian Marter sadly died in 1986, and is unavailable. Actor Christopher Naylor has played Harry in a few stories, but few from this era. All of which means this section is somewhat short, despite covering two and half seasons on TV. The inserts here are mainly Short Trips.

docs.text: Chain Reaction Short Trips #2.4 Released: 28 February 2011 Listened: 2/13/22 This Short Trip is barely even a story, just a kind of a goof, for which the Fourth Doctor is perfect. He’s at a shopping center, waiting for Sarah, and rolls a pound coin across the pavement, setting off a Rube Goldberg chain of events. The cycle repeats a few times, so it bears careful listening. (And I’m not sure how that works with the Laws of Time, but whatever, it’s a Short Trip.) There’s a small twist, but it’s not really important. And that unimportance makes it a fun story.

docs.text: Collector's Item Subscriber Short Trips #2017-1 Released: 21 March 2017 Listened: 8/5/22 This later Short Trip is still fairly vignettey, without a bad guy as such, just a guy messing with things he shouldn’t be messing with. It’s a nice piece for Sarah, though, as it starts in her own era, at a jumble sale, a tradition Sarah is quite fond of. Writer Paul Salamoff has Sarah’s mannerisms down perfectly, especially when she leads a fellow on for information, and then immediately drops the act once she has what she wants. Steven Critchlow narrates, and as usual, does a fantastic job with the Fourth Doctor’s lines. Finally, this story gives the origin of the TARDIS hatstand, which I’m reasonably sure no one has ever asked about.
docs.title: Collector's Item

docs.text: #HarrySullivan Short Trips #9.8 Released: 29 August 2019 Listened: 2/13/22 Yes, this title is pronounced “Hashtag Harry Sullivan,” which makes it hard to alphabetize, and neither Sarah nor Harry should understand the meaning of the word. Yet that’s what the story is about: The TARDIS crew is on a ship full of journalists orbiting a resort planet and running low on life support, because the celebrities won’t allow the paparazzi to land. Amazingly, the Doctor’s usual bluster and charm is ineffective, so the solution is to make Harry temporarily famous. Writer Eddie Robson clearly intends this to be a commentary on the attention marketplace of the early 21st century, and there’s a certain new-series flavor about it, which makes Harry and Sarah stand out somewhat. It’s read by Louise Jameson, as sadly Ian Marter and Elisabeth Sladen are both unavailable. However, Jameson is an excellent narrator, putting just enough impression in the characters’ voices to achieve the effect.
docs.title: #HarrySullivan

docs.text: How to Win Planets and Influence People Short Trips #7.6 Released: 29 June 2017 Listened: 2/12/22 This short trip has a rather unusual structure, with Rufus Hound not narrating, but telling the story in-character as the Monk. Except he’s the keynote speaker at a corporate function, giving a talk on “How to invade the Earth.” Which is, to be fair, an excuse to take lots of cheap shots at humans and their foibles, which James Goss is certainly equipped to do. In the form of anecdotes, the Monk mentions a few recent times that he was defeated by the Fourth Doctor, Sarah Jane, and Harry, probably in chronological order. Which means that Rufus Hound gets to play the Monk imitating all three of them, which he does reasonably well, although his Tom Baker isn’t as stentorian as one might hope. Of course, the joy of Rufus Hound’s Monk is hearing him go apoplectic, which he quite kindly does by the end of the story. It’s not really the best entry, but it is funny.
docs.title: How to Win Planets and Influence People

docs.text: Invasion of the Body Stealers Classic Doctors New Monsters #4.1 Released: 14 March 2024 Listened: 3/24/26 This is another "Classic Doctors, New Monsters" story, and this time it features Sadie Miller as Sarah along with Tom Baker. Unfortunately, I wish the story was a bit stronger. The "new monster" actually is a monster this time, instead of simply an alien like the Hoxx or the Tivolians . Except that the story clearly wants to keep it a mystery, from both the characters and the listener. Which I think may be wasted effort, because even once I heard who it was, I didn't really remember them. The Doctor keeps it a secret from Sarah as well, for no story purpose that I can determine other than drawing out the suspense. There's a slightly clever twist in that the baddies have encountered the Doctor before, but only in a much later incarnation. That doesn't really affect the plot, though, so it's just kinda interesting. The Doctor seems reactive rather than proactive; in fact, he barely saves anyone, and doesn't seem too put out about it. In the end, not a great story.
docs.title: Invasion of the Body Stealers

docs.text: The Pescatons Argo Records Special Released: July 1976 Listened: 2/14/22 This story has a strong up-side and down-side. On the one hand, it’s the first ever Doctor Who audio, recorded in 1976, featuring a remarkably young-sounding Tom Baker and Elisabeth Sladen. As Sladen’s only appearance in this part of the project, that’s welcome. On the other hand, the story is strange, and frankly, not very good. It’s heavily narrated, with small patches of dialog here and there, which is fine, but it’s narrated from the Doctor’s point of view, revealing him to be not just excessively wordy, but also frequently frightened, which just doesn’t fit at all. The bad guys are the Pescatons, a race of humanoid shark-people from a dying planet (in the constellation of Pisces, rather too on the nose). They’re supposedly vicious on a hand-to-hand level, but honestly they’re kind of low-rent, even for a classic-series monster. And yet the Doctor describes them as irredeemably evil, and needing to be destroyed, which is entirely out of character, almost as much as him being afraid of them. Sarah Jane doesn’t seem to have a purpose in this story, as her conversations with the Doctor are usually unimportant, with the big dramatic bits being covered in narration. There’s also a completely unnecessary flashback that doesn’t make a lot of sense, given how short the story is. And the aliens do an absurd amount of damage worldwide, and rack up rather a high body count, yet UNIT is never seen or mentioned, which really makes no sense given where it’s set in Doctor Who history. As a historical artifact, it’s amazing. As a story, it’s fairly terrible. It’s probably best to think of it like a TV story from its era; not able to pull off what it promises.
docs.title: The Pescatons

docs.text: The Wondrous Box Short Trips #3.4 Released: 11 May 2011 Listened: 2/13/22 This Short Trip, in contrast, is a story, although a brief one. The TARDIS lands in P.T. Barnum’s circus in 1885. Of course the Doctor loves a circus, although Sarah Jane is less thrilled. The Doctor delights in pointing out the original Jumbo the Elephant , but the fun ends when a circus performer steals the TARDIS key and accidentally moves it a short distance. Unfortunately, that accident leads to tragedy, and it seems to be one of those times where the Doctor is predestined to be involved with an established historical event. It’s neat if you want to learn a bit about Jumbo and the circus, but otherwise, kind of sad.

docs.text: Blood of the Time Lords Fourth Doctor Adventures #11.1 Released: 16 March 2022 Listened: 3/22/22 This particular set of Fourth Doctor Adventures, released in 2022, takes place specifically just “hours” after “ The Deadly Assassin .” The Doctor is feeling responsible for a change, and lands on Gallifrey’s moon, the Recusary, which is apparently where old Time Lords retire when they’re getting close to death. There’s a lot of continuity stuff going on with this one, but not so much that it becomes a burden. The old hermit friend who the Doctor mentions from time to time gets a name, Ansillon, and is currently running the Recusary, so that makes for some interesting interactions. Of course, there has to be a companion substitute, in the form of Elanora, played by Emma Noakes as a mousy librarian who’s a bit more than she seems. Timothy X Atack produces a story with rather a lot of layers and misdirection, and a villain that I really didn’t see coming. The Doctor is at a pretty arrogant point in his life, without Sarah, having just saved Gallifrey from the Master, and it almost seems like he treats the proceedings with contempt. He certainly succeeds in getting under everybody’s skin. As a bonus, there’s even a hint of explanation about one of the Doctor’s oldest mysteries, although I don’t know if any other story will pick up on it. Definitely worth a listen, and probably a re-listen.
docs.title: Blood of the Time Lords

docs.text: Genetics of the Daleks Time Lord Victorious Special Released: 10 December 2020 Listened: 2/20/22 This story is part of the sprawling Time Lord Victorious storyline…except the connection to that overall plot is quite tenuous. Specifically, it’s a prequel to the “A Dalek Awakens” escape room game, but you don’t need to experience one to enjoy the other. So, viewing this entirely in isolation: The Doctor arrives on a generation ship, halfway through its journey. Unfortunately, some criminals have infiltrated and replaced some of the crew. Worse, they found what seems to be an empty, frozen Dalek shell floating in the Oort Cloud, and they’re letting the science officer experiment on it by himself. Never a good idea. What follows is a tight, well-paced horror story, in which the Doctor is slightly more clever than usual with establishing his bona fides, and the commander is less stupid than usual in accepting his help. Unfortunately, when multiple members of the crew are lying about their identities, for different factions, that may not be enough. The win isn’t quite as clean as it seems to be, because then there couldn’t be an escape room sequel. But credit to Jonny Morris for telling a Fourth Doctor story in the Time Lord Victorious framework without messing up any timelines.
docs.title: Genetics of the Daleks

docs.text: Night of the Vashta Nerada Classic Doctors, New Monsters #2.1 Released: 27 July 2017 Listened: 2/19/22 This is the Fourth Doctor’s first appearance (in produciton order) in the “Classic Doctors, New Monsters” line, and he’s paired up with the Vashta Nerada, which at this point he’s only ever heard of, but hasn’t seen. The story connects to “ Day of the Vashta Nerada ,” the Eighth Doctor story later in the set, but there’s no indication of that here. The Doctor has come to Funworld, a whole planet that’s a fun-fair, because he wants to…have fun. However, it’s closed because something killed the original staff, so the owner has turned up with a bunch of hunters to clear it out. It’s very Jurassic Park , except the raptors are microscopic. The Doctor spends an inordinate amount of time shouting at people, trying to get them to leave, but they’re stubborn and won’t go. Which makes it remarkably like “Silence in the Library,” except there’s no River Song. John Dorney is the writer, but there’s nothing twisty here; it’s just straight-up sci-fi horror. The Vashta Nerada are kind of tricky to do on audio, since they don’t speak and hide in shadows that listeners can’t see, but Dorney does a nice job piling up the tension, especially using the “two shadows” trick. It’s atmospheric, but feels like half a story…because it is.
docs.title: Night of the Vashta Nerada

docs.text: Only Connect Short Trips Rarities #3.3 Released: 28 September 2018 Listened: 2/19/22 Tip for the non-British: “Only Connect” is the name of a game show in which contestants try to find the common link between groups of disparate items. This Short Trip is longer than the previous, but it’s equally a vignette. An architect gets a taxi ride from a strange driver who turns out to be the Doctor, of course. The Doctor claims that he drives a cab because it’s a source of interesting information that may save lives someday. Of course, we’ve never known the Doctor to spend much time as a cab driver, so it doesn’t make a ton of sense. The architect gives the Doctor a bit of info about Chase Manor, site of “ The Seeds of Doom ,” but if this timeline is correct, the Doctor no longer needs that information. I expected there to be a twist, but there really isn’t. John Banks narrates, and does a slightly better job of matching Tom Baker’s tone than Hugh Ross did, but still without being an impression.
docs.title: Only Connect

docs.text: Out of Time Out of Time #1 Released: 26 August 2020 Listened: 2/19/22 This is really a Tenth Doctor story, but it’s a crossover, and for the Fourth Doctor, it definitively takes place here. He’s taking a break after the events of the past few stories, and has gone to a cathedral outside of space and time to have a rest and paint some frescos. And apparently talk about himself a lot. When the Tenth Doctor turns up in the midst of his own identity crisis near the end of his regeneration, there’s some abrasion, but also mutual appreciation, as in the best multi-Doctor stories. When the Fourth Doctor calls out the Tenth on his arrogance, the Tenth Doctor – accurately – replies that it’s rich for the Fourth to call anybody arrogant. And yet, the Tenth Doctor really deserves the criticism at this point in his life. Oh, and there’s Daleks too, but that really just gives the Doctors something else to argue about. Matt Fitton excels at the interpersonal dynamics, and he really nails this one.
docs.title: Out of Time

docs.text: Peake Season Fourth Doctor Adventures #11.5 Released: 21 June 2022 Listened: 6/26/22 This bonus two-parter has the Doctor fanboying over Mervyn Peake , artist and writer of several novels, particularly Gormenghast . As you can imagine, the story is replete with Gormenghast references, most of which I didn’t get. The Doctor is at his most Fourth Doctory in the surreal setting, full of bizarre observations and commentary that drive Peake to distraction, but Peake finds himself liking the Doctor despite himself. David Holt, well-known English actor, does a very impressive job as Peake. It’s a rather strange story, but if you can roll with it, it’s fun.

docs.text: Shellshock Fourth Doctor Adventures #11.4 Released: 21 June 2022 Listened: 6/25/22 The Doctor unexpectedly finds himself in World War I in France, and of course in No Man’s Land, because that’s how these stories always go. This time, though, when the Doctor is knocked unconscious by shelling, he’s taken to a German hospital instead of an English one. Not that it really matters, because something alien is going on that’s affecting both sides equally, but it’s interesting to see the story from the German point of view. He gains a nurse, Hanna Schumann, as a temporary companion, and it’s kind of hard not to see parallels with Molly O’Sullivan , but he won’t meet her for some time yet. Hanna is very patriotic and dedicated to duty, but also believes in doing the right thing, and very willing to give the Doctor sass when he acts oddly or doesn’t explain things, which is most of the time. Much of the story is spent unraveling the mystery, and traveling back and forth through No Man’s Land, which does get a bit tedious after a while. But there really aren’t any baddies to speak of, which is an interesting twist on this kind of story.
docs.title: Shellshock

docs.text: Fourth Doctor Adventures #11.4 Released: 21 June 2022 Listened: 6/25/22 The Doctor unexpectedly finds himself in World War I in France, and of course in No Man’s Land, because that’s how these stories always go. This time, though, when the Doctor is knocked unconscious by shelling, he’s taken to a German hospital instead of an English one. Not that it really matters, because something alien is going on that’s affecting both sides equally, but it’s interesting to see the story from the German point of view. He gains a nurse, Hanna Schumann, as a temporary companion, and it’s kind of hard not to see parallels with Molly O’Sullivan , but he won’t meet her for some time yet. Hanna is very patriotic and dedicated to duty, but also believes in doing the right thing, and very willing to give the Doctor sass when he acts oddly or doesn’t explain things, which is most of the time. Much of the story is spent unraveling the mystery, and traveling back and forth through No Man’s Land, which does get a bit tedious after a while. But there really aren’t any baddies to speak of, which is an interesting twist on this kind of story.
docs.title: Shellshock

docs.text: Someone I Once Knew The Diary of River Song #4.4 Released: 4 September 2018 Listened: 2/19/22 This is a River Song story, but it’s kind of an alternate one. At this point in production order, Big Finish and River had worked their way back through the Eighth , Seventh , Sixth , and Fifth Doctors, with a memory wipe each time. So when they got to the Fourth, they pulled a twist of having the Fourth Doctor not only know River, but he’d always known her, all the way back to Gallifrey. That’s because the baddies in this boxed set are the Discordia, beings who simply go back and rewrite time every time they lose, or want something, or any excuse, really. They’re apparently immune to paradox. What’s going on with River and the Discordia makes a lot more sense if you’ve been listening to the entire box. The Doctor’s part in it is to mostly swoon over River, and attempt to save the day, but it’s River’s story, after all. The schmoopy bits between River and the Doctor are a bit much, especially because Tom Baker sounds closer to his actual age in those scenes. So it’s a bit hard for it to come across as poignant. John Dorney is at his best with paradoxes, but maybe not so much with romance.
docs.title: Someone I Once Knew

docs.text: The Dreams of Avarice Fourth Doctor Adventures #11.3 Released: 21 June 2022 Listened: 6/25/22 The second boxed set of this season was called “The Nine,” and this story is why, as John Heffernan’s Nine makes a return. The Nine’s various voices aren’t quite as distinct as Marc Bonnar’s Eleven, but they actually only play a small part in this story. The Nine is a kleptomaniac, as displayed in his other major appearance in Doom Coalition. This time, though, he’s even more insane than usual, not even willing to part with a cup of coffee. His “companion” Thana from “ Relative Time ” appears in this story, later in her personal timeline, but they’re not getting along. The real highlight here is the temporary companion, Detective Inspector Probert, played by Richard Dixon. Probert starts out arresting the Doctor, but of course that never lasts long. He’s reasonably bright, but completely out of his depth following the Doctor around, so it’s fun watching his policeman’s cynicism turn to confusion and panic, and then reach the stage where he’s just rolling with it. Unfortunately, because the Nine’s mental problems are so severe, he’s fairly predictable, and not too difficult to thwart. As a result, this story falls a little flat.
docs.title: The Dreams of Avarice

docs.text: The Ravencliff Witch Fourth Doctor Adventures #11.3 Released: 16 March 2022 Listened: 3/24/22 In contrast to the previous story, this one is a very Hinchcliffe-style “gothic horror” story, with supernatural elements that turn out to not be so supernatural after all. Writer David Llewellyn captures the tone of the era quite nicely. It’s not specifically stated that it takes place in the 1970s, but it certainly has that feel. You’ve got your usual power plant run by idiots, messing with things they don’t understand, and locals who don’t want the power plant there. British national treasure (and star of “ Kinda ” way back when) Nerys Hughes plays temporary companion (or more, but that will come later ) Margaret Hopwood, a driftwood sculptor. Lucy Pickles plays the other, a local woman who works at the power plant. The Doctor indulges in quite a bit of technobabble, but the main problem is caused by another time-traveling species, so technobabble is to be expected. It’s a tight story, with good tension, and it holds together quite well.
docs.title: The Ravencliff Witch

docs.text: Waiting for Gadot Short Trips Rarities #2.2 Released: 29 September 2017 Listened: 2/19/22 This particular Short Trip is more of a vignette than anything. A wildlife photographer spends months alone on a barren planet waiting for a rare bird, a “gadot,” to come along. Instead, he finds the Doctor, who decides to help him out. The moral is that even when the Doctor helps you, it can lead to unexpected consequences. Hugh Ross is the narrator, and his Fourth Doctor isn’t what you’d call an impersonation, but it more or less captures the tone.

docs.text: The Ninth Doctor The Ninth Doctor had a lot of weight on his shoulders, both in-story and behind the scenes. As the first Doctor of the revived series in 2005, he had to be the Doctor for a new generation, not just more of the same (no offense, Paul McGann). Russell T Davies had to reintroduce all the Doctor Who concepts and make them seem fresh, which he achieved by mostly viewing them through Rose’s eyes, which put a lot of weight on Billie Piper as well. They all succeeded admirably, and yet, Eccleston only stayed for one series, as the result of unspecified bad blood between him and the BBC. It looked for a long time like he was going to be a recalcitrant former Doctor, much like Tom Baker had been for so long. But also like Tom Baker, Big Finish eventually found the right set of circumstances to lure him back. A lot of the stories in this era are “workarounds,” short trips, chronicles, and other things intended to include the Ninth Doctor without having Eccleston available, but now with one huge chunk of the real deal right in the middle.
docs.title: Ninth Doctor

docs.text: The Ninth Doctor and Rose Now we reach 2005, and the beginning of the modern series proper. It took a long time for Big Finish to arrange for Christopher Eccleston and Billie Piper to appear together, so there aren't too many full-cast inserts in this section. Because Rose is around until the regeneration at the end of the season, there’s no more room for solo stories. There are some gaps that can be exploited, though, and Big Finish has done a reasonable job of stuffing stories into the cracks. The Doctor of these stories is a bit less world-weary, a bit less hard, and having Rose along opens him up even more.

docs.text: Identity Check The Ninth Doctor Chronicles #1.4 Released: 4 May 2017 Listened: 3/15/23 This Short Trip from the 2023 collection is the first time in a bit that we've heard Jacob Dudman narrate a Ninth Doctor story. And his Christopher Eccleston impression…is really good! Remarkably good, in fact. The Northerness, the pacing, the delivery, it’s very nearly spot-on. Which is even more remarkable if you’ve just been listening to the real thing, and a welcome change if you’ve been listening to the Nick Briggs version (sorry, Nick). As for the story, it’s fine, but that’s about it. A colony, somewhere in the future. Lots of humans and refugees from other races. It’s after a war, times are hard, and everybody’s mining. So there’s lots of racism going around. Of course, the story involves the most racisty racist of all, who’s hiding a secret, even from himself. Unfortunately, not from the listener, because you can figure that bit out pretty easily. It does give the Doctor a chance to expound on what he thinks of war criminals, which is either poignant or hypocritical, depending on how you look at it. Rose is in the story, but doesn’t really do a whole lot except back the Doctor up, and be slightly more empathetic. Not the best story, but wow, Dudman does a good job.
docs.title: Identity Check

docs.text: Night of the Whisper Destiny of the Doctor #9 Released: 1 September 2013 Listened: 11/15/22 This is the Ninth Doctor’s entry in the “Destiny of the Doctor” 2013 anniversary story, meaning this is technically the Ninth Doctor’s first audio appearance. Unfortunately, he’s played by Nick Briggs, who hasn’t perfected his Ninth Doctor impression yet. Briggs plays both Rose and Jack as well, and while he doesn’t attempt Rose’s accent, he does get the cadence right. His “American” accent for Jack is simply terrible, sounding nothing like Barrowman. Making matters worse, the other actor in the story, John Schwab, is an actual American. The story, by Mark Wright and Cavan Scott, clocks in at well over an hour, making it the longest “Destiny” story. They also seemed to be taking advantage of the audio medium to do things that even the new series would struggle to pull off. The story is set in New Vegas, an entire planetoid of casinos and neon, and features a hoverbike chase, a wolf-man villain, and a vigilante who gets around by means of grapples. The Doctor is angrier and more physical than he’s been in previous stories, and the story as a whole has an unusually high level of violence. On the whole, the story feels kind of rough-draft compared to the other stories in this section. The Eleventh Doctor has a message inserted, as in all the “Destiny” stories, but it’s not even slightly subtle this time, using a giant video screen. It’s OK, but no more than that.
docs.title: Night of the Whisper

docs.text: Retail Therapy The Ninth Doctor Chronicles #1.4 Released: 4 May 2017 If we can use Adam for one of these narrated stories, why not Jackie? Camille Coduri always seems to be up for a Big Finish. She hasn’t often appeared with the Ninth Doctor, which kind of makes sense, as this Doctor really doesn’t seem to care for her much. In fairness, in this story Jackie rambles a lot (probably to give Coduri more lines), and she’s awfully defensive. Basically, she and the Doctor seem to bring out the worst in each other, mostly because they both think they know what’s best for Rose. In this story, Jackie has become part of a multi-level marketing scheme selling “Glubby Glubs,” which are fuzzy pink eggs that exude a sense of restfulness and well-being. Of course the Doctor is immediately suspicious, which puts Jackie’s back up. Unfortunately, because the eggs have a soporific effect, the story itself seems sluggish. The investigation phase takes too long, probably to give Jackie more to do.
docs.title: Retail Therapy

docs.text: The Other Side The Ninth Doctor Chronicles #1.3 Released: 4 May 2017 When Big Finish started doing the “Doctor Chronicles,” they didn’t have access to any of the Doctor or companion actors, so they used what they could. In this case, that’s Bruno Langley, who played Adam ever-so-briefly. You thought there was no gap between “ Dalek ” and “ The Long Game ”? Well, there is if Adam doesn’t visit a different planet, so for him, this story takes place in Birmingham, 2012 (Rose’s future, Adam’s present, and the past when it was recorded and released – yay, time travel!) The plot itself isn’t all that great; there’s a temporal anomaly, left over from the war, and it bounces both the Doctor and Rose back into separate parts of history. It’s the characterizations that are spot-on: Adam acts like a normal human would when confronted with strangeness, which is to say, not like a companion. He also acts like a young genius who’s used to being right all the time, and who held a position of importance up until yesterday, but is now thrust into a situation where he can’t really cope. Rose is displaying way too much faith in the Doctor, because he hasn’t failed her yet. And the Doctor is being unnecessarily snotty towards Adam, somewhat possessive of Rose, and possibly not liking what that says about him. He does change his tune by the end of the story, which is somewhat pointless, given what will happen next. Don’t expect Bruno Langley to appear again, as the actor has been convicted of assault.

docs.text: The Ninth Doctor Chronicles #1.3 Released: 4 May 2017 When Big Finish started doing the “Doctor Chronicles,” they didn’t have access to any of the Doctor or companion actors, so they used what they could. He does change his tune by the end of the story, which is somewhat pointless, given what will happen next. Don’t expect Bruno Langley to appear again, as the actor has been convicted of assault.

docs.text: The Window on the Moor The Ninth Doctor Chronicles #1.2 Released: 4 May 2017 We’re now back to Nick Briggs-narrated stories, including his somewhat congested Ninth Doctor. However, this is the earliest audio appearance of Rose (in production order), sorta-kinda. This story, by Una McCormack, has a “doomed lovers” feel straight out of Wuthering Heights , intentionally. The Doctor and Rose land in a city in the midst of a civil war, where a prince has overthrown the ruling duke, and anybody who complains gets locked up in a glass prison. The Doctor and Rose are separated almost immediately, and because this is a story, bump into the Duchess and the Duke respectively. The prison, made of intelligent glass of some kind, is an interesting image, as are the glass beasts that the prince uses. The city also features a dimensional window onto an English moor in the early 19th century, where a girl named Emily helps out visitors. It’s not the strongest story, but it does evoke a sense of place quite well.

docs.text: The Ninth Doctor Solo These stories take place between the Ninth Doctor’s regeneration and when he meets Rose. We’re either ignoring the second when he looks in the mirror in “ Rose ,” or maybe they all take place in the few seconds after he leaves Rose and Mickey on the street and before he comes back for her. Doesn’t matter; he’s traveling without a companion, is the point. And he’s carrying a lot of pain from the Time War, which is still fresh for him. Originally, this was a fairly small space, occupied by a hodge-podge of stories from different sources. However, when Christopher Eccleston surprised everybody by agreeing to participate in Big Finish in 2021, all those adventures ended up here at first, making it much larger and more appealing.

docs.text: Auld Lang Syne The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 2 #1.3 Released: 4 May 2022 Listened: 10/8/22 Tim Foley has the third story, which takes place in the early 90s, more or less. Mandy Litherland is a young Northern woman who rents out a manor called Foulds House for her family to celebrate the New Year. The Doctor is there, pretending to be the caretaker, because something is wrong with time in this house. It’s almost a Doctor-lite story because the focus stays firmly on Mandy and her fractured family. All of the characters are wonderfully drawn, and clearly bound by love even as they’re rude to one another. The story has a remarkable amount of timey-wimey, as the Doctor’s parts of it take place out of order, and Mandy’s bits are several consecutive New Years Eves, through which she travels the long way around. The only real flaw is a character who’s not what they seem, and it’s pretty easy to spot. It’s tricky to spin a timey-wimey plot and tug at the heartstrings at the same time, but this story pulls it off, making it the standout from this set.
docs.title: Auld Lang Syne

docs.text: Battle Scars Short Trips #9.7 Released: 31 July 2017 Listened: 9/5/22 This story, an affecting short trip, seems as though it’s intended to take place shortly after the Doctor’s regeneration. Only the blue sonic screwdriver sets it after the previous . The Doctor lands in 1912, near the house of the Daniels family, unconscious from an injury. He recovers quickly, but sticks around because Mr. Daniels is having trouble, both with his shipping business, and with his own temper. The Doctor understands the difficulty of reintegrating into normal life after being a soldier, and is able to assist. Connie Daniels, the eldest daughter, is a voracious reader, and introduces the Doctor to the word “fantastic,” which he likes quite a bit. There is a bit of obligatory sci-fi, which is resolved quickly, and even in that, the Doctor is sympathetic to the effects of war. And yes, this is the same Daniels family who Clive mentions in “ Rose ,” the family that was due to sail on the Titanic, but ended up not doing so. Did that bit need explaining? Not really. But it’s handled really well here, so I can’t object.
docs.title: Battle Scars

docs.text: Below There The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 3 #2.1 Released: 3 August 2023 Listened: 10/2/23 This boxed set is called “Travel in Hope,” and for the most part, it has a lighter, friendlier take on the Ninth Doctor, even if that doesn’t necessarily fit the story’s setting. This first one is a claustrophobic, small-cast story that’s perfect for audio, as the Doctor and the main character only interact via radio for the first half of the story. It’s also got a very new-series “used future” feel, where humanity’s technology has advanced, but the way we treat people hasn’t. Capitalism, especially, is still alive and well. Lauren Mooney and Stewart Pringle take advantage of the fact that the listener can’t see what’s going on to make Vyx into a semi-unreliable narrator. The resolution may be a bit of an anticlimax, but it’s in keeping with the tone of the season.
docs.title: Below There

docs.text: Break the Ice The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 2 #2.3 Released: 17 August 2022 Listened: 10/11/22 Speaking of things the Ninth Doctor didn’t get, among them are a Christmas special, and a chance to fight an old god. So Tim Foley serves up both of those things in this story set on a space station orbiting Venus. The crew are doing cryo-suspension research, and it turns out that when you get down to absolute zero, one of the gods of winter can come through. Which gets a bit of fairy tale in what is almost exclusively a sci-fi story. Jack Frost is played by Pip Torrens with obvious relish, sounding every bit as entitled and mischievous as you would expect from a “Jack Frost,” not as much the booming, echoey elder god. Thalissa Teixeira is the companion-substitute, Dr. Lenny Fisk, who’s smart and trusts the Doctor as good companions should, but also suffers from anxiety that leaves her paralyzed at certain points in the story. It’s interesting to see mental illness treated the same as other more recent characters with physical issues, like Ryan or Hebe . It’s a thing, we cope, we get the job done. The ending is a little bit squishy, but what else would you expect from a Christmas special?
docs.title: Break the Ice

docs.text: Cataclysm The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 1 #1.2 Released: 13 May 2021 Listened: 9/12/22 This is the middle part of the “Ravagers” storyline, and unfortunately, it really feels like a middle part. The Doctor at least knows that he was mistaken about the threat Audrey posed in Part 1 , although she’s not making it easy on him. There’s a whole lot of bouncing around in timelines, including the Battle of Waterloo, for no real good reason. The Doctor is able to rescue Nova from her cliffhanger, but then there’s rather too much chasing about through time, trying to track down a “node” that may or may not be linked to the problem. The pacing and the number of scene changes are appropriate to a new-series story, but the overall arc doesn’t seem to be proceeding as quickly as it could.

docs.text: Flatpack The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 2 #3.3 Released: 23 November 2022 Listened: 3/10/23 There’s an unexpected twist to this one, which of course means that John Dorney is involved. This story features Liv and Tanya, in post-pandemic London, after the end of “ Stranded .” Fortunately, both of them know about regeneration, so the Doctor doesn’t have to spend any time explaining, although Liv goes through a bit of an existential crisis that the Doctor can’t really help with. The story involves people getting trapped in a DIY furniture store with a labyrinthine layout, which sounds exactly like IKEA to me, although Dorney says he didn’t have any particular store in mind. The reveal comes slowly, as the Doctor tries to keep Liv and Tanya out of the investigation, then they discover they’re stuck as well, and the Doctor still can’t figure out what’s going on for quite some time. In fact, depending on your ear for voices, you may work it out well before the Doctor does. The solution, as often, is less important than the problem; the Doctor does a thing, and that’s about it. There are a few interesting character touches, like the Doctor’s extreme dismay at losing the TARDIS, which mirrors what happens in “ Father’s Day .” He also seems happier to see Liv than he’s letting on, engaging in some rather bad puns and slowly becoming more sociable. In fact, the Doctor is starting to lose his edginess as a survivor of the war. It’s kind of natural as Chris Eccleston settles into his Big Finish tenure, but that makes it a bit odd when the cycle of pain appears to start over with “ Rose .”
docs.title: Flatpack

docs.text: Fond Farewell The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 1 #4.1 Released: 16 February 2022 Listened: 9/28/22 This is the beginning of the boxed set called “Old Friends,” which will be more appropriate in later stories, but this one also fits the theme. The Doctor attends the funeral of wildlife activist Flynn Beckett, who encountered the Doctor on a recent mission. In the future, if you’re wealthy enough, you can get the contents of your brain temporarily downloaded into a synthetic being, and therefore attend your own funeral. Except Flynn doesn’t remember the Doctor, or his assistant Sasha, or his last mission. And then the murders start. Writer David K Barnes fills this story with new-series features, such as the shifty organization with something to hide and a clueless administrator, things that should be dead but aren’t, and a spooky repeated phrase that makes no sense, as in “Silence in the Library” or “ The Empty Child .” In this case, it’s “I’m still here,” which is creepy enough on its own. The secondary characters are quite dynamic, giving us a tease of adventures the Ninth Doctor had that we didn’t see. Sasha, in particular, has the role of the companion-substitute, but she’s not really a great companion. She lacks the empathy that the Doctor normally likes, which makes her harder to predict. It’s a nice sci-fi trope, but it’s really just a prologue for the rest of the set.
docs.title: Fond Farewell

docs.text: Food Fight The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 1 #1.3 Released: 13 May 2021 Listened: 9/19/22 This story is the big ending to the large arc of this boxed set, and as you would expect, it’s got a decent amount of slam-bang. Big Finish doesn’t always do that with their finales, but since this was the first Ninth Doctor boxed set, it makes sense that they would. However, it’s not just a good guys / bad guys smash-up. The Doctor realizes that he’s gotten something very wrong, even more wrong than he originally thought, and there are consequences to that. Fortunately, he’s got a bunch of friends to help. Our British army officers are still around, as is Dan Starkey’s hilarious Roman legionary, who basically only has one battle plan…which admittedly worked well for the Romans, so hey. And the resolution isn’t a matter of “defeating” anybody, which is appropriate for this war-weary Doctor, but does let down all the chaos that led up to it, a little. It’s also got the whole timey-wimey thing where they run through the plot again, but in the correct order this time, so you can see all the bits you didn’t understand the first time around. As a whole-box story, this one holds together pretty well; Nick Briggs brought his A game.
docs.title: Food Fight

docs.text: Fright Motif The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 1 #2.2 Released: 11 August 2021 Listened: 9/21/22 This story takes place in Paris, post WWII, and features that Big Finish classic, the monster made of sound. Artie Berger is an American pianist who’s come to Paris to make his fortune and escape racism back home. (Played by Damian Lynch, doing quite a decent American accent.) Unfortunately, he’s lost his ability to play, for some reason. The Doctor turns up looking for…something extradimensional, and gets involved. The monstrosity is never really explained, which is fine, really; it’s just a threat to be dealt with. There’s a scene in Notre Dame that probably would’ve been quite difficult to do on TV, so it comes across well on audio. Artie’s boss Maurice starts out as rather a harsh employer, but turns quite sympathetic once his secret is discovered. The post-war setting is perfect for this post-war Doctor, who’s clearly being affected by the whole situation. There’s less sarcasm in this story, and the quickness with which he leaves indicates how much pain he’s still in.
docs.title: Fright Motif

docs.text: Girl, Deconstructed The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 1 #2.1 Released: 11 August 2021 Listened: 9/20/22 This second box is “Respond to All Calls,” and if you think that means the Doctor answering distress signals, you’d be right. Nick Briggs takes a back seat this time, so this story is written by Lisa McMullin, and directed by Helen Goldwyn. And it’s a much smaller, more personal story than the previous set . It’s a missing-persons story, which takes place in Scotland, so it’s full of gorgeous accents. The Doctor continues to be aggressively protective of innocents, and blows off figures of authority. Even with his allies, he’s not interested in explaining much, or rather explains in a way he knows won’t be understood. The actual plot has unfortunate similarities to “Fear Her,” but without the things that made that episode terrible. Detective Jana Lee makes a nice substitute companion, mostly by not being nearly as baffled as other characters.

docs.text: The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 1 #2.1 Released: 11 August 2021 Listened: 9/20/22 This second box is “Respond to All Calls,” and if you think that means the Doctor answering distress signals, you’d be right. Nick Briggs takes a back seat this time, so this story is written by Lisa McMullin, and directed by Helen Goldwyn. And it’s a much smaller, more personal story than the previous set . It’s a missing-persons story, which takes place in Scotland, so it’s full of gorgeous accents. The Doctor continues to be aggressively protective of innocents, and blows off figures of authority. Even with his allies, he’s not interested in explaining much, or rather explains in a way he knows won’t be understood. The actual plot has unfortunate similarities to “Fear Her,” but without the things that made that episode terrible. docs.text: Her Own Bootstraps Short Trips #10.9 Released: 29 September 2020 Listened: 9/8/22 It seems like the Ninth Doctor spent most of his early life cleaning up weapons from the Time War, which is certainly kind of him, but it can’t have done his mental state any good. This time, the weapon has ended up in the hands of Althea Bryce, scientist, time traveler, and thief. The Doctor takes it to Krakatoa, just before it erupts, only to find a very young Althea there, possibly looking to steal it, and in any event creating a bootstrap paradox in a decaying loop, which isn’t good for anybody. The Doctor tries to be careful of the web of time, not telling Althea her fate, but eventually breaks down, and at one point unloads on her with the anger and frustration built up from the war. Usually, when he talks about the war, he’s talking to someone he likes, so he evades and euphemizes, but he believes Althea to be a villain, so he can really let her have it. Getting out of a time loop is no mean trick, so kudos to writer Amy Veeres for thinking of a clever way to pull that off. There’s also a short scene set much later on that marks the first appearance of Rose in this project. Plus the ending can be read ambiguously, so that’s fairly interesting. The story is read by Jacob Dudman, most known for his Eleventh Doctor, but he does a pretty decent Ninth as well.
docs.title: Her Own Bootstraps

docs.text: Human Conflict The Churchill Years #2.2 Released: 15 February 2018 Listened: 9/6/22 This story takes place on a rather broader canvas than the previous . It’s 1941, the war is in full swing, and Churchill is Prime Minister, and looking for any edge he can get in this fight. When he hears of a weapon that can destroy mountains, he sends his best agent, Lt. Fleming – yes, that Ian Fleming – to investigate. They end up with an alien arms dealer who’s fairly willing to sell to either the Allies, the Nazis, or maybe even both. There’s a clandestine meeting in Dundee, where Churchill was once a member of Parliament, but he has only bad memories of it. Writer Iain McLaughlin uses the setting well, getting in a car chase worthy of a spy movie. The Doctor doesn’t actually seem to do a whole lot, just flitting around the edges, until he tries to get rid of the arms dealer, because once again, he’s going to deny either side weapons that are too advanced for this time period. Ian McNeice actually attempts the Ninth Doctor’s northern accent, just a little bit, but more than he did in the last story. This version of Churchill is determined to “do what it takes, no matter the cost” to win his war, even if that means compromising his morals, and the Doctor, especially this Doctor, doesn’t want to see anyone else do that. Unfortunately, he also knows that there’s no way to spare Winston or England the rest of this war.
docs.title: Human Conflict

docs.text: I Was Churchill's Double The Churchill Years #2.3 Released: 15 February 2018 Listened: 10/14/22 This story, from the second Churchill set, doesn’t take itself particularly seriously; even narrator-Churchill comments to that effect. It’s the middle of the war, Churchill is PM, and he’s no fan of television, as the Germans can intercept the broadcasts. Scotsman John Logie Baird (inventor of the television and head of the BBC, who'll eventually appear in "The Giggle"), however, is picking up strange transmissions that can’t exist. When Churchill retires for the evening, he finds a strange mirror in his room, through which he can see a different Churchill. Upon touching the mirror, they swap places, and our Churchill finds himself in a parallel world, in which the US never entered WWI, and Britain was forced to surrender to Germany. This Churchill is a freedom fighter, although WWII isn’t happening. The Doctor, for some reason, is in the parallel world, and wants to get back. Churchill, as it happens, is conversant with parallel worlds, as he ( in the real world ) once wrote an essay imagining what would happen if General Lee won the battle of Gettysburg. Alan Barnes pumps this story full of references, to the R101 and Colditz , to the “howlaround” effect , and to the Doctor’s penchant for carrying a banana . There are also a number of sly TV references, especially when Baird is around. Ian McNiece is more willing to attempt the Doctor’s accent in this story, although it’s still not a very good likeness. It’s fun and goofy, if you like that sort of thing.
docs.title: I Was Churchill's Double

docs.text: Last of the Zetacene The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 2 #2.2 Released: 17 August 2022 Listened: 10/10/22 One side of the Ninth Doctor that we haven’t seen in this series so far is the darker, angrier side that comes out fairly often in Series 1. That side definitely shows up here, as the Ninth Doctor rarely misses a chance to be contemptuous of the super-rich. This story has a quartet of “rich enough to buy planets” types who all get together periodically to play games of chance for super-rare prizes, in this case a Zetacene Swine. It’s the last of its kind, and of course that’s a trigger for the Ninth Doctor, who immediately recruits a companion substitute to help him rig the game and free the swine. Unfortunately, it gets loose before the Doctor can free it, and starts killing the gazillionaires, to which the Doctor isn’t even slightly sympathetic. James Kettle is normally a comedy writer, so there are a number of comedic elements, like a dance revue starring sentient spiders, and one of the players who’s an “aroma enthusiast.” But the story is actually kind of dark, and the plot really isn’t very deep. The big draw here is that one of the players is played by Maureen O’Brien, who played Vicki back in the Sixties. Even though she’s done a pretty good Vicki in the Early Adventures, you’d never recognize her here without the credits. Aside from that bit of trivia, though, the story didn’t really grab me.
docs.title: Last of the Zetacene

docs.text: Lay Down Your Arms The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 2 #3.2 Released: 23 November 2022 Listened: 3/8/23 This one is a pseudo-historical set at a German spa in 1864. You could be forgiven for not recognizing that Bertha Kinzky, young socialite, is the maiden name of Bertha von Suttner . You would be further forgiven for not knowing who that is, and I’m not even sure whether it counts as a spoiler, so I’ll leave it at that for now. Bertha’s mother is trying to match her up with a suitable (read: rich and/or titled) husband, while Bertha herself is trying to make her own way in the world, and has somehow latched onto the idea that she’ll become an opera singer, with the Doctor as her instructor. Naturally, there are aliens, and they’re up to no good, and frankly what they’re up to isn’t nearly as interesting as the dialog. The exchanges between Bertha, her mother, and the Doctor fairly crackle, so credit Lisa McMullin for that. I’m not sure I can forgive her for the “ Two Princes ” reference, though. We also discover that the Doctor’s habit of getting someone’s name wrong to needle them didn’t start with Mickey. Most of the pieces are interesting, but I’m not sure the whole is the sum of the parts.
docs.title: Lay Down Your Arms

docs.text: Monsters in Metropolis The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 1 #3.3 Released: 23 November 2021 Listened: 9/26/22 It’s about time that John Dorney got in on this action, and equally it’s time for some Cybermen, as the Ninth Doctor never encountered them on TV. Except instead of their usual conquering, a lone, broken Cyberman has ended up in 1920s Germany, where a penniless puppeteer has found it, and managed to get it cast in Fritz Lang’s Metropolis in place of Brigitte Helm. Of course, this can’t possibly go wrong in any way. Because it’s a Ninth Doctor story, particularly one from this boxed set, the Cyberman is a danger, but it’s also a sad, lonely, abandoned Cyberman, because that’s the only kind anybody writes anymore. Much like the last story was a love letter to Macbeth , this one is a love letter to Metropolis , with the cast and crew being very excited about making a “celebrity historical.” It lacks the usual twistiness of John Dorney stories, but it does have a very strong sense of foreboding, as characters from 1925 express different opinions about the resolution of the last war, and what it means for Germany going forward. The story is probably more enjoyable if you’re familiar with Metropolis , but it’s still decent even if you aren’t.
docs.title: Monsters in Metropolis

docs.text: Northern Lights The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 3 #1.2 Released: 10 May 2023 Listened: 6/19/23 Sometimes Big Finish does a story to satisfy a particular creator’s personal interest. In this case, it’s Christopher Eccleston’s admiration of Fridtjof Nansen of Norway, an explorer who navigated the Arctic and came very close to the North Pole. Moreover, he was a national hero in Norway, and received a Nobel Prize for his work with refugees later in life. Eccleston didn’t ask for this story; it was commissioned based on him mentioning Nansen in the studio, and he knew nothing about it until he saw the script. However, he’s clearly pleased with the results. Basically, the Doctor comes across Nansen and Hjalmar Johansen as they’re trying to return to civilization. Of course, the Doctor has bumped into some alien explorers on the way (as he does), and now they’re a threat to the human explorers. Except the sci-fi stuff is so minor that it’s almost an excuse. The bulk of the story is the Doctor hanging out with, and being impressed by, Nansen and Johansen. Which is nice, and even inspirational if you want to know more about these historical figures, but it’s not a ton of story. It’s clear that everyone involved is pleased with making the story, but I wonder if it wouldn’t have worked better as a true historical.
docs.title: Northern Lights

docs.text: Planet of the End The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 1 #2.3 Released: 11 August 2021 Listened: 9/22/22 Following a “present” story and a “past” story , we need a “future” story, so this one sees the Doctor following a distress signal to a planet that’s essentially one giant graveyard for countless different species, without a single living person on it. Except for a robot, who’s not “living.” Except, of course, that all is not what it seems. To say more would be spoilery, but the Doctor gets wrong-footed multiple times in this story, and only wins by relying on someone else’s humanity. I’m not normally a fan of stories where the characters do nothing for years, but this one had me legitimately wondering how the Doctor was going to get out of the situation, so kudos to Timothy X Atack for that. On the whole, this set is a nicely diverse set of stories, all quite strong.
docs.title: Planet of the End

docs.text: Red Darkness The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 2 #4.3 Released: 8 February 2023 Listened: 3/14/23 Roy Gill wrote the last story in set 4, and does so again here. Big Finish is treating each set of four as a “series,” so this is again the series finale. This one is a base-under-seige story, with the Vashta Nerada, more or less, and that makes for a very tight story. The standout character in this one is a partially sighted teenager named Callen, and his companion dog Doyle, who speaks using an AI on his collar. Doyle’s got some amazing lines, and contributes to the story in the way that only a dog can, so props to Roy Gill for figuring out how to write like a dog. It also works nicely on audio, because you’ve got characters who might need to have described what other people are seeing, or need to relay other sense information verbally. As a bonus, the story ties very neatly to the first story of the set. It’s a tough listen in some places, because the monsters aren’t gentle, but these characters are so well-drawn they invite you to be invested. The Doctor seems to be softening even more here, and reacts well to both Callen and Doyle, so it’s enjoyable from that angle too. This is a quality set, consistently good throughout.
docs.title: Red Darkness

docs.text: Salvation Nine The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 2 #2.1 Released: 17 August 2022 Listened: 10/9/22 This is the first story of the set known as “Into the Stars.” In contrast with the last box , which was entirely set on Earth, none of these stories are. The Ninth Doctor never met the Sontarans, and this is certainly an interesting spin on the typical Sontaran story. The Doctor stumbles upon a moon that’s about to be attacked by a human fleet, because there’s a colony of Sontarans there. Thing is, the Doctor took a look, and these Sontarans have been here so long they’ve forgotten their history and evolved out of their warlike natures. Or have they? The Doctor, especially this Doctor, isn’t going to fall for that so easily, and a lot of the story revolves around his trying to figure out what happened and whether it’s a feint. Timothy X Atack mines this for just about all the humor he can, which is a good bit. Dan Starkey, of course, is playing the Sontarans, and given the opportunity to play another Strax-like one, he grabs on with both hands. The human captain, whom the Doctor has to stall while he figures out what’s going on, is well portrayed too. She has no reason to believe these Sontarans are different, and no reason to trust the Doctor either, so all her actions are logical given what she knows. It’s nicely plotted, and keeps you guessing, and I’ll never say no to Dan Starkey Sontaran comedy.
docs.title: Salvation Nine

docs.text: Sphere of Freedom The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 1 #1.1 Released: 13 May 2021 Listened: 9/10/22 Now we reach the proper “Ninth Doctor Adventures,” a series released starting in 2021, with Christopher Eccleston returning to the role. With all due respect to Nick Briggs’ voice acting, this is the real deal. Briggs also wrote and directed this first boxed set, called “Ravagers,” because I guess being the Executive Producer has its privileges. Again, giving him credit, he’s produced a story that fits nicely with modern Who , especially this first story, which hits the ground running and doesn’t let up on the pace, much like the first part of “ Rose .” Also much like “Rose,” we focus on the Doctor and companion first, and the plot gets filled in later. Nova, played by Camilla Beeput, is the temporary companion for this story, and she does a nice job of being the kind of companion the Ninth Doctor needs right now: curious and capable, interested in what’s going on, but not big on empathy or adventure. The story starts out on the Sphere of Freedom, a planet run by a corporation that makes virtual reality games. (Which isn’t a problem; the Doctor really likes VR games.) The CEO, of course, is acting all evil and oppressing the populace to get the games made. Oh, and somehow using time eddies that could tear the universe apart. One of these eddies dumps a Roman legion in London, 1959, meaning that the Doctor has to try to keep either side from getting killed, because there’s no UNIT around yet. It also means that we get to hear Dan Starkey practice his Latin as the Centurion. He sounds just a little bit too Sontaran (sorry, Dan), but I think that’s to be expected. All of which adds up to a case where the Doctor turned up, saw an injustice, tried to do a clever thing to fix it without telling anybody what he was up to, and it all went terribly wrong. However, the three stories in this set are one connected story, so this is just the opening act. Sets a nice tone, though.
docs.title: Sphere of Freedom

One of these eddies dumps a Roman legion in London, 1959, meaning that the Doctor has to try to keep either side from getting killed, because there’s no UNIT around yet. It also means that we get to hear Dan Starkey practice his Latin as the Centurion. He sounds just a little bit too Sontaran (sorry, Dan), but I think that’s to be expected. All of which adds up to a case where the Doctor turned up, saw an injustice, tried to do a clever thing to fix it without telling anybody what he was up to, and it all went terribly wrong. However, the three stories in this set are one connected story, so this is just the opening act. Sets a nice tone, though.
docs.title: Sphere of Freedom

docs.text: Station to Station The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 2 #1.1 Released: 4 May 2022 Listened: 10/3/22 After the first “season” went well, Christopher Eccleston came back for another round of boxed sets, starting with this one, called “Back to Earth,” because that’s where the stories take place, with one in the past, one in the recent past, and one in the “present,” which seems to be early 21st Century for the sake of continuity. The “present” story is a properly creepy fairy tale from Rob Valentine. It takes place at a train station in the middle of nowhere, literally in this case, because it’s outside of time, and populated by people who got “lost” in moments of indecision, and are now basically ghosts. The companion-substitute is Saffron Windrose, played by Indigo Griffiths, who’s trying to go home to her parents’ house to tell them that she’s getting married to a woman. She doesn’t expect to be well-received, so she’s ambivalent. Running the whole place is the Grimminy Grew, a monster, maybe troll-like; it’s never really described. The Ninth Doctor is particularly good at standing up against those. He doesn’t get shouty like the Tenth or speechy like the Eleventh; he just says no. The pseudo-science is actually pretty weak, but it would have ruined the fairy tale if it were otherwise. For sense of place and general spookiness, this one is ace.
docs.title: Station to Station

docs.text: The Beautiful Game The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 3 #1.3 Released: 10 May 2023 Listened: 6/20/23 This one seems to be another “indulge an interest” story, but this time it’s football, and it’s writer Katherine Armitage who’s indulging, but Christopher Eccleston is a huge football fan as well, and it appears that the Ninth Doctor also feels positively about it. He’s come to the Royal Hotel, Manchester to see the foundation of the Football League in 1888, except oops, he’s a week early. (Really not bad, considering.) However, there’s also an alien here called a Strike, which is a growly, tentacle thing that somehow feeds on obsessions and mania, and doesn’t let go once it’s started. So football itself is in danger. Naturally, there’s an extremely practical, helpful young woman working at the hotel, whom the Doctor immediately latches onto as a companion-substitute. Except she really doesn’t want any part of the adventure, and keeps insisting that she should know her place. Normally, the Doctor ignores bystanders who don’t want to help out, so it seems a bit odd that he’s leaning on Daphne so much instead of her more outgoing friend Eva. There’s a lot of football references and commentary in this one, like a lot a lot. Much of which goes over my head as an American. The Strike is a rather strange baddie. It’s mostly mindless, and the whole “eats obsessions” thing is really odd. It reminds me a lot of the P’Ting from Jodie Whittaker’s first season. That said, Becky Wright does an amazing job portraying its raspy babble.
docs.title: The Beautiful Game

docs.text: The Bleeding Heart Ninth Doctor Chronicles #1.1 Released: 4 May 2017 Listened: 9/5/22 This story is from the "Ninth Doctor Chronicles" collection, which means that like most Chronicles stories, it’s narrated and only has two actors. Nick Briggs does most of the narrating duties, which means we’re treated to his version of the Ninth Doctor, which sounds a bit more like Nick Briggs with a head cold than it does Christopher Eccleston, but we’ll take what we can get. The story itself takes place a while after his regeneration, but not too long, because he’s still carrying the War Doctor’s red-tipped sonic, but that ends in this story. However, the psychic wounds of the Time War are still fresh, which is why he visits Galen, planet of peace, to try to find some forgiveness for what he’s done. The planet is also used to host peace conferences, because it has a calming effect on everyone on it. In this case, the Harrigain, the hippo-like aliens seen in the comics and in “ Devil in the Mist ,” are seeking peace with a group of jellyfish-like aliens. Which is hard enough, but then people start turning up dead. The other primary character is a reporter played by Claire Wyatt, who does well enough as a substitute companion, but we know she won’t be sticking around. What I didn’t expect was how much this story affects the Doctor, personally, and just how hard it hits. You can almost see the Doctor growing the emotional protective shell he’ll have by the time he meets Rose.
docs.title: The Bleeding Heart

docs.text: The Blooming Menace The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 2 #4.2 Released: 8 February 2023 Listened: 3/13/23 This one, however, is straight-up comedy from James Kettle, who’s a comedy writer, so it works pretty well. It’s a Wodehouse send-up, which is always good fun. London, 1920s, gentlemen’s clubs, and all the gentlemen are falling in love with…giant flowers. So the Doctor sets himself up as a valet for one of the last gentlemen standing. Of course, this is the Ninth Doctor, who really has no time for class differences, so his attempt to act like a valet…never really gets off the ground at all. And of course we’ve got to toss in some gender-bending and mistaken identity, because why not? On the whole, it’s very funny, and would be the standout in a different set.
docs.title: The Blooming Menace

docs.text: The Colour of Terror The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 2 #4.1 Released: 8 February 2023 Listened: 3/11/23 This boxed set is called “Shades of Fear,” and the stories fit the title a bit better than usual. This one takes place in a charity shop in a small town, where aliens called the Vermine are invading through the color red. Which sounds silly, so really they’re invading along the electromagnetic spectrum, specifically the wavelengths that humans see as the color red. But that’s not as much of the point as the secondary characters, including a young man who works at the shop as part of his recovery program for petty thievery, a retired widower played by Frank Skinner, and the shop owner, Mrs. Bevell, played by Susan Penhaligon, a well-known actress who had a minor role in “ The Time Monster ” decades ago. But the point is that Lizzie Hopley has created in Mrs. Bevell a truly reprehensible human being, who spins every event the way she wants it to be, and nothing is ever her fault. You wouldn’t think a shop owner could do much to affect an alien menace, but you’d be wrong. What goes down is less important than the relationships among the humans, and how this Doctor handles them, which is a bit better than you might expect, but he’s starting to heal.
docs.title: The Colour of Terror

docs.text: The Curse of Lady Macbeth The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 1 #3.2 Released: 23 November 2021 Listened: 9/25/22 The Doctor turns up in Scotland, and bumps right into Queen Gruach , or rather Lady Macbeth. The Doctor is immediately star-struck, as this Doctor often is when meeting historical figures. Problem is, she hates Macbeth because she believes he murdered her first husband, her son has gone mute with trauma, and something is replacing all the babies of the town with changelings. Writer Lizzie Hopley is having a ball with this one, as is everybody else, because as actors, they’re all familiar with the Shakespearean Macbeth , and putting a historical spin on it appeals to nearly everybody. And it’s an excuse to bring in all the lovely Scottish voices Big Finish can get their hands on, with Neve McIntosh playing Lady Macbeth, and Lucy Goldie (from “ Girl, Deconstructed ”) making a return. With all that going on, there’s barely enough time to have the monsters in the plot; in fact, they’re kind of underdeveloped. The big threat is really the superstition of the locals, and basically the whole grim situation the people live in. Personally, I found it rather dark for my taste, but apparently the appeal of Macbeth allowed most of the cast and crew to look past that.
docs.title: The Curse of Lady Macbeth

docs.text: The False Dimitry The Ninth Doctor Adventures Series 2 #1.2 Released: 4 May 2022 Listened: 10/7/22 This one is a proper historical, but not a “pure” one, because the modern series doesn’t do that. It’s set in Moscow, in the early 1600s, just after the death of Boris Godunov . Unfortunately, that set off a succession crisis, in which several people claimed to be Dimitry, son of Ivan the Terrible, and therefore the true heir. The one who turns up in this story, though, has some alien help, and with perception filters, almost nothing is who or what it seems. There’s no real companion-substitute in this one, although the monk Sasha fulfills some parts of that role. He’s overshadowed by his mother Oksana, played by Katy Brittain, an old maid in service to the Tsar, with a strongly peasant-class accent, a tendency to wail, and a complete inability to keep a secret for more than thirty seconds. New writer Sarah Grochala is well-versed in the history and culture of this period, and there’s a lot of it on display, but at the expense of the plot, unfortunately. The aliens don’t seem to have a lot of motivation or personality. But as a historical, it’s not bad.
docs.title: The False Dimitry
