docs.text: Operation Dusk Far from Home #1 Released: 27 June 2023 Listened: 7/29/23 The Seventh Doctor is still hanging out with Harry and Naomi here, although they both talk about wanting to go home, to varying degrees. Thing is, for Harry, that’s definitely the 1970s, whereas Naomi has made some friends in the 21st Century, and also feels at home there. (It’s implied, but not stated, that Naomi prefers the state of race relations in the 2010s as well, a fact that goes completely by Harry.) Except before they can do anything about that, they answer a distress call from Winston Churchill, and head for WWII. Churchill doesn’t appear, but the Doctor gets to use his credentials and basically stomp all over the poor MI-5 agents trying to deal with this. Because it appears that there’s a shadow eating people, and we know what that means. We haven’t seen the Seventh Doctor with the Vashta Nerada before, although he sounds great saying their name. He’s also pointlessly cryptic about who they are and what they can do (the MI-5 folks think they might be an Indian resistance group), which very nearly gets people killed. Of course, Vashta Nerada are tricky on audio, because shadows aren’t known for their chattiness, so we get some other alien conspirators too. The bluffs and double-bluffs keep piling up, to the point where it’s tricky to know who’s on which side. And there’s a reference to the Forge that feels like it’s pretty random, but does get sufficiently explained. It’s got a lot of interesting parts, but I’m not sure the sum is worth it.
docs.title: Operation Dusk

docs.text: Scream of the Daleks Sullivan & Cross: AWOL #2 Released: 8 November 2022 Listened: 1/21/23 The Doctor has promised to take Harry and Naomi back to their own time, but naturally he wants to take a few detours first. The first of those doesn’t take them very far, though, just to Chester, on Halloween 1969, the site of a combination concert and fright-fest. After discovering an “aura of evil,” as the Seventh Doctor often does, he and Naomi take off in the TARDIS to discover where in history it’s coming from, accidentally leaving Harry behind. This gives Naomi more of a chance to establish her character, and she’s pretty clearly Action Girl, familiar with time travel, confident she can hold her own physically, and comfortable with the strange. Lisa McMullin takes the opportunity to show us Halloween throughout the history of England, from ancient Samhain to Roman Feralia to the middle ages, because why not? Except that the cry for help they’re following comes from the Daleks. An early Dalek time-travel experiment got stuck in time, and the Daleks figured that if they caused enough horror and tragedy throughout history, eventually the Doctor (or some other time traveler) would turn up to investigate, which is a very Dalek way of problem-solving, but also fairly accurate. Even though it’s only a short two-parter, the story keeps the Daleks a secret until the episode 1 cliffhanger, despite naming them in the title. Which is traditional, and yet fairly absurd. The Doctor really lets loose with how he feels about the Daleks in this incarnation. “Sgt. Pepperpot’s Angry Hate Club Band” is a personal favorite. Compared to other Dalek stories, the threat is a bit low-key.
docs.title: Scream of the Daleks

docs.text: Subterfuge Main Range #262 Released: 17 March 2020 Listened: 3/25/21 In this story, the renegade is the Monk, which isn’t particularly hidden, because you can’t disguise Rufus Hound. This time, he’s interfering in the 1945 election , trying to make sure Churchill wins. Churchill features prominently as a character, played by Ian McNeice as he was on TV, and again we’re given to believe that he’s met various Doctors in random order throughout the ‘30s and ‘40s. There’s a bunch of spying and double-crossing in this story, and pretty much nobody is what they appear to be, other than Churchill himself. There’s a German spy who wants a final revenge before he flees the country, some aliens who just want to go home, and the Monk...well, it’s not really clear what the Monk wants. Personal wealth and power, sure, but it’s not at all clear how helping Churchill win the 1945 election would accomplish that. The Monk just seems to enjoy messing about with English history for some reason. The Doctor is left to put things back on track, which means betraying Churchill -- or at least that’s how the Seventh Doctor handles it. I suspect some of the others might have been less manipulative. The point of this story doesn’t really seem to be the plot, but rather to let Ian McNeice get a lot of time as Churchill and give a famous speech. Which is fine, but not particularly compelling.
docs.title: Subterfuge

docs.text: The Eye of the Storm The Diary of River Song #2.4 Released: 25 December 2016 Listened: 3/21/21 From one new-series tie-in to another. Normally, I credit multi-doctor crossovers to the “newest” Doctor involved, but this story is “owned” by River, so I’m just going to have to cover it twice. Looking at the story from the Seventh Doctor’s point of view, it seems appropriate that it should come at the end of his tenure. He’s not as much playing chessmaster as he’s demonstrating an inability to trust anybody else. He recognizes River, but still doesn’t trust her, so he tries to lock her out of his plan (literally), but it’s less because he’s inherently untrusting and more because he believes he’ll have to violate his code of ethics, and doesn’t want to burden anyone else with that. The story resolves rather abruptly, with River doing something that only River can, and bringing up her own backstory as part of that process. Personally, I’m not too fond of the resolutions where River sees herself as only a tragic adjunct to the Doctor, but this time it saves the world, so OK. And I still find her sparring with the Seventh Doctor while trying to erase his memory to be terribly funny, probably the best such sequence in her series.
docs.title: The Eye of the Storm

docs.text: The Krillitane Relic Classic Doctors New Monsters #5.3 Released: 21 January 2025 Listened: 4/18/26 This one is complicated for a number of reasons. First, the Doctor is traveling with Ray, from " Delta and the Bannermen ," still played by Sara Griffiths. However, it's a 20-years-older version of Ray than we saw before, having been picked up by the Doctor during " Catastrophix ," which hadn't been released yet at the time this story came out. It's also connected to " The Krillitane Feint " from earlier in this boxed set, but that was a long time ago for the Doctor, leading him to believe that he's encountered Zoe again. Even more confusing, the story references Zoe's trilogy of Companion Chronicles , but they're not required listening. This story is by John Dorney, and while it's not twisty like of his stories are, it's unique in that the secondar characters behave more realistically than characters in a Doctor Who story usually would. The security guard tries to piece together what's going on, instead of just shouting at people. When one of his colleagues acts strangely, he reports it to his manager. The manager, being confronted with evidence that one of her employees might not be who she says, does some research to find out. It's all quite reasonable until the slavering monsters turn up and the slaughtering starts.
docs.title: The Krillitane Relic

docs.text: The Night Before Christmas Subscriber Short Trips #2017-4 Released: 18 December 2017 Listened: 3/21/21 This is one of the annual Christmas short trips, this time dealing directly with Clement Clarke Moore , author of “Twas the Night Before Christmas”...in our world, anyway. In this case, reality has been altered so that Christmas is known as a time when demons walk the Earth and steal away the wicked, which people are mostly acclimated to, but Moore has a nightmare (and a poem) about the Krampus, a gigantic evil monster made of candy. Of course, the Doctor has experience with candy monsters , and shows up to put things right. His outfit is rather vaguely described as an early-season one, but he’s traveling alone, and has a sonic with a red light, so it must be later in his tenure. As often happens with Short Trips, Stephen Critchlow narrates, and gives the Seventh Doctor a bit more stereotypical Scottish accent (some of his lines sound like Peter Capaldi delivering them), but does a good job with Moore’s American accent. Writer Nic Ford tells the story from Moore’s point of view, so the language is somewhat colorful and writerly, but only veers over into poetry when Moore is describing his actual poems. It’s a decent Christmas story in the Doctor Who style -- the right trappings, but twisted and just scary enough. Sadly, because “ Better Watch Out ” exists, this is the second-best Big Finish story to feature the Krampus (and there are several appearances in print and comics too), but that’s OK.
docs.title: The Night Before Christmas

docs.text: Subscriber Short Trips #2017-4 Released: 18 December 2017 Listened: 3/21/21 This is one of the annual Christmas short trips, this time dealing directly with Clement Clarke Moore , author of “Twas the Night Before Christmas”...in our world, anyway. In this case, reality has been altered so that Christmas is known as a time when demons walk the Earth and steal away the wicked, which people are mostly acclimated to, but Moore has a nightmare (and a poem) about the Krampus, a gigantic evil monster made of candy. Of course, the Doctor has experience with candy monsters , and shows up to put things right. His outfit is rather vaguely described as an early-season one, but he’s traveling alone, and has a sonic with a red light, so it must be later in his tenure. As often happens with Short Trips, Stephen Critchlow narrates, and gives the Seventh Doctor a bit more stereotypical Scottish accent (some of his lines sound like Peter Capaldi delivering them), but does a good job with Moore’s American accent. Writer Nic Ford tells the story from Moore’s point of view, so the language is somewhat colorful and writerly, but only veers over into poetry when Moore is describing his actual poems. It’s a decent Christmas story in the Doctor Who style -- the right trappings, but twisted and just scary enough. Sadly, because “ Better Watch Out ” exists, this is the second-best Big Finish story to feature the Krampus (and there are several appearances in print and comics too), but that’s OK.
docs.title: The Night Before Christmas

docs.text: The Psychic Circus Main Range #261 Released: 11 February 2020 Listened: 3/24/21 This final trilogy for the Seventh Doctor has him going up against other renegade Time Lords in each story, although the stories themselves aren’t related. In this first one, it’s the Master, although the Richard Dreyfus version, considered the “First Master” depending on how you look at it. Unfortunately, Dreyfus made some impolitic remarks after recording this story, and Big Finish dropped him from appearing again. Stephen Wyatt wrote the story, as he’s the writer of “ Greatest Show in the Galaxy ” and “ Paradise Towers ,” both of which feature heavily here. Unfortunately, because this is a prequel to “Greatest Show” for everyone except the Doctor, that means the Doctor can’t actually resolve anything, without wrecking his own timelines. So we see how the Circus was created, how it was corrupted by the gods of Ragnarok, and how Kingpin became Deadbeat, without fixing any of it. We also see the origin of the Chief Clown (kind of), but we don’t get an explanation of why he’s so chatty in this story, but mostly silent on TV. Although the Master is apparently behind most of it, neither he nor the Doctor physically appear in the story; they spend most of their time as psychic projections. The problem is, I don’t feel like we really needed an origin story for the circus, especially not one tangentially involving Paradise Towers, and there was certainly no need for the Master’s involvement. There’s also no mention of Mags, who was just a companion a short while ago, but there’s no real reason why there would be. It does capture the somewhat surreal feel of the original story, but that’s not necessarily a good thing.
docs.title: The Psychic Circus

docs.text: Doctor Who: The Movie TV Special Released: 14 May 1996 Also known as "Enemy Within," this 1996 production features the end of the Seventh Doctor’s tenure, and the beginning of the Eighth. Unlike other regeneration stories in this project, Big Finish hasn’t tried to set a story in the middle of it. Because of the long gap between the end of the TV series and this movie, the Doctor appears distinctly older, implying that he’s had a long run. It also features the redesigned “gothic” TARDIS, and shows that the Seventh Doctor acquired a new sonic screwdriver sometime after “ Survival .”

docs.text: The Two Masters Main Range #213 Released: 13 June 2016 Listened: 3/20/21 This is the final “five-six-seven” trilogy for this project, but it’s more about the Master than it is about the Doctors. The big surprise is that the “crispy” Master and the “bald” Master swapped bodies before the trilogy started, which explains why he’s acting out of character in “ And You Will Obey Me ” and “ Vampire of the Mind .” The ruse continues through the first couple of parts of this story, and it’s clear Geoffrey Beevers and Alex MacQueen are loving every minute of it. Alex MacQueen had appeared in several sets of “ Dark Eyes ” by this point, but the Seventh Doctor knows him only from “ Dominion .” The story is written by John Dorney, so you can expect a heaping helping of timey-wimey, which mostly takes place in flashbacks, so you can see how the mind-swap was set up. As a bonus, you also find out how the Master got crispy-fried before “ The Deadly Assassin ” (or at least one version of that story), and what the “bald” Master was up to at the beginning of his life. And Dorney throws in his creations the Rocket Men , but at a very down-on-their-luck point in their history, so they’re not really significant to the story. Of course, a major paradox like this threatens the existence of the entire universe, and of course the Masters want to take advantage of that and take over. And even more of course, they can’t get along for long enough to pull it off, at least not once the Doctor sticks his nose in. Which is kind of obvious, especially if you’ve heard the “Masterful” boxed set or seen “The Doctor Falls,” but multi-Master stories were still pretty uncommon in 2016. Alex MacQueen once again demonstrates why he’s a great Master for audio, with lots of variations in his line delivery, pitched all over the place. His Master also seems to be having such fun, which makes a great contrast to Geoffrey Beevers’ Master (who’s in constant pain, so I can’t really blame him). The only disappointment is that the Doctor wraps it all up fairly easily and neatly, which is perhaps normal for the Seventh Doctor at this point, but you’d think it should be trickier to defeat the Doctor’s greatest enemy.
docs.title: The Two Masters

docs.text: The Sixth Doctor The Sixth Doctor had a tempestuous tenure on television, alienating quite a lot of fans (myself included) and BBC executives. He also had a very short tenure, and a temporally confusing companion in Mel, whom he met out of order. That leaves a lot of gaps for Big Finish to slot in new stories, new companions, and character growth. For the most part, the Sixth Doctor has just one companion at a time, which makes a contrast to the First and Fifth Doctor eras that I’ve listened to so far in this project. “Old Sixie” probably has the greatest expansion to his personality of any of the TV characters, and most listeners would agree it’s a vast improvement. There are also quite a few new characters created especially for Big Finish, and at the time of this writing, some of their stories haven’t concluded.

docs.text: The Sixth Doctor and Charley Even the heading on this section is a spoiler, and I can’t hide it for multiple complete stories, so I’m sorry about that. Basically: After Charley leaves the Eighth Doctor , she’s picked up by the Sixth. Charley’s not ready to stop adventuring, so she goes along with him, but she also knows that he didn’t remember her when they first met, so her efforts to keep that knowledge from him hang in the background of all of these stories. That does cause some headaches for this project, because we won’t meet Charley for quite some time yet. Charley’s an experienced traveler at this point, but she doesn’t know this Doctor, which drives a certain amount of drama.

docs.text: Blue Forgotten Planet Main Range #126 Released: 25 September 2009 Listened: 7/24/20 Charley’s story at last comes to an end here, as does Mila’s. There’s a large gap between the last story and this one, for both the Doctor and Mila, and for Charley with the Viyrans. The nominal plot revolves around the Viyrans tracking down one of their particles to Earth, which threatens the entire human race at some unspecified point in time. There are a handful of humans, who we’re supposed to feel attached to, but they’re mostly kept in the dark the entire time, so it’s hard to empathize with them. But that’s not really what the story is about; it’s about Charley and Mila and which one the Doctor believes. Charley seems even older and wiser than she had a few stories ago; she’s clearly hardened from her time with the Viyrans. The Viyrans themselves aren’t terribly impressive as baddies. They aren’t, really; they’re just implacable, and slaves to logic as robots often are. They’re not even a force of nature, because they can be reasoned with, to an extent. They’re still a threat, but not scary as such. It’s possible that Charley overstayed her welcome a bit, but it’s really hard to fault Big Finish or India Fisher for that. -- The stories from the two Charlotte Pollard boxed sets take place here, from Charley’s point of view, anyway. --
docs.title: Blue Forgotten Planet

docs.text: Brotherhood of the Daleks Main Range #114 Released: October 2008 Listened: 7/18/20 This one is complicated . Writer Alan Barnes even tells you in the Extras that you can’t listen to this one while doing something else (which is how I usually listen to Big Finish, so that was a problem). It even has five parts instead of the usual four. There are lots of levels of deception going on in this story, with Daleks who think they’re Thals, missions on a planet that’s a simulation, hallucinogenic spores, and most oddly (and the bit that doesn’t really work, in my opinion) Daleks adopting Communism and its principles of brotherhood and collective effort. Charley, of course, is practicing her own deceptions, and that comes strongly to the fore here. She’s met Daleks before (in “ Terror Firma ,” although this project hasn’t gotten there yet), and furthermore, they know who she is. She also plays into her “experienced adventurer” role more than usual, taking the lead away from the Doctor several times. The story ends up tap-dancing all over the line of revealing the truth, miraculously never quite crossing it. She also reveals her early-20th-century upbringing in her opinions about Communism. In addition, she’s heavily snarky this time, with a cutting comment for just about every occasion. It’s not the most traditional Dalek story, but it is worthy of the attention it demands.
docs.title: Brotherhood of the Daleks

docs.text: Paper Cuts Main Range #125 Released: 25 September 2009 Listened: 7/24/20 This is the middle story in Mila’s trilogy, which makes it a bit of an odd one out, because the first and last stories are tightly connected. For the majority of this story, except for the very beginning and the very end, Mila may as well be Charley, given her actions and reactions. However, it features the Draconians, a species with an outsized reputation, given how rarely they appear. They only had one TV appearance , and few audio appearances . (They show up a bit more in novels and comics, but not really very much.) They’ve got a lot of Japanese influence, consumed with nobility, which fits quite nicely with the Third Doctor, where they originated. This is the Sixth Doctor, of course, but he does his best to hold up Draconian ideals. It’s a court intrigue story, which makes sense given the setting, but it sort of falls down from that point. The intrigue isn’t as twisty as it could be; most characters are pretty straightforward. It’s a very visual story, with elaborate temples, and origami chess pieces, but the descriptions aren’t as subtle as they usually are. There’s a fair amount of characters describing what’s happening right in front of them, which Big Finish normally doesn’t fall victim to. There isn’t really a villain, either, just politicians with their own agendas. And the ending doesn’t really resolve. The Doctor just does some stuff, then leaves before it’s really finished, almost as if he’s aware of the time limit on the CDs. It’s very rare for me to say this, but I think this would have worked better on TV (even with a 1986 budget) than it does on audio.
docs.title: Paper Cuts

docs.text: Patient Zero Main Range #124 Released: 22 August 2009 Listened: 7/20/20 Between the last story and this one, Big Finish shifted the monthly range schedule to feature mostly linked trilogies of stories. Which means that Charley’s stay got extended by a couple of stories, but also that her condition becomes more central to the plot as of now. It’s also rather more continuity-heavy, as stories by Nick Briggs tend to be. It’s the first appearance of the Dalek Time Controller, who would most often be seen bothering the Eighth Doctor . It’s also the first appearance of Mila, who’s difficult to discuss without spoilers, but she’s an entity who’s been hiding in the TARDIS since “ The Chase ,” completely undetected. It also features the Viyrans, and we find out the origin of all the viruses they’ve been so concerned about whenever they appear. In fact, the virus in this story is probably the same as the one Peri had in “ Mission of the Viyrans .” On top of all of which, it’s a Dalek story. The plot itself is kind of slow-boiling, as the story is trying to keep several secrets for as long as it can: Amethyst Station, the Time Controller, Mila, and the virus itself. As a result, the Doctor doesn’t get to do much except stand around, shout questions, and react to things, even up until the end. And the end isn’t really an ending as such, as they’re leaning hard into the trilogy idea. As a stand-alone story, it’s somewhat lacking, but as the first part of the trilogy, it’s better.
docs.title: Patient Zero

docs.text: Return of the Krotons Bonus Release Released: 11 December 2008 Listened: 7/18/20 This special release came out in 2009, when Charley was traveling with the Sixth Doctor. The Krotons hadn’t been seen at all, really, since the Second Doctor episode “ The Krotons .” Unfortunately, because the story is only an hour, it feels like a full-length story with parts of the plot cut out. The Krotons don’t get a lot of development at all; they’re just a generic threat. There’s the usual trope of scientists messing with things they shouldn’t, and a tyrannical leader motivated only by profit, but all of that is taken as read and disposed of almost immediately; the Doctor never even meets them. Unfortunately, the resolution is fairly predictable as well. At least Charley gets to make a “croutons” joke, which has been in my head for decades. As for Charley, once again her secret is confined to just a few hints that the Doctor makes note of. On the whole, pretty throwaway.
docs.title: Return of the Krotons

docs.text: The Avenues of Possibility The Legacy of Time #5 Released: 17 July 2019 Listened: 7/18/20 This is another entry from the Legacy of Time box set released in 2019 for Big Finish’s anniversary. It’s best listened to as part of that set, but this story is relatively independent. The Doctor and Charley intend to visit the Doctor’s friend Henry Fielding, author and founder of London’s first police force (depending on who you ask). Almost immediately they run afoul of some cracks in time, one of which leads to 2009, where Fielding gets to meet D.I. Patricia Menzies, who is apparently now the police authority on “weird stuff,” and even has her own task force. There’s also a portal to an alternate 1951, where Britain is an authoritarian state who’ve taken over the world, and now want to invade the other time zones. The plot zings along, because with only an hour, there’s barely any time to breathe. Still, Charley is game, clever, and unflappable, and Menzies is equally calm and capable. That’s very consistent with their last appearances, but for people listening in release order, it would’ve been some time since these characters last appeared. The Sirens of Time, from the first first Big Finish story , make a brief appearance, and Charley needs to spill her big secret in order to distract them, but thanks to a handy bout of temporal amnesia, the Doctor doesn’t know. It’s more of a fast-paced character piece than it is a mystery, but it’s good fun.
docs.title: The Avenues of Possibility

That’s very consistent with their last appearances, but for people listening in release order, it would’ve been some time since these characters last appeared. The Sirens of Time, from the first first Big Finish story , make a brief appearance, and Charley needs to spill her big secret in order to distract them, but thanks to a handy bout of temporal amnesia, the Doctor doesn’t know. It’s more of a fast-paced character piece than it is a mystery, but it’s good fun.
docs.title: The Avenues of Possibility

docs.text: The Condemned Main Range #105 Released: February 2008 Listened: 7/15/20 From the Doctor’s standpoint (and this project’s), this is his first meeting with Charley. (Poor Sixie; so many of his companions have temporal issues.) She’s savvy enough to know what’s going on and try to hide her knowledge from the Doctor, but she doesn’t do a very good job of it. That’s fine for the moment, because they spend a large part of this story apart. The Doctor is mostly hanging out with D.I. Patricia Menzies of Manchester, who we met before in “ The Crimes of Thomas Brewster ,” but this is their first meeting from her point of view. To her credit, she handles the alien strangeness pretty well. Turns out there’s a thriving, if hidden, alien community in Manchester, with all that goes along with it, including a black market, petty jealousy, and killing for insurance purposes. It’s kind of a new-series concept, which makes sense, as this story focuses around the machinations of the aliens, and one very spooky tower block. Charley gets a fair amount of time alone to show off her skills and experience, but in the end needs the Doctor to be clever in order to solve things. The main plot isn’t as important as Charley’s character work, which goes fairly well.

docs.text: The Doomwood Curse Main Range #111 Released: August 2008 Listened: 7/16/20 Charley continues her charade with the Sixth Doctor, trying to go back to adventuring with him while not letting on how much she knows. In this case, they wind up in what appears to be a rather hammy Victorian drama based on the novel Rookwood . It gets a bit draggy in the middle while the Doctor figures out what’s going on, and the story also needs to explain its literary references for those who aren’t up on their early 1800s novels (which includes myself, mostly). However, with Charley being subsumed by fiction and separated from the Doctor for much of the story, she doesn’t need to worry about keeping her secret. This is one of those where there’s not so much a bad guy as a runaway phenomenon to be stopped, which makes it a little light on the drama. It also features a pre- Captain America Haley Atwell as a bride who turns up a bit later in the story but proves capable and heroic, perfect for the future Agent Carter. Your enjoyment of this will likely hinge on how much you enjoy the setting.
docs.title: The Doomwood Curse

docs.text: The Raincloud Man Main Range #116 Released: 11 December 2008 Listened: 7/19/20 This is yet another story with D.I. Patricia Menzies, for her happening after “ The Condemned ,” but before “ The Crimes of Thomas Brewster ,” and “ The Avenues of Possibility .” Even still, Menzies is pretty comfortable with aliens and time travel, and handles all the weirdness quite well. Well enough that the alien community in Manchester trusts her and comes to her with problems. The plot itself is a bit convoluted, with interplanetary and intertemporal gamblers on board a floating casino, which teleports from Manchester to Rio (which would have made a great visual, if there were any). The baddies are a bit one-note, but an awful lot of bystanders get killed. Charley and her deception, once again, take a big role here, where she’s warned that the consequences of her lies may be very great indeed. This is the last appearance of Menzies as far as this project goes, and it’s safe to say I’d welcome her return, and even taking on a companion role if that were possible.

docs.text: The Red House The Last Adventure #2 Released: 17 August 2015 Listened: 7/18/20 In 2015, Big Finish released a boxed set called The Last Adventure , intended to give the Sixth Doctor a proper regeneration story. It consisted of four parts, each with a different companion, and this is the first to show up in this project. This particular piece is a slightly odd one-hour story, in which the Doctor and Charley encounter a planet of werewolves...kind of. Their story actually isn’t terribly important, as Charley and the Doctor get separated. Charley is rescued by someone calling himself a Time Lord, who wants to stealthily intervene and steal a psychic probe while he’s at it. A Time Lord who knows all about who Charley is, and who sounds exactly like Michael Jayston, meaning it’s the Valeyard. On the whole, it seems like an inconsequential, slightly silly adventure, but the Valeyard’s plan won’t become clear until much later in the boxed set.
docs.title: The Red House

docs.text: These Stolen Hours Short Trips #10.8 Released: 28 August 2020 Listened: 8/28/20 This is almost told in a Companion Chronicles style, with a frame story surrounding a flashback. The frame story takes place, for Charley, in the long gap before “ Blue Forgotten Planet ,” but the flashback takes place hereabouts. It’s a story uniquely fitting for Charley, as she and the Doctor come across a standard temporal anomaly, which turns out to be a woman interfering with her own past to relieve heartbreak. The Doctor doesn’t see it at first, and he’s very disapproving once he figures it out, but Charley understands, and is sympathetic, because she’s doing the same thing. It’s a tiny story, but because it’s from Charley’s point of view, it makes her more understandable than any other story in this segment.
docs.title: These Stolen Hours

docs.text: The Sixth Doctor and Constance (and Flip) There’s a gap at the end of the previous section, in which it’s assumed that Peri’s story has ended, and this era picks up with the Doctor meeting Mrs. Constance Clarke, a code-breaker from Bletchley Park in WWII. Once again, she’s a capable woman with a strong personality capable of standing up to the Sixth Doctor’s bluster, and in this case Constance has her own agenda. After several stories, Flip reappears, letting us know what she’s been up to in the interim. As of the time of this writing, their final status is unresolved, but hopefully we'll get more with them at some point.

docs.text: Absolute Power Main Range #219 Released: 13 December 2016 Listened: 9/2/20 Another spacey future adventure for Constance, as she and the Doctor end up on a planet with a long-dead civilization, significant ruins, and mysterious glyphs. And, of course, a mining corporation owned by a wealthy businessman, Lyam Yce, who doesn’t care about the cultural values, and who has a ditzy-seeming fiance who knows a lot more than she should. Constance gets the spotlight here, although portraying her 1940s cryptography skills as making her a capable xeno-linguist is kind of a stretch, even with the TARDIS giving her a boost. She also gets a romance subplot for the first time, as Yce’s assistant Ammar takes a shine to her immediately. It’s unrequited, of course, and Ammar is kind of a wet blanket, but he manages to come through in the end, and accepts being turned down with good grace. Constance seems to be reminded of the war wherever she goes, and so asks to go home at the end. It’s an OK story, although the climax seems a bit rushed and overdone. It’s not quite as clever as it thinks it is.
docs.title: Absolute Power

docs.text: All for One The Eleven #1 Released: 2 September 2021 Listened: 9/5/21 This release is part of a boxed set simply called “The Eleven,” featuring the Sixth Doctor and Constance. (Not to be confused with the Eighth Doctor story of the same name , which also features the character known as the Eleven.) This story introduces the planet Molaruss, where the natives mostly have two distinct personas, and have mild discrimination against “mono-minds.” There are even institutes where one can go to help your personas get along better. The Eleven has somehow acquired a wife, Miskavel, who has brought him to the institute so that he can get rid of some of his personalities. Although she seems like the innocent victim in all of this, her motivations and manipulations aren’t entirely clear. The Doctor and Constance don’t really seem to have a whole lot to do in this story, as it seems to be mostly setup for later.

docs.text: Children of the Revolution The Quin Dilemma #4 Released: 22 March 2024 Listened: 4/22/26 This story continues directly from " Sibling Rivalry ," the preceeding part of "The Quin Dilemma." Usually, when Big Finish does these multi-part stories, there's some kind of symmetry to them, but this one is odd. The previous two stories of this set were self-contained, but this has been a two-parter with twice the bad guys. I rather wish the story were stronger, though. After handwaving the cliffhanger, the Doctor and Constance join up with some rebels to outwit the Sontarans, because the Doctor is clever. Flip is with her own group, being a strategic genius by accident, and ends up getting all the credit. The two idiot princes learn that the only way out of their predicament is to work together. Much like the last story, the princes have very little effect on the plot; they just hang around and swoop the Doctor away at the end. For the Doctor, Constance, and Flip, the story continues from here to The Firstborn , before they come back here.
docs.title: Children of the Revolution

docs.text: Colony of Fear Main Range #273 Released: 19 January 2021 Listened: 1/21/21 This 2021 release features the Doctor traveling with just Constance (because Lisa Greenwood was unavailable due to Covid), which doesn’t match its predecessors in release order, so it needs to be inserted in a previous run. The TARDIS lands on a colony that’s familiar to the Doctor, and where the colonists are being attacked and infected by parasitic space wasps, which eventually threaten to take them all over. That’s normal base-under-seige, but there’s also a character who knows the Doctor of old, but the Doctor can’t remember him. We eventually find out that it was the Second Doctor who knew him, but the Time Lords apparently wiped his memories. That’s never fully explained, and I find that somewhat annoying. It’s a bit paradoxical for a Big Finish fan, because I’m OK with them introducing new companions and giving them a dozen Main Range appearances, but I’m not OK with them having a new companion turn up who’s never been mentioned before or since. The body count in this one is unusually high, which is also a negative. The major and minor characters are well-drawn with distinct personalities and motivations, but the plot itself is somewhat rote, which leaves this as something of a mixed bag.
docs.title: Colony of Fear

docs.text: Criss-Cross Main Range #204 Released: 15 September 2015 Listened: 8/27/20 It’s time for a new companion, in this case Leading WREN Constance Clarke. Before the story starts, the TARDIS is immobilized on Earth during World War II, and the Doctor has had to insinuate himself at Bletchley Park to try to figure out what the problem is. It turns out to be one of those aliens who are so different their very presence is harmful to humans, and it just wants to go home, or so it appears. The alien bits take kind of a back seat to the historical setting. Matt Fitton has done his research on this one, and is unstinting in his praise of Bletchley and the folks who work there, and their instrumental role in ending the war. Details of the systems and processes abound, but it’s a little tricky to appreciate that and keep track of the plot at the same time. Constance is also part of that praise, as she’s capable, clever, and generally unflappable, which certainly makes her companion material, but she doesn’t get an offer, likely because she has her duties, and is married. However, her husband, part of British Intelligence, whereabouts unknown, is what drives Constance to talk the Doctor into taking her along. That plot won’t resolve for quite a while. A new companion is always a breath of fresh air, and Constance more than most.
docs.title: Criss-Cross

docs.text: Cry of the Vultriss Main Range #263 Released: 15 April 2020 Listened: 9/6/20 The stories in this trilogy were a welcome return at the time, because fans had been waiting three years for this team to reappear. Fortunately, this project doesn’t have that problem. After the events of “Static ,” Constance thinks she doesn’t want to go home just yet, but Flip is starting to feel she should get back to her wedding. However, they’re interrupted by the old standby, a temporal anomaly. In this case, it’s the planet of the Vultriss, a race of avians who are just about to make their first diplomatic contact with the wider galaxy. The chosen ambassadors are Ice Warriors, which leads to a Peladon -ish “are they good guys or bad guys?” plotline. There’s also a rebellion, and an ancient prophecy, plus the time anomaly. Unfortunately, although there are lots of bits and pieces running around, it’s not all that memorable. Most of the characters feel pretty one-note, even the ones who are hiding their true intentions. Once again. Flip’s empathy gets the emphasis, rather than her recklessness; Constance continues to be mostly unflappable. Adele Lynch plays the Ice Warrior Queen, a bit of stunt casting, because she played the title character in “Empress of Mars” on TV. This one definitely has to be an audio, given the high mountain vistas and evolved bird-people everywhere, it likely wouldn’t have worked on TV, even with 2020 effects.
docs.title: Cry of the Vultriss

docs.text: Elevation The Eleven #3 Released: 2 September 2021 Listened: 9/6/21 After the events of the last story , the Eleven is now the ruler of Molaruss, because the residents think that having eleven minds is terribly nifty and efficient, and for his part, the Eleven seems to be trying to do a good job for once. How he’s keeping the more insane personas in line isn’t exactly clear, but probably has something to do with the therapy methods on Molaruss. The Doctor and Constance return, about five years later in the Molaruss timeline, but an undefined “while” in the Doctor’s. It turns out that the Eleven has summoned them back because he’s enacted a plan to give the rest of the population eleven personas, like himself, and wants the Doctor as witness. There’s no grand scheme or nefarious plan; he’s just bored with being the ruler now and thinks this will make the people more interesting. This scheme affects Constance as well, so we get to see aspects of her personality. There’s something of a plot thread there, as Constance is upset and frightened at first, but eventually comes to an accommodation with them. Unfortunately, the story is too short to really explore that aspect. The climax is fairly typical, with a villain who over-reaches rather than the Doctor doing something clever. On the whole, the boxed set is well-named, because it’s really the Eleven’s story, without the Doctor doing much at all. Which is OK for a one-time thing, but he doesn’t have the interest to pull off a series like the War Master. On the whole, the set is OK, not great.
docs.title: Elevation

docs.text: Flight of the Blackstar Main Range #275 Released: 16 March 2021 Listened: 3/16/21 This is the second part of the Main Range finale, “The End of the Beginning.” As with the last part , we begin somewhere in the middle, as Flip has been poisoned by some local fauna, but is recovering in the hospital. (In the real world, Lisa Greenwood couldn’t appear in this story, as a Covid infection had affected her vocal cords, leaving her unable to perform for a while). While trying to let Flip rest, the Doctor decides to take down a group of robotic raiders. Because they’re in the 51st Century, he calls on Calypso Jones, who appeared in the previous story in this project , but it seems like it’s been a while since they’ve all seen each other. Constance seems to have grasped that Calypso is non-binary, and uses the appropriate pronouns, but is completely oblivious that Calypso has a crush on her and keeps attempting to flirt, poorly. The Death Lord interrupts a bit earlier in the story than in "Death and the Desert," but the Doctor and friends dodge him and continue on with the main plot. They infiltrate the robots’ base fairly easily, and in reprogramming their leader, the Doctor discovers another data crystal left for him by his old tutor, but we don’t gain any more information about him. After Calypso has left, the Death Lord shows up and snags the Doctor and Constance. Once again, it’s a decent standalone, if slight, but better listened to as part of the whole.
docs.title: Flight of the Blackstar

Because they’re in the 51st Century, he calls on Calypso Jones, who appeared in the previous story in this project , but it seems like it’s been a while since they’ve all seen each other. Constance seems to have grasped that Calypso is non-binary, and uses the appropriate pronouns, but is completely oblivious that Calypso has a crush on her and keeps attempting to flirt, poorly. The Death Lord interrupts a bit earlier in the story than in "Death and the Desert," but the Doctor and friends dodge him and continue on with the main plot. They infiltrate the robots’ base fairly easily, and in reprogramming their leader, the Doctor discovers another data crystal left for him by his old tutor, but we don’t gain any more information about him. After Calypso has left, the Death Lord shows up and snags the Doctor and Constance. Once again, it’s a decent standalone, if slight, but better listened to as part of the whole.
docs.title: Flight of the Blackstar

docs.text: Order of the Daleks Main Range #218 Released: 9 November 2016 Listened: 8/30/20 Constance’s next trilogy begins with a story bearing one of the most impressive covers Big Finish has ever produced: a stained-glass Dalek. That gives the impression of Daleks invading a medieval monastery, which is in fact what happens, but it’s a medieval monastery on an alien world, which hasn’t had first contact yet. Unlike the last story , this one has a bit of a classic-series feel to it, with various combinations of the good guys running around corridors, finding secret passages, captures, escapes, and recombining again. The Daleks are mostly on the back foot the whole time, which is different than their usual implacable take, but this batch are also more psychic than your usual Daleks, which makes them a bit more insidious. The monks are very like traditional European monks, which seems like a bit of a waste of an alien planet, but it’s got all the monastic cliches in there. The story is written by Mike Tucker, who was an effects designer at the end of the classic series, and designed the first Dalek for the new series, so you can certainly say the man knows his Daleks. Constance is pretty consistent in this story, being capable and even a bit more outspoken than previously. It’s a decent story of Daleks in different circumstances.
docs.title: Order of the Daleks

docs.text: Planet of the Rani Main Range #205 Released: 14 October 2015 Listened: 12/12/20 This is the second Big Finish story with the Rani. It’s a sequel to previous Rani stories, taking place after “ The Rani Elite ,” which was a while ago in the Rani’s timeline, and possibly quite a while in the Doctor’s, but rather recently in this project and in release order. The Rani wants to return to Miasimia Goria, mentioned back in “ The Mark of the Rani ” on TV as a planet where she’d experimented on the populace and deprived them of the ability to sleep. Thanks to the Doctor’s interference, she arrives 16 years after she left, meaning her rule has been usurped by one of her own experiments. From there, it sort of wanders around a bit. Like other Rani stories, she ends up defeated by her own creations, but I’m afraid the getting there really isn’t terribly interesting. Constance isn’t used quite as well as she was in the previous story . She’s determined, and adapts well to being on her own, but she reacts more than she acts. It’s an acceptable episode, but that’s all.

docs.text: Quicksilver Main Range #220 Released: 13 December 2016 Listened: 9/3/20 This one is somewhat twisty, with Constance going home at the very beginning, which gives us an unusual companion departure scene at the start of the story, not rushed before the closing credits. But it doesn’t quite work out that way, as there are aliens in 1944 who need the Doctor’s help, and there’s more to learn about Constance’s husband. We end up with two groups of warring aliens in 1948 Vienna (complete with Ferris Wheel), and Constance’s husband who’s gone deep cover and fallen for another woman. On top of which, one of the groups of aliens has kidnapped Flip from her wedding in 2012 and brought her to 1948 to use as leverage. This leads to a rather impressive scene where Constance believes Flip to be the other woman for a bit. The two of them soon get along like a house on fire, though, and the Doctor almost finds himself crowded out of the story. With all that going on, there’s not a lot of room for the aliens, although giant praying mantises made of glass would certainly have been something to see. The relationships are the key thing, which often happens in Matt Fitton stories, and they’re done quite well here. Everybody has a valid motivation, and there aren’t any clear bad guys. This one ends with both Constance and Flip in the Doctor’s company, and a sense that he’s in trouble now.
docs.title: Quicksilver

docs.text: Scorched Earth Main Range #264 Released: 13 May 2020 Listened: 9/7/20 For someone who’s trying to get home and failing, Constance seems to have a lot of stories set around World War II . Up until now, we’ve seen how well Constance and Flip get along, despite an age gap, widely different backgrounds, and being separated in time by 70 years. This story, though, hinges on the point that they’re really not the same. They’re in France, in 1944, as the occupation is ending, and the Doctor states bluntly that this is somewhere Constance shouldn’t be, mostly because of the potential to damage her timeline. However, Constance is carrying around a lot of hatred towards the Nazis, which is understandable for a person actively participating in WWII, but Flip can’t bring herself around to Constance’s way of thinking, and they disagree when they witness a French collaborator being punished. It’s not a true historical, though, and there’s a creature who feeds on hate, of which there’s rather a lot to go around in this time and place. The crux of the story is about letting go of one’s hatred, even after a war, and it’s played reasonably well, although the resolution may be rather swift for characters who’ve been at war for years. Unusually for Doctor Who (or any western pop culture), there are a few Nazi soldiers portrayed as sympathetic; they even get some snarky lines (as Constance observes, “sarcastic Nazis”). Constance and Flip have some rather pointed dialog themselves, mostly at the Doctor’s expense, thanks to Chris Chapman. The Doctor, for his part, seems a bit off his game in this story, but that’s OK, as the focus is on Constance and Flip. It’s a good story that’s a bit light on the sci-fi.
docs.title: Scorched Earth

docs.text: Shield of the Jötunn Main Range #206 Released: 16 November 2015 Listened: 8/29/20 There are a couple of firsts in this story: Louise Jameson, who commonly plays Leela, is the director, and comics writer Ian Edgington makes his debut as a writer. The Doctor and Constance end up in Arizona, 2029, in a rather unlikely Viking burial mound. The Vikings journeyed there to bury a bit of alien technology that lets “frost demons” travel to Earth. There’s a feel of “innocent displaced aliens in need of help,” but that doesn’t actually last very long. This story has a distinctly different feel, with each episode having its own tone, but it zips along rather well for what’s essentially a base-under-siege story. The Doctor in particular is somewhat more verbally adroit than he has been recently, and doesn’t display quite as much concern for Constance’s safety as he does elsewhere. For her part, Constance is even more capable and cool under pressure than she has been, although she displays some curiosity at being in her own future. All the characters other than the Doctor and Constance are American, and played by actual Americans, but they all have that slight over-enunciation that Americans in Big Finish usually have. The ending is a bit overly convenient, but that’s often the case. The difference in tone makes for a nice contrast as Constance wraps up her first trilogy.
docs.title: Shield of the Jötunn

docs.text: Sibling Rivalry The Quin Dilemma #3 Released: 22 March 2024 Listened: 4/22/26 This chapter of "The Quin Dilemma" is very short, and rather silly. Once again, it starts in the middle, with the Doctor, Constance, and Flip having landed on the planet Geminus, which is in the midst of a civil war. Worse, the Sontarans have invaded, and the natives are too divided to do anything about it. The Doctor and Constance are captured, and spend most of the story getting away. Flip is with the natives, and inadvertently gives them something to rally around so they can fight back. This happens to be the time period where two princes of Arunopal have been sent, one dim but sincere, and the other dim but cruel. Not that it makes any difference; they both try to capture the Doctor, and simply cancel each other's efforts. Unlike " Escape from Holy Island ," this story has a second episode , so this one ends on a cliffhanger. The story is rather underwhelming, and doesn't do much for Flip or Constance, since they're separated the whole time. Dan Starkey plays all the Sontarans, which is always nice, but they're definitely comedic Sontarans this time around, so there's not much threat.
docs.title: Sibling Rivalry

docs.text: Static Main Range #233 Released: 12 December 2017 Listened: 9/5/20 This story has developed a bit of a reputation for being creepy, and it’s well-deserved. The travelers land at an isolated caravan park in the 1980s, one that’s isolated and gloomy, and only made worse by the fact that radios and TVs are forbidden. As the only other campers discover, the rule is in place for a reason -- using electronic devices can raise the dead. Getting to the bottom of what’s going on involves a trip back to the 1940s, where the British armed forces were using the area’s properties in a very creepy manner. This is a rather layered mystery, involving some timey-wimey, and a person forced to stand sentinel for 40 years, which is a little dark for this Doctor, at least at this point in his life. Saying much more would invite spoilers, but even as the situation becomes clear, it remains remarkably creepy; you may want to consider your environment before you listen. The baddies have an interesting vocal effect that Big Finish hasn’t used before, and which becomes a plot point, so that’s nice. Flip isn’t quite reckless in this one, but does display a lot of empathy, one of her character’s strengths. Constance is starting to become concerned about getting back home, and it’s starting to look like the Doctor is stalling on getting them there. Significantly, Constance leaves this story in a cloned body, and the ramifications of that have yet to be seen.
docs.title: Static

docs.text: The Behemoth Main Range #231 Released: 11 October 2017 Listened: 9/4/20 This one is a pure historical, taking place in Bath, 1756. Both Constance and Flip have difficulty adapting to the social standards of the time. Unfortunately, slavery is also prevalent in this period, which forms the core of the story. The Doctor, however, seems to enjoy an evening out with an idle widow, much to Flip and Constance’s dismay. There’s also a runaway rhinoceros, which somehow manages to elude large crowds in the streets of Bath. The initial upper-class silliness takes a rather jarring turn when the slavery subplot moves to the fore. Doctor Who doesn’t have a great record of dealing with African characters, but it’s handled reasonably well here. As often happens in true historicals, the villains are completely vile, instead of having redeeming qualities. The underlying theme is of ownership, and the rights and responsibilities that go along with guardianship of another living being. In a small twist, the Doctor doubts his ability to make a short hop in the TARDIS, but then later lands her on a moving ship on the ocean with no trouble. Flip is notably less reckless than in her previous stint, but still very willing to talk back to people who offend her. It’s grim as pure historicals tend to be, but not entirely bleak.
docs.title: The Behemoth

docs.text: The Darkened Earth Short Trips #8.7 Released: 30 July 2018 Listened: 9/13/20 Constance gets another story set around WWII. It seems to start with the Doctor trying to show Constance the positives of the post-war era, but instead ends up in Germany during the later part of the war, when the English are doing the bombing. That’s enough of a mind-bender for Constance, but of course there’s also an alien involved, one that eats light during blackouts. The story is told first-person, which is unusual for Short Trips, but Miranda Raison has a lovely voice as Constance, so it’s easy to hear a story read by her.

docs.text: The End of the Line The Last Adventure #1 Released: 17 August 2015 Listened: 8/30/20 This episode is a slightly unusual insert. It’s actually the first story recorded with Constance, and the first to be released as well, so for many fans, this was the first time they heard her. It takes place here in the timeline, though, because she’s been traveling with the Doctor for a while. Constance seems a bit different in this story; her RP accent isn’t quite as pronounced, and she’s somewhat snarkier with the Doctor. She’s still capable and take-charge, though, which is useful. The episode is almost a play on “Midnight” from the Tenth Doctor’s era, in that it features a bunch of frightened people stuck on a train that’s lost in a fog. However, there’s some serious timey-wimey going on with colliding parallel dimensions. The Master is the baddie in this story, but using one of his typical disguises, and a clever workaround to use the Anthony Ainley Master without Anthony Ainley. And because this is the Last Adventure, the Valeyard is here too, but because it’s the first story, he’s well in the background. The fact that it’s out of order for the Doctor doesn’t affect the story at all, which is well done. I think this is the most creative of the Last Adventure stories, even though it’s short.
docs.title: The End of the Line

docs.text: The Lovecraft Invasion Main Range #265 Released: 30 July 2020 Listened: 9/7/20 This story was intended for release in June 2020, but as a result of the Black Lives Matter protests at that time, and the fact that HP Lovecraft was a raging racist, some dialog was retooled, and its release was delayed until the very end of July. Given that the story never misses a chance to remind us how horrible he was, or have characters excoriate him for being horrible, or opine on the difficulty of separating the creator from the creation, I wonder what the script was like before the changes. There’s at least a small gap between the last story and this one, as the TARDIS crew have picked up bounty hunter Calypso Jones in the 51st century, where they’re chasing down one of those engineered psychic bioweapons that always seems to get loose, and this one has headed for Providence, Rhode Island, 1937, and HP Lovecraft, shortly before his death, in order to make his fever dreams into reality and destroy the world. That should make for a deeply scary story, but in fact there’s a streak of silliness running through it, because the story never takes the Lovecraft mythos seriously. Case in point: Flip knows about Lovecraft because she sat in on her cousin’s Call of Cthulhu gaming sessions as a kid. The story name-checks all the points you’d be expected to recognize even if you’ve never read Lovecraft (like me): Randolph Carter, Arkham, Miskatonic University, R’lyeh (which even the Doctor can’t pronounce), and of course Cthulhu himself. If you’ve ever wanted to hear somebody actually say “Ia! Ia! Cthulhu fhtagn!” out loud, you’ll get your shot during one of the cliffhangers. Lovecraft, as a character, seems more pathetic than anything, which gives the story a feel of punching down. I’m a little disappointed that the Doctor doesn’t offer any hope for his redemption, but he’s a historic figure, so there’s not much you can do. The story ends without any indication of trying to get Constance or Flip home, or even Jones. I think I expected quite a bit more from this story than I got.
docs.title: The Lovecraft Invasion

docs.text: The Middle Main Range #232 Released: 15 November 2017 Listened: 9/4/20 This one is a high-concept story, where the travelers land on a planet that’s divided into three castes by age: the young, who do nothing but party, the middle-aged, who apparently all have unceasing office jobs, and the elderly, who go...somewhere else. Somewhere else turns out to be a riff on Old Man’s War , because they’re locked into powered armor and forced to fight in a war. This scenario splits up the three travelers fairly quickly, giving them a range of other people to interact with. The Doctor confronts his pacifism (for a bit), Constance gets to use her organizational skills (if not her codebreaking ones), and Flip gets a physical adventure, although she’s still a bit more restrained than she had been in previous stories. The minor characters are the ones who make this story, all of them being nicely realized and well performed. The plot doesn’t so much climax as unravel, with a series of conclusions one after the other. Each tells a piece of the bigger picture, but none are really wholly satisfying. How much you like this one will depend on how appealing you find the concept, or the guest actors.

docs.text: Main Range #232 Released: 15 November 2017 Listened: 9/4/20 This one is a high-concept story, where the travelers land on a planet that’s divided into three castes by age: the young, who do nothing but party, the middle-aged, who apparently all have unceasing office jobs, and the elderly, who go...somewhere else. Somewhere else turns out to be a riff on Old Man’s War , because they’re locked into powered armor and forced to fight in a war. This scenario splits up the three travelers fairly quickly, giving them a range of other people to interact with. The Doctor confronts his pacifism (for a bit), Constance gets to use her organizational skills (if not her codebreaking ones), and Flip gets a physical adventure, although she’s still a bit more restrained than she had been in previous stories. The minor characters are the ones who make this story, all of them being nicely realized and well performed. The plot doesn’t so much climax as unravel, with a series of conclusions one after the other. Each tells a piece of the bigger picture, but none are really wholly satisfying. How much you like this one will depend on how appealing you find the concept, or the guest actors.
docs.title: The Middle

docs.text: The Murder of Oliver Akkron The Eleven #2 Released: 2 September 2021 Listened: 9/6/21 The Doctor and Constance don’t appear in this story, which technically means that it doesn’t belong in this project, but it would be silly to leave it out. It’s a very different kind of story, mostly in the form of a conversation between the Eleven and the titular Oliver Akkron, who’s presented as a fairly important person, and through the course of the story it becomes clear just how important, and what he did to achieve that. The Eleven, for his part, seems to have resolved his condition entirely, and currently claims that the Eight is the dominant persona. He’s become a monk (again), albeit one with a level of fame. There are also cutaways to some scientists who are working to stop some alien parasites, an infestation that’s proving quite fatal to chunks of the population. Miskavel doesn’t appear until the very end, when the story unravels itself. It’s very much a murder mystery in the Doctor Who style, with gobs of timey-wimey, false identities, and unreliable narrators. The fact that every character has more than one persona makes things even more confusing. This story probably benefits from a repeat listen once you know what’s going on. However, it only makes sense as the middle part of this boxed set, and should be listened to that way.
docs.title: The Murder of Oliver Akkron

docs.text: The Sixth Doctor and Evelyn This section takes us back close to the beginning of Big Finish history, where Professor Evelyn Smythe became the first proper “Big Finish companion.” She’s a fascinating choice, being both a professor of history and an older woman, rather different than the Doctor’s normal companions. But she’s what the Sixth Doctor needed, because she has plenty of relevant expertise, so he can’t railroad her with his superior knowledge, and having taught students for decades, she’s not willing to put up with the Doctor’s bluster. Maggie Stables is a fantastic actress in her own right, fully able to keep up with Colin Baker and humanize his Doctor. Unfortunately, she passed away in 2014, and Evelyn’s story was closed out, so there are unlikely to be many further stories with her. Unlike most of the Big-Finish-created companions, the stories in this era don’t match up well with their release order, at least, not in this project. Craig Brawley has created an entirely separate Evelyn timeline to explain the logic.
docs.title: Sixth Doctor and Evelyn

docs.text: 100: 100BC Main Range #100 Released: 26 September 2007 Listened: 6/6/20 This story is the first in the set, but takes place second. Written by Jac Rayner, it’s another true historical, with the only interfering aliens being the Doctor and Evelyn. It’s a mess of timey-wimey, with the travelers accidentally interfering with the conception of Julius Caesar and dealing with the resulting fallout. Evelyn makes a good effort at changing the future, since her last two stories have indicated that’s possible, but the Doctor is trying to put things back on their original track, as he’s aware of the disastrous consequences. The interference and repair are rather silly, but Evelyn is dead serious about her goals, and is willing to play on her status as an older woman with physical infirmities to get what she wants. The Doctor, for his part, is angry with Evelyn for her actions, but rather than just raging, as he might have not long ago, he’s sympathetic to her motivation, if not her solutions. It adds up to a pretty good story.
docs.title: 100BC

docs.text: A Town Called Fortune Companion Chronicles #5.5 Released: 4 November 2010 Listened: 6/14/20 This story is the only Companion Chronicle with Evelyn, and one of the rare ones to feature a Big Finish-created companion. Which makes it somewhat unusual, because we haven’t heard Evelyn as narrator before. It’s also a western, meaning that she has to play a couple of characters with American accents, and it has to be said, does a very good job. Her portrayal of the Doctor isn’t really an imitation, but captures some of his tone and cadence, which is pretty normal for Companion Chronicles. Richard Cordery, who plays the male characters apart from the Doctor, sounds a little stereotypical, even though he’s spent some time in America. The plot itself is pretty twisty, and hinges a lot on deception, and Eveylyn’s research skills to see through that, which is good. Oddly, it’s not told as a flashback to long ago, but as a flashback to the story as it’s ending, which means the frame story actually ends the main plot. Doctor Who has never done particularly well with westerns, but this one is reasonable.
docs.title: A Town Called Fortune

docs.text: Arrangements for War Main Range #57 Released: May 2004 Listened: 7/2/20 Evelyn’s last appearance (for a while) in this project is a dark one, but also a love story. After the events of “ Project: Lazarus ,” Evelyn wants a break, but she also doesn’t want to mope around the Eye of Orion. She wants to go someplace that’s vibrant and full of things she can learn, but also doesn’t have to get involved and save the world. You’d think that wouldn’t be too hard to find, but the Doctor fails spectacularly. They arrive on the planet Vilag, which has three major nations. The first two are at war, but that’s about to be resolved by an arranged marriage of nobility, which is a good thing, because they’ll need to be united in the face of an alien invasion the Doctor knows is coming in about a month. (Why Evelyn thinks they’ll be gone by then, I don’t know.) Of course, the Doctor promptly screws up the arranged marriage (inadvertently, but still) and Evelyn falls for Rossiter, the leader of the third nation, and her feelings are reciprocated. There’s an awful lot of talk about what one is willing to do for love, and accepting of consequences. Oddly, the male half of the arranged marriage never appears, so we don’t know his opinion on the matter. Typically of early Big Finish, there’s more talk than action -- there’s a war and an alien invasion going on, but most of that is in the background. Evelyn does an awful lot of introspection, about the end of her teaching career, and facing mortality. This story and the previous are the only ones in which her heart condition really comes up, and she seems to be taking it quite seriously. The scenes between Evelyn and Gabriel Woolf as Rossiter are excellent, and it would make sense for Evelyn to stay behind here, although she doesn’t, as far as we know. There’s a lot of needless death, and the Doctor has a pretty powerful “Time Lord Victorious” moment, proving to Evelyn that he does care about events around him. The only serious flaws in the story are some political leaders who are way too idealistic and moral (even the bad guys), an alien threat that’s no more than a bogeyman, and rather unrealistic depictions of how simple it is to change the direction of a nation’s entire military. Emotionally, though, it’s a very strong story, and I agree with Craig Brawley that this is a very appropriate ending to Evelyn’s story (at least for the time being).
docs.title: Arrangements for War

docs.text: Assassin in the Limelight Main Range #108 Released: May 2008 Listened: 6/28/20 This story features a number of flashbacks to Robert Ross’s other two stories, with Dr. Knox from “ Medicinal Purposes ” and the Indo from “ Pier Pressure .” However, he never wrote for Big Finish again, so these characters don’t reappear. It takes place in Washington, DC in 1865, on the day of Lincoln’s assassination. However, Knox aims to prevent that, and the reasons exactly why he does so are mysterious for most of the story. Although it seems like this would be a dark story, much like the other two, there are many elements of comedy here, starting with Knox pretending to be Oscar Wilde, and attempting to present The Importance of Being Earnest 30 years too early, and various other snarky comments from both the Doctor and Evelyn. I suspect an American writer wouldn’t play the Civil War and Lincoln’s death for comedy, but it’s a British show, so we roll with it. The American accents aren’t terrible, since they’re all played by actual Americans this time, although they tend to be over-enunciated, but that’s almost always the case at Big Finish. Evelyn seems to have a much better understanding of the Web of Time here than she did in “ 100 ,” although she’s not above trying to make strategic changes. I can see where they were going with larger mythbuilding on this one, but the whole is less than the sum of its parts.
docs.title: Assassin in the Limelight

docs.text: 100: Bedtime Story Main Range #100 Released: 26 September 2007 Listened: 6/13/20 This short one is a bit of a mystery with a twist, but it links into Evelyn’s personal history, which is something of a change. The plot revolves around a family curse, but the Doctor is able to work out what’s really going on. I don’t particularly like stories that resolve with “and then the Doctor waited around for 100 years for the plot to finish,” but because this one is something of a fairy tale, I’ll feel free to disregard it. The twist ending may not be to everyone’s liking, but it takes the story up a level.

docs.text: Bloodtide Main Range #22 Released: 23 July 2001 Listened: 6/9/20 The Doctor takes Evelyn to go meet Charles Darwin, while he’s in the Galapagos Islands with the Beagle . But this isn’t a straight historical; there are Silurians around -- with a Myrka, but no Sea Devils, which is a bit odd. The story feels just a little too long, with the Doctor being captured, then Evelyn being captured. But it gives a certain amount of time for Darwin to work out the theory of evolution by talking with Evelyn. For her part, Evelyn seems to have gotten the message by now about not interfering in history, although she’s not above giving Darwin some encouragement. The story is pretty dark, as is typical for this era of Big Finish; pretty much everyone who’s not a main character or a historical figure ends up dead. The Silurian voices weren’t really intended for long speeches, but the actors try their best to imbue them with emotion. As usual in Silurian stories, the Doctor makes a game effort to get them to coexist with the humans, with shades of “The Hungry Earth,” but in 1835, that’s even less likely than in 2020. There’s also some nonsense about the origins of humanity which is really best left forgotten. It’s a reasonably good Evelyn story, after the hysterics of the last one, but otherwise pretty average.
docs.title: Bloodtide

docs.text: Doctor Who and the Pirates Main Range #43 Released: April 2003 Listened: 6/29/20 This rather oddly named story also has a very unusual structure. Evelyn drops in on Sally, one of her old students, and insists on telling her a story about an encounter she had with pirates, although Sally clearly doesn’t want to hear it. For the most part, the story is absurd, half Pirates of the Caribbean and half Pirates of Penzance . The pirates seem to be the worst sort of cliche. Evelyn’s storytelling skills aren’t very impressive, either, for a history professor. There is some mighty fine singing, from Colin Baker and Helen Goldwyn, many-time Big Finish director, but here playing Sally. The part 2 cliffhanger is probably one of the best Big Finish has ever produced. And the ending has some of the sharpest tonal whiplash the show has ever seen. I’m not sure I would recommend this to new listeners, because it departs so much from the standard formula. But because it does that departure successfully, the story as a whole succeeds.
docs.title: Doctor Who and the Pirates

docs.text: Industrial Evolution Main Range #145 Released: March 2011 Listened: 6/27/20 This story has rather the same frenetic pace as the first of the trilogy , but there’s a lot less going on in the plot. Brewster has been returned to roughly when he came from, but not where, as he now has a factory job. However, there’s two separate groups of aliens running around, which leads to “trouble at the mill.” It seems like there should be a bit of class struggle going on, but what little appears is quickly forgotten. The alien threats are somewhat fuzzy as threats. One has a clear goal, but isn’t very effective, and the other is effective, but we don’t know who or what they are. Evelyn gets a fair amount of sarcasm, if not quite as much as last time. For his part, the Doctor seems harsher than he has been in a while; it’s possible Brewster brings out the worst in him. The voice acting is clear and creates multiple distinctive characters, but they don’t have as much to do as I’d like. Ultimately, it leaves Brewster in a place where he could possibly continue, although he hasn’t been seen since. This is the last story Maggie Stables recorded as Evelyn before her death, which is a bit of a shame because the story doesn’t focus on her, but rather on Brewster. Still, it’s not the end of her story.
docs.title: Industrial Evolution

docs.text: Jubilee Main Range #40 Released: 4 February 2003 Listened: 6/12/20 This story by Rob Shearman is one of the more famous Big Finish stories, because it was the basis for the TV story “Dalek,” from the show’s first return season. The two stories really only have one thing in common, but it’s a big thing: The sole surviving Dalek being held prisoner by humans, and the Doctor encountering it in a dark room. I have to say that Christopher Eccleston played that scene better than Colin Baker did, but the Sixth Doctor is merely encountering his nemesis, whereas the Ninth Doctor has all the weight of the Time War to deal with, meeting a scourge he thought was gone forever. For the rest, though, the humans in this story are remarkably stupid and insane, even the ones who are just pretending to be stupid for nefarious purposes. Evelyn gets the part that Rose played, of the companion who believes a Dalek can be redeemed, even when the Doctor doesn’t. The resolution, though, is dramatically different, with a big chunk of timey-wimey that’s never adequately explained. It leads to a couple of Daleks shouting philosophy at one another, which doesn’t make a ton of sense, and the Doctor speechifying on the dark side of human nature, which is a bit over the top. Bottom line, the parts of this story that inspired “Dalek” are great, and deserve to be remembered, but the rest doesn’t make any sense.
docs.title: Jubilee

docs.text: Medicinal Purposes Main Range #60 Released: August 2004 Listened: 6/13/20 This is another dark story, which starts out as a historical featuring the Edinburgh body-snatchers Burke and Hare , but it quickly takes a turn. When the Doctor learns where they are, he’s eager to meet Burke and Hare, much to Evelyn’s disgust. It’s kind of out of character for the moral crusader Sixth Doctor, but he’s taking the long view of history in this case. But something is going awry with history, as this Robert Knox is rather more than the Scottish Doctor he appears to be. There’s a bunch of timey-wimey going on in the background, but it’s darker than usual, and there are more sinister time-traveling powers involved. This is a tough one on Evelyn, but she’s getting more accustomed to the idea of what can and can’t be changed in history, even though she doesn’t particularly like it. Knox will be back again, but not for a while . This story also features a relatively unknown actor named David Tennant as Daft Jamie. Tennant will go on to star in various other Big Finish stories, but he’s somewhat typecast by that point.
docs.title: Medicinal Purposes

docs.text: Mission Improbable Short Trips #2018-1 Released: 20 March 2018 Listened: 6/30/20 This Short Trip is the first Evelyn story released since Maggie Stables’ death, read by Stephen Critchlow, who as usual manages to capture the characters’ tone, if not their exact voices. Evelyn is already a prisoner when the story opens, bragging to her captor about her imminent rescue by the Doctor, whose skills and daring she praises highly. This is intercut with scenes of the Doctor bumbling his way through the rescue, succeeding mostly through dumb luck. It’s a funny story overall, and reflects Evelyn’s tendency to appear confident and glib even when she had no reason to.

docs.text: 100: My Own Private Wolfgang Main Range #100 Released: 26 September 2007 Listened: 6/6/20 Big Finish chose to mark their 100th Main Range release with a short story anthology, rather than the big blowout event they’d done for the 50th (to mixed reviews). All the stories feature the Sixth Doctor and Evelyn, and they all have a fair amount of “timey-wimey.” The first two aren’t very serious at all. Oddly, the second story in the set takes place first. The Doctor and Evelyn find themselves in a history in which Mozart never died, and continued creating music for centuries, with diminishing results over time. This leads to a very confused pile-up of Mozart clones, some of whom want to kill him, and others who want to save him. It’s as wacky as it sounds, which is what happens when you turn Rob Shearman loose. Significantly, though, Evelyn participates in changing what she knows as history, without bad results.
docs.title: My Own Private Wolfgang

docs.text: Pier Pressure Main Range #78 Released: 11 January 2006 Listened: 6/20/20 This is another rather dark one, as the TARDIS lands in Brighton, 1936, where an alien with mind-control tendencies has been living at the end of the pier for some time. I have a strong feeling this one will make more sense to the English fans, particularly ones who can picture Brighton, and in particular comedian Max Miller , who is an active character in the story. I didn’t know anything about him, but the type wasn’t hard to envision. (There’s also a young actor named Billy who is apparently intended to be William Hartnell .) The plot, though, is rather slow and meandering, spending nearly an entire episode before it gets going, and even after seems to spend a lot of time going back and forth between locations rather slowly. The Doctor is more maudlin and given to speechifying than usual, but Evelyn pretty much tells him that she’s not having any of it, which is her role in these stories. A forgettable episode on the whole.
docs.title: Pier Pressure
