docs.text: The Wrong Doctors Main Range #169 Released: 14 January 2013 Listened: 7/25/20 From Mel’s and the “colorful” Doctor’s point of view, this happened just after the Trial . From the “blue” Doctor’s point of view, it happens here. (Or right after Evelyn departs; doesn’t really matter.) This is a candidate for the most timey-wimey story from the main range, as it’s got two Doctors and two Mels running around, and that’s just the beginning of the temporal shenanigans. Even worse, the title is accurate -- both of these Doctors are in the wrong place at the wrong time, and that place isn’t what it appears to be, either. The younger Doctor is trying to return Mel to her proper place in the timestream after the Trial, but he gets it wrong. The older Doctor is attempting to meet Mel for the first time (from her perspective), but it’s not time for that either. Colin Baker does an excellent job of differentiating the two Doctors, with the younger one sounding much more arrogant, although a lot of that is in the writing. Bonnie Langford has a similar challenge, but the two Mels have to sound mostly the same, but the older one being more confident and capable. The bit of the big corporation mining for temporally sensitive material is a bit silly and overdone, leaving the story without much of a villain, but any villain they could have used would’ve been overwhelmed by the two Doctors anyway. Definitely good for a brain twist.
docs.title: The Wrong Doctors

docs.text: World Enough and Time The Diary of River Song #2.3 Released: 25 December 2016 Listened: 7/29/20 Not the Twelfth Doctor story (which is great), but a story from River Song’s second box set. (It’s a wonder nobody had used the title before, really.) This story is from one of the early River boxed sets, so Big Finish was going through the exercise of having her meet up with all the classic Doctors they had available, while still hiding her identity. This time, she’s trying to investigate an apocalypse that happened in one of her earlier stories, and it leads her to the Golden Futures company, whose managing director, much to River’s surprise, is the Sixth Doctor. Unfortunately, because it’s River’s story, the Sixth Doctor doesn’t come off too well. Golden Futures is distracting him by saddling him with pointless administrative tasks, and he falls for it. It makes me wonder if these stories really should take place here, because the Doctor at this point is more likely to bluster his way into doing what he wants, rather than follow someone else’s agenda. He’s also got a sonic screwdriver, which seems odd. He gets tricked out of a sacrifice play, and then even fumbles the big sciency climax. The plus side is his obvious affection for River (even though he’s never met her, as far as he knows), which River returns, also somewhat unexpectedly. She’s annoyed with him being a bit slow to solve the mystery (as she should be), but she seems to appreciate his kindness. She even says she likes his coat. I kept expecting there to be something deeper to the plot, but if there is, it’s not revealed in this story, which is fine, because it’s still the middle of the set.
docs.title: World Enough and Time

It makes me wonder if these stories really should take place here, because the Doctor at this point is more likely to bluster his way into doing what he wants, rather than follow someone else’s agenda. He’s also got a sonic screwdriver, which seems odd. He gets tricked out of a sacrifice play, and then even fumbles the big sciency climax. The plus side is his obvious affection for River (even though he’s never met her, as far as he knows), which River returns, also somewhat unexpectedly. She’s annoyed with him being a bit slow to solve the mystery (as she should be), but she seems to appreciate his kindness. She even says she likes his coat. I kept expecting there to be something deeper to the plot, but if there is, it’s not revealed in this story, which is fine, because it’s still the middle of the set.

docs.text: Gallifrey The Gallifrey series doesn’t feature the Doctor, and so it’s not something I generally collect, but at the time of this writing (March 2021), I’ve expanded the Big Finish I’m collecting to include some tangential spin-offs, and this is the most elaborate of them. Gallifrey started in 2004, very possibly as a way to create new stories featuring Lalla Ward as Romana and Louise Jameson as Leela, as both actors enjoyed Big Finish, but were limited because Tom Baker wasn’t participating at the time. Eventually the series developed its own recurring characters in Brax and Narvin, who sometimes spilled over into other series. Once Big Finish acquired the rights to more new-series concepts, the Time War became a storytelling option, since there are a number of characters we know were on Gallifrey at the end of the Classic Era, but whose fates are currently unknown.

docs.text: A Blind Eye Gallifrey #1.4 Released: May 2004 Listened: 3/29/21 One of the inevitabilities of Doctor Who spin-offs is that they have a strong tendency to end up on Earth, even when the story and characters have nothing to do with Earth. In this case, the plot moves to a train in Switzerland just before WWII, and drags in Cissy Pollard, Charley’s sister, who is apparently a Nazi sympathizer, and not particularly bright, but it does provide a chance to cast India Fisher, which would have been a substantial draw for fans in 2004. Leela and Romana both know Charley from “ Neverland ,” and the events of that story tie into this one more closely than one might otherwise expect. Charley is a temporal anomaly, and the perception is that she was allowed to live just on the Doctor’s say-so, because Romana is his friend. Therefore, the logic goes, Cissy could be used to create a similar paradox. There’s some pretty deep timey-wimey going on, but that seems to be a hallmark of this series. The question of just what happened to Andred is finally resolved, and that’s pretty dark too. (And breaks another convention about Time Lords as I’ve always understood it.) Romana ends up making some fairly cold choices, which I suspect the Doctor wouldn’t approve of, but as far as Romana’s concerned, the Doctor’s gone, and this is the universe that’s left. Which makes sense given that this series seems to be going for darker and more mature, but that changes after the new series comes around.

docs.text: Annihilation Gallifrey #4.3 Released: March 2011 Listened: 4/24/21 Another episode, another alternate Gallifrey. This time, it’s an alternate far in Gallifrey’s past, not long after the time of Rassilon, when wars are still going on between the early Time Lords (called True Lords at this point) and a nation of vampires. For what seems to be no reason at all, the leader of the True Lords is called Borusa, and played by Katy Manning. To be fair, she does a pretty good job of sounding like a serious warlord, and not like Jo Grant at all, which is definitely playing against type for her. Geoffrey Beevers plays the Lord Prydon, head of the vampires, and apparently has nothing to do with the Master, but it sure sounds like him. Everyone behaves pretty recklessly in this one, from Romana being unafraid to confront the vampires (because she’s apparently immune, and has faced them before in “ State of Decay ”), to Leela subjecting herself to a strange biological procedure that rejuvenates her, restores her sight, and amplifies her other senses, but possibly at the expense of her humanity. She seems to have come out the better for it, which is good, because the blindness subplot got old a while ago. It’s certainly a dark episode, with death and destruction all around, and Romana blaming herself for it. Probably the best of the stories so far from a plot perspective, even though it’s grim.
docs.title: Annihilation

docs.text: Appropriation Gallifrey #3.3 Released: July 2006 Listened: 4/7/21 With the war nominally over, we have to get back to what Gallifrey supposedly does best: scheming! As a result of “ Warfare ,” the Matrix is destroyed, and Romana is too injured to carry out her duties as President. (Except she declared herself Imperiatrix a while back? Or was that just a ruse?) Darkel, still the Worst Ever, is trying to maneuver her way into the Presidency despite the fact that she’s actually under arrest for sedition. And thanks to Chancellor Valyes being under Darkel’s thumb and pulling some constitutional shenanigans, she actually succeeds for a bit. This whole back-and-forth about who’s really the president is a lot less comfortable after the American 2020 election; there’s even a question raised about whether a President can self-pardon. In the background of all of this, several other temporal powers are on the verge of declaring war on Gallifrey, because those races had students at the Academy who haven’t been returned yet (because there was no way to get them off-planet safely during a civil war). Matthias is charged with negotiating with them, and he fails miserably, but basically keeps failing upwards as everybody else sticks more responsibilities on him, to the point where he declares himself Vice President, and therefore President, on the strangest of technicalities. And it’s still not clear exactly whose side he’s on, or whether all of this happened to him by accident. At least Narvin finally declares his loyalty to Romana, but only because the alternatives are much worse. For a bonus bit of fun, Colin Baker has an uncredited cameo as Commander Maxil , but that’s not actually important to the plot. Leela has almost nothing to do this time around, unfortunately. I’ve completely lost the thread of what’s going on in this series. Although I guess it’s realistic that the Time Lords would squabble rather than unite in the face of a new war, that doesn’t make it interesting.

docs.text: Arbitration Gallifrey #5.3 Released: 16 February 2013 Listened: 4/25/21 It’s another episode of “politics for the cruel” on Gallifrey. A Gallifreyan aristocrat who supports Romana for his own reasons abandoned a bunch of his slaves to their deaths some years ago, so Leela’s Outsiders kidnap him and intend to put him on trial. Whether he’s actually guilty isn’t really in question; this is Cruel Gallifrey, so of course he is. In fact, it might even have been legal at the time, a point that’s never raised in the story. It all hinges around whether Leela will bend to help Romana, how much Romana will sacrifice to protect Leela, and how far Narvin will go to protect Romana from her own actions. Stir in the fact that our heroes will likely be going home much sooner than they thought, which is supposed to raise the stakes as both Romana and Leela are determined to do the Right Thing before they go, but in fact it just underlines that nothing they do here really matters (at least, Narvin sees it that way). There are a bunch of absurdities built into this story: The idea that Romana could reform a slave-owning society in just a few months, and that Leela suddenly has a history with slavery on her home world that’s never been mentioned before. Probably most forgivable is the idea of a dramatic courtroom revelation that changes all the spectators’ minds; thanks to real-world politics around 2020, it’s pretty clear that people will deny the evidence of their own eyes and ears if it’s politically expedient, so that part of the story falls flat now. And there’s a dramatic last-second cliffhanger that has no relation to what came before, revealing that Series 5 and 6 are really one six-part series, and that most of Series 5 is just filler, unfortunately. The writing and characterization are stronger than what came before, but the story hasn’t really gone anywhere.

docs.text: Ascension Gallifrey #6.3 Released: 16 October 2013 Listened: 4/27/21 This poor episode has the difficult task of wrapping up this boxed set, which is really an extension of Series 5, wrapping up details back to the beginning of the series, explaining what’s going on with Trey, and possibly kicking off the Time War itself. That’s no easy feat, and honestly, I don’t think this story pulls it off. There’s an awful lot of Matrix-projecting misdirection, including a bit at the end which feels fairly unearned. There’s also a ton of exposition, lots of it coming from K-9, which can be difficult to listen to; poor Leela is almost entirely left out of it. Valyes and Matthias get small roles, but the overall impression is that Gallifrey is severely underpopulated. There’s certainly nobody to stand for President, which results in Romana getting the office against her will. There’s even a connection back to “ Genesis of the Daleks ”...maybe. Gary Russell does like his ambiguous endings, but for the most part, the board is swept clean, for someone else to pick up the pieces later.
docs.title: Ascension

docs.text: Assassins Gallifrey: Time War #2.4 Released: 20 March 2019 Listened: 5/21/21 One of the limiting factors of the Gallifrey: Time War series is that we know where it’s going to end up, which makes it kind of a prequel. It gets darker and darker, but the feeling is that there can’t be too much risk. Characters get pushed away, but not killed off. This story, though, pushes things just about as far as they can reasonably go, where Romana has reached her breaking point, and decides that Rassilon has to go. Narvin, for his part, finds his limits as well, and isn’t willing to go along with assassination. Worse, he’s tempted by both of the factions opposed to him, and promised a new regeneration cycle. Ultimately, though, his loyalty is to Romana as the best hope for Gallifrey’s survival, and they both pay the price for that. Livia represents the politics this time, straddling the fence for so long that she ultimately has no loyalty to anyone, just fear. There are some nice references to Olistra, the General, and even the Doctor, although none of them appear; they’re all stated to be closer to the front lines. And Rassilon himself plays a bigger part here than any previous story. The writing (by Matt Fitton) is appropriate to how Terrence Hardiman (and later Timothy Dalton) play him, as a man who’s entirely confident in his own stature, completely convinced of his rightness, and therefore completely unhinged. It’s a good character and a good portrayal. Although I wasn’t too sure where this boxed set was going, I think the writing here has been stronger than any previous Gallifrey series.
docs.title: Assassins

docs.text: Beyond Gallifrey: Time War #4.3 Released: 4 February 2021 Listened: 5/23/21 This boxed set has been a series of two-handers: Leela and Eris, Narvin and Rayo, and now Romana and Braxiatel. Brax hasn’t been seen since he dumped Ace on Earth back in Volume 1, and he only turns up now to rescue Romana from the cliffhanger she created for herself at the end of Volume 3 . Unfortunately, it seems like the least interesting way to resolve that thread. (The extras admit they created the cliffhanger in case Lalla Ward was unavailable for Volume 4, as she was moving out of the country, but still.) Brax is after one of those apocalyptic Time Lord weapons, which requires going through one of those enigmatic Time Lord not-space-not-time places, this one called “the Beyond,” a name that at least Romana has the good sense to mock. They pass through various alternate timelines, pursued by some Ravenous , from the series of the same name, but nothing really comes of that. In the end, it’s not what it seemed at all, and it pretty much comes down to a reflection on responsibility -- how far will one go to win the war, what sort of collateral damage is justified, and is just running away from it all a moral choice? Speaking of running, the Doctor is mentioned, and although Romana hasn’t met him lately, it’s clear she knows about the War Doctor, and is saddened by what he’s become. Brax seems to be taken off the table for good this time, but c’mon, that never means anything when it comes to Brax. So we’ve had three stories in a row that didn’t really amount to a whole lot; just excuses to split the characters up and have them reflect on their journeys. And now with one episode left, we can bring the big three back together.
docs.title: Beyond

docs.text: Celestial Intervention Gallifrey: Time War #1.1 Released: 22 February 2018 Listened: 5/12/21 This boxed set jumps forward a couple more years of production time to 2018, by which time Big Finish had embraced the idea of the Time War, with boxed sets for the Eighth Doctor , the War Doctor , and the War Master, so it was kind of inevitable that they’d touch on the story of Gallifrey during this period. But this first story makes clear it’s a direct connection to the previous series . Livia is still President, Romana is head of the CIA, with Narvin as her deputy, and Leela is...around. She seems to be a CIA agent now that she’s no longer the President’s friend, but she’s not happy about some of her assignments. The CIA seems to be fully public now, and on equal footing with the High Council and the new War Council when it comes to defense matters. The other “temporal powers” are still around, at least for a few minutes before they all get wiped out by Daleks, and dump some refugees on Gallifrey’s doorstep. General Trave of the War Council uses the refugee crisis to get a promise that the CIA will stay out of their secret weapons program, which is good Gallifrey -style politics. Most of the time Romana seems to be on the back foot, which leaves Lalla Ward playing exasperated the whole time, which got tedious back in Series 2. Narvin doesn’t seem too sharp for the experienced operative he usually is, sending Leela into a high-stakes situation without proper precautions. The real point of this story, though, is to get Gallifrey to formally declare war on the Daleks, which feels like a momentous enough occasion, so that’s well done, and I’m impressed that they didn’t drag that out further. The refugee subplot is a little uncomfortable in 2018, but that was probably intentional. I was expecting a big change in tone, to match the other Time War sets, but this one really just inserts the war into the existing Gallifrey structure, which is an impressive trick, even if it’s not exactly to my taste.
docs.title: Celestial Intervention

docs.text: Collateral Victim Gallifrey: War Room #1.3 Released: 23 August 2022 Listened: 7/8/23 This one is extra timey-wimey, emphasis on “extra.” Which is a good thing, because the Time War we've gotten to see didn’t really have enough of that, but I didn’t expect it from Alfie Shaw; it’s a nice surprise. Basically: The Time Lords eliminated an entire galaxy to prevent the Daleks from using it later. Except it won’t stay gone. Something is bouncing around in time and rewriting history, and Leela, Rasmus, and Veklin get sent to find out what’s up. It’s told in anachronic order…heck, it happens in anachronic order, and time keeps changing, and some of the narrators are unreliable. You may want to take notes as you listen. But among the things that happen is we find out just how ruthless Veklin can be when nobody’s watching. (I’m going to guess this is before her time with Susan.) We also find out that Rasmus lies just as easily as any other Time Lord, and that damages his relationship with Leela. But darkest of all, even Leela isn’t above some creative omission if she thinks it’s necessary, until she gets called on it, anyway. This one’s confusing, but it’s a good one.
docs.title: Collateral Victim

It’s told in anachronic order…heck, it happens in anachronic order, and time keeps changing, and some of the narrators are unreliable. You may want to take notes as you listen. But among the things that happen is we find out just how ruthless Veklin can be when nobody’s watching. (I’m going to guess this is before her time with Susan.) We also find out that Rasmus lies just as easily as any other Time Lord, and that damages his relationship with Leela. But darkest of all, even Leela isn’t above some creative omission if she thinks it’s necessary, until she gets called on it, anyway. This one’s confusing, but it’s a good one.
docs.title: Collateral Victim

docs.text: Collateral Gallifrey: Time War #2.3 Released: 20 March 2019 Listened: 5/21/21 The story of Ysalus continues, at least as a pawn in the larger game. Even though it was time-locked in the previous story , someone has broken the seal, and although none of the characters from there recur, there’s now a resistance, or at least a call for a resistance, trying to raise a standard against the Time Lords. For their part, the Time Lords are continuing the slide into cruelty; they’ve now decided to destroy the planet completely, to deny the Daleks the resources. Romana and Narvin can’t stop it, but they at least want to evacuate the population, and send Eris back five years to get it done. There’s a certain amount of timey-wimey going on here, in which Eris goes back on this mission specifically because we’re told that he did, five years later. Some of what’s going on there may yet be revealed, but at the least Eris has developed a strong distaste for what the Time Lords are willing to do in the war. As much as I’m tired of exasperated Romana, at least genocide is something appropriate for her to be exasperated about. Unfortunately, because we know where this all ends up, there’s a strong sense that things aren’t going to go well at all for Romana and friends.

docs.text: Collision Course The Legacy of Time #6 Released: 17 July 2019 Listened: 2/4/22 "The Legacy of Time" was created as the Big Finish 20th Anniversary Story, with six parts, featuring the Third through Eighth Doctors, but not in that order. This story was intended to be the Fourth Doctor’s story, but in reality it’s more of a Gallifrey story, because Leela and Romana are working together, after their time with the Doctor, but unfortunately there’s not much more placement info than that. All throughout this set, the Sirens of Time have been working in the background, and now we find out what they’re actually doing: Interfering with the first Gallifreyan time flight. If that’s undone, it will create the largest paradox of all, which the Sirens feed on. Through flashbacks, we learn that the Doctor took both Leela and Romana here at separate times, entirely unintentionally, because this is one of those events even the Doctor knows not to mess with. Except Leela and Romana now have to mess with it, in order to set it right, and to work the prototype TARDIS, they need six pilots, which is how they rope in the Third through Eighth Doctors. Once that happens, there’s really no more time for plot subtlety, just giving everybody some lines here and there. Which means there’s a bit of intra-Doctor bickering, but not as much as you’d expect. Romana sounds even more exasperated than usual, which is saying something, but trying to contend with six Doctors is pretty extreme. There’s also a cameo appearance by the First (David Bradley), Second (Fraser Hines) and Tenth (David Tennant) Doctors, basically trying to butt in and turning out not to be needed. As stories go, it’s really not much of one; “ The Light at the End ” made much better use of multiple Doctors. As fanservice, it’s through the roof, and perhaps best appreciated that way.
docs.title: Collision Course

docs.text: Deception Gallifrey: Time War #4.1 Released: 4 February 2021 Listened: 5/23/21 After the interlude of the previous boxed set, it’s time to get back to Time Warrin’. This time, though, Romana is gone, assumed to be in Dalek hands, and also assumed (by Leela, not Narvin) to have Chameleon Arched herself into a human. The first thing Narvin does is hook back up with the Resistance. It’s being run by Eris, the idealistic former CIA agent, last seen in Volume 2, and he’s got some plans he thinks Narvin won’t approve of. The Resistance seems to be a real thing, opposing the Time Lord War Council, but also fighting against Daleks when necessary, and generally agitating for conducting the war in a way that doesn’t burn the universe down. Unfortunately, they’re raided and scattered shortly after Narvin, Leela, and Rayo arrive, so the three of them get accidentally separated. Which makes this mostly Leela’s story, as she’s dragged along with Eris on a rescue mission. The key point here is that Eris wants to save his friends specifically because they’re his friends, and he hasn’t lost sight of that yet, which goes a long way toward making Leela like him, and helping her come around to his cause. We can’t skip out on the politics entirely, enough, so we get intervals on Gallifrey with Mantus, who’s all-in for Rassilon, and Livia, who’s not, but is too afraid of him to do anything. There’s double- and possibly triple-agents, and it’s a bit hard to tell who’s spying on whom, but I’ll let that go for now. And finally there’s a new Rassilon, having regenerated after the assassination attempt at the end of Volume 2. He’s now played by Richard Armitage, who’s bringing everything he’s got to the role. Unfortunately, Rassilon has gone full authoritarian, and may also have become detached from reality, which is kind of unsettling given the real-world political situation in 2020, when this set was recorded. It’s good to have a Leela-centered story to kick off the set, but it’s not entirely clear where this is going.
docs.title: Deception

docs.text: Desperate Measures Gallifrey: Time War #1.4 Released: 22 February 2018 Listened: 5/16/21 After a couple of unorthodox episodes, this story jumps back into traditional Gallifrey with both feet. Narvin and Leela are spying, there’s a double agent, a risky plan, and a Presidential election; what’s more Gallifrey than that? Romana continues to be exasperated that the War Council is shutting the CIA out of decisions, particularly the Resurrection Engine that brings dead Time Lords back to life. She sends Narvin out to destroy the engine, while secretly keeping a back-channel open to the Dalek Supreme, in the hopes of finding a diplomatic solution. President Livia realizes things are going badly and decides to stand down, nominating an Admiral named Valerian as her successor, but Romana decides to run for President again. Valerian is played by the lovely David Sibley, but he runs on a platform of open warfare and radical transparency. I think it’s saying something that he’s clearly supposed to be a right-wing candidate, yet still seems like a better choice than the ones in the US or the UK at the time this story was made. Once he’s able to expose Romana’s channel to the Dalek Supreme, she’s toast in the polls (and rightly so, I must say). But it turns out that the whole thing was a ruse, even the mission to destroy the Resurrection Engine, because as soon as Valerian is invested, it’s used to replace him with (spoiler) a resurrected Rassilon. We pretty much had to reach this point, because the TV show told us who’s President during the Time War, and this series has been sure to line things up neatly with what we already know. As a single episode, it’s pretty much right on the mark, although exasperated Romana isn’t my favorite character, and she’s got plenty to be exasperated about. As a boxed set, it went in a couple of unexpected directions, which I appreciated. Unfortunately, it also closed off those directions, so it looks as though what’s coming next is more of what we’ve already seen.
docs.title: Desperate Measures

docs.text: Disassembled Gallifrey #4.2 Released: March 2011 Listened: 4/23/21 Another episode means another alternate Gallifrey, and in this one, everybody’s straight-up evil. Or at least, the Time Lords are much more heavily interventionist than the mainstream versions. And their imperialist tendencies extend to alternate timelines too; they want to wipe them all out, and anybody from them, including our protagonists. Romana is President again (but evil). Leela is the chief torturer (and evil). There’s another Vansell here, and also evil. But the big thing here is the alternate version of the Doctor, played by Colin Baker. Except, spoiler, he’s evil, and the Presidential Assassin. Which leads to a paradox and a confrontation with Braxiatel. The protagonists get the door to that unpleasant reality shut, but lose the Evil Doctor and Brax. The Doctor won’t appear again, but Brax ends up somewhere else, meeting Bernice Summerfield for the first time (but not from her perspective). On the whole, this one is boring. All the evil moustache-twirling is over the top, even for an actor as gifted as Louise Jameson. And the plot doesn’t appear to be going anywhere.

docs.text: Dissolution Gallifrey: Time War #4.2 Released: 4 February 2021 Listened: 5/23/21 If the war is kicking back into high gear again, this seems like a good time to...have a breather episode where we find out more about Narvin? OK. During the evacuation at the beginning of the last episode, Narvin and Rayo grabbed a TARDIS and made themselves scarce, but without Leela, much to Rayo’s annoyance, because he doesn’t entirely trust Narvin. They’re attacked by a hunter-class Dalek while fleeing, so Narvin has to go to the one place in the entire universe he knows is safe, the Patrex chapterhouse on a hidden ocean planet. There’s only one person there, an old friend of Narvin’s, who seems to have the ability to get inside his head pretty well. It seems that the Patrex chapter has never had much power, preferring to spend time on art and philosophy, which young Narvin found irritating, so he bailed and joined the CIA. So he’s caught between his old desires to get away and get involved, versus his new instinct to protect Rayo, who really wants to get back to a war he doesn’t comprehend so he can do some fighting, believing Leela would want that. It takes Narvin fighting off a Dalek to impress Rayo, but he eventually starts to trust him. There’s nothing wrong with humanizing Narvin, and finally getting some insight into him, but it seems like a bit of an odd time for it. And Rayo himself seems to have turned up at the end of Volume 3, not done much in particular, and now gets written out. It makes you wonder if Big Finish didn’t have all the plans for Volume 4 in place when they finished Volume 3.
docs.title: Dissolution

docs.text: Emancipation Gallifrey #5.1 Released: 16 February 2013 Listened: 4/24/21 Gallifrey came back in 2013 in a reduced mode: Only three episodes instead of four, no extras, no classic-series guest actors, not even individual covers. But most significantly, new writers, although Gary Russell continued to direct. The stories also seem less episodic, which makes for a more drawn-out single plot. Romana, Leela, and Narvin are stuck on the New Gallifrey they ended up on last series, but Leela no longer trusts Romana, and she’s joined the former slaves outside the Capitol. Romana and Narvin are bound together by the need to keep their origins secret, and to push Gallifreyan society to the point where it can get them home, which is making them a lot of enemies. That results in a return to the schemes-and-politics mode of Series 1 and 2, which long-time fans probably appreciated. And, in fact, Romana slips back into exasperated-at-everything mode, and Narvin reverts to being out for himself, but there’s more going on than meets the eye. Alternate versions of Valyes and Matthias from Series 2 and 3 play prominent parts, which is nice for the actors, although the characters are entirely different. Matthias in particular is just a news commentator, no longer part of the action. It’s not nearly as dark as the last series, and there’s a sense that it’s going somewhere.
docs.title: Emancipation

docs.text: Enemy Lines Gallifrey #8 Released: 2 February 2015 Listened: 5/7/21 Released a year after “ Intervention Earth ,” this story initially appears to pick up right where the previous cliffhanger left off...except it promptly shifts back into the past, bringing us back to Romana II and Leela. It seems like it was intended as a legitimate extension from Series 7, keeping the same theme music, and the same half-hour structure, although with six parts instead of four. And yet at the same time, the plot seems to be undoing Series 7 so that it never happens. Braxiatel appears from nowhere and rescues Romana III, who orders him back to an earlier point in time to save Romana II from sacrificing her current life to prevent a spaceship explosion. She doesn’t regenerate in this new timeline, but that may not be enough change, so she also steps down as President, setting off another round of Gallifreyan politics as her rival Livia takes office. Ace is here as well, newly trained, and delighting in confusing Time Lords with Earth slang, but also very loyal to Gallifrey and Romana. But she doesn’t get to interact much, as she’s sent off on a mission. Narvin, unfortunately, exits quite early, having fallen back into “possibly can’t be trusted” status, which is odd after the events of Series 4-6. Ace gets sent on a mission, but her part feels unnecessary; you could have substituted any other CIA agent in the same place. But Series 7 established Ace as part of the Gallifrey story, so here she is. The last couple of parts involve lots of paradoxes and more timey-wimey ball than I can comfortably follow, and I’m pretty good with timey-wimey balls. If I’ve got this correct, most of the events of Series 7 and 8 have un-happened, all the dead characters are back alive, and Gallifrey is reasonably safe for now. Romana is no longer President, although not really disgraced either, and Braxiatel is...something vague and paradoxical. That would probably mean a lot more to me if I were more conversant with Brax from the Benny stories, but I’m not, and he’s been absent from most of the Gallifrey stories, so it kind of falls flat. I guess the primary goal here was to maneuver things so that Romana wasn’t President when the Time War broke out, as Big Finish had just started releasing stories set during the Time War, which is where we’re going next. On the whole, Series 8 is a little better than Series 7, but both are unsatisfying.
docs.title: Enemy Lines

docs.text: Erasure Short Trips #8.4 Released: 30 April 2018 Listened: 7/20/22 Although this story is included in the Fourth Doctor era , the frame story takes place here. Narvin and Leela are in a battle, Leela gets hurt, and Narvin tells her a story to keep her awake. It doesn’t have much impact on the overall story, but Narvin uses it to illustrate that he’s changed a lot since meeting Leela, become a more moral person, and he has a great deal of respect for Leela as a result.

docs.text: Evolution Gallifrey #5.2 Released: 16 February 2013 Listened: 4/25/21 The slower, more drawn-out version of the story continues. Romana and Narvin are sponsoring scientific research into time travel, in the hopes of a breakthrough. Leela is trying to help the former slaves forge a new life outside, but she’s drawn into helping one of them investigate a batch of former research subjects who’ve formed a cult of some kind. Of course, this is a crueler alternate Gallifrey, so ethical standards for use of human subjects in research isn’t quite what you’d expect them to be, and that’s what ties the two threads together. There’s a nice reference to “ Warrior’s Gate ,” which indicates that Romana has seen these sorts of experiments before, and she reacts about as well as you might expect. Although the story is fine by itself, the main plot is a dead end, which makes it seem something like filler.
docs.title: Evolution

docs.text: Extermination Gallifrey #6.1 Released: 16 October 2013 Listened: 4/25/21 Series 6 came out just a few months after Series 5, and they were obviously planned together. But 6 has some of the bells and whistles that 5 lacked, including individual covers and an extras disc. It’s also pretty clear that the first story of this series was intended to be a part of Series 5, as it puts a capstone on Cruel Gallifrey. Both these sets were released in 2013, and both Doctor Who and Big Finish had changed a lot since Gallifrey started. In particular, we knew a lot more about the Time War, and what it did to Gallifrey. That’s still in these characters’ futures, but it colors this episode because if you want to present a multiversal threat that can annihilate Gallifrey, you go to the Daleks, which wouldn’t have been the case in the classic series. Most of the minor characters are forgotten, and our three protagonists spend way too much time trying to convince everybody else just how serious the threat is. Writer Scott Handcock seems to want this to be a war story, with the characters suffering stark terror at their imminent deaths, and pushed well beyond the bounds of their personal ethics by the stresses of battle. All of them are willing to grab heavy weaponry to fight (which Cruel Gallifrey has plenty of), and Romana in particular has enough PTSD from being a Dalek prisoner for 20 years (in “ The Apocalypse Element ”) that she’s more than willing to torture one for information. Unfortunately, she also seems to be trying to talk it to death, and Lalla Ward’s portrayal simply can’t maintain that level of intensity through all the speeches she has to make. Leela, for some reason, won’t kill an unarmed Dalek, which is insane, because she knows what they can do. And Narvin lectures Romana over abandoning Cruel Gallifrey, even after they’ve eliminated the Daleks, when last episode he was all for leaving without a backward glance. I can see what they were going for, but it doesn’t quite come off, resulting in an episode with lots of shouting and heightened emotion, but no real sense of what comes next.

docs.text: Forever Gallifrey #4.4 Released: March 2011 Listened: 4/24/21 And we’ve got yet another alternative Gallifrey, once again unpleasant. This version is fairly similar to the “mainline” Gallifrey, except everyone is slightly more vicious, so Rassilon was assassinated before he finished discovering time travel, and therefore these Gallifreyans don’t have it. They’ve got a bunch of slaves, too, in case we weren’t clear that they’re bad guys. Unfortunately, the way back to the Axis is unstable, so Romana is willing to risk giving these people time travel so that her friends can get home. It’s part of the theme that Romana’s self-doubt and shame is leading her to be more and more reckless. The pointless cameos this time are a one-liner from Colin Baker, because the Doctor is apparently a video commentator in this world, and a longer, but equally unimportant, role for Carole Ann Ford as a kindly slave, but she doesn’t really do anything. Leela stages a revolt, and Narvin seems to be reaching levels of near friendliness with the other two, but he’s still got a pragmatic streak when it comes to morality. It turns out that Rassilon had a very good reason to deny these people time travel, and that reason ends with the three main characters sealing themselves off from the Axis permanently, ending the episode and the series itself on either a cliffhanger or a serious down note, depending on how you view it. Given that Series 3 ended in nearly universal destruction, this series didn’t add much of anything except to write out some characters, and keep the rest stuck in a rather depressing cycle. It’s a poor return after five years of silence, and it would be another couple of years before there was any more of it.

docs.text: Fractures Gallifrey #3.1 Released: May 2006 Listened: 4/6/21 The third series starts off about as dark as the second one ended. The war has been going on for a while, and Romana is definitely on the losing side, somehow, while Pandora has seized most of the power, apparently using the Dogma virus to control high-ranking Time Lords. Except Darkel, of course, who continues to be completely slimy. Leela feels much more comfortable on Gallifrey by helping Romana’s side fight a guerilla war, which is sad enough, so she’s blinded because she hasn’t suffered enough lately. Romana’s K-9 is the only one remaining, and he’s been reprogrammed to be on Pandora’s side, maybe. The plot hinges on Romana trying to get her hands on something to give her side an edge, and encountering yet another Gallifreyan weapon that can potentially destroy the continuum, so of course the Time Lords just locked it away in case they needed it for later. There’s a lot of shouting, and several people trying to do the clever thing that the Doctor always does at the last minute, except none of them are the Doctor, so it doesn’t go very well. There’s an introduction of a doctor with a rather mercenary style. He doesn’t do much in this story, so presumably he’ll be important later. It’s not an inspiring start to the series.

docs.text: Havoc Gallifrey: Time War #2.1 Released: 20 March 2019 Listened: 5/19/21 After the last series, we’re left with just Romana and Narvin as protagonists, which means there’s lots of Gallifreyan politics going on. In this case, with a curveball, because Rassilon is back and installed as President Eternal (never mind that he essentially murdered the newly elected President Valerian to get here). Rassilon uses the excuse of the war to basically set himself up as an autocrat, sidelining the War Council, disbanding the Chancellery Guard, and setting up an Interior Defence Unit loyal only to him. While this is going on, Narvin investigates a murder, because of course there’s a murder, and of course the murderer is from the future with important information about how the war turns out, which is very much against all the rules, but hey, there’s a war on. All of this put together causes Romana to vow to create a resistance, which I’m sure won’t cause any problems in the middle of a war with the Daleks. Narvin doesn’t come off too well in this one, complaining of feeling old and being unable to run down a suspect. Clearly they’re sticking with the idea that he lost his remaining regenerations during their Axis adventures. I’m not sure I particularly like this version, stripped down to two characters, but I’m willing to see where it goes.
docs.title: Havoc

docs.text: Homecoming Gallifrey: Time War #4.4 Released: 4 February 2021 Listened: 5/23/21 So it all comes down to this, the slam-bang ending, and Matt Fitton gets the ball. And for the most part, I’d say it does what it’s supposed to. The story plays out almost like an episode of the TV show, with dramatic rescues, desperate plans that can’t possibly work, heroic sacrifices, and honestly two-dimensional characters who either do the right or wrong thing. Richard Armitage as Rassilon has gone completely over the edge, focusing most of his attention on his “Ultimate Sanction,” which we eventually see play out in “ The End of Time .” If I didn’t know better, this story could be taking place around the events of “ The Day of the Doctor ,” with Daleks storming Gallifrey’s defenses, but this seems to be a pivotal battle that occurs earlier instead. Everybody ends up where they’re supposed to be, per stories that take place later: Leela is set up for the War Doctor stories, Romana is apparently set up for a future chronicled by “Doctor Who: The Experience,” but that’s a remarkably tenuous link. And Narvin is left ambiguous. It’s possible this is the point where the Dalek Emperor falls between times ; it’s deliberately vague. Even for a series whose ending was already known before it started, this particular episode succeeds pretty well. As for the fourth volume, I’m not so sure. It has several nice two-handers, but there are too many loose ends in the character arcs, particularly Eris and Rayo. And the Time War series as a whole seemed to wander all over the place, setting up Volume 1 with a lot of promise of new and returning characters, and then shuffling most of them off the page in favor of classic Gallifreyan politics, then a bunch of one-off stories. It never really found its voice as a series, which is a shame. Looking at Gallifrey as a whole, I can see why some people are so fond of it, but I’m not sure I can muster the same affection. Louise Jameson is fantastic in whatever she does, but Lalla Ward’s Romana is much more palatable when she’s bouncing off the Doctor, instead of with the weight of the universe on her shoulders. If this is the end of the Gallifrey stories for good, I’m OK with that, but with Big Finish, it’s best to never say never.

docs.text: Hostiles Gallifrey: Time War #3.1 Released: 20 February 2020 Listened: 5/21/21 After the events of the last series, Romana and Narvin are exiled from Gallifrey, traveling in a busted TARDIS, and looking for Leela. Which is good in one way, because it means that they don’t need to play politics right now, or act officious, and Narvin doesn’t have his loyalty tested. On the other hand, this is an ordinary sort of Doctor Who adventure, which means it comes off a bit like filler. They end up on a wrecked Time Lord ship, where the only survivor is a scientist who has created a monster, which turns out to be more than it seems. There’s a bit of a link here, as the monster is a Sicari, one of the race of attackers from “ Assassins ,” which in turn were created from paradox, as they’re answering the call from “ Collateral ,” which was sent by a race that has been wiped from history. Maybe that will come to something later on, but right now it hasn’t. It’s an OK episode, but has a feeling of killing time.

docs.text: Imperiatrix Gallifrey #2.5 Released: August 2005 Listened: 4/3/21 This is the climax of the second series, and unlike the first, they don’t intend it to be self-contained. It’s a weird one, seemingly determined to make the story as dark as it can get. Even the structure is odd, with a 70-minute Part 1 and a 30-minute Part 2, for no reason that I can really determine. After the events of the last story, Andred is dead, permanently this time. Darkel is just as evil as ever, so Narvin has to get a semi-redemption arc now. As established in “ Pandora ,” he’s loyal to the office, even if he dislikes Romana personally, and he’s not willing to lie or fabricate evidence in the service of his agenda. Unfortunately, Darkel doesn’t get that, which ends badly for her. Leela is trying to avenge Andred’s death, and solve a bombing at the Academy, and even worse, suffers the death of her own K-9, who never comes back, much to my astonishment. But it’s Romana who goes completely off the chain in this story, taking drastic action and declaring martial law. Supposedly she’s protecting Gallifrey itself and not just her presidency, but that doesn’t play so well in 2021 (and I imagine it sounded bad in 2005 as well). Even more bonkers, Pandora manifests itself in the form of Mary Tamm, playing sort of an evil version of Romana I, who’s quite over the top with the evil gloating and imminent destruction of Gallifrey. It ends on a cliffhanger, making the whole series somewhat dissatisfying.
docs.title: Imperiatrix

docs.text: Insurgency Gallifrey #2.4 Released: July 2005 Listened: 4/1/21 I think this story may be an attempt at a bit of a “ Lower Decks ” episode, as a lot of it takes place in the Academy and focuses on a group of non-Gallifreyan students, which adds several new actors to the mix. Unfortunately, there’s more and more politics here, as various politicians want the alien students expelled from the Academy, and assert that they’re a security risk. Unfortunately, they’re kind of right, because the students idolize the Doctor and other Renegades, and want to “do something,” which doesn’t end well. Leela is a guest lecturer, and ends up advising the students to play it cool, which makes her disappointed in herself. Andred might be starting to have an epiphany, or he might be tricking students into incriminating themselves, or maybe both; it’s hard to tell, and we’ll never know. And Romana carries the Idiot Ball for this story -- robbed of her political allies, she thinks it’s a good idea to commune with the ghost of Pandora, as if she’ll get any good information from that. As a result, she becomes even more irritable, paranoid, and shrill, which I didn’t think was possible. And Darkel just continues being a straight-up baddie, eventually challenging Romana for the Presidency. The whole thing feels a bit over-stretched, and all the characters are miserable most of the time, so it’s not a very fun listen.
docs.title: Insurgency

docs.text: Intervention Earth Gallifrey #7 Released: 2 February 2015 Listened: 5/2/21 At the end of the last series, it seemed that all concerned considered the series to be finished, and certainly Gary Russell did. But two years later, in 2015, a new and different version of Gallifrey appeared, by Scott Handcock and David Llewellyn. There’s no sign of Leela, K-9, or Romana II; instead, we’ve got Ace and Trey, but Narvin is still around. This is obviously set later in Gallifrey’s history, as Romana is on her last term in office, and Ace has been a CIA agent for some time, entrusted to work solo, although the story is deliberately vague on how Ace arrived on Gallifrey or rose up the ranks. It’s also a single four-part story encompassing a bit less than two hours (and no extras), the length of a single Main Range story. The parts are split fairly evenly, with Part 1 featuring Ace and the sort of adventure/exploration you’d expect she gets up to, Part 2 focused on Romana and a “lite” version of the intrigue that Gallifrey was known for, Part 3 with Narvin stumbling rather poorly through a rescue mission, and Part 4 supposedly tying it all together. Stephen Thorne features as Omega, but doesn’t really have all that many lines, as Omega is mostly inhabiting other bodies in this story. Still, the lines he has are properly booming and impressive. Unfortunately, the big threat is never really contextualized, and the confrontation with Omega seems fairly by-the-numbers, featuring both a psychic battle of wills, and dramatic TARDIS piloting, two tropes that rarely come off well on audio. Worst of all, it ends on a cliffhanger, with an absurd deus ex machina escape for one character. If this was intended as a launch for a new era of the Gallifrey series, it comes off rather half-baked.
docs.title: Intervention Earth

docs.text: Lies Gallifrey #2.1 Released: April 2005 Listened: 3/29/21 It looks like the first series did well enough to warrant a second, released in 2005, but still made before the new TV series debuted. The cast is a little bigger this time around, including Mary Tamm appearing as Romana I in flashbacks and Matrix projections, and sounding quite wonderful doing so. The “Free Time” terrorists are still active, and (spoiler) Andred still seems to be one of them, having been influenced by Torvald. But the big thing going on here is apparently a prophecy linking Romana to one of the earliest Time Lord Presidents, a woman who called herself Imperiatrix Pandora, and opposed most of Rassilon’s policies. As a result, this episode is mostly a lot of exposition: primarily Romana and Leela finding out about this prophecy and what all the backstory means. There’s also quite a bit of plotting against Romana on the part of Narvin and Darkel, but to be honest it’s kind of farcical. Narvin attempts to manipulate Wynter, the new Castellan, but it’s so obvious that the only reason it succeeds at all is because Wynter is carrying on the bold tradition that Castellans must be as dumb as a post. I’m not sure it’s great having Romana’s backstory manipulated like this, but it does explain some of the odder things about her.
docs.title: Lies

docs.text: Mindbomb Gallifrey #3.4 Released: July 2006 Listened: 4/8/21 It’s election time on Gallifrey. (Which apparently hasn’t happened in a long time, as each outgoing president normally names their successor, which sounds like a lovely system.) Romana, Darkel, and Matthias are all in the running...except oops, Romana’s been arrested on a charge of High Treason and spends the rest of the episode in a cell. Never mind that Darkel actually committed treason; she’s the Inquisitor, so it doesn’t count. In addition to being the Worst Ever, Darkel adds Stupid to the list, as she’s rather easily manipulated by Matthias into making basic political mistakes. At least, until she fakes an assassination attempt and gains sympathy, but forgets to have the “assassin” silenced afterwards, because Stupid. Narvin finally makes it clear to everybody that he’s on Romana’s side, but Matthias’ motives are still unknown until the very end. Leela once again doesn’t have much to do except try to spy on people, mostly unsuccessfully, because she’s blind and has to rely on a noisy robot dog for help. And what about all those aliens who were about to declare war? They’re not mentioned, so I guess they’re politely waiting for the result of the election before doing anything. There’s a twist that I won’t spoil, but suffice it to say that the election is finally settled, although not the way anyone expected, and Darkel’s story is finished. I really don’t care for what they did to her character throughout this series, and I may decide to believe that she’s not the Inquisitor from the Trial, who was generally impartial, if somewhat inclined to snap.

docs.text: Mother Tongue Gallifrey: Time War #3.3 Released: 20 February 2020 Listened: 5/22/21 So where has Leela been this whole time? Glad you asked, because this story is Leela-centric. It uses the trope where Leela wakes up in a strange place, where she’s a wife and mother, and everybody seems to know her, except she has no memory of this life. But in a twist from the usual trope, the people here are accustomed to “visitors,” and worse, the visitors bounce around to different points in time. (What exactly happens to the “hosts” when the visitor isn’t having a vision is unexplained. The hosts don’t seem to exist as separate people.) Despite the natives knowing about visitors, they’re awfully slow to spot one, even when a person they’ve known for years starts acting strangely. And as usual with these sorts of timey-wimey stories, because Leela is experiencing events out of order, she makes some assumptions about what’s going on in the future, and how to use that knowledge in the past, and that turns out to be disastrously wrong. Writer Helen Goldwyn isn’t so concerned about the plot details, but she is concerned about what happens to a mother who abruptly sees her son’s life at different points, and tries to prepare him for what’s to come. Leela isn’t a parent, but Louise Jameson brilliantly plays her getting over her initial reluctance and quick bonding with her son. Like all the stories in this set so far, it doesn’t seem to connect to anything else, but with Jameson’s acting to appreciate, I don’t mind.

docs.text: Nevernor Gallifrey: Time War #3.2 Released: 20 February 2020 Listened: 5/22/21 The Quest for Leela continues, with another Doctor Who -type story. This time, it’s the sort where they land on a seemingly normal planet, only to gradually discover that something is deeply wrong. And Narvin waxes nostalgic about a Kobayashi Maru -type test from the Academy, where the solution is not to care about which timeline survives, so you know that’s going to come up. Basically, there’s a pre-industrial community who’s caught in a time loop, except there’s lots of bleed-through from paradox and other badness, which Romana figures is the result of the Time War. Unfortunately, that leads to lots and lots of talking while they try to explain this to each other and the audience. I get that it’s supposed to be spooky and atmospheric, but unfortunately I found it a little dull. I noticed the sound design a lot more in this story, and not in a good way. There’s a cowbell that’s a little too loud and frequent, as if the goat is having a fit right on top of the microphone, as well as some scratching and knocking sounds that seem to last through the entire story. Exasperated Romana sounds a bit less exasperated in this one, but the heavy sigh is still her go-to reaction, which is unfortunate.

docs.text: Panacea Gallifrey #3.5 Released: August 2006 Listened: 4/8/21 The last story in this series has a distinctly different tone. Everybody has a distinctly sarcastic turn, which makes the dialog snappy, but not really fitting with what came before, nor appropriate to the tone of the series. Romana isn’t President anymore, and isn’t in immediate danger, but she’s snapping at absolutely everybody. Braxiatel is back, but nobody really knows whose side he’s on now. And Arkadian is back from Series 1, but everyone is treating him as a very serious threat now, which doesn’t seem to be warranted. The big threat is the Dogma virus, created by Free Time a long time ago, and modified by Pandora. It seems to be running rampant through the population, and the potential cure is even worse. No matter what course of action they take, it looks like Gallifrey is doomed...which is where it ends, on a cliffhanger. That’s fairly disappointing to me in this project, because Series 2 and 3, at least, seem to have gone nowhere in particular. For fans at the time, though, it was far worse, as this story was released in 2006, and there was no continuation until 2011. Whether it’s worth the wait remains to be seen.
docs.title: Panacea

docs.text: Pandora Gallifrey #2.3 Released: June 2005 Listened: 3/31/21 If the last episode was a break, this time we’re right back in it. The Pandora entity is supposed to be trapped in the Matrix, but of course it doesn’t stay there, breaking out and hiding in people’s minds. The politics continue apace, but they’re really not that sophisticated, and require their target (Wynter, mostly, but sometimes Leela or Romana) to be remarkably gullible. Narvin shows some signs of growing into a loyal opposition -- he’s willing to take someone down for political reasons, but he’s not willing to lie or fake evidence to get it done. Darkel, however, is nasty and manipulative, which really doesn’t match her characterization in “ Trial of a Time Lord ,” but we need a bad guy. The limited cast hurts the political machinations somewhat, especially when Leela and Andred are the only choices for acting Castellan, as none of the other Chancellery Guards have voice actors (even though Maxil was mentioned in a prior episode). The thread of the injured Time Lord is resolved, and giving credit where it’s due, I didn’t figure out who it was until a few minutes before the reveal, as there’s some timey-wimey involved, so that was well done. And the story ends with Braxiatel being taken off the table, robbing Leela of her most savvy political advisor, which I didn’t anticipate. The politics are a bit boring, but the overall arc seems to be better constructed than the last series.

docs.text: Partisans Gallifrey: Time War #2.2 Released: 20 March 2019 Listened: 5/21/21 The way to avoid this set getting completely bogged down in Gallifreyan politics is to introduce an away mission and a third party. In this case, it’s the planet Ysalus, which is rich in the fuel the Daleks need for their time machines. It’s been a non-entity up until now, but there’s a world war at some point in its history, which can be influenced. If the more brutal side wins, eventually the people react to that and form a pacifistic world government. If the other side wins, the brutal side launches a final strike that wipes out all life on the planet. Romana favors the pacifistic government, and sends Narvin and Eris to ensure that, while Rassilon sends an agent to ensure all life is wiped out. (I’m not sure why that hurts the Dalek plans; maybe it destroys the resource they need.) They don’t spend much time on Narvin having to help the brutal side, which seems like an interesting dilemma, because he never gets that far. Instead, he’s pretty ineffectual while Rassilon’s agent walks all over him with her plan, mostly because Narvin can’t bring himself to completely mistrust another Time Lord, or tolerate seeing one hurt. Which is kind, but he is supposed to be cunning and duplicitous, so. Eris, for his part, is almost completely idealistic, and decries what both sides are trying to do, and even Narvin’s stop-gap solution. One wonders how he joined the CIA at all, or if there’s more going on. The politics are actually reasonable this time, with Romana and her War Council counterpart doing the dance of warning each other off while each pretending they know nothing about the covert mission. Una McCormack has created some decent moral dilemmas here, as we actually see the Time Lords doing despicable things in the war, instead of being told about them in vague generalities. Probably the best story of the Time War series so far.

docs.text: Reborn Gallifrey #4.1 Released: March 2011 Listened: 4/18/21 The fourth series was released much later, in 2011, after the new series had taken off, and Big Finish had a higher profile. There’s a much better opening theme, more fitting with other Big Finish offerings, although the cover designs are mostly the same. Story-wise, it picks up shortly after the previous series ended, with a fake-out “everything is awesome” scene that turns out to be a dream. However, there’s a retcon that Brax’s hidden planetoid is actually the Axis, from “ The Axis of Insanity ,” although it’s described as though it’s common knowledge. The Axis leads to aborted timelines, and the main characters decide to investigate one, although it’s not clear whether they’re looking for a way to solve the problem from Series 3 , or just escape to a new reality. Anyway, they find an alternate Gallifrey in which Romana is still in her first incarnation, and Leela is a celebrity, having helped the Doctor find the Key to Time. Everybody acknowledges that this is an alternate reality, but everyone except for Leela presumes that the rules of society are the same as the Gallifrey they knew, so they can navigate here. Mary Tamm at least gets to play Romana this time, although an alternate one, and this is her final appearance in this series. Vansell, former CIA director who Narvin replaced, also appears here, in alternate form. It seems like it didn’t come to anything, but it remains to be seen whether this is setup, or just something episodic. The pacing feels slightly off, and the characterizations seem to have shifted a bit. Narvin and Brax are both on the “untrustworthy” list, despite having proven themselves in Series 3. It feels a bit off, listening to them one after the other.
docs.title: Reborn

docs.text: Renaissance Gallifrey #6.2 Released: 16 October 2013 Listened: 4/26/21 This is a tightly contained story with a small cast, because it has one major job to do: Introduce Romana III, also known as “Trey,” played by Juliet Landau. Trey has a much softer tone that makes a contrast with the strident Romana, so they’re quite distinct from an audio perspective. She’s also being created at a point in the larger Doctor Who story where there have now been a number of examples of reincarnations of the same Time Lord meeting each other and not necessarily being trustworthy. Trey claims to have come from a future where Gallifrey was destroyed by the Dogma Virus, and took so long to rebuild that the other temporal powers tore apart the Web of Time without proper guidance. She wants Romana to break the laws of time by overwriting the present with the future, restored Gallifrey, to avoid the Dark Ages. That sort of lost cause appeals to Romana’s sense of heroic danger (probably cultivated by the Doctor), and so of course she’s up for it. Narvin, not so much, and Leela isn’t really sure what to make of it. Trey’s calm persuasion draws both of them to her side, with grave consequences to Romana. There’s definitely something strange going on with Trey, and the whole story has something of a dreamlike quality, with characters acting against their own interests, and realizing it, all against a background of a completely empty Gallifrey. It’s an interesting counterpoint after the Dalek carnage in the last story, and it’s still not clear where this boxed set is going.
docs.title: Renaissance

docs.text: Soldier Obscura Gallifrey: Time War #1.2 Released: 22 February 2018 Listened: 5/16/21 This story is kind of a quick sideline that deals with just Braxiatel and Ace on a mission to check on one of those bizarre Time Lord weapons that nobody should ever use, and which Brax always seems to know a lot about. In this case, he’s left it in the charge of his old military mentor, Danna, in a region of spacetime so damaged that even looking at it causes insanity, which is a very Time-War-ish detail. Most of the story involves Brax acting very Brax, enigmatic to the point of being untrustworthy, knowing a lot more than he really ought to, while still seeming pretty friendly. Brax’s overall behavior isn’t too far from the Seventh Doctor’s, so Ace falls into a pretty familiar pattern, operating on limited information and complaining about it. Brax even implies that he’s evaluating her abilities as an agent, and favorably impressed. However, Brax is willing to be a bit more ruthless than the Doctor, and is likewise unwilling to make the sacrifice play, even if that could have stopped the war early on. I haven’t read or listened to the Benny stories where this version of Brax appears most, so I’m not sure whether that’s consistent, but it’s an interesting character study. Spoilers: The end of this story leads to Brax wiping Ace’s memory of her time on Gallifrey and depositing her back on Earth, which ends her involvement in the Gallifrey story and presumably sets her up for the founding of A Charitable Earth and the handful of “older Ace” stories that exist. It’s probably good that Ace doesn’t get caught up in the War, because there’s no good escape for her in that direction, but it seems a shame that she’s out of the series so early. I like this one because it’s different from the other Gallifrey stories, but that’s probably not going to last.
docs.title: Soldier Obscura

docs.text: Spirit Gallifrey #2.2 Released: May 2005 Listened: 3/30/21 Because series 2 is longer than series 1, there’s room for a breather episode like this one, to develop characters and set up the rest of the story. The Pandora threat is temporarily contained (or the K-9s are containing it, which writes them out of the story), so Romana takes Leela for a bit of R&R, to a planet designed as a retreat for heads of state. Romana’s not dumb, so she chooses a place with lots of wilderness and natural beauty, as an olive branch to Leela. Unfortunately, she burns any goodwill she’d earned by stomping all over Leela’s religious beliefs -- not Xoanon , but a general indiginous-sounding belief in a guiding spirit, which is likely why she’s never mentioned it before. The vacation is interrupted by a Time Lord who’s so badly injured he’s unrecognizable and can’t communicate, but also won’t regenerate, and no one knows why. Leela and Romana get pulled into a psychic experience that swaps parts of their personas -- Leela gains Romana’s knowledge, while Romana gets Leela’s instincts (which come with heightened senses). It’s not a total body swap, but each actor gets to behave a bit like the other. In practice, that means Louise Jameson gets to say a lot of long words and be irritated, which is a lot better than Lalla Ward, who adopts Leela’s speech patterns in a way that sounds like a bad parody. A body swap is a cliche sci-fi way of getting two disparate characters to appreciate the other’s point of view, and really shouldn’t be necessary here, as both characters are smarter than that, but it serves the purpose. And it’s good to get away from the intrigue for a while.
docs.title: Spirit

Leela and Romana get pulled into a psychic experience that swaps parts of their personas -- Leela gains Romana’s knowledge, while Romana gets Leela’s instincts (which come with heightened senses). It’s not a total body swap, but each actor gets to behave a bit like the other. In practice, that means Louise Jameson gets to say a lot of long words and be irritated, which is a lot better than Lalla Ward, who adopts Leela’s speech patterns in a way that sounds like a bad parody. A body swap is a cliche sci-fi way of getting two disparate characters to appreciate the other’s point of view, and really shouldn’t be necessary here, as both characters are smarter than that, but it serves the purpose. And it’s good to get away from the intrigue for a while.
docs.title: Spirit

docs.text: Square One Gallifrey #1.2 Released: April 2004 Listened: 3/27/21 This one is kind of a creepy episode, and not in a good way. It may have been better when it was released, but it sure hasn’t aged well. There’s a temporal summit going on, but the terrorists from last episode are still a worry, so Romana sends Leela to the conference in the guise of an exotic dancer (iew!) to ferret them out. To make matters worse, there’s a delegate who’s a walking harassment suit, and it turns out he murders women too. Another Time Lord negotiator is introduced, but she’s just as bad as Narvin, if not worse. There’s some timey-wimey taking place around the conference, which is a bit odd, as you’d think a bunch of temporal powers would be able to notice and stop such a thing. On top of which, there’s some language that really doesn’t belong in a Doctor Who story, but I guess Big Finish was trying to be a bit edgy at the time. I think we’re supposed to get the sense that Leela and Romana are starting to work better together, but the way Romana takes advantage of and belittles Leela in this one, I’m not really seeing it.
docs.title: Square One

docs.text: Stolen Futures The Eighth of March #2.1 Released: Listened: 5/23/23 It’s kind of hard to know where to place this one, as it features Romana during her time with the Tharils, not long after “ Warrior’s Gate .” I’m putting it in the Gallifrey section, because that’s where Romana is. She, Biroc, and some others are busy rescuing captured Tharils, but not all of her team want to let the humans go unpunished, and Romana’s just not getting that. It results in a lot of timey-wimey bouncing around, using the semi-mystical time travel that the Tharils use. That’s gotta be frustrating for Romana, since she’s not in control. In fact, she’s not in control of a lot in this story. I’ve mentioned elsewhere that Lalla Ward seems to have one emotion for Romana, and that’s “exasperated,” which can be very tiresome. In this story, with lives at stake and little power of her own, she’s reduced to shouting a lot, with mixed effect. The story is written by Lizbeth Myles and directed by Louise Jameson, which must have been kind of funny for Lalla Ward, at least. Unlike other Eight of March stories, this one seems like a common-or-garden Romana story, without anything marking it for International Women’s Day. Unfortunately, it’s kind of forgettable.
docs.title: Stolen Futures

docs.text: The Devil You Know Gallifrey: Time War #1.3 Released: 22 February 2018 Listened: 5/16/21 This boxed set is taking shape as a series of self-contained stories, which isn’t what I expected. Romana made it clear in the teaser of the previous story that the Doctor has refused to help -- presumably this is one of the Eighth Doctor’s various refusals -- so she has no choice but to turn to the Master, who’s currently incarcerated on Gallifrey. For the Master, this happens in the middle of the first War Master boxed set, after “Beneath the Viscoid” and before “The Good Master,” which is confusing, because the first War Master boxed set is last in his personal timeline, but also because the war hasn’t been going very long at this point, so the Master’s activities are all pretty early in the war. Narvin is pretty clear that asking the Master for help is an insane idea, but Romana seems desperate, and she sends Leela along to keep an eye on him. Leela has plenty of previous experience with the Geoffrey Beevers version of the Master, but as she notes right away, that Master is pretty straightforward about his evil, whereas the War Master is much more sly and genial (and don’t we just love him for it?). The plot, such as it is, involves a non-Gallifreyan fighter who has one of those horrible temporal weapons, and in this case, it split him into two separate people with conflicting timestreams. One believes the Daleks were responsible for the destruction of his world; the other thinks it was the Time Lords. The joy of this story comes from Leela and the Master interrogating the two separate men and trying to work out who’s telling the truth. Of course, Leela and the Master have entirely separate motives for wanting this information, and honestly, Leela really isn’t up to the task of keeping this Master in check. In a way, it feels a lot like a War Master story that Leela just happens to be in. (It was written in consultation with Matt Fitton, and recorded with the War Master set, much before the rest of Gallifrey: Time War .) Spoiler: Much like the last story, Leela gets taken off the board at the end, setting her up for where she eventually appears in the War Doctor sets -- as if there wasn’t enough continuity mess going on here. It’s leading me to wonder just what the goal for this boxed set is, since it seems to be bringing back characters just to write them out. But with the acting going on in this one, it’s hard to complain.
docs.title: The Devil You Know

docs.text: The First Days of Phaidon Gallifrey: War Room #1.4 Released: 23 August 2022 Listened: 7/13/23 You’re gonna need a cheat-sheet in Gallifreyan history for this one, so it’s appropriate that it’s written by super-fan Fio Trethewey (formerly known as Sophie Iles). So: Phaidon was the home of the Warpwrights, an advanced race that was just getting started with time travel, back when Romana was in charge and “the temporal powers” were a thing. Except whoops, the Daleks wiped them out in the early days of the war. (All of this being “Previously, on Gallifrey .”) And now it’s back, except it shouldn’t be, and that’s bad. Something has crashed on Phaidon, the Daleks want it, which means the Time Lords do too. So Leela and the General are sent to find out all sneaky-like, which lasts about five seconds. The other surprise is that Narvin is here, and alive, and working with the Resistance. Because we can’t have Gallifrey without Narvin, and of course there’s a Resistance. His reunion with Leela is rather emotional, drifting perhaps into the author channeling how the fans feel rather than Narvin’s actual character. Leela plays it very restrained, though, because Louise Jameson is brilliant. And the General proves himself as one who obeys orders, but who will also Do The Right Thing if properly motivated. I’m not sure that subplot was needed, but it gives Ken Bones more to do. I’m not exactly sure where the series is going. Richard Armitage clearly isn’t meant to be a recurring character, and I doubt they’ll get Timothy Dalton. So how far is this going to go, and who’s it about? That all remains to be seen. It’s not riveting, exactly, but it is interesting.
docs.title: The First Days of Phaidon

docs.text: The Inquiry Gallifrey #1.3 Released: April 2004 Listened: 3/28/21 After the events of “ Weapon of Choice ,” there were threats of an inquiry into Romana’s actions, and in this story, we get it. It’s a thin excuse to bring back Linda Bellingham as Inquisitor Darkel from the Trial for a guest appearance, but that’s OK. Except that events proceed too quickly for a stately Gallifreyan inquiry to keep up with. The plot fairly rockets along in this one, a sharp contrast with previous stories, and skipping over some action scenes that I would have expected to see played out. Narvin and his assistant Torvald are being sneaky and skulky, Leela is still looking for info on Andred and not trusting anybody, Braxiatel is being enigmatic and playing both sides, and Romana is frequently exasperated. Oh, and the impossible weapon from part 1 not only exists, but was built by the Time Lords and then destroyed, as we see in some tantalizing flashbacks...except the flashbacks aren’t reliable, because of some impressive timey-wimey that I didn’t think was possible on Gallifrey, but there it is. And we get the first reference to the Braxiatel Collection, which some people think is harmless, but others think is a crime. As a part 3 story, it succeeds more than most of them do, giving a solid motivation to continue to part 4.
docs.title: The Inquiry

docs.text: The Last Days of Freme Gallifrey: War Room #1.1 Released: 23 August 2022 Listened: 7/4/23 Oh, Big Finish. Despite the Gallifrey series having a perfectly suitable wrap-up in the last story , they can’t leave it alone. Bounce forward to 2022, and the War Room series was released, which I assume is going to run for several boxed sets. The good news is this isn’t really a prequel anymore; we’re smack in the middle of the war. Strangely Sexy Rassilon (Richard Armitage) is completely bonkers by this point, and has an iron grip on Time Lord society. But he’s too focused on his “Ascension” plan, and basically leaves the running of the war to others. The bad news is that Romana is off the board, both K-9’s are dead, and Narvin is who-knows-where, so that leaves poor Leela imprisoned by characters you’d rather she wasn’t hanging around with. The Time Lords think Leela has some uses, either as a scout, or as a guinea pig for some mad scientist to mess around with her DNA. They go the “scout” route first, sending her off on a mission with Veklin and the General, and when those two are the sympathetic characters, we’re not in a good place. Incidentally, the Carolyn Pickles version of Ollistra is around, somehow resurrected from the Matrix. The Jacqueline Pearce version is mentioned to be out there as well, but as Jacqueline Pearce is no longer around, they need to write around that. (I think her Ollistra wouldn’t put up with Rassilon’s crap, anyway.) It’s possible we’re up to the War Doctor in his personal timeline; hard to tell. Anyway, Leela’s mission is to make sure a planet is destroyed with no survivors, so the Daleks can’t force them to ally later in the timestream. You can imagine what Leela thinks of that, and the mission goes sideways almost immediately, so credit to Lou Morgan for not dragging that out. The leader of the Fremians is an oddly trusting sort, willing to spend a lot of time expositioning to Leela while he’s supposed to be planning a planetary evacuation, but maybe that’s just what his people are like. It seems like this is going to be an awfully dark and grim story, but it does lighten up once Leela starts to get some agency of her own. Plus, y’know, Beth Chalmers as Veklin is rarely a bad thing.
docs.title: The Last Days of Freme
