docs.text: The Passenger Gallifrey: War Room #1.2 Released: 23 August 2022 Listened: 7/6/23 It’s starting to look like this series is going to be more of an ensemble than Leela’s story, as she doesn’t do all that much in this episode. Instead, we add Rasmus to the mix, played again by Chris Jarman. We also get a survivor story: a Time Lord shows up with amnesia, claiming to be the survivor of a Dalek attack. If he’s telling the truth, he’s got a pile of valuable information and tech, assuming he can remember it. We get several interrogation scenes of varying politeness, as David Llewellyn uses them to flesh out each interrogator’s character and motivations. The only problem is that Ollistra, Rasmus, and the General seem to flip back and forth rather too quickly, and more than once in the story. Admittedly, Llewellyn keeps us guessing, and also reveals some deep, nasty backstory for both Ollistra and the General, but that part isn’t exactly surprising. Everybody in this set has skeletons in their closets, except for Leela (because she would have destroyed them).
docs.title: The Passenger

docs.text: Unity Gallifrey: Time War #3.4 Released: 20 February 2020 Listened: 5/22/21 With a title like “Unity,” and the last story in the set, you know they’re going to be getting the band back together, or part of it, anyway. The problem is, thanks to time travel, it’s been a rather long time for Leela, and she’s more than a little resentful of Time Lords and their war, and not exactly happy to see Romana and Narvin. She’s been living on a planet far from the war, protecting a mother and her teenage son, for a few decades. And to be fair, Romana and Narvin turning up attracts a bunch of attention that she really doesn’t need. Louise Jameson plays the conflict well; Leela will help Romana out of a sense of duty for their old friendship, but she’s pretty bitter about it, and doesn’t really return Romana’s affection. That will take time they don’t have to spare, because the Daleks make their first appearance in this Time War series, three boxed sets in. The end of the story offers yet another cast shake-up, which sort of makes it feel like the whole story was in service to the cliffhanger. On the whole, this boxed set is good, but not as good as volume 2, because of how episodic this one is. I normally think episodic in the boxed sets is a good thing, but when you’re in the middle of a long-running plot like this one, episodic can feel like wasting time.
docs.title: Unity

docs.text: Warfare Gallifrey #3.2 Released: June 2006 Listened: 4/6/21 Although this one is entitled “Warfare,” it seems more like politics. Romana’s troops are ensconced within the ruined Academy, so within the Capitol itself, so Pandora can’t move against them as easily. Darkel continues to be the Worst Ever by attacking under a flag of truce, while at the same time scheming to replace Pandora. Romana’s side has its own questionable entity, Lord Matthias, who may be a double or triple agent, or may just be playing both sides. To the story’s credit, we don’t know yet. Narvin continues to display loyalty to Romana while disliking her personally, bringing us dangerously close to liking him. Leela has supposedly become a crack strategist, and a dangerous hand-to-hand fighter despite being blind, which I think says more about Pandora’s soldiers. Pandora seems to be banking on the idea that with Pandora in Romana I’s body, that makes Romana II an anomaly...kind of? Except for a couple of lines as Romana I, poor Mary Tamm has nothing to do except spout cliche villain dialog. The ending is rather unexpected, though, as Romana makes a big sacrifice play that comes with great cost. The pacing of this series is very odd; Pandora was built up as a big threat from the first story in Series 2 , and now it’s suddenly over halfway through Series 3? That doesn’t seem to make a lot of sense.
docs.title: Warfare

docs.text: Weapon of Choice Gallifrey #1.1 Released: March 2004 Listened: 3/27/21 The kick-off of this series is fairly Gallifreyan, with intrigues and plots, but not really the strongest story. Then again, it’s from 2004, so there isn’t any new-series influence to the plot or pacing. It sets up the recurring characters and where they’ve been: Romana is now president, and considered a fairly radical reformer, which makes you wonder how she got elected, because the aristocracy is all against her. That leaves her sounding annoyed and exasperated much of the time, which Lalla Ward can do well, but it doesn’t make her the most sympathetic character. Leela, however, has lost Andred (under mysterious circumstances), and that leaves her with no place in Gallifreyan society, and wanting to join the outsiders before Romana calls her in to help. We get Braxiatel as Romana’s frequently enigmatic advisor, and Narvin as the head of the CIA, frequently overstepping his authority and being a general jerk most of the time. The plot stems from “ The Apocalypse Element ,” where a weakened Gallifrey is just one of many “temporal powers,” which means politics as they try to stay on top. But there’s a group of “Free Time” rebels who’ve stolen the plans for a Time Lord weapon that shouldn’t exist. However, Romana out-thinks them without too much difficulty, leaving the episode feeling rather light. It’s a start, if not a great start.
docs.title: Weapon of Choice

docs.text: Gallifrey #1.1 Released: March 2004 Listened: 3/27/21 The kick-off of this series is fairly Gallifreyan, with intrigues and plots, but not really the strongest story. Then again, it’s from 2004, so there isn’t any new-series influence to the plot or pacing. It sets up the recurring characters and where they’ve been: Romana is now president, and considered a fairly radical reformer, which makes you wonder how she got elected, because the aristocracy is all against her. That leaves her sounding annoyed and exasperated much of the time, which Lalla Ward can do well, but it doesn’t make her the most sympathetic character. Leela, however, has lost Andred (under mysterious circumstances), and that leaves her with no place in Gallifreyan society, and wanting to join the outsiders before Romana calls her in to help. We get Braxiatel as Romana’s frequently enigmatic advisor, and Narvin as the head of the CIA, frequently overstepping his authority and being a general jerk most of the time. The plot stems from “ The Apocalypse Element ,” where a weakened Gallifrey is just one of many “temporal powers,” which means politics as they try to stay on top. But there’s a group of “Free Time” rebels who’ve stolen the plans for a Time Lord weapon that shouldn’t exist. However, Romana out-thinks them without too much difficulty, leaving the episode feeling rather light. It’s a start, if not a great start.
docs.title: Weapon of Choice

docs.text: The Tenth Doctor The Tenth Doctor defined Doctor Who for a new generation, much like the Fourth Doctor did for the classic series. He’s cool, he’s confident, he’s funny, and a little bit sexy, which caused his companions to fall for him. Even better, David Tennant himself was a super-fan since his childhood, and loved just about everything about being the Doctor, on-screen and off. He appeared in several Big Finish roles before being cast as the Doctor, and apparently wanted to do more. Although he’s had a very successful career since leaving the role (breaking the classic-series typecasting curse), he seems to be willing to come back as often as possible. However, his busy schedule meant his appearances were somewhat limited, until the 2020 pandemic. He discovered the joy of recording from home, most famously with Staged , his series with Michael Sheen, but also in a large number of Big Finish stories, expanding this era nicely.
docs.title: Tenth Doctor

docs.text: The Tenth Doctor and Donna Donna Noble was created as a character who was clearly unsuited to being a companion, one that even the casual viewer could see didn’t belong. Except…the Doctor makes some people better versions of themselves when he touches their lives, and Catherine Tate absolutely knocked it out of the park, making Donna brash, snarky, and sympathetic at the same time, which folks didn’t really expect. Plus, Tate and David Tennant get along like a house on fire, and they’re brilliant as a comic duo. Which not only meant that Tate got upgraded to full-time companion in the fourth series, but also that she’s been entirely willing to do Big Finish work, especially when Tennant is involved. So there are a fair number of inserts in this section.
docs.title: Tenth Doctor and Donna

docs.text: Death and the Queen The Tenth Doctor Adventures #1.3 Released: 16 May 2016 Listened: 11/19/22 In which Donna finally gets to be treated like royalty. Landing on the French Riviera in the late 1800s, Donna attracts the attention of Prince Rudolph of Goritania, which the Doctor has never heard of. Turns out he was basically out in the world to locate a bride, which means this story is about the same as “ The Auntie Matter ,” but without the Wodehouse parody. The Doctor is a profoundly annoying gooseberry during that part of the story, mostly told in flashbacks. It seems he’s rather afraid of losing yet another companion to falling in love. So when he turns up on the day of the wedding, and then horrible invaders follow close behind, he goes into Doctory high gear trying to figure out what’s going on. He’s actually wrong an unusual number of times in this story, while at the same time proclaiming how clever he is. Beth Chalmers appears as a remarkably capable maid who’d make a perfect companion, a fact the Doctor keeps mentioning. Ultimately, Donna gets a large chunk of the big save, which is nice, but the whole thing has a fairy-tale feel that just sort of vanishes once it’s over. On the whole, I don’t think the first boxed set quite settled into the groove of the Doctor/Donna relationship. It’s close, but not as accurate as later stories.
docs.title: Death and the Queen

docs.text: Death's Deal Destiny of the Doctor #10 Released: 3 October 2013 Listened: 11/3/22 Appropriately, the first audio with Donna in this project is from the “Destiny of the Doctor” series, and it’s narrated by Catherine Tate, with David Tennant not around. Which means that Tate has to play the Tenth Doctor, and while she doesn’t attempt his accent, she’s got his delivery and timing down cold, which you would expect of a comedic actress known for a wide range of roles. The Doctor and Donna follow a distress call to the planet Death’s Deal, the deadliest planet in the galaxy, because it’s covered with aggressive coral and slug-type creatures that eat almost anything that lands on the surface. There’s also a handful of bystanders, because the Doctor needs a bunch of people to try to save (and mostly fail), and Donna needs people to yell at for being insensitive. Of course, one of them is a sentient molusc-creature that Donna has trouble with at first, but then he saves her life later on. Author Darren Jones hasn’t written a lot for Big Finish, and what he has, has been almost entirely in the new-series eras. That said, he seems to have the new series style down pretty well, with good pacing and an air of mystery.
docs.title: Death's Deal

docs.text: No Place The Tenth Doctor Adventures #3.1 Released: 16 May 2019 Listened: 11/17/22 After several stories with parts of the family, we’ve got everybody together this time: the Doctor, Donna, Wilf, and Sylvia, all played by their respective TV actors, and boy does it feel good to hear Bernard Cribbins. He’s a wonderful moderating influence on all of them, but especially on Sylvia. And they kinda need it this time. For reasons that aren’t entirely clear at first, they’re all pretending to be a family renovating an old manor house, supposedly haunted, for the benefit of a reality TV show and its host Justin. Which means that the Doctor and Donna have to pretend to be married, and be shmoopy at each other, and you can hear David Tennant and Catherine Tate trying so hard to make the other crack up, to the point it nearly takes you out of the story. Because it’s a reality TV show, you only get to hear the bits where Justin is filming, meaning the listener has less idea of what’s going on than usual. It turns out that the Noble family has something of a history with this house, and so does Justin. It’s a properly spooky episode, although not quite so much of a jump scare or creeping dread as spooky and uncertain. It’s a quality story, and it’s great to have the full cast.
docs.title: No Place

docs.text: One Mile Down The Tenth Doctor Adventures #3.2 Released: 16 May 2019 Listened: 11/5/22 It’s funny that this story from the second set appears so early in the timeline, but it makes sense. Donna is still a bit new, obsessing about her shoes, willing to go along with the official tour, and referring to the sonic as the “buzzy thing.” She convinces the Doctor to take her to Vallarasee, a water planet with magnificent underwater cathedrals made of coral. The native Vallarasee are water-breathers, but the Galactic Trust has come in to “preserve” the city…by draining it of water and turning it into a tourist attraction. And bringing in the Judoon to police the place, which means we get Nick Briggs voicing them, and David Tennant speaking bits of Judoonese, because of course. There’s even a “junior Judoon” with a higher-pitched voice and a slightly open mind, giving hope for the species. Of course, this is a Tenth Doctor story, so disaster is always imminent, in the form of the air dome collapsing. Almost all of the characters have serious flaws, from the oblivious human administrator to the racist tourist to the cultural appropriator. And the Doctor spares none of them his contempt as he’s saving them, his arrogance coming through fairly strongly. He’s trying to be nicer to Donna; although he clearly doesn’t want to do touristy things, Donna’s still getting her feet wet, as it were. This is the first story in this project with both Tate and Tennant together, and their banter naturally sparkles, even in this period where they’re still being a bit tentative with each other. Some interesting guest casting here, including Rakie Ayola, who played the Hostess in “ Midnight ,” and Eleanor Crooks and Christopher Naylor, who will later go on to play Naomi Cross and Harry Sullivan .
docs.title: One Mile Down

docs.text: Technophobia The Tenth Doctor Adventures #1.1 Released: 16 May 2016 Listened: 11/5/22 When this story came out in 2016, it was the first new-series story with the original actors, and there was a lot of excitement around it, enough to crash the Big Finish servers. I admit to being part of that excitement myself; hearing the series 4 theme again after so long put a big stupid smile on my face. Looking at it in the context of this larger project, though, it’s kind of a middle-of-the-road story, something very typical of the period in which it’s set. The Doctor and Donna are in London, “a few years” after Donna’s native 2008, although she’s being careful not to learn anything that could disrupt the timeline. In particular, the smartphone revolution has happened while she was gone, and Donna doesn’t care for “swipey stuff,” although the Doctor is in his element. Except that all over London, people start losing their ability to interact with technology, and then to become actively afraid of it (hence the title). The Doctor and Donna are immune for a while, but even they start to be affected eventually. The focus is on the mystery, and also on Donna interacting with people, usually with her trademark empathy. The aliens themselves really aren’t all that impressive, but that’s not the point. The banter between the Doctor and Donna is good, but not sublime. Which is fine, really; it’s a good start.
docs.title: Technophobia

docs.text: The Creeping Death The Tenth Doctor Adventures #3.3 Released: 16 May 2019 Listened: 11/21/22 While aiming for the Swinging 60s, the TARDIS ends up in the Great Fog of 1952. Which is an event that has to happen, but an invasion of microscopic aliens that feed on pollution is something the Doctor can stop. Apparently, most of the cast learned about this historic event from the same episode of The Crown where I learned about it, which seems a bit sad since I’m not English. There’s a lot of running around and shouting, even by the Tenth Doctor’s standards, and there’s a bunch of nicely drawn secondary characters, half of whom end up dead, and two of whom are a gay couple, which is a no-go in 1952. A bit of guest-casting in this one with Lauren Cornelius, who will later play companion Dodo Chaplet . Also, Big Finish regulars Helen Goldwyn and Stephen Critchlow have minor parts. I think this one impacts a lot of the cast and crew differently than it does me, because of the closeness they feel to London in the 50s. And that’s going to be a wrap for Catherine Tate in this project.
docs.title: The Creeping Death

docs.text: Time Reaver The Tenth Doctor Adventures #1.2 Released: 16 May 2016 Listened: 11/6/22 This Jenny T. Colgan story has an interesting high concept: a weapon that stretches the perception of time for the victim, so seconds last hours. Obviously, that’s pretty horrific if you’re using it on someone in pain, but it’s equally horrific as a drug: people want to extend pleasurable experiences, so use the weapons on themselves. All of this takes place on a “crossroads” planet, a way-station that millions of people pass through every day, and where legal enforcement is sketchy at best. It’s a bit odd that the Doctor seems very fond of it, although he does like a bit of anarchy in some incarnations. The mobster characters I could take or leave, but the secondary protagonists are relatable and well played. The only fail in this story is that it’s really hard to portray someone having their personal time stretched to infinity on audio. You end up with characters narrating what they’re seeing to themselves, sometimes really slowly; that could have been done better. At the end, the Doctor declares a desire to visit a library, so we know what that means .
docs.title: Time Reaver

docs.text: Wild Pastures The Tenth Doctor Chronicles #1.3 Released: 18 April 2018 Listened: 11/16/22 This is a “Chronicles” story, so instead of David Tennant, we get Jacob Dudman, who does a perfectly decent Tenth Doctor, in pacing and intonation if not exactly in pitch. We also get Jacqueline King as Sylvia…really? Turns out the Doctor suspects something is fishy at a local old-folks home, so he drops Donna off someplace sunny and goes to fetch Wilf to help him infiltrate…except Wilf’s not around, and Sylvia likes the look of the home as a rest break, so she buffaloes the Doctor into taking her along instead. This goes about as well as you might imagine. Sylvia is nasty, acidic, displays no self-awareness, and is borderline racist and definitely ageist. Even compared to the version of Sylvia from “Kidnapped,” this one is nasty. James Goss must have a hell of a mother, is all I can say. The Doctor spends a fair amount of time elsewhere, captured, or missing a lot of his faculties, which means that Dudman is in narrator mode more often than not (which he does quite well), and that Sylvia carries the bulk of the story. Which, well…it’s a good thing it’s an hour-long story, because Sylvia wears thin rather quickly. Jackie Tyler may be unsuited to this sort of thing, but she could still be fun to hang out with. I can’t imagine anyone enjoying hanging around Sylvia. When the chips are down, though, she gets the job done, mostly through the same bull-headedness that gets Donna through. It’s nice to see the Doctor wrong-footed from time to time, even if Sylvia gets to be smug as a result.
docs.title: Wild Pastures

This goes about as well as you might imagine. Sylvia is nasty, acidic, displays no self-awareness, and is borderline racist and definitely ageist. Even compared to the version of Sylvia from “Kidnapped,” this one is nasty. James Goss must have a hell of a mother, is all I can say. The Doctor spends a fair amount of time elsewhere, captured, or missing a lot of his faculties, which means that Dudman is in narrator mode more often than not (which he does quite well), and that Sylvia carries the bulk of the story. Which, well…it’s a good thing it’s an hour-long story, because Sylvia wears thin rather quickly. Jackie Tyler may be unsuited to this sort of thing, but she could still be fun to hang out with. I can’t imagine anyone enjoying hanging around Sylvia. When the chips are down, though, she gets the job done, mostly through the same bull-headedness that gets Donna through. It’s nice to see the Doctor wrong-footed from time to time, even if Sylvia gets to be smug as a result.
docs.title: Wild Pastures

docs.text: The Tenth Doctor and Martha Martha Jones, my absolute favorite companion of the modern series. So smart! And capable – she saves the Doctor’s life three times in her first story! The only modern companion to leave of her own volition until Ryan! And she absolutely rocks a leather jacket. However, Freema Agyeman has had a stellar career since leaving the show, starring in Law & Order UK , Sense8 , and New Amsterdam , all of which has kept her pretty busy, so she hasn’t had much time for Big Finish. After one appearance in Torchwood, she recorded The Year of Martha Jones, which takes place during the “year that never was” in the middle of the Series 3 finale. Unfortunately, that means we've got no stories (yet) with David Tennant and Freema Agyeman together.

docs.text: Backtrack The Tenth Doctor Chronicles #1.2 Released: 18 April 2018 Listened: 10/22/22 The second entry in the Tenth Doctor Chronicles series, with Jacob Dudman again playing the Doctor, backed up by John Culshaw, so between the two of them, they manage quite a few characters, mostly aliens, although Culshaw does a handful of different American accents pretty well, especially by Big Finish standards. The story itself is kind of standard, with the Doctor and Martha landing on one of those time-tourism ships that never seems to know what they’re actually doing. Unfortunately, there’s also a fungal infection on board, and the Doctor just leaves Martha to deal with that while he goes off to poke at the engines. But because Martha is unbelievably awesome, she manages to use a futuristic medical kit to cure a bunch of aliens she’s never seen before of a fungal infection she’s never seen before, and is mutating anyway because of exposure to temporal radiation. True to Series 3, especially this part of it, the pacing kicks in from the start and never really lets up. Which is good, because a fungus doesn’t make for a complex bad guy. It probably would’ve looked hokey on TV, so audio is a great place for it. It slots quite nicely into this spot, but doesn’t really stand out.

docs.text: Cold Vengeance The Tenth Doctor Adventures #2.3 Released: 23 November 2017 Listened: 11/16/22 The Tenth Doctor met Daleks , Cybermen , Sontarans , and (eventually) Zygons, but he missed out on Ice Warriors . Matt Fitton aims to fix that. And these aren’t the noble, federation-joining Ice Warriors of the future, but angry, vindictive Ice Warriors. In large part, it’s a classic “base under siege” story, which doesn’t fit as well in Series 2 as the goofier stories, except it’s a lot like “ Tooth and Claw ” in that the Doctor and Rose are both overconfident, which means they don’t listen to the people around them, and that causes trouble. The Ice Warriors aren’t too big on listening either, which leads to the whole problem of generations of war and revenge that can’t end because nobody knows how to stop anymore. As often in Matt Fitton stories, the relationships between the characters are the important bits, between the Doctor and Rose, and between Brona and Callum Volta, mother-and-son space pirates. And even with Lorna, the recycling collector who nobody listens to until it’s too late. This one’s a bit darker than the other stories in the set, but it sets up future sets nicely…if there ever are any.
docs.title: Cold Vengeance

docs.text: Infamy of the Zaross The Tenth Doctor Adventures #2.1 Released: 23 November 2017 Listened: 10/15/22 With all respect to Jacob Dudman, this is the real deal. David Tennant, Billie Piper, Camille Coduri, and a Series 2 feel. John Dorney is known for his time-twisting stories, but this time, he brings the funny. Jackie calls Rose and the Doctor back to Earth to thwart an alien invasion in…Norwich. And nowhere else. And the invaders aren’t really too impressive, although they are a legitimate threat. Of course, there’s more going on here, and the Doctor doesn’t like it. The lightheartedness of the story is a nice fit for early Series 2, and the Doctor and Rose are operating quite well as a team, and individually. Even Jackie is more competent than last time we saw her, and she gets to go to space for the first time. There’s even a brief reflection on the price of fame, and why some people are willing to pay it anyway, which is kinda sad. But not for long, because that’s not what these stories are about. And it wouldn’t be Series 2 without a brief mention of Torchwood. I’m a fan of this story because it’s one that could only be told in modern Who .
docs.title: Infamy of the Zaross

docs.text: The Sword of the Chevalier The Tenth Doctor Adventures #2.2 Released: 23 November 2017 Listened: 11/15/22 The second story of this set (which doesn’t take place immediately after the previous ) is a “historical celebrity” story, and the celebrity in this case is the Chevalier d’Eon , a French spy and expert fencer living in England in 1791. The Chevalier had lived as both a man and a woman at different times in their life, and doesn’t seem to have had a definitive expression. They’re played by Nickolas Grace using a rather indeterminate voicing, and in truth, neither the Doctor nor Rose actually care all that much, although Rose is somewhat curious. As it turns out, the Chevalier is a bit of an egotist, but they have the fencing abilities to back it up. The villain is an alien slaver with three separate faces and personalities, although one of them is deceased. Which is seriously creepy, and suggests a lot of potential for other stories with this species or the criminal organization they belong to, although none has appeared yet. With that much setup going on, the ending is actually a bit weak, more appropriate for a Moffat-era story than Series 2, but on the whole, Guy Adams does a good job of bringing a lot of pieces together.
docs.title: The Sword of the Chevalier

docs.text: The Taste of Death The Tenth Doctor Chronicles #1.1 Released: 18 April 2018 Listened: 10/15/22 Even though Big Finish had already published some stories with David Tennant by the time this was recorded, they went ahead with their plans to make narrated “chronicles” stories with the Ninth through Twelfth Doctors. They’d tapped Jacob Dudman because of his amazing Eleventh Doctor impression, and he does a half-decent Tenth as well, with the mannerisms down perfectly, but the voice itself sounds a touch younger. It’s different enough from his narrator voice to make a nice contrast. This is very much a Series-2-type story, with the Doctor and Rose arriving at a resort planet to discover that something’s not right. The guests are being fed something addictive that makes them gorge themselves. If you guessed the Slitheen are involved, you’d be right. It’s kind of nice to see the Slitheen with the Tenth Doctor, but it’s equally nice to see that while they acknowledge the use of vinegar as a weapon, they’re not running around killing Slitheen with it, which didn’t really sit right. docs.text: Death in the New Forest Tales from New Earth #2 Released: 6 March 2018 Listened: 10/28/22 With Devon now part of Senator Hame’s team, he takes a trip to the New Forest – a continent populated entirely by sentient trees – to tell Thorn’s family how he died. Except he can’t find them, because there’s people going missing here too. Which brings him right smack into the Doctor, who’s investigating the disappearances along with Sapling Vale, a cutting of Jabe of the Forest of Cheem , which means she can be played by Yasmin Bannerman, which is always good fun. Sadly, David Tennant isn’t here, so Devon mostly narrates the story, meaning that Kieran Hodgson has to imitate the Doctor. And he does a reasonably good job, especially when the Doctor gets excited and shouty, which to be fair, he does a lot. From there it gets pretty complicated. There are some sentient termites who are the prime suspects, and have a legitimate claim to the continent, but of course the Doctor thinks it can’t be that easy, and Devon thinks the Lux are involved, and it turns out they are trying to convert the trees to Lux-ism, starting with their religious leaders. But the whole thing turns out to be more complicated than that. The story turns into a runaround, with lots of shouting and sonic-ing that doesn’t necessarily make sense, but it’s decent fun.

docs.text: Escape from New New York Tales from New Earth #1 Released: 6 March 2018 Listened: 10/27/22 This 2018 release is one of those where Big Finish had the rights to new-series characters, but didn’t have access to the primary actors, so they did what they could. Which in this case was revisit New Earth, seen in “ New Earth ” and “ Gridlock ,” and in the same time period as “ The End of the World .” Which, admittedly, is a fairly well-drawn setting, because Russell T Davies does like dropping concepts that leave a lot off-screen, so why not? The main character for this one is Devon Pryce, played by Kieran Hodgson, a young man with a very unfortunate story. His parents were New Humans, created by the Sisters of Plenitude in “New Earth” as lab animals, and after that, they got caught in the Gridlock, and then died while Devon was still young. So he grew up in a kind of monastic society dedicated to maintaining the elevators, and has a boyfriend who’s a sentient shrub, which is all really very Davies. Except that an organization called “the Lux” is helping to fund the society of New Earth, and spreading their religion…and kidnapping people. Oops. Fortunately, Novice Hame (still played by Anna Hope), now Senator, is just the cat for the job, and runs into Devon during her investigations. Except this is a set-up story, and we don’t get to know much other than the Lux are bad. The Doctor doesn’t appear, so technically it doesn’t belong in this project, but, well. Special props to Dan Blasky for pulling off an excellent American accent as the Duke of Brooklyn.
docs.title: Escape from New New York

docs.text: Free Speech Short Trips #10.X Released: 29 December 2020 Listened: 4/20/26 This story is one of Big Finish's Paul Spragg Memorial stories, meaning that Eugenie Pusenjak is a new writer, and she's starting with a pretty high concept: a planet where speaking literally costs money, enforced by chips embedded in people's tongues before they become adults. Writing apparently also costs, but that's just handwaved. Sign language isn't mentioned, which I think is a pretty serious oversight, but I'll let it go. The story is told in the form of the protagonist being interrogated by police, and of course, it costs to answer. Needless to say, the Tenth Doctor is antithetical to this society, and he's not having any of it. Jacob Dudman both narrates and plays the Doctor, and if anything, the Doctor doesn't have enoough lines. Other Doctors might have quietly encouraged rebellion, but I'm sure the Tenth would take a more direct approach. There's also a scene of a high-stakes poker game that takes up a lot of time, but doesn't seem necessary to the story. The whole speech thing is an indictment of the British class system and the idea of "knowing one's place." Maybe it's because I'm American, where not only is the class system weaker, but free speech is considered a core value, but this one just isn't working for me.
docs.title: Free Speech

docs.text: Quantum of Axos Tenth Doctor, Classic Companions #3 Released: 14 September 2022 Listened: 11/3/22 The final story features Ace, in the present, and in her current role as CEO of A Charitable Earth. It’s a little tricky to say where this falls in Ace’s personal timeline, but it seems to be before Sarah Jane’s funeral, and possibly after “The Power of the Doctor,” although the story is purposely vague about that, and Big Finish probably couldn’t have known anything about Ace’s role in that story (or did they?). Ace is in full control here, very much the CEO and investigator, sniffing out alien goings-on right away. Although admittedly, it’s Axos, which have been trying to find a hole in their time-loop since the 1970s, and don’t appear to have adapted all that well to the 21st century, despite the fact that mimicking other life forms is their thing. Once again, the emphasis is on the companion’s relationship with the Doctor, rather than on the main plot. Unlike the others, Ace has changed a lot since her time in the TARDIS, and it’s good character growth. Fortunately, Sophie Aldred plays it brilliantly. It helps that we’ve just recently seen her on TV, but she presents a sharp difference to 1989 Ace, even vocally. It looks like this story ends here, and they don’t really have plans for more, which may be for the best, given that the TV series is getting more prone to pulling in classic companions.
docs.title: Quantum of Axos

docs.text: Soul Music Subscriber Short Trips #2021-1 Released: 16 March 2021 Listened: 4/20/26 Placed here rather arbitrarily. This is the last ever of the bonus Subscriber Short Trips, but there's nothing particularly special to indicate that. It's a Tenth Doctor story, and it's a little unusual in that it takes place in Las Vegas, which isn't somewhere the Doctor seems to have gone often, although he does mention that the landscape reminds him of Gallifrey a bit. The time period isn't specified, but there's a tower that seems to be the Stratosphere, and a fountain that's probably the Bellagio. It seems that the Doctor brought some humanoid aliens here some time ago, because the climate is similar to their lost planet. Except now something is making them all sick, and they can't determine the cause. Writer Victora Saxton is leaning hard on the melancholy that the Tenth Doctor feels when he thinks about home, and that part works pretty well. However, when Doctor Who pushes together a spiritual experience with a scientific explanation, the writer has to be careful of where the edges meet, and I don't think that quiet works in this story. It's decent, but that's about all.
docs.title: Soul Music

docs.text: Splinters Tenth Doctor, Classic Companions #1 Released: 14 September 2022 Listened: 10/31/22 This boxed set is a trio of recent adventures featuring the Tenth Doctor meeting companions from the classic series…sort of. They’re not always what they seem. The box’s arc starts off with the Doctor randomly finding K-9 Mark II floating in space. (Except not quite randomly; K-9 got here after the events of Gallifrey and the Time War.) He requests the Doctor’s help in tracking down anomalies left over from the Time War, with the first one being on 16-century Earth…where Leela is, unusually. Leela has no memory of how she got here, but she’s been helping to defend the village against the Spriggan, a creature of myth that steals the children of the village on their 18th birthday. Louise Jameson is a treasure, and it’s fantastic to see her working with any Doctor, because Leela pretty much takes them in stride. The story itself has a new-series feel to it, in that its pacing rarely lets up, which plays to the Tenth Doctor’s strengths of running a lot and talking very quickly. Ultimately, the story has more fairy-tale in it than I like, and although John Dorney puts a good explanation on it, that doesn’t really do it for me. Louise Jameson makes it worth it, though.
docs.title: Splinters

docs.text: The Cats of New Cairo Tales from New Earth #4 Released: 6 March 2018 Listened: 10/29/22 It’s finale time, and we’ve got more guest stars in the form of Adjoa Andoh, who aside from Francine Jones, played one of the cat nuns in “ New Earth ,” and plays that same cat’s cousin here. Plus James Dreyfus (before he was the Master , and before he was not the Master) plays the “Exalted High Persian.” Because we’re going to New Cairo, which is kind of Cat HQ on New Earth, where all the orders are based. There aren’t any humans, so Devon encounters plenty of racism. Cats are still accustomed to being worshiped, it seems, and they’ve got a bunch of sentient camels to do that for them. They’re also willing to cut a deal with the Lux, because if there’s one thing these cats can do above all else, it’s look out for themselves. The Doctor doesn’t really appear much in this one, mostly because he’s locked out by the Lux, but a bunch of the characters we’ve met in the previous stories pitch in to help out. Because of course cooperation is what wins against the selfish. We never do learn much more about the Lux than we already knew. They’re a Big Bad, but exactly what they are and how they work remains a mystery. On the whole, the boxed set is coherent and decent storytelling, but not really required listening. It’s pretty good, and that’s it.
docs.title: The Cats of New Cairo

docs.text: The Last Line The War Master #7.4 Released: 16 June 2018 Listened: 10/30/22 If you’ve got the option of putting David Tennant and Derek Jacobi together, then you take it. How can you pull that off without ruining “ Utopia ”? Simple: You use the Master from during the Time War, before he uses the Chameleon Arch, and the Doctor from afterward, specifically this gap, where losing the Master is still raw for him. Sure, the War is Time Locked, but they don’t make Time Locks like they used to. From the Master’s point of view, he’s been on trial this whole boxed set, and he’s run out of tricks, so he uses his final option to call the Doctor for help. The majority of the story, though, is told from the Doctor’s point of view, which helps the suspense. He’s pretty sure the Master’s up to something, and so is the listener, but what? And the beauty of it is, there’s no way of knowing if this was an elaborate plan, or if the Master just tossed the Doctor into the room like a live grenade and took advantage of the chaos. It’s a very talky episode, but why not, with these two doing the talking? Writer Lizzy Hopley says in the comments that she tried for a while to avoid just having the two of them in a room talking, but then changed her mind and went all-in. I suspect this story wouldn’t have worked out as well with a different Doctor, because the Tenth is quite arrogant, though he hides it well, and has no difficulty taking dubious actions based on his own ideas of justice. Of course, the Master comes out ahead, because it’s his story, but that doesn’t make it any less gripping.
docs.title: The Last Line

docs.text: The Skies of New Earth Tales from New Earth #3 Released: 6 March 2018 Listened: 10/29/22 We’ve had cats, and trees, so why not get a little crazier? This story takes place on several floating islands above New Earth, mostly inhabited by sentient bird-people, one of whom is played by Nina Tussaint-White (Mels). There are also sentient “solar bears” who live on clouds and get around with jet packs, because why not? The primary bear we meet, Oscar McLeod, is played by Toby Hadoke with a comical Scandinavian accent. Devon is here to investigate the Lux, but they’re not doing a lot this time. Instead, there’s another power company, Cloudburst, who can generate energy by “fragging” the clouds (the parallels are pretty obvious). Of course, the birds and bears aren’t thrilled about that, and think the process is dangerous, which, whoops, it is. And since the Lux want rid of Cloudburst, they’re willing to exploit that. At least, until the Doctor shows up to put a stop to it with some judicious sonic-ing. Kieran Hodgson’s Tenth Doctor is getting better, especially on lines like “Brilliant!” but it lets him down a bit when he’s got to do exposition, sounding more like a Matt Smith impersonator with a head cold, which is unfortunate. The Lux are apparently defeated in this one, but with one story left to go in the box, we know better.
docs.title: The Skies of New Earth

docs.text: The Stuntman Tenth Doctor, Classic Companions #2 Released: 14 September 2022 Listened: 10/31/22 Moving on from Leela, Nyssa is up next. In her personal timeline, she’s commanding the hospital ship Traken , just as she was in “ A Heart on Both Sides ,” but that doesn’t seem to have happened for her yet; she hasn’t started her family yet either. However, the Doctor finds her as a stunt person in a massive movie studio, with a protective stuntman father. Which is a strange thing for Nyssa to be doing, because it’s a virtual reality simulation. Nyssa’s “father,” Kent Novum, is actually K-9, who entered the VR to protect Nyssa, but got caught in the narrative. Which allows John Leeson to play a human, and one his own age as well. Kent is a fantastic character, quite a bit braver and more emotional than one might have expected for K-9. Leeson manages to carry the scene in which “Kent” realizes he’s in fact a robot dog, which has got to be a challenge for any actor. Unfortunately, the bad guy isn’t nearly as well realized, and Nyssa spends rather too much time in distress, and not being herself. Writer Lizzie Hopley seems to be trying to focus on the relationships here, and John Leeson overshadows the other actors, making this story probably the weakest of the set.
docs.title: The Stuntman

Leeson manages to carry the scene in which “Kent” realizes he’s in fact a robot dog, which has got to be a challenge for any actor. Unfortunately, the bad guy isn’t nearly as well realized, and Nyssa spends rather too much time in distress, and not being herself. Writer Lizzie Hopley seems to be trying to focus on the relationships here, and John Leeson overshadows the other actors, making this story probably the weakest of the set.

docs.text: The Tenth Doctor Solo (again) Every Doctor needs a solo period where Big Finish can squeeze in stories, and the BBC provided Big Finish with a whopping huge one in 2009. Only a handful of specials aired in that year, all considered to be part of Series 4, and not only was the Doctor canonically without a companion for that period, he also spent a long time between televised stories. With an invitation like that, various writers have squeezed in two whole epic storylines (so far): Dalek Universe from Big Finish, and the Time Lord Victorious multimedia storyline from…well, primarily James Goss, but lots of people. And we’ve got some River Song and multi-Doctor stories too. But all good things must end, and this era comes to a close with multiple stories set in the last minutes of “ The End of Time .”

docs.text: Buying Time Dalek Universe #1.1 Released: 14 April 2021 Listened: 11/30/22 Hang on kids; this is where things get confusing. Most Big Finish stories don’t rely too heavily on continuity, especially the modern-series ones. Dalek Universe is a big exception. You’ll need to know who Anya Kingdom is (last seen by the Fourth Doctor in the “Syndicate” stories). You’ll also need to know Mark Seven (last seen in the “ Dalek Protocol ” prequel), and it helps to know how both of those tie in to “ The Daleks’ Master Plan ,” which is a First Doctor story from 1966, and it’s a lost story, so nobody’s actually seen it in its entirety in decades. But, all that aside, the story chugs along at a good pace, appropriate for a new-series story. It starts in the middle, with Anya and a Space Security Service team searching a wreck for survivors, except that Anya’s really looking for Mark, and finds the Doctor, who has no idea how he got there. There’s some sharp character work going on here too, with the Doctor still being angry at Anya over the Ann Kelso identity – except he never told her about his relationship with Sara Kingdom or Bret Vyon , so he’s at least compartmentalizing, if not being downright hypocritical. On top of which, Mark and Anya apparently had some disagreement since we saw them last. In Terry Nation style, the plot has no problem hopping between planets, where we get several more characters, including Mark Gatiss, mostly unrecognizable as an unscrupulous CEO who’s about to introduce time technology way ahead of schedule. It’s also a John Dorney story, and therefore has one hell of a cliffhanger. This is good stuff, all the way around.
docs.title: Buying Time

docs.text: Churchill Victorious The Churchill Years #2.4 Released: 15 February 2018 Listened: 11/26/22 The concluding story of this boxed set finds Churchill on V-E Day, and yet rather out of sorts. Basically, the war is won, but he can’t celebrate, because there’s so much else to do. Most of the staff is out celebrating, so after a rather disastrous attempt to cook himself lunch, he goes through intelligence reports, and finds one about power outages near Piccadilly. So he goes out in “disguise” to see what he can do about it, because that’s a perfectly sensible thing for the Prime Minister of an entire nation to do. Fortunately, this is Doctor Who , where strange power outages always mean alien activity, so he ends up finding one who’s captured the Doctor. Most of the story is played just for laughs, almost entirely at Churchill’s expense. You can’t really have a big conflict on V-E Day, since the war is over, but you can have a small story. The Doctor is kept off-screen for most of the story, which saves Ian McNeice from trying to imitate David Tennant too often, although to be fair, he does it better than in the first boxed set . The goal here seems to be giving us a peek into Churchill’s psyche without the war to sustain him, and, well, you can kind of see how he lost the next election. This is one of those stories that probably has a greater impact on British listeners.
docs.title: Churchill Victorious

docs.text: Cycle of Destruction Dalek Universe #2.1 Released: 14 July 2021 Listened: 12/4/22 We got a lot of Anya’s background in the last story , so now it’s Mark’s turn. Although Mark is a fairly typical Terry Nation sort of character, subsequent stories reveal that he’s actually pretty advanced for the 41st Century, quite a bit ahead of other robots or A.I. Which makes him unique, but does beg the question of where he came from. Turns out, it’s an advanced A.I. research project, which has been forgotten about, accidentally or deliberately, by the Powers That Be, leaving a bunch of androids and staff in a base on a deserted planet, surrounded by woodland and alien bears. This is one of those stories where, if you figure out the twist before the main characters, they come off looking rather slow. The flashbacks to Mark’s “childhood” are pretty intense, even tear-jerking, and make it pretty clear how he feels about Daleks and why. Despite having not turned up yet, they’re clearly a looming presence throughout the galaxy, and in most people’s personal histories. There are also rather a lot of bears in this story, who sound like they might be adorable.
docs.title: Cycle of Destruction

docs.text: Echoes of Extinction Time Lord Victorious audio Released: 16 April 2021 This is the somewhat odd vinyl release that was part of the Time Lord Victorious storyline, except that for the Eighth Doctor, it’s kind of a prequel, and for the Tenth, it’s more of a coda. Oddly, although the Time Lord Victorious revolves around the Tenth Doctor, because of the multimedia format, this is the only piece in which David Tennant portrays the Tenth Doctor. And boy, does he portray him. The Doctor is extremely Doctory in this story, talking a mile a minute, charming people, judging people, and being very, very sorry. It’s short, even by Big Finish standards, only about a half-hour, so there’s not much time for fakes or misdirection, and yet it feels complete, possibly because of the greater pace of Tenth Doctor stories. It’s also got some impressive guest actors, from Burn Gorman (Owen from Torchwood ) playing the monster to Arthur Darvill (Rory) playing a starship trooper to Mina Anwar (Gita Chandra from The Sarah Jane Adventures ). This story almost certainly would benefit from listening to both halves in order, but it’s not really a huge deal. The Doctor can’t really remember the first half of the story , so it’s OK if the listener doesn’t either. What’s interesting is that the Doctor makes a compassionate choice. He’s no longer interested in just stopping the monsters, or being “fire and ice and rage.” You can see he learned something from the Time Lord Victorious , and maybe he’s more at peace with himself after “ The Day of the Doctor .” This is a Doctor very close to the end of his time, and it’s impressive that Alfie Shaw managed to portray that. This is also the end for David Tennant in this project, at least for the time being.
docs.title: Echoes of Extinction

docs.text: Expiry Dating The Tenth Doctor and River Song #1 Released: 25 November 2020 Listened: 11/23/22 This particular boxed set was a 2020 release, which means it was a pandemic recording. In fact, it was kind of thrown together in a hurry when it became clear that David Tennant was willing and capable of recording from his home during lockdown. And he did a lot of it, but this was where it started. It’s also interesting in storytelling terms, because this era is the one spot where River can interact with the Tenth Doctor, after the Library, but before his regeneration. Thing is, he knows very little about River at this point, and he knows a lot more by “The Time of Angels,” so what happened in the interim? Well, this did. And it could just come off as blatant fanservice, unless the writers were very careful and the actors were very good…which they all happen to be. This story, by James Goss, is at the beginning, so it’s kind of tentative, so Goss rather cleverly set it up as a series of letters between the Doctor and River. River’s doing her enigmatic thing, where she has to get the Doctor to do something, but can’t tell him exactly what or why, so she has to manipulate him into it, and of course he pushes against that, which is exactly what River knows he’ll do, etc., etc. It ends up as a proper Moffat-y puzzle box, so you may want to listen multiple times if you want to really get your head around it, or you can just go with the flow. There are also some lovely cameos from other Doctors, who seem to be enjoying themselves immensely. But for the most part, it’s a two-hander between David Tennant and Alex Kingston, and it comes off brilliantly.
docs.title: Expiry Dating

docs.text: Fear of Flying Short Trips #11.5 Released: 15 February 2022 Listened: 11/26/22 This Short Trip is from the 2022 collection, which means it’s a fairly long Short Trip. It’s read by Ayesha Antoine, a frequent Big Finish contributor, but not often used as a narrator. It’s told from the perspective of Hawa Hassan, an aspiring actress in the 22nd century. Unfortunately, she’s been struggling, and she needs to fly to her next audition, but she’s terrified of flying. The story makes the experience sound nearly identical to 21st-century flying, with the only real difference being the propulsion system. And just like now, there are some people afraid to fly, and some overly chatty, bordering on rude, passengers. Guess which one the Doctor is. He seems to be doing his usual motormouth act, with the effect of making Hawa increasingly nervous, but is he just being thoughtless, or is he winding her up for a reason? This is writer Paul Verhoeven’s only Big Finish work to date, but he captures the Tenth Doctor’s dialog style well, and Antoine does a reasonably good job of capturing the cadence, although she doesn’t try for an impression. The twist is pretty nice, perhaps a bit predictable, but predictable can still be good if it’s well-executed, and this one is.
docs.title: Fear of Flying

docs.text: Ghosts The Tenth Doctor and River Song #3 Released: 25 November 2020 Listened: 11/26/22 The last of the Tenth and River stories is a bit of a mind-bender by Jonny Morris. The Doctor meets River on the “most haunted planet in the galaxy,” known for its graveyards and ghosts. But of course that can’t be all that’s going on, and there’s almost nothing I can reveal without ruining it. What’s especially wonderful about this one is that the Doctor and River trust one another a lot more than previously. They’re both keeping secrets, and they each know the other has a good reason for that, but aside from that, there’s a level of trust. As a result, they’re more companionable than elsewhere, even more so than the Eleventh Doctor, because the Doctor believes they’ve come to an understanding. The dialog between the two is sharp, but neither has the upper hand. They’re just working on a mystery together, and it’s always fun to see the Tenth Doctor working something out in his head. On the whole, this boxed set is great for its special place in their relationship, where they can be mostly honest with one another. There aren’t any plans to do more of these, but I certainly wouldn’t object.
docs.title: Ghosts

docs.text: Hounded The Churchill Years #1.2 Released: 14 January 2016 Listened: 11/26/22 This is another of the Churchill stories, the first for the Tenth Doctor. Which means that David Tennant isn’t playing the part; Ian McNeice is more-or-less filling in for him, as well as playing the narrator. Much like the other stories in this set, McNeice doesn’t try for an impersonation, but rather tries to match the cadence and pace. Unfortunately, the Tenth Doctor speaks a mile a minute, and it’s kind of hard for McNeice to do. As a result, writer Alan Barnes gave the Doctor fewer lines, which is honestly uncharacteristic for him, and results in a sort of an “off” feeling to the story. The plot focuses on Churchill’s “black dog,” a metaphor he himself used to describe occasional bleak moods. Whether Churchill was actually manic depressive is a question for scholars, but this is Doctor Who , so of course the black dog is a creature that can physically manifest and drain the life energy out of people. A lot of the action falls to Hetty Warner , Churchill’s private secretary, who by 1941 is starting to take matters into her own hands regarding Churchill’s well-being, including summoning the Doctor. She serves as a nice companion-substitute, being quite capable and determined. Unfortunately, we won’t be seeing her again.
docs.title: Hounded

docs.text: Last Chance The Tenth Doctor Chronicles #1.4 Released: 18 April 2018 Listened: 12/15/22 In this story, Guy Adams gets his Douglas Adams on. Specifically, he tells a story about conservation, but the narrative style is very Adams-y, with a completely despicable bad guy acting rather nonsensically. The Doctor bumps into Lady Christina deSouza on the plains of Africa. It’s been quite a while for him, but not nearly as long for her. He’s busy rounding up last-of-their-kind creatures from Earth history, because the baddie is trying to kill them. In this particular case, they’re racing to save the last Great Auk. The story is too short for there to be a lot of twists or peril, really, because the baddie is mostly too stupid to be any real threat. There’s also a lot of narration, which cuts down on the dialog time. The main appeal is Lady Christina, and how she feels about the Doctor, which is to say, pretty entitled, but that’s Lady Christina for you. She’s not all that impressive, but she’s not really a companion.
docs.title: Last Chance

docs.text: Out of Time Out of Time #1 Released: 26 August 2020 Listened: 11/27/22 This is the first of three Big Finish crossover stories that were recorded in lockdown, when David Tennant suddenly had a lot of time on his hands. A Fourth/Tenth Doctor crossover was always high on just about everybody’s wish list, and this story pretty much fit the bill. The Doctor is coming off his Time Lord Victorious binge , and is in his extended “I don’t want to go” period of dodging the summons from the Ood . He’s companionless, and directionless, which brings him to a cathedral outside of time, where the Fourth Doctor is recovering after the events of “ The Deadly Assassin .” Basically, the Tenth Doctor fan-goobers all over the Fourth, while still maintaining his own superiority by dint of experience. The Fourth Doctor finds the Tenth to be arrogant, as well as a reminder of his own mortality – logically, if the Tenth Doctor exists at all, the Fourth no longer does. And yet he doesn’t regard that as a loss, but as a continuation of his own life, an attitude the Tenth Doctor doesn’t share. We’ve also got Daleks invading the cathedral and killing people, but it’s a little bit pro-forma, and honestly, that’s fine. docs.text: Precious Annihilation The Tenth Doctor and River Song #2 Released: 25 November 2020 Listened: 11/24/22 Although a bunch of time seems to have passed for the Doctor since he last met River, this is the very next story in the boxed set. The Doctor’s attitude toward River has softened a bit, and he’s not quite so anxious to figure out who she is. On the flip side, he’s not real happy about her tendency to escalate situations and resort to violence. This story isn’t as timey-wimey as the previous , but that’s a really high bar. It’s still fairly timey-wimey, taking place in both 1912 and the 1600s. They’re investigating the Cheapside Hoard , from which some of the gemstones have turned out to be explosive (oops), a dramatic deviation from recorded history. River’s got some skills that are a surprise to the Doctor, and she loves frustrating him with what he doesn’t know at this point. She’s also ridiculously flirty, almost as much as I’ve ever seen her. Mind you, the Tenth Doctor deserves some flirting. The Doctor’s arrogance is on display here too, both the “I can save anybody” and the “time has to do what I say” varieties. Lizzie Hopley has crafted a story that’s fun, with historical details, but really asks a big question, specifically “How far would you go for someone you love?” And acknowledging that the answer can be pretty scary indeed.
docs.title: Precious Annihilation

docs.text: Table for Two, Dinner for One Short Trips #12.5 Released: 2 February 2023 Listened: 3/15/23 This Short Trip is from the 2023 collection, and also read by Ayesha Antoine. Like the last, it’s first-person, told by Mandy, who badly fumbled her relationship with a friend / would-be boyfriend, and who believes she’s meeting him at a restaurant to get closure. Except that’s not even slightly what’s going on. New writer Jennah Dean gives Mandy a distinct voice: she’s smart, has a clever way with words, is too polite for her own good, and eventually proves to be more self-aware than most of us trying to get over heartbreak. The Doctor stays offscreen for most of it, but when he does appear, he makes an impact, running over everything with the Tenth Doctor’s characteristic overconfidence. The story also takes advantage of the fact that he’s just recently left Rose behind for good, and is starting to heal from that, except there’s some really dark times ahead he doesn’t know about. This one creates a really vivid atmosphere, making the story very easy to picture.
docs.title: Table for Two, Dinner for One

docs.text: The Dalek Defence Dalek Universe #3.2 Released: 13 October 2021 Listened: 12/11/22 We’re down to the final two-parter by Matt Fitton, and yes, we can now, finally , have some Daleks. In fact, we can have a bona-fide sequel to “ Destiny of the Daleks .” It seems that the Earth Forces prisoner transport that Davros was on at the end of that story ran into some trouble, and had to pass off its cargo to another ship, which the Doctor and Anya are now on, in between the Dalek and Movellan battle fleets. Which is bad news for everybody involved, because the only option is to defrost Davros and use him as a bargaining chip. It’s an interesting dynamic, seeing this version of Davros – “Destiny” and “ Genesis ” were recent for him; skipping over long periods of suspended animation, he’s still relatively young. He does recognize the Doctor right away, though. For the Doctor, however, he last saw Davros in “ Journey’s End ,” going way off the deep end and trying to destroy reality. So there’s some bitterness there. In fact, the Doctor spends large parts of this story insisting that he knows best, only to get ignored by absolutely everybody, including Anya at times. All of which sets up a cliffhanger in which the First Movellan turns out to be real, and someone we know.
docs.title: The Dalek Defence

docs.text: The First Son Dalek Universe #3.1 Released: 13 October 2021 Listened: 12/10/22 We’re now on the third boxed set of this story, so maybe now it’s time for some Dal-–nah, have some Movellans ! And River Song, because why not? Except is it River? There’s a Movellan who looks just like River, but she continually denies that’s who she is. She’s also got a “son,” Kamen Vers, who seems to be some kind of advanced Movellan – more organic, and definitely more emotional. Except he’s got the mind of a supercomputer, the body of an android, and the morality of a two-year-old; never a good combination. They’re all hiding out on a planetoid made of crashed spaceships, along with a bunch of human refugees, and a bunch of Movellans who’ve gone insane, all of them hiding from Dalek and Movellan fleets in the vicinity. There’s a bunch of waffle about the “first Movellan,” who Kamen seems to regard as both a father and a god, also a bad combo. The real core of the story is River’s “is she or isn’t she?” which doesn’t unravel until nearly the very end. In fairness to Lizzie Hopley, that part is well done, and will keep you guessing. The rest of the story feels like filler.
docs.title: The First Son

docs.text: The Gates of Hell Out of Time #2 Released: 2 June 2021 Listened: 11/28/22 It’s a bit odd that these Tenth Doctor crossovers are occurring all in a row like this, but that seems to be the way they were intended. This time it’s the Fifth Doctor and the Tenth vs. the Cybermen. These are my two favorite Doctors, so you’d think that I’d be over the moon about this story, but unfortunately, I’m not. Unlike the last story, there’s no dancing around the Doctor’s identity, and no admiring each other unawares. They just meet up, recognize each other from “ Time Crash ,” and get on with the story. In addition, the Tenth Doctor defers to the Fifth a bit, instead of citing his greater experience as in the last story. Per writer David Llewellyn, this is a reference to Peter Davison being David Tennant’s father-in-law in real life; however, it makes the story seem somewhat odd. The Fifth Doctor comes off as being slower, more contemplative, which isn’t really fitting. Granted, anybody looks slow compared to the Tenth Doctor, but the Fifth was full of youthful energy. It’s like it was written for Peter Davison as he currently is, not the Fifth Doctor from the 80s. As for the story, it’s a Cyberman invasion of Paris in the 1800s, which messes up the timelines something fierce, which is what draws both Doctors to investigate. Although the plan is somewhat timey-wimey, it actually doesn’t take all that much effort to stop, which is a little disappointing. Of note in the guest cast is Mark Gatiss, unfortunately unrecognizable playing a Frenchman. Also Shelley Conn plays a Time Agent named Tina Drake, with an American accent that’s slightly more natural than most Big Finish Americans, but still not really great. It feels like Tina should be a recurring character, but she hasn’t, as yet. Unfortunately, this story is mostly unmet potential, which is a bummer.
docs.title: The Gates of Hell

docs.text: The House of Kingdom Dalek Universe #1.3 Released: 14 April 2021 Listened: 12/3/22 Should we see some Daleks in this Dalek Universe event? Nah, have some Mechonoids instead. They translate remarkably well to audio, where their habit of spitting out random numbers and words makes them sound just as awkward as their big round bodies look. They’re implacable, though, as good robot menaces always are, which is useful in this story, as they’re helping to terraform Neptune. The story is mostly about putting Anya through the wringer, though, as we find out rather a lot about her past, and meet her grandfather Merrick. We learn that her mother was killed by Daleks while Anya was still young, and she blames her grandfather for not saving her. So of course the Doctor reveals (to Merrick, not Anya) that he knew Brett and Sara, but not how they died. Although Anya’s venom causes both the Doctor and the listener to think that Merrick has been unfairly accused, it’s a good bit more complicated than that. The story ends on another cliffhanger, because this isn’t really three boxed sets as much as it’s a nine-part story.
docs.title: The House of Kingdom

docs.text: The Jago and Litefoot Revival Short Trips #7.3 Released: 22 December 2020 Listened: 12/16/22 This particular Short Trip had a number of unusual features at the time of its release (2017): It was a two-part story told over two releases, it had two narrators, Trevor Baxter and Christopher Benjamin, and it was told in the style of a Companion Chronicle, with Jago and Litefoot each recounting a part of the story, experienced from their own perspective. Most of all, though, it featured the Tenth and Eleventh Doctors, although not together. The Tenth Doctor, during his “farewell tour” at the very end of “ The End of Time ,” encounters George Litefoot on Minos. Whereas the Eleventh Doctor visits Henry Gordon Jago at the New Regency theater. Most of the story is honestly setup, told in the rather wordy style of Jago & Litefoot, as Litefoot prepares to relate the story to a scientific club and Jago interferes, with the intent of spicing up the story. Even within the flashback, it takes a while to get going, mostly making the point that Jago & Litefoot were bored, not having bumped into any aliens in a while. Once it finally picks up speed, it stops on a cliffhanger. Two cliffhangers, really. It’s hard to call this one a Tenth Doctor story and the other an Eleventh, because it’s really two stories told in parallel, but I’m choosing to do it this way because I can. Which means this is more or less it for the Tenth Doctor in this project, but as we all know, he doesn’t want to go.
docs.title: The Jago and Litefoot Revival

docs.text: The Lost Dalek Universe #2.3 Released: 14 July 2021 Listened: 12/8/22 The Doctor isn’t in a good place right now. Mark’s been killed by a Dalek, and even though the Doctor didn’t know him that long, he’s still pretty tired of this stuff. Plus, he and Anya are in a rapidly disintegrating ship with a malfunctioning time drive, which drops them in an empty bubble universe. Even better, it’s one of those bubble universes built as a prison for a Being From Before Time, who did a Bad Thing. The being naturally wants to get out, which it can only do in the consciousness of a mortal, and being immaterial, the only thing it can do is mentally torment the Doctor and Anya until one of them agrees. The Doctor’s got plenty of torment-fodder, but he’s been through this sort of thing before, and he’s not biting. For Anya, though, the Lost can reveal what happened to Brett Vyon and Sara Kingdom , and what the Doctor had to do with that. Rob Valentine seems to be trying to paint an equivalence between the Doctor’s lie of omission about the Kingdoms and Anya’s deception around Ann Kelso , but I don’t think I buy it. Anya didn’t really have much choice about Ann’s fate. I’m not overly fond of an “it never happened” resolution, and neither is the Doctor, really, but at least the consequences stick, and the Doctor and Anya are forced to tell some truth. On the whole, the point of this second boxed set seems to be making the Doctor very sad, but also confronting him with the results of his actions. We’re six episodes in, though, and there’s still a notable absence of Daleks.
docs.title: The Lost

docs.text: The Shattered Hourglass Short Trips #10.12 Released: 22 December 2020 Listened: 4/20/26 In " The End of Time ," the Doctor mentions that while he was stalling, he named a galaxy "Alison." This is that story. It rather particularly takes place after The Time Lord Victorious, when the Doctor has realized his own mistakes, and is determined not to let anyone else repeat them. Of course, this is still the Tenth Doctor, so he's going to be arrogant and high-handed while he does it. In this case, he goes up against the Time Agency, and pretty much knows everything that's going to happen before they do. The Seventh Doctor would be proud. Robert Napton, in his only Doctor Who contribution, captures both the Tenth Doctor's voice and his physicality, not a bad trick in a short audio story. Neve McIntosh is always a delight to hear, especially narrating in her own native accent. This one might be a bit predictable, but that's OK when it's done well.
docs.title: The Shattered Hourglass

docs.text: The Triumph of Davros Dalek Universe #3.3 Released: 13 October 2021 Listened: 12/13/22 The First Movellan turns out to be Mark Seven, tying together Terry Nation properties in a way that…kinda makes sense, but wasn’t really necessary, and smacks of narrative convenience. If you listened to these as they came out, it’s been months since Mark died, and you’ve probably forgotten about him. But if you’re listening all in a row like this, it’s only been a couple of episodes, and you’ve got a high chance of seeing it coming. I’m not sure we needed a “Genesis of the Movellans” story, because they’re really not all that interesting, except as a foil for the Daleks. As for Davros, he continues to be a complete amoral slime, helping the Movellans out until he has the opportunity to screw them over in favor of his Daleks, who don’t actually want him around. And the Doctor takes kind of a back seat in this one. He’s started actively trying to avoid mucking up the web of time, probably because he knows where Davros needs to end up next , and really doesn’t want to mess with that. With the ending known, it kind of takes some of the air out of the climax. In a Matt Fitton story, you’re really more interested in the character relationships, and it is interesting to see how Anya and the Doctor have healed the fracture that started a very long time ago ( for him ), but I’m not sure that she ends up as a better person because of it. She really hasn’t changed all that much. The Doctor ends up back where he needs to be, and decides to go visit Elizabeth I, leading directly to the anniversary story .
docs.title: The Triumph of Davros

docs.text: Dalek Universe #3.3 Released: 13 October 2021 Listened: 12/13/22 The First Movellan turns out to be Mark Seven, tying together Terry Nation properties in a way that…kinda makes sense, but wasn’t really necessary, and smacks of narrative convenience. If you listened to these as they came out, it’s been months since Mark died, and you’ve probably forgotten about him. But if you’re listening all in a row like this, it’s only been a couple of episodes, and you’ve got a high chance of seeing it coming. I’m not sure we needed a “Genesis of the Movellans” story, because they’re really not all that interesting, except as a foil for the Daleks. As for Davros, he continues to be a complete amoral slime, helping the Movellans out until he has the opportunity to screw them over in favor of his Daleks, who don’t actually want him around. And the Doctor takes kind of a back seat in this one. He’s started actively trying to avoid mucking up the web of time, probably because he knows where Davros needs to end up next , and really doesn’t want to mess with that. With the ending known, it kind of takes some of the air out of the climax. In a Matt Fitton story, you’re really more interested in the character relationships, and it is interesting to see how Anya and the Doctor have healed the fracture that started a very long time ago ( for him ), but I’m not sure that she ends up as a better person because of it. She really hasn’t changed all that much. The Doctor ends up back where he needs to be, and decides to go visit Elizabeth I, leading directly to the anniversary story .
docs.title: The Triumph of Davros

docs.text: The Trojan Dalek Dalek Universe #2.2 Released: 14 July 2021 Listened: 12/7/22 The Doctor, Anya, and Mark are still looking for time-travel tech to help the Doctor get back where he belongs. They’re trying to track down a temporal scientist named Arborecc, which leads them to an SSS station that houses both medical facilities and research labs. Except this is one of those human outposts where they’re trying anything they can to defeat the Daleks, no matter how unethical, or how much it costs in human lives. The key element of this story is to put the Doctor through the wringer, emotionally, and at that it succeeds. He’s back on the wrong side of the Time War, and the Daleks are once again taking away things that are important to him. Elsewhere, we get to see an old friend of Mark’s, surprising everybody with the idea that Mark has old friends, even one who has a crush on him. Plus we get Dalek voices by a bunch of actors who aren’t Nick Briggs, which is an unusual twist.
docs.title: The Trojan Dalek

docs.text: The Wrong Woman Dalek Universe #1.2 Released: 14 April 2021 Listened: 12/1/22 Surprise, the Doctor has regenerated into a woman, but it’s Gemma Whelan, not Jodie Whittaker. Obviously, something funky is going on here, but it’s a lot of fun to hear Whelan act like a newly regenerated Time Lord, reveling in the mania and rushing all about. ( Spoiler: It’s not the Doctor, it’s the Monk, or rather “the Nun” as she prefers to be known now. Once you know, it’s hard to miss, because Whelan’s dialog is very nearly as plummy as Rufus Hound’s is.) Outside of that, there’s an awful lot of timey-wimey going on in this story, most of it continued from the previous, and John Dorney usually does a good job of keeping his timey and his wimey straight. It becomes clear to the Doctor that he’s been brought back to before the Time War, which is an impressive trick, and without the TARDIS, he’s stuck here. And we know how well he responds to being stuck. Mark gets to be rather superhero-y in this one, and also seems just a touch more arrogant than the last story, even though he’d deny it. Once the big twist is resolved, the rest of the story is good, but doesn’t quite come up to the same level.
docs.title: The Wrong Woman

docs.text: Wink Out of Time #3 Released: 8 June 2022 Listened: 11/28/22 The third and final crossover (even the Doctor is starting to think this is odd) unites the Sixth and Tenth Doctors, and sets them up against Weeping Angels. Writer Lisa McMullin tosses out several Angel-related high concepts, like what would happen if an Angel feasted on a Time Lord with several regenerations left (the Angel gets very powerful and reproduces), or what would happen if the Angels came across a planet where the natives had no sense of sight (buffet, is what happens). Much like the previous story , the Doctors don’t waste any time establishing their respective identities and get right to business. However, unlike the last story, any respect between the two is grudging. The Sixth Doctor is fairly spikey, criticizing both the Tenth Doctor’s hyper-verbosity, and his taste in interior decorating. For the Tenth Doctor’s part, the Sixth Doctor’s coat is way too easy of a target. However, he does suggest the Doctor might look better in blue, which the Sixth Doctor hadn’t considered yet, indicating this is probably early in his timeline. Lisa McMullin deserves praise for dealing with the Angels on audio, which is no mean trick, but she pulls it off without any clunky dialog. She also doesn’t spend too much time trying to explain sight and color to the sightless characters, although it does pop up when least expected. On the whole, the clever storytelling makes up for a lack of Doctory banter, which makes this better than “ The Gates of Hell ,” but not as good as “ Out of Time .”
docs.title: Wink

docs.text: The Third Doctor The era of the Third Doctor represented a major change in the format of the show, and for the most part, the Big Finish series reflects that. The most prominent change was that the show was in color, but along with that, the pacing became more dynamic and action-oriented. At the same time, Jon Pertwee played the Doctor as a more physical character than his predecessors. He was more physically imposing, and more likely to take charge of a situation. In addition, he spent a lot of his era exiled to Earth, for budgetary reasons, but that also means that he had a “home base” and a regular cast of supporting characters in UNIT. Although I’ve divided the eras by companion, the UNIT characters are often present in these stories. Exactly which UNIT actors were available for a story varied, especially after the death of Nicholas Courtney in 2011. Although there are some Companion Chronicles from this era, Big Finish drew a line separating out the first two Doctors for their extended Chronicles series and the Early Adventures. Instead, in 2015, they made a deliberate decision to recast the Doctor for the first time, bringing in Tim Treloar. They seem to have done this with great care and even trepidation, going very slowly to see how the audience would react to a recast Doctor. However, the reception seems to have been positive, leading them to risk recasting the Brigadier in 2019, and Liz and Sarah Jane in 2021.
docs.title: Third Doctor

docs.text: The Third Doctor and Jo The era with Jo Grant is pretty extensive, as she had three TV seasons, more than Liz or Sarah, but it’s also extensive within Big Finish, because Katy Manning has been one of the more enthusiastic participants, voicing not only Jo, but Iris Wildthyme as well. Katy does a decent job of sounding like her younger self, and although not perfect, you get used to it quickly. In narrated stories, her version of the Doctor sounds...well, a lot like Jo trying to imitate the Doctor, so that’s fair. Jo always was kind of an odd fit within UNIT, and these stories vary from showing her as part of the UNIT team, to displaying her independent streak. The Doctor regained his ability to travel in the middle of this era, allowing Big Finish to nicely split stories set on Earth with stories on other planets. Most of the latter don’t have much UNIT in them, and feel more like traditional Doctor/companion stories. Katy has also worked on the Third Doctor Adventures series with Tim Treloar, helping to ease concerns about the recasting with her enthusiastic support, so most of those (thus far) appear in this era.
