docs.text: The Gulf Third Doctor Adventures #7.2 Released: 18 May 2021 Listened: 7/10/21 Now we return to a story with someone actually playing Sarah Jane. It’s not Elisabeth Sladen, sadly, but it’s Sadie Miller, her daughter, which has to be the next best thing. This one is also an alien planet, and an ocean world like “ Scourge of the Cybermen ,” but a dramatically different story. Instead of a big colony, it’s a small artist commune set up in a former industrial facility, with just a few people resident. All of the artists are women, which makes the Doctor the only male character in the story, but that’s never a plot point. As often happens in these situations, the TARDIS is unreachable, there’s a psychic entity picking off the residents one at a time, and if that’s not enough, the sea is poisonous. There’s a tight tension, similar to what you’d find in “ Horror of Fang Rock ” or “Midnight,” although I don’t think it leans into the horror as much as either of those. Sarah Jane gets to put her investigative skills to good use, as well as her empathy. Sadie Miller isn’t going for a direct impersonation, as recast actors often don’t. As a result, sometimes she doesn’t sound much like Sarah, but other times she’s dead on, especially in cases of the snarky asides that Sarah enjoyed. Tim Treloar stretches a bit as the Doctor, and sometimes you can see him with a line that Pertwee might have done differently, but on the whole, it’s quality work. It’s a solid story, but not a particular standout.
docs.title: The Gulf

There’s a tight tension, similar to what you’d find in “ Horror of Fang Rock ” or “Midnight,” although I don’t think it leans into the horror as much as either of those. Sarah Jane gets to put her investigative skills to good use, as well as her empathy. Sadie Miller isn’t going for a direct impersonation, as recast actors often don’t. As a result, sometimes she doesn’t sound much like Sarah, but other times she’s dead on, especially in cases of the snarky asides that Sarah enjoyed. Tim Treloar stretches a bit as the Doctor, and sometimes you can see him with a line that Pertwee might have done differently, but on the whole, it’s quality work. It’s a solid story, but not a particular standout.
docs.title: The Gulf

docs.text: The House that Hoxx Built Classic Doctors New Monsters #3.1 Released: 28 July 2022 Listened: 8/3/22 In production time, it’s been a few years since the first two sets of CDNM stories, but this is one of the earliest in the chronology. The formula gets changed up a bit this time, as we’re incorporating the Third Doctor, and in this boxed set, the Doctors have companions with them, in this case Sarah Jane. We’re also stretching the definition of “monster” quite a bit, as this story features the Hoxx of Balhoon, brother to the Moxx of Balhoon from “The End of the World” on TV. The story appears to take place in roughly the same time period, as the Hoxx is also interested in Earth conservation, and has convinced Galactic Heritage to reconstruct an old manor house on the otherwise empty Earth. Of course, if you rebuild an English manor house, you’re inevitably going to get ghosts along with it. In addition to the Hoxx, there’s his ward Francesca, a Fleeceling (evolved sheep), and a butler named Butler. Butler is rather sinister and ghostly, but that’s because he’s a holographic life form, and a glitching one at that. Tim Foley lays the references on fairly thick here, for fans of the new series, as well as a few hidden classic references as well. The atmosphere is properly spooky, and it’s hard to determine on first listen just who’s behind all the spookiness. Sadie Miller continues playing Sarah Jane, and sounds even more like her mother this time. Dan Starkey plays the Hoxx, in a departure from his normal roles, and you’ll never know until the credits. It’s a nice tight story all around.
docs.title: The House that Hoxx Built

docs.text: The Paradise of Death BBC Radio Released: 27 August 1993 - 24 September 1993 Listened: 2/12/22 This story, along with “ The Ghosts of N-Space ” was produced by BBC Radio in 1993, which means it stars Jon Pertwee, Elisabeth Sladen, and Nicholas Courtney in their respective roles, which Big Finish, sadly, cannot claim. Listening to this really brings into focus how good a job Tim Treloar, Sadie Miller, and John Culshaw are doing. It’s written by Barry Letts, and…well, it’s kinda disappointing for a Barry Letts story. Yes, there’s a political message, not particularly subtle, but the plot has some questionable turns, and a lot of the secondary characters are little more than caricatures. Bonus companion Jeremy Fitzoliver is particularly odious; he’s like a parody of a fan. He can’t seem to do anything right, and is constantly exclaiming “Oh, I say!” and other insipid drivel. You get the impression that not even Sarah likes him very much; the Doctor and the Brig are clearly just tolerating him. There’s rather a lot made of a planet that makes extensive use of VR to keep the populace placated. There’s a cool opening scene at a new amusement park that really goes nowhere, just an excuse to get UNIT involved. Unfortunately, the story seems to know that it’s on audio, and fights against the limitations: the single-user VR rigs mean that characters have to describe what they’re seeing out loud, and a climactic arena fight is described by onlookers rather than being “shown.” One gets the feeling that modern Big Finish could overcome those problems, but we’re a few years too early for that. But still, hearing the classic actors again is worth the price of admission.
docs.title: The Paradise of Death

docs.text: Council of War Companion Chronicles #7.12 Released: 11 June 2013 Listened: 7/4/21 This one is slightly unusual in a number of ways. It’s the only Companion Chronicle featuring John Levene as Sgt. John Benton, for a start. It also has the narration split between Benton and secondary character Margery Phipps, even though it’s told entirely in the present tense. Finally, it’s written by Simon Barnard and Paul Morris (creators of the Scarifyers audio stories), which means it’s not a terribly serious story. Paul Morris admits that he wanted to take advantage of a throwaway line that Benton knew how to ballroom dance, and the story grew from that. It involves Benton going undercover as a town councillor in Kettering, a task that would normally go to Mike Yates, but Mike is still recovering from being mind-controlled in “ The Green Death ,” which is why the story is set here. Benton and Phipps end up being kidnapped by aliens for extremely silly reasons, but Benton’s knowledge of military history allows him to come up with a plan, yet without involving much in the way of violence, which keeps it as a fitting Doctor Who story. There’s a bit of Doctor-ex-machina at the end, but that’s only to be expected in a Companion Chronicle. In this sort of story, the main narrator is called upon to voice several characters, and it must be said that neither John Levene’s Doctor nor his Brigadier are very believable. In fact, this is probably the poorest rendition of the Doctor I’ve heard from a former companion actor. Fortunately, they’re not really in it that much. It’s a fine story, good for a laugh.
docs.title: Council of War

docs.text: Landbound Short Trips #7.X Released: 29 December 2017 Listened: 7/4/21 This is one of the bonus short trips normally released in December, but it’s not a Christmas story, nor is it a traditional Doctor Who story, nor a typical Short Trips vignette. Instead, it takes place over three different points of the Third Doctor’s life, three times that he encounters a former ship’s captain who lost his ship and crew under mysterious circumstances. Taken together, the three incidents help him deal with his exile on Earth, the restoration of his freedom, and the loss of Jo. As with “ The Prisoner of Peladon ,” there’s a hint here that without a companion, the Doctor doesn’t quite understand what humans need or want, although he’s trying. Nick Briggs reads this one, and his Third Doctor voice isn’t the most accurate, but he gives it a good shot. The voice he uses for the ship’s captain is pretty much the same one Briggs uses whenever he needs a Northern accent, which seems a little overdone, but it’s not bad. One of the longer Short Trips, this one is decently atmospheric.
docs.title: Landbound

docs.text: Supernature Third Doctor Adventures #11.1 Released: 23 February 2023 Listened: 3/4/23 This 2023 release more or less exists because of real-world circumstances. Katy Manning, while a gifted voice actor, was no longer finding it easy to portray young Jo anymore. And Stewart Bevan, who played Professor Cliff Jones, had recently died, so they decided to have the character die as well, which sets up Jo’s arc here. It’s the modern day, and Jo’s feeling a bit bereft without Cliff, although her extended family is carrying on his work of feeding the world. She goes to investigate strange happenings on the Isle of Wight, and runs into the Third Doctor. For him, it’s only a little bit after “ The Green Death ,” and he’s still hurting from Jo’s departure. That means Jo knows an awful lot about the Doctor’s future that she can’t tell him, and also means that the Eleventh Doctor was dancing around the truth when he talked to Jo in “The Death of the Doctor,” but that’s pretty typical for him. Because this is Matt Fitton writing, the emphasis is on Jo and the Doctor’s feelings on seeing one another again, but it’s also been 50 years for Jo, and no time at all for the Doctor, so the older, more capable Jo keeps throwing him and his 70s attitude off-stride. Of course, there’s also a plot going on here, but only a small one, as it’s a two-part story. There’s a secretive organization trying to develop a new weapon using alien technology, because of course there is, and it’s harming the local wildlife, so Jo and the Doctor show up to stop it. There’s no indication of what this organization actually is, but they don’t like UNIT, and they use the phrase “For King and Country,” which could indicate a link to the Forge, or could simply be because King Charles is on the throne now. Regardless, the story achieves its goal of putting the Doctor and 2023 Jo back together again for more adventures.
docs.title: Supernature

docs.text: Terror of the Master Masterful audio novel Released: 2 January 2021 Listened: 7/3/21 This is a Big Finish audio novel, a proof-of-concept released a few months before the first official entry in that series. That means it’s a narrated story, not a full-cast recording. However, because it’s read by John Culshaw, who is easily capable of impersonating the Doctor, the Master, the Brig, Yates, and Benton to a very accurate degree, it has a full-cast quality to it. Given that it’s set after Jo, but before Sarah, he’s relieved of having to do many women’s voices. This period was also during the construction of the “Whomobile,” which gives the story a nice hook to talk about pollution, which concerned the recently-departed Jo, and also Mike. In fact, even the Master seems concerned about rising pollution levels on Earth, but of course his method of dealing with it is entirely horrible, teaming up with an ameboid creature who can both absorb and emit carbon dioxide in large quantities. As usual with this version of the Master, he’s chosen an ally whose goals aren’t entirely aligned, and makes his plan rather precarious. The audiobook format, as opposed to Big Finish’s usual full-cast dramas or low-cast “chronicles,” means that the story is much longer, about three and a half hours, although the plot itself isn’t much more involved than a typical story. However, it does give you a chance to experience the internal thoughts of the characters, which is especially interesting when it’s the Master. Big Finish adds period-appropriate background music and sound effects, which really makes the whole story more like a heavily narrated “chronicle,” than an audiobook. It was a good experience, and I’m happy to try it out again.
docs.title: Terror of the Master

docs.text: The Conservitors Third Doctor Adventures #11.2 Released: 23 February 2023 Listened: 3/5/23 Jo’s first trip this time around is to a human colony in the 49th century. It’s a fairly well-developed planet, but it has a rather new-series concept: Every person has a personal risk rating, like a credit score, and if your score gets too high, you’ll lose privileges (up to imprisonment) to keep you safe. Of course, Jo and the Doctor have only been there a couple of minutes before deciding to join the rebellion, and because this is a one-hour story, they find a rebel group quite quickly. The Doctor spends a fair part of this story sidelined or hobbled, and Jo’s the one wielding the Sonic most of the time. Which gives the Doctor a chance to be protective (Jo has a family now, after all), and for Jo to thwap him upside the head with her lifetime of experience. She’s practiced at civil disobedience, getting arrested, recognizing when movements turn fanatic, and she’s even got form disarming bombs. Which is handy, because this rebellion isn’t just a civic movement; it’s also personal for several of the characters involved. Relatively new writer Felicia Barker leans hard into new-series influences here. You could probably swap out the Third Doctor for the Tenth or Eleventh with very little change to the story itself. But that’s OK, because it’s a Jo story.
docs.title: The Conservitors

docs.text: The Iron Shore Third Doctor Adventures #11.3 Released: 23 February 2023 Listened: 3/5/23 The next trip for the Doctor and Jo is…kinda strange. They end up on an ocean planet, in a shipyard that’s fallen on hard times because of a “curse.” There are also indigenous people who object to the folks who built the dock. Jo’s on their side, naturally, but not nearly as much as I would have expected her to be. She’s also sympathetic to the suffering dockworkers, who believe themselves victims of a curse. Basically, everybody’s miserable, and nobody wants to talk about their problems straight away, which leaves the Doctor and Jo operating in ignorance for a while. When the monster finally does appear, it seems to be a “misplaced alien causes trouble accidentally” situation…except that’s not what’s going on, not remotely. Very oddly for this series, the story is narrated by Jo, and opens with a scene where the Doctor is badly hurt, with the rest told in flashback. That puts the emphasis on Jo and Katy Manning’s narration skills, but I’m not really sure it was necessary. The story is very atmospheric, but also kind of confusing. It feels like there should be more to solve the natives’ plight. It’s never really clear whether this is a space-faring civilization or not, probably because it was originally set in Liverpool, but got moved to an alien planet.
docs.title: The Iron Shore

docs.text: The Prisoner of Peladon Companion Chronicles #4.3 Released: 25 September 2009 Listened: 7/3/21 This is an unusual Companion Chronicle in that there’s no companion. There is, however, the returning character of King Peladon, played by David Troughton, son of Patrick Troughton, close friend to the franchise, and frequent Big Finish actor. In traditional Chronicles fashion, it’s told as a flashback, as a story King Peladon is telling to his daughter Thalira, the future queen . The flashback is set five years after “ The Curse of Peladon ,” during a Martian Civil War, in which Martian refugees took refuge on Peladon, with the King’s blessing. Of course, because this is Peladon, nothing goes quite the way it’s supposed to, there’s a mystery and intrigue, and Ice Warrior politics plays into all of it. There’s also a rare moment of the Doctor getting called out for going too far, similar to what Donna believed about him. That works best when the Doctor is without a companion, and having it delivered by a king is a nice touch. Alpha Centauri is present, because of course it is, but Troughton is forced to perform its voice, and he’s no Ysanne Churchman (but who is?). Nick Briggs provides the voice for the Ice Warriors, as he often does, but sounds much more clearly like himself than usual. This is also a very rare directing credit for Nicola Bryant. Although they never went back to that well again, it was a nice effort.
docs.title: The Prisoner of Peladon

Of course, because this is Peladon, nothing goes quite the way it’s supposed to, there’s a mystery and intrigue, and Ice Warrior politics plays into all of it. There’s also a rare moment of the Doctor getting called out for going too far, similar to what Donna believed about him. That works best when the Doctor is without a companion, and having it delivered by a king is a nice touch. Alpha Centauri is present, because of course it is, but Troughton is forced to perform its voice, and he’s no Ysanne Churchman (but who is?). Nick Briggs provides the voice for the Ice Warriors, as he often does, but sounds much more clearly like himself than usual. This is also a very rare directing credit for Nicola Bryant. Although they never went back to that well again, it was a nice effort.
docs.title: The Prisoner of Peladon

docs.text: The Thirteenth Doctor The Thirteenth Doctor marked a distinct change from what had gone before. Most obviously, the Doctor was played by a woman for the first time, Jodie Whittaker. We also saw three companions in the TARDIS for the first time in the modern series. Even more interesting, one of them was a grandfather. Showrunner Steven Moffat exited as well, resulting in a full turnover of everybody in front of and behind the camera. Unfortunately, although Chris Chibnall’s era had a ton of potential, I think it left something to be desired. The writing wasn’t as strong as in previous seasons, and the shorter seasons (down to 10 episodes initially) left less time for us to get to know most of the characters, including the Doctor. The pandemic shortened Series 13 even more, and left us with some big mysteries with the “Timeless Child” reveal. Unlike many modern-era Doctors, not only was Jodie willing to return, along with Mandip Gill, but Jo Martin’s Fugitive Doctor and Sacha Dhawan’s Master also returned for series of their own.
docs.title: Thirteenth Doctor

docs.text: Redacted BBC Sounds Released: 17 April - 19 June 2022 Listened: 10/21/22 This was an audio-only story produced by BBC Sounds, in 10 parts, to keep fans occupied during the long wait from “ Legend of the Sea Devils ” to “ The Power of the Doctor .” The story centers around three young, queer podcasters Abby McPhail, Shawna Thompson, and Cleo Proctor, who together run a podcast called “The Blue Box Files,” dedicated to the strange and conspiratorial, especially incidents related to a mysterious blue box. When people start disappearing, the women investigate, only to discover that people aren’t just disappearing, they’re being erased from history, and from people’s memories too. A few folks you might expect to be active in 2022 turn up, including Rani Chandra, Larry Nightingale , and UNIT, including Kate and Osgood . There are plenty of references, mostly small, and mostly new-series. The Doctor makes small cameos until the final episode, in which she’s pretty Doctor-y until the day is saved. I’m not much of a podcast person myself, but the story seems to reflect the culture of young podcasters pretty well, especially those who deal in the unusual. Cleo seems to be the primary character, and the least traditionally “companion-y,” but she does fairly well for herself, and never lacks for a snarky comment. It’s a nice introduction to the world of audio for the Thirteenth Doctor, and hopefully a sign of things to come.
docs.title: Redacted

docs.text: The Power of the Doctor TV Centenary Special 2022 Aired: 23 October 2022 This episode is the end of Series 13, the end of the Jodie Whittaker era, and part of the BBC’s Centenary celebrations. As such, Chibnall throws absolutely everything at the wall here. The Master is back again, working with Daleks and Cybermen. Dan almost dies, and asks to leave, which he does before the plot even gets going. There’s a lot going on back on Earth, so at UNIT, Kate calls in Ace and Tegan for help. (Squee!) The Master steals the Doctor’s body, forcing her to an interior regeneration-y place where she chats with the incarnations of the First, Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Doctors, all looking like their actors currently do. (More Squee!) Tegan and Ace get to interact with AI versions of their own Doctors, settling past differences (Super Squee!) After they win, the Doctor asks Yaz to leave, as her time is ending. (Awwww.) Graham and Dan form a support group for former companions, and invite Yaz, Tegan, Ace, and Kate, as well as Mel , Jo , and Ian ! (Mega Squee!) The Doctor has a beautiful, calm, regeneration into…David Tennant? ( What? )
docs.title: The Power of the Doctor

docs.text: The Twelfth Doctor The Twelfth Doctor is spiky, grumpy, and hard to get to know. After two rather lovable incarnations, Stephen Moffat wanted to go for something different. So he cast a much older actor, Peter Capaldi, and made him rather uncertain about himself. Although he’s much less friendly, he’s a lot more fundamentally honest, particularly with regard to himself and his place in the world. He’s also the Doctor who changes the most as a result of his experiences, as his costume, his hair, and his persona get more relaxed as the seasons pass. Like Tennant, Capaldi is also a known super-fan, but unlike Tennant, hasn’t jumped at the chance to do Big Finish. Initially he said he didn’t want to consider it until Jodie Whittaker’s tenure ended. Lately, he’s been indicating he’s just not interested. With Jenna Coleman also busy, we’ll have to wait and see what the future holds.
docs.title: Twelfth Doctor

docs.text: The Twelfth Doctor and Bill And then there was Bill Potts. Moffat finally introduced a traditional companion, rather than a huge mystery in the shape of a person. Bill has a humble background, but a fierce curiosity and desire to learn, which causes the Doctor to take her on as a student. Having a traditional mentor / learner relationship is good for this Doctor, as it’s a role he falls into naturally. Having a consistent home base he keeps returning to also allows Bill to have her own life, which is a benefit to her. Of course, Nardole is around, always nagging him about Missy in the basement, but you can’t have everything. This series is fairly recent, so no one involved has done Big Finish yet, meaning the only inserts are a couple of audiobooks.

docs.text: Emancipation of the Daleks Audio Novels #3 Released: 19 July 2022 Listened: 1/18/23 The first Big Finish product featuring Bill is this audio novel, which like the other novels is six hours long, divided into three parts, so at least there’s plenty of Bill to go around. It’s written by Johnathan Morris, who’s a good fit for the Twelfth Doctor, and narrated by Dan Starkey, who does a very nice Capaldi impression, possibly a touch better than Jacob Dudman’s. He also manages to catch Pearl Mackie’s speech rhythms, without trying to directly imitate her. Which is good, because Bill was particularly skilled at asking questions with her eyes, and that’s tricky to capture on audio. And she’s got plenty to question. A version of Bill from 20 years in the future turns up, which catapults them and the TARDIS into an alternate 2017 where a Dalek saucer crashed on Earth in the 1990s…and humanity ended up enslaving the Daleks instead of the other way ‘round. The second part starts with an extended flashback that details the life of this timeline’s Bill Potts, from the moment it diverged from the main one. It’s reminiscent of the Monks trilogy in a way, although for Bill, that hasn’t happened yet. And wow, is it grim. Probably grimmer than almost all but the darkest full-cast audios. And the third part takes place in yet another timeline, as the Daleks try to fix what went wrong, from their point of view. It’s very much Bill’s story, taking advantage of the fact that we never got to learn much about Bill on TV, specifically her relationship with Moira, her foster mother, and any friendships she had as a child. Jonathan Morris takes advantage of the fact that the listener understands the rules of changing history, and anticipates several of our questions, such as what happened to the Doctor and Nardole of the divergent timeline, or can we grab Missy from the vault to help (no, that’s a terrible idea). And the listener knows Bill’s eventual fate, so you’re wrong-footed at least part of the time. The more villainous, or at least amoral characters are fairly two-dimensional, although there’s a case to be made that while they may have been merely unpleasant in the original timeline, the opportunities provided by Dalek tech cause them to become full-blown evil, which seems a little bit forced. Of course, ultimately it’s a divergent timeline story, so you know how it has to end, but the getting there is a decent amount of fun. I’m looking forward to more Bill stories in the future, because she really is awesome.

docs.text: The Twelfth Doctor and Clara Clara marks the first companion since Mel to stick around through a regeneration, but then, Clara’s a special case who’s met all the Doctor’s previous selves. Unfortunately, with her puzzle box function fulfilled, Moffat didn’t seem to know how to characterize her, opting for “control freak,” apparently. She appears to consider herself the Doctor’s equal, if not superior, but her “impossible girl” history doesn’t really justify that. Or maybe it’s just how she deals with the new Doctor’s constant insults. Regardless, Jenna Coleman stuck around for two seasons, which was apparently one longer than she’d originally intended to. Now, she’s either busy, or doesn’t like doing audios, or both, so the only inserts in this section are a couple of chronicles.

docs.text: The Charge of the Night Brigade Tweflth Doctor Chronicles #1.1 Released: 13 February 2020 Listened: 1/6/23 Let’s get this bit out of the way: Jacob Dudman’s Twelfth Doctor isn’t as good as his Eleventh Doctor. He does get the cadence right, and the mannerisms, but the voice still sounds a bit like he has a head cold. Which is fine; I don’t think anybody expected a pitch-perfect Capaldi impersonation. This story takes place during the Crimean War, around 1855, and features Mary Seacole and her British Hotel, which conflicts with the Thirteenth Doctor story “War of the Sontarans,” but that takes place in an alternate timeline, so you can make it OK. (There’s also no mention of the fact that the Seventh Doctor, Ace, and Hex are nearby in Scutari , but there’s no reason to mention it.) The pacing of this story is a bit slower than previous new-series stories, in keeping with the pace of Season 8. The Doctor is described as wearing his white shirt and frock coat, and knows who Clara is, so it’s still early days for him, but he’s not nearly as spiky as one would expect from this era. Maybe without Clara to snark at, he’s a little kinder. He’s certainly kind to Mary Seacole, and acknowledges her place in history. He doesn’t show his normal contempt for soldiers either, even though he’s in the middle of a very bloody war with no proper medicine. There are a few snide remarks, but nothing beyond what any of the Doctors might usually say. As for the monster, it’s nothing much to write home about. Potentially a bit scary, but really not all that threatening.
docs.title: The Charge of the Night Brigade

docs.text: War Wounds Tweflth Doctor Chronicles #1.2 Released: 13 February 2020 Listened: 1/7/23 Following the Chronicles tradition, if you can’t get a major character’s actor, round up a minor one! In this case, that’s Sam Anderson as Danny Pink . The Doctor comes looking for Clara at Coal Hill, she’s on a field trip, so Danny tries to tell the Doctor to get lost, but ends up with an inadvertent ride in the TARDIS. To a planet in the middle of a war, featuring both humans and saurians on both sides. A setup like that is going to plow straight into Danny’s background as a soldier, and the Twelfth Doctor’s extreme dislike of soldiers. Which honestly never made that much sense to me, given that he’s a UNIT advisor, but it’s a part of Series 8 that sticks out, so here it is. Sam Anderson does some amazing work with his grunts and gasps, convincingly simulating sliding down a steep slope and into a watery gully. However, that means Jacob Dudman is tasked with all the other characters, of which there are several, and honestly, his American woman doctor doesn’t quite come off. The whole point of this story is for the Doctor and Danny to clash, which they definitely do. Unlike the last story , the Doctor is quite nasty in this one, and Danny overreacts as well. The Doctor’s insistence on calling Danny “P.E.” is grating, but serves to underscore the few times he calls him “Danny.” Eventually, of course, they come to an understanding, which should have happened on TV, but never did. And there’s a fairly clumsy Chekov’s Gun to reset their relationship to the status quo before the end. You knew it had to happen, and there’s no elegant way to do it, but that doesn’t really make it better. Given the restraints on the writer, the story comes out as well as it can, primarily due to the efforts of the actors.
docs.title: War Wounds

docs.text: The Twelfth Doctor Solo As always, Big Finish needs a space for solo stories, and once again, the TV show was kind enough to provide one. A lot goes on between “ Hell Bent ” and “ The Pilot ,” but mostly it involves the Doctor settling into his role as lecturer at St. Luke’s. Which puts him in one place for long enough to have a consistent set of stories in a fixed setting. Or taking him away from the fixed setting. Whatever. Most of the Big Finish Twelfth Doctor stories go here.

docs.text: A Song for Running Subscriber Short Trips #2019-4 Released: 10 December 2019 Listened: 1/7/23 This is one of those stories where the Doctor helps a child to help a lost alien. They’ve done that sort of thing before, but it seems a bit odd coming from the Twelfth Doctor, given his past difficulties in understanding children. It almost seems more like an Eleventh Doctor story, with the Doctor being unusually candid with the little girl, and talking about Susan. Perhaps that’s why he put her photo on his desk at St. Luke’s. Anyway, the plot itself isn’t anything spectacular, but the way it’s told is quite different, with the little girl hearing the alien in the form of a song. Stephen Critchlow is the narrator, and while he does a rather good Twelfth Doctor, he also has to portray a little girl and a high-pitched alien, neither of which are really in his wheelhouse. It’s good enough, for what it is.
docs.title: A Song For Running

docs.text: Dead Media Short Trips #9.9 Released: 30 September 2019 Listened: 1/8/23 One thing a Doctor Who writer really seems to enjoy is the opportunity to write something like Douglas Adams. I’m not certain if that’s what Ben Tedds was aiming for when he entered the Paul Spragg Memorial Short Trip contest, but that’s certainly what he got. The high concept: Dracksil Forg sells ideas. The right idea to the right person, every time. They even come with a money-back guarantee if any foreseeable circumstances go wrong. And the Doctor, of course, is anything but foreseeable, so Dracksil ends up with a lot of unhappy customers once the Doctor starts tracking him down. Which is pretty much all that happens. The story is mostly a vehicle for a high concept, and an excuse to use a lot of Adams-like names and dialog, and a bunch of ridiculous plans. But it’s nice to see a short story that tries to be exactly what it is, successfully.

docs.text: Distant Voices Tweflth Doctor Chronicles #1.3 Released: 13 February 2020 Listened: 1/8/23 Back to the Chronicles , but no guest actor from TV this time. Instead we have Emily Redpath as Cameron, a tour guide at Rochester Castle. Except that things are timey-wimey, and Cameron and the Doctor find themselves in 1215, during King John’s siege of the castle, and it later turns out that things are even more timey-wimey than that. The Doctor is back to being cranky in this one; there’s some slight elements of mellowing, but he’s pretty short with stupid people and soldiers, which unfortunately there’s quite a bit of in all time periods. Not Cameron, though. Cameron’s boss Alex, however, is quite stupid, and happens to sound an awful lot like Jacob Dudman’s Eleventh Doctor. I guess you eventually run out of voices. Probably the weak link of this set.
docs.title: Distant Voices

docs.text: Field Trip Tweflth Doctor Chronicles #1.4 Released: 13 February 2020 Listened: 1/8/23 Closing out the set, we’ve got Ingrid Oliver as the special guest, playing Osgood . Ingrid is no stranger to Big Finish, or to playing Osgood for that matter, so she’s quite comfortable here. And she’s smart enough to keep pace with the Doctor, so he doesn’t really get a chance to be cranky. The Doctor turns up at UNIT to borrow Osgood for a special mission…and it turns out that what he needs are her bureaucratic skills, as he’s trying to stop an invasion by convincing a bunch of civil servants not to do it. Which Osgood isn’t real happy about, but Una McCormack isn’t just going to let it go at that. There’s a chase scene, and some spying, and sabotage, and Osgood needing to act fairly brave, which she does, because Osgood is awesome. We know that she’s companion material, and also that she doesn’t get to be one, so this is as close as we’re going to get. As Ingrid herself notes in the extras, there are plenty of stories hinting that Osgood might get a TARDIS trip, but this is the first time it actually happens.
docs.title: Field Trip

docs.text: Flight to Calendra Tweflth Doctor Chronicles #2.1 Released: 3 November 2021 Listened: 1/9/23 These next three stories are really one story, released in a boxed set entitled “Timejacked!” Much like with the Eleventh Doctor Chronicles after #1, this is a full-cast audio, but with Jacob Dudman playing the Doctor, not narrating. Without hearing Dudman’s native accent for contrast, you can get more into his Twelfth Doctor performance, and while it never really fools you into thinking it’s Peter Capaldi, it is a reasonable Twelfth Doctor. This story is explicitly set after the Doctor has been at St. Luke’s for a while, but just before he meets Bill. As in the last story, the fact that he stayed in one place for an extended period allowed people to find him if they’re determined enough. In this case, a novice time agent named Keira Sandstrom, who’s in way over her head. She’s supposed to be observing the planet Calandra, but it’s really boring, so she pushed their technology forward to the point where she could use it to augment her vortex manipulator and get to Earth. Which, oops, broke the vortex. Which is bad. So she forces the Doctor to help her out, at gunpoint. (She disables Nardole before the story starts, relieving that problem.) Being the Twelfth Doctor, he gets plenty of opportunity to pile on the scorn and sarcasm. However, Dudman’s performance doesn’t quite reach the level of scathing that Capaldi could be, even in this “calmer” period of his life. He just sounds vaguely bored with the whole thing, which more or less works, admittedly. Keira’s messing around not only broke the vortex, but also left Calendra with a teleportation system that accidentally makes zombified copies of people, called “the Confused” in a great leap of euphemism. Once that problem is fixed, they head off to fix everything else Keira broke.
docs.title: Flight to Calandra

docs.text: Split Second Tweflth Doctor Chronicles #2.2 Released: 3 November 2021 Listened: 1/9/23 While Part 1 was written by Matt Fitton, Parts 2 and 3 are both written by Lou Morgan, which kind of implies a tighter connection, but I’m not sure I agree. This part is mostly the Doctor and Keira trying to fix subsidiary cracks in time, which aren’t really that dramatic, as far as cracks in time go, and are solved by tossing in a time grenade at the right moment. The other major thing that happens is that Keira starts to grow on the Doctor. As a time agent, she’s a bit more capable than normal companions when it comes to the timey-wimey stuff, but she’s still naive enough to let the Doctor act superior. So she triggers both his professor tendencies and his protective tendencies, and seems to be sincerely helping out, all of which makes the Doctor warm to her. Is that likely for the Twelfth Doctor, especially after she shot one of his guitars? I’m not so sure. He does seem to have a soft spot for bored young time-travelers, so maybe. Bhavnisha Parmar plays Keira – you’ve seen her playing Yaz’s younger sister Sonya on TV – and admittedly she’s amazingly charming and likable, but with a selfish and short-sighted streak. Being confronted with the consequences of her actions seems to be making a difference, though. It also introduces Mrs. Havilland, who is, apparently, a random passerby in Bath who got too close to one of the cracks. Probably isn’t important.
docs.title: Split Second

docs.text: The Astrea Conspiracy Short Trips #9.2 Released: 28 February 2019 Listened: 1/7/23 In recording order, this is the first appearance of the Twelfth Doctor in Big Finish. As a Short Trip, it’s narrated, by Neve McIntosh, who is more than capable of reproducing Capaldi’s Scots accent. The Doctor is written as slightly more whimsical and cavalier than he was previously, but this is probably part of his mellowing prior to Series 10. As for the story itself, it’s about Aphra Behn , who used the alias Astrea as a spy, and later as a pen name. Lizbeth Myles is pretty good with historicals, and sticks very close to the historical record here. It’s mostly told from Aphra’s point of view, so although the Doctor says he’s caused a paradox to English literature and is trying to fix it, we have only his word for that. In fact, the Doctor behaves inscrutably, and to Aphra, incomprehensibly, throughout the story, but that’s just the Doctor being Doctory. As a debut, it’s quite good.
docs.title: The Astrea Conspiracy

docs.text: The Three Flames Short Trips #10.5 Released: 2 February 2023 Listened: 3/20/23 This story is by Sophie Iles, superfan, and takes very good advantage of the short trip format. It’s told from the point of view of a family of aliens fleeing the destruction of their home planet, and being rescued by the Doctor after their ship crashes. In that kind of format, seeing the Doctor from the outside, he looks kind of insane. While the Twelfth Doctor is kind of cranky, he’s already starting to mellow, and when he’s being legitimately helpful, he’s more useful than his two predecessors being motor-mouthed and trying to distract everybody from danger. Dan Starkey reads this one, and although he does a pretty good Twelfth Doctor, there’s no need for his particular talents. It’s a small story, and works nicely that way.
docs.title: The Three Flames

docs.text: The Weight of History Tweflth Doctor Chronicles #2.3 Released: 3 November 2021 Listened: 1/13/23 I have to admit, I was underwhelmed by this conclusion. It could be the way I listened to it, in bits and pieces over the course of a week when I was mostly occupied with something else. But still, there are pieces I didn’t care for. A second Keira turns up, claiming to be Future Keira, which has some entertainment value. Except it’s pretty obvious from jump what’s really going on, and how it ties back to the first story . The Doctor definitely should’ve worked that out immediately, and Keira probably should have too. Mrs. Havilland pops up as the big bad, another rogue time agent taking advantage of the mess Keira made, but she’s ruling godlike over the temporally shattered bits of Calandra. She also seems to have gone binky-bonkers, which is the least engaging type of villain. It’s nice for the Doctor to have somebody to rage at, but he probably wouldn’t waste his breath, because she certainly ain’t listening. If anything, the trilogy is too short. There isn’t enough space for the callback to Part 1 to be a surprise, and we don’t have much time to get used to Keira. She goes pretty hard for redemption in this story, but given how she started off, it seems too quick of a turnaround. Lucky for her, her story continues .
docs.title: The Weight of History

docs.text: The War Doctor The War Doctor is a bit of timey-wimey retconning by Steven Moffatt that totally shouldn’t have worked, and yet it did, brilliantly. He needed a Doctor who’d fought in the Time War, but the Eighth was a bad fit, and Christopher Eccleston declined to return. Hence the invention of a new incarnation who denied his own name, played impeccably by Sir John Hurt. And that should have been it, really, as Big Finish at the time didn’t want to show the Time War itself. But when Sir John asked if he could continue to play the Doctor on audio, what could they do? Say no? So with the rights to new-series concepts obtained as of 2013, four boxed sets of the War Doctor were recorded. Unfortunately, one of the reasons John Hurt had wanted to do audio was because he had cancer, and wanted a role he could do without overexerting himself. After his passing, four boxed sets seemed like a reasonable place to leave it. Except in 2021, they cast Jonathon Carley, who does an uncanny John Hurt impression, and went back to the beginning of the War Doctor’s life, leaving the two halves of this era entirely out of order. And the 60th anniversay of the show threw in yet another curveball into the middle of the war.
docs.title: War Doctor

docs.text: Once and Future Big anniversary stories now seem to require gathering as many Doctors together as possible. That's getting harder to do on TV, but strangely easier to do in Big Finish, at least for the time being. In 2023, Big Finish had the original actors for the Fourth through Tenth Doctors, and official recasting for the First, Second, Third, and War Doctors. Not to mention a bunch of companions, spin-off characters, and original creations. Fitting them all into one story is asking for trouble, but a series of shorter episodes, that's reasonable. So we have this, where an "unidentified" Doctor is hit with a "degenerative" weapon, which results in him manifesting his other selves, past and future (don't squint too hard at that last bit). We're not supposed to know who the original is, but this is a Time War weapon if I've ever seen one, so that means it gets slotted in here.
docs.title: Once and Future

docs.text: A Genius for War Once and Future #3 Released: 20 July 2023 Listened: 7/25/23 This instance features the Seventh Doctor, and frankly a sidestep from the main plot, if we even know what that is. The unstable Seventh Doctor is snatched out of time, and taken to that nasty courtroom space station again, because he’s particularly needed. Seems the Daleks found Davros tucked away in a cupboard somewhere, but when they didn’t immediately start worshipping him as their creator, he got ticked off, so they dropped him on the prison moon of Falkus and left him there . Of course, being Davros, he’s taken control of the prison computer, genetically engineered a whole bunch of Kaleds to serve him, and then sent a message to the Time Lords offering to betray the Daleks…if the Doctor comes to rescue him. It’s pretty obviously a trap, so why not grab the chessmaster Doctor to resolve it? There’s plenty of Davros-y double- and triple-crossing, because of course there is. There’s also a reference to the legend of the hybrid from Series 9 of the new series, one that actually makes a lot more sense than the answer we eventually got. docs.text: Once and Future #3 Released: 20 July 2023 Listened: 7/25/23 This instance features the Seventh Doctor, and frankly a sidestep from the main plot, if we even know what that is. The unstable Seventh Doctor is snatched out of time, and taken to that nasty courtroom space station again, because he’s particularly needed. Seems the Daleks found Davros tucked away in a cupboard somewhere, but when they didn’t immediately start worshipping him as their creator, he got ticked off, so they dropped him on the prison moon of Falkus and left him there . Of course, being Davros, he’s taken control of the prison computer, genetically engineered a whole bunch of Kaleds to serve him, and then sent a message to the Time Lords offering to betray the Daleks…if the Doctor comes to rescue him. It’s pretty obviously a trap, so why not grab the chessmaster Doctor to resolve it? There’s plenty of Davros-y double- and triple-crossing, because of course there is. docs.text: Past Lives Once and Future #1 Released: 3 May 2023 Listened: 5/4/23 This multi-part series is Big Finish’s contribution to Doctor Who ’s 60th anniversary. And they’re making a serious effort to make this hard to place by mashing up several different threads of the Doctor’s life. Sometime during the Time War, an unspecified version of the Doctor is hit with a “degenerative weapon,” which causes him to regenerate into past incarnations. It starts out chronologically, letting all the other Big Finish Doctors get a line or two, but doesn’t stay that way. The phenomenon settles down when the Doctor reaches the TARDIS, stabilizing on the Fourth Doctor. He’s got the Fourth’s personality and appearance, but the memories of a much later Doctor (and presumably the clothes, but nobody mentions that). The Doctor can’t exactly remember what he’s trying to do, only that it involves finding the Monk. Which means we’ve got Rufus Hound being especially Rufus Houndy. He’s got some scheme of his own going on, and seems to be unaware of the War, but he does know about Jenny, so who knows where he is in his timeline. He does pick up Sarah Jane, moments after she’s dropped off in Aberdeen , which totally backfires on him, because Sarah’s not one to be pushed around. They all end up in early 2010s London, which allows them to encounter Kate Stewart and Osgood. This seems to be pretty early in their tenure, as Osgood is completely star-struck. Kate does a bit better, but refers to Osgood as her “personal assistant” several times, which is hardly how she’d be referred to later, so definitely early days. I don’t know how to reconcile that with Osgood not having met the Doctor or traveled in the TARDIS until much later in her timeline, so maybe it’ll all get rewritten. The plot isn’t really much of anything, mostly a runaround after a macguffin that some aliens want to use to get revenge on the Doctor. The resolution is less bloody than you’d expect, especially for a UNIT story, which is nice. The big point, though, is to let Sarah have some conversation with the Doctor who she last saw less than an hour ago, from her point of view. Obviously, she never entirely comes to terms with being left behind, but this helps some.

docs.text: The Artist at the End of Time Once and Future #2 Released: 14 June 2023 Listened: 6/19/23 Moving on, the Doctor is in his fifth incarnation in this chapter. Although “ Past Lives ” emphasized that this was a later Doctor inhabiting the form of the Fourth, this one just seems to be the Fifth, with maybe a few more memories. The big guest star is Georgia Tennant, Peter Davison’s daughter, which is why she’s in this particular story. Fortunately, he remembers her , so we don’t have to go through the “you’re not really my daughter” thing (although he forgets again by the end). The other big twist is that the story involves the Curator, the Colin Baker version , instead of the Tom Baker version, although the Doctor doesn’t recognize his form. The Curator takes a more active role in this story than we’ve seen before; he’s creating a number of works of art, indicating talents he hasn’t shown previously. He’s also trying to take direct action to stop some bad things from happening, which is very unlike what we’ve seen before. He’s very Curator-y in that he’s constantly being enigmatic for the sake of it (or so it seems), and he loves to take the long view. However, the actual menace turns out to be rather banal and perhaps even a bit silly. James Goss is very good at writing families, and fortunately this one isn’t nearly as dysfunctional as he portrays the Noble family. The plot, unfortunately, feels kinda thin.

docs.text: Coda: The Final Act Once and Future #8 Released: 22 November 2024 Listened: 3/15/26 For reasons I never really understood, the last part of "Once and Future" was released a full year after " The Union ." However, as the title suggests, it's not the finale, but rather a coda. It picks up with the War Doctor immediately after leaving River and Susan, still suffering from the effects of the degenerative weapon. But the main attraction here is this was the first appearance of Jo Martin as the Fugitive Doctor. She'd get her own series shortly, but this is the beginning. She's pretty much the version of the character seen in Flux, preferring to act alone, generally being short with people, and definitively willing to use violence. Which is probably why she's matched up with the War Doctor in this story, except, as often seems to happen in their stories, we don't see either of them do anything all that terrible. And because this miniseries always brings in random other characters, we get a short visit from Vienna Salvatore, and a longer one from Bernice Summerfield. Why Benny didn't turn up in " Time Lord Immemorial ," where she was specifically mentioned, is anybody's guess, but she's here now. She's met her share of Doctors, but doesn't know these two. What she does know is that neither of them are acting Doctor-ish, and that bothers her. For his part, the War Doctor is unusually reckless; he needs an army, so he ends up recruiting Queen Elizabeth's (not his first choice, but it's what he got). Elizabeth remembers the War Doctor, as he attended her wedding , but for him, that hasn't happened yet. There's a lot of mistaken identity and people being lied to in this story, possibly to set up a new big bad, but if that's the case, they haven't reappeared as of this writing.

docs.text: The Martian Invasion of Planetoid 50 Once and Future #5 Released: 12 September 2023 Listened: 9/21/23 Things get even more confused here, if that were possible, because the Doctor in this story is the Tenth (or maybe, just maybe, the Fourteenth, but probably not). And the mash-up characters are the Paternoster Gang and Missy. Because David Tennant never got to play with Michelle Gomez, and isn’t that a shame? It starts out with Stephen Noonan’s First Doctor, finding himself in Victorian London in the middle of HG Wells’ Martian Invasion, which he knows full well is fictional. Once Missy sticks her hand in, though, we get the Tenth Doctor, which should be impossible. Tennant does a good job of portraying a Tenth Doctor who’s actually an earlier Doctor and therefore doesn’t really know who or what the Tenth is like. We also get confirmation that the Doctor’s outfit is changing with each of these regenerations, including, apparently, the sonic screwdriver. Is the plot any good? Well, we’ve seen stories before where the Master has screwed something up and calls the Doctor to come save him. That’s more of a Roger Delgado / Antony Ainley thing, though. With Missy doing her “crazy ex-girlfriend” act, it comes off somewhat differently. However, there’s some indication that Missy is also suffering from regenerative issues, so maybe she’s not entirely herself. For what it’s worth, the Tenth Doctor is having none of Missy’s approach. It’s probably a good thing that this Doctor can’t remember the John Simm Master, or things might have gone differently. This one is more of an actor’s workshop than a story, and Strax doesn’t steal any scenes, which just shows how good the actors in question are.

docs.text: The Union Once and Future #7 Released: 25 October 2023 Listened: 10/8/23 The Doctors this time around are the Eighth and Fourth, splitting time more or less equally. And the timey-wimey elements are Susan and River, from relatively late points in their respective timelines. Susan remembers River as one of her teachers at Coal Hill , and doesn’t wig out too much when River reveals a lot more about her relationship with Susan’s grandfather. The action takes place on the Diamond Array, which is a fairly blunt reference to the 60th anniversary. The baddie turns out to be The Union, another renegade Time Lord, but one we’ve seen before. She’s played by Maureen O’Brien, and I certainly wouldn’t have known it was her if not for the credits. It's a Matt Fitton story, so relationships are at the forefront. Not just the Doctor's relationships with River or Susan, although those are promient. It's also the Doctor's relationship with themself...or selves, really. Although the Doctors sniping at each other is fairly standard in multi-Doctor stories, the Doctor asserts here that he's at peace with his past and future selves, leading all of them to turn up for a line or two. Except, well, it turns out that there is one Doctor that the others don't accept, and that's why this story appears at this point in the chronology. As with several other stories in this collection, I wish there had been a bit more plot. Finding an excuse to put all the Doctors together is the main thing, but the plot contrivance was a bit weak.

docs.text: Time Lord Immemorial Once and Future #6 Released: 5 October 2023 Listened: 10/8/23 We swap from David Tennant to Christopher Eccleston, which still doesn’t make a ton of sense, but this is the only anniversary special he’s likely to participate in, so we’ll let that go. Eccleston has said he doesn’t want to participate in multi-Doctor stories, which is why there are no other de-generations in this story. However, apparently David Warner doesn’t count, as he’s playing an alternate-universe Doctor, and hey, he’s David Warner. Unfortunately, his Doctor doesn’t get a whole lot to do, and his voice sounds weaker than usual. It’s hard not to remember that this is the last thing Warner recorded before his death. Because we have to throw in more timey-wimey elements, the Lumiat is here, although nobody recognizes her, and she has a hard time proving her bona fides. (She's mostly here because Gina McKee and Christopher Eccleston starred in Our Friends in the North together.) In fact, she seems to be borrowing Missy's "crazy ex-girlfriend" act, but without the malice. Also, there’s Liv Chenka, pulled from a time after she’s met Helen, but before Stranded . Of course, Liv is always delightfully cranky, so it doesn’t really matter when you’ve pulled her from; she’s the same. The story, well…I’m sure there is one, but it’s a little hard to tell. It’s mostly a runaround, taking place at one of those outside-time, cross-dimensional places, called the “Time Lord Immemorial,” which is somehow a location and a person, neither of which seem like memorials. There’s another one of those absurd Time Lord prophecies, but nobody really seems to need to do anything; it all just happens. This is one of the weaker installments of the story, sorry to everyone involved.

docs.text: Two's Company Once and Future #4 Released: 16 August 2023 Listened: 8/21/23 After a couple of questionable entries, we get one that actually plays into the overarching storyline, and also plays with the mashup concept that was introduced in the first story. The TARDIS lands in London, 2006, because the Doctor, wearing the Third Doctor’s body, is looking for something called “esoterium.” Harry Sullivan is part of a very secret project working with esoterium. In fact, it’s so secret that only Harry and (a person who Harry believes to be a future version of) the Doctor are involved. Except that’s not the Doctor, it’s the Eleven; just not the one you were expecting. I’m not sure where in Harry’s timeline this is, but the Doctor thinks he looks older in 2006, so I guess it’s after he got back where he belongs. Meanwhile, because it’s 2006, Jackie Tyler is around, playing with alien doodads Rose left in her room, and getting set up as a cleaner for Lady Christina deSouza. Except it’s 2006, so Christina hasn’t met the Doctor or UNIT yet. Jackie certainly has, though, and is just as terrible as always about keeping her mouth shut. (Which means nobody involved is going to remember this story; cliche, but there it is.) Although the Third Doctor gets more screen time than other “cameo” Doctors in this series, he ends up regenerating into the Sixth right in front of Harry, conveniently proving who he is. Old Sixie is perfect for this story, as he’s a fountain of snark, and Harry’s on the receiving end of most of it, not undeservedly. The actual resolution is a bit muted, but that’s fine, as it’s the interaction of the characters that’s important in this story. And it gives the Doctor another step along the path.

docs.text: The War Doctor Adventures This set of stories, starring Sir John Hurt, come toward the end of the War Doctor’s tenure, thus relieving Sir John of the burden of trying to sound like his younger self. It’s one of the first instances of Big Finish stepping into the modern series, and it’s almost tentative at times. It clearly wasn’t planned as a long arc of four boxes, as some other stories are. In fact, they were just starting to get rolling when it was cut off, so there isn’t much closure or direct connection to “ The Day of the Doctor .” The other thing that’s lacking is a sense of atrocity. We’re told that the War Doctor did things so terrible that his other regenerations disowned him, but there’s little evidence of that here.

docs.text: A Thing of Guile The War Doctor #2.2 Released: 22 February 2016 Listened: 8/30/22 The second story, by Phil Mulryne, is the weak link in this boxed set. There’s yet another Dalek weapon hidden on an asteroid, so Ollistra brings a strike team to go get it. She ensures the Doctor’s cooperation by sticking an “artron leash” on him, which means he can’t go too far away from her. Why Ollistra would want to go on this particular mission is a mystery, as she’s hardly a commando, and making the Doctor stick by her doesn’t make the best use of his talents. The other two Time Lords who tag along also aren’t suited to commando missions, with predictable results. It turns out there are two secret weapons here, and the Doctor pronounces both of them too horrific to use. Which is starting to get a little repetitive, as at least one of them is pretty bad, but not exactly beyond the pale for the Doctor to use. Ollistra seems to be off her game in this story. Every other time she appears, she’s several steps ahead of the Doctor, who’s innovative when he’s improvising, but his broad motivations are fairly easy to manipulate. This time, though, she seems caught out several times, not least of which at the very end. This one is serviceable, and that’s about it.
docs.title: A Thing of Guile

docs.text: Eye of Harmony The War Doctor #3.3 Released: 6 October 2016 Listened: 9/2/22 This last story is written by Ken Bentley, who’s an extremely prolific Big Finish director, but rarely writes. It’s a tight story with a small cast that takes place entirely aboard a battle TARDIS. It turns out that Heleyna was the traitor all along, not because she’s pro-Dalek, but because her grandfather was a pacifist who got killed very early in the war. Her plan is to give the Daleks access to the TARDIS’s link to the Eye of Harmony, which will wipe the Time Lords from existence. That results in a chase through the interior of the TARDIS, which takes a lot of inspiration from “Journey to the Centre of the TARDIS” more than any other story where we’ve seen a TARDIS interior. Helenya’s rage-driven grief is almost overwhelming, and a lesser actor would just be a screaming annoyance, but Honeysuckle Weeks sells it perfectly. Bentley’s writing is a little too heavy on the exposition, but it kind of has to be, since only the most dedicated fans will know how the Eye of Harmony works without some explanation. The Doctor is also more aggressive in this one, being rather quick to grab some guns. He also cites having “no choice” several times, and whether he really doesn’t, or just believes he doesn’t, is really what makes the War Doctor. Overall, this boxed set is better than the second one, but there’s still that overall feeling of “ordinary adventures” rather than war-specific ones.
docs.title: Eye of Harmony

docs.text: Legion of the Lost The War Doctor #2.1 Released: 22 February 2016 Listened: 8/29/22 This second boxed set aims for a more “ordinary” pace, as much as the Time War has such a thing. The box is called “Infernal Devices,” which we know there were a lot of in the Time War, and we know from “Day of the Doctor” that the Doctor has strong opinions about a lot of these devices, and who should be able to use them. In this first story, by John Dorney, we actually get two: the boringly named Annihilator, which erases species from time retroactively, but also some rather nasty resurrection technology. Time Lords are always doing the resurrection thing during the war, but this one is particularly nasty, as it involves partnering up with some “technomancers” from the dawn of time who worship the sort of demon-things that the Seventh Doctor would regularly stomp upon. The story doesn’t really have the usual John Dorney twistiness, but it does have David Warner playing an evil wizard, and that’s pretty hard to beat. Plus the Doctor spends more time being appalled than tired this time around, so John Hurt gets to shout in shock and outrage more than he did last time. It’s not necessarily the strongest story, but it’s not bad.
docs.title: Legion of the Lost

docs.text: Pretty Lies The War Doctor #4.1 Released: 23 February 2017 Listened: 9/3/22 This boxed set is “Casualties of War,” the fourth and final set. It may have been originally planned as four, and I think they were going to take a pause after this one, but they certainly hoped to continue with more. Which is a shame, because John Hurt’s death in early 2017 put a final end to it. The Doctor seems a lot crankier in this story, much more disgusted with himself and short-tempered with everyone around him. Which makes a bit of a contrast, because there’s a war historian following him and Ollistra around, trying to preserve the moment for posterity. The reporter is clearly star-struck, and provides some inappropriate comic relief as a result. The Doctor is still behaving fairly Doctor-y in terms of his plan, but he’s being clear that there will be deaths he’s unable to prevent. It seems as though he’s heading toward the bleakness that will lead him to use the Moment. Ollistra, however, while remaining irritated with the Doctor, shows considerable leadership skill in helping a badly outgunned city defend itself. Although John Hurt and Jacqueline Pearce play wonderfully off each other, putting them together all the time is starting to make me wonder whether Ollistra lacks anything better to do than personally hound the Doctor all the time.
docs.title: Pretty Lies

docs.text: The Enigma Dimension The War Doctor #4.3 Released: 23 February 2017 Listened: 9/4/22 Having retrieved Leela, the Doctor and Ollistra return to Gallifrey to find…a thing. One of those impossible things hanging in space such that you can’t follow its dimensions. An Enigma, you might say. And the Daleks are holding its “people?” hostage so that it will wipe out the Time Lords. However, when your ultimate weapon has a mind of its own, you never quite know what it’s going to do (foreshadowing!). It isn’t a slam-bang ending, because as Nick Briggs himself points out, we know how the war ends, and we can’t mess with that, so this has to be an ending without being the ending, so why not make it quieter? Leela is used to good effect here as an outsider who’s not part of the war, although it does go a bit too far in the “noble savage” direction. Toward the end, though, it’s quite chilling as Ollistra tries to turn the situation to her advantage, and the Doctor realizes that maybe the only way to end the time war is to wipe out both sides. He’s terribly bleak and grim, and you can see “Day of the Doctor” happening not long after this. I used to think this series didn’t really have a proper ending, but I’m revising that opinion now. John Hurt got some time to be the Doctor, maybe not as up-beat as other Doctors, but he did have his moments of happiness and victory. And in the end, they put him where he needed to be. I’m not really sure how much further they could have taken it. Sadly, this marks the end for both John Hurt and Jacqueline Pearce in this project. Two actors whose passing is a loss to the entire acting community.
docs.title: The Enigma Dimension

docs.text: The Eternity Cage The War Doctor #3.2 Released: 6 October 2016 Listened: 9/1/22 How about we bring in another outside group who want in on the Time War, but nobody else wants them? Yeah, the Sontarans, but both sides can safely ignore them because they don’t have any temporal weapons…until now. They’ve used them to kidnap Ollistra, and they’re willing to give her to whichever side offers an alliance. So Ollistra’s aide Heleyna recruits the Doctor to lead a strike team to rescue her. They get some rather unexpected help from a boy named Kalan, who’s remarkably helpful, even in dangerous situations, but he says he really wants the Sontarans off his planet. Dan Starkey plays the Sontarans, and he’s excellent as always, but honestly they’re in over their round heads, and they don’t know it. The real story comes from the mystery of who the traitor is, and there’s an obvious candidate, which means it’s not them. Ollistra tries gamely to use her manipulation skills on the Dalek Time Strategist, but to no avail. In fact, she’s on the wrong foot most of the time in this story, which is a shame, because Jacqueline Pearce is awesome, but less so when she’s not being cunning. Heleyna is played by Honeysuckle Weeks, who brings unexpected strength to the character when she has to shut somebody down. Unfortunately, this again feels like a middle story, so it’s not all that memorable.
docs.title: The Eternity Cage

docs.text: The Heart of the Battle The War Doctor #1.3 Released: 14 December 2015 Listened: 8/29/22 This story is a direct continuation of the previous, and plans come unraveled fairly quickly. Seretrix is revealed to be a sincere peace advocate, trying to reach a deal with the Daleks. He was sent by Ollistra, who clearly never wanted him to succeed. And of course the Daleks don’t want to make peace; they’re just buying time and space to put together a new assault on Gallifrey. Seretrix is portrayed as quite idealistic and foolish for thinking his plan could work, but the Doctor has been on the side of hope a few times in the past, even when Daleks are involved. Nick Briggs’ goal seems to be to put the Doctor in another situation where there are no good choices, just less-bad ones. Which is kind of unfair, because “there’s always another way” is the rule the Doctor lives by, and he almost always gets away with it…except for the War Doctor. I’ve complained before that we don’t really see the Doctor commit atrocities in this series, but what he does here is pretty bad, and he doesn’t dodge it, although he does pile on the guilt. Ollistra is the real monster here, and she’s either unaware of it, or simply doesn’t care. Her cold calculation is enough to shake Veklin, who shows the first glimmers of who she’ll later become (and already was, in this project, but whatever). I recall being a bit dissatisfied with this set when it came out, but now I see it as quite strong.
docs.title: The Heart of the Battle

docs.text: The Innocent The War Doctor #1.1 Released: 14 December 2015 Listened: 8/28/22 This boxed set, “Only the Monstrous,” is the first writing Big Finish, and Nick Briggs specifically, did for the War Doctor, and it’s clear that they’re being very, very careful with how to portray him. This is the same Doctor we’ll see later in “ The Day of the Doctor ,” one who’s tired, weary down to his very soul, and no longer cares if he lives or dies. He claims to have done terrible things, but they’re in his past, and we don’t really know what they are. His reaction to being called by his name feels more earned here than it does in the “ Begins ” stories, because he thinks he really has renounced his beliefs. Of course, this is proper John Hurt, and with all deference to Jonathan Carle, there’s a very clear difference. Carle is gravely all the time, because it’s an impersonation, but Hurt is a master of his instrument. The gravel comes and goes; he can take it down to a whisper for effect, and when he shouts, which is rare, his rage and self-loathing spills out in every direction. For a character who’d only appeared in one story, Hurt is in complete control. In this particular story, the Doctor is missing, believed dead, after doing something stupidly heroic, again, but may have disrupted the Daleks’ access to time travel. While he’s recuperating on a remote planet, he meets pseudo-companion Rejoice, who nurses him back to health. In return, he saves her planet from what seems to be a rather ordinary invasion force, basically doing what the Doctor used to do, but he finds no peace in it, because he knows he has to go back. And it’s Ollistra who’s going to insist on that, played here by the lovely Jacqueline Pearce. She’d reprised her Blake’s Seven role as Servalan for Big Finish before, and nobody can touch her when it comes to affable evil. Beth Chalmers’ Veklin also appears, but she’s an unfinished form of Veklin, just a caricature of the good soldier. Which is funny, because the character is much better fleshed out in stories that chronologically come earlier. Also, the Doctor doesn’t seem to know her, but I’m going to let that slide. I wasn’t sure if Nick Briggs could pull off a story that would capture the War Doctor properly, but this is very effective.
docs.title: The Innocent

docs.text: The Lady of Obsidian The War Doctor #4.2 Released: 23 February 2017 Listened: 9/3/22 Four boxed sets in, it was about time to introduce other Classic-series characters, in this case Leela. We know from Gallifrey: Time War that she was conscripted to be a front-line fighter, and apparently somewhere along the line, she was injured by a Dalek weapon and believed dead. She was flung far away, and her timeline was scrambled such that she remembered all of her possible lives as having equal weight. Running into anyone or anything that reminded her of her previous life causes her physical pain. Of course Louise Jameson dives headfirst into such a role, and she’s magnificent. The pain of finding out she never had children, even though she remembers them, is hard to take as a listener. John Hurt’s voice is trapped between joy at seeing her again, and compassion for her pain; it’s an amazing thing. There’s some story in here too, with Leela and her people fighting off entities called the Unlived – potential beings from possible timelines, trying to get a foothold in this universe. They look truly terrifying on the cover, but aren’t really described in the story. And Ollistra takes it on herself to force the Time Lords to defend a helpless planet, which is a bit odd, to be honest, but her character seems to be taking a turn toward the good guys’ side. And Veklin gets a cameo, appearing in the nick of time. It feels like this was meant to be the start of a new arc in the series, but sadly, it doesn’t turn out that way.
docs.title: The Lady of Obsidian

docs.text: The Neverwhen The War Doctor #2.3 Released: 22 February 2016 Listened: 8/31/22 This story really seems to get at what this boxed set is supposed to be about, which makes sense, since it was written by Script Editor Matt Fitton. The “Neverwhen” sounds like one of those lovely Time War entities Russell T Davies invented for Christopher Eccleston and David Tennant to toss off in one-liners and then never explain. It also definitely puts the “time” in the Time War. It apparently creates a zone where timelines are in flux, so armies and their gear shift up and down their own evolutionary scale, from high-tech armor and weapons to stone knives and bearskins. Worse, when they die, they come back in the next cycle. This is one the Doctor would legitimately consider an “infernal device,” but he’s also forced to deal with it in a way other than just wrecking it outright, and to accept the consequences. Ollistra is in much better form this time, mostly leading the Doctor around by the nose and cornering him every time he’s about to wriggle out of a moral trap. Even with that, she still thinks she’s doing the right thing, which makes her even more terrifying. There’s also a nice plot twist that you can see coming just a bit before the Doctor does, which is very satisfying. Definitely the best story of the set. On the whole, it’s not a bad idea for a boxed set, although having all three stories take place in sequence makes it look like the Doctor spent the whole war destroying each side’s weapons, which is hardly terrible. It also makes you wonder what weapons the Doctor considers acceptable to fight a war with, because it’s not entirely clear.
docs.title: The Neverwhen

docs.text: The Shadow Vortex The War Doctor #3.1 Released: 6 October 2016 Listened: 9/1/22 This new boxed set is called “Agents of Chaos,” and deals with various entities working for and with the Daleks during the war. Specifically in this story, agent Lara Zannis, played beautifully by Neve McIntosh. Although we know that Earth was kept out of the Time War, hey, it’s a Time War, so that could change. Lara’s job is to bring the Daleks through the quantum shield to Earth in 1961. And for maximum fun, West Berlin in 1961, because we need more paranoia in this story. Writer David Llewellyn makes good use of the cold war setting, with both MI6 and the KGB getting involved, and a temporary companion who’s a member of the Stazi, of all things. It’s interesting to note that the KGB has a file on the Doctor, even in 1961 (that file’s going to get a lot fatter over the next few decades). The actual resolution isn’t all that strong, but the War Doctor does cross a line that he normally wouldn’t, so that’s a thing. This one is worth it for the atmosphere.
docs.title: The Shadow Vortex

It’s interesting to note that the KGB has a file on the Doctor, even in 1961 (that file’s going to get a lot fatter over the next few decades). The actual resolution isn’t all that strong, but the War Doctor does cross a line that he normally wouldn’t, so that’s a thing. This one is worth it for the atmosphere.
docs.title: The Shadow Vortex

docs.text: The Thousand Worlds The War Doctor #1.2 Released: 14 December 2015 Listened: 8/28/22 Having established that the Doctor is alive and well, Ollistra immediately tries to put him to work, on a commando team with Veklin and two other Time Lords, trying to rescue a Time Lord strategist who’s trapped behind enemy lines. Except that the Doctor doesn’t take orders, and doesn’t do commando missions, so of course he heads off to do the rescue himself, with the others trailing along behind. It’s interesting that in this story, Veklin is dogmatic, short-tempered, and has no idea how to handle the Doctor, yet Ollistra is much more patient with him, nearly amused, and knows exactly how to push his buttons. It turns out that the planet is the same one from the previous story , but 30 or so years later, meaning Rejoice is played by a different actress now. There’s a lot of “middle story” going on here, as things are set up for later revelations, and the pieces get moved into place. It doesn’t really stand on its own very well, though.

docs.text: A Mother's Love The War Doctor Begins #5.1 Released: 16 May 2023 Listened: 5/28/23 A lot of Big Finish spin-off series last four boxed sets, and that’s it. Looks like the War Doctor is going beyond that, though, because there’s a new set called “Comrades in Arms.” Judging by the tone of this first one, the War Doctor gets to have some actual friends, and maybe behave a bit more like the Doctor. Because this story sees the return of Case, the Dalek-built cyborg from series 2, “ Warbringer .” She’s been working with Veklin as an agent, but just now Veklin is badly hurt, so they make for an advanced Time Lord hospital called Haven. The Doctor ends up there as well, answering a distress call, but there’s no sign of distress. In fact, there’s no sign of anybody, except for Runa, the daughter of the caretakers, and “MOM,” the station A.I. You know it’s never a good idea to let an A.I. run a hospital , and the Doctor is suspicious right away. However, he’s also a lot kinder and friendlier than we’ve seen him before, very nearly Doctor-ish. That’s possibly because he’s interacting with a child, and with Case, whom he feels concern for. Still, he doesn’t object very strongly when the A.I. addresses him as “Doctor.” Ajjaz Awad is back as Case, and it’s always nice to hear Beth Chalmers in anything, but especially as Veklin. There’s an auto-tuned quality to the vocal effect on the A.I. this time which is unusual, but also very effective. It’s also fun to hear all the British actors trying to pronounce “mom” instead of “mum.” The story itself you can kinda predict, including the resolution, but the characterizations are great.
docs.title: A Mother's Love
